setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
My first week in the ER was not what I expected. I knew it would be busy, but I did not understand how many different kinds of hard could fit into one shift. There were alarms, people calling for supplies, families asking questions, and nurses moving quickly from one room to another. I was nervous the whole first day. I wanted to help, but I was also afraid of getting in the way.

One of the first moments that stayed with me happened during a wound cleaning. The patient was a man who had gotten hurt at work. The nurse was cleaning a deep cut, and he was trying hard not to react, but I could see that he was scared. His wife was supposed to be there, but she was stuck in traffic and had not made it yet. The nurse asked if I could stay by his side.

I held his hand while they cleaned the wound. I did not know what to say at first. I just told him that his wife was on her way and that he was doing a good job. He squeezed my hand every time it hurt. I remember thinking that I had not done anything medical in that moment. I did not place an IV or give medication. But I was still helping. He did not have to be alone while something painful was happening to him. That taught me that nursing is not only about skills. Sometimes it is about being the person who stays.

Later that week, there was a code in the ER. I was not part of the team in the room. I was sent to restock gauze and other supplies nearby. At first, I felt disappointed. I wanted to see what was happening and learn from it. Then I heard the team counting through the curtain. Their voices were steady and loud over everything else in the department.

I stood there with gauze in my hands and listened. It made the situation feel real in a way that class had not. I understood that emergencies do not pause because someone is new or because someone feels ready. Everyone had a job, even if that job seemed small. The team needed supplies ready. They needed the room to keep moving. I learned that being useful does not always mean being at the center of the action. It means doing what needs to be done well, especially when things are stressful.

Another day, I was trying to draw blood from a patient with diabetes and very difficult veins. I missed the first time. Then I missed again. By the third try, I felt terrible. The patient was kind, but I knew he was tired of being poked. I was embarrassed and frustrated with myself. My instructor talked me through it and reminded me to slow down, take a breath, and look again instead of rushing because I was nervous.

On the fourth try, I got it.

I felt relieved, but I also felt humbled. I did not walk away thinking I had mastered blood draws. I walked away knowing that I still have a lot to learn. That patient gave me more patience than I probably deserved that day. I thanked him, and I meant it. He reminded me that every skill I practice is happening to a real person, not just a practice arm in lab.

My first week in the ER showed me that nursing will ask a lot from me. It will ask me to stay calm when I feel nervous, to keep learning when I make mistakes, and to care for people during some of the worst moments of their lives. I know I am only at the beginning of my education. I will miss things, ask questions, and need help. But that week made me even more sure that nursing is where I belong.

I want to become the kind of nurse who can be steady in a crisis, honest when I need to learn, and kind when someone feels scared. Sometimes that may mean holding a stranger’s hand. Sometimes it may mean restocking gauze. Sometimes it may mean trying again after I miss. My first week in the ER taught me that all of those moments matter.

b.text:
In the skills lab, the plastic arm never flinches. It has thick, blue rubber veins that never roll, never collapse, and never bleed when you mess up. 

My third day in the ER, I met a real arm. It belonged to an older man with diabetes who had been poked so many times over the last twenty years that his skin felt tough, like an old baseball glove. I prepped the site, anchored the vein, and slid the needle in. Nothing. I tried again on the other side. Nothing. By the third miss, my face was burning hot under my mask, my hands were shaking, and I was about ready to apologize and run out of the room to find my preceptor. 

The man just looked at me, let out a tired breath, and said, "Take a second, kid. Try one more time. I’ve got all day." I took a deep breath, backed out, found a tiny vein near his wrist, and went in slow. Dark red blood finally filled the tube. He gave me a small nod, and I taped a cotton ball over the puncture. That fourth stick taught me more about nursing than any textbook: when you fail, you don't get to run away and feel bad for yourself. You take a breath, adjust, and do the job right because the person in the bed needs you to.

The ER moves fast, and as a first-year student, most of my job was trying to stay out of the way while still being useful. On Thursday, an ambulance brought in a woman in cardiac arrest. The room exploded into motion—doctors, respiratory therapists, nurses shouting numbers and drawing meds. I froze in the doorway until a nurse shoved a box into my chest and said, "Go restock the gauze in cart three." 

I felt embarrassed, like I was being sent to sit at the kids' table. But as I stood outside the bay, stuffing packages of 4x4 gauze into the plastic bins, I could hear them through the curtain. "One, two, three, four, five..." counting out chest compressions. Steady and loud. I realized then that somebody has to make sure the gauze is there when the bleeding starts, and somebody has to make sure the suction tubes are ready. It wasn't glorious, but it mattered. Being a nurse isn't always about being the hero in the middle of the room; it’s about making sure the machine keeps running so the patient has a chance.

Later that same shift, a man came in with a nasty, infected laceration on his leg that needed a deep cleaning. The doctor said it was going to hurt. The man looked terrified. His wife was his rock, but she was stuck in bumper-to-bumper traffic on the interstate, thirty miles away. He had nobody with him. When the doctor picked up the scrub brush, the man reached out into the empty air, and I stepped in and put my hand in his. He squeezed down so hard my knuckles ground together. He didn't say a word, and neither did I. I just stood on my sore feet, leaned against the rail of the gurney, and let him squeeze until the doctor was finished. 

Before this rotation, I thought being a good nurse was mostly about knowing your lab values, your dosages, and your anatomy. Those things matter, of course. You can't help anyone if you don't know the science. But walking out of the ER at the end of that first week, my scrubs stained and my back aching, I realized the hard part is the human part. It’s staying calm when your hands are shaking, doing the grunt work without complaining, and standing still so a scared stranger doesn't have to hurt alone.

Nursing school is the hardest thing I have ever done, and paying for it on my own makes it even harder. Between tuition, gas to get to clinicals, and the hours I have to spend studying instead of working a full-time job, money is tight every single month. This scholarship would take off some of that financial weight so I can focus on passing my classes, sharpening my skills, and getting back onto the floor. I know I have a lot left to learn, but I also know I'm meant to be there, and I’m ready to put the work in.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
# Let Our Teenagers Sleep: Why 8:45 Is Right for Millbrook

My kids are exhausted. Not the "I stayed up too late" tired—the bone-deep, adolescent-body tired that no amount of willpower fixes. And I'm not alone. Every parent with a middle or high schooler knows this struggle.

Next month, our school board will vote on moving start times to 8:45 a.m., and I'm urging them to say yes.

Here's the science: the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high school students get 8-10 hours of sleep on school nights. Our current 7:30 start time makes that nearly impossible. When my daughter has to be out the door by 7, she's getting up around 6:15. Even if she's in bed by 9:30—which rarely happens with homework and activities—that's nine hours in bed, maybe eight of actual sleep.

The research isn't theoretical. Lincoln Middle School ran a pilot program last year with a later start time. The results? Attendance went up. First-period grades improved. We're not talking about transforming education overnight, but these are real gains for real kids, right here in Millbrook.

I know the immediate objection: bus schedules. But I've read the proposal carefully. It already includes a re-tiered route plan. Yes, there will be adjustments. Yes, the district and transportation department have work to do. But "it's complicated" isn't a reason to leave teenagers chronically sleep-deprived.

My son's bus comes at 7:15 a.m. Under the new plan, it would come later. That's not a crisis. That's actually solving a problem we've lived with for years.

The pushback I hear most is about sports and after-school activities. I get it—I'm driving my kids to soccer and debate club. But here's what I know: a well-rested kid performs better at everything. School. Sports. Everything. One parent told me she was worried about evening activities ending later. They do. But the alternative—having kids wake up when their bodies are literally wired to sleep—isn't working.

This isn't about mollycoddling teenagers. It's about basic biology. Adolescent circadian rhythms shift around age 13. This is established science, not opinion. An 8:45 start time aligns school with how teenagers' brains actually work.

The Lincoln pilot showed it works. The proposal addresses logistics. The science is clear.

Our school board has a chance next month to give our kids something their bodies desperately need: sleep. I hope they take it.

b.text:
**Let Our Kids Sleep: Why 8:45 is the Right Call for Millbrook**

Every morning at 6:15 a.m., I fight the same losing battle: dragging my two middle-schoolers out of bed. They are exhausted, cranky, and running on fumes. I know I’m not the only parent in Millbrook living this daily struggle, which is why I’m writing to strongly support the school board’s proposal to push our start time to 8:45 a.m.

This isn’t just about letting kids sleep in; it’s about basic biology. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that adolescents get 8 to 10 hours of sleep, noting that their natural sleep cycles shift later during puberty. It's not a choice; it's chemistry. When we force them into classrooms before the sun is fully up, we are fighting their biology.

We don’t have to guess if a later start time works. We already have the data from right here in our backyard. When Lincoln Middle ran their pilot program last year, the results spoke for themselves. Chronic absenteeism dropped, and first-period grades went up across the board. Teachers noticed kids were actually engaged instead of staring blankly at their desks. Our kids aren’t lazy; they’re just sleep-deprived. When they actually get enough rest, they show up and they succeed.

I’ve heard the main argument against this change: the buses. Parents are worried about traffic, longer commutes, and scheduling nightmares. It's a valid concern for working parents. But if you actually read the board’s proposal, you’ll see they’ve already solved this. The plan includes a re-tiered bus schedule that staggers the routes efficiently. The transportation department has mapped it out, and the logistics simply work. We shouldn't let a solvable routing puzzle stand in the way of our children's health and academic success.

Next month, the school board will vote on this proposal. I urge the board members to look past the fear of change and look at the facts. And I urge my fellow parents to support this shift. Let’s give our kids the chance to wake up, eat a real breakfast, and actually be ready to learn. An 8:45 start time is a simple change that will make a massive difference for Millbrook’s students. Let’s vote yes.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
If your house is anything like mine around 6:30 every morning, it isn't pretty. As the parent of two middle-schoolers here in Millbrook, my day starts with dragging two half-conscious kids out of bed, nagging them to find their shoes, and shoving breakfast into their hands before they stumble out the door in the dark. 

It’s exhausting, and it turns out, it’s completely unnecessary.

Next month, our school board will vote on whether to move our middle and high school start times to 8:45 a.m. I’ve read through the board’s proposal carefully, and I believe voting "yes" is the single most common-sense move we can make for our kids’ health and education.

This isn't about letting teenagers be "lazy." The American Academy of Pediatrics has pointed out for years that biological shifts during puberty make it nearly impossible for teens to fall asleep before 11:00 p.m. Pre-teens and teens need between 8.5 and 9.5 hours of sleep for healthy brain development. Forcing them awake at dawn directly undermines their physical and mental well-being.

We don’t have to guess whether a later bell works—we already have local proof. When Lincoln Middle ran their pilot program with an 8:45 start, the results spoke for themselves. Attendance improved, morning tardiness dropped significantly, and first-period grades went up. Teachers reported that students were actually awake and participating, rather than resting their heads on their desks. 

I know some neighbors have valid concerns, particularly about how this impacts family logistics and busing. I was worried about the transportation puzzle myself. But the proposal specifically solves this by re-tiering the district’s bus routes. By staggering the pick-ups between the different grade levels, the district can make the 8:45 start happen using our current fleet, without blowing up the budget or stranding younger students. The logistics are already figured out.

Change is rarely easy, and adjusting morning routines takes effort. But our current schedule is asking our children to fight their own biology every single morning just to make the opening bell. 

When the board votes next month, I urge them to listen to the medical experts, look at Lincoln Middle's success, and approve the 8:45 start time. Our kids deserve to walk into first period alert, healthy, and ready to learn.

b.text:
**A Later Start Time is the Right Choice for Millbrook’s Middle Schoolers**

As a parent of two middle schoolers in Millbrook, I’ve spent years watching my kids struggle to wake up for the 7:30 a.m. bell. Like many of you, I’ve seen the yawns at the breakfast table, the rushed mornings, and the way their energy flags by first period. That’s why I’m relieved the school board is finally considering an 8:45 a.m. start time—and why I hope the community will support it.

The science is clear: middle schoolers need more sleep. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. to align with adolescents’ natural sleep cycles. When kids don’t get enough rest, it affects everything—mood, focus, even their immune systems. Chronic sleep deprivation isn’t just about being tired; it’s linked to higher rates of anxiety, depression, and lower academic performance. Our current start time isn’t just inconvenient—it’s working against our kids’ well-being.

We don’t have to guess what a later start would look like. Lincoln Middle School’s pilot program last year showed real results: attendance improved, and first-period grades went up. Teachers reported students were more alert and engaged. That’s not a coincidence—it’s what happens when we listen to the research and give kids the rest they need to thrive.

I know some parents worry about logistics, especially bus schedules. But the proposal already addresses this by re-tiering routes, so elementary and high school start times would shift slightly to accommodate the change. It’s not perfect, but it’s a workable solution—and one that prioritizes the age group that needs it most. Middle schoolers are at a critical stage, juggling harder coursework, social pressures, and physical changes. They deserve a schedule that sets them up for success, not one that leaves them exhausted before the day even begins.

Change is always hard, and I don’t take lightly the adjustments this will require for families. But when I think about the difference an extra hour of sleep could make for my kids—for all our kids—I believe it’s worth it. Let’s give them the best chance to learn, grow, and start their days with energy, not exhaustion. The school board votes next month, and I hope they’ll do the right thing for Millbrook’s students.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
Why the State’s 15% Cut to Apprenticeship Funding is a Bad Deal for Everyone

I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with our local IBEW. I’m writing this because the state is looking at a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding, and it needs to stop. Some lawmakers think they can balance the budget by slashing our programs, but they aren't looking at the actual numbers. When you look at the real math, cutting apprenticeship funding is exactly the wrong move.

Let’s look at my own class. We started with 24 apprentices. Today, 21 of us finished the program and are working full-time journeyman jobs. That’s a pretty solid track record. We aren't just sitting in classrooms; we are out there wiring buildings, keeping the power on, and doing the hard work that keeps this state moving. 

This program doesn't just give us a job; it gives us a real career and a path to the middle class. As a first-year apprentice, I started out making around $19 an hour. By the time we top out as journeymen, we’re making about $46 an hour. That kind of wage progression means people get off state assistance programs fast. We buy houses, we buy trucks, and we spend our money right here in our local communities. We pay our own way and we pay taxes.

Now let’s talk about what this costs the taxpayers, because I know the state cares about the budget. The total public cost for an apprentice who finishes the program is about $14,000. Compare that to a four-year college student. The average public subsidy for a student who finishes a four-year degree is around $48,000. We are giving the state a highly skilled, tax-paying worker for less than a third of the cost of a traditional college degree. If the state wants to save money and build the workforce at the same time, they should be doubling our funding, not cutting it by 15%.

A 15% cut means fewer tools, fewer instructors, and fewer people getting the chance to learn a trade. It means fewer journeymen to build and maintain the state's infrastructure. To the legislators reading this: look at the numbers. Spending $14,000 to create a journeyman who makes $46 an hour is the best deal in the state budget. Don't cut the very program that trains the people who build the state.

b.text:
**Don’t Pull the Plug on What Works**

Right now, there’s a proposal in the state budget to slash apprenticeship funding by 15%. That’s a bad idea, and I’ve got the numbers to prove it.

I’m a third-year apprentice with the IBEW. When my class started, there were 24 of us. Twenty-one finished and are out on the job today working as journeymen electricians. That’s an 88% completion rate. We’re earning good wages, paying taxes, and keeping the lights on across this state—literally.

Here’s what the path looked like for us. Apprentices start at around $19 an hour. It’s a living wage from day one, and every year we get a raise as our skills grow. By the time we top out, we’re making around $46 an hour as journeymen. Nobody in my class had to lean on food stamps or housing aid for long. Most of us were off any kind of public assistance within the first year or two, because the paychecks actually covered life. That means the state’s investment in us pays itself back fast.

Now let’s talk about what that investment actually costs. The total public money put into each apprentice who completes the program runs about $14,000. That’s it. Compare that to the average taxpayer subsidy for a student who finishes a four-year college degree: over $48,000. For nearly three and a half times the cost, you often get a graduate with debt, a degree that might not lead straight to a job, and no guarantee they’ll stay in-state. With apprenticeships, taxpayers get a skilled, licensed worker bolted directly into the local economy. We’re not moving away—we’re wiring your hospitals, schools, and factories.

A 15% cut hits the pipeline hard. Fewer slots open up. Fewer folks get a shot at a career that doesn’t require student loans or a trust fund. That means fewer journeymen a few years down the road, right when our state needs every set of skilled hands it can get to rebuild infrastructure and handle the energy transition. It’s shortsighted and it doesn’t save money in the long run. You’re just pushing people toward paths that cost the public more and deliver less.

Legislators talk a lot about “workforce development” and “return on investment.” Well, here’s the real deal: $14,000 for a near-guaranteed job with zero debt and a good wage. That’s a deal any business would take. The state should too.

Brothers and sisters, if you’re reading this, don’t just shake your head. Call your state rep and your state senator tomorrow. Tell them to reject the 15% cut and fully fund apprenticeship programs. Tell them my story. Tell them our numbers. And if you’re a legislator holding this newsletter: come ride with us for a day. I’ll show you what your dollars build. Don’t cut the one thing that’s working exactly the way it’s supposed to.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/4 Just wrapped up a kitchen remodel on Maple Ave and found something that’s worth sharing—because it could save you a ton of time, money, or both. Pulled up the old flooring and discovered the joists weren’t just sagging… they were *split* under the original load-bearing wall.

2/4 Home was built in the ‘50s, and the previous layout had a non-load-bearing wall running parallel to the joists. At some point, someone moved it—right onto the weakest point of the span. No sistering, no extra support. Just… hope? Cost to fix: ~$2,800 in labor/materials to sister 8 joists and add a beam.

3/4 The real lesson? **Don’t assume the last guy knew what they were doing.** If you’re moving walls, even non-load-bearing ones, check the framing underneath. A $200 inspection before demo could’ve saved this homeowner thousands. And if you’re a homeowner? Ask your contractor how they’re verifying structural integrity.

4/4 Bonus: If you’re in an older home and see cracks in drywall or doors that stick, don’t just patch it—get under the floor or in the attic. Those “cosmetic” issues might be your only warning. Stay safe out there.

b.text:
Maple Ave kitchen demo. Pulled the drywall for the new soffit and immediately knew something was off with the floor above.

Previous owner notched a 2x8 joist 2" deep for a dryer vent right at the bearing wall. "Repaired" it with a scrap 1x4 and drywall screws. Been carrying half the kitchen load for probably 20 years.

Fixed it right: full sister LVL, adhesive, proper nail schedule, moved vent through the wall. Cost us a day and ~$390 in lumber/glue. Would've been a sagging ceiling and a $3k callback if we'd framed over it.

Actual lesson: old houses don't hide well. Before you close anything up, open the joists and look. Fifteen years in and this still bites people—demo never lies.

✅ 15% of your week: Building out our help center. Right now it’s 4 Google Docs we threw together last year with half-answered questions. ✅ 10%: Quick 15-minute check-ins with me and Jake (our product lead) every other day to flag trends. If 6 dispatchers email about the same load board sync bug in one day, you’ll tell us, and we’ll prioritize fixing it that week. You’ll talk directly to the people building the tool — no 3 layers of management to pass feedback through.
✅ 5%: Small, team-related stuff that pops up — testing a new feature before we launch it to make sure it’s actually useful for dispatchers, drafting a quick customer email if we have a 10-minute outage, stuff like that. No “other duties as assigned” garbage where you end up ordering lunch for the whole office (we’re all remote, so you’d just be ordering your own lunch anyway).

What we’re not looking for: 5+ years of SaaS support experience, a fancy college degree, or someone who’s memorized every customer support framework.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
I bought the Jarvik L2 six months ago because I needed a desk that could keep up with 8-hour coding days, dual monitors, a laptop stand, and a mechanical keyboard that I absolutely hammer on. Here’s what I think after daily use, no sugarcoating.

The motor is fast and quiet—shockingly so. Transitions take about 10 seconds, and the sound is a low hum that doesn’t travel through walls. That matters to me because I often switch positions at 6 a.m. while my partner sleeps. Zero complaints here. It also lifts my roughly 80 pounds of gear without any hesitation, no lag or grinding.

But the stability at full standing height is a problem. At my preferred 43.5 inches, the desk wobbles when I type with any force. Not just a tiny shiver—the monitors visibly tremble. I use a tactile-switch keyboard and bottom out hard, and the bounce is distracting enough that I sometimes drop the desk an inch or two just to settle it. If you type like a butterfly, maybe you won’t notice. For me, this is the desk’s biggest flaw.

The memory presets are a nice idea, but they drift. I set four heights, and every couple of weeks my standing preset has crept up about a centimeter—I’ll hit the button and end up uncomfortably high. It’s easy to fix (just re-save it), but a memory function that doesn’t remember is just a mislabeled button.

The included cable tray is garbage. It’s a shallow metal trough held on by flimsy plastic clips. I tried to fit a surge protector, monitor cables, and a USB hub in it; the clips popped off within a month. Now it hangs at an angle, cables spilling everywhere. It’s barely usable, and I’ll be buying a proper under-desk tray. A complete afterthought.

Everything else is fine. The laminate top has survived coffee spills and hadn’t scratched yet. The frame feels solid, and the dual motors run smoothly. But these don’t redeem the wobble at full height or the useless add-ons.

I paid $549 on sale. For that price, I can tolerate the wobble, the finicky presets, and a cable tray that’s basically landfill. But at the regular $749? Absolutely not. That puts it in direct competition with desks like the Fully Jarvis or Uplift V2, both of which I’ve used in offices and are noticeably more stable. At $549, it’s a decent deal for a fast, quiet desk that mostly gets the job done. Pay a dollar more, and you’re being overcharged.

b.text:
**6-Month Review: The Jarvik L2 Standing Desk**

I bought the Jarvik L2 in February - 60x30, laminate top, black frame - with my own money. No affiliate links here, nothing to sell you.

I'm a remote software engineer. This desk gets 9-10 hours a day, 5 days a week, dual 27" monitors on an arm, MacBook, heavy mechanical keyboard.

After 6 months of actual use:

**The motor is legitimately good.**

It's fast and quiet. Jarvik claims 1.4"/sec and that's about right - it goes from my sitting height (28.5") to standing (44.5") in ~11 seconds. And it's quiet enough that I can adjust it mid-Zoom call without muting. My old Flexispot sounded like a forklift. This one is just a low hum.

**It wobbles at full height.**

I'm 5'10" and I stand at 44.5 inches. At that height, if I'm really hammering on the keyboard or leaning to grab something, there is noticeable side-to-side wobble. The monitor shake is visible. At sitting height it's rock solid. At 40" it's fine. At full max height (47") it's borderline unusable for me if I'm typing hard. If you're over 6' and plan to stand tall all day, this is not the frame you want.

**The memory presets drift.**

I have preset 1 at 72cm and preset 2 at 113cm. After 2-3 weeks, preset 1 will stop at 71cm or 73cm. It's consistently off by about a centimeter. Not the end of the world, but annoying when you expect it to hit your exact ergonomic position every time. I've had to recalibrate it twice in 6 months by holding down+up until it resets.

**The cable tray is garbage.**

Throw it away. It's thin, stamped metal, too shallow to hold a power strip plus cables, and the included wood screws stripped out of the pre-drilled holes on day one. I replaced it with a $35 under-desk tray from Amazon that holds everything. For a company selling a $700+ desk, this tray is insulting.

**Verdict:**

At the $549 sale price I paid, it's a good desk. The motor alone makes it better than anything else in that price range.

At $749 full price? Absolutely not. For that money, buy a Uplift V2 or Fully Jarvis frame and get a more stable frame and presets that actually stay put.

If you can get it on sale and you're under 6 feet and don't mind fixing the cable management yourself, it's worth it. If you see it at $749, close the tab.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam – 14 months / ~140k miles in. Honest rundown.**

Hey folks. Figured I'd put my 2 cents in since I've been running the Roadstar DC4 for about 14 months now, 140k miles on the odometer with it, front and rear cams. Not writing a manual, just stuff I wish someone had told me before I ordered it.

The big one. The thing that justifies the price tag no matter what else you think about this cam: it caught a lane-change accident on I-20 outside Shreveport. Some idiot merged into my trailer, full contact, no contact zone. Rear cam had the whole thing. Filed the claim with the footage attached, adjuster approved it in 9 days. Nine. Last time I had a claim without video I sat on it for 6 weeks waiting for "further review." That alone paid for this thing four times over, easy. You know how it goes.

Now the stuff that ain't great.

Rear cam at night past about 30 feet gets real grainy. If you're trying to ID a plate on a truck in a rest area parking lot, forget it. For the road footage, the brake lights ahead, the general "what happened" of a night collision, it's fine. It's a dash cam, not a night-vision scope. Just know going in.

Suction mount is garbage. I'm not kidding. Fell off twice in July in Texas, both times I'm pulling in and I'm like "that's a weird thud sound." Switched to the adhesive mount after the second one and haven't had a problem since. Don't even try the suction thing in summer if you're running anywhere south of Nebraska.

App pulls footage over wifi. Just... just don't count on it. Most truck stops the wifi's locked behind a paywall, password changes every 20 minutes, or it's barely got a bar to begin with. I've stopped trying to pull clips from my phone. Just pop the SD card into the laptop at the end of the week. Took me three months to stop fighting the app and do it the dumb simple way.

Bottom line: camera's solid, the insurance-saving factor is real, the mounts and app need to go in the trash. Keep it, swap the mount, ignore the software.

Happy to answer questions if y'all got any. Back to the road, I'm 40 miles behind schedule.

— T.

b.text:
**RoadStar DC4 Dash Cam – 14 Months & 140K Miles In**

Been running the RoadStar DC4 for over a year now, and it’s mostly held up to the abuse. The front cam is solid—day or night, footage is clear enough to make out license plates at highway speeds. The rear cam? Not so much. Night footage gets grainy past 30 feet, but it’s still better than nothing.

Biggest win? Caught a four-wheeler sideswiping me during a lane change. Insurance had the claim approved in nine days instead of the usual six weeks. Worth every penny for that alone.

The suction mount is garbage in summer heat—fell off twice before I swapped it for the adhesive mount. Stick with the adhesive; it hasn’t budged since.

The app’s a joke. Needs Wi-Fi to pull footage, which is useless at most truck stops. I just pop the SD card and transfer files to my phone. Not ideal, but it works.

Battery life’s decent—no issues even in extreme temps. Build quality’s solid, no random shutdowns or overheating.

Bottom line: If you need a no-frills dash cam that’ll hold up to long-haul abuse, this one’s a solid pick. Just skip the suction mount and don’t expect miracles from the rear cam at night.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text: They had a shot at state, but the season ended in round two against a team they’d already beaten by twenty in week three. The loss stings because, in the second half, the run game that had been working all night was abandoned—even though the team was only down three. That’s where it died. You don’t ditch what’s working when the margin’s that small. Dez Kowalski threw for twenty-three forty, a new school record, but you can’t hang stats on the wall when the play-calling gets cute. The season didn’t end because of a lack of talent; it ended because we stopped running the ball when we should’ve kept driving it.

b.text:
Eight wins and a playoff exit. That’s the headline. But if you’re looking past the final score in Round 2, the real story isn’t about a sudden collapse—it’s about a choice made when it mattered most.

Let’s get the obvious out of the way. Dez Kowalski put up numbers that’ll live in the record books forever. 2,340 passing yards. A new school standard. That’s worth a nod. So is going 8-2 and proving you could handle a regional powerhouse when you blew them off the field by 20 points back in Week 3. This group showed up when expected.

Playoffs, though, don’t care about résumés. They care about what you run when the noise drowns out the practice reps. In the second half, sitting on a three-point cushion, the offense shifted gears. They took the ball out of the hands of their runners and started living on the sideline. The run game was working. The interior push was creating seams. The backs were reading blocks cleanly. Yet the playbook flipped toward vertical shots against a defense that spends its whole week preparing for long passes. That wasn’t a calculated adjustment. It was hesitation wearing a coaching headset.

When you walk away from what’s producing with single digits on the board, you cede control. You play into the opponent’s strength and strip your own team of rhythm. Dez can stack yardage all December, but a quarterback can’t manufacture leverage alone. This team knew how to eat clocks, punish tackles, and force opposing coordinators to call timeouts. They abandoned their teeth right when they needed to bite.

There’s no shame in losing to a team you proved you could beat months earlier. Shame comes from changing your identity the moment the pressure rises. Beating someone once is a statement. Doing it twice is a habit. Dropping the run game in the third quarter turned a habit into a cautionary tale.

The record stands. The milestone stands. But the lesson hangs heavier. Championships aren’t won by chasing stat lines. They’re decided by trusting your foundation when the floor starts shaking. If this staff and those seniors remember that before cleats hit grass again, next fall won’t look like this one.

a.text:
# The Market Didn't Crash. Some Sellers Just Haven't Gotten the Memo.

Last spring, the median home in my zip code sold in eight days. This spring, the median is thirty-four.

I've watched people read that number — 8 to 34 — and hear one thing: crash. Inventory's piling up, buyers are gone, the party's over, get out while you can.

That's not what's happening. Here's what's actually happening.

List prices in my zip are still up 6% year over year. Showings per listing have dropped by half. Read those two facts together, because they are the entire story: sellers raised their prices while buyer traffic collapsed underneath them. Nothing else changed. The buyers didn't disappear. They just stopped paying the number.

I have three sellers right now who are past 60 days on market and will not drop their price. I've shown them the data. I've shown them the six competing listings within a mile that are also sitting. I've shown them what the last four closed sales in their own subdivision actually sold for. And every one of them has told me some version of the same thing: "The right buyer will come along."

They won't. Not at that price. And I'd rather say that to you here than nod along and let it cost them another sixty days.

Here's the part buyers already understand and sellers haven't accepted yet. A buyer today walks in with the last six months of sold data in their pocket. In 2021, buyers were guessing. In 2025, they pull comps in the driveway before they knock. When a house is listed meaningfully above what the same street closed at in March, the buyer doesn't counter. They don't come back. The conversation ends before it starts. That's what shows-per-listing dropping by half looks like on the ground — not rejection, just silence.

And silence has a clock on it. This is the part sellers underestimate most. A listing at day 14 is new. A listing at day 34 is *stale*. Buyers assume something's wrong — foundation, roof, neighbor's dog, divorce, something. The showing requests thin out. The offers that do come come in low, because the buyer assumes you're stuck and prices it in accordingly. The longer you sit, the less you get per showing. That's not market psychology. That's arithmetic.

I'll run the numbers because I run them with every seller. Say you're asking $425,000. You sit ninety days, then cut. Compare that to cutting to $399,000 on day 14 and selling in ten days. You've paid three months of taxes, insurance, utilities, and the lawn guy. You've paid whatever it costs you to carry the next house, or to rent, or to stay put a season longer than you wanted. And the buyer pool at $399k is meaningfully bigger than the pool at $425k — you're now competing with houses that looked out of reach last month. In most of the cases I've run, the seller who cuts early nets *more*. Not less. More.

Now the uncomfortable part, and I'll write it because I've done it. Some of this is on us. Agents take overpriced listings because we're afraid the seller will call the agent down the street who will. I've done it. I've told a seller their number was high, watched them pick someone who wouldn't, and then watched the house sit all summer. Every one of those listings drags the median up and the showings down, and makes it harder for the seller next door who priced it right. We're not innocent bystanders in this.

So here's the position, and I'm not going to wrap it in "it depends on many factors," because it doesn't.

Fourteen-day average for the houses priced correctly. Thirty-four-day median overall. Same zip code, same spring, same buyers.

Those numbers only exist together because price is the one variable sellers fully control, and a lot of them are refusing to touch it.

If you're a seller sitting at day 30 with no offers, you don't have a marketing problem, and you don't have an agent problem, and you certainly don't have a market problem. You have a price problem. The market is telling you so, politely, once a week, every time your phone doesn't ring.

This isn't a crash. Crashes are when prices fall whether you like it or not. I'm telling you the opposite: the market is fine, buyers are here, and money is still changing hands in under two weeks in my zip code. What's happening is a recalibration, and the only people losing money in it right now are the ones still pricing like it's last April.

Sellers who price it right are selling. Sellers who don't are donating their carrying costs to a buyer who hasn't shown up yet.

That's not the market being difficult. That's a decision.

b.text:
# No, Our Local Housing Market Isn’t Crashing—It’s Waiting For Sellers To Catch Up

Last Saturday, I spent 20 minutes chatting with three different parents at my kid’s rec soccer game, all asking the same question: Is the local housing market crashing?

They’d all seen the same red flags: the house on the corner of Oak and 5th that’s had a for-sale sign in the yard since March, the headlines about rising mortgage rates, the gossip from their cousin who’s a realtor in Arizona saying prices are tanking. Let me cut through the noise, straight from someone who’s been selling houses here in this suburb for 10 years, who’s out showing properties every weekend, who’s currently got three sellers sitting on 60+ days on market refusing to drop their price: This isn’t a crash. It’s just sellers who haven’t caught up to the new pace of the market.

Let’s run the numbers for our zip code, no fluff:
- Last spring, median days on market was 8. Eight. That means half the houses listed were under contract before most people even had time to schedule a second showing. I listed a 3-bed with a half-finished basement last April that got 19 offers in 3 days, $45,000 over asking.
- This spring? Median days on market is 34. That’s a huge jump, and it’s the number everyone’s panicking about.
- Showings per listing are down 50% from last year. Where a new listing might get 30 showings in the first weekend last spring, now it’s more like 10 to 15—if it’s priced right.
- And here’s the kicker that confuses everyone: average list prices are still up 6% year over year. Sellers are still asking more than they were last spring—but buyers aren’t biting on the ones that cross the line of what the market will actually bear.

Wait, how can days on market be way up, showings way down, but prices still climbing? Because that 34-day median isn’t being dragged up by a market-wide crash—it’s being dragged up by a handful of overpriced listings that are sitting there collecting dust.

The homes that are priced for today’s market? They’re still selling in under 2 weeks. Last month I listed a 4-bed in the Westdale school district at $425,000—exactly what my comparable sales analysis said it was worth, not a penny more—and we had 8 offers in 6 days, sold for $15,000 over asking. Two weeks ago, a colleague listed a 2-bed condo near Main Street for $210,000, and it went under contract in 9 days, no price drop. These aren’t outliers. They’re the norm for homes priced fairly.

The problem is the sellers who are still pricing their homes like it’s spring 2023, when rates were a full point lower, buyers were waiving every contingency just to get a foot in the door, and you could list your house for 10% over what it was worth and still get a bidding war.

I’ve got three of those sellers right now. One couple remodeled their kitchen in 2022 and is convinced their house is worth what their next-door neighbor got last May—never mind that their neighbor had 21 offers, and their house has been on the market for 68 days with exactly two offers, both $30,000 below their asking price. Another seller inherited his mom’s ranch and thinks “sentimental value” adds $50,000 to the price tag. The third is a young family that’s already bought their next house out of state and thinks “waiting it out” will get them their dream price. All three have refused to drop their price. All three are contributing to that 34-day median days on market number that’s making everyone think the sky is falling.

Let me be clear: There is no crash. Buyers are still out there. We still have way less inventory than we did pre-2020, and buyers are still willing to pay a fair price for a good house that’s priced correctly. What they’re not willing to do is overpay for a house that’s listed at a 2023 frenzy price when mortgage rates are higher and they have more time to shop around.

If you’re a buyer right now: Don’t let the “for sale” signs that have been up for two months fool you. Those are the overpriced ones. The well-priced homes are still moving fast, so you still need to have your pre-approval in order and be ready to act when you find one you love. But you also don’t have to waive your inspection or appraisal to compete anymore, which is a nice change from last year’s chaos.

If you’re a seller thinking of listing this summer: Do yourself a favor and price it right from the start. The longer your house sits on the market, the more buyers will assume there’s something wrong with it, and the less you’ll likely end up getting. That 6% year-over-year price increase is real for well-priced homes, but you don’t get that if you list 10% over what the market will bear and let it sit for three months.

And if you’re one of those sellers who’s been on the market for 60+ days and you’re convinced your house is “worth more”? I hate to break it to you, but your house is worth what a buyer is willing to pay for it. Right now, buyers aren’t willing to pay last year’s prices. It’s not the market crashing. It’s the market going back to normal—and normal means you can’t just slap a sky-high price on your house and expect buyers to line up around the block.

If you’re curious about what your house is actually worth in today’s market, or you’re a buyer looking to navigate this weird in-between period, shoot me an email or give me a call. I’m happy to walk you through the numbers, no sales pitch, just the straight talk I’ve been giving this community for 10 years.

See you at the Memorial Day parade next weekend— I’ll be the one handing out popsicles and talking real estate, as usual.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
## The Market Didn't Break. The Clock Just Changed.

I've had three separate conversations this month that went almost word for word the same way. Seller sitting at the kitchen table, sixty-some days on market, maybe four showings total, and they look at me and say some version of: "We're not giving it away."

Nobody's asking you to give it away. I'm asking you to price it like it's 2025.

Here's what's actually happening in our zip code. Last spring, the median days on market was eight. Eight. You listed on a Thursday, you had offers by Sunday night, and half of them were waiving inspection and throwing in an appraisal gap. This spring, that number is thirty-four. That's not a rounding error. That's a different market wearing the same clothes.

And yet list prices are up six percent year over year. Six percent, while showings per listing have been cut clean in half. Read that sentence again, because it's the whole story. Sellers are asking more money from fewer buyers who are taking four times as long to decide. That math doesn't work, and it's not going to start working because we want it to.

So let me say the thing everyone's dancing around: this is not a crash. I've been doing this ten years, I remember what a bad market smells like, and this isn't it. Homes are still selling. Good homes, priced right, are going in under two weeks — I've closed three like that since February. Buyers are out there. They're employed, they're pre-approved, they toured your house on a Saturday and they liked it.

They just didn't like it *that* much.

What we have is a pricing problem dressed up as a demand problem. And the reason it's so hard to shake is that sellers are anchored to a nine-week window in 2022 when their neighbor's split-level went thirty grand over ask to a guy who'd never seen it in person. That was the anomaly. That was the fever. We all knew it at the time and said so out loud, and then somehow it became the baseline against which every listing since has been judged.

I have a seller right now — good people, lovely house, genuinely one of the nicer kitchens on their street — who has been on the market since early March. We've had two showings in the last three weeks. I brought them a comp analysis showing three comparable homes that sold in the same window, all of them priced eight to twelve thousand below where we are. Their response: "Those houses don't have our lot."

Maybe not. But the market doesn't price your lot. Buyers price your lot, and right now buyers are pricing your lot at less than you are.

Here's what I wish more sellers understood about the mechanics of this. In an eight-day market, overpricing costs you almost nothing. The market is moving so fast it catches up to your mistake in two weeks and you sell anyway, and you tell yourself you were smart to hold firm. In a thirty-four-day market, overpricing is expensive and the expense compounds. You burn your first two weeks — the only two weeks when every buyer with a saved search gets an alert with your address on it — talking to nobody. Then you sit. Then the days-on-market counter starts doing your negotiating for you, badly. Then when you finally do cut, buyers don't read it as a deal. They read it as a question: what's wrong with it?

The price drop you refuse to make in week three is almost always smaller than the price drop you'll accept in week ten. I have watched this play out enough times that I'd put money on it.

The flip side, and this is the part I want to shout from the parking lot: the sellers who *are* getting it are doing great. Not surviving. Doing great. Price it at what the last three comps actually closed at, not what your neighbor listed at and later withdrew. Clean it out. Fix the thing you've been meaning to fix for four years. Take the pre-listing inspection seriously. Those houses are going pending in ten, twelve days, at or near ask, with normal contract terms and buyers who show up to closing happy. There is nothing wrong with this market for people who are willing to meet it where it is.

So no, I'm not going to tell you the market is complicated and depends on many factors. It depends on one factor right now, and that factor is whether the seller has updated their internal calendar. The buyers already have. Rates did that for them. They're methodical now. They tour four houses instead of one. They go home and think about it. They come back for a second showing before they write. That's not weakness — that's what a normal market has always looked like, and we're just out of practice.

The pace changed. The price expectations didn't. That gap is where the thirty-four days lives.

Close the gap and you'll be moving by summer. Don't, and I'll see you in September, taking less than I'm telling you to take today.

b.text:
# The Market Didn't Crash. Some Sellers Just Haven't Caught Up.

If you've been watching our local market and reading the headlines, you might think we're headed off a cliff. Days on market nearly quadrupled. Showings have been cut in half. And yes, those numbers are real — they're happening right here in our zip codes. But before you start panicking or waiting for a massive price correction, let me tell you what's actually going on.

**This is not a crash. It's a correction in expectations.**

Last spring, a well-priced home in our area was getting multiple offers in under a week. Eight days on market was the median, and sellers were in the driver's seat. That pace has slowed to about five weeks. Some people look at that shift and see collapse. I look at it and see a market that's returning to something more balanced — something that's actually healthy.

Here's the piece that's getting lost in the conversation: list prices are still up six percent year over year. Six percent. That's not the sign of a market in freefall. That's a market where sellers are still confident — perhaps too confident in some cases.

And that's where the problem actually lives. I have three sellers right now who have been on the market for more than sixty days and are refusing to adjust their price. They're looking at last spring's numbers and expecting last spring's results. But last spring's buyer who would've lined up for that house with minimal negotiation doesn't exist anymore — at least not at that price point. Those buyers have either adjusted their expectations, gotten more selective, or in some cases, stepped back entirely.

Meanwhile, the sellers who are pricing it right — really pricing it to the current market, not the market of twelve months ago — are still selling in under two weeks. That tells you everything you need to know about where the demand actually is. The buyer is still there. They're just not willing to overpay anymore.

I get it. Nobody wants to hear that they need to come down in price. When you've watched your home's value climb the way it has over the past several years, it feels like a loss to ask for less. But asking for less than you wanted isn't the same as losing money. Those sellers who are holding firm on overpriced listings aren't protecting their equity — they're watching their homes grow stale, losing leverage with every passing week.

The market didn't change overnight. It shifted. And the agents and sellers who adapt to that shift — who price smart, who market effectively, who trust the data over their gut — are still getting deals done quickly and at strong numbers.

So if you're selling right now and you're frustrated because the phone isn't ringing the way it did last spring, you're not alone. But the answer isn't to hold your ground and hope. The answer is to look at what's actually happening and make the smart move. The market will reward you — if you meet it where it is.

*If you're thinking about listing and want an honest conversation about where your home falls in this market, I'm always happy to talk.*

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
Let Juniors and Seniors Leave for Lunch

Every day at 11:42, our lunch wave turns into a scramble for chairs. People end up sitting on the floor in the hallway or standing around trash cans trying to eat because there is nowhere else to go. Our school should allow open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. It would fix a real space problem, it has already worked in schools near us, and students are clearly ready for it.

The most immediate reason is space. Our cafeteria only seats 220 people, but there are 340 students assigned to that lunch wave. That math does not work. When more than a hundred students do not have a seat, lunch is not really a break. It is loud, crowded, and stressful, and custodians and lunch supervisors have to deal with the overflow. Letting juniors and seniors who want to leave go off campus would take pressure off the cafeteria for everyone, including freshmen and sophomores who would stay.

The other thing is that we know this policy can work because nearby schools are already doing it. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow open campus lunch for upperclassmen. According to their published attendance stats, none of them have seen a rise in tardiness since they started it. That matters because the biggest worry adults have about open lunch is that students will not get back in time for fifth period. In these three districts, they do get back. There is no reason to assume our school would be different.

Some teachers and parents might still argue that only some juniors and seniors are responsible enough to handle leaving campus. But at this point most of us are driving to school, holding part-time jobs, and applying to college. Going out for lunch and getting back on time is a pretty basic level of responsibility. I surveyed 80 students at our school and 71 said they were in favor of open campus lunch. That shows students actually want this privilege and understand what comes with it.

Open campus for juniors and seniors is not about getting out of school. It is about trusting upperclassmen with a normal choice and solving an overcrowding problem at the same time. The cafeteria cannot fit us, other schools have proven it does not cause tardiness issues, and students support it. It is time for our school to make the change.

b.text:
Open Campus Lunch Is Overdue for Juniors and Seniors

Every day during B lunch, about 340 students try to eat in a cafeteria built for 220. Some of them sit on the floor by the vending machines. Some eat standing up in the hallway outside the gym, which is technically against the rules, though nobody enforces it because there is nowhere else to send them. A few just skip lunch and go to the library. This is the situation our school has chosen instead of a policy that three nearby districts already use without problems: letting juniors and seniors leave campus for lunch. Open campus lunch for upperclassmen would solve a real overcrowding problem, and the evidence from schools around us shows it can be done without hurting attendance or student safety.

The overcrowding is not an exaggeration or a matter of opinion. The cafeteria has 220 seats. The B lunch wave has 340 students. That means on any given day, roughly 120 students have no place to sit, and that number does not go down when it rains and the courtyard is closed. Juniors and seniors together make up close to half of that wave. If even a third of them left campus, the cafeteria would go from overcrowded to full, which is a very different thing. The school has spent years treating this as a scheduling puzzle, adding a third lunch period one year and then removing it when it cut into class time. Open campus is the only fix that does not require rebuilding the cafeteria or rearranging the master schedule.

The most common objection is that students who leave for lunch will come back late, or not at all. This is a fair concern, but it is also one we can actually check, because other districts have already run the experiment. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow open campus lunch for upperclassmen, and all three publish attendance data. None of them show a rise in tardiness after adopting the policy. This matters because these are not distant schools in some other state with a different culture; they are districts a short drive away, drawing students from similar communities, dealing with the same traffic and the same fast food places. If open campus caused a wave of tardy students, it would show up in their numbers. It doesn't.

Students at our school also clearly want this. I surveyed 80 students across grade levels, and 71 said they were in favor of open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. That is almost 89 percent. I will be honest that 80 students is a small sample and I was not able to randomize it the way a real study would, so the exact percentage should be taken loosely. But the size of the gap is hard to dismiss. Even if the real number is closer to 75 percent, that is still a policy with overwhelming support from the people it would affect. Schools regularly ask for student input and then explain why it cannot be acted on. This is a case where the input points in one direction and the practical evidence points the same way.

Some will argue that open campus is a privilege upperclassmen have not earned, or that it creates a liability for the school if a student is hurt off campus. On the first point, the policy can easily be tied to standing. Fairmont, for example, revokes the privilege for students with excessive absences or discipline referrals, and our school could do the same. That turns open campus into an incentive rather than a giveaway. On the liability question, the three districts I mentioned all require a signed parent permission form, which shifts responsibility to families the same way a field trip form does. This is a solved problem, not a new one.

Our school does not need to be the first to try this. It needs to be the fourth. The overcrowding in the cafeteria is measurable and getting worse, students strongly support a change, and the districts closest to us have already shown that the main fear about open campus lunch does not come true. Juniors and seniors are a year or two from being trusted to manage their own time in college or at a job. Trusting them to eat lunch and come back on time is a reasonable place to start.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After 12 years of selling homes in Asheville, I’ve noticed something simple that keeps proving true:

Buyers who walk the neighborhood at 7am before we ever tour the house usually end up happier with the home they buy.

Not because they’ve “researched harder.”
Not because they’ve found some hidden trick.

Because they’ve seen what the street actually feels like.

I learned that lesson clearly with the Pruitts on Sycamore Street.

They were first-time buyers, excited, a little overwhelmed, and understandably focused on the house itself. But before we met to tour, I suggested they drive by early one morning and take a walk around the block.

That morning changed everything.

They noticed the quiet. The neighbors out with coffee. The light on the trees. The way the street felt at the start of a normal workday, not just during a showing when everything is polished and still.

By the time we toured the house, they weren’t just reacting to finishes and square footage. They were already picturing life there. And when they made their decision, it was with a lot more confidence and a lot less second-guessing.

That’s what I keep seeing. A house can look perfect in the middle of a scheduled showing, but the neighborhood is what you live in every day.

So if you’re house hunting, especially as a first-time buyer, try this: walk the street early. See who’s up. Hear the sounds. Notice the pace.

It can tell you more than a pretty listing ever will.

b.text:
Twelve years in, you stop guessing and start noticing patterns.

One that’s held up every time: the buyers who walk the neighborhood at 7 a.m. before we tour the house are the ones who still love the place two years later. Not because the house changes, but because they actually know what they’re buying into.

I learned that with the Pruitts. They were under contract on a little craftsman just off Sycamore Street, and the inspection was clean, the numbers worked, everything looked good on paper. But I’d watched enough buyers grow quiet six months after closing to know that paper isn’t the whole story. So I told them to grab coffee at the shop on the corner, walk the full length of Sycamore at 7 a.m. on a Tuesday, and then call me.

They did. They saw the retired guy three doors down who hoses off his driveway every morning and waves whether you wave back or not. They heard the school bus stop at the end of the block, which meant kids, which meant the Pruitts—who were expecting their first—wouldn’t be the only young family on the street. They realized the “quiet” street they’d driven through at 5 p.m. on a Saturday was actually alive in a way they liked at 7 a.m. on a weekday.

They closed three weeks later, and last I checked they were still happy. Not because the house was perfect, but because Sycamore Street felt like home before they ever walked through the front door.

I don’t have a statistic for this. I just know that when buyers fall in love with the context around the house, the house itself tends to stick.

By shifting the windows for elementary, middle, and high schools, the district can handle the new schedule using the fleet we already have, without costing taxpayers extra money. setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/
I raised Tallyup's prices 40% overnight. Every customer, no exceptions.

A week later, 30 of my 140 customers were gone.

What I got wrong, and what I changed:

2/
The backstory: like every indie hacker, I'd absorbed the advice.

"You're undercharging."
"Just charge more."
"Raising prices is the highest-leverage move in SaaS."

So one day I did. Every customer. Same day. Bigger number on the next invoice.

3/
No grandfathering.
No heads-up.
No "here's why."

Just a charge 40% higher than what they signed up for.

That was the whole mistake — but it took losing 30 customers to see it.

4/
The cancellations started almost immediately.

30 out of 140, gone in seven days.

And these aren't faceless accounts. Gym owners run small businesses. They notice every line item, and they'd taken a chance on a solo founder's tool.

5/
Here's the thing: the price probably wasn't the problem.

New customers might have paid it without blinking.

The problem was changing the deal on people who had already said yes. A price hike with no warning doesn't feel like strategy. It feels like a broken promise.

6/
What I changed:

→ Existing customers keep their original price
→ New pricing applies to new signups only
→ Any future increase gets announced well in advance, with a reason and a way to push back

The deal you sign is the deal you keep.

7/
I also emailed every customer who cancelled and offered their old price back.

Most didn't take me up on it.

Trust is fast to spend and slow to earn back. I knew that in the abstract. Now I know it for real.

8/
The "just charge more" advice isn't wrong. It's incomplete.

Charge more for new customers, fine. But your existing customers already made a deal with you. Honor it — or at least warn them before you change it.

9/
Rebuilding now, one gym at a time.

If you've raised prices on existing customers as a founder — how did you handle it? Genuinely asking.

b.text:
I raised Tallyup’s prices 40% on everyone overnight.

Within a week, 30 of our 140 customers had left.

Here’s the pricing mistake—and what I changed afterward 🧵

1/ I treated pricing like a spreadsheet problem.

The product had improved. The old price felt too low. A 40% increase seemed reasonable to me.

But customers didn’t experience it as a spreadsheet update.

They experienced it as a surprise bill.

2/ The biggest mistake wasn’t raising prices.

It was changing the deal without giving customers:

• Advance notice  
• Time to evaluate  
• A clear explanation  
• Any recognition for supporting Tallyup early

I optimized for simplicity on my side and created uncertainty on theirs.

3/ I also assumed existing customers saw the product the way I did.

I saw everything we’d built.

They saw the specific job they hired Tallyup to do: help track member retention.

More features don’t automatically make a sudden price increase feel fair.

4/ Losing 30 customers in a week made the lesson impossible to ignore:

Pricing isn’t just about what the product is worth.

It’s also about trust, timing, and how you communicate change.

5/ What I changed:

• No more overnight increases  
• Existing customers get advance notice  
• Pricing changes come with a clear reason  
• Early customers are treated differently from new signups  
• Customers have time to decide, ask questions, or adjust

6/ I’m not saying never raise prices.

Small SaaS companies need sustainable pricing.

But “we need to charge more” doesn’t mean “everyone pays 40% more starting now.”

The rollout is part of the pricing decision.

7/ My takeaway:

Raise prices when the business needs it.

Just don’t confuse having the right destination with taking the right route.

I learned that one by losing 30 of 140 customers in a week.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
**Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8 Months of Almost-Daily Sourdough**

I’ve run the Corlane SM6 nearly every day for eight months, mostly for farmers market sourdough. It has also worked through double batches of stiff bagel dough, which is where this mixer really proves itself.

The motor is the highlight. A double batch of low-hydration bagel dough—heavy, stiff, and exactly the kind of thing that makes weaker mixers stall or overheat—kneads without stalling. The mixer doesn’t sound like it’s struggling, and the head stays stable. For weekly market production, the SM6 has been dependable in a way I didn’t fully expect at this price.

The downsides are specific and real. The bowl-lift lever squeaks, and I have to WD-40 it about once a month. That’s not difficult, but it’s annoying on a $429 mixer. The included dough hook is too short for the deep bowl, so it leaves unincorporated flour and dough at the bottom. I bought a third-party dough hook, which solves the problem but adds extra cost and means the out-of-box accessory isn’t quite right for bread dough. And at $429, the Corlane is $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid bowl-lift model.

**Verdict:** For heavy dough bakers—sourdough, bagels, stiff whole-grain loaves—this is a buy. The motor is the reason to choose it. For cookie and cake bakers, skip it. You’ll pay more than the KitchenAid and inherit the squeak and hook issue without getting any real benefit. This is a bread mixer, not an all-purpose mixer.

b.text:
**Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8-Month Review**

Eight months ago, I unboxed the Corlane SM6 to replace the hand mixer I’d been beating to death with weekend market sourdough. Since then, it’s run nearly every day—sometimes twice a day—and it’s become the workhorse I was hoping for, with a few caveats that matter.

The motor is the real story. I mix double batches of stiff bagel dough, the kind that makes lesser machines smell like burning plastic and stall out mid-knead. The SM6 doesn’t blink. It powers through 75% hydration sourdough and shaggy rye without slowing down or heating up. If you’re buying this for heavy dough, the guts are absolutely there.

But Corlane cut corners on the details. The bowl lift lever squeaks like a rusty gate, and I’ve had to hit it with WD-40 every month to keep it from grinding. Worse, the included dough hook is too short for the deep bowl, leaving a dry ring of flour at the bottom every single mix. I ditched it after two weeks and bought a third-party spiral hook that actually reaches the base. Factor that extra $25 into your total cost.

Speaking of cost: the SM6 is $429, which is $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid Artisan. You’re paying that premium for torque, not polish.

Here is the actual verdict. If you knead heavy dough weekly—sourdough, bagels, pizza, babka—buy this mixer. The motor justifies the price and the minor annoyances. But if you are mostly creaming butter for cookies and whipping cake batter, skip it. You will spend extra money on power you will never use, and you will still be oiling that squeaky lever for no good reason.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After 12 years of helping buyers—mostly first-timers—navigate the Asheville market, I’ve realized that the secret to long-term home happiness isn’t found on an inspection report or a spreadsheet. The buyers who end up truly loving their homes years down the road are almost always the ones who walk the neighborhood at 7:00 AM before our scheduled tour. 

I always think about my clients, the Pruitts, when they were looking at a cottage on Sycamore Street. On paper, the house was perfect, but they were understandably nervous. It was their first purchase, and they wanted to be absolutely sure. I suggested they get up early, grab some coffee, and just walk the block on a weekday morning. 

By walking the street at 7:00 AM, they saw the neighborhood wake up. They saw who was walking dogs, how the morning traffic moved, and how quiet the block actually was when the rest of the world was starting their day. They got a feel for the rhythm of the street in a way that a Saturday afternoon open house could never replicate. 

They bought the house, and to this day, they tell me that early morning walk was the moment they knew they were actually home. 

If you're searching for a home right now, don't just look at the house. Go stand on the sidewalk at 7:00 AM on a Tuesday. It tells you everything the listing description can't.

b.text:
After twelve years of doing this mostly with first-time buyers in Asheville, I've started keeping a mental list of "this couple is gonna be okay." It's not about credit scores or pre-approval amounts. It's something much dumber than that.

I started noticing it around year three or four. You're standing in a kitchen with granite countertops and somebody goes, "Oh, is there a grocery store?" Or, more rarely, "How loud is the truck at 6:30?" And then the couple who actually walks the block at seven in the morning before our Saturday tour, those people just... know. They know the rhythm of the place before anyone's staging anything for them.

The Pruitts, four or five years ago. They were looking in West Asheville, nervous, two kids under six, first real home. I had a 9:30 showing on Sycamore Street that day, a mid-century bungalow they'd been talking themselves into for weeks online. I was doing my usual "arrived, locked the box, pretending not to be nervous with my hands" routine when I pulled up and there they were. Both of them. Walking the street. Mrs. Pruitt in her bathrobe slippers with the kids asleep in the car, Mr. Pruitt just walking behind her pointing at things.

They'd been up since six. Couldn't sleep with the anxiety, she told me, and they figured they'd come see it "in real life" before seeing it "on Zillow life." And what they noticed: the school bus hits the intersection at 7:04, sharp enough to wake a toddler. The neighbor's dog barks at 5:45 every single day. The church parking lot fills up Sunday morning and there is no turning in. And the light on the east side of the house, the one that makes every sunset photo look unreal, is actually just... okay, at seven a.m. It's a different kind of beautiful. They needed to know it before they needed to love it.

We toured the bungalow. They put in an offer. Thirty-six years old, one bathroom, a kitchen that I gently called "character." They're in year four now, and I got a text in September from her, a photo of the porch with the kids doing homework. "You were right that we needed the light," she wrote, "but more than that we needed to know about the bus."

I don't do this job to sell kitchens anymore. I do it so people land somewhere that fits the Tuesday-morning version of their life, not the Saturday-afternoon open-house fantasy. And the people who walk the block at seven a.m., even just once, even in their bathrobe slippers, they save themselves some kind of grief I've never seen quantified in a spreadsheet but I've seen in the faces of people who skipped that step and found out about the dog, or the bus, or the truck, on the thirty-second morning of month two.

If you're house hunting and the showing isn't until ten, come early. Walk it. Bring coffee. Notice the garbage truck day. Watch which way the sun actually hits. I'll be the agent in the parking lot pretending to check my phone. Walk up and say hi. I'd rather you see it quiet and real at seven than pretty and performative at noon.

That's the whole "secret." That's twelve years of data. Go walk the street.
