setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: My 6-Month Review

I’ve used the Jarvik L2 as my full-time desk for six months, usually eight to ten hours a day. The short version: the frame and motor are good, the stability is merely acceptable, and the included cable tray is terrible.

I paid the $549 sale price. At that price, I’d buy it again. At the regular $749 price, I would not.

## Motor: Quiet and Fast

The motor is the L2’s best feature. It moves quickly enough that switching positions never feels like an interruption, and it’s quiet enough to use during a call without announcing to everyone that I’m raising my desk.

The motion is smooth, with no alarming jolts when it starts or stops. After six months of frequent adjustments—typically four to six per workday—the motor still sounds and performs the same as it did when new.

## Stability: Fine Until Full Height

At seated and moderate standing heights, the L2 feels solid. My monitors stay put, and normal typing doesn’t create noticeable movement.

At full height, it wobbles. I’m a fairly hard typist, and when the desk is near its maximum extension, I can see movement in my monitor arms. It’s mostly front-to-back rather than side-to-side, but it’s obvious enough to be distracting.

This isn’t a dealbreaker for me because my normal standing preset is below maximum height. Taller users who need the desk fully extended should take the wobble seriously. A stable frame at mid-height does not automatically mean a stable frame at full extension, and the L2 is proof of that.

## Memory Presets: Useful but Imprecise

The controller is simple, and the memory buttons make switching between sitting and standing easy. Unfortunately, the presets drift by roughly a centimeter.

I’ll save a height, return to it later, and find the desk slightly higher or lower than expected. One centimeter doesn’t sound significant, but it’s enough to change wrist and elbow positioning. I occasionally have to tap the controls to correct it.

The presets are still useful, but they aren’t precise. On a desk with a $749 list price, they should be.

## Cable Tray: Garbage

The included cable tray is the worst part of the desk.

It’s too small for a power strip plus the collection of adapters and excess cable that comes with a real workstation. Access is awkward, cable routing is poorly considered, and it does very little to keep heavier cords from sagging or escaping.

I gave up on it and installed a larger third-party tray. That solved the problem, but buyers shouldn’t have to replace a basic accessory immediately—especially at the regular price.

If you use multiple monitors, a dock, speakers, and a desktop PC, budget for a separate cable-management setup.

## Six-Month Verdict

The Jarvik L2 gets the fundamentals mostly right. Its motor is quiet, fast, and still reliable after six months of daily use. It feels stable at the heights most people will use, but the wobble at full extension is real. The drifting memory presets are irritating, and the cable tray belongs in the recycling bin.

At **$549**, the L2 is worth it. The motor performance and overall frame quality outweigh the flaws, especially if you don’t need maximum height and are willing to replace the cable tray.

At **$749**, skip it. For that price, I expect better full-height stability, accurate presets, and cable management that isn’t an afterthought.

b.text:
Six months into owning the Jarvik L2, here’s exactly where it succeeds and where it cuts corners. I’m a remote software engineer running a heavy dual-monitor setup, cycling between sitting and standing four to six times a day. If you’re comparing standing desks and want raw, unfiltered data after half a year of daily use, read on.

**The Motor**
Genuinely good. Fast. Dead silent. There’s no whine, no grinding, no stuttering on lift or descent. It transitions smoothly and quietly, which matters when you’re stepping away from commits or jumping into back-to-back calls. If acoustic isolation is a priority, this passes.

**Stability**
Firm at mid-range heights. Fails at maximum extension. When I hard-type through debugging sessions or lean into aggressive keypresses at full height, the desktop plate flexes and monitor arms visibly shiver. It’s not a structural failure, but it’s tactile and distracting. I’m 6’2”, and the wobble at peak elevation is consistent. Add a wider base or a center crossbar and it would hold up; instead, you’re trading stability for reach.

**Memory Presets**
Convenient until they aren’t. The four factory profiles have drifted roughly a centimeter since unboxing. Standard daily cycles, home office temperatures, no mechanical abuse. The calibration slipped enough that I’ve had to reprogram mine twice. Nice feature on paper. Practically, it requires periodic manual correction.

**Cable Management**
Garbage. Thin, stamped-metal tray that bows under its own weight if you run anything beyond two lightweight cords. The integrated clips pop out immediately. The mounting hardware fights standard under-desk routing geometry. I tore it off in week two and ran everything through a simple nylon sleeve. It delivers zero value and costs you fifteen minutes of teardown time.

**Verdict**
Buy it at $549. Ignore it at $749. 

At the discounted price, you’re paying for a quiet, reliable dual-motor system and a functional work surface that justifies the wobble, preset drift, and missing cable solution. At full retail, you’re overpaying for mid-tier stability and assembly shortcuts that drag the experience below the $700 mark. 

Run the L2 on a sale. Keep a cheap bubble level nearby to recalibrate your presets quarterly. Rip the cable tray out on day one. Otherwise, keep shopping.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
## The Market Isn’t Crashing. Sellers Are Just Still Pricing for Last Year.

If you’re watching homes sit longer this spring and wondering whether the local market has suddenly fallen apart, my answer is no.

What we are seeing is not a crash. It’s a correction in expectations.

In our ZIP code, the median days on market has gone from eight days last spring to 34 days this spring. That is a meaningful change, and sellers should take it seriously. At the same time, list prices are still up 6% year over year—even though showings per listing have dropped by about half.

Those numbers tell a very clear story: sellers are still asking more, while buyers are showing up less often. That gap is why inventory is lingering.

The problem is not that there are no buyers. There are buyers. Well-priced homes are still selling, often in under two weeks. The difference is that today’s buyers are more selective, more payment-conscious, and far less willing to chase a home that feels overpriced from the moment it hits the market.

I am seeing this firsthand. I currently have three sellers whose homes have been on the market for more than 60 days, and none of them wants to reduce the price. In each case, the resistance is understandable. They remember last spring, when homes could receive multiple offers almost immediately. They have neighbors who sold at peak enthusiasm. They see headlines about prices still being higher than last year.

But last year’s strategy does not automatically work in this year’s market.

A home can be worth more than it was a year ago and still be priced too high for today’s buyer. Those are not contradictory statements. Sellers need to stop treating last year’s sale prices as a guarantee and start treating current buyer behavior as the real market signal.

The first two weeks matter more than ever. That is when a listing gets the most attention, the most online traffic, and the strongest pool of active buyers. If a home enters the market at an aspirational price and receives limited showings, no offers, or repeated feedback about price, waiting rarely fixes the problem. It just gives buyers more reason to wonder what is wrong with it.

A listing that has been sitting for 60 days does not become more attractive because the seller holds firm. It becomes stale. And stale listings often sell for less than they would have if they had been positioned correctly from day one.

This is the market we have now: not a bargain-basement market, not a panic market, and not the frantic market of a year ago. It is a market that rewards accuracy.

Sellers who price based on what they hope to get may wait. Sellers who price based on what buyers are willing to pay are still moving. The homes selling quickly are not necessarily the cheapest homes. They are the homes that make sense for their location, condition, competition, and monthly payment.

The good news for sellers is that prices have not collapsed. Demand has not disappeared. A properly priced, well-presented home can still command serious attention. But the era of testing the market with an inflated price and expecting buyers to negotiate upward is over—for now.

The market is sending sellers a message. The smart ones are listening.

b.text:
## The Market Isn’t Crashing. Sellers Are Simply Behind It.

Last spring, the median home in my ZIP code spent just eight days on the market. This spring, that figure has climbed to 34 days. Showings per listing have fallen by roughly half.

Those numbers sound dramatic—and they are. But they do not mean our local housing market is crashing.

They mean the pace has changed, and too many sellers are still pricing their homes for last year’s market.

List prices remain about 6% higher than they were a year ago. That tells me seller expectations have continued rising even as buyer activity has cooled. Buyers today have more time, more choices and less willingness to overlook an inflated price. They are not disappearing; they are becoming selective.

I see this disconnect firsthand. I currently have three sellers whose homes have been on the market for more than 60 days, and all three are resisting a price adjustment. They remember hearing about multiple offers, bidding wars and homes selling over asking price in a weekend. Understandably, they want that outcome for themselves.

But the market does not care what a seller wants, what a neighbor received last year or how much money an owner put into the kitchen. Buyers compare a home with what is available today. If the value is not there, they move on.

The clearest evidence is what happens to homes that are priced correctly: They are still selling, often in less than two weeks.

That is not a crash. A crashing market does not consistently reward well-priced, well-prepared homes with quick sales. What we have is a market that has shifted from automatic urgency to price sensitivity.

For several years, sellers could start high and assume the market would catch up. That strategy is now risky. The first two weeks of a listing are when buyer attention is strongest. If a home enters the market overpriced, serious buyers may skip it, while everyone else watches and waits for a reduction. By the time the seller finally adjusts, the listing has accumulated days on market and buyers begin wondering what is wrong with it.

Often, nothing is wrong with the house. The original price was wrong.

Sellers also need to stop treating a price reduction as a defeat. If a home has been listed for 30, 45 or 60 days with limited showings and no serious offers, the market has already delivered its verdict. Refusing to respond does not protect the home’s value. It simply extends the listing and may ultimately result in a lower sale price than a realistic starting price would have produced.

My advice to sellers right now is direct: Price for the market you are entering, not the market you remember.

Look closely at recent sales, but pay equal attention to the active listings competing for the same buyers. Prepare the home properly. Address obvious condition issues. Make access for showings easy. Most importantly, take the first two weeks seriously.

Buyers should not mistake longer market times for a collapse, either. The best homes are still moving quickly, and waiting for a dramatic drop in prices could mean missing the right property. What buyers have gained is not unlimited leverage but breathing room—the opportunity to compare homes, inspect carefully and negotiate without the frenzy of last spring.

Our local market has slowed. It has not fallen apart.

The sellers succeeding this spring are the ones who understand that distinction. They are not chasing last year’s peak or testing an aspirational price. They are meeting today’s buyers where they are—and they are still getting sold.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
The fluorescent lights buzzed overhead as I tied my apron strings tight, the same way I had every Saturday since sophomore year. The restaurant smelled like garlic and fish sauce, a scent that clung to my clothes long after I left. Dad always said, "You want college? You help pay for it." So I did.

That Saturday, the register system crashed. No warning, just a blank screen and a line of customers stretching to the door. Mom cursed in Vietnamese, Dad rubbed his temples, and I grabbed a stack of order pads. "I'll write them by hand," I said. For six hours, I scribbled down orders—pho ga, bun bo Hue, com tam—calling them back to the kitchen in my broken Vietnamese. My hand cramped, but the line moved. By closing, the pads were smeared with grease and soy sauce, but we’d made it through.

In the back, near the walk-in cooler, I taught Minh, a new hire, how to fold spring rolls like my grandma taught me. "Not too much filling," I said, pressing the edge of the rice paper with my thumb. "And roll tight, or it’ll fall apart in the fryer." He fumbled at first, but by the end of the shift, his rolls looked almost as good as mine. Almost.

During my breaks, I sat on a milk crate in the cooler, my calc textbook propped against a stack of tofu. The cold seeped through my jeans as I worked through derivatives, the hum of the compressor drowning out the noise from the dining room. Sometimes, I’d lose track of time and Mom would bang on the door. "You’re not paid to do homework in there!"

By midnight, the dishes were done, the floors mopped, and the chairs stacked on tables. I counted my tips—$87 that night—and tucked the bills into my backpack. Outside, the parking lot was empty except for Dad’s old Honda. He was already asleep in the driver’s seat, waiting to take me home. I slid into the passenger side, my muscles aching, and closed my eyes as the car pulled away.

b.text:
The register died at 11:40 on a Saturday in October, twenty minutes into lunch rush. The screen froze on order #34, two bowls of pho, and my dad smacked the side of it twice, which is his fix for everything. Nothing. He called the company from the kitchen and the company said Monday. The dining room had six tables eating and two more walking in the door.

He tore a to-go pad off the stack under the counter and handed it to me. "You write."

So I wrote. Table numbers, dishes, prices off the menu I've had memorized since I could see over the host stand. I did the tax in the margin — 8.25 percent, I've done that math enough times that I trust it — and kept a running total on the back page. My dad unlocked the cash drawer with the little emergency key he keeps in his shirt pocket. I counted change back to people the old way, ones on top of the fives. At four o'clock I added everything up against the cash in the drawer. We were off by $2.25. I found it in twenty minutes: I'd written a 3 that looked like an 8 on table twelve. After that I did every ticket twice. The register came back Monday, and there's a stack of order pads in my locker at school in case it ever dies again.

I've worked at my family's Vietnamese restaurant every weekend since sophomore year. Friday nights, Saturdays, Sundays. I host, run food, work the takeout counter, and fill in on whatever station is short, which is usually all of them. The restaurant is in a strip mall between a nail salon and a phone store. It seats forty-two. I know that number because I've pushed the tables into party arrangements more times than I can count.

Last month we hired a new kid, Marcus, seventeen, first job. My dad handed him to me for the spring rolls, because spring rolls are mine. My grandma taught me the fold at this same counter when I was ten, by saying "Again" every time one came out wrong. You dip the rice paper for two seconds — longer and it goes soft and sticky. Filling goes in the bottom third, not the middle. Fold the bottom edge up over it, fold the sides in, roll forward, seam down. Grandma's test was to hold it by one end and shake it. If anything moved, again. Marcus's first five fell apart in his hands. His ninth held. He looked up at me like he'd passed something, which I guess he had. Last Saturday he rolled sixty for a birthday party and nobody at the party could tell whose were whose.

Breaks are thirty minutes when it's slow and ten when it's not. There is exactly one quiet room in the building: the walk-in cooler. I keep a plastic stool in there between the bean sprouts and the crates of Thai chiles, and I do my calculus homework sitting on it, jacket zipped, breath showing. Last year the chapter on related rates and the lunch rush happened at the same time, so I worked the ladder-against-the-wall problem in eleven-minute pieces, with the door sliding open — "Two more spring rolls, table five" — between part b and part c. My notebook has a soy sauce stain in the shape of Michigan. I have not tried to get it out.

People ask what it's like, working weekends, and I never know what to say, because it's not like anything. It's just what my Saturdays are. I know the 12:30 church crowd orders number five by habit. I know the front door sticks when it's humid. I know which regulars pay in exact change and which ones tip in fives because fives are what the ATM gives. When my friends post pictures from the lake I'm usually in the same apron, and honestly, some Saturdays I wish I were at the lake. Then a party of ten walks in and I don't think about the lake again until we close.

Next Saturday I'll be there at ten to open. If the register works, fine. If it dies, the order pads are in my locker and I already know the tax.

Best,

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**Let Our Kids Sleep. The Numbers Say We Should.**

Every school morning at 6:20, I stand in my daughter's doorway and say her name three times before she moves. She is thirteen. She is not lazy. She is doing exactly what her body is built to do at that age, which is sleep.

That's why I'm asking the school board to approve the 8:45 start time when it votes next month.

I'm not a doctor, but the doctors have been clear on this. The American Academy of Pediatrics says middle and high schools should start no earlier than 8:30, because teenagers' internal clocks genuinely shift later during puberty. They physically cannot fall asleep at 9:30 the way a second-grader can. Ask them to be at their desks by 7:40 and you are guaranteeing they show up short on sleep. The AAP ties that chronic shortfall to worse grades, more depression, more car accidents among teen drivers, and more sick days. That's not a parenting opinion. That's the pediatricians.

We don't have to take it on faith, either. Lincoln Middle ran this as a pilot, and the results are in the proposal for anyone to read. Attendance went up. First-period grades went up. The kids who used to sleep through pre-algebra started actually doing pre-algebra. When a change works in our own district, with our own kids and our own teachers, I don't know what more evidence we're waiting for.

I know the objection. I've heard it at soccer practice and in the pickup line: "It'll wreck the buses." I had the same worry, so I read the transportation section twice. The proposal doesn't add buses. It re-tiers the routes, so elementary runs first and middle school runs second, instead of the other way around. Same fleet, same drivers, same number of trips. It's a schedule change, not a budget request. If someone has read that section and found a hole in it, I'd like to hear it, but "the buses" isn't an argument on its own anymore.

Will it be an adjustment? Sure. Some families will need to rethink before-school care. Practices may shift. I'm willing to do that, because the alternative is what we're doing now, which is asking twelve- and thirteen-year-olds to fight biology every single morning and then wondering why they're irritable, distracted, and falling behind.

We tell our kids that when the evidence changes, you change your mind. Here's a chance for the grownups to model it.

Vote yes on 8:45.

b.text:
**Let Our Middle-Schoolers Sleep**

I have two kids at Millbrook Middle, and every school morning starts the same way. My seventh-grader's alarm goes off at 6:20. By 6:40 he's eating cereal with his eyes half shut, trying to remember whether he has his gym clothes. The bus comes at 7:05. First period starts at 7:50.

He's thirteen. His body doesn't work that way, and neither does any other thirteen-year-old's.

That's not a parenting complaint — it's biology. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m., because at puberty kids' internal clocks shift later by as much as two hours. They physically can't fall asleep at 9 p.m. the way they did in fifth grade, and they still need eight to ten hours. We can keep telling them to go to bed earlier. Their bodies stopped listening.

That's why I'm supporting the 8:45 start time the board is voting on next month.

And it's why I paid attention to the Lincoln Middle pilot. Attendance went up. First-period grades went up. Not by a miracle — by kids showing up awake and staying that way. Teachers said the same thing at the forum: fewer heads on desks, more hands in the air. That's what a schedule change buys you. Not a new curriculum, not a new program. Just students who are actually there.

Now, the bus question. I've heard it at every meeting: "You can't just move the start time, the buses can't do it." It's a fair worry. But the proposal already answers it. It re-tiers the routes — elementary first, then middle and high — so the same buses and the same drivers cover the same students. No new buses, no extra runs, no line in the budget. The district's transportation director walked the board through the tiers at the last meeting and said the plan works. That's exactly what re-tiering is for, and it was built into this proposal from the start.

I'm not asking for anything exotic for my kids. I'm asking that they be awake for first period. Lincoln already showed us what that looks like. I hope the board says yes.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
**Coming Home**

The airport was the same one I'd left from, which threw me. Same carpet, same smell of popcorn and floor wax. I came down the escalator with a duffel over one shoulder and saw my wife before she saw me. Our daughter was holding her hand.

She was six. She'd been five when I left, and in my head she was still five, so the first thing that happened was that I was wrong about her.

She got behind her mother's leg and stayed there. I squatted down on the carpet in my uniform with the duffel beside me and said her name. She looked up at her mom to check. Her mom nodded. She came out about half a step and stopped. I didn't reach for her. I don't know why. It took a minute, and then she let me pick her up and she was heavier than I remembered, which sounds like a stupid thing to say, kids grow, but that's the thing I remember. Like I'd been carrying a weight in my head for a year and it was the wrong weight.

Two weeks later my wife gave me the grocery list and sent me out. Her list said cereal. That was my whole job.

I stood in the cereal aisle for twenty minutes. I know because I checked my watch, and I checked my watch like I was timing something. There were forty kinds. Maybe more. I picked up the Cheerios we used to buy and put them back because it had been a year and I didn't know what she ate now. I picked up something with a cartoon on it and put that back too, because she might have outgrown it and I didn't want to be the guy who came home with the wrong box. I read the backs of boxes. I did the math on sugar per serving for no reason.

A woman came around me, reached past my shoulder, took a box without looking at it, and kept walking. Never slowed down. I stood there and watched her go and felt something I couldn't name, and then I took the Cheerios and went to the register.

Sleep was the other thing.

For a year I slept where the door mattered. You slept facing the door. If you rolled over in the night you rolled back. I never thought of it as anything. It was just how you slept, the way you put your boots a certain way.

At home, the bedroom door was shut. My wife likes it shut. Dark. First week I'd come awake at 0300 with my eyes already open and pointed at the door, and it was closed, and there was hallway light in a line under it. I'd lie there and listen to the house. The fridge. My daughter breathing down the hall.

After a few nights I got up and opened it. Just a foot. Then I went back to bed. My wife asked me about it the next morning. I said the room felt small. That was true enough and it was the whole answer.

It took a couple of months. Somewhere in there I quit waking up at 0300, and somewhere after that I quit getting up to check. The door's still open at night. I don't think about it much.

b.text:
My daughter was six when I came home from my second deployment. At the airport, she stood behind her mother’s leg and held on to her jeans. I could see one eye and part of her forehead.

I had pictured her running to me. I hadn’t told anybody that, but I had pictured it plenty.

I set my bag down and crouched. My knees popped.

“Hey, kiddo.”

She pulled her face back out of sight. Her mother reached down and rubbed her shoulder.

“It’s Dad.”

“I know,” she said, but she stayed where she was.

I didn’t know whether to keep talking or give her a minute. There were people coming around us with rolling bags. I moved my bag closer so nobody would trip over it.

Finally she looked at me again.

“Your hair’s different.”

“Yeah. Pretty short.”

She came out from behind her mother, but not all the way over. I stayed down there until my legs started to hurt. Then she let me put my arms around her. She kept hers at her sides for a second before she put them around my neck.

On the way to the car, her mother carried a bag and I carried the rest. Our daughter walked between us, holding her mother’s hand. She told me where they had parked.

A few days later, I went to buy groceries. I wanted to do something useful without having to ask how to do it. My wife had made a list. Milk, bread, eggs, cereal. A few other things.

I got as far as the cereal.

There must have been forty kinds. More, if you counted the different sizes. I stood there with one hand on the cart and read the boxes. I picked one up, checked the price, and put it back. Then I picked up another.

I wasn’t looking for anything special. That was the trouble. Any of it would have been fine, but I couldn’t get from looking at a box to putting it in the cart.

A woman said, “Excuse me,” and I moved so she could reach past me. She took a box without stopping to think about it. I watched her go around the end of the aisle.

I checked my phone. I’d been standing there close to twenty minutes.

I was a staff sergeant. I had spent the last year making decisions people needed me to make. Now I was blocking a grocery aisle because I couldn’t pick breakfast.

I called my wife.

“What kind of cereal?”

“Whatever you want.”

I didn’t say anything.

“The yellow box,” she said. “She’s been eating that one.”

There were two yellow boxes. I bought both.

When I got home, my daughter helped unpack. She took one of them out of the bag.

“I don’t like this kind anymore.”

“Okay.”

She took out the other one.

“This one’s good.”

I put it on top of the refrigerator and went back out for the milk I’d left in the car.

At night, I wanted the bedroom door shut.

My wife had been leaving it open so she could hear our daughter. If I closed it, she would get up and open it again. Neither of us said much about it at first. I’d close it on my way back from the bathroom. Later, when I woke up, it would be open.

For a year I had slept facing the door. I still did. I could be worn out and ready to fall asleep sitting up, but once I lay down, I needed to turn that way. If my wife spoke from behind me, I answered without rolling over.

One night she asked, “Does it have to be closed?”

“I sleep better.”

“I need to hear her.”

I knew that. Our daughter’s room was down the hall. Sometimes she called for water or had a bad dream. Her mother had been the one getting up.

We left the door halfway open that night. I lay there looking at the strip of hallway. The house made noises I didn’t remember. The refrigerator shut off. A pipe knocked after somebody used the bathroom. I got up once and checked the front lock, although I had checked it before bed.

In the morning my wife asked if I’d slept.

“Some.”

That was true. I had.

We kept leaving the door open. Some nights I got up and pushed it partway shut. Some nights I stayed in bed. I didn’t make a plan for it or keep track.

My daughter started coming to my side of the bed when she woke up. The first time, she stood there so quietly that I didn’t hear her until she touched my arm. I jerked awake and scared her.

“What?”

She stepped back.

I lowered my voice. “What do you need?”

“Water.”

I took her to the kitchen. She wanted a particular cup, and I opened two wrong cabinets before she pointed to the right one.

After that, I told her to say my name from the doorway.

One night I heard, “Dad.”

The bedroom door was open. She was standing in the hall in her pajamas, holding her cup with both hands.

“Water?”

She nodded.

I pushed the blanket off and sat on the edge of the bed. She waited while I found my slippers.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
On the Maple Ave kitchen remodel, we pulled back the drywall and found a 4-inch notch cut into a main load-bearing joist by a previous owner.

We couldn’t ignore it. Had to sister the joist with LVL and add a steel plate. That added $1,200 to the budget and two days to the timeline.

Lesson: Never assume framing is sound until you expose it. Structural surprises are the norm, not the exception, in older Pittsburgh homes.

Always allocate a contingency fund for hidden structural work. It’s cheaper than the alternative.

b.text:
1/4
We just opened up the ceiling on our Maple Ave kitchen remodel (1910 Pittsburgh home). 

What we found: a previous "pro" had notched out 90% of a main load-bearing floor joist to run a 3-inch plumbing drain. It was literally hanging by a 1-inch splinter of old-growth pine.

2/4
To fix it safely:
- Had an engineer spec the repair.
- Slowly jacked the sag out of the joist to avoid cracking the bathroom tile directly upstairs.
- Sistered it with an LVL and rerouted the drain line.

Total cost: $3,200 and 3 days added to the schedule.

3/4
The lesson for homeowners:
This is why a 10-15% contingency fund isn't optional on old homes. If we hadn’t opened this ceiling, that floor would have eventually failed under the weight of the new kitchen island. Always budget for what you can’t see.

4/4
The lesson for contractors & architects:
Never write a contract that guarantees a flat price for structural work before drywall comes down. Build an "exploratory demolition" clause into your contracts. It protects your margins and sets honest expectations from day one.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
After sitting in on close to 200 interviews the last couple years, I've started listening for one question.

"What's the last project here that failed?"

Had a candidate for an Ops Supervisor role ask it just like that last month. No softening it.

I told him about our attempt to move one building to staggered start times last fall. Looked clean on the whiteboard. Fell apart in under two weeks because we didn't account for inbound detention from two of our biggest customers. Carriers started missing windows, OT blew up, leads were running freight themselves.

He didn't move on. He just said, "So who finally called it? And what did you keep from it?"

We spent the next ten minutes talking about that mess. I learned more about how he thinks, how he talks to drivers, and how he pushes back on a plan in those ten minutes than I do from any "tell me about a time" question I ask.

If you're interviewing right now, steal that question.

And hiring managers, what do you say when someone asks you that honestly?

b.text:
I’ve sat in on roughly 200 interviews in logistics recruiting. The candidates I remember aren’t the ones with the smoothest answers. They’re the ones who ask the sharpest questions.

One question keeps showing up from the best ones:

“What’s the last project here that failed?”

I had a candidate ask it last month for an ops manager role. We’d done the normal back-and-forth. Then she asked it.

I told her about the carrier portal we tried to launch. We wanted to replace three legacy systems with one portal. We built it, trained the team, announced it. Then adoption flatlined. Small carriers kept emailing PDFs because the portal couldn’t handle their exception cases. We ended up running both systems for six months longer than planned.

She didn’t nod and move on. She leaned in.

“So the exception cases were the issue. Did you find that out before or after launch?”

After.

“Who caught it first? Your ops team or the carriers?”

The carriers. Our ops team was too close to the build.

“Did the next version start with the exception cases instead of the happy path?”

Yes. That was the fix.

Then she said, “I’ve been on the other side of that. We rolled out a new TMS and forgot the drivers who still used paper manifests. I spent three months doing workarounds. I’d rather know now that you’ll talk about it.”

That’s the thing. She wasn’t digging for dirt. She was checking if we could be honest about a failure, if we actually learned from it, and if the next person who joins will be set up to succeed.

People who only ask about wins are reading the brochure. People who ask about failures are deciding whether to actually work here.

If you’re interviewing, ask the uncomfortable question. If you’re hiring, have an answer ready. Not the polished one. The real one.

What’s the last failed project you’ve talked about in an interview? Or the last one you’ve asked about?

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
**Why I'd Shoot Your Wedding in November (And Used to Try to Talk You Out of It)**

For my first few years doing this, I treated winter as the off-season. Not a slow season—the *off* season. When a couple asked about a January date I'd say yes, but I'd also mention that the days were short and the trees were bare and had they considered May? I thought I was being helpful.

I've shot eleven winter weddings in the last two years, and I've stopped saying any of that. Here's what changed my mind.

**The light is actually better.**

This is the one I didn't expect. My assumption was that winter light would be weak and gray, and June light would be full and golden. What I actually get in June, most of the time, is flat overcast. It's fine. It's flattering in a bland way. Nobody squints. But it also has no direction, so faces don't get shape and backgrounds go a little muddy.

In November, around 3pm, the sun is already low, and it's coming through trees with no leaves on them. That's the part that matters. Bare branches break the light up into something that has edges and texture without being harsh, because the sun isn't high enough to be harsh. It's the kind of light I spend all summer hunting for at 7:30pm, except it's happening at 3 in the afternoon, which is when you're actually available for portraits. I'm not asking you to leave your reception for twenty minutes to catch it. It's just there.

I have portraits from a December wedding two years ago that I still use as the example when I'm explaining to summer couples what I'm hoping for at golden hour. They were shot at a public park with a chain-link fence out of frame. It was 41 degrees.

**I'm not sharing the venue with four other vendors.**

Every June Saturday, I pull into the venue parking lot and there's already a florist unloading, a DJ running cable, a second photographer for the wedding in the other hall, and a catering truck with the door open. The coordinator is doing her best but she's running two events. I'm negotiating for ten minutes in the good room before the other party's cocktail hour starts.

In February, I pull in and it's me and the caterer. The coordinator knows your name and mine. If I want to shoot in the lobby with the big windows, the lobby is empty. If we're running twenty minutes behind, nobody's waiting on the space behind us. That kind of slack sounds small, but it's the difference between me getting the shot I planned and me getting the shot that was available.

**It costs you about 30% less.**

I'm listing this last because it's the reason everyone already knows about, and I don't want it to sound like the only reason. But it's real. Venues, and most vendors including me, price winter dates lower because demand is lower. That's the whole mechanism. Same room, same florist, same photographer, roughly a third off, because it's not June.

You can spend the difference on more coverage, a second shooter, an album—or nothing. Nothing is a fine choice too.

**What I'm not going to pretend.**

It gets dark early. If your ceremony is at 4:30, we're doing portraits before, not after, and I'll be firm about that. Outdoor time is shorter and colder, and I'll ask you to trust me for fifteen minutes in a coat you'll take off for the picture. And if you have your heart set on peonies or a garden ceremony, I'm not going to tell you a snowy sidewalk is the same thing. It isn't.

But if you're flexible on the month, and you're weighing a November or February date against something in high season, I'd stop thinking of winter as the compromise. From where I stand—behind the camera, in the parking lot, at 3pm—it's not the compromise. It's frequently the better day.

If you want to see the winter work specifically, [it's here](#). If you have a date in mind, [reach out](#) and I'll tell you honestly what the light's going to be doing.

b.text:
**Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now**

I’ve been shooting weddings around here for six years, and if you had told me at the beginning that I’d grow to genuinely love winter weddings, I probably would have laughed. I used to think the season was a compromise: too dark, too cold, too many things that could go wrong.

Then I shot 11 winter weddings in the last two years. That changed my mind.

Not because I suddenly became sentimental about cold feet and bare trees. I’m still not going to pretend every winter wedding is some cozy, fairytale event. Some couples hate the cold, some families can’t travel in icy weather, and not every venue works for a season where the sun disappears before your guests are comfortable.

But for the right couple, winter is not just a sensible backup plan. It can actually make the day better.

One obvious reason couples consider it is money. Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for the couple than peak-season dates. That number matters if you are trying to protect budget for a venue, flowers, a photographer you love, or an actual wedding night instead of a mortgage payment.

But the pricing is not the only reason I like shooting them now.

The light is part of it.

In June, I often get that flat, overcast afternoon light that is technically “usable” but honestly kind of boring for portraits. It’s soft, sure, but it doesn’t do much. It doesn’t create shape, depth, or drama. Sometimes it makes every portrait look like it was shot on the same gray Monday.

Winter light is different.

Around 3 p.m. in November, when the sun is already low, it cuts through the bare branches in a way that feels specific to that season. It gives portraits something summer portraits often lack: contrast, warmth against cool shadow, and a real sense of place. You can stand in front of a leafless tree and suddenly the photograph has edges, texture, and mood. I’ve learned to chase that light instead of avoiding it.

Another reason winter feels better: logistics.

In June, I often show up to a venue and share the parking lot with three or four other vendors doing the same thing. That’s fine in theory, but in practice it means everyone is loading in at once, everyone is fighting for the same small space, and the whole day starts a little compressed.

Winter weddings usually breathe more. There are fewer other events on site. I have room to unload. I can walk the space. I can plan my shots without constantly stepping over someone else’s gear. For couples, that can make the day feel calmer. For me, it means I can be more present instead of spending the morning managing chaos.

That doesn’t mean winter weddings are easier. They are not.

You still need a plan for cold hands. You need a timeline that does not pretend sunset is at 8:30 p.m. You need to account for guests who may need coats, blankets, or a bar area that doesn’t turn them into ice sculptures during cocktail hour. If you are the couple who wants a bare-shoulder gown in a garden at golden hour, a winter date might fight you.

But if you are open to a day that feels a little quieter, a little sharper, and a little less crowded, winter can be a very smart choice.

I think a lot of couples make the mistake of assuming winter weddings should feel like a toned-down version of summer. They don’t. The best winter weddings are not pretending to be something they are not. They use the season. They lean into the early darkness, the bare landscape, the heavier fabrics, the candles, the low light, the intimacy of staying inside longer.

And for me as the photographer, those conditions often produce stronger images than the generic “pretty outdoor wedding” summer can deliver. There is more range. More texture. More reason for a photo to feel like it happened in that exact moment.

So if you’re deciding when to book, don’t just ask, “Can we have a wedding in winter?”

Ask if a winter wedding actually fits the day you want.

Do you care more about a specific date, a budget, a venue, or the type of light you like in photos? Are you excited about the atmosphere of a cold-weather celebration? Can you live with shorter daylight and maybe jackets over outfits during portraits? If the answer is yes, winter is not just the “cheaper” option. For a lot of couples, it is simply the better option.

I shot enough of them recently to know that for sure.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
I have worked every weekend at my family's Vietnamese restaurant since sophomore year. Saturdays start early and run late.

One Saturday the register system died right in the middle of lunch. Screens went black. People kept walking in. I grabbed the old paper pads we keep in the drawer and wrote every ticket by hand. Table 4, two orders of pho with rare steak, one no onions, spring rolls, extra chili. I tore them off and stuck them on the wheel. The cooks asked me to rewrite a couple that got smudged. My hand cramped by dinner, but we filled every order that way.

I show new hires how to fold the spring rolls the way my grandma does it. Rice paper flat, filling in a thin line, bottom edge up first, sides tucked in tight so no air pockets form, then roll it closed and wet the last edge to seal. Loose ones fall apart in the fryer. The last kid I trained kept leaving them soft. I made a few next to him, slow, then watched him try until his looked right.

Breaks are short. Calculus needs quiet, so I take my book into the walk-in cooler. I sit on a milk crate in my jacket and work the problems while the compressor hums. Cold air keeps the numbers clear. When time is up I put the book back in my bag and step out to the floor again.

b.text:
The register went black around two on a Saturday. The dining room was full enough that the floor had become a maze of chairs and trays. My father pressed buttons that should not have been pressed. My mother looked at the line by the door and said, “Write it down.”

I took order slips. I knew which ones were for dine-in and which ones were for pickup, because I have done this since sophomore year. I started writing. Pho no beef. Bun cha, grilled pork, less carrot pickle. Spring rolls, six, no peanut sauce. Two plates of broken rice with egg.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots (Before the Ground Freezes)

Every January we get the same call. Water pouring through a ceiling, basement flooding, a wall soaked through. Almost every time, the cause is the same: a hose left connected to an outside spigot that froze and split the pipe.

This is a ten-minute job. Here's how to do it right.

## Step 1: Find and Shut Off the Interior Valve

Somewhere inside your house—basement, utility room, crawl space—there's a shutoff valve on the line feeding each outdoor spigot. Find it and turn it off.

If you have a frost-free spigot (the kind with a long stem), you still need to shut this valve off. Frost-free doesn't mean freeze-proof, especially if water is trapped in the line.

## Step 2: Disconnect the Hose

**This is the part people skip, and it's the one that costs them thousands.**

A hose left connected traps water inside the spigot. That water freezes, expands, and cracks the pipe—often inside the wall where you can't see it until it thaws and starts leaking. We see this constantly. Disconnect every hose, coil it up, and store it in the garage or basement.

Don't just leave it lying on the ground next to the spigot. That's not disconnected.

## Step 3: Drain the Spigot

Open the outside faucet all the way. Then go back to the interior shutoff valve—there should be a small brass cap on the side, called a drain cap. Unscrew it with a bucket underneath. Let whatever water is in the line drain out.

If your valve doesn't have a drain cap, just leave the outside faucet open. Air needs somewhere to go.

## Step 4: Install a Foam Faucet Cover

Go to any hardware store and pick up a foam faucet cover. They cost about three dollars. Slide it over the spigot and secure it.

Is a foam cover enough on its own? No. You still need to do the shutoff and draining. But it adds an extra layer of insulation and keeps cold air from drafting into the opening.

## What If You Don't Have an Interior Shutoff Valve?

A lot of older Minneapolis homes—especially around South Minneapolis and Northeast—don't have interior shutoffs for the outside spigots. If that's your situation, give us a call. We can install one. It's not a huge job, and it's a lot cheaper than a burst pipe in January.

## The Quick Version

1. Shut off the interior valve
2. Disconnect the hose (seriously, do this)
3. Drain the spigot
4. Put on a $3 foam cover
5. No interior shutoff? Call us

Do this before the ground freezes. Once we're into consistent freezing temps, you're rolling the dice.

Questions or need help? Call us at **(612) 555-0147**. We're a family-owned shop in Minneapolis and we've been keeping pipes from bursting for over thirty years.

b.text:
## How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots

If you’ve got outdoor spigots on your Minneapolis home, winterizing them is one of the easiest ways to avoid a burst pipe call in January.

The big mistake we see most often is leaving a hose connected. That traps water in the line, and when temperatures drop, that water freezes, expands, and can split the pipe or the spigot. Most of our January burst-pipe calls start with a hose left on outside.

Here’s how to do it right.

### 1. Shut off the interior valve
Most homes have a shutoff valve for exterior spigots inside the house, usually in the basement, utility room, or near the main water line. Turn that valve off before the first hard freeze.

If you do not have an interior shutoff for your outside spigot, call us. We can help you figure out what you’ve got and whether it needs to be updated.

### 2. Drain the spigot
After the interior valve is off, go outside and open the spigot so any water left in the line can drain out. Leave it open long enough for the water to stop running.

If there’s a drain cap or bleed point on the inside shutoff, use that too if your setup has one.

### 3. Disconnect every hose
This is the step a lot of people skip. Disconnect garden hoses, sprinklers, splitters, and hose timers from the spigot.

Even one hose left attached can hold water in the line and keep the spigot from draining properly.

### 4. Put on a foam cover
A basic foam spigot cover costs about $3 and gives you a little extra protection against wind and cold. It’s not a substitute for shutting off and draining the line, but it’s a good final step.

### Quick checklist
- Shut off the interior valve
- Open the outside spigot and drain it
- Disconnect all hoses and attachments
- Install a foam cover

That’s it. A few minutes now can save you from a frozen pipe, water damage, and an expensive repair later.

If you don’t have an interior shutoff for your outside spigots, or you’re not sure whether your setup is winterized correctly, give us a call. We’d be happy to take a look before the cold really sets in.

**What happened:**
During our routine deployment yesterday, we ran a database update that accidentally locked up a critical table in our database for much longer than expected. This made it impossible for customers to access the service. We caught it quickly, reversed the change, and service came back online.

We’re not going to be taking custom wedding cakes anymore. At least not for a while, maybe not for a long while.

There are only three of us here, and most days I’m in at 4am to get the ovens going. I sat down last week and actually added up what a wedding cake takes, and between the emails and the consults and the tasting boxes I make up for free, it’s about 14 hours before I even turn the mixer on for the real cake. I love that part, I do, sitting with you and sketching and tasting frostings, but when there are only three of us it turns into a whole second full-time job.

And honestly this year was just hard. We had three weddings cancel pretty last-minute after we’d already bought and prepped everything for them. I get it completely, plans change and life happens, but as a little shop we just ate all of that cost and we don’t have any wiggle room to do that.

The biggest thing though is I noticed I was spending so much time in the back on wedding stuff that I wasn’t paying attention to the front case. And that case — the morning buns and the croissants and the chocolate chip cookies that you come in for on a Tuesday — that’s what actually pays our rent. That’s our day to day, and I want to be good at that again.

It’s been such an honor to do what we’ve done. Thank you if you trusted us with your wedding, really.

We’ll still be here at 7am with coffee and everything in the case, and we’re still doing little birthday cakes and everyday stuff. Just not the big custom wedding ones.

Come say hi this week, okay?

b.text:
**A Change to Our Wedding Cake Orders**

Hi friends,

I've been putting off writing this one, mostly because I know some of you have been part of the wedding cakes we've made over the years, and those cakes carry a lot of good memories for me. But here it is: we've decided to stop taking custom wedding cake orders.

I want to explain why, because you all have been so good to us and you deserve more than a quiet line disappearing from the website.

When someone orders a wedding cake, the cake itself is honestly the easy part. It's everything around it that adds up. Between the consultations, the tastings, the sketches, the emails back and forth about ribbon colors and sugar flowers, each wedding order takes about fourteen hours of time that never shows up on an invoice. There are three of us here. Fourteen hours is a lot of hours when you're also the person mixing the morning croissant dough at 4am.

And this year we had three weddings cancel at the last minute. I understand that life happens, truly, and I don't hold it against anyone. But by the time a cancellation comes in, we've usually already bought the butter, the eggs, the fondant, sometimes cleared a whole day's production schedule to make room. Three times over, that's real money for a shop our size, and it stung.

The biggest reason, though, is simpler than either of those. Every hour we spent on wedding cakes was an hour we weren't spending on the everyday case. The sourdough, the morning buns, the cookies your kids press their noses against the glass to look at. That case is the heart of this place. It's what keeps the lights on, and honestly, it's what I love most. When wedding season got busy, I could feel the everyday stuff getting less of me, and that never sat right.

So we're choosing the case. We're choosing being here, rested enough to be cheerful when you come in, with the shelves full of the things you actually stop by for.

If you're planning a wedding, we can still be part of your day in smaller ways. We're happy to do sheet cakes, dessert tables, big boxes of pastries for a brunch reception, that kind of thing. Just no more tiered custom cakes with all the trimmings. And if you need a recommendation, ask me, there are some wonderful cake artists around here who do that work full-time and do it beautifully.

Thank you for understanding, and thank you, as always, for keeping this little place going. Come see us. The morning buns come out around 7.

With love (and flour on everything),

your baker

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The couples who ditch the exhaustive shot list almost always end up with the best photos.

Not because planning is bad. Planning is essential.

But on a wedding day, the moments that matter most rarely happen because they were written down in column C of a spreadsheet.

At the Barrera wedding, rain changed everything. We moved the plan, the people, and the ceremony setup under a pecan tree—and suddenly the day became less about executing a perfect timeline and more about being present in it.

That’s where the photographs lived:

The quick glances while everyone adjusted to the weather.  
The laughter when the plan changed.  
The family and friends gathering close beneath the branches.  
The feeling of “this isn’t what we expected, but it’s still ours.”

I’ll always make time for the important family combinations, meaningful heirlooms, and the people you absolutely need photographed. Give me those priorities.

But you don’t need to direct every image.

The best wedding photography comes from a couple trusting their photographer enough to notice what’s unfolding—not just what’s on the list.

b.text:
After 8 years and hundreds of weddings, I've noticed a pattern: the couples who hand me a shot list and then let go of it get better photos than the ones who stick to it minute by minute.

Case in point: the Barrera wedding.

Rain moved in about an hour before the ceremony. The outdoor setup they'd planned for months was suddenly underwater. We ended up moving everything under this massive old pecan tree on the property, no arch, no draping, no aisle runner in place, just the tree and everyone crowded in under it.

It wasn't the plan. It wasn't on any shot list. And it produced some of the best images I've shot all year.

Here's what I think is actually happening: a shot list is a security blanket. It's couples trying to control an outcome months in advance because the whole process feels overwhelming. Totally understandable. But weddings don't run on schedules, they run on weather, on emotions, on 80 people in one place at one time. The second something doesn't go as planned, a rigid list becomes a source of stress instead of a source of comfort.

The couples who do best are the ones who tell me what matters to them (grandma's ring, dad's reaction, the first look) and then let me handle the rest. That trust is what lets me actually see what's happening in front of me instead of checking boxes.

The Barrera's didn't get the wedding they planned. They got a better one. And they got photos they'll be looking at for the next 50 years.

If you're planning a wedding right now: bring me your must-haves, then let the day do what it's going to do. That's usually where the best photos are hiding.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
After nearly 200 interviews over the last nine years, I’ve noticed a pattern that separates good candidates from great ones. It isn’t the questions about salary or growth path. It’s the question about failure.

Most people want to hear about our biggest wins. The top performers want to know where we stumbled.

Here’s how that conversation usually looks.

Candidate: I read about the warehouse automation rollout last year. Can you tell me what didn’t go as planned?

Me: We underestimated the training time for the floor staff, which caused delays in Q3.

Candidate: How did you adjust the timeline afterward, and what’s the new protocol for change management?

That shift from “what went right” to “how did you recover” tells me everything about their mindset. They aren’t just looking for a job; they’re looking to solve the problems we’re already trying to fix.

If you’re on the market, don’t be afraid to ask about the rough patches. It shows you’re ready for the real work.

b.text:
Some of the best candidates I’ve met in roughly 200 interviews have asked a version of this:

“What was the last project here that didn’t work out?”

Not the biggest success. Not the five-year vision. The thing that went sideways.

In logistics, that can tell you more about a team than a polished answer about “fast-paced environments.”

Here’s how that conversation might go:

Candidate: “What was the last project that failed?”

Hiring manager: “We rolled out a new scheduling process, but had to pull it back.”

Candidate: “What did you miss?”

Hiring manager: “We didn’t get enough input from the people running the shifts.”

Candidate: “And did those people have more say in the next rollout?”

That follow-up is the part I notice.

They’re not just checking whether we make mistakes. Of course we do. They’re trying to understand whether anything changes afterward—and whether the people closest to the work get heard.

As an in-house recruiter, I want us to have an honest answer ready. Not a success story dressed up as a failure.

Candidates are making a decision too. They deserve to know what happens here when the plan doesn’t survive contact with the operation.

setup: A high-school biology teacher is writing a cover letter to a customer success hiring manager at the edtech company.

a.text:
Dear Hiring Manager,

As a high school biology teacher for the past eight years, I didn’t just teach science—I managed a revolving portfolio of over 150 daily users. For the last two years, [Company Name]'s platform has been the backbone of my classroom, and I am eager to transition from a power user to your next Customer Success Manager.

The core of teaching perfectly mirrors customer success: driving adoption, onboarding users, and managing stakeholders. Every semester, I successfully onboarded new cohorts of 30 students with wildly different tech-literacy levels to complex software workflows. When issues escalated, I regularly mediated with high-stress stakeholders—anxious, frustrated parents—de-escalating tensions and turning detractors into collaborative partners to reach a shared goal.

My experience with [Company Name] specifically goes far beyond my own classroom. Because I championed the platform, I stepped up as the campus admin for your product. I trained my fellow teachers on best practices, troubleshot tier-one tech issues before they ever reached your support desk, and drove department-wide adoption by showing reluctant educators exactly how the tool would save them time. 

I know firsthand what your users need, where they get stuck, and how to guide them to value quickly. I would love the opportunity to bring my deep product knowledge and eight years of relationship management experience to your Customer Success team to help other schools achieve those same results.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]  
[Your Phone Number]  
[Your Email]  
[Link to LinkedIn]

b.text:

For the past two years, I have used [Product Name] in my high-school biology classroom—not as a prospective customer, but as the teacher responsible for making it work for students, families, and colleagues. I have seen firsthand how the right edtech platform can reduce friction, strengthen learning, and give educators more time to focus on students. I would be excited to bring that customer perspective to a Customer Success role at [Company Name].

Over eight years in the classroom, I onboarded roughly 30 new students each semester, adapted instruction for different levels of comfort and confidence, and built trust with families navigating questions, concerns, and occasional frustration. Teaching demanded the same skills that drive strong customer success: listening carefully, identifying the real issue behind a question, communicating clearly, and helping people feel capable with a new process or tool.

As my campus’s administrator for [Product Name], I supported implementation beyond my own classroom. I managed account and user needs, troubleshot issues, answered colleague questions, and helped educators use the platform in ways that matched their goals. That experience gave me an understanding of both the daily realities of educators and the value of proactive, practical support.

I’m drawn to Customer Success because I enjoy helping people turn a product into meaningful results. I would bring empathy, organization, product familiarity, and a deep understanding of the school environment to helping [Company Name]’s customers succeed.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
Over the last two seasons, my varsity girls’ soccer team has had nine games rained out, delayed, or relocated to an opponent's field because our grass doesn't drain. 

Nine times, parents rearranged their work shifts for nothing. Nine times, visiting teams sat on idling buses waiting for a call. And nine times, I had to walk into a locker room of teenagers who did everything right—trained all summer, kept their grades up, showed up ready to compete—and tell them they couldn’t play on their own home field because three hours of rain turned the pitch into a retention pond.

Worse than the schedule disruptions is the safety hazard. Last October, one of my starting midfielders stepped into a mud-covered rut near the sideline. Her foot stuck, her body twisted, and her ACL went. Her season was over in a split second, followed by surgery and nine months of painful physical therapy. It didn’t happen because of a hard tackle or a freak collision. It happened because the district expected teenage girls to sprint at full speed on uneven, waterlogged dirt. 

Next month, the school board will vote on the upcoming facilities budget. Turf for the girls' soccer field needs to be approved. Period. 

I know what the pushback will be. Someone will clear their throat and bring up the cost. But nobody seemed to worry about the price tag back in 2019, when the board found the money to put down a brand-new turf field for the boys’ football program. 

Five years later, the boys play every single scheduled game, rain or shine, on a smooth, modern, reliable surface. Meanwhile, the girls are still out back, sharing space with the geese, waiting for the mud to dry, or being packed onto a bus on two hours' notice to forfeit our home-field advantage. 

I don't coach to make a political statement, and I certainly don't do it for the writing credits. I do it because I care about these kids, and I get a small stipend at the end of the term to make sure they are coached properly and kept safe. Right now, the district isn't holding up its end of that deal. 

The board needs to look at the budget, remember what year they put turf on the football field, and do what should have been done five years ago. Fund the turf. Let the girls play.

b.text:
**Headline: It’s time to turf the girls’ soccer field — enough mud, enough injuries, enough double standards**

Last Tuesday, I stood in ankle-deep water on the west end of West High’s girls’ varsity soccer field and texted 22 kids that their senior night game was canceled.

Full disclosure: I coach girls’ soccer and track here for the stipend, not because I fancy myself a writer. I’d rather be on the field running drills than sitting at my kitchen table typing this, but someone’s got to say what everyone who’s ever set foot on that field already knows: it’s a disaster, and it’s past time we fixed it.

In the last two seasons, we’ve had 9 games either rained out entirely or moved to other schools because the field floods. Two inches of rain, and the west end turns into a pond that takes three days to drain. It’s not just the water, either. The field is pocked with ruts, some six inches deep, left by maintenance trucks that get stuck in the mud when they try to patch the drainage that never works.

Last October, one of my juniors, Mia Carter, tore her ACL stepping in one of those ruts during a JV game. She didn’t get tackled, she didn’t trip over another kid. She just planted her foot to pass, hit a rut, and went down. Surgery, 9 months of rehab, missed her entire junior soccer season and most of track. Her family paid $8,000 out of pocket even with insurance. I asked the district if they’d help cover it. I never got a straight answer.

Let’s be clear: this isn’t just about mud and canceled games. It’s about fairness. The boys’ football field got turf back in 2019. The district paid for half, the football booster club raised the other half, and it was done in time for the season. That turf’s great — don’t get me wrong. The football team uses it for 5 home varsity games a year, plus a handful of JV and youth league scrimmages.

My soccer teams — varsity, JV, and the middle school program that uses the field in the spring — play 18+ home games a season. We practice three days a week on it, track uses it for field events when the track’s being resurfaced, and rec league teams use it all summer. That’s hundreds of kids using that field every year, and we’re still playing on grass that’s unsafe half the time.

I know what the school board’s going to say: turf is expensive. I’ve sat through enough budget meetings to hear the line about “limited capital funds” and “prioritizing core needs.” But let’s do the math, plain and simple. The district spends $12,000 a year on that soccer field: re-sodding the west end, filling ruts, renting portable pumps to drain the water after storms. That’s $12,000 every single year, money that just disappears into the mud. A new turf field costs around $1.2 million. At $12,000 a year in maintenance, that pays for itself in 10 years — before you even count the money we save on not having to rent other fields for playoffs, not having to pay for substitute teachers when our kids miss class for early dismissals to away games that should’ve been home, and not having to deal with liability claims from kids who get hurt on a field we know is unsafe.

And it’s not like we’re asking the district to foot the whole bill. The soccer booster club has raised $40,000 in the last three years — car washes, bake sales, sponsorships from every local auto shop and diner within 10 miles. We presented that to the board last year, and they told us we didn’t have enough “community buy-in.” What’s buy-in, exactly? Do we need to draw 2,000 people to a Friday night game? Our games are on Tuesdays and Thursdays, when people are at work or feeding their little kids. Our crowds are smaller, but our kids show up every day, same as the football players. They work just as hard, they compete just as hard, and they deserve the same safe, playable field.

I’m not here to give you a speech about how youth sports build character or teach teamwork or any of that stuff. You already know that. I’m here because I’m tired of watching 14-year-old girls cry because their first varsity game got canceled. I’m tired of watching a 17-year-old senior miss her last home playoff game because we had to move it 30 minutes away. I’m tired of taping up ankles before every practice and worrying that next time, it’s going to be another ACL, another broken ankle, another kid who gets hurt because we won’t spend the money to fix a problem we know exists.

The

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
Six months ago, I bought the Jarvik L2 standing desk to replace a static butcher-block setup in my home office. I work remotely as a software engineer, which means this desk gets used 45 to 50 hours a week, holding a 34-inch ultrawide, a vertical 27-inch secondary display, studio monitors, a laptop dock, and a heavy mechanical keyboard. 

I don’t use affiliate links, and I bought this with my own money. Here is the reality of living with the L2 after half a year of daily use.

### The Motor and Lifting Mechanism
The dual motors are genuinely good. They are whisper-quiet—more of a low-pitched hum than the whiny electric grind you get on sub-$400 Amazon specials—and they clear the travel range fast (roughly 1.5 inches per second under load). Transitions don't interrupt calls, and the anti-collision sensor is sensitive enough to stop before crushing an armrest without throwing false positives. From an electro-mechanical standpoint, the lifting columns perform well.

### The Annoyances: Wobble and Drift
Now for the trade-offs:

**1. High-extension wobble.** 
I’m 5'11". At my preferred standing height (around 43 inches), the desk is stable enough. But at full extension (48 inches), lateral rigidity falls apart. If you are a heavy typer—especially on tactile or clicky mechanical switches—your monitors will shake. It’s not going to dump a cup of coffee, but the micro-vibrations on mounted displays are noticeable and annoying when reading code. If you are over 6 feet tall, the structural stability at your standing height will be a compromise.

**2. Memory preset drift.** 
The handset looks sleek, but the firmware has a calibration retention problem. Over the course of three to four weeks, my standing preset drifts upward by about a centimeter. I only notice because my shoulder alignment starts feeling slightly off, and a quick check with a tape measure confirms the height readout is lying. Power cycling the controller and resetting the zero-point fixes it, but I shouldn't have to recalibrate my desk's digital brain once a month.

**3. The stock cable management tray is garbage.** 
Don’t factor the included cable tray into your buying decision. It’s stamped sheet metal that flexes under the weight of a single heavy-duty surge protector and a couple of power bricks. The mounting brackets also leave almost no clearance for bulky plugs. I threw it in the recycling bin within forty-eight hours and bolted a third-party wire basket underneath instead.

### The Verdict
The Jarvik L2 is a classic mid-tier product masquerading as high-end hardware. 

* **At its $749 MSRP:** Hard pass. At that tier, you should be looking at an Uplift V2 Commercial or a Deskhaus frame that offers real crossbar stability, better controller firmware, and usable wire management out of the box.
* **At the $549 sale price:** Buy it, with reservations. If you can snag it on sale, the smooth, quiet motor drive justifies the cost—provided you’re willing to spend an extra $40 on an aftermarket cable tray and don't mind a slight monitor wobble while typing at full extension.

b.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6 Months Later

I’ve been using the Jarvik L2 as my full-time remote-work desk for six months now. I bought it myself, no review unit, no affiliate links. This is the desk I use for coding, video calls, writing, and occasionally eating lunch over my keyboard like a degenerate.

Short version: the Jarvik L2 is a good desk with a few annoying flaws. At the $549 sale price, I’d buy it again. At $749, I’d keep shopping.

## What I Like

### The motor is quiet and fast

This is the L2’s best feature. The height adjustment is noticeably quicker than my old desk, and the motor noise is low enough that I can adjust it during a call without sounding like a blender next to the mic.

It goes up/down smoothly under normal load. I usually raise it after lunch, lower it when I’m done for the day, and it doesn’t hesitate. For a desk I move a few times a day, that matters.

### The memory presets are convenient

There are preset buttons, and in theory they’re great. I use them daily. I don’t want to hold the button and eyeball the height every time.

In practice, they mostly work — but not perfectly. More on that below.

## What I Don’t Like

### It wobbles at full height when I type hard

This is the big one.

At sitting height, the desk feels fine. At a lower standing height, it’s mostly fine. But at my full standing height, there is noticeable side-to-side and front-to-back movement if I’m typing aggressively.

I’m not talking about gently resting my hands on the desk. I mean when I’m writing code quickly, hitting keys with actual force, or moving the mouse around during a frustrating debugging session, the monitor shifts just enough to be annoying.

It doesn’t feel unsafe. It doesn’t feel like the desk is going to collapse. But it feels less stable than I want from a desk at this price.

If you are a light typist, you may not care. If you are a mechanical-keyboard person who types like they’re mad at the compiler, you will notice.

My workaround: I lowered my standing height by about an inch. It helped, but I shouldn’t have to compromise ergonomics because the frame gets nervous at full extension.

### The memory presets drift about a centimeter

The presets are close, but they’re not consistent.

I have my standing height saved, and most days the desk stops roughly where I expect. But over the past few months, I’ve noticed it drifts by about a centimeter. Sometimes it’s slightly high. Sometimes slightly low. It’s not enough to make the desk unusable, but it’s enough that I end up micro-adjusting after every preset move.

That defeats part of the point of having presets.

If Jarvik fixed this with a firmware update or better calibration, I’d upgrade my opinion. As it stands, the presets are useful but not reliable enough to fully trust.

### The cable tray is garbage

I hate the cable tray.

It feels like an afterthought. It doesn’t hold enough, it doesn’t route cables cleanly, and it makes cable management feel worse than if I’d just used velcro ties and a power strip.

For a desk marketed to people who presumably own more than one electronic device, this is a miss.

I ended up removing it and using my own cable management underneath the desktop. If you buy the L2, do yourself a favor and skip the included tray unless you enjoy disappointment.

## Build Quality

The frame itself feels solid enough. The finish is fine. The desktop is decent, though I’d still recommend getting a desk mat if you write or type hard.

The controls are simple. The handset isn’t fancy, but it works. I don’t need Bluetooth, RGB, or a smartphone app to make my desk go up and down. I need it to go to the right height and stay there. The L2 mostly does that, with caveats.

## Who Should Buy It

Buy it if:

- You can get it on sale around $549
- You want a quiet, fast motor
- You need a desk for mixed sitting/standing throughout the day
- You don’t type like you’re punishing the keyboard
- You plan to use your own cable management

Skip it or look elsewhere if:

- You’re paying $749
- You need maximum stability at full standing height
- You want memory presets that are actually precise
- You expect the included cable tray to be useful

## Verdict

The Jarvik L2 is a solid midrange standing desk with a great motor and a few irritating execution problems.

At $549, those flaws are easier to accept. You’re getting good performance for the money, especially if you catch it on sale.

At $749, the wobble and preset drift become harder to ignore. For that much, I expect better stability and more consistent height memory.

Final rating: 7/10 at $549. 5.5/10 at $749.
