setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
This spring, 40 percent of my soybean and corn acres stayed unplanted past the May 31 prevented planting deadline. I didn’t need an adjuster to tell me why—the sky simply wouldn’t quit raining. What I did need to calculate was how to absorb the financial shock. When USDA hikes the regional prevented planting base rate by 22 percent, that percentage points straight at my bottom line. Across my insured acreage, the increase adds roughly $46,000 to my out-of-pocket costs this year.

That $46,000 doesn’t land evenly. Because of the current federal acreage caps on prevented planting premiums, the penalty falls hardest on family operations like mine. The program restricts eligibility to a flat percentage of crop-insured acres, a rigid limit that ignores scale. Large neighboring operations can spread risk across thousands of acres, purchase coverage in multiple counties, or absorb the loss through diversified revenue streams. We can’t. When rain washes out the same percentage of our fields, the cap locks us out of the very coverage we paid premiums for. Instead of filling the gap, we’re forced to drain operating capital, carry more debt, or delay critical reinvestment in equipment and inputs. Meanwhile, the bigger players navigate around the limitation and emerge structurally stronger after every wet spring.

There’s a direct legislative path to correct this. Support Senate Bill 214. The bill eliminates the arbitrary acreage cap on prevented planting premiums and replaces it with a scaling structure that accounts for farm size, historical yields, and regional weather extremes. It doesn’t raise overall program costs or expand eligibility beyond actual insured acreage; it simply restores proportionality so the safety net works for the farms that form the backbone of our local economy.

If you’ve ever watched a planter sit idle while the planting window burned, you know variability isn’t a talking point here—it’s Tuesday. But we still control the policy side of this equation. Contact your state senator. Tell them we need SB 214 moved forward and voted on before the next planting season begins. The ground will decide what gets seeded again this year. Let’s make sure our coverage doesn’t shrink while we’re still picking up the pieces from last spring’s deluge.

b.text:
This spring I got 60% of my acres planted by the late May deadline. The other 40% sat underwater while the rain kept coming. That’s not a new story—what’s new is the bill.

USDA jacked the prevented planting base rate 22% in our region this year. For my operation, that means roughly $46,000 in additional premium costs for coverage I didn’t choose to need. I’ll absorb it because the alternative is worse, but I’m not writing about the weather. I’m writing about the math.

Here’s what the numbers don’t show on the rate sheet: the acreage cap. Because of how the subsidy structure is built, that 22% increase hits family operations like mine harder proportionally than the bigger spreads nearby. We carry a heavier load per acre, and when you’re only planting 60% of what you planned, every capped dollar stings worse.

There’s a fix sitting in the legislature. SB 214 would adjust the acreage cap so family farms aren’t shouldering a disproportionate share of a federal rate hike we had no hand in setting. If you’re reading this, you’re likely in the same boat—literally, this spring. Call your state senator and representative. Tell them to pass SB 214. We’ve got enough unpredictability to manage without the policy stack working against us too.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
**The Girls’ Soccer Field Needs Turf—Now**

In the last two seasons, our girls’ soccer team has had nine games either rained out or moved because our grass field floods.

Nine games.

That means nine changes for families, bus schedules, officials, opposing teams, athletic trainers, teachers, and athletes who already have enough on their plates. It means trying to find field space somewhere else, sometimes with little notice. It means senior nights moved, home games becoming away games, and players losing the chance to compete in front of their own community.

And that is before we even talk about safety.

Last October, one of my players tore her ACL after stepping in a rut on our field. An ACL injury is not a scraped knee. It is surgery, months of rehabilitation, missed seasons, missed opportunities, and a long road back for a teenager who should have been worrying about school, friends, and whether we could win the next game.

No field is perfectly safe. Soccer is a physical sport, and injuries happen. But we should not accept preventable field conditions as part of the game. We know this field floods. We know it develops uneven spots. We know games are being lost because it cannot handle normal weather. Continuing to patch, mow, seed, and hope for the best is not a real plan.

The school board is considering next year’s facilities budget. Turf for the girls’ soccer field needs to be in it.

This is also a fairness issue. The boys’ football field received turf in 2019. That investment gave football a reliable, playable surface when the weather turns bad. It gave that program a field built to withstand heavy use and provide consistency underfoot.

Our girls deserve the same basic standard.

This is not an argument against football. Football players deserve a safe, dependable field. They got one. Good. But our girls play a competitive outdoor sport on a field that routinely becomes unplayable. They deserve a safe, dependable field, too.

I coach girls’ soccer and track at a public high school. I am not writing this because I enjoy writing letters to the newspaper or because I think every problem can be solved with a new facility. I coach because I care about the students in front of me. I also know what it looks like when adults ask athletes to make do with conditions we would not accept for other programs.

We tell girls that their athletics matter. We tell them to work hard, be committed, and represent their school with pride. Then we send them onto a field that floods after rain and has ruts that can change a season in one step.

Words are cheap. Facilities budgets show what a school actually values.

A turf field would mean fewer cancellations and fewer moves. It would mean a more consistent playing surface. It would mean our athletes can prepare for games without wondering whether rain earlier in the week has made their home field unusable. It would mean parents and community members can schedule around games with more confidence. Most importantly, it would mean we are taking player safety seriously.

Yes, turf costs money. So do repeated repairs, rescheduled transportation, lost event revenue, and sending teams elsewhere because our own field cannot be used. So does an injury that may have been avoided with a more reliable surface. The question is not whether turf has a price tag. The question is whether we are willing to keep paying the cost of doing nothing.

The board has a chance to fix a problem that has been obvious for years. Put turf on the girls’ soccer field. Give these athletes the safe, reliable facility they have earned.

b.text:
**Put Our Girls On Turf Too**

The last two seasons, my team has had nine games rained out or moved. Not delayed. Rained out or moved to another school's field because ours was underwater.

I coach girls soccer and track at the high school. I'm not a writer, I do it for the coaching stipend. But I'm tired of telling 16-year-olds we don't have a place to play because it rained yesterday.

Our field is the low grass field behind the school. It doesn't drain. After any real rain it's ankle-deep mud for three days. We practice in it, we slide all over it, and we try not to get hurt in it. We sprint around the swampy spots and we tell parents to bring boots to sit on the hill.

Last October one of my sophomores tore her ACL in a game. She wasn't hit. She was dribbling, stepped in a rut in our own field where the grass had washed out, and her knee went. She missed basketball season and she's missing this whole season. I coach track, too. I know what a bad surface looks like. That field is a bad surface.

This is a safety problem and it's a fairness problem.

The boys football field got turf in 2019. It's great. It drains, it's lined, they never lose a home game to weather. Our girls have been playing on a field that floods if you look at it wrong for six more years. If this were the football field, it would have been fixed a long time ago. Actually, it was.

I get it, turf isn't cheap. The board has a lot to pay for. But we are not asking for a stadium or lights or a press box. We are asking for a flat field that works when it rains. A field where we don't have to bus to the other team's school and call it a "home" game. A field where kids aren't worrying about what hole they're going to step in.

The school board votes on the facilities budget next week. Put turf for the girls soccer field in it.

Our girls deserve the same shot the boys have had since 2019 - to actually play their home games, on their home field, without getting hurt.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now

After six years shooting weddings almost entirely in the same metro area, I didn't expect to become a winter wedding person. I did. Actively.

I've shot 11 of them in the last two years, and I now tell couples who are flexible on dates to seriously consider it. Not because "weddings are beautiful year-round" — because winter gives you specific advantages you don't get in June.

First, the practical one: my winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for the couple. Same coverage, same albums, same me running around fixing your veil. It's just off-season, so I price it that way. If budget is part of why you're debating dates, that difference is real.

Second, the light. Everyone assumes summer = better photos. It's not. Give me the light through bare trees around 3pm in November over flat overcast June light any day. In June here, we get that bright white-gray sky that washes everything out at noon and then we’re racing the harsh evening sun. In November, the leaves are gone so the light actually comes through the branches instead of getting blocked, and by 3pm it's low, warm, and directional. It sculpts faces instead of flattening them. Some of my favorite portraits from the last two years were taken in 20 minutes in a park in November while everyone stayed warm in coats between shots.

Third, the day itself is calmer. In June, I pull up to a venue and I'm sharing the parking lot with 3 or 4 other vendors — another wedding flipping out of the ceremony space, a corporate event loading in, a DJ double-parked behind the caterer. We're all negotiating for the same patch of shade at the same golden hour. In winter, it's usually just us. Your venue team isn't exhausted from their third wedding that weekend. We get the good getting-ready room, not the overflow one. We can take our time and actually use the whole space for photos without waiting for another party to clear out.

Winter weddings aren't for everyone. It gets dark early, you need a coat plan, and you have to embrace it. But if you want better light for portraits, a less hectic venue, and a date that costs you about 30% less on photography — winter is worth a look.

If you're deciding between seasons, tell me what you're picturing and I'll tell you honestly what that date would look like to shoot.

b.text:
# Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings

*Or: a confession from a photographer who spent years dreading them.*

For my first few years shooting weddings in this city, winter inquiries felt like a calendar problem. I said yes because January needed filling, not because I wanted the job. Somewhere along the way, that flipped. I've shot eleven winter weddings in the last two years, and they're now the bookings I look forward to most. Since a lot of couples asking me "when should we book?" are really asking "when is the best wedding," let me make the case for the season nobody plans for.

## The light. I'm serious about this one.

In November, around 3 p.m., the sun is already low. It comes in sideways through the bare branches, and those leafless trees break it into shafts and patterns that no lighting kit I own can replicate. There's direction to it. It gives a face shape.

Here's the part that might get me in trouble: that light is better for portraits than what we often get in June. Flat overcast June light is like a giant ceiling fixture — even, forgiving, and forgettable. Everyone is lit identically from every angle, which sounds kind and is actually the problem. Portraits need light with an angle and an opinion, and bare-tree light at 3 p.m. in November has both.

And because the sun sets early, your best-light portraits happen mid-afternoon — when your makeup is fresh and you've still got energy — instead of at 7:30 p.m., after you've been on your feet for eight hours and the schedule has already slipped twice.

## Nobody is fighting over your Saturday.

In June, I pull into a venue lot and there are regularly three or four other vendors there — another photographer's van, a videographer, a florist's delivery, all of us on overlapping timelines.

You feel that even if you never see the parking lot. It's why the getting-ready suite has a stranger's garment bag in it. It's why the coordinator is impossible to find, why the room flip starts while your grandmother is still sitting in it, why everyone is rushing. In January, the venue is yours. My timeline holds. The staff isn't stretched thin, so they're not rushing you either.

I know "the parking lot was roomy" sounds like a photographer convenience. It isn't. Calm is the thing I need most on a wedding day, and winter days have it.

## The part you already guessed: it's cheaper.

Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for couples than peak-season dates. That's not a gimmick — it's how the industry prices the slow months, and it adds up fast. That difference is your videographer, or a real chunk of your venue, or the honeymoon.

But I want to be honest about the other side of it, because I've had couples seem almost apologetic about booking a discounted date: I'm not shooting eleven of these a year out of charity. The discount exists because demand is lower. I keep saying yes anyway because these have become my favorite weddings to shoot — the calm, the light, the day that actually runs on schedule. You're not getting a lesser wedding at a lower price. You're getting the same wedding at the time of year fewer people want it.

## Yes, it's cold. Plan for it, don't fear it.

I won't pretend otherwise. We plan around it: portraits in twenty-minute bursts with a warm room to retreat to, and a timeline that puts the outdoor portraits in that good light instead of after dark. And coat shots are not a compromise — a great coat is a better portrait prop than a shawl pretending it isn't freezing. The short day is a constraint, but it's the kind that makes the timeline better, not worse.

## If you're flexible on your date

Ask me about winter. After six years shooting in this area, I know exactly which spots near you hold that low November light at 3 p.m. — and my winter calendar has room in it.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text: Six months with the Jarvik L2, and I’m bored of dancing around the same three gripes. The motor lives up to the hype—dead quiet even at top speed, no rumble or delay when I flip it from sit to stand. But the moment I drop my hands into a heavy typing session at full height, the desk decides it’s a boat in a choppy sea; it wobbles enough that I can feel the vibration through my wrists. The memory presets are a joke: they “save” positions that drift about a centimeter left or right, so “save at 38 inches” actually means 37 or 39 depending on the mood of the motor. And the cable tray? Garbage. It’s flimsy, sits too high for most keyboards, and anything heavier than a power brick slides right off. If you find it on sale for $549, it’s a decent budget play—the motor alone beats most desks at $800. At $749, though? I’d rather pay the premium for something that doesn’t feel like it’s holding together with prayer and MDF. No affiliate links, no sugarcoating: the L2 is a noisy, wobbly, preset-drifting compromise that only earns a seat in your setup if the price is right.

b.text:
# Six Months With the Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: Buy It at $549, Not $749

I’ve used the Jarvik L2 as my full-time remote software engineering desk for six months. Two 27-inch monitors on a dual arm, a full-size mechanical keyboard, a laptop dock, a mic arm, and various bricks and cables live on it. I bought it myself on sale for $549. No sponsorship, no affiliate links. If you’re researching this desk, here’s the part the spec sheet won’t tell you.

## The motor is quiet and fast

This is the best thing about the L2. It’s quick and genuinely quiet. Jarvik rates it around 1.6 inches per second; I timed my 28-inch sit-to-stand travel at about 12 seconds. No grinding, no high-pitched whine, no slowdown under roughly 70 pounds of gear. I’ve moved it during Zoom calls and nobody has ever asked what the noise was. Six months in, it sounds exactly the same as it did on day one.

## It wobbles at full height when I type hard

Now the bad part. At the top of its travel — around 47–48 inches to the desktop with my 1-inch top — the desk wobbles front-to-back when I type aggressively. I bottom out MX Browns on a steel plate, and my monitors visibly jitter. Side-to-side is acceptable; fore-aft is not. It’s not going to tip over, but if you’re a heavy typist or you insist on standing at the very top of the height range, you will feel it.

Drop the desk 2–3 inches below max and about 80% of the wobble disappears. I re-torqued the frame bolts at month two; that helped a little. It did not fix it. This is fairly normal for this price class, but don’t let anyone tell you the L2 is rock solid at full height.

## The memory presets drift about a centimeter

Four preset buttons, easy to program. Going up, they’re accurate. Coming back down, they stop about 1 cm high. Worse, my sit preset creeps roughly 1 cm upward over a week of normal use, so by Friday my elbows are a hair too high until I reset it and tap the down arrow.

I’ve recalibrated the controller twice. The drift comes back. If you’re the only user and you don’t mind nudging the height once a day, you’ll live with it. If you share the desk or want button-perfect precision every time, this will annoy you.

## The cable tray is garbage

The included cable tray is the worst part of the package. Thin metal, sharp unfinished edges, and barely deep enough for a 6-outlet power strip plus one laptop brick. Mine sagged immediately, the screws started tearing at the underside of the desktop, and it cut my hand once. I ripped it off in month one and bought a $35 aftermarket tray.

Jarvik should either delete this thing from the box or include a tray that can actually hold real-world cable management. Budget for a third-party solution, or plan to screw a power strip directly to the underside of the top.

## Build has held up otherwise

The 60x30 laminate top itself has been fine: no chips, no warping, no coating peeling after six months of daily use. Assembly took me about 40 minutes alone. The grommet holes are useless if you use a clamp-on monitor arm, but that’s true of most desks.

## Verdict

At $549, yes — buy it. That price gets you a quiet, fast, good-sized desk that is stable enough for real work as long as you don’t camp at max height.

At $749, no. For full price you can do better: better stability at standing height, tighter tolerances, and cable management that isn’t a joke. I paid $549 and I’m satisfied. If it’s $749 when you’re shopping, wait for the sale or buy something else.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
Members of the City Council:

I own a small independent coffee shop on Main Street, and I urge you to reject the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour. This is not a minor adjustment. It triples the hourly rate—a 200% increase—for people visiting downtown businesses.

For my customers, the practical impact is especially clear. Their average visit lasts 22 minutes. Under the current one-hour minimum, they already pay for more than twice the time they typically need. That minimum charge would rise from 50 cents to $1.50, adding a dollar to the parking cost of a visit that usually takes less than half an hour. The current minimum already covers their visits. Tripling its price makes a short stop more expensive without giving them anything more.

My concern is based on experience, not just speculation. In 2019, following a similar parking rate increase in the next town over, I tracked my own register activity for six weeks. That tracking showed an 18% drop in foot traffic during the period. Register-based tracking is not a controlled study, and I cannot claim that parking prices alone caused the decline. But an observed decline of 18% is a serious warning for a small business, and it deserves consideration before this council adopts a similar increase.

The city’s own report says meter revenue covers only 4% of the downtown budget. That figure does not mean parking revenue is irrelevant, but it does raise an important question: What budget problem will this increase actually solve? The council should show the expected net revenue, account for possible changes in parking demand, and explain why that benefit justifies tripling the cost to visitors.

Please keep the current rate while evaluating alternatives, including shorter billing increments for short visits. Downtown needs customers who can stop for coffee, pick up an order, or browse a neighboring shop without reconsidering the trip over parking costs.

For an independent business, those brief visits are not incidental. They are how we stay open.

b.text:
To the Members of the City Council:

I am the owner of a small independent coffee shop on Main Street and I submit this testimony in opposition to the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from fifty cents to one dollar fifty per hour.

a.text:
**RoadStar DC4 Dash Cam — 14 Months / ~140,000 Miles**

I’ve had the RoadStar DC4 in my truck for about 14 months now and put roughly 140k miles on it. For the money, it’s been worth having.

Main reason: it caught a lane-change accident that involved me, and the footage got my insurance claim approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6-week headache. That alone paid for the camera several times over.

Front camera footage is solid in daylight and decent at night. Rear camera is usable, but don’t expect miracles after dark. Anything past about 30 feet starts getting pretty grainy. It’ll show what happened close behind the truck, but it’s not going to read a plate from way back at night.

One thing to skip: the suction mount. Mine fell off twice during summer heat, which is not what you want when you’re rolling down the interstate. I switched to the adhesive mount and haven’t had an issue since.

The app is my biggest complaint. You need Wi-Fi to pull footage through it, which is pretty useless when you’re parked at most truck stops with weak or overloaded service. I quit messing with the app and just pull the SD card when I need video. Faster and less aggravating.

Bottom line: not perfect, rear night footage could be better, and the app is more trouble than it’s worth. But it’s reliable, records what matters, and already saved me a pile of time with insurance. I’d buy it again, just use the adhesive mount from day one.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
**6-Month Review: Jarvik L2 Standing Desk**

I bought the Jarvik L2 standing desk exactly six months ago. As a remote software engineer, I am stationed at this desk for 8 to 10 hours a day. I don’t do sponsored content, and there are zero affiliate links in this post. If you are researching this desk, here is exactly how it holds up to real, daily use. 

**The Good: The Motor**
The dual-motor system on the L2 is genuinely excellent. It is remarkably quiet—I routinely adjust it from sitting to standing during Zoom standups without muting my mic, and nobody hears a thing. It’s also incredibly fast. It clears the distance to my standing height in about five seconds and doesn't struggle or groan, even when lifting a dual 27-inch monitor setup, a heavy duty mount, my MacBook, and a pair of studio monitors. 

**The Annoying: Wobble and Drift**
The desk has two specific engineering flaws that you need to know about. 

First is the stability at height. When I am seated (around 29 inches), the desk is a rock. However, when I raise it to my standing height (42 inches) and type hard, the desk wobbles. I use a mechanical keyboard with heavy tactile switches, and my aggressive typing translates straight into lateral monitor jiggle. It’s not going to collapse, but if you are an aggressive coder, the screen shake will annoy you.

Second, the electronics have a bizarre quirk: the memory presets drift. Over a few months of use, my saved "standing" preset slowly creeps off target by about a centimeter. I end up having to manually dial it back in and re-save the preset every eight weeks. It feels like a lazy firmware issue that shouldn't exist on a modern desk.

**The Garbage: The Cable Tray**
Do not factor the included cable management into your buying decision. The tray Jarvik includes is absolute garbage. It’s a rigid, awkwardly designed piece of flimsy metal that doesn't hinge down for easy access. It barely has the clearance to hold a standard surge protector, let alone chunky monitor power bricks or a laptop charger. I threw it out in week two and drilled in a $25 third-party wire basket. Assume you will need to do the same.

**The Verdict: Buy the Sale, Skip the MSRP**
Jarvik lists the L2 at an MSRP of $749, but they constantly run sales dropping it to $549. 

At $749, this desk is absolutely not worth your money. If your budget is in the mid-$700s, go buy an Uplift V2. You will get better electronics, zero preset drift, and far superior lateral stability at full extension. 

At $549, however, the L2 is worth it. If you can catch it on sale, the quiet, lightning-fast motors and thick desktop make up for the flimsy cable tray and the minor firmware drift. It’s a solid workhorse for a home office, just refuse to pay full price for it.

b.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6 Months In

I've been standing at this thing roughly four hours a day since March. Here's what I actually think, now that the honeymoon is over and I've had time to get annoyed at it.

**Setup:** 60" x 30" bamboo top, dual 27" monitors on a single crossbar arm, Keychron Q1 (heavy, aluminum, I type like I'm angry at it), a laptop on a riser, and the usual desk detritus. Call it 45 lbs of load, well under the 265 lb rating.

## The motor is genuinely great

This is the thing I'd tell you first. The dual-motor lift is fast — I timed it at about 6.5 seconds to go from my 29" sitting height to my 44.5" standing height, which works out to roughly 1.5"/sec. That's not a spec-sheet number, that's me with a stopwatch and a loaded desktop.

More importantly, it's *quiet*. I measured around 44 dB from where I sit, which is quieter than my Mac Mini under load. I've raised it mid-meeting on Zoom probably fifty times now and nobody has ever asked what that noise was. My previous desk (an Autonomous SmartDesk) sounded like a garbage disposal and I'd time transitions around calls. Not an issue here.

Six months, no motor stutter, no one-leg-lags-behind desync, no reset dance required. The controller has never dropped its calibration. That's the boring stuff that actually matters and Jarvik got it right.

## The wobble is real and it's height-dependent

At sitting height, rock solid. At 38-40", fine. Above about 42" — which is where I actually stand, I'm 5'9" — it develops a front-to-back sway when I'm typing hard. Not a shimmy. A slow, low-frequency wobble, maybe 2-3mm of travel at the monitor tops, with a period long enough that you can watch your text cursor drift.

To be specific about the trigger: normal typing is fine. Aggressive typing on a 1kg mechanical keyboard is not fine. Hitting Enter hard is not fine. Leaning on the desk edge to read something is definitely not fine.

I tried the obvious fixes. Moving the crossbar arm from the rear edge to a clamp closer to center helped maybe 20%. Adding a diagonal brace kit from a third party helped more, call it 50%, but now there's a bar across my knees at sitting height and I hate it. What actually fixed it for me was dropping my standing height to 43" and switching to a lower-profile keyboard when standing. That's a workaround, not a solution, and it's fair to hold it against the desk.

This is a two-stage leg design. If you're over 6'0" and you type with force, I'd look at a three-stage frame with a thicker upper segment, or just accept it. Everyone who tells you their two-stage desk is rock solid at 46" is either short or lying.

## Memory presets drift about a centimeter

This one bugs me more than it should because it's so obviously fixable in firmware.

I have four presets. Preset 2 is my standing height. When I set it, it was 43.0". Six months later, hitting preset 2 lands me at 43.4", sometimes 42.9". It's not a slow one-way creep — it wanders. The variance is roughly ±1cm, consistently.

Why do I care about a centimeter? Because my monitor height is tuned to my eye line and a centimeter is enough that I notice my neck angle change. I've re-saved the preset three times. It drifts back.

My theory is the controller counts motor revolutions rather than reading an absolute encoder, and the coasting distance after the stop signal varies with load and direction of travel. Arriving from below lands consistently higher than arriving from above. If you're precise about this stuff, expect to nudge it manually. The controller does have single-inch-increment tap adjustment, which helps, but I paid for presets so I wouldn't have to.

## The cable tray is garbage

Not "mediocre." Garbage.

It's a shallow stamped steel channel, maybe 2.5" deep and 20" long, mounted with two screws into pre-drilled holes on the underside. Problems, in order of severity:

1. It's too small. Two monitor power bricks and a 10-outlet strip do not fit. Pick two.
2. It has no lid, no retention, nothing. Anything you put in it that isn't wedged in works its way out over a few weeks of height changes and ends up hanging.
3. The mounting holes are positioned so the tray sits directly where my knees go at sitting height. I banged my kneecap on the corner of it hard enough to swear, twice, before I gave up.

I removed it in month two and replaced it with an under-desk basket ($22, screwed into the bamboo directly) plus a handful of adhesive cable clips. Total cost of fixing Jarvik's cable management: about $30 and an hour. Budget for that.

The included cable management overall is an afterthought. The velcro straps are fine. The power cable that runs from the controller to the outlet is exactly long enough at sitting height, which means at full extension it's taut. Mine has pulled out of the wall socket once. Get an extension.

## Assembly and build

Took me 70 minutes solo. Instructions are picture-only and mostly clear, though the step where you attach the feet has the orientation ambiguous and I got it backward the first time. Hardware is bagged and labeled. All the bolts were the right length, which sounds like a low bar but I've assembled desks where it wasn't.

The bamboo top is good. Six months of a coffee mug, a water glass, and a cat who has decided the desk is hers, and there's one faint ring near the back-left corner that I caused by leaving a wet glass overnight. Edges are well finished, no splintering. The underside has proper threaded inserts, not just wood screws into particle board, which is why I felt comfortable mounting my own cable basket.

Powder coat on the frame is even. No chips. The feet have adjustable levelers that actually work, which mattered because my apartment floor slopes.

## What I'd tell you to buy instead, conditionally

If you type gently, or you're under 5'8", or you use a laptop and a low-profile keyboard: the wobble complaint doesn't apply to you and this is an easy recommendation.

If you're tall and heavy-handed: three-stage frame, or spend more.

If you need presets to land within a millimeter: not this desk.

## The verdict

I paid $549 during a sale. At $549, this is a good desk. The motor is the expensive part of a standing desk and Jarvik didn't cheap out on it — it's fast, quiet, and hasn't given me a single problem in six months of daily cycling. The top is real bamboo, properly finished, with real threaded inserts. The wobble and the preset drift are annoyances I've worked around. The cable tray is a $30 problem.

At $749, no. At that price you're within spitting distance of desks with three-stage legs and better controllers, and the two flaws that annoy me are exactly the flaws that money solves. Paying full retail for this desk means paying premium prices for mid-tier rigidity and firmware.

It goes on sale often. Wait for it.

*No affiliate links here, as always. I bought this with my own money and Jarvik doesn't know who I am.*

a.text:
Jarvik L2 After Six Months

I paid $549 for the Jarvik L2 last winter and have used it every workday since. Dual 27-inch monitors, mechanical keyboard, the usual remote-engineer setup. I switch heights 8–12 times a day.

The motor is the best part of this desk. It is quiet enough that I raise it during standup calls and nobody comments. Full travel from 28" to 46" takes about 14 seconds. No grinding, no hesitation. Dual motors, advertised 220 lb capacity; my setup is well under that and it never strains.

It is worse with both screens mounted on a dual-arm. I can live with it, but I notice it every time I hammer out a block of code. If you type lightly or keep the desk lower, you may not care. I type like I mean it.

The four memory presets work until they don’t. They drift roughly a centimeter over a few weeks. I end up tapping the up/down buttons to correct. Recalibrating is simple but I shouldn’t have to do it. For someone who switches all day, this is a real annoyance.

The included cable tray is junk. Thin plastic, two flimsy clips, sags under a laptop brick and a USB hub. I ripped it off in week two and replaced it with a $22 metal tray from Amazon. The grommets are fine. The tray is not.

Desktop is a 1.2" laminate. No warping, no peeling after six months. Edges are decent. Assembly took 45 minutes with one other person; the instructions were adequate. Crossbar is solid. The wobble is in the legs/columns at extension, not the frame joints.

b.text:
**Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6-Month Review**

I bought the Jarvik L2 six months ago as a remote software engineer who codes 8–10 hours a day and switches between sitting and standing. Paid $549 on sale. Full price is $749. Here’s the unfiltered report after daily use.

**The motor is excellent.**  
It is quiet and fast. Full travel (sitting to standing) takes about 12–13 seconds. At desk height I barely notice the hum. No grinding, no strain sounds even after hundreds of cycles. This is the best part of the desk. If you raise and lower multiple times a day, the motor alone justifies looking at this frame.

**Stability falls apart at full height.**  
At max standing height the desk wobbles when I type hard. Not a gentle sway—actual side-to-side movement that I feel in my wrists and that makes my monitors shake. Soft typing or mouse work is fine. Aggressive keystrokes (debugging, rapid navigation) make it annoying. I keep it 2–3 cm below max now and the wobble drops to acceptable. Crossbar is decent but not rigid enough for a heavy dual-monitor + laptop setup at full extension. If you’re tall and need max height, this will bother you.

**Memory presets drift.**  
The four presets work, but after a few weeks they start landing about 1 cm off. I recalibrate every month or so. Not catastrophic, but for a desk in this price range I expect the positions to hold. The control panel itself is responsive and the display is clear.

**Cable tray is garbage.**  
Thin stamped metal, poorly finished edges, and the mounting screws strip easily. It sags under a modest power strip + a few cables. I replaced it with a third-party tray after two months. Budget for that if cable management matters to you.

**Everything else**  
Desktop is solid laminate, no warping. Legs feel sturdy when locked. Assembly took me 45 minutes alone. No weird smells after the first week. Frame has held up to daily height changes without developing new noises.

**Verdict**  
At the $549 sale price I paid, yes—buy it. The motor is that good and the core frame is usable if you don’t max the height. At $749 full price, no. You’re paying for a motor that belongs on a better desk and then getting mediocre stability, drifting presets, and a throwaway cable tray. Shop the sales or look at competitors in the same range that don’t force the stability compromise.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots (And Avoid a January Burst Pipe)

Every January, our phone blows up with emergency calls for burst pipes inside basement walls. Nine times out of ten, the culprit is an outdoor hose spigot that wasn't properly shut down before the ground froze. 

Freezing water expands with incredible force. If water gets trapped in your spigot or the line feeding it, it will split the copper pipe inside your wall, and you won't know it until gallons of water are pouring into your basement.

Here is the exact step-by-step process we tell all our Minneapolis customers to follow every autumn.

---

### Step 1: Disconnect Your Hoses (The #1 Mistake Homeowners Make)
If you only do one thing on this list, do this. Leaving a garden hose connected to the spigot is the single biggest cause of frozen pipes we fix in the winter. 

When a hose stays attached, it prevents water from naturally draining out of the spigot body. That trapped water freezes, expands backwards into your home, and cracks the pipe inside the wall. Disconnect all hoses, drain them, and roll them up for the winter. 

### Step 2: Shut Off the Interior Valve
Go inside your home—usually in the basement, utility room, or crawlspace directly behind where the outdoor spigot sits—and locate the shutoff valve for that specific line. Turn the handle clockwise until it is completely closed. 

### Step 3: Drain the Line and Spigot
Once the inside valve is shut, head back outside. Turn the outdoor spigot completely on and let any remaining water drain out into the yard. 

Next, go back inside to that interior shutoff valve. Most modern ball valves or gate valves have a small brass cap on the side called a bleeder cap. Hold a small cup under it, unscrew the cap, and let the small amount of trapped water drain out. Once it stops dripping, screw the bleeder cap back on hand-tight. 

**Pro-tip:** Leave the outdoor spigot turned *open* all winter long. If any tiny amount of moisture freezes inside the pipe, leaving the faucet open prevents pressure buildup.

### Step 4: Install a $3 Foam Cover
Head down to the local hardware store and grab an insulated foam spigot cover. They cost about three bucks. Slip the rubber loop over the spigot handle, push the foam dome tight against your exterior siding, and pull the plastic slider tight. This blocks drafty winter winds from blowing straight into the brass fixture.

---

### Can’t Find an Interior Shutoff Valve?
Some older homes in Minneapolis don't have interior shutoff valves for outdoor plumbing, or a previous owner remodeled and covered them up. 

If you look behind the spigot inside your house and there is no valve, do not just leave it to chance. Give our team a call. We can come out, install a dedicated interior shutoff valve or a modern frost-free sillcock, and make sure your home is completely protected before the deep freeze hits.

b.text:
**How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots (Minneapolis)**

Shut the interior valve, open the outside spigot to drain it, disconnect the hose, and put a $3 foam cover on it. That is the whole job.

Start inside: find the shutoff valve feeding the spigot—usually in the basement, crawl space, or utility room along the pipe running to the wall. Turn it off. Go outside, open the spigot, and let the line empty. Leave the outside handle open a crack all winter so any leftover water has room to expand.

Disconnect the hose first. This is the mistake that drives most of our January burst-pipe calls: leaving a hose attached traps water in the pipe, it freezes, and the spigot or the line inside your wall splits. Even if you have a frost-free sillcock, the hose can back up water toward the valve. Disconnect it, drain it, and store it.

When the line is empty, screw on a cheap foam cover from any hardware store. It helps against wind chill, but it is not a substitute for draining the line.

If you don’t have an interior shutoff for the spigot, call us. We can install one, or we can handle the winter prep properly, but the real fix is that inside valve. It takes five minutes now, or it can cost you a repair when the first real freeze hits.

Need it done? Give us a call. We’re local, and we actually answer.

We’re hiring Ridgepoint’s first dedicated support person.

We’re a three-person SaaS team that helps small trucking dispatchers schedule loads. Right now, “support” means the three of us founders answering tickets whenever we’re not building or selling. It’s falling apart. Dispatchers need help in real time, and we’re slowing them down.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
If your baseboards are cold, you likely have air trapped in the lines blocking the hot water from circulating. You can fix this yourself in about fifteen minutes with a cup and a flathead screwdriver or radiator key. 

**1. Shut off the boiler and circulator.** Don't try to do this while the system is running. Shut the power off at the emergency switch so the water settles and the pump isn't pushing more air through the lines.

**2. Start at the unit closest to the boiler.** You need to go unit by unit, starting at the boiler and working your way out to the end of the line. The mistake that causes most of our "cold radiator" service calls is when people only bleed the upstairs bedrooms and entirely skip the basement loop. Don't skip the basement—that is usually where the air actually is.

**3. Find the bleeder valve.** Pull the cover off the end of your baseboard unit. You'll see a small brass valve on the pipe with a slotted screw head or a square fitting for a radiator key. 

**4. Open the valve slowly.** Hold your cup right underneath the valve. Turn the screw or key counter-clockwise just a little bit until you hear air hissing out. 

**5. Wait for a steady stream of water.** Let it hiss and spit until the air is gone. Once the water flows out into your cup in a solid, steady stream with no sputtering or hissing, the air is cleared from that unit.

**6. Close it snug, but don't overtighten.** Turn the valve clockwise until the water stops. Make it tight enough to seal, but do not crank down on it hard. If you overtighten it, you will crack the valve seat and you'll be calling me to come out and solder in a replacement.

Work your way through every baseboard in the house. Once you're done, flip the boiler back on and let it run. The heat should distribute evenly now, but if you still have dead spots after bleeding the entire system, you might be dealing with a stuck zone valve or a failing circulator pump. Give us a call and we'll come get it sorted out.

b.text:
**How to Bleed Your Baseboard Heating (And Why You Should Start in the Basement)**

If the upstairs is toasty and the basement baseboard is cold, you're not crazy — the air is almost always down there. Here's the whole job, start to finish.

**What you'll need**
- Radiator bleeder key (or a flathead screwdriver that fits the slot)
- Old towel
- Small cup or container
- About 45 minutes

**1. Shut off the circulator — not the whole boiler, just the pump.**

Flip the burner switch to "off" or kill the breaker to the boiler. You want the pump dead so it's not pushing water past you while you're working. If you have a dedicated circulator relay, that's even better.

**2. Let it cool down.**

Fifteen minutes minimum. Hot system + open bleeder = a face full of pressurized water. Worth the wait.

**3. Start with the basement loop.**

This is the part most homeowners skip, and it's the reason we get three "cold radiator" calls every October. Air rises, but in a closed hydronic system it pools at the high points of the loop — and on most homes with a basement boiler, the high point of the heating loop is right at the basement ceiling or the basement-level baseboard itself. If you only bleed the upstairs, you leave the biggest pocket in place and chase your tail all day.

**4. Find the bleeder valve on each baseboard unit.**

It's on the end cap, usually the supply end (the end closer to where the feed line comes in). Looks like a small square stem or a slotted nipple. One per unit.

**5. Work unit by unit, starting at the boiler and moving outward.**

Same direction the water flows. Bleed, close, move to the next. This pushes the air column out ahead of you instead of letting it run back into a unit you already did.

**6. Bleed it.**

- Tuck the towel around the end of the baseboard.
- Hold the cup right under the valve.
- Crack it open slowly. Quarter turn max.
- Hissing = air still coming out. Let it run.
- When the water comes out in a steady stream with no spitting or hiss, you're done at this valve.
- Close it. Snug is enough. If you reef on it, you'll crack the brass seat and trade a cold room for a leak.

**7. Repeat on every unit in the house.**

Same drill. Cup, towel, slow open, listen, close. Don't skip the ones that "feel fine" — the air will migrate to those by next winter if you do.

**8. Restart and recheck.**

Turn the circulator/boiler back on. Give it 20 minutes to push water through the whole loop. Then walk the house and touch every baseboard. The cold ones should be warming up. Go back and check each bleeder for any seepage — sometimes they need a quarter turn more once the system is hot and pressurized.

**When to stop and call us:**

If a unit stays cold after a proper bleed, the problem usually isn't air anymore. Stuck zone valve, failed circulator, sludge in the loop — those are jobs for a tech, not a homeowner with a key. Same thing if a bleeder won't stop dripping after you close it, or if the system pressure has dropped noticeably on the gauge. (If your boiler doesn't have a pressure gauge, that's its own problem.)

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/ I raised Tallyup's prices 40% on every customer overnight. A week later, 30 of 140 had cancelled. Here's what I got wrong and what I'm doing differently now.

2/ The reasoning felt solid. The product had gotten meaningfully better since launch. New customers were already paying more without blinking. Existing customers were on the old price and I figured the value was obvious.

3/ So I changed the Stripe plans, sent one email saying "prices are going up starting next billing cycle," and went to bed.

4/ The cancellations started before I woke up.

5/ What the replies taught me: it wasn't really the number. Gym owners run on thin margins and budget month to month. A 40% jump with no warning read as "this guy doesn't understand my business." Which, for a retention tool, is a bad look.

6/ A few said they'd have stayed at the new price if I'd just given them time. A few said they'd have stayed if I'd asked what they thought first. Most just left quietly.

7/ What I changed:

Existing customers are grandfathered at their old price for the rest of the year. If you signed up trusting a number, that number should mean something.

8/ New pricing only applies to new signups. Anyone who cancelled over this got an email offering their old rate back, no strings. Some came back. Not all.

9/ Going forward, any price change gets a real heads up. Months, not one billing cycle. And I'll talk to customers before I decide, not after.

10/ The lesson isn't "never raise prices." It's that the way you raise them tells customers what you think of them. I told 140 people I thought of them as line items. 30 of them believed me.

11/ Still here, still building. Back to the work.

b.text:
I made a pricing mistake with Tallyup.
  
Raised prices 40% overnight. Lost 30 of our 140 customers in a week.

Here’s what happened and what I changed. 🧵

1/ I thought we were underpriced. Competitors charged more, and I felt our value justified the jump. So I bumped every plan by 40% and sent a “new pricing” email. No warning. No grandfathering. Just an update.

2/ Within 24 hours, cancellations started rolling in. A few angry DMs. Then more. By the end of the week, 30 customers had left. That’s 30 people who trusted a tiny indie tool, and I blindsided them.

3/ I panicked. This is a bootstrapped SaaS; every customer counts. The immediate fix: I reverted the price for every existing customer and told them their rate was now locked indefinitely. I apologized publicly and privately.

4/ What I changed permanently:
  
– New customers now see the higher price, but with a clear 30-day notice promise if it ever changes.  
– Existing customers are grandfathered for life. No exceptions.  
– Any future price tweaks will be tested with a small subset first, never blanket overnight.

5/ The lesson: pricing isn’t just about value. It’s about trust. I broke trust by moving fast and not thinking about the humans on the other side. A 40% hike with no warning is a great way to burn relationships you spent years building.

Now I treat pricing like a conversation, not a surprise.

Dear City Council Members and Members of the Public Record,

My name is [Your Name], and I own [Coffee Shop Name], a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. First, the math on my customers. My register shows that the average customer visit to my coffee shop is 22 minutes. If a regular comes twice a week, that is $104 more per year. If they come three times a week, it is $156 more per year. b.text:
Members of the City Council,

My name is [Name], and I own a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am writing to oppose the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour.

This proposal would triple the hourly rate—a 200% increase—for customers who come downtown to shop, eat, and support local businesses. For a small business like mine, that increase matters. Customers do not experience parking costs as an isolated fee; they add it to the cost of every coffee, meal, or purchase they make downtown. Even a modest increase can influence whether someone chooses to visit Main Street, how long they stay, or whether they go somewhere with free parking instead.

I have firsthand evidence of how a similar increase affected downtown activity. In 2019, after the town next door raised its parking rates, I tracked my register and customer activity for six weeks. During that period, I observed an 18% drop in foot traffic. I recognize that this tracking does not prove that the parking increase alone caused every bit of that decline, but the timing and scale of the change are concerning. An 18% reduction in customers is significant for any small business operating on narrow margins.

The proposed increase also does not appear to match how long most of my customers actually visit. Their average visit is approximately 22 minutes. Under the current system, the one-hour minimum already covers that typical visit. Raising the rate from 50 cents to $1.50 would therefore triple the cost for customers whose parking needs have not changed. They would pay substantially more without receiving additional parking time or a meaningful improvement in their experience.

Most importantly, the city’s own report indicates that meter revenue covers only 4% of the downtown budget. That figure suggests this increase will not solve the city’s broader financial challenges. Even if the rate increase produces additional revenue, it will address only a very small portion of the downtown budget while placing a disproportionate burden on the local businesses and customers who rely on downtown activity.

I understand that the city must manage its budget and parking system responsibly. However, a policy that triples parking costs, risks reducing foot traffic by a measurable amount, and contributes to only 4% of the downtown budget deserves careful reconsideration. The city should evaluate alternatives that support revenue needs without making Main Street less accessible and less attractive to customers.

I respectfully ask the Council to reject the increase from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour, or at minimum to delay it and conduct a more complete analysis of its likely effect on downtown businesses, customer visits, and overall revenue. Our downtown businesses are part of the city’s economic foundation. Policies intended to strengthen downtown should not make it harder for customers to visit and for small businesses to remain open.

Thank you for considering my testimony.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
**The Run Game That Wasn’t**

The Titans finished 8-2. That’s the kind of record that usually gets you a parade, not a postgame handshake at the state quarterfinal. But after falling in Round 2 to the same team we beat by 20 back in Week 3, you have to ask why the script flipped.

Dez Kowalski is special. His 2,340 yards are a school record, and he carried us for most of the year. But passing records don’t seal fourth quarters when the ground game dies.

Here’s the hard truth: we lost because we abandoned the run in the second half. It was working. We were only down three. Instead of grinding, we opened the book too wide. That was a coaching call, not a player failure.

Dez has the arm. The line has the grit. But next year, if we want to finish games instead of just playing in them, we need to trust the run when the lights are brightest. 8-2 is great. But we’re chasing something better.

b.text:
**Season worth remembering, playoff loss worth questioning**

The final score is going to sit there for a while, and that’s the cruel part about playoff football. One week you’re still playing, the next you’re spending the whole winter wondering what happened.

What happened for our team shouldn’t be buried under the result. An 8-2 season is something to be proud of. This group played hard, played tough, and gave the town a fall worth talking about.

But I’m not going to pretend Friday night didn’t leave a bad taste.

This was a loss the team didn’t have to take. Not against this opponent. Not the way the game was set up. Not when they were only down three and still very much in control of their own fate.

They lost because they stopped doing what worked.

For long stretches, the run game was moving the chains and keeping the offense ahead of the sticks. It was physical, it was balanced, and it gave the team a chance to control tempo. Then, somewhere in the second half, the team got away from it. I still don’t understand why.

You don’t abandon your best weapon when the game tightens up. You lean on it. You make the other team adjust to you. Instead, the offense became one-dimensional, and that’s exactly what a good defense wants.

That’s what made the loss so frustrating. This wasn’t a case of being overmatched. This wasn’t a team getting punched in the mouth and never answering. They were right there. They had already beaten this same team by 20 back in Week 3. They knew they belonged.

And maybe that’s part of it. Sometimes the hardest thing in sports is to stay simple when the lights get brighter. You start pressing. You start searching for the big play instead of trusting the thing that got you there.

Still, this season was bigger than one bad stretch in one game.

Dez Kowalski set a school record with 2,340 passing yards. That’s not a small thing. That’s the kind of number people will be talking about around this program for years, and it should be celebrated. He made plays all season and gave this offense a real identity through the air.

But records don’t erase decision-making, and this loss still falls on the choices made when the game mattered most.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
The fluorescent lights in the ER buzzed like they always do, too bright and too steady. My first week, and I was already learning that time moves different here. Slower when someone’s hurting, faster when everything’s falling apart.

I remember the man with the deep gash on his forearm. He’d been cutting wood when the saw slipped. His wife was on her way, but traffic was bad, and he kept glancing at the door like he could will her there faster. The nurse told me to stay with him while she prepped the supplies. I didn’t know what to say, so I just held his hand. His palm was rough, calloused from work, and he squeezed mine a little too tight when the antiseptic touched the wound. “You’re doing great,” I told him, even though I wasn’t sure if that was true. He exhaled like he’d been holding his breath for hours.

Then there was the code. I’d only seen them on TV before, but this was nothing like that. No dramatic slow-motion, no one shouting for a crash cart—just a team moving fast, voices low and urgent. I got sent to restock gauze, which felt stupid at first, like I was in the way. But through the curtain, I could hear them counting compressions. “One, two, three…” The numbers were steady, but the air in the room wasn’t. I stood there with my arms full of supplies, listening, until someone called for me to bring more gloves.

And the blood draw. The diabetic man with veins like spiderwebs. I missed the first time, then the second, then the third. His skin was thin, bruising easy, and I could see the frustration in his eyes. “I’m sorry,” I kept saying, like that would make it better. The nurse watched me the fourth time, her arms crossed, and I took a deep breath before trying again. When the needle finally went in, I almost cried. He just patted my shoulder and said, “It’s okay, kid. You’ll get better.”

I don’t know if I did anything important that week. I held a hand. I restocked gauze. I missed a blood draw three times. But I think that’s the point—it’s not always about the big moments. Sometimes it’s about showing up, even when you’re scared, even when you’re not sure you’re doing it right. I’m still not sure. But I know I want to keep trying.

b.text:
My first week in the ER, I mostly tried to stay out of the way.

I'm in my first year of nursing school. I don't know much yet. I know how to wash my hands right and check blood pressure and not touch stuff I'm not supposed to. That first week was the first time I was around real sick and hurt people, not just class stuff.

The first day, there was a man with a bad cut on his leg that they had to clean out. It hurt and he was scared. His wife was trying to get there but she was stuck in traffic. The nurse said I could stand with him. I held his hand while they cleaned it. He squeezed so hard. He was my dad's age, but he just held on and looked at the wall. I didn't really know what to say, so I just said you're doing good, almost done. His wife walked in right when they finished. I was glad she made it, but I'm glad I was there for the part she missed.

Another day there was a code. I wasn't supposed to go in the room. They sent me to the back to restock the gauze. I was in the supply room stuffing gauze into the bins and I could hear them through the curtain. I could hear them counting, one, two, three, real steady for the chest pushes. Someone calling out what to do next. I just stood there and listened and kept stacking. I felt pretty useless. I kept thinking I should be doing more. But somebody has to make sure the gauze is there when they yell for it. That stuck with me.

The one I still think about was a blood draw. He was a diabetic guy and his veins were bad, they roll and they're hard to find. I missed three times in a row. Three sticks and no blood. He didn't get mad, which almost made it worse. My face was hot and my hands were shaking. I wanted to quit and tell the nurse to just do it. She told me to take a breath and try one more time. On the fourth try I got it. Blood came back in the tube and I almost couldn't believe it. He smiled and said, see, you got it. I said sorry about ten times and he just said it's okay.

I know I'm just starting. I have a lot to learn. But that week showed me what the job really is. It's holding someone's hand when their person can't be there yet. It's getting the gauze ready when you can't be in the room. It's saying sorry and trying again when you mess up.

This money would help me a lot. I work part time now and school costs a lot with gas and books and everything else. It would help me work less and focus more on school so I can finish and be good at this. Thank you for reading this.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
The season ends not with a bang but with a head-scratcher. Our high school football team finished 8-2 and made a solid run to the second round of the state playoffs, only to fall to a squad they had dismantled by 20 points back in Week 3. Dez Kowalski put an exclamation point on his year with 2,340 passing yards—a school record that will stand for a while.

But records and regular-season wins don’t decide playoff games. What decided this one was the decision to abandon the run in the second half. The ground game was working. They were only down three. Yet the ball kept going in the air, the clock kept running against them, and a winnable contest slipped away. Stick with what’s moving the chains when you’re that close. That’s football 101, and it cost them a deeper run. 

Solid season, no question. Just a tough way to learn the lesson.

b.text:
**8-2 And Out - That's The Frustrating Part**

Well, that's it. Friday night in the cold closed the book on this Wolves season, 8-2 with a second-round exit to a team we beat by 20 back in week 3.

It stings because it shouldn't have ended there. This was a good team. A really good team. Dez Kowalski throwing for 2,340 yards and setting the school record tells you that much. Those kids have a lot to be proud of.

But I'm not going to just recap the record and pat everyone on the back. You heard me say it Monday on the air and I'll say it here - we coached ourselves out of that game.

We were down three points to start the second half. Three points. That's nothing. And the run game was working. We were gashing them between the tackles all night.

Then we just stopped. 

We came out in the third quarter and decided we needed to throw our way back into it. Five straight pass plays on that opening drive, all incomplete or short. You can't tell me that's playing to your strengths when you're only down a field goal.

I get it. You have a kid like Dez who just rewrote the record book, you want to put the ball in his hands. But Friday night wasn't the night for it. They couldn't stop the run, and we got away from what was actually moving the chains because the scoreboard made us panic.

A three-point deficit in the third quarter is not a reason to abandon your identity. That's playoff football. You stay patient.

This team was good enough to play next week. 8-2, wins over teams that pushed them, a quarterback who made history. They deserved better than a one-and-done in November against a team they already handled.

Tough loss. Tougher way to lose. I'll talk more about it on the show tomorrow morning at 8.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
If you’ve stopped by the shop lately or browsed our site wondering where the wedding cake page went, I wanted to share a little of what’s been going on behind the counter.

First, please know this wasn’t a decision I took lightly. For years, making wedding cakes was one of the most tender, joyful parts of our work. Standing in a quiet kitchen with a couple’s whole story, translating it into buttercream and flowers and a flavor you hope they’ll remember forever — there’s nothing like it. I loved that we got to be a tiny part of something so big.

But after this past year, I’ve had to be honest with myself about what our little three‑person bakery can actually hold, and custom wedding cakes have quietly slipped outside that circle.

Here’s the unglamorous truth: every single custom order was eating up about fourteen hours of free consultation, tasting, sketching, and back‑and‑forth before we ever turned on the oven. That’s fourteen hours we weren’t in front of the case, weren’t filling the cookie jar, weren’t rolling croissants while the rest of the neighborhood was still asleep. And because we run on a shoestring crew, that time always came right out of the things that keep our lights on day to day.

Then this year we had three last‑minute cancellations — three couples who, for completely understandable life reasons, had to pull the plug after the ingredients were ordered and some of the prep already done. No fault, no drama, just a quiet email and a whole lot of butter, cream cheese, and specialty chocolate that nobody was going to eat. In a bigger operation, maybe you absorb that. For us, it meant the loss hit our grocery bill in a way we felt down to our bones.

And underneath all of it was a simpler humming truth: the everyday case is what pays rent. The morning regulars who grab a scone and a coffee on their way to work. The loaf of sourdough someone picks up twice a week. The chocolate chip cookie that makes a kid’s after‑school stop a little brighter. Those small, steady things are the heartbeat of this place, and I realized that every time I said yes to a wedding, I was saying a quiet, frantic no to a portion of that rhythm.

So we’re stepping back. Not because we don’t still get sappy over love stories, and not because we’ve forgotten how to build a tall, beautiful cake. Just because I want to be fully here for the bakery you’ve built with us — the one that’s open before sunrise, that smells like brown butter and yeast, that has a worn wooden counter where you lean and tell me about your day. That’s where my whole heart is right now.

If you have a celebration coming up — a bridal shower, an anniversary, a Tuesday that just needs to feel special — please still come talk to us. We’ll have whole cakes you can order from the flavors we already bake for the shop, simpler and just as lovely, without the custom carving and sugar‑flower weeks. I think you’ll find them pretty wonderful, and they come without the hidden weight that the big ones carried.

Thank you for understanding, and for trusting us with your mornings, your afternoons, your everyday hunger. That’s the wedding gift you’ve been giving me all along, and I don’t take it for granted.

With flour on my apron and a lot of love,
[Your name]

b.text:
If you’ve been following along here for a while, you know we try to keep this bakery as personal and hands-on as we can. That’s one of the best parts of being a small shop: I get to know so many of you by name, I get to bake the things you come in for every week, and I get to spend my days making the treats that end up at your tables for birthdays, coffee breaks, Tuesday afternoons, and all the ordinary little celebrations that make up real life.

That’s also why I want to share a change with you directly, in plain language.

We’re no longer taking custom wedding cake orders.

That isn’t an easy thing to write, because I know wedding cakes can be deeply meaningful, and I’m honored every time someone even thinks of us for something that important. But the truth is that custom wedding cakes have become too much for our tiny bakery to carry well.

A single wedding cake order takes an enormous amount of time. Between the back-and-forth emails, consultation time, tastings, planning, design work, and all the coordination that comes with making something that has to be exactly right, each one eats up about 14 hours of time that pulls me away from the bakery floor and away from the bread, pastries, cakes, and cookies you actually see in the case every day.

And because we’re small, that time matters a lot.

This year alone, we had three last-minute cancellations. When that happens, we’re left with ingredient costs we can’t recover, plus all the time that already went into planning and preparation. For a larger business, that might be easier to absorb. For a three-person bakery, it’s a real strain.

More than anything, I’ve had to be honest with myself about where our energy needs to go. The everyday case is what keeps this bakery going. It’s what pays rent, covers payroll, and keeps the lights on. It’s also what most of you come in for, week after week. That’s the heart of the business, and I need to protect that.

So this isn’t us saying no to weddings. It’s us saying yes to the part of the bakery that’s sustainable, steady, and true to what we do best.

We’ll still be here with cakes for smaller celebrations, special desserts, and all the things that make a gathering feel complete. And if you’re planning a wedding, I truly wish you all the sweetness in the world as you find the right fit for your day.

Thank you, as always, for supporting this little bakery and for understanding the realities behind what it takes to keep it running. I’m so grateful for every one of you who shows up for us, and I want to keep showing up for you in the ways we can do well.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
I’ve had three golden doodles, two huskies, and a corgi come through the salon this week alone, all with their owners saying the same thing: “I gave them a bath to loosen the mats, but they just got worse.” If that sounds familiar, you’re not alone—it’s the most common mistake I see with double coated and curly coated pups between grooming visits, and it’s such an easy fix once you know why it happens.

Wet matted fur is basically just felt: when the tangled hairs get saturated and then dry, they shrink and lock together way tighter than they were when dry, to the point where sometimes even our professional dematting tools can’t work through them without hurting your pup. That’s why the number one rule of at-home mat prevention is always, always brush before you bathe, never after. I know it feels backwards—you’d think water would soften things up, right? But trust me, I’ve spent way too many hours picking at felted armpit mats that could’ve been avoided with five minutes of brushing pre-bath.

For double coats and curls, a good slicker brush is your best friend—skip the soft bristle brushes that just glide over the top layer of fur and never touch the undercoat where mats actually start. Instead of scrubbing in circles like you’re washing a car, use short, straight line strokes. Circles can catch loose fur and twist it into new tangles, plus they irritate your dog’s skin if you press too hard. Short, even strokes get down to the undercoat without yanking, and they’re way easier on your wrist, too.

When you’re brushing, don’t just go over the top of their back and call it done. Mats almost always start in the spots you don’t think to check first: behind the ears where their collar rubs, under the front legs where their fur bunches when they walk or curl up, even along their belly where they lay on the carpet. Start there when your pup is still calm and willing to sit still, work in small sections so you don’t miss anything, and lift the top coat up as you go to make sure you’re getting all the way down to the skin. For double coated breeds, it’s easy to think their coat is fine because the top layer looks fluffy, but there can be a whole mess of tangled undercoat hiding underneath that turns into a mat in a day if it gets wet.

If you do spot a little mat forming before bath time, don’t dive in with the brush right away. Grab some dog conditioner—either regular stuff diluted a little with water, or a leave-in detangler if you have it—and work a tiny bit into the mat with just your fingertips. Gently separate the hairs as much as you can by hand first, working from the ends of the fur up toward the skin so you don’t pull. Once you’ve loosened it up as much as possible with your fingers, then you can go in with the slicker or a wide-tooth comb to work out the rest. It takes an extra minute, but it’s way less stressful for your pup than yanking a brush through a tight mat.

If you’re ever not sure if you’re doing it right, just pop by the salon anytime we’re open—no appointment needed. I’ll even let you test out our slicker brushes and show you how to hold them so you don’t tire out your arm, and we can check those tricky behind-the-ear spots together. The goal is to keep your pup’s coat comfy and mat-free between grooms, so you don’t have to stress when they roll in dirt at the park down the street or get caught in a rainstorm on your walk home.

b.text:
# How to Keep Your Dog's Coat from Matting Between Grooming Visits

If you've got a double-coated or curly breed at home, you already know how fast the fur can go from soft and fluffy to tangled and tight. The good news is that a little regular upkeep between your visits to us makes a huge difference, and it's easier than most people think once you know a couple of key things.

The single biggest mistake I see, and I mean I see it constantly, is people bathing the dog first because they figure the water will loosen everything up. It does the exact opposite. Wet matted fur doesn't relax, it shrinks and tightens into what's basically a felt pad, and then there's not much anyone can do with a brush. So the rule to remember is simple: always brush before the bath, never after. Get the coat detangled while it's dry, then wash.

When you brush, reach for a slicker brush and work in short, straight line strokes. A lot of folks brush in little circles thinking they're being thorough, but that just tangles the coat back around itself. Short lines, moving through the fur in one direction, is what you want.

Take it in sections rather than trying to do the whole dog at once. Start behind the ears and under the front legs, because that's where mats almost always show up first. Those spots rub and move constantly, so they knot up before anywhere else. If you stay on top of those two areas, you're winning half the battle.

And if you do spot a mat already forming, don't grab the brush and start yanking at it. Work a little conditioner into it with your fingers first and gently loosen it apart by hand before any brush or comb ever touches it. That saves your dog a lot of discomfort and saves the coat too.

Keep this up a few times a week and you'll notice the difference at your next appointment. If a mat ever gets ahead of you, don't stress about it. Bring your pup in and we'll take care of it.
