setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
**How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots (And Avoid a January Disaster)**

Every January, my team gets flooded with emergency calls for burst pipes. Nine times out of ten, it’s because of one simple mistake made in October or November with an outdoor spigot. 

In Minneapolis, we don’t just get cold weather—we get deep, sustained freezes that will find any weakness in your plumbing. Here is exactly how to winterize your outdoor spigots today. It takes five minutes and can save you thousands of dollars in water damage.

### Step 1: Disconnect your garden hoses (The Big Mistake)
If you only do one thing on this list, do this. Leaving a garden hose attached to your spigot is the number one cause of frozen pipes we see. Even if you have a "frost-free" spigot, leaving a hose connected traps water inside the faucet. When that water freezes, it expands back into the pipe inside your warm basement, splits the copper, and sits there waiting to flood your home the moment things thaw out. Unhook your hoses, drain them, and roll them up for the winter.

### Step 2: Shut off the interior valve
Go inside your house—usually the basement, utility room, or crawl space directly behind where the outdoor spigot is located. Look for a shutoff valve on that water line. It will either be a round wheel handle (gate valve) or a straight lever (ball valve). 
* Turn the wheel clockwise until it stops, or turn the lever so it is perpendicular to the pipe. 

### Step 3: Drain the spigot from the outside
Once the indoor valve is shut, go back outside. Turn the outdoor spigot handle all the way on. Let any trapped water drain out completely. Leave the outdoor valve open all winter. If any water does manage to trickle past the indoor valve, leaving the outdoor faucet open gives it room to escape rather than freezing and cracking the pipe.

*(Pro-Tip: If your indoor shutoff valve has a tiny brass cap on the side—called a bleeder valve—place a bucket under it and unscrew the cap slightly. This lets air into the line so the remaining water can drain out. Screw it back on tight when you're done.)*

### Step 4: Install a $3 foam cover
Go to your local hardware store and grab a Styrofoam faucet cover. They cost about three dollars and take ten seconds to install. They loop over the spigot handle and clamp tight against your siding, keeping the bitter Minneapolis wind from freezing any residual moisture left in the faucet. It’s cheap insurance.

---

### What if you don’t have an interior shutoff valve?
A lot of older homes in Minneapolis either don't have interior shutoffs for their outdoor spigots, or the valves have been walled over during basement remodels. 

If you can’t find your shutoff valve, or if you try to turn it and it’s frozen solid, don’t force it and risk snapping the handle. Give us a call. We can install a proper indoor shutoff valve or replace your old outdoor spigot with a modern, frost-free model before the hard freeze sets in.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots

Every January we get the same calls: a burst pipe behind the wall, water in the basement, and a homeowner who had no idea a garden hose caused it. The good news is that winterizing your outdoor spigots takes about ten minutes and costs almost nothing. Here's how to do it right.

## Step 1: Shut Off the Interior Valve

Most outdoor spigots have a dedicated shutoff valve inside your house, usually in the basement or crawlspace along the wall where the spigot comes through. Follow the pipe from the spigot back inside and look for a small valve. Turn it clockwise to close it.

If you can't find an interior shutoff for your outdoor spigot, don't guess. Give us a call. A lot of older Minneapolis homes either don't have one or have it buried somewhere unexpected, and it's worth knowing before the cold sets in.

## Step 2: Drain the Spigot

Once the interior valve is closed, go back outside and open the spigot all the way. Let any water still sitting in the pipe drain out. This is the step people skip, and it matters. Water left in that line is exactly what freezes, expands, and cracks the pipe.

Leave the spigot open for the winter once it's drained.

## Step 3: Disconnect Your Hoses

This is the big one. **Leaving a hose connected over the winter is the single most common cause of the burst-pipe calls we get in January.**

Here's why: even with the valve shut, a connected hose traps water against the spigot and back into the pipe. When it freezes, it expands, and the pipe splits. You often won't even know until the spring thaw, when it starts leaking behind your wall.

So disconnect every hose, drain them, and store them in the garage or shed.

## Step 4: Add a $3 Foam Cover

Pick up an insulated foam spigot cover from any hardware store. They run about three dollars and slip right over the spigot. It's cheap insurance against a freeze, especially on exposed spigots that catch the wind.

## The Bottom Line

Shut the valve, drain the line, disconnect the hoses, and cover the spigot. Ten minutes now saves you a flooded basement and a repair bill later.

And if you can't locate your interior shutoff valve, or you'd rather have someone handle it, give us a call. We'd much rather help you winterize in the fall than dig out a burst pipe in January.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
1. Shut off the circulator pump and boiler at the control switch or breaker. Bleeding a pressurized, running system forces fresh air back in, wastes time, and can damage the pump seals.

2. Find the bleeder valve on each baseboard unit. It’s a small brass fitting, usually half an inch across, located on the end cap where the supply and return pipes meet. Every unit in the loop gets one.

3. Cup a small container directly underneath the valve. Keep a shop rag folded over the rim to catch drips. You’re only going to release a few ounces per unit.

4. Open the valve slowly using a dedicated bleeder key or a flathead screwdriver. Turn counter-clockwise just enough to break the seal. You’ll hear air hiss out, followed by sputtering water. Keep it cracked until the stream runs completely steady and silent—that means the air pocket is gone.

5. Close the valve by turning clockwise until it stops, then tighten it firmly with one additional quarter-turn. Snug is all it takes. Overtightening shears the rubber washer or cracks the valve seat, which turns a three-minute maintenance task into a leaky fixture replacement.

6. Work your way through every unit in the loop, always starting with the baseboard closest to the boiler and moving outward to the farthest room. Water carries air as it circulates, so purging from the source pushes trapped pockets cleanly out through each valve.

The single biggest reason I show up to houses for cold radiator calls is that homeowners only bleed the upstairs units and completely ignore the basement loop. Air rises with the heat and migrates with the water flow, which means it consistently settles in the lowest part of the system—the basement circuit. Skip that loop and the rest of your house will stay cold regardless of what you do upstairs. Purge the basement first or treat it equally, and your zones will balance fast.

Once you’ve run through every unit, verify the system pressure on the gauge. It should read 12 to 15 psi when the boiler is cold. Top off with a filling loop or garden hose adapter if needed, restart the boiler, and let each zone pull hot. 

If you complete this entire process and still get lukewarm floors or major temperature swings, the culprit is usually a worn circulator, partially closed zone valves, or sediment buildup in the piping. Call us out, and we’ll diagnose it properly before the first hard freeze.

b.text:
If your baseboard heaters are knocking, clanking, or staying lukewarm while the boiler runs, air is trapped inside the lines. Water can't flow through an air pocket, which leaves you with a cold room. 

Bleeding the air out is a simple job you can do yourself in about 20 minutes before you crank the heat up for the season. Here is the exact order and method to do it right.

### Step 1: Kill the power to the system
Before touching a valve, turn off your boiler and the circulator pump at the emergency switch. Never bleed a system while the pump is running. A running pump can actually pull more air into the lines, and you run the risk of pumping hot water or air pockets right past your bleeder valves. Let the system settle and cool down for a few minutes so you don't burn yourself.

### Step 2: Start at the basement loop (Do not skip this)
The single biggest mistake that triggers cold-radiator service calls to our shop is people bleeding only the upstairs units. Air rises, so logic tells you it’s all on the top floor—but in hydronic systems, air pockets frequently get locked into the lowest loops first. If you leave air in the basement baseboards, it will eventually push up into the rest of the house. 

Always bleed unit by unit, starting with the baseboard closest to the boiler (usually in the basement) and working your way out and up through the house.

### Step 3: Find the bleeder valve
Pop off the end caps on the metal baseboard housing. You are looking for a small metal valve soldered into the pipe at the end of the finned tube. It will have a tiny discharge nozzle on the side and either a square stem (which takes a radiator key) or a slotted top (which takes a small flathead screwdriver).

### Step 4: Catch the water and open slowly
Hold a small cup or rag directly beneath the valve spout. Insert your key or flathead screwdriver and turn the valve counterclockwise very slowly—usually just a quarter to a half turn is all it takes. 

You’ll hear a sharp hissing sound as trapped air escapes. Hold steady. 

### Step 5: Wait for a solid stream and close snug
Keep the valve open until the hissing stops completely and a steady, unbroken stream of water spurts into your cup. 

As soon as you get solid water, turn the valve clockwise to close it. **Tighten it until it’s snug, but do not crank down on it.** These valves are soft brass. If you overtighten them, you’ll crack the internal valve seat, turn a small bleed job into a dripping leak, and end up having to call us to drain the whole system and sweat on a new valve.

### Step 6: Repeat down the line
Move to the next baseboard unit along the zone, working away from the boiler, and repeat the process. Once you’ve hit every unit—basement included—head back to the boiler, check your system pressure gauge (a standard residential system usually sits around 12 to 15 PSI cold), turn the power switch back on, and let the pump circulate.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
**What the 22 Percent Actually Cost Me**

USDA raised the prevented planting base rate 22 percent in our region this year. On my operation — about 3,000 acres of corn and beans — that came to roughly $46,000 in additional premium. Not $46,000 in lost yield, not $46,000 in equipment. Forty-six thousand dollars in extra premium on a policy I bought before I knew what kind of spring we were going to have.

Then I got the spring we had. Thirteen inches of rain between the second week of April and the May 25 final plant date for corn, which is close to double our thirty-year normal for that window. I got 1,800 acres in the ground. Twelve hundred acres I did not, and no amount of standing at the edge of the field looking at it was going to change that. I know I'm not alone; I've had the same conversation with half the people reading this.

So I paid 22 percent more for coverage in the exact year I needed to use it. That's how insurance works some years, and I'm not going to complain about paying a premium and then filing a claim. That's the deal.

The acreage cap is a different story. That one isn't bad luck. That one is written down on purpose.

Here's how it works, and I'd encourage anybody who hasn't looked closely to pull out their policy and check me on this. The eligible acreage under the enhanced coverage is capped per covered entity — 500 acres, flat, regardless of the size of the operation behind it. I farm as one entity. My grandfather set it up that way, my dad kept it that way, and I never had a reason to change it. So of my 1,200 prevented planting acres, 500 are eligible. Forty-two percent.

An operation nine miles from me farms somewhere north of 11,000 acres. It's a good outfit and I have nothing bad to say about how they treat their ground or their neighbors. But that operation is structured across four entities, which means it carries 2,000 acres of eligible cap. Their prevented planting acres this spring came in lower than mine proportionally — they're spread across three counties and didn't catch the same rain — and every acre they claimed fell under the cap with room to spare.

Same rule. Same rain event. One of us gets covered on 42 percent of the problem and the other gets covered on all of it. The difference isn't farming practice or risk management or how well anybody keeps their tile up. The difference is how many LLCs the operation is divided into.

I want to be careful here, because this argument gets made badly sometimes. I'm not asking anybody to punish scale. Scale isn't a moral failing and consolidation isn't going to be fixed by a crop insurance rule. What I'm saying is narrower than that: a flat per-entity cap is functionally a discount for operations with the size and the accounting to split themselves up, and a penalty for the ones that never had a reason to. It rewards a paperwork decision. That's it. And when you stack a 22 percent rate increase on top of a cap structure that already tilts against mid-size family operations, you get a year like this one, where the premium hike lands on everybody and the coverage lands unevenly.

The obvious response is that I should restructure. Maybe I will. But I'd point out that the cost of restructuring — legal, accounting, redoing every lease and loan document — is itself a fixed cost that's easier for a bigger operation to absorb. So even the fix favors the same people the rule already favors.

**SB 214**

SB 214 would replace the flat per-entity cap with a percentage-of-insured-acres cap that applies to the operation as a whole, however it's organized. Under that structure, my 1,200 acres and the 11,000-acre outfit's acres get treated on the same proportional basis. Nobody loses coverage they'd otherwise have. As I read the fiscal note, the change comes close to a wash for the state — it redistributes eligibility rather than expanding it.

That's the whole bill. It is not ambitious. It does not solve the rate increase, which is a federal question and a longer fight. It corrects one line of arithmetic that is currently producing an outcome I don't think anybody sat down and intended.

The Senate ag committee is expected to take it up this session. Two things worth doing:

First, call your state senator's office and say, plainly, that you farm in this county, that you had prevented planting acres this spring, and that

b.text:
# The 22% That Came Out of My Pocket

The USDA raised the prevented planting base premium rate 22% this year for our region. For my operation, that worked out to roughly $46,000 in additional cost, and that's on top of a spring where I could only get 60% of my acres in the ground before the late May deadline.

I want to walk through the numbers, because I think most of us felt the pinch but haven't sat down and added it all up.

When the rain finally let up enough to plant, the calendar had already decided my season for me. Prevented planting coverage is exactly what it's for—it's the safety net that keeps a bad spring from becoming a lost year. But the 22% rate increase means that safety net costs dramatically more to hold onto right when we needed it most.

Here's the part that stings worse, and it's the reason I'm writing this: the way the acreage caps are structured, family operations like mine absorb this increase at a higher effective rate than the larger operations nearby. A big operation can spread its planted and prevented acres across a larger base, so the cap doesn't bind the same way it does for us. When you're farming a family-sized footprint, the cap hits earlier, and every percentage point of premium increase lands on fewer acres to carry it. The 22% isn't evenly distributed, even though the announcement reads like it is.

I've farmed my whole life on ground my great-grandfather broke. I'm not looking for sympathy—wet springs come with the territory. What I'm asking is that the rules be fair when the wet spring arrives. Right now, they aren't.

Senate Bill 214 would fix the acreage cap so that family operations aren't paying a disproportionate share of these premium increases. It's a targeted fix. It doesn't cost the state much, and it doesn't change anyone's coverage—it just makes the cap reflect the reality of how mid-sized family farms are structured.

Our state legislators read this newsletter, and I hope they read this piece. Call their offices. Write them. Tell them you support SB 214, and tell them why: not because farming is hard—everybody knows that—but because a 22% premium increase that falls hardest on family operations is a policy choice, and policy choices can be changed.

I paid my $46,000 this year. I'd rather pay for a wet spring than for an unfair rule. Right now I'm paying for both.

a.text:
**How to Bleed Air Out of Baseboard Heating Before Winter**

Shut off the circulator or boiler first.  

Find the bleeder valve on the end of each baseboard unit. Hold a cup underneath it. Open the valve slowly with a radiator key or flathead screwdriver until water comes out in a steady stream with no hissing air. Close it snug—do not overtighten or you will crack the valve seat.

The mistake that causes most of our cold radiator calls is people only bleeding the upstairs units and skipping the basement loop, which is usually where the air actually is.

b.text:
Trapped air is the number one reason your baseboards are gurgling or failing to heat up. Bleeding the lines is an easy fix, but doing it out of order will just leave you with cold rooms and a mess. Here is exactly how we do it in the field.

**1. Shut off the boiler and circulator pump**
Don't try to bleed a running system. The circulator pump will just push more air around the pipes or suck new air in. Flip the red emergency switch or turn off the breaker to your boiler so the water is sitting completely still.

**2. Start at the boiler and work your way out**
Find the bleeder valve on the end of each baseboard unit, usually tucked behind the small metal access panel. You need to go unit by unit, starting with the baseboard closest to the boiler and working your way down the line to the furthest one. 

**3. Catch the water and crack the valve**
Hold a small cup directly under the valve. Use a bleeder key or a small flathead screwdriver to open it slowly. You’ll hear a hiss as the trapped air escapes. Leave it open until the hissing stops and you get a steady, solid stream of water with no sputtering.

**4. Close it snug, but don't crank it**
Once it's just water, close the valve. Give it a firm, snug turn, but do not overtighten it. These brass valve seats are soft, and older ones get brittle. If you bear down too hard, you’ll crack the seat and end up with a steady drip that requires replacing the whole valve.

**The Mistake That Causes Most of Our Service Calls**
Here’s the part most homeowners get wrong. When the upstairs bedrooms are cold, people grab a cup and only bleed the upstairs baseboards. But in a two-story house, air gets pushed to the highest physical point of the piping, which means people skip the basement loop, which is usually where the air actually is. 

If you bleed the upstairs units and the radiators are still cold, go down to the basement. Find the main supply and return lines and bleed any valves on that basement loop. Nine times out of ten, that’s where the air pocket is actually hiding.

a.text:
### Coming Home

When I came home from my second deployment, my wife and daughter met me at the airport.

My daughter was six years old. I had seen pictures of her while I was gone, and we talked when we could. Still, pictures and phone calls are not the same as standing in front of somebody.

When I walked toward them, she went behind her mother’s leg.

She did not cry. She just held on and looked at me from the side. I stopped a few feet away. I wanted to pick her up, but I did not want to scare her. Her mother said my name and told her it was Dad.

I knelt down. I said hello.

My daughter kept looking at me. After a little while, she came out from behind her mother. She let me hug her, but she held herself stiff at first. I remember the smell of her hair. I remember the airport noise around us. People were talking, bags were rolling over the floor, and somebody made an announcement I could not understand.

I had pictured that moment many times. In those pictures, she ran to me.

Instead, she had to figure out who I was.

A few days later, I went to the grocery store with my wife. I needed cereal. That was all.

I stood in front of the cereal shelves and looked at the boxes.

There were rows of them. Some had cartoon characters. Some had marshmallows. Some were supposed to be healthy. Some had less sugar, more fiber, whole grains, extra protein, or something else printed on the front. There were flakes, squares, rings, clusters, and little pieces shaped like animals.

I stood there for about twenty minutes.

I would pick up a box, read it, and put it back. Then I would pick up another one. I had been gone for a year. While I was away, the grocery store had continued being a grocery store. New products had come in. Old ones had moved around. There were too many choices.

My wife came down the aisle and asked if I was ready.

I told her I was still deciding.

She looked at the shelf, then at me.

I finally picked a box. I do not remember which one.

At home, I had trouble sleeping. Before the deployment, I had slept with the bedroom door open. My daughter’s room was down the hall. I was used to hearing the house settle, the air conditioner come on, or one of the kids moving around. With the door open, I could see part of the hallway from the bed.

Overseas, I slept facing the door.

That was how I had learned to sleep. Even when I was tired, I put myself where I could see the entrance. I did not think about it much. I would lie down, check the door, and close my eyes. If I woke up, I checked it again.

At home, the bedroom door stayed open, but I kept turning toward it. The hallway was dark. I could see the edge of it from the bed. Every small sound brought me awake.

One night, I got up and closed the door.

The room felt too quiet. I lay there for a while, then opened it again.

The next night I tried leaving it open. I put a pillow behind my back so I would not roll toward the door. That helped for a little while. Then I heard something in the hall and was awake again.

My wife was already asleep. I watched her breathing and listened to the house.

It took time to sleep with the door open the way I had before. I had to get used to the hallway being a hallway and not an entrance I needed to watch.

My daughter also needed time. For a while, she stayed close to her mother when I came into a room. Then she started asking me to read to her. She would bring a book and sit beside me, not quite touching me at first.

One evening, she fell asleep against my arm while I was reading. I stayed still until my arm went numb.

I did not move it.

b.text:
**Second Time Back**

The first time I came home from a deployment my daughter was three and she ran at me so hard she knocked the wind out of me. I remember thinking that was the hardest part of the whole thing, getting my breath back in front of everybody at baggage claim.

The second time she was six. I came down the escalator and saw my wife right off, standing where we said she'd be, and then I saw about half of my daughter. The other half was behind her mother's leg. She had her hand wrapped in the fabric of her mom's jeans and she was looking at me the way you'd look at a dog you didn't know yet.

I'd lost some weight. I had a mustache I'd grown on a bet and forgot to shave. A year is a big piece of a six-year-old's life. I knew all that in my head. It still landed somewhere lower than my head.

I didn't rush her. I put my bag down and got on one knee, which is a thing they tell you to do with kids and also a thing I'd been doing a lot of that year for other reasons. I said hey. She didn't say anything. My wife said, "Baby, that's Daddy," in the voice you use when you're trying not to make a thing into a thing.

What got her out was her shoes. They had little lights in the heels and I said, "Did those come like that or did you put those in yourself," and she said she didn't put them in, they came like that, and she stepped out about a foot to show me. I told her they were the best shoes I'd seen in a year, which was true. She let me hold her hand to the truck. She didn't hug me till we were home and I'd shaved the mustache off. My wife said later she'd been asking about me the whole drive to the airport, so it wasn't that she didn't want me. She just had to make sure.

About four days after that I went to the grocery store by myself for the first time. My wife gave me a list. Milk, bread, eggs, a couple other things, and cereal. She didn't write down what kind. Why would she.

I want to be accurate about this. It was not forty kinds of cereal. It was one whole side of an aisle, top to bottom, both directions, and I stopped counting at forty. For a year I had eaten what was put in front of me at the time it was put there. When there was a choice it was between two things and usually one of them was gone. I stood in that aisle and I read boxes. I read them like they were going to tell me something. Fiber. Whole grain. Marshmallows. Some kind with a cartoon bee on it that I did not remember existing.

A woman with a cart came around me once, and then a while later she came around me again the other way, and I realized how long I'd been standing there. My cart had milk and bread in it. That was all I'd managed.

The thing I kept getting stuck on was that I didn't know what my daughter ate now. When I left she ate the ones with the tiger. I did not know if that was still true. I could have called my wife. I had a phone in my pocket. I stood there instead. I think I was ashamed to call home and ask a question like that, like it was proof of something.

I ended up putting two boxes in the cart. The tiger ones and a plain one for me. When I got home my daughter told me she didn't eat the tiger ones anymore, she ate the honey ones, and she said it kindly, like she could tell I'd tried. My wife didn't say anything about how long I'd been gone. The plain ones I ate for about a month. They were fine.

The door took longer than the cereal.

Over there I slept facing the door. Everybody did. You put your rack so you could see it, you kept your boots where your feet would find them, you kept your weapon where your hand would. Nobody had to tell me to do that after the first week. It's just how you lay down. Twelve months of it and it wasn't a habit anymore, it was just how sleeping worked.

At home our bedroom door stays open. It's always stayed open, since she was a baby, so we can hear her down the hall. My side of the bed is the side away from the door. The first night back I lay down on my side and inside of a minute I'd rolled over to face the door. My wife was between me and it. That bothered me in a way I couldn't have explained if she'd asked, and she didn't ask, she just kind of watched me settle and unsettle for a while and then went to sleep.

I tried the other side for a couple nights. Told her I wanted to be closer to the bathroom. She let me have that one. On that side I could see straight down the hall to my daughter's door, and I did, for hours. Every time the house made a noise I was up on one elbow before I knew I was doing it. The house makes a lot of noises. I'd forgotten that. Ice maker. The dog turning around in her bed. The furnace.

I tried closing the door. Got up to do it around one in the morning like I was going to the bathroom and just shut it on the way back. My wife woke up and said, "We'll never hear her," and she was right, so I opened it again.

So then it was just a matter of lying there. I don't have a technique to tell you about. I did not breathe in through my nose and out through my mouth or count backwards from a hundred. I just lay on my own side with my back to the door and made myself stay there. It felt like I was leaving something open. I'd last twenty minutes and turn over. Then it was an hour. I'd tell myself, she's the one who's been hearing that hallway all year, she's got it. Then I'd turn over anyway.

Somewhere around the second month I woke up one morning and I was facing the wall. I'd been facing the wall all night. I lay there and looked at the wall for a while. There's a crack in the paint by the outlet that I'd never noticed.

Some nights I still turn over. My wife says she can tell when I've done it by how the bed moves, and she'll put her hand on my back, and I'll turn back. She doesn't say anything about it and neither do I. The door stays open. My daughter is nine now and eats the ones with the marshmallows, and I know that without asking.

setup: A retired rural mail carrier is writing a letter to the Kettle Falls Courier urging residents to oppose the post office counter closure at the July 28 forum.

a.text:
To the Editor,

I am not much of a writer, but I felt I had to say something about the plan to close our post office counter service. I drove the 38 miles of Route 4 for 22 years before I retired last year, so I know this town and the folks who live in it. 

The postal service claims the Kettle Falls branch is losing $40,000 a year, and they are using that as their excuse to shut the counter down. But anyone paying attention knows why the numbers look like that. They cut the counter hours to just 8 a.m. to noon. Of course foot traffic dropped after that—most folks are at work during those hours. The USPS is pointing at a problem they made themselves to justify leaving us high and dry.

This isn't just about numbers on a spreadsheet. It's about our neighbors. Take Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She’s in her 80s and relies on the mail for her heart meds. When she needs a money order, she relies on our local counter. If it closes, she can’t exactly drive twenty minutes over to Fairview to get her business done. 

There is a public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall, and the USPS district manager is going to be there. I am asking everyone in Kettle Falls to show up. We need to pack the room and tell them face-to-face what closing this counter will actually do to our town.

b.text:
To the Editor,

I’m not a writer. I drove Route 4 for 22 years—same 38-mile loop—before retiring last year from a small town called Kettle Falls, and I still know this place.

USPS says our branch loses $40,000 a year and wants to close the counter. That figure is only there because they already cut hours from 8 to noon. Of course traffic dropped after that. They’re pointing at a problem they made themselves.

It’s not just numbers. Mrs. Halloran on Kettle Hill is in her 80s. She gets her heart meds by mail, and once the counter closes she can’t drive 20 minutes to Fairview just to get a money order. She shouldn’t have to.

The USPS district manager is coming to a public forum July 28 at the grange hall. I hope people show up—not just for me, but for Mrs. Halloran and anyone else who can’t make that trip.

Sincerely,
A retired Route 4 carrier
Kettle Falls

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/
I raised Tallyup prices 40% on everyone overnight.

No warning. No grandfathering.

Lost 30 of our 140 customers in a week.

Here’s what happened and what I changed.

2/
I just flipped the prices in billing and let it go live.

Thought gym owners tracking member retention would see the value and stay.

They didn’t.

3/
Cancellations started coming in immediately.

Small gyms especially. “This came out of nowhere.” “We can’t do this.”

30 gone in a week.

4/
I spent that week talking to people who left and people who stayed.

The sudden jump was the problem more than the number itself.

They felt blindsided.

5/
What I changed:

Remaining customers stay on their old price.

New customers pay the new price.

I never raise prices on existing people without talking to them first.

6/
Biggest lesson: the customers who already believed in you got you here.

Don’t surprise them.

b.text:
1/ I messed up pricing on Tallyup.

I run a small subscription tool that helps gym owners track member retention.

I raised prices 40% on everyone overnight. Lost 30 of our 140 customers in a week.

Here's what happened:

2/ No warning. No grandfathering. Just a new price.

I told myself it was cleaner to rip the bandaid off.

It wasn't clean. It felt like a surprise bill to people who trusted me early.

3/ The feedback wasn't really "too expensive."

It was "you surprised me."

That's on me. I broke trust over something I could have just communicated.

4/ What I changed:

Put existing customers back on their old plan, new pricing only going forward, and emailed everyone to own the mistake and lay out how I'll handle pricing changes from now on.

5/ Lesson for other indie founders:

Don't raise on everyone overnight. Grandfather. Give warning. Let people choose.

I had to lose 30 of 140 in a week to really get it.

setup: A high-school biology teacher is writing a cover letter to a customer success hiring manager at the edtech company.

a.text:
Dear [Hiring Manager's Name],

For the past two years, I've been one of your users. I ran [Product] in a high-school biology classroom of 150 students a year, served as the campus admin for our department, and fielded the questions that came in when a colleague couldn't find the gradebook sync or a student's login broke the night before a test. I know your product from the side you're trying to reach: the teacher who has forty minutes to make it work before the bell rings.

I'm applying for the Customer Success role because that's the job I've been doing informally, and I want to do it fully.

Eight years of teaching taught me the parts of this work that are hard to train. Every semester I onboard 30 new people at a time, most of whom did not choose to be there, and get them functional and invested within two weeks. I've sat across from parents who were furious about a grade, a policy, or something that wasn't my decision, and left those conversations with the relationship intact and a plan they agreed to. I've been the person other teachers came to when the tool wasn't cooperating, which meant learning it deeply enough to troubleshoot fast and translate what I found back to people who didn't want a lecture.

I also know why a school renews or quietly lets a license lapse. It's rarely the features. It's whether someone on campus feels supported, whether the first month went smoothly, and whether anyone from the company ever checked in after the sale.

I'd like to be that person for your schools. I understand the calendar, the budget cycles, the politics of a department meeting, and the difference between a tool teachers tolerate and one they defend.

Thank you for your time. I'd welcome the chance to talk.

Sincerely,
[Name]

b.text:
Dear [Hiring Manager],

Two years ago, I brought [Product Name] into my high school biology classroom. I also onboarded three other science teachers to it, helped our campus IT director troubleshoot rostering on a Sunday, and fielded late-night login questions from parents. None of that was in my job description. It's the job I want now.

For eight years I've taught high school biology, which means every semester I've done what customer success teams do: onboard 30 new users, drive adoption, train colleagues, calm frustrated stakeholders, and keep a long list of accounts from churning. I didn't have the title, but the work was identical.

When [Product Name] released a new feature last spring, I built the training deck my department used to roll it out. When teachers at other schools asked how we used it, I ran a workshop after hours. When a parent threatened to pull her student from the program over a gradebook error, I escalated through support, documented the issue, and made sure it didn't repeat the next semester.

That's customer success — onboarding, adoption, retention, escalation. I just did it with report cards instead of renewal contracts.

What I bring that most CS candidates can't: two years on the customer side. I know where the product wins teachers over and where it loses them. I know what a great CSM looks like from the receiving end, because I've leaned on a few. And I know how to champion a product inside an organization, because I was my school's unofficial [Product Name] lead for two years running.

I'd love to bring that perspective to your team.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/4  
On the Maple Ave kitchen job, we opened the ceiling to reroute plumbing and found a floor joist that had been heavily notched for an old drain line.

It wasn’t an obvious failure, but it had taken far more material out of the joist than was acceptable.

2/4  
The fix meant temporarily supporting the floor, removing the damaged section, sistering the joist, and reworking the plumbing so the problem didn’t get repeated.

That added about **$[amount]** and **[number] days** to the job.

3/4  
The expensive part wasn’t the lumber. It was the access, temporary support, extra labor, inspection, and schedule disruption.

This is why “we’ll figure it out when the cabinets are out” can turn into a real change order.

4/4  
The lesson: before finalizing a kitchen layout, inspect the framing and map the plumbing paths.

A joist is not a convenient place to make a hole just because the pipe needs to get through. Small shortcuts in framing can become expensive corrections years later.

b.text:
1/ Opened up the kitchen ceiling on the Maple Ave job Tuesday. Three joists notched more than halfway through for an old cast iron drain line that got abandoned decades ago. Nobody ever sistered them. Floor above had a sag the homeowner thought was "just old house charm."

2/ Fix was 6 sistered joists, new blocking, and a half day of plumbing rerouting we didn't plan for. About $2,800 and pushed the schedule 3 days. Homeowner wasn't thrilled but I'd flagged the possibility in writing before demo, so the conversation was easy.

3/ The lesson isn't "old houses have surprises." Everybody knows that. It's that the change order conversation happens at contract signing, not when you're standing under a cut joist. I put a line in every proposal: concealed conditions = documented, photographed, priced before we proceed.

4/ 15 years in and the jobs that go sideways are almost never about the framing. They're about expectations nobody set. The joists were a Tuesday problem. Bad paperwork would've made them a lawsuit.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
# Why I've Fallen in Love with Winter Weddings (And Why You Should Consider One)

Let me be upfront: when I first started shooting weddings six years ago, I dreaded the off-season. January and February felt like dead months, and I thought weddings in the cold were just couples being "budget-conscious." I was wrong. Totally wrong.

In the last two years alone, I've shot eleven winter weddings. Not because I needed the work—my calendar fills up just fine. I kept saying yes because winter weddings have become some of my absolute favorite days to photograph.

Here's why.

## The Math Actually Makes Sense

This isn't a little discount. Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for you. That's real money—money you can put toward a longer bar, a better band, or a honeymoon you'll actually remember. And let me be honest: I've seen couples throw the money saved on not-hiring-a-photographer-because-it-was-too-expensive at a better flower arrangement or a dress they wouldn't have splurged on otherwise. The work doesn't suffer. My gear doesn't care what month it is.

## The Light is Genuinely Better

Here's the part that surprised me most. Around three o'clock in November, when the sun drops low and the trees are bare, the light that comes through those branches is honestly better for portraits than the flat overcast light I get on most June days. I don't say that lightly. I've shot hundreds of weddings in this metro area, and I've watched how the light behaves year after year. The winter sun angles are lower, softer, warmer—more flattering on skin, more glow on a veil, more drama on a suit jacket. In June, I'm often fighting harsh midday shadows or thick cloud cover that mutes everything. In November, I just point my camera and the light does most of the work.

## No Parking Lot Drama

This one is small but it matters. In June, by the time I roll up to a venue, I'm usually sharing the parking lot with three or four other vendors—the florist, the DJ, the caterer, the coordinator—all circling for spots, all arriving at the same time. In winter, I pull up and there's space. It sounds trivial, but when you're on a tight timeline and the couple has a specific sunset portrait window, not having to navigate vendor loading chaos makes the whole day run smoother.

## Eleven Weddings in Two Years Still Isn't Enough

I keep saying yes to winter weddings because they book fast. Couples who figure this out early tend to lock in the best dates. November and December dates—especially the Saturday after Thanksgiving—are still available in most cases, but not for long. And here's the thing: the couples who book winter weddings tend to be a little more adventurous, a little less stressed about checking every box, and a little more willing to just enjoy the day. That energy makes my job better, and it makes your photos better.

## So If You're Looking at Dates

I'm not telling you to rush. I'm telling you that if you haven't considered a winter wedding, you're missing out on cheaper rates, better light, and a relaxed vibe that's hard to recreate in peak season. And if you *have* considered one, now you know why my calendar is already starting to fill up.

Let's talk.

b.text:
Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now

I used to treat winter as the leftover season. Couples booked May through October, I shot May through October, and that was that. Then the last two years happened: eleven winter weddings. I stopped treating them like a discount category and started noticing what they actually give me as a photographer, and what they give you.

The light is the first thing. Around 3 p.m. in November the sun sits low and the trees are bare, so you get this directional, textured light cutting through branches that I cannot get in June. June overcast is flat. It is even, it is safe, and it is boring for portraits. I will take the November version every time.

The second thing is purely logistical and I did not expect to care this much. In June I am regularly sharing a venue parking lot with three or four other vendors unloading at the same time. In winter I am not. That extra space and the slower pace change the whole day for me. I can set up without rushing, I can move you without dodging another crew, and the portraits do not feel like they are happening in a traffic jam.

You also pay less. Winter bookings here run about 30 percent cheaper than peak dates. That is not a vague “off-season savings” line; it is the number I see on contracts. You get the same coverage, the same editing, and (in my experience) better light and a calmer day.

I still shoot plenty of summer weddings. I just stopped pretending winter is second-best. If you are still deciding dates, that is the version I would book if I were you.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
Why Juniors and Seniors Should Have Open Campus Lunch

Every day at 11:42 the bell rings and 340 of us try to fit into a cafeteria that only has seats for 220. People end up sitting on the floor in the hallway, standing around tables waiting for someone to leave, or scarfing down food in five minutes so they can get out. We have a lunch period that is supposed to be a break, but right now it's just stressful and crowded. Our school should allow open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. 

The most immediate reason is space. We literally do not have enough room for everyone we put in that lunch wave. With 340 kids and only 220 seats, more than a hundred students don't have anywhere to sit. If even a third of juniors and seniors left campus to get food or just eat somewhere else, the cafeteria would finally be usable for the sophomores and freshmen who stay, and for the upperclassmen who prefer to stay. It's a practical fix to a physical problem we already have.

Some people worry that if students leave campus they won't come back on time, or that it will cause problems in the community. That hasn't been the case at schools near us. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow open campus lunch for their upperclassmen, and their published attendance reports showed no rise in tardiness after they changed the policy. That matters because those districts are a lot like ours, and they have already tested it. If it made kids late, we would see it in their numbers. We don't.

The other part is that this is something students actually want, and we're old enough to handle it. I surveyed 80 students at our school across all grades and 71 of them said they were in favor of open campus for juniors and seniors. That's almost 90%. This isn't just about wanting Chick-fil-A. Most juniors and seniors can drive, a lot of us have jobs and other responsibilities outside of school, and we are about to be expected to manage our own time in college or at work next year. Being trusted to leave campus for 45 minutes and come back is a pretty basic way to start learning that responsibility.

I know the main argument against it is safety and liability. People say students could get in car accidents or get into trouble off campus. That's a valid concern, but keeping 340 kids packed into a room built for 220 isn't exactly safe either. And limiting it to juniors and seniors makes sense precisely because we are the oldest students. We are held to a higher standard with grades, attendance, and behavior, and if someone abuses the privilege it can be taken away. The other districts show you can do it without creating a bigger problem.

Open campus lunch for juniors and seniors would relieve our overcrowded cafeteria, it has already been shown to work without increasing tardiness nearby, and it's something the majority of students support. It's a small change that would make the school day work better for everyone.

b.text:
# Room to Breathe: Why Our School Should Allow Open Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors

Every day at 11:40, three hundred and forty students funnel into a cafeteria built to seat two hundred and twenty. The math does not work, and everyone who has ever eaten lunch sitting on the floor outside the gym already knows it. Our school should adopt an open campus lunch policy for juniors and seniors — a policy that would let upperclassmen leave school grounds during their lunch period. This is not a request for a privilege so much as a practical solution to a problem the school has not otherwise addressed, and the experience of nearby districts suggests the risks administrators worry about do not actually materialize.

The most immediate argument for open campus is that our current lunch arrangement is physically overcrowded. With 340 students assigned to a lunch wave and only 220 seats available, more than a third of the students in that wave have nowhere to sit down. The overflow spills into hallways and stairwells, which creates exactly the kind of congestion and supervision headache that administrators say they want to avoid. Letting juniors and seniors leave would reduce the number of bodies in that room without requiring the school to build anything, hire anyone, or restructure the master schedule. It is the cheapest fix available.

The strongest evidence that open campus can work here is that it already works nearby. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow open campus lunch for upperclassmen, and none of their published attendance data shows an increase in tardiness to fifth period since the policies were adopted. This matters because tardiness is the objection administrators raise first. The concern is reasonable in the abstract — students who leave might not come back on time — but three neighboring districts have effectively run the experiment for us, and the numbers did not move. If open campus reliably produced late students, it would be visible in the data of the districts closest to us, and it is not.

Student support for the policy is also overwhelming. In a survey I conducted of eighty students at our school, seventy-one said they were in favor of open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. That is nearly nine out of ten. A survey of eighty students is not a district-wide referendum, and I administered it myself rather than through the school, so it should be read as a strong indication rather than proof. Still, when a proposal has that level of buy-in from the people it affects, it is worth taking seriously — especially since a policy students actually want is a policy students are more likely to follow.

Critics will argue that open campus creates safety and liability problems, and this concern deserves a real answer rather than a dismissal. Students driving off campus and returning in a hurry is a genuine risk. But the same students already drive to school in the morning and away from it in the afternoon, and the school does not treat those trips as unacceptable dangers. Districts that allow open campus manage the risk with straightforward measures: parent permission forms, revocation of the privilege for students who abuse it, and grade and attendance requirements for eligibility. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade have not abandoned their policies, which suggests the risk is manageable at the scale of a normal high school.

Open campus lunch is not a radical idea. setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
Opening the Doors: The Case for Upperclassmen Open Campus Lunch

Every day during fourth period, the bell rings and a frantic footrace begins. The destination is not an exciting assembly or an early dismissal, but the cafeteria—a space designed to secure a seat before the room reaches a breaking point. For juniors and seniors balancing advanced coursework, jobs, and extracurriculars, the thirty-minute lunch block should offer a genuine break in the day. Instead, it is spent navigating long lines and congested tables. Implementing an open campus lunch policy for upperclassmen is not merely a request for more freedom; it is a practical solution to our school’s severe space constraints, backed by overwhelming student support and successful precedents in our neighboring districts.

The most immediate argument for open campus lunch is simple mathematics: our school does not have enough room to seat its students. Our cafeteria has an official seating capacity of 220 people, yet our current lunch wave forces roughly 340 students into the room at the exact same time. That leaves over one hundred students every day balancing trays on their laps in the hallway, sitting on the radiator covers, or standing near the garbage cans just to eat. By allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus for lunch, the school would naturally cut the cafeteria population down to a manageable number. This would immediately eliminate overcrowded hallways, shorten food lines, and create a safer, calmer environment for underclassmen who remain on campus. 

The primary administrative hesitation toward open campus lunch is usually the fear that students will return late or skip their afternoon classes. However, regional data shows this fear is unfounded. Three nearby districts—Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade—already permit open campus lunch for their upperclassmen. According to published attendance statistics from all three districts, none of them experienced a measurable rise in afternoon tardiness after implementing the policy. When students are granted a privilege that they value, they actively protect it by watching the clock and returning on time. High school juniors and seniors are on the verge of entering college or the workforce, where time management is an essential expectation. Letting them practice that responsibility in a controlled, daily setting actually reinforces good habits rather than breaking them.

Furthermore, this change aligns directly with what the student body wants and is ready for. In an informal survey conducted across our junior and senior classes, 71 out of 80 respondents—nearly 89 percent—expressed strong support for an open campus policy. Most students indicated they would use the time simply to grab food closer to home, run quick errands, or eat in a quieter environment where they can decompress. To address any lingering safety concerns, the school could easily implement basic guardrails, such as requiring parental permission forms and establishing minimum GPA or attendance benchmarks to maintain off-campus eligibility. 

Our current closed-campus model forces hundreds of students into an inadequate space while ignoring the proven success of neighboring schools. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave for lunch would instantly solve our cafeteria overcrowding, give students the opportunity to practice real-world accountability, and treat upperclassmen like the young adults they are. It is time for our administration to follow the evidence, trust its students, and open the doors.

b.text:
**Open Campus Lunch: A Practical Privilege for Upperclassmen**

Every day, 340 students at our school file into a cafeteria with 220 seats. The math doesn't work, and everyone who has survived that lunch wave knows it. Students eat sitting on hallway floors, balanced on the edges of trash cans, or standing in line so long that by the time they get food, half the period is gone. The district could spend years and millions of dollars expanding the cafeteria, or it could try something far simpler: let juniors and seniors leave campus for lunch. Our school should adopt an open campus lunch policy for upperclassmen because it would immediately relieve overcrowding, it is what the student body overwhelmingly wants, and nearby districts have already proven it can work.

The overcrowding problem alone justifies the change. A cafeteria built for 220 people cannot comfortably hold 340, and the difference isn't abstract. That's 120 students per lunch wave without a seat, every single day. Beyond being uncomfortable, it's a genuine health concern. Students who spend twenty minutes in line and ten minutes hunting for somewhere to sit end up rushing through meals or skipping them entirely. Open campus lunch addresses this without a single construction dollar. Even if only a portion of juniors and seniors chose to leave, the students who stayed would actually have a place to eat.

Students themselves clearly support the idea. In a survey I conducted of 80 students at our school, 71 said they were in favor of open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. That's nearly nine out of ten. Admittedly, 80 responses isn't the entire student body, but it's a strong signal of where opinion sits. It also makes sense when you consider who this policy would affect. Juniors and seniors are sixteen to eighteen years old. Many of them drive, hold jobs, and manage their own schedules outside of school. Within two years, every one of them will be in college, trade school, or the workforce, where nobody assigns them a lunch table or watches the clock for them. Being trusted with one unsupervised hour is not a radical leap. It's reasonable practice for the independence they're about to have.

The most common objection is that students won't come back. Administrators worry about tardiness, kids skipping afternoon classes, and the school's responsibility if something happens off campus. These concerns are fair, but they're predictions, and predictions can be checked against evidence. Three nearby districts, Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade, already allow open campus lunch for their upperclassmen. Their published statistics show no rise in tardiness since the policies were put in place. Three different communities had the same fears ours does, and the feared outcome simply didn't happen. On top of that, the policy can be designed to protect itself. Limit it to juniors and seniors, require students to sign out or show ID at the door, and revoke the privilege permanently for anyone who returns late. That structure punishes the individual rule-breaker instead of assuming every student will be one.

Right now, more than a hundred students eat lunch without a seat while a workable solution sits just outside the cafeteria doors. The students want it, the overcrowding demands it, and three neighboring districts have shown it succeeds without the problems critics predict. The administration should pilot open campus lunch for juniors and seniors next semester and judge it by the same attendance data that has vindicated it elsewhere. Upperclassmen are asking to be trusted with one hour a day. All the available evidence says they'll handle it.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
**The Market Didn't Crash. Your Listing Price Did.**

Last spring, the median home in our zip code sold in eight days. Eight. This spring? Thirty-four. Showings per listing have been cut in half. And yet, list prices are still up six percent year over year. If you're waiting for a crash, stop holding your breath. What we're seeing isn't a collapse—it's a standoff between sellers who are living in last year's market and buyers who finally have room to think.

Right now, I have three sellers who've been on the market for sixty-plus days. All three are refusing to drop their price. All three are convinced the right buyer is "just around the corner." Here's the truth I told them, and I'll tell you: that buyer isn't coming. Not at that price. The buyers are still here, but they're not desperate anymore. They're not waving inspections, they're not engaging in bidding wars, and they're certainly not paying 2021 premiums for 2023 interest rates.

The agents and sellers who have adjusted are doing just fine. In fact, homes priced correctly—*actually* correctly, not "let's shoot for the moon and see what happens"—are still selling in under two weeks. The inventory isn't flooding the market. The sky isn't falling. The fundamentals of our local market are still solid. What changed is the frenzy, and some sellers are having a hard time accepting that the feeding frenzy is over.

If you're selling, you need to make a decision. You can price your home for the market that exists today and sell it, or you can price it for the market that disappeared last summer and let it sit. There is no third option where you get last year's price with this year's patience. The data is right there: thirty-four days on market, half as many showings, and prices that are only up because the *right* inventory is still moving.

And if you're buying? This is the breathing room you've been waiting for. You can tour a home twice. You can sleep on it. You can negotiate. But don't expect a fire sale. The homes that sell quickly are still moving at strong numbers because they're priced with eyes wide open.

This isn't a crash. It's a correction in expectations. The sellers who recognize that will move on with their lives. The ones who don't will be decorating for the Fourth of July in a house they listed in April.

b.text:
Not a Crash. Just Sellers Who Won’t Listen.

Last spring, the median home in my zip went from contract to sold in eight days. This spring, it’s thirty-four. List prices are still up six percent year over year. Showings per listing are down by half. And I have three sellers right now—three—refusing to drop price after sixty-plus days on market. They aren’t wrong about their houses. They’re wrong about the clock.

This is not a market crash. It is a market that finally hit the speed limit.

For two years, buyers were desperate, inventory was thin, and pricing roughly meant “add ten percent and wait for the weekend war.” That era is dead. The new pace is measurable: price it right, and you’re still under contract in under two weeks. Price it like it’s 2021, and you’re collecting dust while fresh listings steal what little traffic is left.

The split is stark. The homes that came in at honest, current-value pricing moved fast—often in days, with real buyers, not ghosts. The ones priced on hope are sitting, and their owners are acting like the market is “complex” when really they just haven’t accepted that urgency is gone.

Take my three. One is comparing to a March sale that went eight percent over ask after a bidding war that no longer exists. Another won’t budge because “we put in the new kitchen,” as if buyers are no longer comparing every dollar across twenty listings. The third is waiting for “the right buyer,” who apparently stopped showing up because she won’t even book a second tour.

Here is the real opinion: this isn’t some complicated economic puzzle requiring months of analysis. It’s a seller-correction problem. Buyers are still out there, but they’re pickier, more discreet, and they have options—just fewer of them. That means your listing either fits their reality immediately, or it becomes the one they skip.

The data does not lie. Median days on market tripled. Traffic halved. But prices haven’t cratered because supply is still tight and homeowners who bought low aren’t panic-selling. What’s happening is a discipline market. The ones pricing to the new pace are selling. The ones pricing to their memory of spring 2022 are explaining to me why they need “one more weekend” on day sixty-three.

If you own a home here, stop treating this like a negotiation with the universe. Price for the pace that actually exists. The buyers who are left have options, and they are not paying a premium for a seller’s emotional holding cost.

The market didn’t break. The sellers who haven’t caught up did. Price it right, and you’ll still be done in under two weeks. Price it like last year, and you’ll be here with me, watching the calendar turn, wondering why the market “crashed” when all it did was move on without you.
