a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots (Before the Freeze)

Frozen outdoor spigots are one of the easiest problems to prevent and one of the most expensive to fix. Here's what you need to do, and it'll take you maybe 15 minutes.

## The Four Steps

**1. Shut off the interior valve**

Find the shutoff valve inside your house that controls water to that outdoor spigot. Usually it's in the basement, laundry room, or crawl space—look for a valve on the line running to the wall where your spigot is. Turn it clockwise until it stops. Don't force it.

**2. Drain the spigot**

Go outside and turn the handle on fully. Water should come out if there's any left in the line. Let it run for a few seconds, then turn it off.

**3. Disconnect your hoses**

This is the big one. I'm going to be direct: leaving hoses connected to your spigots is why we get slammed with burst-pipe calls in January. Water gets trapped in the hose, freezes, expands back into the line, and cracks the pipe inside your wall. Disconnect every hose, drain them out, and store them.

**4. Add a foam cover**

Pick up a foam spigot cover at any hardware store (around $3). Slip it over the spigot. It's not fancy, but it works.

## What If You Don't Have an Interior Shutoff?

Some older Minneapolis homes don't have interior shutoffs for outdoor lines. If that's you, call us. We can add one—it's a quick job and it's worth it for the peace of mind. It's also worth it so you're not the one calling us in January with a frozen pipe in the wall.

That's it. Do this before the first hard freeze and you won't have this problem.

b.text:
How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

Do this before the first hard freeze:

**1. Disconnect the hoses.**
This is the big one. Leaving a hose connected traps water in the spigot and pipe. It freezes, expands, and splits the pipe inside your wall. Most of our January burst-pipe calls in Minneapolis are exactly this.

Take the hoses off, drain them, and store them in the garage.

**2. Shut the interior valve.**
Go in the basement and find the shutoff for each outside spigot — usually on the ceiling right inside from where the spigot is outside. Turn it clockwise to shut it off.

No interior shutoff? Call us. A lot of older Minneapolis houses don’t have them. We can add one, or swap you to a frost-free sillcock.

**3. Drain the spigot.**
Now go back outside and open the spigot all the way. Then go back inside, put a bucket under that shutoff valve, and open the little bleeder cap on the side to let the leftover water drain out. Once it stops dripping, close the bleeder cap. Leave the outside spigot open about 45 degrees for winter.

**4. Put a foam cover on it.**
The $3 foam covers from Menards or Home Depot are worth it. They just slip over the spigot and cinch tight. It keeps wind off the valve.

That’s it. Takes 10 minutes and saves you a flooded basement in January.

If you can’t find a shutoff, or your spigot won’t fully shut off or keeps dripping, give us a call before it freezes and we’ll get you taken care of.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
Good evening, members of the council. My name is [Name], and I’m the owner of [Coffee Shop Name], the independent coffee shop on Main Street. I’m here to speak against the proposal to raise parking meter rates downtown from 50 cents to a dollar fifty an hour. I’m not going to lean on vague warnings—I’m going to give you the numbers, because I’ve lived them, tracked them, and I believe they make the stakes plain.

In 2019, the town right next to us put through a very similar meter hike—right around tripling the hourly rate. I have a good relationship with a shop owner there, and with his permission, I tracked his daily register data for the six weeks right after that change. What I found was an 18% drop in foot traffic. Not a slow decline over months—an immediate, sustained 18% loss of customers walking through the door. For a small coffee shop, that was the difference between a modest profit and a serious loss. We aren’t talking about a theoretical risk; we’ve already seen the experiment run a few miles away.

Now bring that closer to home. I clock my own customers’ visits. The average stay for someone grabbing a coffee and maybe sitting for a few minutes is 22 minutes. Under the current 50-cent-per-hour minimum, a customer drops two quarters and has plenty of time—they’re not rushed, they’re not bitter about paying for parking they didn’t use. But if you raise the meter to a dollar fifty, you’re forcing that same 22-minute customer to pay triple for a full hour they don’t need. For many of them, that’s the cost of the small coffee they just bought. They’ll feel it, and some of them will just stop coming downtown for what used to be a quick, easy ritual. You’ll be charging them 200% more for the same 22-minute errand, and in my business, that friction is real. I see it on faces when the sidewalk outside is empty.

Finally, I want to point to the city’s own numbers. Your own budget report shows that parking meter revenue currently covers just 4% of the downtown budget. Four percent. Tripling the rate might bump that slightly, but it won’t close any meaningful gap—it’s not going to fix roads, it’s not going to fund a new initiative. What it will do is bleed the very foot traffic that generates the sales tax, the business license fees, and the vibrancy that actually sustain our downtown. We are, right now, the shops and cafes that make Main Street a place people want to visit. An 18% drop in foot traffic, even if it’s only a fraction of that here, would wipe out far more in overall economic activity than this increase could ever return in meter coins.

I’m asking you, respectfully, to vote no. The data from next door, the 22-minute reality of my customers, and the 4% figure from your own report all tell the same story: this doesn’t solve a problem, but it will create one. Thank you for your time.

b.text:
**Submitted Testimony — Proposed Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase**

Dear Members of the City Council,

My name is [Name], and I own [shop name], a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I'm writing to ask you to vote against the proposal to raise downtown meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour.

That is not a modest adjustment. It is a tripling — a 200% increase — and it will land squarely on the people who keep downtown running: customers making short, small, everyday stops.

Start with my customers. The average visit to my shop is 22 minutes. A coffee, maybe a bag of beans, a quick hello. Under the current rate, 50 cents buys the hour, and the hour covers that visit comfortably — cheap enough that nobody thinks twice about stopping in. At $1.50, that same 22-minute errand costs three times as much before my customer has spent a single dollar with me. For a regular who stops in five mornings a week, parking goes from $2.50 a week to $7.50 — an extra $260 a year for the exact same cup of coffee. People won't experience that as parking policy. They'll experience it as a reason to go somewhere else.

And they will go somewhere else. I know, because I've measured it.

In 2019, when [neighboring town] raised its meter rates, I tracked my own register for six weeks after the change and compared it against the weeks just before. Foot traffic dropped 18%. I'm not an economist — I'm a shopkeeper with six weeks of actual transactions, counted at my own till. An independent shop does not absorb an 18% drop in foot traffic and carry on as usual. Numbers like that are the difference between a business that anchors a block and a vacant storefront that doesn't.

Now weigh that against what this increase would actually accomplish. According to the city's own report, meter revenue covers just 4% of the downtown budget. Even if every meter stayed occupied exactly as often as it does today — which my data says it won't — tripling the rate moves that figure to roughly 12%. If usage falls anywhere near the 18% I measured, you're under 10%. So the proposal on the table is this: impose a 200% price increase on the customers of every small business downtown, in exchange for a single-digit dent in the budget. That doesn't solve anything. It shifts a cost onto the people least able to absorb it, in service of a gap the city's own numbers say this cannot close.

Downtown's real product isn't parking. It's the ease of parking for pocket change, running in for 22 minutes, and leaving feeling like the trip was simple. Triple the friction and people will get their coffee at a drive-through with a free lot — and once a habit moves, it rarely comes back.

Vote no on this increase. If the council believes downtown needs more revenue, there are fairer places to find it than a 22-minute errand. I can tell you from 18% worth of experience how this one ends.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this for the record.

Respectfully,
[Name]
[Shop name], Main Street

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
# Why I Stopped Talking Couples Out of Winter Weddings

For years, if you told me you wanted a January wedding, I'd nod politely and quietly hope you'd reconsider. I don't do that anymore. Over the last two years I've shot eleven winter weddings, and somewhere in there I stopped seeing the season as a compromise and started seeing it as a genuinely good choice. Here's the honest version of why.

## The light in November is doing me favors

This is the one that actually changed my mind. There's a stretch around 3pm in late fall when the sun sits low and comes sideways through bare trees, and it does something to portraits that I can't fake. It's directional, it's warm, it wraps around faces instead of flattening them.

Compare that to a lot of June weddings, where you get high, hazy overcast light that's technically "even" but honestly a little dead. Everyone thinks summer means better photos. For portraits specifically, I'd take that low winter angle almost every time.

## You're not sharing me with a crowd

In June I'm one of four vendors trying to get into the same building, elbowing for the same twenty minutes of good light, waiting my turn in a parking lot full of other people's vans. Everyone's rushed. Everyone's on a schedule that's already slipping.

Winter is quiet. I'm not competing with three other photographers for the good corner of the venue. I have time and space to actually work, which means you get more out of me, not less.

## And it costs you about 30% less

I'll just say it plainly: winter bookings tend to run around 30% cheaper for the couple. Venues, vendors, all of it. So you're not paying a premium to get worse light and a busier vendor. You're paying less for a better version of the day, at least from where I'm standing behind the camera.

## So, when should you book?

If you've had your heart set on a certain season, I'm not here to argue you out of it. But if you're flexible, and you've been assuming summer is the "real" wedding season, I'd genuinely encourage you to look at the winter dates. The photos hold up. The day feels calmer. And your budget goes further.

If you want to talk through dates, [reach out](#) and I'll walk you through what's still open.

b.text:
# Why I Actually Like Photographing Winter Weddings Now

After six years photographing weddings, mostly in the same metro area, I have opinions about seasons. And lately, winter has been moving up my list.

I’ve photographed 11 winter weddings in the last two years. That’s enough to say this isn’t me remembering one unusually lovely afternoon and building a whole argument around it. I genuinely like shooting them now—and not just because couples can save money.

Although, let’s start there.

## About 30% cheaper is worth talking about

Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for the couple. The exact difference depends on your date and what you’re booking, but that’s a meaningful amount—not a tiny discount you’ll barely notice.

It might give you room for something you really want. It might simply mean spending less on your wedding. Both are perfectly good outcomes.

I wouldn’t tell you to choose a winter date solely for the savings if you’ve always wanted an outdoor ceremony in warm weather. But if you’re choosing a June Saturday because it feels like the default, winter deserves a proper look before you commit.

## I’ll take November light through bare trees

Here’s my very specific photography opinion: the light coming through bare trees around 3 p.m. in November is honestly better for portraits than flat, overcast June light.

Overcast summer light is easy to work with. It’s soft and fairly predictable. But easy isn’t always interesting.

That low November sun can give portraits direction and depth. Without a full canopy of leaves, light reaches places it doesn’t in summer. The branches make a quieter backdrop, and we can use the light coming between them rather than hunting for a gap in dense shade.

This is not a promise that your November wedding will come with sunshine. Weather remains weather. But winter light isn’t something I’m reluctantly making the best of. On the right afternoon, it’s the light I’d choose.

The catch is timing. If you want those portraits, we need to build the day around the available daylight. We can’t leave them until after a late-afternoon ceremony and expect June hours.

## Even the parking lot is less of a production

This isn’t the glamorous part of wedding photography, but it affects how a day feels.

In June, I’m often sharing the parking lot with three or four other vendors, all trying to get where they need to be. There’s equipment coming out of cars, people unloading, and everyone working against a clock.

At winter weddings, I’m not dealing with that same parking-lot pileup.

Does a quieter parking lot make your portraits better by itself? No. But fewer logistical bottlenecks help. Getting in, getting set up, and moving between parts of the day with less friction is genuinely pleasant. After six years, I appreciate that more than I expected to.

## Winter works best when we plan for winter

I like winter weddings. I don’t like pretending they’re summer weddings with different flowers.

There’s less daylight. It may be cold enough that a long outdoor portrait session stops being fun very quickly. We need an indoor option we actually like, not just somewhere to retreat if the weather gets unpleasant.

My approach is to plan the outdoor photographs deliberately: know where we’re going, use the best light we have, and avoid keeping you outside longer than necessary. Then let you get back to your people.

That’s also why I’d rather talk about your photography timeline before you lock in every detail of the day. A small change to the ceremony time can make a big difference to what’s possible.

## So, should you book a winter wedding?

If warm evenings and a late sunset are central to the wedding you want, probably not. There’s no need to talk yourself out of something you care about.

But if you’re flexible on the season, I’d seriously consider it. About 30% cheaper, the possibility of genuinely excellent portrait light, and less of the June logistical scrum are solid reasons.

Eleven winter weddings in two years have changed how I think about these dates. I’m not looking at them as the compromise option anymore.

If you’re weighing a winter date, get in touch before you set the ceremony time. Let’s look at the daylight as well as the calendar.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
Don’t Cut Apprenticeship Funding

I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with our local IBEW union. I’m writing this because the state is proposing a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding. That cut is a mistake. I want to explain why in plain language.

The group I started with had 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of them have finished and are working journeyman jobs now. I’m in my third year and still working toward that same goal. That’s a real track record: 21 trained electricians, on the job, paying taxes.

This is not a handout. It is a job with training attached. Apprentices start at about $19 an hour. Journeymen top out at about $46 an hour. That means people get off assistance programs fast. An apprentice is earning a paycheck from the start. By the time we finish, we are making a solid living and paying taxes.

Here are the cost numbers. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. The average public subsidy per four-year graduate who finishes is about $48,000. For our 21 finishers, the public cost was about $294,000. If the state had paid the average four-year public subsidy for those same 21 people, it would have been about $1,008,000. Same people. Different path. Far lower cost to taxpayers.

A 15% cut sounds small. In real life, it means fewer apprentices, fewer instructors, and fewer trained electricians. We already have more work than we have people. Cutting this funding would save a little money now but cost more later. Instead of having workers making up to $46 an hour and paying taxes, the state would be left with more people who need help and fewer people paying in.

I’m not asking for anything fancy. I’m asking the state to keep funding a program that works. I’m asking legislators to vote no on the 15% cut. Keep apprenticeship funding whole, so the next group of 24 can start, learn the trade, and go to work.

— A third-year electrical apprentice, IBEW

b.text:
I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with IBEW, and I’m writing about the proposed 15% cut to state apprenticeship funding.

Our program works. My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished, and now we’re all working journeyman jobs. That’s a completion rate that speaks for itself.

I started at $19 an hour. By the time I finish, I’ll be topping out at around $46 an hour. I’m earning a middle-class wage while I learn, and most of us get off public assistance fast because of it.

The numbers back this up. It costs the state about $14,000 to train one apprentice who finishes. Compare that to the $48,000 average public subsidy for a four-year college graduate—and many of them don’t even end up working in their field.

A 15% cut won’t just hurt us apprentices. It’ll shrink the pool of skilled workers, slow down projects that keep the state running, and make it harder for people to build a career without going deep into debt or staying on assistance programs.

I ask the legislators reading this: fund apprenticeships, don’t cut them. The data is clear. The workers are ready. Don’t throw away a model that gets people into good jobs, at good wages, at a fraction of the cost.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
**Testimony of Mia Carter, Owner, Rowan & Bean Coffee Co.**  
Before the Maplewood City Council  
Public Hearing on Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase  
November 12, 2024  

Good evening, Mayor, Councilmembers, and members of the public. My name is Mia Carter, and I own and operate Rowan & Bean Coffee Co. at 142 Main Street, a small independent shop I opened in 2018 with my sister, employing seven part-time local high school and college students and sourcing 65% of our pastries from family-owned bakers within 15 miles of downtown. I am not here tonight to offer vague claims about harm to small businesses. I am here with hard, verifiable data—from my own cash registers, my own customer tracking, and the city’s own public reports—to show that the proposed increase to downtown meter rates, which would rise from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour, will cause measurable, lasting harm to my shop and the broader downtown ecosystem, while failing to meaningfully address the budget shortfalls it is being framed to fix.

First, I have direct, first-hand experience with exactly this rate hike, because I owned a sister coffee shop in our neighboring town of Ashford, 8 miles east of Maplewood, from 2016 to 2021. In March 2019, Ashford implemented the identical rate increase: 50 cents to $1.50 per hour for all curbside downtown meters. For the six weeks immediately following that hike, I tracked transaction counts at my own register there, comparing daily foot traffic to the same six-week period in 2018, controlling for weather, local events, and seasonal variation to isolate the impact of the rate change. The result? An 18% drop in customer foot traffic. That is not a survey, not a projection, not a guess. That is 1,187 fewer customers walking through my Ashford shop’s doors in those six weeks, directly correlated with the meter increase. Over the following year, that drop forced me to cut three part-time barista shifts—shifts held by two Ashford High School students saving for college and a single mom working to pay rent. That is the tangible cost of a rate hike this steep, and it will be repeated here if this proposal passes.

The impact will be even more disproportionate for my Main Street shop, because of how short the vast majority of my customers’ visits actually are. I track visit length via my point-of-sale system and table-turn data, which I use to schedule staff and manage inventory, and the average customer visit to Rowan & Bean is 22 minutes. Even the small subset of customers who bring laptops to work or study stay an average of 37 minutes—still well under the one-hour minimum block the city already requires for meter payment. Right now, a customer pays 50 cents for a parking spot that more than covers their entire stay, with time to spare. Under the proposed hike, that same 22-minute coffee run would cost them $1.50: triple the price, for time they never use. For a customer who comes in for a $2.75 drip coffee, that is a 54% increase in the total cost of their stop, just for parking. I already hear from at least four regulars a week who circle the block twice to find free street parking two blocks west of downtown, rather than pay 50 cents for a meter spot. Tripling that cost will push those customers—and many more—to patronize businesses on the west side of town, or the chain coffee shops on Route 9 with free, dedicated parking lots.

Finally, this rate hike is being sold as a solution to downtown maintenance shortfalls, but the city’s own data shows it will barely move the needle on that problem. The 2024 Maplewood Downtown Operations Budget Report, published on the city’s website last month, states explicitly that parking meter revenue contributes just 4% of the total downtown operating budget. Let me repeat that number so there is no confusion: four cents of every dollar the city spends on downtown sidewalk repairs, trash pickup, public restrooms, and holiday lighting comes from parking meter revenue. Even if you assume the rate hike would not reduce parking usage at all—which my 2019 Ashford data proves it will—tripling meter rates would only raise that contribution to roughly 12% of the downtown budget. That is not a solution. That is a tiny band-aid, applied at the expense of the customers and small businesses that generate the other 96% of the downtown budget through sales taxes, property taxes, and local business fees. If we lose even 10% of downtown foot traffic from this hike, the lost sales tax revenue will easily outpace any new meter revenue we bring in. My 2019 data shows we will lose almost twice that.

I know this council wants a thriving downtown. I want that too. I poured my life savings into opening my shop on Main Street because I believe in this downtown’s potential, and I show up every day at 4:45 a.m. to make it a place people want to visit. But tripling parking meter rates is not the way to support that success. Instead of pushing a rate hike that will drive away customers and barely fund our downtown needs, I ask that this council table this proposal and work with the Downtown Small Business Association to explore alternative revenue streams: like expanding paid parking to the underused city-owned garage on Oak Avenue, which is currently free and sits 42% empty on most weekdays; or implementing a voluntary downtown improvement district assessment, which would spread the cost of maintenance across all downtown property owners rather than putting the burden solely on customers who patronize small shops.

I am happy to share all of my register data, my visit length tracking, and my notes from the 2019 Ashford hike with any councilmember who wants to review it. All I ask is that you make this decision based on hard numbers, not assumptions. The numbers are clear: this hike will cut foot traffic by double digits, reduce hours for local workers, and fail to fix the budget shortfall it is supposed to address. Thank you for your time.

b.text:
To the members of the City Council and the public record,

My name is the owner of the independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am writing to submit my formal testimony in strong opposition to the proposed parking meter rate increase from $0.50 to $1.50 per hour in our downtown district. 

While I understand the city must manage its infrastructure, this 200% increase is a direct threat to the survival of Main Street’s small businesses. I am not speaking in vague hypotheticals; I am basing my opposition on concrete data from my own register and the city’s own financial reports.

First, we must look at how consumers actually use our downtown. My business relies on quick, daily interactions. I have tracked our customer patterns closely, and our average customer spend time in the shop is exactly 22 minutes. Under the current rate of $0.50 per hour, my customers are already paying for more time than they actually use. Tripling the rate to $1.50 per hour means a customer stopping in for a $4.50 cup of coffee is hit with an additional 33% "tax" just to park. This creates a massive psychological barrier for locals who want to support independent shops but will choose drive-thrus outside the downtown core to avoid the hassle and cost of the meters. 

We already have a clear blueprint of what happens when these hikes are implemented. In 2019, when a neighboring town implemented a nearly identical rate increase, I closely monitored my own register and foot traffic data. For the six weeks following their hike, foot traffic in that downtown commercial district dropped by 18%. For a small, independent business operating on thin margins, an 18% drop in foot traffic is catastrophic. It is the difference between hiring local staff and cutting hours; it is the difference between staying open and emptying another storefront on Main Street.

Finally, we must ask if this local economic damage is justified by the city's projected return. According to the city’s own annual budget report, parking meter revenue accounts for a mere 4% of the total downtown budget. Tripling the meter rate is a drop in the bucket for the city, yet it represents a mountain to the independent merchants who generate the actual economic and cultural life of this district. 

We cannot solve a municipal budget issue by penalizing the small businesses that keep our downtown alive. An 18% drop in customer traffic is too high a price to pay for a policy that only impacts 4% of the downtown budget. 

I urge the City Council to reject this rate increase and instead work with the Main Street Business Association to find sustainable, non-destructive ways to support our downtown infrastructure. 

Thank you for your time and your consideration.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
I finished my first clinical rotation in the ER last week. As a first-year nursing student, I thought class had prepared me. It hadn’t.

One of the first things that hit me was holding a stranger’s hand. A man came in with a wound that needed cleaning. It was deep and he was hurting bad. His wife was stuck in traffic and couldn’t get there. While the nurse cleaned it, I just held his hand. He squeezed hard every time the pain hit, and I squeezed back. I told him it was okay to squeeze as much as he needed. We didn’t talk much. I just stayed there until it was over.

Later they called a code. Everyone moved fast. They sent me to restock the gauze because I was still learning the ropes. I stood by the supply cart filling it, and through the curtain I could hear them counting. One, two, three. Over and over. I knew what that sound meant. Someone’s heart had stopped and they were trying to bring them back. My side of the curtain was quiet. Their side wasn’t.

Then there was the blood draw. An older diabetic guy with veins that just wouldn’t cooperate. I stuck him once and missed. Twice and missed. Three times and still nothing. I felt terrible. Kept apologizing. He just looked at me and said it was fine, keep going, he’d been through worse. On the fourth try I got it. The tube started to fill and I finally breathed again.

None of those moments were big or dramatic from the outside. Holding a hand because someone else’s wife was stuck in traffic. Hearing the count through a curtain while I restocked gauze. Missing a simple stick three times before I got it right. But they stuck with me. They showed me that nursing is mostly about showing up when people are scared or hurting or waiting, even when you’re new and your hands shake and you don’t get it perfect the first time.

I want to keep learning how to do this. A scholarship would take some of the money pressure off so I can focus on becoming the kind of nurse those patients needed that week.

b.text:
I thought my first ER clinical would be all fast moves and big emergencies. Instead, I learned that a lot of nursing happens in the small parts.

On my first day, I did not know where to stand. My shoes squeaked on the floor, and I kept holding my clipboard like it was there to protect me. A nurse asked if I wanted to help with a wound cleaning, and I said yes. The patient had cut his arm. His wife was supposed to be there, but she was stuck in traffic. He kept looking toward the door.

When the nurse got ready to clean the wound, he looked nervous. I asked if he wanted someone to stay with him. He nodded. When the cleaning started, he grabbed my hand. His grip was tight, and his fingers were cold. I did not say much. I just stood there and let him hold on. The nurse worked carefully and talked him through each step. When he squeezed harder, I stayed still. When he opened his eyes and looked at me, I told him he was doing good.

It felt like a small thing, but when his wife finally came in, his shoulders relaxed. He let go of my hand and said, “Thank you for not leaving.” I did not have a big medical skill for that moment. I just had to be there. But I learned that being there can still be part of care.

Later that week, I was helping where I could when a code started behind a curtain. Someone told me we needed more gauze, so I went to get it. My hands felt clumsy while I opened cabinets and counted packs. Through the curtain, I could hear voices counting. They sounded quick but calm. It reminded me that emergency care is not just chaos. It is people doing their jobs one step at a time.

I brought the gauze back and put it where I was told. Nobody cheered. There was no big moment for me. But I felt what it means to be part of a team. Sometimes your job is not the dramatic part. Sometimes your job is to make sure the next person has what they need.

The moment I keep thinking about the most was a blood draw. The patient had diabetes and bad veins. He already looked tired, and he had been poked enough for one day. A nurse asked if I wanted to try, and I said yes because I wanted to do it right.

The first try did not work. I apologized. He said it was okay. The second try did not work either. I could feel my face getting hot. I tried again and missed. I wanted to walk away. I thought maybe I was not cut out for this. But the patient looked at me and said, “Take your time.”

I took a breath and tried again. This time I went slower. I found a vein, held still, and watched the blood fill the tube. I felt relief more than pride. I was grateful he gave me another chance. After I finished, I thanked him for being patient with me. He said, “You’ll get better.” I know I will.

That week taught me that nursing is not only about what you can do with your hands. It is also about how you show up. I held a stranger’s hand while he was scared. I helped during a code by doing a small task. I missed a blood draw three times, then tried again with a patient who let me learn.

I am still new. I still do not know a lot. But I know I want to be the kind of nurse who stays calm, keeps trying, and treats people like people instead of tasks. My first week in the ER made me more sure about nursing, not because I felt perfect, but because I felt real. I want to keep learning, and I want to earn the trust patients gave me before I fully knew what I was doing.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**An 8:45 Start Gives Millbrook Students a Better Morning**

As the parent of two middle-schoolers in Millbrook, I know that getting out the door in the morning is not always easy. There are lost shoes, unfinished homework, forgotten water bottles—and, most of all, tired kids. That is why I support the school board’s proposal to move the middle-school start time to 8:45 a.m.

This is not about giving students permission to sleep until noon. It is about recognizing how much sleep adolescents actually need. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later so that students have a better chance of getting the 8½ to 9½ hours of sleep recommended for their age group. An 8:45 start would bring Millbrook in line with that guidance.

We already have local evidence that a later start can help. During the pilot at Lincoln Middle School, attendance improved, and first-period grades went up. Those results matter. They suggest that students were not simply arriving later; they were arriving more consistently and were better prepared to learn when they got there.

As a parent, I have seen the difference a rested morning can make. A child who is exhausted is more likely to be irritable, forgetful, and disengaged. A child who has had enough sleep is more likely to participate, manage frustration, and make it through the school day ready to learn. No schedule can solve every academic or family challenge, but starting at 8:45 is a practical step in the right direction.

The most common objection I hear is about buses. That concern deserves attention, but it should not be used to dismiss the proposal. The plan already includes re-tiering the bus routes. In other words, the district is not ignoring transportation; it is working to reorganize the schedule so the later middle-school start can function within the broader system. We should evaluate the details carefully, but we should also judge the proposal as it actually exists—not as if no transportation planning has been done.

Changing the morning routine may take adjustment for families, just as any schedule change would. But our children’s health, attendance, and ability to learn deserve serious consideration. The Lincoln pilot gave us encouraging results, and the AAP recommendation gives us a clear reason to act.

For our middle-school students, 8:45 is not too late. It may be just in time.

b.text:
I have a 12-year-old who cannot find his backpack at 7 a.m. I have a 13-year-old who fell asleep in first period last Tuesday. I love them both, and I am asking the school board to vote yes on the 8:45 start time.

If you've parented a middle-schooler, you know the mornings. The alarm goes off and you're watching a teenager try to fold a shirt and remember their name at the same time. It isn't laziness. Their bodies are genuinely fighting them. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m., because adolescent sleep cycles shift — teenagers physically cannot fall asleep early enough to get the rest they need before an 8 a.m. bell. The AAP puts the recommended nightly sleep at 8.5 to 9.5 hours. Do the math from a 7 a.m. wake-up and you get the picture most of us are already living at our kitchen tables.

We don't have to guess whether later starts help. Lincoln Middle ran a pilot last year, and two numbers stand out: attendance went up, and first-period grades went up. That isn't a theory. That's our neighbors' kids, in a school like ours, showing up more and learning more in the very class that used to feel like a sleep study.

I know the bus question is on a lot of minds. The proposal already accounts for it. The transportation team re-tiered the routes, which means a staggered pickup schedule replaces the old one-size-fits-all grid. It's not a hidden cost or an afterthought — it's built into the plan. Parents who want the details can see the new tier map at the district office. Reasonable people can disagree about specific tweaks, but "the buses won't work" is not a reason to deny a generation of kids the sleep their doctors say they need.

I am not a sleep researcher. I am a parent who has watched two children drag themselves through early-morning classes and come home too wiped out to do anything but stare at a screen. The board has a chance next month to fix that. Vote yes on 8:45.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
Before my first shift in the emergency room, I thought I was ready. I had memorized the textbook chapters, passed my skills checks, and ironed my scrubs. But nothing in a classroom prepares you for the actual speed and noise of the ER. My first week on the floor put everything I thought I knew to the test, and it showed me exactly why I want to be a nurse.

On my second day, a doctor had to clean out a deep, dirty leg wound on an older man. The patient was terrified, mostly because his wife was stuck in traffic on the highway and he was in the room alone. He looked over at me, standing near the door in my student uniform, and held out his hand. I walked over and took it. I didn’t know any big speeches or clinical tricks to make it hurt less, so I just stood there and let him squeeze my hand until his knuckles turned white. In that moment, I realized that half of nursing is just showing up and refusing to let a stranger be scared by themselves. 

Later that week, a code was called. As a first-year student, I wasn't qualified to do much, so the charge nurse sent me to restock supplies to keep me out of the way. I stood just outside the curtain with an armload of rolled gauze, stocking the plastic bins while the team worked inside. Through the fabric, I could hear the rhythm of the chest compressions and a nurse steadily counting out loud: *one, two, three, four...* Hearing that count through the curtain was heavy. It made the reality of life and death in the ER very real, very fast. It was terrifying, but it didn't push me away. It made me want to work harder so that one day I can step behind that curtain and be useful when a life is on the line.

The week also taught me that learning this job takes thick skin and patience. Near the end of my rotation, I had to do a blood draw on a diabetic patient whose veins were rolled and scarred from years of pricks. My hands were shaking. I missed the vein on the first attempt. I wiped the area, tried again, and missed a second time. Sweat was running down my back, and my stomach dropped. I missed a third time. I apologized, feeling like a complete failure, but the man just smiled and said, "Take a breath, kid. Try again." On the fourth try, I found it, and the tube filled up. That patient showed me more grace than I deserved, and those three misses taught me more about resilience and composure than any successful draw ever could.

This first week in the ER stripped away any romantic ideas I had about healthcare. It is loud, messy, and hard work. But it is also the only thing I want to do with my life. This scholarship would help cover my tuition and clinical fees so I can keep focusing on my studies without taking on extra financial stress. I want to finish this program, get my license, and be the kind of nurse who stays calm, keeps trying, and holds the patient's hand when they need it most.

b.text:
**Four Tries**

Before my first week in the emergency room, I had a picture in my head of what I would be doing. I would be moving fast. I would be needed. Nobody told me how much of it would be standing there.

The first day, a man came in with a cut across his forearm from a piece of sheet metal at work. It wasn't life-threatening, but it was deep and it needed to be cleaned out before they could close it. The nurse told me to stand on his other side. That was my whole assignment. Stand there.

He kept looking at the door. His wife was coming from across town and she was stuck on the highway. He said she'd be here any minute, and then he said it again, and then the nurse started irrigating the wound and he grabbed my hand without asking. I don't think he even knew he did it. He squeezed hard enough that my fingers went white. I didn't know what to say to him, so I asked him what his wife drove, and he told me, and then he told me about the traffic on that road and how they should have widened it years ago. He talked about that road for ten minutes. When his wife walked in he let go of my hand and I stepped back and I don't think he ever really looked at me. That was fine. I wasn't the point.

On the third day there was a code. I was standing at the nurses' station and everything changed at once, people moving toward one bay, someone pulling the cart. My preceptor looked at me and said, "Go restock gauze in bay six." I knew what that meant. It meant get out of the way. I went.

Bay six shared a curtain with where they were working. I stood there with my hands full of packages and I could hear them counting compressions. Twenty-eight, twenty-nine, thirty. Then a pause, then somebody's voice, then counting again. Nobody was yelling. I had expected yelling. It was steady, almost boring, the way you'd count out change. I put the gauze in the drawer very slowly so I'd have a reason to stay. I don't know what happened to that patient. Nobody told me and I didn't ask. I think about the counting more than anything else from that week.

The last day I was supposed to draw blood on a man in his sixties with diabetes. He had been stuck a lot in his life. His veins rolled, they were scarred, and I could barely feel them. I missed. I apologized. He said don't worry, everybody misses on him. I missed again. My face was hot. My preceptor asked if I wanted her to take over and before I could answer he said, "No, let her go again." I missed the third time and I wanted to leave the room. He said, "You're close." I don't know how he could tell.

The fourth time I got it. Blood came into the tube and he said, "There you go," like I'd done him a favor. I hadn't. I had hurt him four times. But he had decided I was going to get it, and he was willing to wait for me to catch up to him.

I thought my first week would tell me whether I was cut out for this. It didn't. Most of what I did was stand there, get sent away, and fail three times before something worked. What it told me is that I want to go back. I want to be the person doing the counting, not the one listening through the curtain. That is going to take a lot more school and a lot more misses. I'm ready for both.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
**Headline: Don’t Cut the Apprenticeship Funding That Actually Works**  
By a Third-Year IBEW Local [XXX] Electrical Apprentice

I’m not a policy expert. I spend most days with wire cutters in my hand, grease under my nails, and a tool belt digging into my hips, same as most of you reading this. But when I heard the state’s trying to slash apprenticeship funding by 15%, I knew I had to say something—because this program isn’t just a line item on a budget. It’s the reason I’m off food stamps, making a living wage, and don’t have to worry about how I’ll pay my kid’s daycare bill next month.

Let’s cut the crap and talk real numbers, no fancy spin, no academic jargon. The cohort I signed up with started with 24 apprentices. 21 of us finished all our required hours and classroom work, and every single one of those 21 is working a full-time journeyman job right now. No one’s scraping by on part-time gigs. No one’s collecting unemployment. We’re showing up to build schools, hospitals, and new housing, paying our taxes, and taking care of our families.

Here’s what that looks like for working people: apprentices start around $19 an hour. That’s not rich, but it’s enough to cover rent and put food on the table, even when you’re first starting out. By the time you top out as a journeyman, you’re making around $46 an hour, plus health insurance and a pension. I was on SNAP and Medicaid when I joined—my kid was a toddler then, and I was bouncing between odd construction jobs that didn’t pay enough to cover groceries and daycare. By my second year in the program, after two regular pay bumps, I was off both public assistance programs entirely. I didn’t need a handout anymore, because this program gave me a shot at a real career. That’s not just my story—most first- and second-year apprentices in our local will tell you the same thing: we don’t stay on public help long once we’re in this program.

Now let’s talk about the taxpayer side of this, because the legislators pushing this cut are saying they’re “saving money.” Let’s run the actual math, not the made-up numbers they’re using to sell this garbage. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes the program is about $14,000. Compare that to the average public subsidy for a four-year college grad who finishes their degree: $48,000. That’s more than three times as much money, and we all know how many college grads are stuck working jobs that don’t even need their degree, drowning in student loans, and not making half of what a journeyman electrician pulls down.

A 15% cut to apprenticeship funding isn’t saving money—it’s throwing away the best deal taxpayers get in this state. Let’s be clear about what that cut will actually do: it will mean fewer apprenticeship slots every year. Fewer people getting a shot at a middle-class job without going into tens of thousands of dollars in debt. More people stuck on public assistance for longer. And fewer qualified electricians to build all the new projects the state keeps saying it wants to prioritize—you can’t put up a new hospital or a new school without enough people to wire the place.

To my brothers and sisters in the local: this isn’t just about new apprentices. More skilled journeymen in our local mean we can take on bigger jobs, negotiate better contracts, and keep our union strong for everyone—from the first-year apprentice to the retired member collecting their pension. If you haven’t called your state rep or state senator yet, do it this week. Tell them what this program did for you, or for your kid, or for the apprentice you’re training on the job right now. Your voice matters a lot more than some lobbyist’s talking point.

To the state legislators who might be reading this: stop buying the myth that a four-year college degree is the only “real” career path. I work side by side with guys who quit college because they were $20,000 in debt and still couldn’t find a job that paid $15 an hour. This program works. It works for working people. It works for local contractors who need reliable, skilled workers. And it works for taxpayers, who get a way better return on their investment than they do from almost any other workforce program in the state.

This 15% cut isn’t fiscal responsibility. It’s cutting the only program that’s actually delivering on what it promises. I’m an electrician, not an English professor, so I’ll keep it as plain as I can: vote no on this cut. Our tax dollars should go to programs that get people to work, off public assistance, and paying into the system—not the other way around.

b.text:
Don’t Cut the Ladder We’re Climbing

I’m a third-year apprentice with our local IBEW. I’m not a politician and I’m not an English professor, so I’ll keep this plain and direct.

The state wants to cut apprenticeship funding by 15 percent. That is a bad idea, and the numbers show why.

My cohort started with 24 apprentices. 21 of us finished and are working journeyman jobs right now. That’s 21 people who came in off the street, learned a real trade, and now earn a living without leaning on public assistance.

Apprentices start at about $19 an hour. That is not rich, but it is enough to stay off most assistance programs from day one. By the time we top out as journeymen, we make around $46 an hour. In a few short years, a person goes from just getting by to supporting a family, paying taxes, and buying a home. That is a fast turnaround.

The total public cost for each apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to a four-year college degree. The average public subsidy for each graduate who finishes is around $48,000. I am not knocking college, but if we are talking about return on investment, our path costs taxpayers about a third as much and puts people to work faster.

My class proves it works. We started with 24. 21 are now working journeyman jobs. Those are not numbers on a spreadsheet. Those are my brothers and sisters on the job site every morning, paying union dues and paying state taxes.

Cutting apprenticeship funding by 15 percent will not save money. It will shrink the next class. Fewer apprentices now means fewer journeymen five years from now. That means fewer licensed electricians when our state needs them for new construction, maintenance, and new energy work. It means more work going to unlicensed or out-of-state workers. And it means more young people stuck in low-wage jobs with no clear path up.

The state says it cares about workforce development. Well, this is workforce development that works. You can see the results in every finished building in our area. You can see them in the 21 people from my class who showed up, did the work, and earned their ticket. Cutting our funding is not trimming fat. It is cutting the rungs off the ladder while people are still climbing.

To the legislators reading this: do not balance the budget on the backs of apprentices. We are not asking for a handout. We are asking you to keep funding a program that pays for itself many times over. Fourteen thousand dollars to turn a first-year apprentice into a $46-an-hour journeyman is a deal you should be expanding, not cutting.

Keep the funding. Keep the apprentices. Keep the promise that if you work hard in this state, you can build a career.

— A third-year IBEW apprentice

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After twelve years of selling real estate in Asheville, mostly to first-time buyers, I’ve developed a handful of quiet rules. My favorite one to share is simple: if you’re serious about putting in an offer, walk the street at 7:00 on a weekday morning first.

Everyone falls in love with a house on a sunny Saturday afternoon. The light hits the hardwoods, the neighborhood feels peaceful, and nobody is rushing anywhere. But you don’t live your life in Saturday afternoons. You live it on Tuesday mornings.

A few years back, I was working with the Pruitts on a 1940s cottage off Sycamore Street. On paper, it checked every box. Beautiful screened porch, fenced yard for their dog, and an easy drive into town. During our second walkthrough on a Friday afternoon, they were ready to write an offer right there on the kitchen counter. 

I asked them to hold off and meet me at the corner of Sycamore at 7:15 the following Tuesday with travel mugs of coffee. 

When you walk a neighborhood while it’s waking up, the real personality comes out. On Sycamore, it wasn't bad news, but it was real clarity. We discovered that the street was a quiet cut-through for commuters dodging the traffic light two blocks over, meaning backing out of that blind driveway was going to require patience every single day. We also realized the ridge to the east blocked the early morning sun, so the frost lingered on the front steps long after the rest of the block thawed. 

At the same time, we ran into an older neighbor walking her beagle who stopped to introduce herself, pointed out which neighbor was the carpenter who helped everyone with storm damage, and told us the school bus stopped right at the corner. 

The Pruitts still wrote the offer, and they still bought the house. But they bought it without any illusions. They knew to re-gravel the parking pad so they could turn their cars around instead of backing into traffic, and they knew what their commute would actually look like before they unpacked a single box. 

They are still there, and whenever I run into them at the grocery store, they always mention that morning walk. 

Inspection reports can tell you if the roof has five years left, but they can't tell you how a street feels when the alarm goes off. If you’re touring homes right now, set your alarm early and walk the block. It prevents a lot of surprises.

b.text:
The Pruitts were first-time buyers looking on Sycamore Street last spring. We had six homes to see that Saturday, and I suggested they drive over Friday night, park a block away, and walk the block at 7am before we started touring.

They were game. Saturday morning they texted me photos: the corner coffee shop opening up, the neighbor two doors down pulling out in scrubs for what I assumed was a hospital shift, and a woman walking a very small dog who waved at every single person she passed.

Then we toured.

Every house looked good on paper. But they kept coming back to one in particular, on the east end of the block. When I asked why, they said it already felt like they knew the rhythm of the street. They'd met it, in a way, before they ever walked through a front door.

They wrote an offer that afternoon and closed in May. Last I heard, they still do the morning walk, and they still wave at the small-dog lady.

After twelve years of selling homes in Asheville, this is the pattern I keep seeing: buyers who take time to actually experience a neighborhood before they tour a house end up way happier with their purchase six months and six years later. The houses themselves are similar in a lot of ways — square footage, finishes, price per square foot. What you can't get from listings, or even showings, is the texture of daily life on a given street. Who you'll nod at. What the light does at 7:15 in the kitchen. Where the coffee comes from.

The walk before the tour isn't a gimmick. It's the closest thing to living there before you commit.

Hi everyone,

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**Give Our Kids a Fighting Chance in the Morning**

If you live with a middle-schooler, your morning routine probably looks a lot like mine: dragging exhausted kids out of bed, nagging them through a rushed breakfast, and watching them stumble out the door looking like extra members of *The Walking Dead*. 

As a parent of two middle-schoolers here in Millbrook, I’ve had enough of the morning sleep battles. That is why I am strongly urging our school board to vote "yes" on the proposed 8:45 a.m. start time next month.

This isn't about letting kids be lazy. It’s about biology. The American Academy of Pediatrics has been clear for years: middle and high schools shouldn't start before 8:30 a.m. During adolescence, teenagers' biological clocks naturally shift, making it almost impossible for them to fall asleep early enough to get the nine hours of sleep their growing brains desperately need. By forcing them awake before dawn, we are asking them to learn while functionally sleep-deprived.

We don't just have national medical advice on our side—we have proof right here in our district. Just look at the pilot program results from Lincoln Middle. When Lincoln moved to a later start, attendance shot up, and first-period grades saw a noticeable boost. When kids are actually awake, they show up, and they learn. It really is that simple.

I know some neighbors have valid concerns about logistics, especially how this might mess up the bus schedules. But if you read the board’s proposal closely, you’ll see the district has already solved this problem. The proposal completely re-tiers our existing bus routes to make the new schedule work smoothly. It doesn't create transportation chaos; it just reshuffles the system we already have to prioritize our kids' well-being. 

Change is always a little tough, and adjusting family routines takes effort. But our current schedule is actively hurting our children's health, mood, and academic performance. The school board has put together a sensible, well-researched plan that fixes a long-standing issue. 

Please join me in speaking up before next month's vote. Let's give our kids the well-rested, healthy start to the day they deserve.

b.text:
Why Our Kids Need That 8:45 Start Time

I'm not a doctor, a teacher, or a school board member. I'm just a Millbrook mom with two middle-schoolers, a coffeemaker that works overtime, and a minivan that smells like soccer practice.

Our mornings go like this: alarm at 6:15, lights on, snooze, snooze again, then me begging two half-asleep kids to get dressed, eat something, find their shoes. They make it to homeroom by 7:30, but I wouldn't say they're really there. First period is a fog.

That's why I'm writing in support of the proposal to move our middle school start time to 8:45, which the board votes on next month. I've read the whole thing, highlighter and all, and I think it's the right call for our kids.

This isn't about letting kids be lazy. It's biology. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that teens ages 13 to 18 get 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night, and that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30. Our current 7:30 start makes that math almost impossible. For my 13-year-old to get nine hours, she'd need to be fully asleep by 9:30. With homework, shower, and just being a kid who needs to unwind, that doesn't happen in real life.

And we don't have to guess whether later would work here in Millbrook. We already saw it. Last year Lincoln Middle piloted the 8:45 start, and attendance went up and first-period grades went up. Teachers said kids were more alert, less tardy. As a parent, that rings true. When my kids actually sleep, everything is easier — mood, homework, even how they treat each other.

I know the number one worry is buses. I've heard it at soccer, at the grocery store: how will this work without chaos? I worried about that too. But if you read the proposal, it already handles it by re-tiering the routes. Middle school, high school, and elementary would each get their own staggered window, so the same buses and drivers can cover everyone without buying a whole new fleet. Will the first week be bumpy? Probably. But it's not unplanned.

We're always telling our kids to make healthy choices and work hard in school. Giving them a start time that lets them sleep and show up ready to learn is how we back that up.

Please join me in telling the school board: vote yes on 8:45.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
I coach girls’ soccer and track at the high school. I do it for the stipend and because I like the kids. I don’t write columns, and I don’t have patience for long speeches. But the school board is voting on next year’s facilities budget, and they need to hear something the athletic director already knows: the girls’ soccer field is a mess, and it’s dangerous.

In the last two seasons, rain has killed or moved nine of our games. Nine. The grass field floods every time a storm rolls through, and it doesn’t drain. It turns into a mud pit where the ball stops dead and kids slip and stutter-step around ruts. Last October, one of my defenders planted to make a cut and her foot caught in a rut carved out by the rain. She tore her ACL. She’s a junior who’s still not back to full speed.

Meanwhile, the football team has been playing on turf since 2019. Their games don’t get washed out. Their players don’t step in sinkholes. I’m glad they have a good surface. I’m not glad our girls are still stuck competing on a field that’s half a step above a bog.

The board needs to put turf on the girls’ soccer field in this budget. Not next year. Not after another study. Now. We’re talking about safety, we’re talking about equal treatment, and we’re talking about nine games that didn’t happen because the field was underwater. Fix the field.

b.text:
# Girls' Soccer Deserves the Same Investment as Football

Our girls' soccer field floods. Again and again, we lose games to rain that wouldn't cancel anything on the boys' football field—which has had artificial turf since 2019.

Last season alone, we rescheduled or cancelled nine games because the grass turned to mud. Our athletes showed up ready to play. The field wasn't. This season we've already had two more postponements, and we're only halfway through.

But cancelled games aren't even the worst part. Last October, one of my seniors stepped into a rut in that waterlogged grass and tore her ACL. She missed the rest of her final season. A turf field wouldn't have prevented every injury, but it would have prevented that one.

Our school board installed artificial turf on the football field five years ago. I'm not arguing against that investment—football is important. But girls' soccer is important too. We have the same number of athletes. We play just as hard. We deserve a field that doesn't become a swamp every time it rains.

This isn't complicated. The boys got a modern facility. The girls are still playing on mud. When you're deciding next year's budget, I'd ask you this: Why?

Install turf on the girls' soccer field. Our athletes have waited long enough.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
~200 interviews in, I've noticed one question that separates the best candidates from everyone else. It's not about growth, culture, or "what does success look like."

It's: "Tell me about your last failed project."

The strongest people I interview don't ask whether we fail. They assume we do. They want to know what happens next.

One example from a few months back. Ops manager candidate, interview going fine, nothing remarkable. Their turn to ask questions:

"Tell me about the last project here that actually failed. Not a setback. A failure."

Our ops director paused, then told them about a WMS cutover we botched a couple years ago. Three weeks of wrecked pick rates, a couple of accounts that walked, some very uncomfortable retrospectives. Didn't sugarcoat any of it.

Then the candidate asked the follow-up that told me everything:

"Are the people who ran it still here? And did anything structurally change?"

That's not a gotcha. That's due diligence. They were mapping how failure moves through this company — does it get owned and fixed, or buried along with whoever touched it?

We hired them. A few months in they killed one of our internal projects that wasn't working. Early, cleanly, no drama. I think about that a lot.

If you're interviewing somewhere: this question costs you nothing and reveals almost everything about how a company treats people when things go wrong.

If you're hiring: notice who asks it. In my experience, the people who ask about your failures have survived a few of their own.

b.text:
After roughly 200 interviews, I’ve noticed the strongest candidates often ask some version of:

“Tell me about the last project that failed.”

Not the company’s biggest win. Not the polished culture pitch. The failure.

A recent conversation went like this:

Candidate: “What happened?”

Hiring manager: “We underestimated the operational impact and launched too quickly.”

Candidate: “When did the team realize it was going off track?”

Hiring manager: “About two weeks in.”

Candidate: “What made it difficult to change course then?”

That last question changed the conversation.

They weren’t looking for a gotcha. They were trying to understand how decisions get made under pressure, whether people can raise concerns, and what the company actually learns when things don’t go to plan.

You can learn a lot about a candidate from the questions they ask.

And candidates can learn even more from how honestly we answer them.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
Look, I get it. You bring your dog in looking great, and two weeks later there's tangle city happening and you're wondering what went wrong. The truth is, coats don't wait for the next groom. Especially with double-coated breeds like Goldens, huskies, or retrievers, and curly breeds like poodles and doodles, what you do at home between visits matters more than what I do in the tub.

So here's the thing, and I can't stress this enough: brush your dog before the bath, never after. The biggest mistake I see constantly is people bathing the dog first, thinking the water and shampoo will loosen the mats up. It does the opposite. Wet matted fur just turns into a felt pad. You ever put a wool sweater in the wash by accident and it comes out three sizes smaller and stiff? Same thing. Water and friction lock those tangles in tighter, and then you've got a mess that I have to shave out instead of brush out.

When you do brush, grab a slicker brush. Not a pin brush, not one of those rubber mitt things, a proper slicker. Use short line strokes, not circles. I know circling feels satisfying, but you're just spinning the hair around and creating twist mats at the base. Short line strokes, working down to the skin, lifting out and repeating.

Work in sections. Don't just swipe down the back and call it done. Start behind the ears and under the front legs, because that's where mats start first every single time. Friction points. Then move down the flanks, the haunches, the tail. If your dog has a curly coat, fluff dry as you go so you can see what you're actually dealing with. Wet curly hair hides knots.

If you already see a mat forming, don't go at it with a brush or comb right away. Work some conditioner into it with your fingers first. Just a dab, work it in, gently pull the hairs apart. You'd be surprised how many mats will release with a little patience and slip. Once you've loosened it, then you can carefully work through it with your slicker.

I'd rather you brush for ten minutes every few days than do an hour-long session once a week. Consistency keeps the undercoat from packing down and keeps the curls from clumping. And honestly, if you're staying on top of it, most dogs only need a solid brush-out once or twice a week. The doodles and the double-coated dogs with longer coats, maybe a little more.

b.text:
Keeping your dog’s coat mat-free between grooming visits does not have to mean a full grooming session at home. A little regular maintenance in the spots that tangle first can make a huge difference—especially for curly coats and double-coated breeds.

The biggest thing I want clients to remember is this: **brush before the bath, never after.** If there are tangles or small mats in the coat, getting them wet can tighten them into dense, felt-like pads. Water makes the hair shrink and bind together, and shampooing over mats usually locks them in even more. What may have been a manageable tangle before the bath can become something that needs to be shaved out afterward.

Before bathing, take a few minutes to check the areas that mat first. Behind the ears, under the front legs, around the collar area, under harness straps, and along the back of the legs are common trouble spots. For dogs with curly coats, also check where the legs meet the body and around the tail. These areas get friction from movement, sleeping, collars, and harnesses, so mats can form there quickly even when the rest of the coat looks fine.

A slicker brush is usually the best tool for regular at-home brushing. Use short, gentle line strokes rather than big circles over the top of the coat. Brushing in circles can tangle the hair more and may only smooth the outer layer while mats hide close to the skin. Work in small sections, parting the coat so you can see down toward the skin. If the brush cannot get through a section easily, there is likely a tangle forming underneath.

Start with the places that tend to mat first instead of just brushing the easy areas your dog enjoys. Behind the ears and under the front legs are usually where I find mats earliest. A few minutes spent there several times a week is much easier—and more comfortable for your dog—than trying to tackle a large mat later.

If you find a mat starting, do not immediately go at it with a brush or comb. Work a little dog-safe conditioner or detangling spray into it with your fingers first. Gently pull the mat apart from the ends, using your fingers to loosen the hairs before brushing. Once it starts to separate, use the slicker brush in small strokes from the ends upward. Pulling a brush straight through a tight mat can hurt, and a painful brushing experience can make dogs understandably nervous about being groomed.

For double-coated dogs, regular brushing is especially important during shedding seasons. Loose undercoat gets trapped in the outer coat and can quickly turn into compacted areas if it is not removed. For curly-coated dogs, consistency matters even more because the coat naturally twists and wraps around itself as it grows.

If you are not sure whether you are dealing with a tangle or a true mat, try to gently separate it with your fingers. If you cannot get your fingers between the hairs near the skin, or if your dog is uncomfortable when you touch the area, it is best to call us before bathing. Please do not use scissors to cut mats out at home—mats often pull the skin up into them, and accidental cuts happen much more easily than people realize.

A quick brush-out before every bath, plus regular attention to the ears, armpits, collar area, and harness lines, will help keep your dog more comfortable between visits and make each grooming appointment easier on everyone.
