setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
# The Girls' Soccer Field Needs Turf. Here's Why That's Not Optional.

I've coached girls' soccer and track at this school for years, and I'm not going to pretend I love writing op-eds. I do this for the stipend and because I care about these kids. But I'm asking the school board — and this town — to fix something that's gone unfixed for too long: our girls' soccer field floods, it's dangerous, and it's been treated like a lower priority than the boys' football field for six years running.

Let's start with the numbers, because they're not close. Over the last two seasons, we've had nine games rained out or relocated because our grass field can't drain. Not postponed by a day — cancelled, or moved to a field forty minutes away, cutting into study time, sleep, and family schedules for forty-plus girls and their parents. Meanwhile, our opponents with turf fields play through the same weather without blinking.

Then there's what happened last October. One of my players planted her foot in a rut — the kind that forms when a grass field takes on water all season and never fully recovers — and tore her ACL. She's out for a full year. Surgery, months of rehab, a season and a half of her high school career gone, because the ground she was playing on wasn't safe. That's not bad luck. That's a facilities problem with a name and a face attached to it now.

Here's the part that makes this personal for me, and for a lot of parents who've already called and emailed the board: the football field got turf in 2019. It drains fine. It doesn't grow ruts. Nobody's tearing an ACL stepping in a divot out there. I'm not saying football doesn't deserve a good field — it does. I'm saying our girls deserve the same standard, and they've been waiting six years for it.

I know turf isn't cheap. I know budgets are tight and there are a dozen good uses for every dollar. But I'd ask the board to weigh that cost against what we're already paying: rescheduled games, lost practice time, a kid's knee, and a message to forty girls that their season matters less than the boys' does. That message gets sent whether we mean it or not, every time it rains and only one team's field is playable.

This isn't a want. It's overdue. I hope the board votes like it.

b.text:
**Our Girls Deserve a Field They Can Actually Play On**

Over the last two seasons, our girls’ soccer team has had nine games rained out or moved because our grass field floods.

Nine games. That means players, families, officials and opposing teams have made plans, only to have them canceled or relocated because the field cannot handle ordinary weather. It means lost home games, lost revenue and lost opportunities for our athletes to compete in front of their classmates and families.

It also means we are asking students to play on a surface that can become unsafe.

Last October, one of our players tore her ACL after stepping into a rut on the field. I am not going to pretend that a new surface eliminates every sports injury. It does not. Soccer is physical, and injuries happen. But we should not be putting our athletes on a field with ruts, standing water and uneven footing when we have the ability to provide something safer and more reliable.

The school board is considering next year’s facilities budget. Installing turf on the girls’ soccer field should be part of that budget.

This is not a request for luxury. It is a request for a basic athletic facility that works.

The boys’ football field received turf in 2019. That investment made sense. Football needed a dependable field, and the school made the decision to provide one. But girls’ soccer deserves the same consideration. Our athletes work just as hard. They practice in the same weather, represent the same school and compete under the same academic and athletic expectations.

This is also a fairness issue.

We should not have one group of athletes playing on a dependable, all-weather surface while another group is routinely displaced by rain. We should not tell girls that their games can be moved, shortened or canceled because their field is not a priority. If the school is willing to invest in facilities for one program, it should be willing to invest in facilities for another program with a demonstrated need.

The current field does not just create inconvenience. It affects the quality of the season. When games are moved, families have to rearrange work schedules and transportation. Opposing teams have to travel again. Coaches have to rebuild practice plans. Senior nights and other events become harder to schedule. Players lose the experience of playing at home, in front of their community.

And when a game is moved to another field, that field may not be ideal either. We end up scrambling for space instead of giving our athletes the stable, well-maintained facility they deserve.

A turf field would allow us to keep more games at home and make better use of the schedule. It would provide a more consistent playing surface and reduce the damage caused by wet conditions. It would give the school a facility that can serve students more reliably instead of sitting unusable after every heavy rain.

I understand that the district has competing needs. Facilities budgets are not unlimited, and every project has to be examined carefully. But fairness should be part of that examination. So should safety. So should whether students are actually able to use the facilities we already ask them to depend on.

Our girls are not asking for special treatment. They are asking for equal treatment.

They show up early. They stay late. They play through heat, cold and pressure. They represent this school with pride. The least we can do is give them a field that drains, holds up and does not turn a season into a series of weather-related cancellations.

The school board should put turf for the girls’ soccer field in next year’s facilities budget. It is the fair decision, the practical decision and the responsible decision.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
I went into my first clinical thinking I would feel like a nurse. Instead I felt like a kid wearing scrubs that were too big, trying not to get in anyone’s way.

By Monday afternoon I was already lost in the ER supply closet when a nurse poked her head in and said a man in room four needed someone to hold his hand. His wife was stuck across town in traffic, and they were cleaning gravel out of a road rash that ran from his shoulder to his elbow. I followed her back and stood on the side where his wife would have been. The nurse warned him it was going to hurt. He gripped my hand before she even started. He didn’t say much, just squeezed hard when the saline hit, and I squeezed back. That was the whole thing. I didn’t do any actual nursing. But he didn’t let go until his wife ran through the door twenty minutes later, and I realized that sometimes being there is the job.

The next day a code got called in the bay next to where I was shadowing. My preceptor told me to step out and restock the gauze cart. I was glad to have something to do with my hands, but standing in the hallway I could hear them through the curtain. Someone counted compressions. One and two and three and four. Over and over. I kept counting in my head even after I stopped hearing them. I had never been that close to it before. I didn’t see the patient, but I understood why the ER runs through supplies so fast, and why nobody walks in that room unless they have to.

Then there was the blood draw on Thursday. Diabetic patient, older guy, veins like cooked spaghetti. I missed the first stick. I missed the second. By the third I was sweating through my shirt and apologizing every time he flinched. He just said, “You’re learning, it’s alright.” I didn’t believe him. I almost asked my preceptor to take over, but she stood back and said, “Try the other arm. You’ve got it.” The fourth stick went in. I saw the flash of blood and almost cried. He said, “There you go,” like he knew it would happen all along. I taped the tubing down and cleaned up and realized I had spent more time with him than I would have if I’d gotten it on the first try. That’s not an excuse for missing three times. But it taught me that nursing isn’t about doing everything perfect right away. It’s about not walking away when you’re embarrassed.

That week stripped away a lot of what I thought nursing was. I didn’t save anyone’s life. I didn’t know enough to be useful in a code. I stuck a guy four times and probably hurt his feelings. But I also held a stranger’s hand so he wasn’t alone, and I stayed in the hallway while someone fought to come back, and I kept trying on that blood draw until I got it because the patient let me. I learned that ER nursing is mostly showing up, paying attention, and not quitting when you feel stupid.

I’m a first-year student, so I still have a lot to learn. But after that first week, I know I want to keep going. I want to get good enough that I can be in the room during the code instead of outside it. I want to hit the vein on the first try. Most of all, I want to be the kind of nurse who stays late enough to hold someone’s hand until their family gets there. This scholarship would help me stay in school and get there faster. I’m ready to put in the work.

b.text:
First Week in the ER

I didn't expect my first clinical rotation to teach me as much as it did. I thought I would mostly watch. I did watch, but I also held a stranger's hand, restocked a supply closet while someone down the hall might have been dying, and stuck a needle in the same man's arm four times trying to get blood. I learned more in that one week than in a whole semester of lectures.

The first day I was assigned to follow a nurse named Trish. She was fast and kind and did not seem nervous about anything, which made me feel better about being very nervous about everything. By midmorning she had me bringing patients water and blankets, which I thought was too simple to matter, until I watched a man drink a cup of water I had handed him and close his eyes like he had been waiting for it all morning.

The moment I keep coming back to happened that same morning. An older man came in with a deep cut on his forearm that needed cleaning and packing. His wife was on her way, but she was stuck in traffic on the interstate. He was in pain and trying to stay still and I could see his hands shaking. Trish asked him if he wanted someone to hold his hand and he looked at me, this total stranger, and said okay. I sat next to him and held his hand while the nurse cleaned out the wound. He squeezed tighter than I expected when it hurt the worst. His wife made it about forty minutes later, and by then my own hand was cramping up. He thanked her on the way in, and his wife grabbed my other hand and just cried for a second. I didn't say anything. I didn't know what to say. I just stood there.

Two days later I was in the back supply room, counting gauze and restocking gloves, when the alarm went off. A code. The curtain was pulled shut where they were working on the patient, but I could hear them counting. One, two, three, four. Compressions. Someone called out meds. The rhythm of it was steady and loud, and I remember standing there thinking how everyone in that room knew exactly what to do except me, and I was three feet away sorting 4x4s by size. I finished restocking the cart. I didn't know what else to do. That night I went home and read my BLS chapter twice.

The last thing I want to tell you about is a man I'll call Mr. D. He came in for high blood sugar and needed blood drawn. The veins in his arms were hard and scarred from years of diabetes and probably a lot of sticks before mine. My instructor let me try. I missed the first time. I missed the second. I missed the third. By the fourth try my hands were sweating and I could feel him staring at the ceiling, trying to be patient. I got it on the fourth. He said "thank you, sweetheart" when I labeled the tube, and I had to walk out of the room before I cried, not because I was upset, but because he had been so kind to me even after I had hurt him three times.

I don't think I went into nursing because I wanted to hold hands or start IVs. I think I went in because I wanted to be useful to people on the worst day of their life, or at least a hard one. That week showed me the job is mostly small things. A cup of water. A hand to hold. Counting to four over and over. Trying four times instead of giving up. I want to keep learning how to do the small things well, and I want to keep showing up on the hard days, even the ones where I feel like I'm just restocking gauze in the next room.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
The state legislature is currently looking at a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding, and as a third-year electrical apprentice with this IBEW local, I can tell you exactly why that is a terrible idea. I am an electrician, not an English professor, so I am going to skip the fancy speeches and just look at the hard numbers. 

Let’s look at my own group. My apprenticeship cohort started with 24 people. Out of those, 21 finished the program. That is a massive success rate. Those 21 men and women aren't sitting at home looking for work. They are out in the field right now, working full-time journeyman jobs, paying taxes, and building this state's infrastructure. 

When we start out as apprentices, we make around $19 an hour. By the time we finish and become journeymen, we top out around $46 an hour. If the state wants to know the fastest way to get people off public assistance programs, this is it. You train them for a career that pays a wage they can actually live and raise a family on. Apprentices get off government assistance fast because we are put straight to work. Gutting the funding that makes this possible doesn't save the state money in the long run. It just keeps people broke.

But here is the math that really proves how backward this proposed cut is. The total public cost for an apprentice who finishes their training is about $14,000. Compare that to a traditional college student. The average public subsidy for a student who finishes a four-year degree is somewhere around $48,000. 

I don't have anything against people who go to college, but the state needs to explain why it wants to cut funding for a program that costs a third of the price and actually guarantees a high-paying job at the end of it. We are delivering a better return on the state's investment, hands down. 

To my brothers and sisters in the local, we need to make some noise. Call your state representatives and tell them to vote against this cut. And to the legislators reading this: do the math. Apprenticeships work. We are the ones wiring your hospitals, schools, and businesses. Do not pull the ladder up on the next group of apprentices trying to get to work. Keep our training fully funded.

b.text:
**Don't Cut What Works**

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with the IBEW. I work full time and go to class. I'm not an English professor, so I'll keep this plain.

The state is talking about a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding. That's a bad deal for everybody, and it won't save money in the long run. It will cost us more.

Look at my own cohort. We started with 24 apprentices. 21 of us finished and are working now as journeymen. That's 21 people who didn't drop out, who learned the trade, and who are working. That's what this program does. It works.

When you start as an apprentice you make around $19 an hour. You're working, you're paying taxes, you're learning. When you top out as a journeyman you make around $46 an hour. At that wage you're off any assistance programs fast. You're buying a house, you're supporting a family, you're paying a lot more in taxes. You go from getting help to giving back.

And it doesn't cost the public much to make that happen. The total public cost for one apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to a four-year college grad. The average public subsidy for one four-year grad who finishes is about $48,000. I'm not knocking college, we need all kinds of workers. But if we're talking about where tax dollars go further, $14k to create a journeyman electrician making $46 an hour is a bargain compared to $48k.

We are short on electricians. Every contractor I talk to is looking for more hands. Houses, schools, hospitals, new factories - somebody has to wire them. If you cut funding by 15%, that means fewer spots, fewer instructors, less training time, less safety training. It means my local can't take in the next class of 24. Maybe we only take 15. That means fewer taxpayers later and more jobs that don't get done.

I hear politicians say we need to cut waste. This isn't waste. This is the opposite of waste. You put $14k in and you get a worker who will pay that back ten times over in taxes and who will work for the next 30 years.

I'm asking the other brothers and sisters reading this newsletter to speak up, and I'm asking any state legislator who sees this to think twice. Don't cut funding for something that is working. If you want to save the state money, keep paying for apprenticeships.

We started with 24. We finished with 21 journeymen. That's a good return. Don't mess with it.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam – 14 Month / 140k Mile Review**

Put about 140,000 miles on the Roadstar DC4 over the last 14 months in my rig. Figure that’s enough road time and cab vibration to give an honest take for anybody looking at one.

Here’s the straight truth on it:

**The Good**
* **Saved my bacon on an insurance claim.** A four-wheeler chopped my front bumper taking a sloppy lane change. Cam caught the whole thing clear as day. Insurance had the claim approved in 9 days flat instead of the usual 6-week fight. It paid for itself right there.

**The Annoying (And How to Fix It)**
* **Ditch the suction mount.** The suction cup dropped off the windshield twice last summer when the cab got hot. Don't bother with it. Use the adhesive mount right out of the box and save yourself the headache. Hasn't moved an inch since.
* **Forget the phone app.** The app makes you connect to Wi-Fi to pull footage off the camera, which is completely useless at most truck stops. Don't waste your time fighting the app—just pull the SD card and slide it into a reader or laptop. It’s ten times faster anyway.
* **Rear camera night vision is mediocre.** Daytime rear footage is solid, but at night it gets grainy real quick past 30 feet. It’ll still prove if somebody rear-ended you, but you won't be reading license plates at a distance in the dark.

**Bottom Line**
It isn't perfect, but it’s tough, it runs constantly without freezing up, and the front video quality is sharp enough to protect your CDL when someone else screws up. Mount it with the tape, pull the card manually, and it’ll do the job. Worth the money for an owner-operator.

b.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam — 14 months / 140k miles**

Figured I'd put some real miles on this thing before writing it up. Here's where I landed.

**The good:**

It earned its keep back in the spring. Four-wheeler cut across my lane, clipped me, and of course told his insurance I drifted into him. Front cam footage said otherwise. Claim approved in 9 days. My last claim without footage took 6 weeks. That alone paid for the camera several times over, so if you're running without one, that's the whole argument right there.

Daytime footage front and rear is solid. Plates are readable, no complaints.

**The bad:**

Rear cam night footage gets grainy past about 30 feet. Close stuff is fine, but if someone's tailing you at a distance in the dark, don't count on reading a plate. Front cam handles night better.

The suction mount is junk in the heat. Fell off my windshield twice last summer, once while I was rolling. Switched to the adhesive mount and it hasn't budged since. Just skip the suction mount and go adhesive from day one.

**The annoying:**

The app needs wifi to pull footage. Sounds fine until you realize truck stop wifi is garbage or nonexistent half the time. I gave up on the app and just pull the SD card and stick it in my laptop. Works fine, just know going in that the app is basically useless on the road.

**Bottom line:**

Not perfect, but after 140k miles it's still recording every day and it already saved me a claim fight. Buy the adhesive mount with it, keep a spare SD card, and don't expect miracles from the rear cam at night. Would I buy it again? Yeah.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8 Months of Daily Market Sourdough

I've been using the Corlane SM6 almost every day for eight months, mostly to develop and mix double batches of stiff sourdough and bagel dough for my farmers market stand. Here's what actually matters.

**The motor is genuinely strong.** I regularly throw a double batch of bagel dough at this thing—the kind that makes cheaper mixers strain and wheeze—and it powers through without stalling or getting hot. The bowl also rotates smoothly without the weird wobble I had with my old KitchenAid. That's the main reason I switched.

**The bowl lift lever squeaks.** Not occasionally. Consistently. I WD-40 it once a month and it helps for about two weeks. It's annoying enough that I notice it every single time I use the mixer, but not annoying enough to regret the purchase.

**The dough hook is too short.** The deep bowl that comes with the SM6 is genuinely useful for large batches, but the standard hook doesn't reach the bottom. I bought a third-party extended hook for $30 and now it works perfectly. Corlane should include this from the factory.

**The price is a real consideration.** At $429, it's $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid. You're paying for the stronger motor and better design—but only if you actually need them.

**Skip this mixer if you mostly bake cookies, cakes, and cookie dough.** The KitchenAid will do that work just fine and costs less. Buy the Corlane if you're regularly mixing stiff dough multiple times a week. If you're serious about sourdough or bagels or any heavy dough work, this mixer will save you time and frustration for years.

b.text:
## Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: 8 Months of Almost-Daily Market Sourdough

I’ve been using the Corlane SM6 stand mixer for eight months now, and it has become one of the main tools behind my farmers market sourdough production. This is not a “baked a few loaves over the holidays” review. I use this mixer almost daily, often for stiff, high-load doughs, and it has been doing real market-bakery work in my home kitchen.

If you’re trying to decide whether the SM6 is worth buying, here’s the honest answer after months of heavy use.

### Motor and Dough Performance

The biggest thing the SM6 gets right is torque. I regularly mix double batches of stiff bagel dough, and the mixer does not stall, bog down, or feel like it’s struggling through the knead. That has been the single biggest selling point for me.

For sourdough production, especially when I’m mixing firmer doughs or pushing larger batches, the motor feels confident from the moment the ingredients come together through the final knead. It doesn’t whine, overheat, or hesitate when the dough gets dense. If your main frustration with stand mixers is that they tap out on heavy bread dough, this is where the SM6 earns its place on the counter.

I’ve mixed enough market batches on it to know that this is not a mixer that wants to live only in cake-batter land. It wants to work.

### The Bowl Lift: Functional, but Annoying

Here’s the part I don’t love: the bowl lift lever squeaks. Not subtly, either. It’s annoying enough that I’ve had to lubricate it with WD-40 about once a month to keep it from sounding like it needs an oil change mid-mix.

It still works. It lifts, locks, and holds the bowl securely. But for a mixer at this price point, I expect the mechanical parts to feel smoother out of the box and stay smoother over time. The squeak isn’t a dealbreaker for me because the mixer itself performs well, but it is a recurring maintenance issue that I think buyers should know about before purchasing.

If you’re the kind of baker who wants everything to feel perfectly polished and silent, this will bother you. I’ve made peace with it because the motor performance is that good, but I do wish Corlane had solved this better.

### The Stock Dough Hook Is a Miss

The dough hook that comes with the SM6 is too short for the deep bowl. In practical terms, it doesn’t engage the dough as well as it should, especially when I’m mixing larger or stiffer batches. I ended up buying a third-party dough hook to fix the problem, and that replacement made a noticeable difference.

This is disappointing because the mixer shouldn’t need an immediate aftermarket fix to do its main job properly. The SM6 is strong enough to handle serious dough, but the included hook does not fully take advantage of that capacity.

If you buy this mixer for bread and heavy dough work, I’d budget for a better hook from the start. It’s an extra cost, but in my experience it was necessary.

### Price: More Expensive Than the Equivalent KitchenAid

The Corlane SM6 costs $429, which is about $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid. That’s not a tiny difference, especially for home bakers who are already spending money on flour, bannetons, dutch ovens, and a dozen other things they swore they didn’t need.

That higher price is only justified if you actually need the SM6’s strengths. For me, the motor performance under heavy dough loads is enough to make up for the extra cost, the squeaky bowl lift, and the need to replace the hook. But if you’re not regularly kneading stiff dough, you probably won’t feel the benefit enough to justify paying more.

### What It’s Actually Good At

The SM6 is best for bakers who regularly work with:

- Stiff sourdough doughs  
- Bagels  
- Pretzels  
- Large batches of bread dough  
- Double loaves or market production batches  
- Low-hydration or high-resistance doughs  

It is not a mixer I would recommend mainly for:

- Cookies  
- Cake batter  
- Whipped cream  
- Light occasional baking  
- Bakers who want the most polished user experience without maintenance quirks  

### The Verdict

Buy the Corlane SM6 if you knead heavy dough every week. It has the power, stamina, and dough-handling confidence to handle serious bread work, and after eight months of near-daily market sourdough use, I would still choose it for that purpose.

Skip it if you’re mostly making cookies, cake batter, or light occasional dough. For that kind of baking, you do not need to spend $429 on this mixer, and the quirks are harder to excuse.

For heavy dough bakers, it’s worth it. For everyone else, save your money.

I carried Route 4 out of the Kettle Falls post office for 22 years. Same 38 miles, same boxes, same people. I know this town, and I know what that counter means to it, so I've got something to say about the plan to close it.

The Postal Service says the branch loses $40,000 a year. Maybe it does. But they cut the window hours down to 8 to noon, and then they act surprised when fewer people come in. Of course traffic dropped. You can't shut the door most of the day and then point at the empty lobby like it's our fault. That's not a losing office. Take Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She's in her 80s. Her heart medicine comes by mail, and I used to hand it to her myself. When she needs a money order, she walks down to that counter and gets one. She doesn't drive. Twenty minutes to Fairview might as well be two hundred for her. Tell me what she's supposed to do.

There are a lot of Mrs. Hallorans here. Older folks, folks without cars, folks who don't do their banking on a phone. The counter isn't a luxury to them. It's the errand.

There's a public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall. I'll be there, and I hope the district manager is listening, because this decision was made somewhere far from Kettle Falls by people who have never stood at that window on a cold morning.

If you care about this, show up. That's the only thing that's ever worked around here.

[Name]
Kettle Falls

b.text:
To the Editor:

I’m no writer. I’m just a retired mail carrier. I drove the same 38-mile Route 4 for 22 years before I retired last year, so I know this town.

USPS says our branch loses $40,000 a year. But that’s only because they already cut the counter hours to 8 a.m. to noon. Folks around here work during those hours. Of course traffic dropped after that. Now they point at those numbers and say, “See? No one uses it.” That’s a problem they made themselves.

a.text:
1/ On the Maple Ave kitchen, we opened the ceiling over the sink and found two 2x8 floor joists cut midspan years ago to fit a drain. The floor still felt solid, but the cut was in the worst possible spot for load transfer.

2/ We temp-supported the floor, got an engineer’s note, sistered the damaged joists with LVL, and added hangers/blocking. Total cost to the client: about $2,600 and 2 extra days.

3/ Lesson: on older Pittsburgh houses, assume someone already made a mess behind the finish. Open early, price structural contingencies in writing, and don’t let a pipe route get solved with a saw.

b.text:
1/ Opened up the ceiling on our Maple Ave kitchen remodel this week and found a classic Pittsburgh old-house surprise. Sometime in the 80s, somebody completely severed a floor joist just to run a PVC drain line. The bathroom floor upstairs was practically floating.

2/ We had to halt drywall prep, bring in the engineer to spec a fix, reroute the plumbing, and properly sister the joist. It cost the client about $1,200 out of pocket and set our schedule back two days. Never a fun phone call to make, but it had to be done.

3/ The lesson for homeowners: this is exactly why you need a 10-15% contingency budget. If a contractor tells you they know exactly what's behind an 80-year-old plaster ceiling before they open it, they're lying. You have to financially plan for the unknown.

4/ The lesson for guys newer to the trade: don't just cover this stuff back up because it's "not in the original scope." In residential remodeling, you touch it, you own it. Have the hard conversation with the client immediately, fix the structure, and sleep well at night.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
I've sat in on roughly 200 interviews over 9 years. The candidates who impress me most almost always ask some version of the same question.

"What was the last project here that failed?"

Not "what's the culture like." Not "what does success look like in this role." They want the failure story.

Had one a few months ago. Senior ops candidate, second round, going well. She asks: "What's the last initiative that didn't work here — and what happened to the people who ran it?"

That second half. That's the actual question.

I told her about a route optimization tool we rolled out two years back. Big vendor, big promises. Dispatchers hated it, adoption collapsed within a few months, and we quietly went back to the old process.

She didn't nod and move on. She asked: "Whose idea was it, and where is that person now?"

Honest answer: the director who championed it is still here. He ran the post-mortem himself. One thing that came out of it — dispatchers now sit in on every pilot before we buy anything — is standard practice.

She told me that was the answer she'd been hoping for. Her last employer had a failed rollout and pinned it on one analyst, who was gone within a month. She left shortly after.

That's what I've figured out about this question: candidates aren't testing whether you fail. Everyone fails. They're testing what failure costs the person attached to it.

If you're interviewing somewhere, ask it. Pay attention to whether the interviewer hesitates, and whether the failure story has a villain.

And if you're on my side of the table: the quality of your answer tells them more about working here than anything on the careers page. If your honest answer ends with "and we fired them," expect the best candidates to politely finish the process and take another offer.

b.text:
One question consistently changes the tone of an interview:

“What’s a project that didn’t go the way you hoped—and what happened after?”

I’ve probably had this come up in around 200 interviews. The strongest candidates don’t ask it to catch anyone out. They’re trying to understand how work actually happens when the plan meets reality.

In logistics, it might sound like this:

Candidate: “What’s a recent project that failed?”

Me: “We rolled out a new scheduling process at one site. The timeline was aggressive, training wasn’t consistent across shifts, and adoption stalled.”

Candidate: “What did the team do once you realized it wasn’t landing?”

Me: “We paused the wider rollout, brought in the site leads earlier, rebuilt the training, and restarted with a smaller pilot.”

Candidate: “If I joined, how much room would I have to raise a concern before a project gets that far?”

That last question tells me far more than “What does success look like in this role?”

It tells me they’re thinking about judgment, communication, accountability, and whether the company learns—or just moves on to the next initiative.

Job seekers: asking about failure isn’t negative. It’s one of the fastest ways to find out whether a company is honest about its operating reality.

Hiring managers: have a real answer ready. Candidates can tell when “our weakness is that we care too much” is doing the talking.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
**1/7**
Made a big pricing mistake last week. Raised prices 40% overnight for all 140 Tallyup customers. Lost 30 of them in 7 days. Here’s what happened, what I changed, and why I’m sharing this (no fluff, just real numbers).

**2/7**
Context: Tallyup is a simple subscription tool for gyms to track member retention. I’m the solo founder. Been building in public for a while—this felt like a gut punch.

**3/7**
The mistake: I assumed customers would see the value in the price increase. I’d added features, improved support, and thought the new pricing reflected that. But I didn’t test, didn’t communicate early, and didn’t grandfather anyone.

**4/7**
The fallout: 30 cancellations in a week. Some were polite (“love the tool, but can’t justify the cost”), others were blunt (“this is ridiculous”). MRR dropped ~20% overnight. Not catastrophic, but painful.

**5/7**
What I changed:
1. **Grandfathered existing customers** at their old price for 6 months. Gave them time to adjust or leave without feeling punished.
2. **Added a mid-tier plan** for smaller gyms who couldn’t afford the new pricing.
3. **Over-communicated**—emailed everyone personally, explained the mistake, and shared the changes.

**6/7**
What I learned:
- **Pricing is emotional**. Even if the math works, people hate sudden changes.
- **Test assumptions**. I should’ve surveyed or rolled out the increase gradually.
- **Indie SaaS is fragile**. Losing 20% of revenue stings when you’re bootstrapped.

**7/7**
The good news: Most customers stayed. A few even upgraded to the new mid-tier. And I’ve got a better pricing model now. If you’re a founder, don’t make my mistake—talk to your customers *before* you pull the trigger.

(And if you’re a gym owner who left, I get it. Hope you find a tool that works for you.)

b.text:
1/ I made the worst pricing mistake of my solo SaaS career last month — and lost 30 of our 140 Tallyup customers in 7 days.
Build in public means I own the bad just as much as the wins. Here’s what went down, what I broke, and what I changed:

2/ For context: I’m the solo founder of Tallyup, a tiny subscription tool that helps gym owners track member retention. I’d been crunching numbers for weeks and realized we were undercharging by a lot — the 40% price hike made total sense on paper. My smooth-brain mistake? I rolled it out for *every existing customer* overnight. No heads up, no grace period, no exceptions.

3/ The fallout was immediate and brutal: 30 customers churned in the first week. A lot of them were early users who’d stuck with me since launch, when the tool was half-broken and I was answering support tickets from my couch after my day job. A handful left angry DMs, and they were 100% right to be mad.

4/ First fix: I sent a raw, no-fluff email to every remaining customer within 24 hours. No corporate excuses, no “we’re adjusting to market conditions” garbage. Just: I messed up. The overnight price hike was unfair. All existing customers are getting their original price back, permanently.

5/ For the 30 people who’d already left? I followed up individually with the same apology, a link to reactivate at their old rate, and a note that I’d have their account fully restored in 2 minutes flat if they wanted to come back. No sales pitch, no fine print — just me owning my mistake.

6/ The big lesson I learned the hard way, for any other indie SaaS founders in the chat: Your existing customers are your entire moat when you’re tiny. They’re the ones who refer friends, leave honest reviews, and put up with your janky v1 features. Burning them for a quick revenue bump is never worth it.

7/ I don’t have a flashy “and then we grew 20% overnight” ending to this yet. We’re still rebuilding trust with the folks who stuck around, and a few of the churned customers have come back, but this was a huge, expensive wakeup call.

8/ I post all this because so much build in public content only highlights the wins, but the messy, stupid mistakes are where the real learning happens. If you’re navigating pricing as an indie founder, drop your questions below — I’ll answer every one with the unfiltered truth. 🫡

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
# The Market Didn't Slow Down. Sellers Just Haven't Noticed Yet.

Let me tell you what's actually happening in our zip code this spring, because the headline numbers are getting read the wrong way.

Last spring, the median home here sold in 8 days. This spring, it's 34. That's a big jump, and I've watched sellers see that number and start bracing for a crash. Meanwhile, list prices are still up 6% year over year. Showings per listing, though, have dropped by half.

Put those three facts next to each other and you get the real story: buyers are still here, they're still paying strong prices, but they are no longer in a panic. They're not showing up to fifteen houses a weekend and firing off offers on twelve of them. They're being selective. And selective buyers move slower.

That's it. That's the whole shift. The market didn't fall apart. It just stopped rewarding lazy pricing.

Here's where I'll be honest, because I think honesty is more useful than hedging. I have three sellers right now who've been on the market 60-plus days and won't drop their price. Every one of them is pointing at that 6% number and saying, "The market's up, so my price is fine." But 6% is what *correctly priced* homes are commanding. It is not a coupon you get to staple onto an overpriced listing. A house that's been sitting for two months isn't proof the market is soft. It's proof the price is wrong.

Because the homes priced right? They're still going in under two weeks. I'm watching it happen. The 34-day median is being dragged up by the stubborn listings, the ones chasing last spring's frenzy. Strip those out and the well-priced homes are moving almost as fast as they did a year ago.

So no, I'm not going to tell you the market is "complex and depends on many factors." Here's my actual advice: price it to today, not to what your neighbor got in a bidding war fourteen months ago. Buyers have their footing back, and they can tell the difference between a home priced to sell and a home priced to sit. The ones priced to sell are still selling.

The frenzy is over. The market is fine. The only thing that's crashed is the seller's ability to name any number and get it.

If you're thinking about listing this year, that's not bad news. It just means the strategy changed. Let's price it right the first time and skip the 60 days of watching it sit.

b.text:
# The Market Has Slowed. Sellers Need to Catch Up.

Eight days. That was the median time a home spent on the market in my ZIP code last spring.

This spring, it’s 34.

That’s not a crash. It’s a change in pace—and too many sellers are still pricing their homes as though buyers have eight days to make a decision.

After 10 years selling real estate in this community, I understand why sellers get attached to a number. They remember what the neighbor got. They’ve watched their equity grow. They’ve already figured out what the proceeds could buy next.

But none of those things tells us what a buyer will pay today.

Here’s the disconnect in our local numbers: List prices are up 6% year over year, while showings per listing have dropped by half. Sellers are asking for more money at the same time they’re getting substantially less attention.

An asking price isn’t proof of value. It’s a proposition. Buyers get to respond.

Right now, a lot of them are responding by not scheduling a showing.

## This Is a Pricing Problem, Not a Market Collapse

Homes priced right are still selling in under two weeks. That’s the fact I keep coming back to when someone asks whether our market is falling apart.

Buyers haven’t disappeared. They’re just not treating every new listing like an emergency.

Last spring’s eight-day median encouraged sellers to expect immediate interest and fast decisions. This spring’s 34-day median demands a different approach. You can’t keep last year’s expectations, add 6% to the asking price, and act surprised when the first weekend passes quietly.

A slower market makes pricing mistakes harder to hide.

I currently have three sellers whose homes have been on the market for more than 60 days and who are refusing to reduce their prices. I understand their reluctance. Nobody enjoys hearing that the number they planned around isn’t getting results.

But my advice is direct: If your home has been available for two months without a buyer, waiting longer at the same price is not, by itself, a strategy.

It’s a bet that the next buyer will see something the previous buyers didn’t.

## “We Can Always Come Down” Has a Cost

Sellers often want to start high because they don’t want to leave money on the table. Fair enough. My job is to help them get the strongest result, not talk them into giving anything away.

But starting too high has a cost, too.

You miss buyers who would have considered the home at a realistic price. You spend the listing’s first weeks testing an ambition instead of competing for an offer. Then, when you finally adjust, you’re explaining why the house is still available.

A price reduction isn’t a personal defeat. It’s a response to evidence.

And the evidence shouldn’t have to become overwhelming before we acknowledge it. Few showings, no offers, and weeks of silence are information. Sellers don’t have to like that information, but ignoring it won’t improve their position.

## Price for the Buyer Who Exists Today

My view of this spring’s market is straightforward: Sellers haven’t caught up to the new pace.

That doesn’t mean every home needs a dramatic price cut. It means the asking price needs to earn a buyer’s attention now—not make sense in a conversation about what happened last spring.

The sellers doing that are still moving. The ones holding out for yesterday’s urgency are spending a lot more time on the market.

I’m not telling sellers to panic. I’m telling them to compete.

There’s a big difference between protecting your equity and protecting an asking price. A good selling strategy knows which one matters.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
Over roughly 200 interviews, I’ve noticed a clear pattern in the final ten minutes.

Most candidates ask about daily routines, tech stacks, or growth opportunities. Standard, safe questions.

The strongest candidates ask something that forces me to put the employer-branding pitch aside:

"Can you tell me about the last major project here that failed, and what happened next?"

A few months ago, an operations candidate asked me this. 

I gave him the unvarnished version: we spent four months rolling out an automated scheduling pilot at two of our cross-docks. The dispatchers hated it. It added ten minutes of manual overrides per route instead of saving time, and we ultimately had to pull the plug and start over.

Instead of just nodding, he asked: 

"When you pulled the plug, did the project lead stay on to run the rebuild, or did leadership reassign it?"

That single question told me more about his maturity than the previous 40 minutes of his resume walkthrough. He wasn’t trying to trap me. He was evaluating our psychological safety. He wanted to know if we treat failure as a learning loop or a career penalty.

Experienced candidates know every company breaks things. The only real question is whether you handle it with a blameless post-mortem or a scapegoat.

b.text:
After ~200 interviews, here's a pattern I can't unsee:

The strongest candidates ask about the projects that didn't work.

Most people ask about growth, roadmap, "what does success look like in this role." Fine questions. Safe questions.

But every so often someone asks: "Tell me about a project that failed recently. What happened?"

Had one last month. When I brought up a warehouse routing rollout we'd scrapped, most candidates would nod and move on. This one asked why we scrapped it, who made that call, and whether we'd try again with a different approach.

That's not a candidate trying to impress me. That's someone figuring out how we handle being wrong—because they're deciding if they want to work here as much as I'm deciding if I want to hire them.

The failed-project question tells them more than any polished win story ever could. How we talk about failure is how we'll talk about theirs.

If you're interviewing soon, ask it. And pay attention to how long it takes us to answer.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer After 8 Months of Market Sourdough

I bought the Corlane SM6 last March because my old mixer started dying on 1,200-gram batches of stiff bagel dough. I bake almost every day for the Saturday market: two or three loads of sourdough, plus bagels twice a week. The SM6 has been on the counter the entire time.

The motor is the reason to consider this machine. A double batch of 65% hydration bagel dough (about 1.8 kg of very stiff stuff) never made it hesitate. No stalling, no overheating, no that-smell-of-hot-plastic. It just chewed through it on speed 2 for eight minutes. KitchenAid’s equivalent 5-quart bowl-lift would have been screaming by minute four. That extra torque is real.

Two problems showed up fast. The bowl-lift lever started squeaking after six weeks. I hit it with WD-40 once a month and it stays quiet for three weeks, then starts again. Annoying, not fatal. Worse: the stock dough hook is too short for the deep bowl. On a 900-gram loaf it barely reaches the bottom third of the dough. I ordered a third-party spiral hook ($28) and that fixed it. Corlane should have shipped the right length in the first place.

Price: $429. That’s $80 more than the KitchenAid Professional 5 Plus that most people would compare it to. You’re paying for the extra power and the bigger bowl. If you mostly mix cookie dough and cake batter, that extra money is wasted. Those jobs don’t need this motor.

If you knead heavy dough every week—sourdough, bagels, pizza, pretzels—buy it. The motor earns the extra $80. If that’s not you, skip it and get the KitchenAid. I wouldn’t own anything else at this point.

b.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: 8 Months of Nearly Daily Use

**Quick take:** The motor is worth the money. The accessories aren't. Full verdict at the bottom.

---

I've been running the Corlane SM6 for eight months now, and it gets used almost every day. I bake sourdough for a weekend farmers market stall, so this isn't a "unboxed it and made two batches of banana bread" review — this machine has mixed hundreds of batches of dough since it landed on my counter. Here's what eight months of hard use looks like.

## The motor is the whole reason to buy this mixer

The test that kills most home stand mixers is stiff, low-hydration dough — and I run the SM6 through that test constantly. A double batch of bagel dough, stiff enough that plenty of consumer mixers would stall out or walk themselves across the counter, runs through this machine without hesitation. No stalling, no straining, no standing there with my hand on the bowl waiting for it to recover. I can walk away and weigh out the next ingredient while it kneads.

If you've ever heard a mixer bog down in the middle of a bread dough, you know how quickly that becomes a dealbreaker. In eight months of near-daily bread work, the motor has never done that to me once. That is the entire case for this mixer.

## Two real problems

**The bowl lift lever squeaks.** Not a catastrophic issue, but it's a monthly maintenance item — I hit it with WD-40 about once every four weeks or it gets genuinely annoying. For a machine at this price, it shouldn't squeak out of the box, and it shouldn't squeak eight months later either.

**The included dough hook is too short for the bowl.** This is my biggest complaint. The SM6's bowl is deep, and the stock hook doesn't reach far enough down — dough at the bottom of the bowl just sits there, not getting worked in. I ended up buying a third-party hook, which solved the problem completely, but it means the hook that ships with the mixer is effectively useless for exactly the kind of dough this machine is built for. Factor that into the price.

## Speaking of price

The SM6 is $429. The comparable KitchenAid is $349. So the real math is: an $80 premium over KitchenAid, plus the cost of a replacement dough hook on top.

## Verdict

**If you're kneading heavy dough every week — bread, bagels, low-hydration anything, double batches — buy it.** The $80 premium buys you a motor that genuinely doesn't stall where other mixers in this class will, and after eight months I trust it with my market bread. Deal with the hook swap, keep a can of WD-40 under the sink, and it earns its spot on the counter.

**If your mixer mostly sees cookie dough and cake batter, skip it.** You'd be paying an $80 premium, plus a new dough hook, for a motor you'll never stress. Buy the KitchenAid and put the savings toward something else.

That's not a hedge — there's exactly one question that determines the answer, and it's whether stiff dough is a weekly event in your kitchen. For me it is, and I'd buy the SM6 again tomorrow.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
**How to Keep Your Dog's Coat from Matting Between Grooming Visits**

If I could give every dog owner one piece of advice, it's this: never put a matted dog in the bathtub. I see it all the time — someone gives their pup a bath at home thinking the water will loosen the tangles, and by the time they come in to me, what started as a few small knots has dried into a solid felt pad against the skin. Water doesn't loosen mats. It locks them in tighter, and once that happens there often isn't a humane option besides clipping them out.

So the rule at home is simple: always brush before the bath, never after. Get the coat completely tangle-free first, then bathe.

When you brush, grab a slicker brush and use short line strokes — little strokes in one direction — not circles. Brushing in circles just winds the hair around itself and tightens whatever's already tangled. Work in small sections instead of going over the whole dog at once, and start behind the ears and under the front legs. That's where mats almost always begin, because of the friction from collars, harnesses, and all that leg movement. If those spots are clear, the rest of the coat usually follows pretty easily.

This matters even more with double-coated breeds — goldens, huskies, shepherds — where the soft undercoat tangles down at the skin where you can't see it, and with curly coats like poodles and doodles, where the hair seems to knot itself overnight. For those coats especially, a few minutes of brushing every couple of days beats an hour-long battle once a month.

And if you run your fingers through and feel a mat already starting, don't reach for the brush or comb first. Work a little conditioner into it with your fingers and gently tease the hairs apart with your fingertips. Once it loosens up, then you can ease through it with the brush. Going straight in with a tool pulls at the skin, hurts your dog, and teaches them to dread brushing — which makes everything harder next time.

Brush before the bath, keep an eye on those trouble spots, and your dog stays comfortable between visits. And if you're ever not sure about your technique, just ask at your next appointment — I'm happy to show you on your own dog. It's a lot easier to learn hands-on than from reading about it.

b.text:
# Stop Matting Before It Starts

Here's the thing I see all the time in my salon: dog owners bathe their pups first, thinking the water and shampoo will loosen those pesky mats. I get it—that seems like it should work. But it actually does the opposite. When you wet matted fur, it compresses everything together and turns it into basically a felt pad. Once that happens, you're looking at a much harder problem to solve.

So start with your brush, not the tub. A slicker brush is your best friend here, and the technique matters. Use short, gentle line strokes—not circular motions. Those circles actually work the mat tighter instead of loosening it. Think of it like you're combing through the coat, following the direction the hair grows.

Now, where do mats actually form first? Behind the ears and under the front legs. If your dog has a double coat or curly fur, these spots are basically mat magnets because of how the hair sits and moves. Start your brushing routine in those problem areas and work in sections so you don't miss anything.

But here's what you do if you already spot a mat forming: don't grab the brush yet. Work a little conditioner into it with your fingers first. Let it sit in there for a minute. This softens the mat and makes it so much easier for your brush to glide through without yanking.

Do this two or three times a week between your grooming appointments, and you'll be shocked at the difference. Your groomer will thank you too.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
Testimony for the City Council Record

Members of the City Council:

I am the owner of a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am submitting this testimony about the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from $0.50 per hour to $1.50 per hour.

This proposal is not a small adjustment. It is a $1.00 increase, raising the rate by 200% and tripling what a driver pays for the same hour of parking. For my business, that matters because my customers are not parking all day. Their average visit is 22 minutes. Under the current hourly minimum, a customer can park, come in, order, and leave within that time for $0.50. Under the proposed rate, the same 22-minute visit would cost $1.50 because the customer must pay for a full hour. That means customers would pay for 60 minutes to use 22 minutes, and they would pay $1.00 more for the same short stop.

The current hour minimum already covers my customers fine. A 22-minute visit is less than half of the paid hour, and the existing 50-cent rate already encourages turnover without punishing people for stopping downtown.

I have seen what this kind of increase can do. In 2019, after a similar parking hike in the next town over, I tracked my register for six weeks and saw foot traffic drop 18%. That is not a general concern or a vague warning; it is the number I recorded over six weeks. When parking becomes more expensive, people notice, and small, quick visits are the first to disappear.

The city’s own report also shows that meter revenue covers only 4% of the downtown budget. That is a specific number, and it should matter in this decision. If meter revenue is only 4% of the downtown budget, then increasing parking rates from $0.50 to $1.50 per hour is not solving the city’s budget problem. It is shifting the cost of a very small revenue source onto customers, employees, and small businesses.

For these reasons, I urge the council not to approve the increase from $0.50 to $1.50 per hour. If the goal is to manage parking turnover, the current rate already does that for businesses like mine. If the goal is revenue, the city’s own 4% figure shows that this increase is too small to solve the budget issue but large enough to risk measurable harm to downtown traffic. Please keep the current rate, or at minimum adopt short-term parking pricing that reflects the 22-minute reality of downtown visits instead of forcing customers to pay for a full hour at triple the old rate.

b.text:
**Testimony on Proposed Parking Meter Rate Increase**

Good evening, City Council members. My name is [Your Name], and I am the owner of [Coffee Shop Name], a small independent business on Main Street. I am here to speak against the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour. While I understand the city’s need to generate revenue, this change will disproportionately harm local businesses like mine without addressing the root issues of downtown funding.

In 2019, a neighboring town implemented a similar rate hike, raising their meter fees from 50 cents to $1.25 per hour. Over the following six weeks, I tracked my own register data and observed an 18% decline in foot traffic. That drop directly translated to lost sales, making it harder to cover overhead costs like rent, utilities, and payroll. If this proposal passes, I fear we will see the same trend here—customers deterred by higher costs, choosing to shop elsewhere or avoid downtown altogether.

Most of my customers spend an average of 22 minutes in my shop. Under the current system, the one-hour minimum at 50 cents already covers their visit comfortably. Doubling or tripling the rate for such a short stay feels punitive, not practical. My customers aren’t the issue—many are regulars who support multiple small businesses in a single trip. If parking becomes more expensive, they may consolidate their visits or opt for areas with free parking, reducing the vibrancy of our downtown.

I also reviewed the city’s own report on parking meter revenue, which states that meter fees currently cover just 4% of the downtown budget. This proposed increase won’t solve the larger funding gaps—it will only place an undue burden on the small businesses and customers who keep our downtown alive. If the goal is to support local commerce, we should explore alternatives that don’t risk driving customers away.

I urge the City Council to reconsider this rate hike and instead focus on solutions that strengthen, rather than strain, our small business community. Thank you for your time and consideration.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
# Why I've Come Around on Winter Weddings

I'll be honest: for the first few years of my career, I thought of winter as the off-season. The time to catch up on editing, update my portfolio, and wait for May.

Then the winter bookings started coming in, and I stopped waiting for May. I've shot eleven winter weddings in the last two years, and at this point, if you told me I could only shoot one season for the rest of my career, November through February would genuinely be in the running. Here's why.

## The light is better than you think. Actually, it's better than June.

This is the part nobody believes until they see the photos.

Everyone assumes summer means great light, but around here, June often means one of two things: harsh midday sun that makes everyone squint, or a flat, gray overcast sky that turns every portrait slightly dull, like someone lowered the contrast on the whole day.

Compare that to a November afternoon around 3pm. The sun is already low, coming in at an angle through bare trees, and the light that filters through those empty branches is soft, directional, and warm. It sculpts faces instead of flattening them. Some of my favorite portraits from the last two years were shot in exactly those conditions — no leaves, no lush greenery, just that low golden light doing the work. The catch is that golden hour comes early in winter, so we plan portraits around 3pm instead of 7pm. But once you're planning for it, it's not a compromise. It's an upgrade.

## Your vendors aren't stretched across four other weddings

Here's something couples don't usually see: in June, when I pull into a venue parking lot, I'm often one of three or four vendors' vehicles arriving for weddings happening the same day, sometimes at the same property. Everyone — the florist, the caterer, the DJ — is running between events, watching the clock, thinking about their next load-in.

At a winter wedding, I pull into that same lot and it's basically just us. Your wedding is the event that day. That changes the whole energy. Vendors aren't rushing. The venue staff isn't split between two receptions. If your ceremony runs fifteen minutes long, nobody's sweating it. I have room to slow down, try that one extra portrait idea, wander off with you two for ten more minutes of couple photos — because there's nowhere else I have to be.

## And yes, it costs less. Meaningfully less.

Winter dates typically run about 30% cheaper for couples across the board — venues, vendors, the works. That's not a small discount. On a full wedding budget, that's the difference that pays for the honeymoon, or the better photography package, or just not starting your marriage with a bigger loan than you needed.

You're not getting less wedding for that money. You're getting a less crowded calendar, which happens to come with a smaller invoice.

## What winter actually asks of you

I won't pretend there are no tradeoffs. The early sunset means we build the timeline around light, which sometimes means doing portraits before the ceremony. It's cold, so we plan for it — quick outdoor sessions, warm layers between shots, and honestly, some of the coziest, most emotional indoor reception photos I've ever taken.

But "we planned around a 4:45 sunset" is a much smaller problem than "our photos are flat and our vendors were racing to their next event."

If you're deciding between a peak-season Saturday and a winter date, I'm happy to talk through what your specific day would look like in each. But after eleven winter weddings, I can tell you: the couples who book December aren't settling. Some of them just figured it out first.

*Want to see winter galleries from real weddings I've shot? [Reach out] and I'll send some over.*

b.text:
## Why I’ve Genuinely Fallen for Winter Weddings

Six years ago, if you’d asked me when I wanted to shoot weddings, I would have said late spring through early fall without hesitating. Everyone does. Warm weather, long evenings, green trees, easy driving—on paper, it sounds like the dream.

And I still love a good summer wedding. But after shooting more off-season weddings over the last couple of years, I’ve realized something that surprised me:

I actually love winter weddings now.

Not in a “well, every season has its own beauty” sort of way. In a very practical, photographer-brain, I’m-honestly-having-more-fun way.

There are a few reasons for it.

### The light is better than people think

Couples often worry that winter means dark, gray, depressing photos. I get it. But winter light can be gorgeous in a way people don’t expect.

In November, especially around 3 p.m., the sun sits lower and the light comes through bare trees in this soft, directional way that I love for portraits. It’s not harsh. It’s not flat. It has shape. It has mood.

Honestly, I’ll take that over a flat overcast June day many times.

Summer light can be beautiful too, but it’s not automatically better. Bright midday sun can create hard shadows. Overcast summer days can look dull and washed out. Winter gives me something different to work with—more texture, more atmosphere, more dimension.

And bare trees? They’re not the disadvantage people think they are. They create natural framing, interesting lines, and a sense of place. They let light through in ways full summer foliage doesn’t. Some of my favorite portraits from the last couple of years were shot in conditions couples initially worried would be “too bleak.”

They weren’t bleak at all. They were striking.

### Winter weddings are calmer

This is the part nobody really talks about when they’re choosing a date.

In June, I might show up to a venue and realize I’m sharing the parking lot with three or four other vendors all shooting different events, or the space feels crowded, or the timeline is tight because everything is booked back-to-back.

Winter weddings often feel different.

There’s more breathing room. Fewer events competing for the same spaces. Less chaos. Sometimes venues are more flexible, timelines feel less rushed, and the whole day has a quieter rhythm.

That matters for photos.

When a day feels calmer, couples usually feel calmer. And when couples feel calmer, they photograph more like themselves. Less performance. Less stress. More real.

That’s always going to make better images.

### Your photos can feel more like yours

Winter weddings have a built-in sense of atmosphere.

Maybe it’s the earlier sunset, the candlelight, the layers, the texture of a coat or shawl, the moodiness of a dark sky behind a venue at dusk. Maybe it’s the fact that winter weddings often feel more intentional because the couple chose them for a reason, not just because it was the “default” wedding season.

Whatever it is, I’ve noticed that winter weddings often end up feeling more distinctive.

They don’t look like every other summer wedding at the same venue in the same golden hour slot. They have their own tone.

I like that.

### It can also be a smarter booking decision

This is the practical part.

Winter bookings often run about 30% cheaper for couples. That’s not a tiny difference. For a lot of couples, that’s the difference between affording the photographer they really want and feeling stretched too thin.

I’ve shot eleven winter weddings over the last two years, and I keep coming back to the same conclusion: couples considering an off-season date should seriously consider it.

Not because it’s cheaper—though it can be.

But because the day can feel more personal, the light can be surprisingly beautiful, and the experience can be calmer than the peak-season version.

If you’re trying to decide between a June date and a winter date, I wouldn’t automatically choose June just because that’s what everyone does.

Some of my favorite work has come from weddings couples planned outside the box.

And if you’re nervous about winter light? Don’t be.

That 3 p.m. November glow through bare branches might end up being one of the best parts of your gallery.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
Last Tuesday morning, my seventh grader fell asleep next to his cereal bowl. Not theatrically—just quietly, face-down, at 6:45 a.m. If you have a middle-schooler in Millbrook, you probably have your own version of this story. The backpack zippers that won’t move fast enough. The argument over whether a hoodie counts as a winter jacket. The blank stare when you ask if they remembered their lunch. By the time we’re in the car at 7:15, I feel like I’ve already done a full day’s work.

That’s why I’m urging our school board to pass the proposal to move middle school start times to 8:45 a.m. when they vote next month. And it’s why I’m asking other parents to let the board know we’ve read the plan, and we support it.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has been clear for years: middle schoolers should not start class before 8:30 a.m. It’s not about coddling kids. It’s biology. Teenagers’ natural sleep shifts later, meaning the 7:30 a.m. alarm hits them in the middle of what their bodies treat as the night. My eighth grader is sharp and funny at 3 p.m.; at 7:45 a.m., he stares at math problems like I’m speaking another language.

We don’t have to guess whether a later start works. Lincoln Middle ran a pilot last year with an 8:45 start. Attendance went up. First period grades went up. Teachers said kids were actually engaged, not just upright. Those are real results from a school a lot like ours.

I’ve heard the worry about bus logistics. Will routes collide? Will elementary kids be left waiting? But the proposal already re-tiers the routes. High school and elementary keep their current start windows; middle school shifts into the later slot. The buses don’t disappear—they just run in a smarter order. The board has done the homework on this.

People sometimes say kids should just go to bed earlier. I invite anyone who thinks that to try putting a hormone-soaked thirteen-year-old to bed at 9 p.m. Their brains simply don’t release melatonin on an elementary-school schedule anymore.

We have a chance to align our school day with what doctors recommend and what our own eyes see every morning. The board votes next month. Let’s not let bureaucratic inertia override a plan that helps kids show up rested, ready, and awake enough to learn. Let’s start middle school at 8:45.

b.text:
**An 8:45 Start Is the Right Choice for Millbrook**

As the parent of two Millbrook middle-schoolers, I know that getting teenagers out the door in the morning can feel like a daily test of endurance. But the debate over an 8:45 school start is about more than making mornings easier. It is about giving students a better chance to arrive at school awake, ready to learn and able to succeed.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later. Adolescents generally need eight to ten hours of sleep each night, yet their changing body clocks make it difficult for many of them to fall asleep early. Telling a 13-year-old to “just go to bed sooner” sounds reasonable, but it often does not match the biology of adolescence.

We also have evidence close to home. In the Lincoln Middle School pilot, attendance improved and first-period grades went up after the school adopted a later start. Those are not abstract benefits. They mean more students in their seats and more students learning during a period that too often begins with tired faces and half-open eyes.

The most common objection I hear is about buses. That concern is understandable. Families depend on reliable transportation, and changing one school’s schedule can affect the entire system. But the proposal before the board does not ignore that problem. It already re-tiers the bus routes to accommodate the 8:45 start. Any new system will require adjustment, but bus logistics should be something we solve—not a reason to reject a schedule that better serves students.

There will undoubtedly be complications involving sports, after-school activities and family routines. Our household will have to adjust, too. Still, the current early schedule also has costs: rushed mornings, missed breakfasts, late arrivals and children trying to learn while exhausted. We should not treat those costs as unavoidable simply because we are used to them.

This proposal is not a cure-all, and it will not turn every teenager into a cheerful morning person. But the AAP recommendation, the Lincoln pilot and plain common sense all point in the same direction.

When the school board votes next month, I hope its members choose the 8:45 start. Millbrook’s students deserve a school day built around when they are most able to learn.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After 12 years selling homes in Asheville, mostly to first-time buyers, I've started asking people to do one thing that feels a little annoying at first.

If they love a house online, I ask them to walk the neighborhood at 7am before we tour it.

The buyers who do it almost always end up happier later, even if they don't buy that house. You just learn different things at 7am.

The Pruitts are why I keep asking.

Last spring they were stuck on a little 1920s bungalow on Sycamore Street in West Asheville. It checked all their boxes online, and they wanted to see it that Saturday. I told them I would book it, but could they do me a favor and walk Sycamore and the two streets over at 7am first, before we went inside?

They texted me from the sidewalk on Tuesday morning. The woman next door was already out watering her garden and stopped to chat and ask if they were thinking of moving in. The guy across the street was loading his kid and a cello into a Subaru for early orchestra practice. And two old black Labs from three doors down dragged their owner straight over to say hello.

We walked the house at 9am. They still loved it, but now they weren't just buying the house, they knew what Tuesday on Sycamore actually felt like.

They closed in May. I ran into Maya at the River Arts farmers market last week and she said those same Labs still come to say hi every morning when she's making coffee.

You can learn a lot about a house at 2pm on a Saturday. You learn a lot more about whether you want to live there at 7am on a Tuesday.

b.text:
I've been selling houses in Asheville for 12 years, mostly to first-time buyers. One thing I keep noticing: the ones who walk the neighborhood at 7am before we even go inside tend to end up a lot happier with the house later.

The Pruitts on Sycamore Street are the ones I think about.

They liked the house but kept circling back to the street. The listing photos made it look busier than they wanted. I told them to go walk it at 7 the next morning, before our showing.

They showed up already smiling. Said it was quiet except for birds and a few people walking dogs. You could smell coffee from the place around the corner. They wrote the offer that afternoon.

They still send me pictures of their porch at sunrise. It's not complicated. You just get a better sense of what living there actually feels like.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

Most of our January emergency calls come from homeowners who skipped this step. A single burst pipe can cost thousands in water damage, but protecting your outdoor faucets takes minutes.

Here is the checklist to stop pipes from freezing:

1.  **Shut the interior valve.** Look for a valve inside your house that controls water to the outside spigot. Turn it off.
2.  **Open the outside spigot.** Let the water drain out completely until it stops flowing.
3.  **Disconnect all hoses.** This is the biggest mistake. If you leave a hose attached, water stays trapped in the pipe and freezes, causing a burst.
4.  **Install a foam cover.** Buy a cheap insulation cover (about $3) and snap it over the spigot.

**Don’t have an interior shutoff valve?**
If your home doesn't have a way to cut the water from inside, call us. We can install one before the first hard freeze so you're not stuck in January.

Do this now while the weather is still okay. Your pipes (and your wallet) will thank you.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots (Minneapolis Homeowner's Guide)

Every January the phone rings the same way. There's water where water shouldn't be, and when we trace it back, it's almost always the same thing: a hose somebody left connected to the outside spigot since October.

Ten minutes this fall prevents that call. Here's the whole job.

## Step 1: Shut Off the Water Inside

Go to your basement or utility room and find the pipe that feeds your outdoor spigot. Within a few feet of where it heads outside, there should be a shutoff valve — either a quarter-turn lever or a round handle. Close it. If it's a lever, it's closed when the handle sits perpendicular to the pipe.
