setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
One question has come up repeatedly in roughly 200 interviews:

“What was the last project that didn’t go as planned?”

The strongest candidates don’t ask it to catch us out. They’re trying to understand how we work when the plan breaks.

Recently, a candidate asked about a logistics system rollout that had to be paused after the first implementation created extra manual work for the operations team.

I explained what happened, where our assumptions were wrong, and what we changed before restarting.

They followed up with:

“Who had the authority to stop the rollout, and how early could the warehouse teams raise concerns?”

That was a much better question than “What’s the culture like?”

It showed they were thinking about decision-making, feedback loops, and whether problems could be surfaced before they became expensive.

We also got into what I would do differently as the hiring manager. I didn’t have a polished answer, because the honest answer involved trade-offs and things we missed.

That conversation became more useful than any rehearsed response about strengths, weaknesses, or five-year plans.

Candidates: you don’t need to ask for confidential details. Ask about a real setback and what the company learned from it.

Hiring teams: if every interview answer sounds perfect, you may not be giving candidates enough evidence to evaluate the job.

b.text:
After roughly 200 interviews for our logistics teams, one specific moment consistently separates strong candidates from the ones we end up fighting to hire.

It happens at the end of the call, right when I ask, "What questions do you have for me?"

The candidates who usually get the offer don't ask about company culture perks or ideal start dates right away. They ask about our last failed project.

Here’s how that conversation usually goes:

Candidate: "What’s the biggest operational project that fell apart here recently?"

Me: "We tried rolling out a new route-optimization tool to three regional hubs last year. The software wasn't ready for our edge cases, drivers hated the interface, and on-time deliveries dipped for two straight weeks."

Candidate: "How did leadership react to that dip? Did they blame the hubs, or did they pivot?"

Me: "We pulled the tool from two hubs, kept it in one to debug, and put two fleet supervisors in the daily product feedback calls until it actually worked."

Candidate: "Good. That tells me failure isn't swept under the rug here, and field feedback actually influences tech decisions. That’s what I needed to know."

Average candidates want to know what success looks like on day one. Top candidates want to know what happens when things go wrong on day thirty. 

When a candidate asks about your worst moments, they aren't trying to catch you in a trap. They're checking for psychological safety, accountability, and how your teams handle pressure.

If you’re interviewing soon—on either side of the desk—don't just talk about the wins. Ask about the mess. You’ll learn more about a company in those five minutes than in the rest of the interview combined.

setup: A co-founder is posting a LinkedIn hiring announcement for a first customer support hire to potential applicants and customers.

a.text:
Up until now, the three of us at Ridgepoint have answered every single customer support ticket, chat, and email ourselves. 

It worked when we had twenty users. It is officially not working anymore. 

We build scheduling software for small trucking dispatchers. When our users reach out to support, it’s usually because a truck is sitting at a dock, a driver is waiting on an address, or a rate con didn’t parse correctly. They are busy, stressed, and working in an industry where delays cost real money. 

We need to hire our first dedicated Customer Support specialist to take this over. 

Here is what the job actually looks like day to day:

- Answering 30–50 tickets and chats a day with fast, clear, human responses (no canned corporate speak).
- Getting on a quick screen share when a dispatcher who isn’t very tech-savvy is stuck and just needs someone patient to walk them through it.
- Replicating weird edge cases, figuring out what actually broke, and handing clean bug reports directly to our engineer.
- Writing our help center from scratch. Right now, half our documentation lives in my head or in scattered Notion docs. You’ll turn that into actual self-serve resources.
- Feeding user frustration directly into our weekly product roadmap. You will know what's broken before anyone else does.

What we’re looking for:
- You’ve done software support before, or you have a background in logistics/dispatching and know how this industry talks.
- You’re comfortable with early-stage chaos. There is no 50-page training manual yet—you’ll be helping us write it.
- High empathy, thick skin, and great written communication. Trucking moves fast and dispatchers don't have time for fluff.

This is a fully remote, full-time role. You’ll be employee #4, working directly with the three founders every day. 

If this sounds like the kind of problem you want to solve, send me a DM here or email me directly at [email address] with a quick note on why you're interested and what you've worked on before.

b.text:
We're hiring our first support person at Ridgepoint, and I want to skip the usual "we're a family, we move fast, ping pong table" post and just tell you what the job actually is.

Right now the three of us founders take turns answering tickets between building product, doing sales calls, and everything else a 3-person company has to do. It's not working. Someone emails about a load not syncing to their dispatch board at 6am because that's when trucking dispatchers start their day, and it sits for two hours because whoever's turn it is was in a customer call. We've had a few people almost churn over response time alone, which is the dumbest reason to lose a customer.

So here's the actual day to day if you take this job:

You'll be on Intercom and email from early morning to mid afternoon, because our customers are dispatchers who start work before sunrise. Most tickets are things like: a load didn't pull over from a broker email correctly, someone can't figure out how to reassign a driver mid-route, a rate confirmation didn't attach right. You'll need to actually learn how trucking dispatch works, not just our software, because half the questions are "is this a Ridgepoint bug or is this just how dispatching works." You will talk to some cranky dispatchers who have been burned by other software before. That's fine, we like builders who don't get rattled by that.

You'll also be the first line back to us on bugs. If three customers ask about the same weird thing in a week, that's a pattern we need to know about, and you're the one who'll catch it before we do.

No support team to manage yet, no ticket queue software with fifteen integrations. It's you, Intercom, our internal docs (which need work, we know), and direct Slack access to the three of us when something's above your pay grade.

This isn't a "wear many hats, own your role" line. It's genuinely: you're support, full stop, and doing it well matters more to our retention right now than almost anything else we could hire for.

If you've done support for a small B2B tool before, especially anything logistics, trucking, or ops-heavy, and you want to be the person who actually shapes what support looks like here instead of inheriting someone else's playbook, message me. Job link in comments.

It’s a risk we can’t keep taking, not when we’re a tiny team working before dawn to make sure you have fresh croissants and sourdough by 7 a.m.

I’ll miss the creativity and the joy of making something truly one-of-a-kind for couples, but I also know this is the right choice for us. Our heart has always been in the daily bake, in the ritual of pulling something warm from the oven and handing it to you with a smile. That’s what we do best, and that’s where we want to keep putting our energy.

Thank you for understanding, and for continuing to support us in all the ways you do. We’re not going anywhere—just refocusing on what makes this little bakery tick.

[Your Name]

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
Look, I know it’s tempting to throw the dog in the tub and hope the water works some magic, but please—don’t do it if there’s already a tangle situation going on. Wet matted fur is basically just a recipe for a felt pad, and once that happens, we’re looking at a much bigger problem (and a much shaggier dog) than when you started. 

The absolute golden rule here is to brush before the bath, not after. If you wait until the dog is already wet and sudsy, you’re essentially just packing those knots tighter against the skin. I see this mistake all the time, and it usually turns a quick brush-out into a full-on de-matting session that neither of us has time for.

So, what’s the game plan? First, grab a slicker brush and forget about those big, circular motions. We’re doing short, line strokes here. And seriously, section the dog off. Start right behind the ears and under those front legs—that’s where the trouble almost always starts first. You want to tackle the easy stuff and the high-risk zones before the water ever touches the coat.

And if you spot a mat starting to form before the bath? Don’t just attack it with a brush right away. Take a moment to work some coat conditioner in with your fingers. This helps loosen the grip without turning that mat into a permanent fixture. Trust me, a little prep work with the conditioner saves you from the frustration of fighting a knot later. Your future self (and your groomer) will thank you.

b.text:
Between grooming visits, the biggest thing I see with double coated and curly breeds is mats that could have been caught early if the brushing happened at the right time. And here's the part most people get backwards: you brush before the bath, never after. Once that coat gets wet, any tangles you missed turn into a felt pad that's ten times harder to get out. So if you're doing an at-home bath, get the brush out first and make sure the coat is completely dry and tangle-free before water touches it.

When you do brush, use a slicker brush and keep your strokes short and straight—no circles. Circles just push the hair around and tighten any knots that are already forming. Work in sections, and don't skip the spots where mats love to start: behind the ears and under the front legs. Those areas rub and trap moisture, so they mat up first even if the rest of the coat looks fine. If you feel a mat starting while you're brushing, stop right there. Don't dig at it with the brush or a comb. Work a little conditioner into the mat with your fingers, let it sit for a minute, then gently tease it apart with your fingers or a wide-tooth comb. That conditioner gives the hair some slip so you're not just yanking and making it worse.

And please, don't bathe the dog first thinking the water will loosen things up. It does the opposite—wet matted fur shrinks and locks in tight, and then you're stuck with a solid clump that usually has to be shaved out. So remember: dry brush first, short strokes, behind the ears and under the front legs, conditioner on any mat before you touch it with a tool. That'll keep your dog comfortable between visits and make your next appointment a whole lot easier on both of us.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
The register died on a Saturday in March, which is the worst day for anything to die. My dad hit the power strip twice and said a word in Vietnamese I'm not supposed to know. The screen stayed black. There were eleven tables seated and four more on the sidewalk looking at their phones.

I got the pad of green order tickets we keep in the drawer under the soy sauce, the ones nobody has used since before I was born, and I started writing. Pho tai, no onion. Bun cha gio, extra fish sauce on the side. Table six wanted their check split three ways and I did the math on the back of the ticket with a pen that kept skipping. I don't know how many I wrote. My handwriting got worse and worse until the last ones looked like a doctor's. My mom read every one of them anyway. She has been reading my dad's handwriting for twenty-six years, so mine wasn't a problem.

We didn't lose a single order. We were forty minutes behind by seven o'clock and a man at table two told me he'd waited longer at the DMV, which I think he meant nicely.

---

We hired a guy named Marcus in the fall. Nineteen, worked at a car wash before. My grandma was supposed to teach him the spring rolls but her hands were bad that month, so she sat on the milk crate by the prep table and pointed and I did the showing.

The fold is not hard. That's the thing people don't believe. You wet the wrapper but not too much, you put the filling in a line a little below the middle, you fold the bottom up, then the two sides in, then you roll it tight and you don't stop rolling once you start. Marcus's first ten came out like little pillows. Too loose. They'd blow open in the oil.

My grandma said something and I told him, tighter, and he said tighter how, and I couldn't explain it in English or in Vietnamese, so I put my hands over his hands and we rolled one together. It came out fine. He did the next four hundred that day and by the end they were all fine. He still works there. He's faster than me now.

---

There's a shelf in the walk-in cooler above the cases of Coke where nobody puts anything, and that's where I do calc.

It's thirty-eight degrees. My break is fifteen minutes and I take it at 3:40, after lunch and before the dinner people. I bring my notebook and a pencil because pens get weird in the cold. I sit on an upturned bucket with my back against the beer boxes.

It's loud out there. Order up, the fan hood, my uncle's phone playing a game show at full volume, somebody's kid. In the cooler it's just the compressor kicking on and off. I can hear my own pencil. I've done most of a semester of related rates in there with my coat on over my apron, and once I fell asleep for six minutes and my mom found me and said I was going to get pneumonia and be useless.

I got a 94 on that unit test. I don't think the cooler had anything to do with it. It's just quiet, and it's the only door in that building that locks from the inside.

---

Last Saturday we were slammed again. The register works now — my cousin replaced it with an iPad thing that my dad refuses to touch. I still keep the green tickets in the drawer under the soy sauce. I moved them to the front, actually, where you can reach them without looking.

b.text:
On the Saturday our register system died, I found a stack of order pads under the counter and started writing.

At first, I tried to keep everything neat. I numbered the tickets and wrote each item on its own line. Then the phone rang, a customer wanted to split a check, and the kitchen needed to know whether “no onion” meant no green onion, too. My handwriting got worse. I started circling things hard enough to tear the paper.

I have worked every weekend at my family’s Vietnamese restaurant since sophomore year. Usually, I can get through a shift without thinking much about the order of things: answer the phone, enter an order, check the bags, wipe the counter. Without the register, I had to think about every step. I added totals on a calculator and checked them twice. When someone came to pick up food, I searched through my handwritten tickets while trying not to look like I was searching.

We got through dinner. Afterward, I put the tickets in order and checked that we had accounted for everything. There was still cleaning to do.

Most weekends are less eventful. I refill things, carry things, and answer questions whose answers are printed on the menu. Sometimes I look at my friends’ messages about Saturday plans while I’m waiting for an order to come out. I would rather be with them than restocking takeout containers. I don’t think that cancels out how much I care about the restaurant.

When a new hire needed to learn how to fold our spring rolls, I showed her the way my grandma had shown me. Keep the filling together. Bring the bottom over it, fold in the sides, and roll firmly without pulling so hard that the wrapper tears.

I did the first one too fast.

She asked me to do it again, so I slowed down. We stood next to each other and folded them one step at a time. Hers came out loose on one end. I pointed to where she could tuck the wrapper tighter, and she tried another. I wanted to reach over and fix it, but I kept my hands on my own roll.

On breaks, I sometimes take my calculus homework into the walk-in cooler. It is cold, obviously, and not a good place to stay long. But it is quiet, and for a few minutes nobody is asking me for extra sauce. I stand with my notebook open and try to finish a problem before I need to go back out.

Some pages have a full solution. Others have two lines of work that make very little sense when I return to them later. At home, I retrace what I was doing, finish the problem, and set out what I need for school.

Next weekend, I will be back at the restaurant. I’ll bring my homework, though I won’t count on finishing it there. If the register works, I probably won’t notice. The order pads are still under the counter.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
My daughter was six when I came home from my second deployment. At the airport, she stood behind her mother’s leg. I could see one eye and part of her forehead.

I had been thinking about seeing her for months. I figured she would run to me. I had pictured putting my bag down so I could catch her.

Instead, I put my bag down and stayed where I was.

“Hey, kiddo.”

She pulled back behind her mother. She didn’t recognize me at first. She knew I was coming home. Those turned out to be different things.

Her mother put a hand on her head and told her it was okay. I crouched down, which wasn’t comfortable after the flight, and asked her about the stuffed animal she was holding. She showed me its face without coming any closer.

People went around us with their suitcases. Somebody was holding flowers. I stayed down there and listened while she told me the animal’s name.

Eventually she stepped out. I didn’t reach for her right away.

On the walk to the car, she held her mother’s hand. I carried my bag and tried not to walk too fast.

A few days later, I went to the grocery store. We needed milk and some other things. I said I would get them. I wanted to do an ordinary job without anybody needing to help me.

I got through most of the list and stopped in the cereal aisle.

There must have been forty kinds. More, counting the different sizes. The same cereal came in a regular box, a family box, and a box big enough to feed a squad. There were versions with almonds, without almonds, with less sugar, with extra something.

I stood there for about twenty minutes.

I’d pick up a box and read it, then put it back. I wasn’t looking for anything special. I just couldn’t settle on one. Every time I thought I had, I saw another.

A woman said, “Excuse me,” and I moved my cart. Later she came through again from the other end. I was still there.

I had made decisions on deployment. Some had mattered a great deal. Now I couldn’t put cereal in a cart.

I finally took the kind I remembered eating before I left. At home, I put it in the cupboard and the milk in the refrigerator.

“What took so long?”

“Couldn’t find a few things.”

Nobody asked which things. I was glad of that.

At night, I slept facing the bedroom door. I had done it for a year, and I kept doing it after I got home. If I woke up turned the other way, I rolled back.

My wife liked the door open so we could hear our daughter. I wanted it shut. With it open, there was a stretch of hallway I couldn’t see from the bed.

The first few nights, I got up and closed it after my wife fell asleep. Then our daughter would need something, and my wife would get up, and the door would be open again.

We had a short argument about it one morning. We were both tired. I said I slept better with it closed. She said our daughter had been able to come in whenever she needed to for the whole year I was gone.

I didn’t have much to say to that.

I tried leaving it open a few inches. The latch would click when the air came on, so I opened it farther. I lay on my side and watched the doorway. Sometimes I got up to check the hall even though I knew what was in it: the bathroom, the linen closet, my daughter’s room.

During the day, she got used to me being around. She asked me to open things. She brought me papers from school and explained which ones I was supposed to keep. Sometimes she started telling her mother something, then remembered I was sitting there and told me too.

I learned which cereal she ate. It wasn’t the one I had bought.

One night I woke to her standing in the bedroom doorway. I lifted my head too fast, and she stopped.

“What’s wrong?” I asked.

“I need water.”

There was a cup in the bathroom, but I got up and went to the kitchen with her. She waited while I took a glass down. I filled it halfway so she wouldn’t spill it carrying it back.

She drank standing by the sink, both hands around the glass. Then she handed it to me.

I walked her back to bed. She climbed in and pulled the blanket up, and I moved a stuffed animal out from under her shoulder.

“Night, Dad,” she said.

I went back to our room. My wife shifted when I got in, then settled. I lay down facing the doorway. I could hear our daughter cough once down the hall.

The door stayed open.

b.text:
I came off the plane and went through the line with everybody else. They had a little area set up for families. I saw my wife first. She had our daughter with her. The girl was six.

I walked over. She looked at me and then she stepped behind her mom’s leg and held on. She didn’t come out right away. I said her name. I got down on one knee so I wasn’t standing over her. After a minute she came around, but she stayed close to her mom.

A few days later I went to the grocery store. We needed cereal. I walked down the aisle and stopped. There were rows of it. Boxes stacked high. Different colors, different names. I counted maybe forty kinds. I stood there looking at them. I couldn’t decide. I just stood there. A woman with a cart asked if I needed help finding something. I said no. I grabbed a box of the plain kind we used to get and put it in the cart.

At night I still slept facing the door. That’s how it was over there for a year. You kept the door in sight. Now I leave the bedroom door open because that’s what we do at home, but I catch myself turning toward it anyway. I have to turn back over. It takes a while some nights.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam Review – 14 months / 140k miles in**
Fellow owner-ops, quick take on the Roadstar DC4 I’ve had mounted since I bought this rig last year. No fluff, just what’s mattered out on the road.

First, the win that made this thing worth every penny: back in March, some four-wheeler cut me off changing lanes, then tried to claim I merged into him. Camera caught the whole thing clear as day, and my insurance approved my claim in 9 days instead of the usual 6 weeks of back-and-forth. That alone paid for the cam twice over. Front footage is sharp day and night, no issues there.

Now the downsides. Rear cam night footage gets grainy as hell past 30 feet – fine if someone’s riding your bumper, but don’t expect to read plates of cars way back after dark. The suction mount fell off twice in 90+ degree summer heat, bounced right off my dash. Swapped to the adhesive mount it comes with, zero problems since.

Also, the app is basically useless for pulling footage on the road. It needs WiFi, and we all know truck stop WiFi is either non-existent or slower than a weigh station on a holiday weekend. I just yank the SD card and plug it into my laptop when I need clips – not a huge hassle, but skip the app entirely.

Verdict: Solid pick if you want reliable front cam coverage and don’t mind skipping the app. Skip it if you need crisp rear night footage at distance, but for most of us? It’s held up through 140k miles of potholes, heat, and rain, and it’s already saved me a ton of headache.

b.text:
**Roadstar DC4 – 14 Months / ~140k Miles**

I’ve had the Roadstar DC4 mounted for 14 months while putting roughly 140k miles on this rig. Here’s the straight breakdown for any owner-ops considering it.

The headline reason I bought it paid off immediately. A driver rolled through my lane change and clipped my quarter panel. The front cam caught license plate, impact angle, and everything leading up to it. My insurer processed the claim in 9 days instead of the normal 6-week drag. That footage literally paid for the unit ten times over.

Night performance on the rear lens is the weak spot. Past roughly 30 feet, the footage turns noticeably grainy. Fine for daytime traffic, but don’t expect clean plate reads or yard maneuvering shots after dark.

Mounting tip: scrap the suction cup. It popped loose twice during peak summer heat. Switched to the included adhesive pad and it’s been dead quiet since.

Skip the app unless you plan to stay parked next to a strong hotspot. It requires active Wi-Fi to pull footage, which doesn’t exist at most truck stops. I just power down, yank the SD card, and dump clips straight to my laptop. Faster, zero drama.

Bottom line: Reliable crash documentation, handles high-mileage vibration fine, and forces the insurance company’s hand when you need it. Just use the adhesive mount, forget the app, and accept the rear lens isn’t built for deep-night visibility. Works for long-haul reality. Recommended.

setup: You're Nadine Alvarado, emailing the daycare owner after a near-miss pickup mistake involving Mia and asking what happened and what changes are being made.

a.text:
Hi Nadine,

I completely understand why that call scared you, and I'm sorry you had to get it. Let me walk you through exactly what happened.

Yesterday I had a substitute helper covering for me for part of the afternoon. A woman came to pick up Mia who wasn't on your approved pickup list. To her credit, the sub didn't recognize her and didn't just hand Mia over — she stopped, called you directly, and waited for your okay before doing anything. That's exactly the instinct we want in that moment, and it's why nothing actually happened here. Mia was never released to anyone unapproved.

That said, I want to be straight with you: she shouldn't have gotten that far in the first place. The process is supposed to be that if someone isn't on the list, we don't even get to the point of a phone call — we just don't let them near the door without ID and without me or a lead staff member checking it against the list first. That step got skipped yesterday, and that's on me for not making sure it was airtight before I stepped away.

So here's what's changing starting today: I'm adding a formal ID check at drop-off pickup for anyone who isn't a parent I personally recognize, no exceptions, no matter how confident they seem. And I'm sitting down with the sub before she works another shift here to go through exactly how that check works and why it matters, step by step, not just a quick reminder.

I take this seriously because Mia's safety is the whole reason I do this job, and I don't want you to feel like you have to second-guess dropping her off here. If you want to talk through it in person or add anything to her pickup list, I'm happy to do that whenever works for you.

Thank you for bringing this to me directly.

Ellie

b.text:
Nadine,

I'm not going to give you the polished version. Yesterday my substitute was at the door, didn't recognize the person asking for Mia, and instead of just saying “not on the list” she called you to confirm. You said it wasn't okay, Mia stayed inside, and nothing worse happened—but she never should have gotten to that phone call. The second a name or face didn't match the approved list, that person should have been told no, period.

That's on me. I need this tighter, not softer. We're putting an ID check right at the door before anyone gets past the threshold—no exceptions, no “they look familiar,” just verify and release. And I'm retraining that sub personally before she works here again; she won't step foot in the building until she's walked through pickup with me face-to-face.

I run this like someone whose license and eight kids' safety depend on it, not like a drop-off service, and yesterday I let that slip. You shouldn't have had to be the safety check.

Call me if you want the straight details, or if you want to come by and see the new setup. Otherwise you'll see it in action tomorrow.

Thanks for being direct with me.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/3
Maple Ave kitchen job last week. Pulled up three layers of subfloor and found four consecutive 2x8 joists notched about 70% through so a plumber in 1982 could run a 3” drain line. 

The previous owner had a 400 lb cast iron range sitting directly over the cut. Pure friction and prayer keeping it up.

2/3
The fix: shore up the basement, engineer-approved sistering with LVLs back to the center carrying beam, and re-routing the waste line correctly. 

Total cost to the homeowner: $3,800 and a 4-day schedule hit before we could even start setting new cabinets. 

3/3
The lesson: A 15-20% contingency on pre-1950s Pittsburgh homes isn't contractor fluff. It’s an insurance policy against the guy who worked on the house forty years ago with a Sawzall and zero supervision. Always budget for what's hiding under the subfloor.

b.text:
1/3
Maple Ave kitchen demo last week. Pulled down the ceiling below to check mechanicals and found two 2x10 floor joists completely cut in half. Not notched—clean through. 

A plumber dropped a 4” cast iron drain right through the middle of the span decades ago. The entire kitchen floor above was basically suspended on 3/4” subfloor and luck.

2/3
Fixing it wasn't just slapping a board next to it. It meant an engineer spec, rerouting the stack, and sistering full-span LVLs with heavy-duty structural hangers. 

Total damage to the client: $3,800 change order and 4 days lost on the schedule before we could even think about cabinet prep.

3/3
The takeaway: in 100-year-old Pittsburgh homes, demo is an archeological dig of every bad shortcut taken over a century. 

When a GC insists on a 15–20% structural contingency on an older remodel, it’s not padding the budget. It’s paying for the invisible sins of the guy who worked on the house in 1982.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
# Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now

If you’re trying to decide when to book, most people will tell you to grab a Saturday in June. After six years of shooting weddings almost entirely in this metro area, I understand the instinct. But “popular” isn’t the same as “better,” and June has some real downsides I don’t think couples hear about enough.

I’ve shot 11 winter weddings in the last two years. For this post, I’m counting November through March as winter around here, and those 11 dates taught me something I didn’t expect

b.text:
I Used to Chase June Weddings. Now I Actually Prefer November.

Six years of shooting weddings in this area, and I’ll be straight with you: I used to treat winter dates like something couples settled for. Then I started looking at the proof. In the last two years, I’ve shot 11 winter weddings, and they’ve changed my mind entirely.

Here’s the part your budget will care about: winter bookings run about 30% cheaper than peak-season dates. That’s real money that can go back into your experience—or your pocket.

But here’s the part I care about: the light.

A flat overcast day in June is genuinely a harder portrait situation than a clear November afternoon at 3pm. In June, that gray sky turns into a giant, boring softbox. In November, the sun sits lower and cuts through bare trees, giving me directional light with depth and texture. I’m not trying to be poetic. Side-by-side, the November portraits from this area have more dimension and drama than the flat June ones. The light is honestly better.

And the logistics actually work. In June, I’m regularly sharing the venue parking lot with three or four other vendors, unloading gear around each other, and competing for the same shady spot during cocktail hour. Winter weddings give me room to breathe, set up without obstruction, and focus on you instead of the timeline traffic jam.

You’ll need a coat. The sun will set earlier. But if you’re browsing photographers and trying to decide whether an off-season date is a compromise, I want you to hear it from someone who’s been in the parking lot: it’s not.

I still have limited winter availability for next season. If you’re considering a November or winter date, reach out before the spring rush starts.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
# The Cereal Aisle

I flew home from my second deployment in October. My wife met me at the airport with our daughter, who was six.

I had a picture of that girl taped inside my locker for a year. In the picture she was five and missing a front tooth. The one at the airport had both her teeth back and was taller than I remembered, and when I came walking up she got behind her mother's leg and held on to it and looked at me like she was trying to place me. My wife put her hand on the back of our daughter's head and said, "That's Daddy." She didn't come out from behind the leg right away. I knelt down and waited. It took her a minute. I don't blame her. A year is a long time when you're six. A year is most of what you can remember.

She came around eventually. But I think about that minute a lot.

A few days later my wife sent me to the store for milk and a couple other things. I got the milk fine. Then she'd written cereal on the list, and I went to the cereal aisle, and I stood there.

I want to explain this right. There were maybe forty kinds of cereal. Probably more. I stood in front of them and I could not pick one. It wasn't that I couldn't decide which one tasted best. It was that I couldn't make the machinery in my head do the thing it was supposed to do. Over there you eat what they give you and you're grateful and you don't think about it. You don't stand in front of forty choices with nobody shooting at you and nothing to do but pick. I stood there long enough that a stocker asked me if I needed help finding something. I said no. I stood there some more. I want to say it was twenty minutes. It was a while.

I finally grabbed the one with the toucan on it because my daughter had that when she was little, and I left.

At home the hardest part came at night. For a year I'd slept facing the door. You do that so you can see it. You do it without thinking after a while, your body just turns you that way. And we kept our bedroom door shut at home, always had, and I couldn't do it. I'd lie there with the door shut and it felt wrong, like something was going to come through it and I wouldn't know. So I started leaving it open. My wife asked why. I said I liked the air. That wasn't it. I turned so I could see the open door and the hallway, and that was the only way I could get to sleep for a long time.

It got a little better. The door thing took months. My daughter warmed up faster than I did, honestly. By Christmas she was climbing on me like I'd never left.

I still don't love the cereal aisle.

b.text:
**Coming Home**

The airport was the same one I'd left from, which threw me. Same carpet, same smell of popcorn and floor wax. I came down the escalator with a duffel over one shoulder and saw my wife before she saw me. Our daughter was holding her hand.

She was six. She'd been five when I left, and in my head she was still five, so the first thing that happened was that I was wrong about her.

She got behind her mother's leg and stayed there. I squatted down on the carpet in my uniform with the duffel beside me and said her name. She looked up at her mom to check. Her mom nodded. She came out about half a step and stopped. I didn't reach for her. I don't know why. It took a minute, and then she let me pick her up and she was heavier than I remembered, which sounds like a stupid thing to say, kids grow, but that's the thing I remember. Like I'd been carrying a weight in my head for a year and it was the wrong weight.

Two weeks later my wife gave me the grocery list and sent me out. Her list said cereal. That was my whole job.

I stood in the cereal aisle for twenty minutes. I know because I checked my watch, and I checked my watch like I was timing something. There were forty kinds. Maybe more. I picked up the Cheerios we used to buy and put them back because it had been a year and I didn't know what she ate now. I picked up something with a cartoon on it and put that back too, because she might have outgrown it and I didn't want to be the guy who came home with the wrong box. I read the backs of boxes. I did the math on sugar per serving for no reason.

A woman came around me, reached past my shoulder, took a box without looking at it, and kept walking. Never slowed down. I stood there and watched her go and felt something I couldn't name, and then I took the Cheerios and went to the register.

Sleep was the other thing.

For a year I slept where the door mattered. You slept facing the door. If you rolled over in the night you rolled back. I never thought of it as anything. It was just how you slept, the way you put your boots a certain way.

At home, the bedroom door was shut. My wife likes it shut. Dark. First week I'd come awake at 0300 with my eyes already open and pointed at the door, and it was closed, and there was hallway light in a line under it. I'd lie there and listen to the house. The fridge. My daughter breathing down the hall.

After a few nights I got up and opened it. Just a foot. Then I went back to bed. My wife asked me about it the next morning. I said the room felt small. That was true enough and it was the whole answer.

It took a couple of months. Somewhere in there I quit waking up at 0300, and somewhere after that I quit getting up to check. The door's still open at night. I don't think about it much.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Review – 14 Months, 140k Miles**

Hey folks,

I’ve been running the Roadstar DC4 on my current rig for about 14 months now. I’ve put roughly 140,000 miles on it in that time, so I wanted to share a quick real-world review for other owner-operators considering it.

First off, the main reason I got this was for liability protection. It paid off big time. The front cam caught a lane change accident on video. That footage got my insurance claim approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6 weeks we all dread. That alone is worth the price of the unit.

That said, there are some quirks you need to know about. The rear camera’s night footage gets pretty grainy past 30 feet. If you’re trying to document something happening further back in the dark, you might not get clear details.

Mounting was another issue. The suction mount fell off twice during the summer heat. I ended up switching to the adhesive mount, which has held up fine since.

Lastly, the app is inconvenient. It needs WiFi to pull footage, which is useless at most truck stops where I don’t have a strong connection. I just pull the SD card and transfer it manually on my laptop now.

Bottom line: It’s a solid camera for insurance protection, but don’t expect perfect night vision or seamless app integration. If you can work around the mount and connectivity issues, it does the job.

b.text:
**RoadStar DC4 Dash Cam – 14 Months, 140K Miles In**

Got this thing installed right when I bought my current rig. Front cam is solid – daytime footage is sharp enough to read plates clear as day, and it held up through everything from desert heat to mountain snow. No issues there.

The rear cam is where things get mixed. Daytime is fine. Nighttime? Anything past 30 feet starts getting grainy and you lose detail. Fine if you're documenting a close call, not fine if someone tags you from two car lengths back.

The accident test is the big one though. Some yahoo merged into my lane near Amarillo last spring. Hit the camera, pulled the footage, insurance had my claim approved in 9 days. Every other claim I've ever filed took 6 weeks minimum. That's the whole reason most of us run these things, and on that front it delivered.

Mounting was my only real complaint. The suction cup fell off twice in summer heat – once on I-10 in Arizona, once in a Walmart parking lot in Georgia. Switched to the adhesive mount and haven't had a problem since. If you run hot routes, skip the suction cup entirely.

The app needs WiFi to pull footage, which is pointless at 95% of truck stops. I just pull the SD card and dump it to my laptop. Not a dealbreaker, but they should fix that.

Bottom line: front cam is great, rear cam is decent but not great at night, and the insurance payoff alone justifies the price. If you're on the fence, get one. Just buy the adhesive mount upfront and skip the headache.

Rating: 4/5. Would buy again.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
After interviewing over 200 people throughout my career, I’ve noticed a distinct pattern. 

The absolute best candidates—the ones who end up being the highest performers and the most resilient teammates—almost always ask some version of the same uncomfortable question. 

Usually, it comes at the end of the interview when I ask, "What questions do you have for me?"

Instead of the standard queries about culture or day-to-day duties, they ask: 

"What was your team’s last major failed project, and how did people react to it?"

Here is how that conversation usually goes:

Candidate: "I know every company has setbacks. What’s the last project on your team that completely fell apart, and why?"

Me: "Honestly, we tried to roll out a new routing software update last year. It was supposed to save our dispatchers two hours a day, but the integration failed, we lost real-time tracking for six hours, and we had to roll the whole thing back."

Candidate: "And what happened next? How did the leadership team handle the mistake, and what did the post-mortem look like?"

That second question is where the magic happens. 

They aren’t asking to catch me in a gotcha moment. They are trying to figure out if we have psychological safety. They want to know if we point fingers when things go sideways, or if we actually run blameless post-mortems and pivot. 

Top talent doesn't expect your company to be perfect. They just want to make sure you aren't pretending to be. 

If you are a job seeker, try asking this in your next interview. You’ll learn more about a company’s true culture in two minutes than you will in two weeks of reading reviews online. 

And if you are a hiring manager, don’t sugarcoat your answer. If you pretend you’ve never failed, the best candidates will see right through it.

b.text:
I've sat in on roughly 200 interviews at our company. The candidates who end up being the strongest hires almost always ask some version of the same question:

"Tell me about a project here that didn't work out."

Not "what's the culture like." Not "what does success look like in 90 days." Those are fine. But the failed-project question changes the whole conversation.

Recent example. We were interviewing for an ops analyst role, and near the end the candidate asked our hiring manager about the last initiative that got shelved. The manager paused, then told her about a warehouse slotting overhaul we'd rolled out too fast — pilots looked great, full rollout fell apart because we hadn't accounted for how differently our seasonal sites run.

Her follow-up: "When it started going sideways, how long before someone said so out loud?"

The manager laughed and gave her an honest answer (longer than it should have been). They spent ten minutes talking about how the team handles bad news now. That was the moment he decided to hire her.

Here's why the question works. Anyone can vet a company on its wins — that's what the careers page is for. Asking about failure tells you how the company actually behaves under pressure. Do they blame a person or examine a process? Do they get cagey or get specific?

And it tells us something too. This candidate isn't shopping for a place where nothing goes wrong. She's checking whether it's safe to be the one who flags a problem.

If you're interviewing anywhere right now, ask it. The answer — and how comfortable they are giving it — will tell you more than the entire job description.

setup: You're everyone at the startup. Yesterday's 40-minute outage was caused by a bad database migration during deploy.

a.text:
All systems are fully operational, healthy, and have been completely stable since yesterday afternoon. 

Here is a breakdown of what happened during yesterday's downtime, why it occurred, and what we’re changing to prevent it going forward—especially for those of you fielding questions from customers.

**What happened**
Yesterday around 2:00 PM, the platform was unavailable for roughly 40 minutes. 

**Why it happened**
During a routine software deploy, we ran a database update (migration) to support new features. Usually, these finish seamlessly in the background in a few seconds. In this case, the update unexpectedly "locked" a critical database table to make changes. While that table was locked, the rest of the application couldn't read or save data, effectively bringing the system to a halt.

**How it was fixed**
Once we identified the lock, the engineering team rolled back the update. As soon as the rollback completed, the database unlocked, and all services recovered immediately. 

**What we’re doing to prevent this**
Moving forward, we are changing how and when we run these updates:
* Any significant database changes will now only be run during scheduled, off-peak maintenance windows (late evening) rather than during normal daytime deploys.
* We’re adding extra checks to our testing process to catch potential locks before updates ever touch the live system.

A huge thank you to everyone who jumped in to manage customer messages while we were heads-down on the fix. If any of your customers are asking for a follow-up, feel free to use the context above, or reach out to me directly if you need a tailored response for an account. 

Let me know if anyone has any questions.

b.text:
Yesterday’s outage is fully resolved. The product is back to normal, and there is no ongoing impact.

Around 2pm yesterday we were down for about 40 minutes. A routine deploy included a database change that held a table locked much longer than expected, which blocked the rest of the system. We rolled that change back, confirmed everything was healthy, and the service stayed up after that.

If you heard from customers during that window, that matches what we saw. We’re sorry for the disruption.

Going forward, this kind of database change will run in a planned maintenance window, not in the middle of a normal deploy, so we don’t take the same risk again during the workday.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
I work every Saturday and Sunday at my family’s Vietnamese restaurant, 10:30 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., have since sophomore year.

Last month the register died at 11:42 a.m. on a Saturday, right as the lunch rush line stretched past the front door. The screen flickered pink for three seconds, then went dark. Dad smacked the side of the cash drawer three times—that used to work when it got stuck on the coupon screen—but this time the receipt printer just spit out a single blank slip.

We didn’t have a backup system. Mom yelled from the kitchen pass, her hair stuck to her forehead, that if we told everyone to come back later we’d lose half the day’s sales, which we couldn’t afford because the walk-in fridge broke two weeks before. I grabbed the stack of yellow legal pads we keep under the counter for inventory, a handful of golf pencils sharpened down to nubs, and started writing tickets by hand.

I wrote each order down twice: one for the kitchen, one for me to ring up later when we figured out how to total everything. #3 crispy pork banh mi, no pickled daikon, extra mayo on the side for the guy from the auto shop down the street who always wears a grease-stained flannel even when it’s 85 degrees out. Two vegetarian spring rolls, no peanut sauce, for the soccer mom

b.text:
Saturdays start at six a.m. The doors lock behind me after my shift yesterday, but by five-thirty, the smell of fish sauce and fried shallots is already in the air. I’ve worked this counter every weekend since I was a sophomore. There’s no hidden agenda or sudden passion project behind it. It’s just inventory, prep, and covering stations when someone calls out. I show up. I stay for the full shift. I leave when the closing list is done.

Last month, the register system died right before the lunch rush. The screens went black. The card readers spat error codes. My dad glanced at the tangled cords, then at me. “Just take cash and write orders,” he said. So I pulled the yellow book from under the counter and started writing. Table number. Dish. Modifications. Seven A. Phở bò tái. Extra bean sprouts. Eight C. Bánh mì. No pickled daikon. I wrote tickets until my hand cramped, matched each paper slip to the right plate, and called numbers out over the exhaust fan. People handed me folded twenties and singles. I logged them. I didn’t troubleshoot the wiring or fix the software. I just kept the queue moving until a technician arrived two hours later. It was slower. It was fine.

Breaks are twenty minutes, sometimes less. Usually, I go to the walk-in. The door seals out the noise and the heat. The fluorescent light hums at a steady pitch. I set my laptop on a stack of frozen protein trays and open the calculus PDF. Derivatives. I work through problems until the battery dips below thirty percent, then close it when the floor manager needs me to restock napkins or clear tables. My supervisors know I sit in there when I need to. I know where my highlighters are. Sometimes I lean back against the cinderblock, eat a stale apple, and stare at integration by parts until it makes sense. The temperature stays constant. The schedule changes anyway.

In October, we hired a kid who’d never made summer rolls. I walked him through the setup. Wet the rice paper just enough so it doesn’t tear. Lay it flat. Lettuce. Basil. Cilantro strips. Shrimp halves, tails removed. Noodles folded tight. But the real part is the fold. My grandmother’s method isn’t written down anywhere. You lift the left corner, tuck it over the filling, then bring the right side in first. Tight, but not crushed. He split the paper on the first four. Filling spilled onto the bamboo board. I didn’t speed him up. I just rolled another one, set it beside his, and said, “Ease into it. Don’t force the paper.” On the fifth try, it held. He slid it onto the plate. It wasn’t textbook perfect, but it wouldn’t fall apart. That’s what matters when you’re learning the station.

I don’t usually think about how it all connects. The machines break. The cooler gets cold. The rolls get tighter. Classes run their own calendar. This place runs on a different one. I cover the shift. I turn in homework before deadlines. Some weekends feel long. Most just feel normal. The tickets clear. The notes get reviewed. I clock out, wash the ink off my palms, and drive home.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
## A $46,000 Increase for One Wet Spring

This spring, I was able to plant only 60% of my soybean and corn acres by the late-May deadline. The rain kept coming, and the fields stayed too wet to work. That left a large share of my operation facing prevented planting coverage.

At the same time, USDA raised the base prevented-planting premium rate in our region by 22%. For my farm, that increase adds approximately $46,000 to this year’s costs—before accounting for lost production, machinery expenses, input commitments, and the income we will not receive from those acres.

The acreage cap makes that increase even harder on family operations. The cap does not affect every farm in the same way. For a farm like mine, where each acre represents a larger share of the operation’s total revenue, the added premium cost takes a bigger proportional bite. Larger operations nearby may absorb the same rate increase across more acres and more production. Family farms do not have that same cushion.

This is not about avoiding responsibility or asking taxpayers to cover every bad outcome. We pay premiums, manage risk, and make planting decisions based on the best information available. But when a federally determined rate jumps 22% in a year when weather prevents planting, the acreage cap can turn an already difficult situation into a disproportionate financial burden for farms like mine.

Senate Bill 214 would fix the acreage-cap problem and make the program more equitable for family-sized operations. It would not eliminate the risks of farming or guarantee a profit. It would simply ensure that the program’s limits do not penalize smaller operations more severely than larger ones.

I encourage farm bureau members and other producers to contact their legislators and support SB 214. A $46,000 increase is not an abstract policy number for my farm. It is a real cost tied directly to a wet spring and a program structure that needs to be corrected.

b.text:
The 22% Prevented Planting Premium Hike Is a Family-Farm Tax

The prevented planting base premium rate in our region went up 22 percent this year. For my operation, that is not an abstract number. It is $46,000 in added premium cost before I put a single seed in the ground.

This spring, I got 60 percent of my soybean and corn acres planted by the late May final planting date. The other 40 percent sat underwater. That is exactly the situation prevented planting coverage was designed to address. I still have land payments due, property taxes due, equipment notes due, and seed already committed. The prevented planting indemnity does not make me whole. It keeps a bad year from turning into a forced sale.

But here is what should bother every farm bureau member in this county: the 22 percent base rate increase is not being applied in a way that matches the actual risk on family farms. Because of how the acreage caps work, my operation pays the increase on a much larger share of my total acres than the bigger operations nearby. A large operation with thousands of acres can absorb the rate hike across a broader planted base. My family operation cannot. The result is that I pay $46,000 more for the same coverage at the exact moment 40 percent of my ground is producing nothing. That is a tax on being a family farm.

SB 214 fixes that. It would adjust the prevented planting acreage cap so that the premium calculation reflects a farm’s actual planting history and prevented planting exposure, not a one-size-fits-all cap that punishes smaller operations. It does not create a new payment. It does not add a new program. It simply makes the premium structure fairer.

This matters beyond my fencerows. The $46,000 I now have to send to the insurance pool is $46,000 I will not spend at the local seed dealer, the elevator, the implement dealer, or the tire shop. When family operations get squeezed disproportionately, the whole county absorbs the loss.

I am not asking for a bailout. I am asking for a premium structure that does not treat a 1,200-acre family operation as if it had the same cash reserves as a 12,000-acre corporation. SB 214 is the narrow fix that would do that.

Call your state senator this week. Ask them to support SB 214. If we wait until next spring’s premium bills arrive, the 22 percent will already be locked in.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
Friday night was a tough pill to swallow. Finishing a high school football season 8-2 is a fantastic achievement by any local standard, but when that second loss sends you packing in Round 2 of the state playoffs, it stings. It burns even more when the team ending your season is the exact same squad you ran off the field by 20 points back in Week 3.

Look, nobody can take away what this offense accomplished this fall. Dez Kowalski was nothing short of electric under center. He threw for 2,340 yards this year, shattering the school record and giving us highlight-reel throws every single week. If you had told me in August that we’d have a 2,300-yard passer, I’d have printed state championship tickets right then and there. 

But Friday night proved that a shiny passing record doesn’t win a gritty November playoff game on its own. I’ll just say what everyone shivering in the bleachers was already thinking: we panicked. We completely abandoned the run game in the second half, and for the life of me, I can't figure out why. 

We were only down by three points. A single field goal. More importantly, the ground game was actually working. We were getting push up front, moving the chains, and controlling the tempo. Instead of sticking to the script and wearing out a defensive line we already proved we could bully, the play-calling suddenly turned into a frantic 7-on-7 drill. 

When you start dropping back on every down in a tight, one-possession game, you let the opposing defense pin their ears back and ignore the run entirely. That’s exactly what happened. The pass rush teed off, the drives stalled, and we watched a winnable playoff game slip right through our fingers. 

You don't reinvent the wheel when you're only trailing by three. It's a bitter end to an undeniably great season, and a harsh lesson in playoff football. Congratulations to Dez and the seniors on an unforgettable 8-2 run, but that second-half play sheet is going to keep this coaching staff awake until August.

b.text:
Round 2 Wasn't Good Enough

That one stings this morning. 8-2, and done in Round 2 of state.

Stings worse because it's the same team we beat by 20 back in Week 3. We know we're better than that.

I said it on the radio Saturday and I'll say it here — we gave this one away.

Dez Kowalski set the school record with 2,340 yards this year. Heck of a season for that kid, and he earned every yard.

But the pass is what lost us Friday.

We were only down 3 at halftime and we were handling them up front. Just go back and watch our last drive of the second quarter when we ran it straight down the field for the score.

Then we come out in the second half in the shotgun throwing it all over the place. For what? Down three is nothing. You don't have to panic.

In my opinion the coaches panicked. Stopped doing what was working to try to look fancy.

The kids didn't lose this game. That second-half game plan did.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
**They Had the Hammer. They Put It Down.**

Eight and two is a good season. I want to say that up front, because what follows is going to sound like a man who forgot it.

Dez Kowalski threw for 2,340 yards this fall, and nobody in the history of this program has done that. He earned every one of them. The kid played the last three weeks with a shoulder he wasn't talking about and kept putting the ball where it needed to be. Years from now his name is going to be on a board in that gym and it belongs there.

But we lost in the second round of the state playoffs to a team we beat by 20 in September, and I don't think we lost because they got better. I think we lost because we stopped doing the thing that was working.

Go back and look at the first half. We ran the ball, we ran it well, and we ran it right at them. They didn't have an answer. The line was getting a push on nearly every down and our backs were falling forward for four, five, six yards at a clip. That's how you build a lead against a team that's out for revenge — you make them tackle for two hours until they don't want to anymore.

Then halftime happened, and whatever was said in that locker room, the plan that came out of it was a different plan. Down three. Three points. And we came out throwing on first down, throwing on second down, and finding ourselves in third-and-long against a defense that finally got to sit back and rush the passer.

I understand the temptation. When you have the best quarterback in school history, every play call that isn't a pass feels like leaving money on the table. But a three-point deficit isn't an emergency. It's a field goal. It does not require you to abandon what got you there and start playing the other team's game.

That's what happened. We took the one thing they couldn't stop and set it aside voluntarily, and by the time the fourth quarter got tight we'd lost the rhythm up front and couldn't get it back. Kowalski ended up throwing into coverage that wouldn't have existed if the safeties still had to worry about the run. Nobody made him do that. The situation didn't demand it. It was a choice.

I've heard people this week blame the officiating, and I've heard people say the other team just wanted it more. I don't buy either one. The officiating was ordinary and the other team wanted it exactly as much as they did in Week 3. The difference was that in Week 3 we kept our foot on the gas, and in Round 2 we changed drivers at the half.

None of this makes it a bad year. The seniors leave with a record most classes here would trade for, and the juniors got a taste of what November football feels like. That matters. But the honest lesson from that game isn't about heart or toughness or wanting it. It's simpler and it's more fixable than that.

When something is working, keep doing it. Especially when you're only down three.

b.text:
The season ended Saturday in the second round of the state playoffs, but it should be remembered as much for what this team accomplished as for how it lost.

An 8-2 record is nothing to dismiss. Neither is a school-record 2,340 passing yards by Dez Kowalski, who gave this team a steady presence at quarterback all season. And yet, the playoff loss will sting because it felt avoidable.

This was a team the Tigers had already beaten by 20 points in Week 3. In the rematch, the offense found success running the football early. That was the formula working against a familiar opponent.

Then, in the second half, the run game largely disappeared.

That decision changed the game. The team was down only three points, not facing an insurmountable deficit. There was no need to panic or suddenly make the offense one-dimensional. The running game was producing, the defense was keeping the margin within reach, and the situation called for patience.

Instead, the offense leaned away from what had been working and put more pressure on Kowalski and the passing game. Kowalski has earned plenty of credit for his record-setting season, but asking one player to carry the offense late in a playoff game is not always the best answer—especially when the ground game is giving you something.

That is the frustrating part of this loss. It was not simply that the team ran into a better opponent. It was that the game seemed to be there for the taking, and the offense moved away from its best option before the deficit demanded it.

Still, one questionable second half should not erase an excellent season. An 8-2 record, a state playoff win and a new school passing record represent real progress and plenty of reasons for this program to be proud. Kowalski’s season will be remembered in the record book, and the seniors leave having raised expectations for everyone who follows.

But good teams learn from disappointing endings. This one should remind the coaches and players that playoff football is often about trusting the plan when the pressure rises. When the run is working and you are down three, stay with it.

That may be the lesson this team carries into next season—and the difference between a promising year and a deeper playoff run.

a.text:
Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

For the past two years, your software wasn't just a tool in my high school biology classroom—it was the backbone of my curriculum. After eight years in education, I am transitioning into Customer Success, and there is no product I would rather champion than the one that transformed my own teaching.

Having used [Company Name] daily, I understand your platform from the user’s perspective better than most. I already speak your customers' language because I was your customer.

Teaching is, at its core, high-stakes Customer Success. Every semester, I onboarded 30+ new, diverse users per period, driving engagement and ensuring rapid time-to-value. I regularly de-escalated high-tension situations with angry parents through proactive communication, empathy, and clear action plans. Managing retention, driving adoption, and navigating complex stakeholder dynamics are already second nature to me.

Two years ago I set up your product for my biology classroom. By last spring I was the campus admin, running it across five teachers' sections and training colleagues who'd never opened it.

That's the short version of why I'm applying for Customer Success.

Teaching is onboarding on a forced deadline. Every semester, 30 new users arrive with no training, no manual, and no patience for a tool that slows them down. I learned to get a class running on a new platform in one 50-minute period and keep it running through fire drills, snow days, and the week before break. When something broke mid-lab, there was no ticket queue — I had to diagnose it, work around it, and explain it to 30 teenagers at once.

I also spent eight years managing frustrated stakeholders. A parent who thinks the software lost her kid's grade is a customer who thinks the product lost her data. Same conversation: listen, verify, fix what you can, and be honest about what you can't. I got good at it.

And I filed the tickets. I know which parts of your product make teachers give up in week two, because I watched it happen and I talked colleagues back from it.

I'm leaving the classroom, but I'm not leaving teachers. I want to be the person who helps a school get to the version of the tool I got to — the one that saved me four hours a week.

That's the job I'm asking for.

b.text:
# How to Bleed Air Out of Baseboard Heating Before Winter

Shut off the boiler and circulator before you touch any bleeder valves. If the system has been running, give it a few minutes so the water in the lines is not hot enough to burn you.

## 1. Start with the baseboard closest to the boiler

Work unit by unit, starting nearest the boiler and moving outward through the loop. Do not jump from room to room.

This is where a lot of homeowners get it wrong: they bleed the upstairs units and skip the basement loop. In most of our cold-radiator calls, the air is sitting in the basement or lowest part of the system, not just upstairs.

## 2. Find the bleeder valve

Look at the end of each baseboard unit. You should see a small bleeder valve, usually with a square key head or a screw slot, depending on the valve type. Some units have an end cap or trim piece that lifts off for access.

## 3. Put a cup or rag underneath it

Have a small cup, jar, or rag under the valve before you open it. Some water will come out, and it can drip onto the floor or baseboard.

## 4. Open the valve slowly

Use the correct bleeder key or a flat-head screwdriver. Open the valve just enough to hear air hiss. Do not crank it open, and do not remove the valve core.

Let it spit and hiss until the air is out. When water comes out in a steady stream with no sputtering or air bubbles, close it.

## 5. Close it snug, but do not force it

Tighten the valve just until it stops leaking. Snug is enough. Overtightening can crack the valve seat or damage the seal, and that can turn a simple bleed job into a leaking valve.

## 6. Repeat on every baseboard

Go through each unit on the loop, one at a time, moving away from the boiler. Include basement baseboards, utility-room units, and any low sections of the house.

## 7. Turn the system back on and check

When every valve is closed, turn the boiler and circulator back on. Check the boiler pressure gauge and bring the pressure back to the normal cold-fill range if needed. If you are not comfortable adding water to the system, stop there and call us.

Walk the house again after the system runs for a while. If a unit still gurgles, stays cold at the top, or heats unevenly, there may still be air in the line or a different flow problem.

If you are in our service area and your baseboards are still cold after bleeding, give us a call. We can track down the trapped air, check the circulator, and make sure the loop is moving hot water the way it should.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The couples who get my best photos are the ones who never sent me a shot list.

Eight years of weddings, and the pattern holds.

The Barrera wedding is the proof I point to.

They didn't give me a list. No spreadsheet of family formals, no Pinterest board, no must-have poses. Just: we trust you, photograph what happens.

Then it rained. An hour before the ceremony, everything already set up on the lawn, and the sky just opened.

We moved the whole wedding under a pecan tree at the edge of the property. Chairs squeezed in tight. Rain coming down past the branches while they said their vows. Every guest pressed close together under the canopy.

No shot list would have covered that. No shot list could have.

So I photographed the wedding they actually had, not the one they'd planned. Those are the photos they still talk about.

A shot list documents the day you imagined. Trust gets you the day that happened. The second one is always better.

To couples choosing a photographer: ask them how they handle a rained-out ceremony. The answer matters more than the portfolio.

Fellow vendors — what's your pecan tree wedding? The one where the plan fell apart and the work got better?

#weddingphotography #TexasHillCountry #weddingvendors

b.text:
Hot take for every engaged couple deep in Pinterest wedding planning right now: The couples who ditch the rigid shot list always end up with their all-time favorite photos.

Full transparency upfront: I’m not saying you can’t have 2-3 non-negotiables (if a photo with your 92-year-old grandma is top of your list, that’s a no-brainer we’ll make happen). But after 8 years as a full-time Texas Hill Country wedding photographer, shooting around 35 weddings a year, I can say the galleries that stick with me (and the couples, years later) are the ones where the rigid, 2-page color-coded shot list got left in the car.

Case in point: last spring’s Barrera wedding.
They’d sent over a detailed shot list a month out—every family combination, every posed wedding party portrait, every timeline beat mapped down to the minute. Then 45 minutes before the ceremony, the Hill Country sky opened up. No backup indoor venue, no tent on standby, just a giant, gnarled old pecan tree at the edge of their family property and a whole lot of willingness to roll with it.

We threw the entire shot list out the window. No herding 12 cousins mid-cocktail hour to check a group photo box. No rushing the couple to a sunlit field for golden hour shots when the rain kept drizzling. Instead?
We got the groom’s abuela squeezing his cheeks so tight his smile crinkled, right after he said vows under the pecan tree’s dripping branches.
We got the flower girl chasing a tiny tree frog through the mud in her sparkly tulle dress, her flower petals stuck to her rain boots.
We got the couple sneaking off for 10 minutes to share a brisket taco (Hill Country wedding staple, duh) while rain pattered on the leaves above them, no one rushing them to the next thing.
We got the best man’s impromptu, tearful speech he’d been too nervous to give on the original timeline, because the rain bought us an extra hour of hanging out under the tree.

None of those moments were on a shot list. None of them were posed. All of them are the photos the Barreras still text me about 18 months later—the ones framed above their couch, the ones their family asks for copies of every holiday. When you’re not constantly checking a list to make sure you got “the shot,” you’re actually living your wedding day. And that’s the stuff that makes photos feel like you, not a generic Pinterest template.

For engaged couples scrolling while researching photographers: If the thought of checking 50+ photo boxes on your wedding day feels overwhelming, you don’t have to do it. I’m always down to chat through how to build a timeline that prioritizes the moments that actually matter to you, no rigid checklist required.
For fellow wedding vendors and photographer friends in my network: This is why I always build extra buffer time into every wedding timeline, and why I never frame my work around checking a pre-written list. The job isn’t to deliver a set of expected shots—it’s to capture the day as it actually unfolds. Drop a comment below about a time a last-minute, unplanned shift led to your favorite wedding memory. I’d love to hear it.
