setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
**Coming Home**

When I came home from my second deployment, my wife and daughter met me at the airport.

My daughter was six. I had been gone a year, which is a long time when you are six. Before I left, she used to run at me full speed and expect me to catch her. At the airport, she stood behind her mother’s leg.

I could see one eye and part of her face. My wife put a hand on her shoulder and told her, “It’s Daddy.”

I was still in uniform. I had my bags with me. There were people all around us hugging and taking pictures. I wanted to kneel down and open my arms, but I did not want to make it worse. So I stood there and said hello.

She looked at me for a few seconds. Then she came out from behind her mother, but she stayed close to her. I hugged my wife first. After that, my daughter let me hug her, though her arms stayed at her sides.

By the time we got to the car, she was talking to me. Mostly she told me what had changed. She had a different teacher. Her friend had moved away. She could ride her bike without training wheels. There was a new restaurant near our house. She had lost two teeth.

I sat in the passenger seat and listened. The roads looked familiar, but not exactly. There were new buildings and new signs. My wife drove. My daughter talked from the back seat. Every so often, I turned around to look at her, just to make sure she was there.

A few days later, I went to the grocery store by myself.

My wife had given me a short list. Milk, bread, eggs, cereal. It should have taken twenty minutes.

I got to the cereal aisle and stopped.

There were cereals from one end of the aisle to the other. Bright boxes, plain boxes, family size, low sugar, high fiber, chocolate, cinnamon, fruit, marshmallows. Some were supposed to help your heart. Some were shaped like little cookies. Some had cartoon animals on the front.

I did not know what to pick.

Before I deployed, I had bought cereal plenty of times. I must have. But standing there, it felt like somebody had asked me a question with forty correct answers and forty wrong ones.

I picked up a box and read the side. Then I put it back. I picked up another one. A woman pushed her cart around me, reached past my shoulder, grabbed a box, and kept going. She did not even slow down.

I stood there for about twenty minutes.

Finally, I bought the cereal my daughter used to like before I left. When I brought it home, she told me she did not like that kind anymore.

At night, I had trouble sleeping.

For the past year, I had slept facing the door. I did it without thinking. Even when there was no reason to worry, I wanted to see the entrance. I wanted to know what was on the other side.

At home, my wife slept on the side of the bed closest to the door. She always had. I did not want to ask her to switch, so I lay on my side and looked past her.

She liked the bedroom door open. That way she could hear our daughter if she called during the night. I wanted it closed.

The first few nights, I got up after my wife fell asleep and shut it. In the morning, she opened it again. Neither of us said anything about it.

One night, she woke up while I was standing beside the door.

“What are you doing?” she asked.

“Nothing,” I said.

I left the door halfway open and got back into bed.

For a while, every sound in the house woke me up. The refrigerator kicked on. Pipes knocked in the wall. A car drove past. Our daughter got up to use the bathroom, and the floor creaked under her feet.

Sometimes she came into our room after a bad dream. She would stand in the doorway until one of us noticed her. Then she would walk around to my wife’s side of the bed.

After a few weeks, she started coming to my side.

The first time, she tapped me on the shoulder and whispered, “Dad.”

I opened my eyes. She was standing there in her pajamas, holding a blanket.

“Can’t sleep,” she said.

I moved over and let her climb in. She lay between us, taking up more room than a six-year-old should be able to take. Her foot pressed into my leg. My wife stayed asleep.

I looked at the open bedroom door. The hallway beyond it was dark.

After a while, my daughter’s breathing slowed. The house made its usual noises. I stayed awake a little longer, facing the door. Then I closed my eyes.

b.text:
# The Cereal Aisle

The flight from Germany was long but quiet. I slept some, which surprised me. When we landed at Dallas-Fort Worth, I carried my bag through the terminal and saw my wife standing near baggage claim with our daughter. Lily had just turned six. She was wearing a purple dress and her hair was done up in braids I didn't recognize. My wife saw me first and smiled and started to wave, but Lily stepped back and hid behind her mother's leg. She peeked around at me with one eye like she was deciding whether I was safe.

I stopped walking.

I'd talked to her on the phone almost every week. Sent her drawings I'd done of her dog, of our house, of things she'd recognize. But I'd been gone a year, and I guess a man in uniform with a shaved head and a bag over his shoulder wasn't quite what she had pictured. She stayed behind that leg until my wife knelt down and pointed at me and said something I couldn't hear. Then Lily came forward slow, looking up at me with her mouth open a little, and I knelt down too. She touched my face with her hand like she was checking if I was real. Then she grabbed me around the neck and I picked her up and she was heavier than I remembered. I held her for a while. My wife put her hand on my back. People moved around us with their roller bags.

The first week home, I drove to the grocery store for milk and eggs. My wife had made a list. I found the eggs fine. The milk was fine. Then I turned down the cereal aisle.

I stood there for what must have been twenty minutes. There were forty kinds of cereal. Maybe more. Cereal with marshmallows in it. Cereal with flakes and clusters. Cereal in a box with a cartoon on it. Cereal in a bag. Cereal with a label that said it was good for your heart. I'd been eating eggs and toast and whatever else they had at the chow hall, and before that, MREs, and the idea of choosing between forty kinds of cereal was something I couldn't get my arms around. It wasn't that I couldn't read the boxes. I just couldn't make the decision. A woman with two kids in her cart came through the aisle and grabbed a box of Cinnamon Toast Crunch without slowing down and kept walking. I watched her do it like she'd performed a trick.

I left without the cereal. I told my wife they were out of the kind she wanted.

The sleeping took longer to sort out. For a year I'd slept on my side, facing the door. It wasn't something I decided to do. My body just did it. In the barracks you slept a certain way, and in a sleeping bag you slept a certain way, and after a while it wasn't a choice anymore. Back home, my wife slept on the left side of the bed, and I'd sleep on the right, which put my back to the door. I'd lie there and feel it. Nothing was wrong. I knew nothing was wrong. But I'd turn over and face the door anyway, and my wife would roll over too in her sleep and put her hand on my arm.

After about a month, she said to me one morning, "Do you want to leave the door open?"

I said sure. She'd started leaving it cracked, then open a little more each night, like she was helping me get used to it. The first night it was all the way open, I lay there listening to the house. The dishwasher running. The furnace clicking on. Lily coughing once down the hall. I could hear everything. I lay on my back and stared at the ceiling and listened to the house make its sounds and eventually I slept.

Some nights I still turn over and face the door. But most nights now I sleep on my side with my back to it, and my wife's hand on my arm, and the door open, and the house quiet.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
**Testimony Submitted to the City Council Regarding the Proposed Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase**

Submitted by [Your Name], Owner, [Business Name], [Address], Main Street

Members of the Council,

Thank you for accepting written testimony. I own [Business Name] on Main Street. I want to speak against the proposal to raise downtown meter rates from $0.50 to $1.50 per hour, and I want to do it with numbers rather than adjectives, because I think the numbers are the strongest argument I have.

**First, the size of the increase.**

This is not an adjustment. It is a 200 percent increase — the rate triples in a single step. I have not seen any other downtown cost, including my own lease, move by that much at once. Whatever the merits of raising rates eventually, the magnitude here is the problem, and it is worth stating plainly at the top of the discussion.

**Second, what happened when a neighboring city did this.**

When [Neighboring Town] raised its downtown meter rate in 2019, I did not want to guess at the effect, so I tracked it. For six consecutive weeks after the change took effect, I logged daily transaction counts against the same six-week window from the prior year. Foot traffic came in 18 percent below the comparison period.

I want to be honest about what that figure is and is not. It is one operator's data from one commercial district, not a controlled study, and I cannot rule out every other variable in those six weeks. But it is real, it is measured, and it is more evidence than has been presented in support of this proposal. If this Council has data showing a downtown retail corridor absorbed a tripling of meter rates without a measurable traffic decline, I would genuinely like to see it before you vote. In its absence, 18 percent is the best available estimate of what we are being asked to accept.

For my shop, an 18 percent drop is not a rounding error. It is the difference between covering payroll and cutting a shift.

**Third, the increase is badly matched to how people actually use downtown parking.**

The average visit to my shop is 22 minutes. My customers come in, order, wait a few minutes, and leave. They are not occupying a space for an hour, and they are not the long-term parkers this policy is presumably aimed at.

But there is no 22-minute option at the meter. There is a one-hour minimum. So today, a customer buying a $4.50 coffee and pastry pays $0.50 to park — an 11 percent surcharge on their purchase, and an effective rate of about $1.36 per hour of parking they actually use. Under the proposal, that same customer pays $1.50 — a 33 percent surcharge on the same order, at an effective rate of roughly $4.09 for every hour of parking they actually consume.

That is the transaction my customers will be evaluating at the meter, and it is the number that decides whether they come to Main Street or to a shopping center with a free lot. The current 50-cent hour minimum already covers a 22-minute visit comfortably. The proposed rate does not make short visits more efficient; it just makes them three times as expensive.

**Fourth, and most importantly: this does not solve the problem it is being offered to solve.**

The city's own report states that meter revenue accounts for 4 percent of the downtown budget. Four percent. Even a perfectly executed tripling — assuming zero behavioral change, zero decline in occupancy, zero lost sales tax from businesses like mine — moves a line item that constitutes one twenty-fifth of downtown spending.

And it will not be a perfect tripling, because the 18 percent figure suggests fewer people will park downtown at all. The Council should ask staff a direct question before voting: what is the projected net revenue after accounting for reduced occupancy, and how does that net figure compare to the sales tax receipts generated by the foot traffic it displaces? I suspect that analysis has not been run. It should be, because a policy that risks 18 percent of Main Street's customer traffic to improve a 4 percent budget line is not a solution. It is a trade the city loses on both ends.

**What I am asking for.**

I am not asking that rates never change. I am asking for three things:

1. **Reject the $1.50 rate as proposed.** If an increase is necessary, phase it — to $0.75, hold for twelve months, and measure.
2. **Create a short-stay option.** A 15- or 30-minute rate, or a free first 20 minutes, would align meter policy with a 22-minute average visit and protect exactly the turnover a merchant district needs.
3. **Require a net revenue analysis before any vote,** including projected occupancy loss and downstream sales tax impact, measured against the 4 percent figure in the city's own report.

I have run my business on this street for years and I intend to keep doing it. I am asking the Council to make this decision with the numbers in front of it.

Respectfully submitted,

[Your Name]
Owner, [Business Name]
[Address] | [Phone] | [Email]

b.text:
# Testimony Regarding Proposed Parking Meter Rate Increase

My name is [Your Name], and I have owned [Coffee Shop Name] on Main Street for [number] years. I am submitting this testimony in opposition to the proposed parking meter rate increase from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour.

I understand the city faces budget pressures, but I believe this rate increase will harm downtown businesses without meaningfully addressing the city's financial needs. I want to present three specific concerns based on data I have gathered and reviewed.

First, I have direct evidence of how parking rate increases affect foot traffic in similar markets. In 2019, the neighboring municipality implemented a comparable parking rate increase. I tracked my sales register data for six weeks before and after that increase. The result was an 18 percent decline in customer visits during that period. My customers are not commuters or all-day parkers—they are coffee drinkers. My data shows the average customer visit is 22 minutes. The current one-hour minimum already covers their parking needs with time to spare. A tripling of the hourly rate will discourage these short-visit customers from coming downtown at all.

Second, I want to address whether this increase actually solves the city's budget problem. According to the city's own parking revenue report, meter revenue currently covers 4 percent of the downtown district budget. Even if this rate increase generates additional revenue, the math is clear: parking meters are not and cannot be the solution to downtown funding gaps. We would be creating a genuine hardship for local businesses and their customers in exchange for addressing perhaps 4 or 5 percent of a much larger problem.

I urge the city council to explore alternative revenue sources that do not penalize people for shopping and dining downtown. Our small businesses depend on accessible, affordable parking to survive.

Thank you for your consideration.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**An 8:45 Start Is Worth Getting Behind**

As the parent of two middle-schoolers in Millbrook, I know that getting kids out the door in the morning will never be effortless. There will still be missing shoes, unfinished breakfasts and someone remembering a permission slip at the last possible moment. An 8:45 school start won’t fix all of that.

But it could help our children arrive ready to learn. That’s why I support the proposal the school board will vote on next month.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later, giving adolescents a better chance to get the sleep they need. As children reach adolescence, their natural sleep schedules shift later. Telling them to “just go to bed earlier” sounds sensible, but it doesn’t fully account for that change.

Of course parents still have a job to do. Phones need to be put away. Bedtime routines matter. But families’ efforts and a sensible school schedule should work together, not against each other.

We also have something more concrete than a national recommendation: the Lincoln Middle pilot. Attendance improved, and first-period grades went up. Those results don’t promise that every student will suddenly love mornings or earn straight A’s. They do give us a practical, local reason to believe a later start can help. More students showing up, and doing better in the first class of the day, is worth taking seriously.

The bus question deserves a serious answer, too. Families need transportation they can count on, and changing school schedules affects parents’ workdays and other children in the household.

I’ve read the proposal closely. It already re-tiers the bus routes to accommodate the later start. That doesn’t mean every concern disappears, but it does mean transportation hasn’t simply been ignored. The useful questions now are about how those routes will work, when families will receive details and how problems will be handled—not whether anyone remembered the buses.

I don’t expect a perfect transition. I do expect the board to weigh the inconvenience of making a change against the daily cost of keeping a schedule that works against adolescent sleep needs.

Our kids spend those first-period minutes trying to learn, whether they’re alert enough or not. We should give them a better shot.

Next month, I hope the board votes yes on 8:45—and follows through with clear transportation information and careful attention to how the change is working.

b.text:
Every weekday morning at 6:15, I stage the same battle. I walk into my kids’ rooms, flip on the lights, and try to coax two exhausted middle-schoolers out of bed. By the time they grab their backpacks and head out the door for the early bell, they’re practically sleepwalking.

If you have teenagers or pre-teens in Millbrook, you know this routine all too well. That is why I am strongly urging our school board to approve the proposal to move our middle and high school start times to 8:45 a.m. when they vote next month.

This isn’t about letting kids be lazy or indulging bad bedtime habits. It’s basic biology. The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. to align with adolescent sleep cycles. During puberty, biological rhythms shift, making it difficult for teens to fall asleep before 11:00 p.m. Expecting them to absorb algebra at 7:30 in the morning simply works against how their brains are wired.

We don’t have to guess whether a later start time works—we already have local proof. Look at the results from the pilot program at Lincoln Middle. When they shifted to a later schedule, attendance improved and first-period grades went up significantly. Teachers reported fewer heads on desks and more kids actually awake and ready to participate. 

I understand why some parents and community members are hesitant. Change is tricky, and the biggest concern I’ve heard around town is the bus schedule. But if you look closely at the district's proposal, this issue has already been thoroughly addressed. The plan re-tiers the existing bus routes, staggering elementary and secondary pickups so our current fleet can handle the change smoothly, without blowing up the budget or leaving families stranded.

Our kids only get one shot at these critical school years. Right now, we’re sending them into the classroom running on empty before the day even starts. 

When the board votes next month, let’s choose common sense, real data, and our children’s health. Please reach out to our school board members and tell them to vote "yes" on the 8:45 a.m. start time.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
# How to Bleed Air Out of Your Baseboard Heating Before Winter

If your baseboards gurgle, or one room stays cold while the rest of the house heats fine, you've probably got air trapped in the system. Bleeding it out takes about 20 minutes and no special skills — here's how to do it right.

## What You'll Need

- A radiator key or a flathead screwdriver (depends on your valve type)
- A small cup or bowl
- An old towel, just in case

## Step 1: Shut Off the Circulator and Boiler

Before you touch anything, turn off the boiler and circulator pump. You don't want the pump pushing water around while you're trying to bleed a valve, and you don't want to be working with scalding water. Give the system a few minutes to settle.

## Step 2: Find the Bleeder Valve on Each Baseboard

Look at the end of each baseboard unit — usually behind the end cap, you'll find a small valve with either a square stem (that's what the key is for) or a slotted screw head. Every unit on the system should have one.

## Step 3: Cup Underneath and Open the Valve Slowly

Hold your cup under the valve and open it slowly. Don't crank it — a quarter to half turn is usually plenty. If there's air in the line, you'll hear it hiss out. Let it run until you get a steady stream of water with no sputtering or hissing. Steady water means the air is out of that section.

## Step 4: Close It Snug — Not Tight

Once the water runs steady, close the valve until it's snug and the drip stops. **Do not crank it down.** Overtightening cracks the valve seat, and then instead of a free 20-minute job, you've got a leaking valve and a service call.

## Step 5: Work Unit by Unit, Starting Closest to the Boiler

Start with the baseboard nearest the boiler and work your way outward through the loop. Air moves through the system, so bleeding in order gets it all out instead of chasing it around the house.

## The Mistake That Causes Most of Our Cold Radiator Calls

Here it is: **people bleed the upstairs units and skip the basement loop.**

We get called out every fall for "cold radiators," and more often than not, the homeowner already bled every baseboard on the main and second floors — but never touched the basement. That's usually exactly where the air is sitting. If your system has a basement zone or any baseboard down there, bleed those units too. Don't skip them because the basement doesn't need to be warm — trapped air down there affects the whole system.

## After You're Done

Turn the boiler and circulator back on and check your pressure gauge. Most residential systems should sit around 12–15 psi cold. If bleeding dropped your pressure below that, the system needs water added back — some setups have an automatic feed valve that handles this, others need it done manually.

If you're not sure how to add water, or you've bled everything (basement included) and you've still got cold spots, that's when it's worth having someone take a look. Could be a stuck zone valve, a failing circulator, or a bigger air problem that needs a power purge.

Give us a call and we'll get you sorted before the real cold hits.

b.text:
# How to Bleed Air Out of Your Baseboard Heating Before Winter

If a baseboard runs cold along part of its length, or a whole zone barely warms up while the rest of the house is fine, you've got air in the line. Air pockets block water flow, and bleeding them out is a twenty-minute job you can do with a screwdriver. Here's the process, start to finish.

## What You'll Need

- A flathead screwdriver or a bleeder key (a couple bucks at any hardware store)
- A cup and a towel
- Twenty minutes

## Step 1: Shut the Boiler Off First

Flip the boiler off at its switch and let the circulator come to a stop. You want the system still while you bleed it — moving water carries air pockets past the bleeders instead of letting them collect where you can actually get at them. It also keeps hot water from coming at you under pressure if the boiler's been running.

## Step 2: Find the Bleeder Valve

Each baseboard unit has a small bleeder valve at one end, right where the finned pipe meets the end of the unit. Sometimes it's tucked behind the end cover — pop the cover off if you have to. Most valves open with a flathead screwdriver; some take a bleeder key.

## Step 3: Put a Cup Under It

Water comes out when you open the valve. Cup underneath, towel beside it.

## Step 4: Open It Slow

Open the valve about a quarter turn, slowly. You'll hear hissing — that's the air escaping. Keep it open until water runs out in a steady stream with no sputtering and no hiss. Sputtering means there's still air in that run; steady water means the unit's clear.

## Step 5: Close It Snug — and Stop

Snug the valve closed and leave it there. Do not crank on it. Overtightening cracks the valve seat, and a cracked seat means a slow drip behind your baseboard cover that you won't find until it's stained the wall. A firm snug is all it takes.

## Step 6: Work From the Boiler Outward

Go unit by unit, starting with the baseboard closest to the boiler and working your way out to the farthest loop. Bleed every unit, including the ones that seem to be heating fine.

## The Mistake That Causes Most of Our Cold Radiator Calls

When we get called out for a baseboard that won't heat, the story is almost always the same: the homeowner bled all the upstairs units, called it done, and skipped the basement loop entirely. The basement loop is usually where the air is actually sitting. You can bleed the whole first floor, get clear water out of every valve, and still have an air-bound system — because the pocket doing the damage never got a bleeder opened on it. If you only bleed one loop, make it the basement.

## When You're Done

Flip the boiler back on, let it run a full cycle, and put your hand along each baseboard. They should heat evenly end to end. If you've bled every unit — basement included — and a loop still runs cold, the problem is past what a bleeder valve can fix: low system pressure, a weak circulator, or a stuck zone valve. That's when to give us a call, and we'd rather come out now than after the first cold night.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
USDA raised the prevented planting base rate 22% in our region this year. On my farm, that is about $46,000 in extra premium costs—before I even turn a wrench.

This spring I got 60% of my corn and soybean acres planted by the late May deadline. The rest never made it; it would not stop raining for weeks, and that 40% went straight to prevented planting. When you are already writing off a big chunk of the farm, a 22% hike is not a nuisance fee. It is a real hit to cash flow.

What makes it worse is how the acreage caps are structured. Because of them, this cost lands proportionally harder on family operations like mine than on the larger farms nearby. Bigger acreage buffers the shock; my ground is exactly the size that gets squeezed. Fourth-generation or not, I do not have the balance-sheet padding to treat a $46,000 surprise as background noise.

That is why SB 214 matters. It fixes the acreage cap so family farms are not punished for being family-sized. If you read this in the newsletter, do not just skim past it. Call your state legislators and tell them to support SB 214. We need that cap corrected before the next rain comes.

b.text:
# When the Rain Won't Stop and the Bill Keeps Climbing

By late May this year, I had 60% of my acres in the ground. The other 40% sat under standing water, waiting on a break in the weather that never came before the final planting deadline passed. Any of you who farmed through this spring know exactly what that felt like — watching the calendar and the radar at the same time, doing math you didn't want to do.

What I didn't expect was to get hit twice. Once by the weather, and once by USDA.

This year, USDA raised the base rate on prevented planting premiums by 22% in our region. For my operation, that increase alone comes out to roughly $46,000 in additional cost — not for a payout, not for coverage I'm glad to have, but simply for the privilege of insuring against a risk that just became a reality on my own farm. That's $46,000 that isn't going toward equipment, inputs for next season, or the note at the bank. It's gone, and it's gone because of a rate change, not because of anything I did differently.

Here's the part that ought to concern every family operation reading this: the way the acreage caps are structured, this increase doesn't land evenly. Operations like mine — mid-sized, family-run, without the acreage base to spread the cap across — absorb a proportionally larger hit than the bigger operations down the road. Two farms can have the same percentage of prevented planting acres, and the smaller family operation pays a heavier premium burden per acre because of how the cap is written into the formula. That's not a market outcome. That's a policy design flaw.

I want to be clear about what this means in practice. A 22% base rate increase sounds like a modest technical adjustment when you read it in a USDA bulletin. It is not modest when you're the one writing the check, and it is especially not modest when the structure of the cap means family farms shoulder more of it, acre for acre, than the larger operations that have more acreage to absorb the same percentage increase.

This is exactly the problem SB 214 is written to address. The bill would fix the acreage cap calculation so that prevented planting coverage costs scale fairly regardless of operation size — closing the gap that currently penalizes smaller and mid-sized farms for the same weather risk everyone in the region is exposed to. It doesn't ask for special treatment. It asks for the cap to work the way most of us assumed it already did: proportionally, not punitively.

I'd encourage every member of this bureau to read SB 214, talk to your neighbors about it, and reach out to your state legislators before the session moves further along. Numbers like $46,000 aren't abstract to those of us who've already paid them this year. They're the difference between a hard year and an unrecoverable one. If we want family operations to still be here for a fifth and sixth generation, the policy has to reflect that math — not work against it.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The couples who ditch the shot list always end up with the best photos.

I don’t say that as a photographer who dislikes planning. I’ve been a full-time wedding photographer in the Texas Hill Country for eight years, and I shoot around 35 weddings a year. In that time, the pattern is consistent: a long shot list turns a wedding day into a checklist. Trust turns it into a story.

The Barrera wedding—the one that got rained out—is the example I keep coming back to.

The original setup wasn’t going to work, so we moved everything under the pecan tree. No one was thinking about a posed list at that point. We were responding to the weather, the light, and the people right in front of us. What could have been a ruined timeline became the most memorable part of the day—and the photographs from under that tree are the ones that tell the real story of the day.

If you’re a couple researching photographers: bring your priorities, your timeline, and your trust. Then let your photographer watch for the moments you didn’t plan.

If you’re a vendor: the most valuable thing we bring to a wedding day isn’t a rigid plan. It’s the ability to adapt and the willingness to be present for what’s actually happening.

The best photos are never the ones on the list.

#WeddingPhotography #TexasHillCountry #WeddingVendors

b.text:
The couples who ditch the shot list always seem to end up with the best photos.

Not because shot lists are bad. They are helpful. But a wedding day is alive, and the best images usually happen when you trust the moment more than the checklist.

At the Barrera wedding, rain took over the day. We moved everything under the pecan tree, set the original plan aside, and stopped trying to force what we thought the day was supposed to look like.

What we got instead was one of the most honest, joyful galleries I have delivered.

Crowded under branches.
Laughing through the weather.
Completely real.

After eight years of photographing weddings full time, I have learned this: my job is not just to check off poses. It is to notice what is happening, protect your time, and make space for the moments you will actually remember.

If you are planning a wedding, bring your must-have family photos. Bring your vendor list. Then give yourself permission to let the rest unfold.

Sometimes the backup plan becomes the best part.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
There's a lot that goes into the loaves and pastries you see here every morning, and I wanted to share a little about how we think about our days. As you know, the ovens start humming at 4am most days, and with just three of us running the place, every hour counts. After a lot of thought, we've decided to step back from custom wedding cakes.

It's been a bittersweet choice. We love celebrating your milestones, but the process is incredibly demanding. Just the consultations and tastings alone can eat up nearly 14 hours of work per cake, often without any guarantee of the final bake. This year alone, we faced three last-minute cancellations that meant we'd already used up the ingredients for cakes that never made it to a table. It became clear that these big projects were pulling focus away from the everyday items we make for you—the sourdough, the morning pastries, the simple slices that actually pay the rent.

Moving forward, we want to pour that energy back into the bread and treats that bring us together day after day. We hope you understand, and we can't wait to keep serving you through the regular seasons of life. Thank you for being part of our story.

b.text:
I’m writing this between the first batch of croissants and the phone ringing—still 4:30 a.m., still covered in flour—because if I don’t say it clearly now, it’ll keep nagging at me through every prep list until I just quietly stop answering emails.

We’re stepping away from custom wedding cakes. Not because they weren’t beautiful—they were, and some of them made me cry—but because they’re taking more than they give back, and I need to explain that without sounding like I’m blame-shifting.

Here’s the honest math, straight from the kitchen. Each wedding order eats up about fourteen hours of free consult and tasting time. That’s fourteen hours of meeting at the counter, scheduling tastings, tweaking fondant colors, and talking through timelines when I should be baking the sourdough, the danishes, or the loaf that pays the rent at six in the morning. For a three-person shop, that’s not just extra work; that’s another part-time job where the time isn’t paid, and I can’t keep that up without the rest of the shop suffering.

Then there’s the gut-punch part. We had three last-minute cancellations this year. Three. Each one meant ingredients—fondant, chocolate, fruit, butter—that we’d already bought sitting in boxes with nowhere to go. We’re small enough that one lost order stings for weeks, and three of them make me want to cry into my mixing bowl because I know exactly how many pieces of everyday bread that money could have bought.

Most of all, it was pulling me away from the everyday case. That’s the heart of this place. You come in Thursday for a warm loaf, you grab a croissant with coffee, you call in a birthday tray or an office order on a Tuesday. That daily rhythm is what keeps the doors open and the oven running. When I’m spending evenings sketching tier diagrams and replying to “just one more change,” the display gets sparse, the regulars wait longer, and the whole thing feels like it’s slipping away from the people who actually support us.

I’m not bitter, and I’m not turning into some corporate bakery with rules. I just need to protect the hours where I bake for all of you. If you’re planning a birthday, an anniversary, or just a Tuesday that needs cake, come in and talk to us—we’ll still make something wonderful, just without the grand-tier, multi-meeting kind of build. But those big wedding orders, with all the custom architecture and the no-paid-consult hours? We have to let them go so the rest of this shop can survive.

Thanks for reading this far, and for being the reason I still get up at 4 a.m. I’ll see you at the counter soon—probably covered in flour, probably a little more tired, but still here for the everyday stuff that actually matters.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
Every Saturday since sophomore year, I've been at my parents' restaurant from ten in the morning to ten at night.

One Saturday in October the register system died. The screen went black and nothing brought it back. My dad called the company and they said someone could come Monday. It was 11:30 and we had a lunch rush coming. I grabbed a stack of order slips from the back office and a pen. I wrote down every order by hand, added the tax, totaled it. The math wasn't hard but doing it fast while people were waiting was. I underlined each total twice because that's what the printed receipts did. For four days I ran the front with a pen, a calculator, and a shoebox of cash. A few customers said they liked the handwritten tickets. One guy called it "charming." It wasn't charming. It was the thing that had to happen so we could keep taking orders.

We hired a new server in September. Her name is Destiny and she goes to the school across town. This is her first job. My grandma still comes in on weekends to make the spring rolls, and she's particular about the fold. If you can see the shrimp through the wrapper, it's wrong. The shrimp should be centered. One Saturday my grandma was tired and asked me to show Destiny. I'd watched my grandma do it hundreds of times. I'd done it maybe fifty. I showed Destiny how to soak the wrapper for four seconds, lay the lettuce flat, fold the sides in, roll tight. My hands knew what to do even though I'd never thought about explaining it. Destiny's first three came out loose and she kept apologizing. I told her it took me a long time too, which is true. I didn't tell her my grandma said my first ones looked like egg rolls.

On breaks I do homework in the walk-in cooler. It's forty degrees in there and it smells like cilantro and raw pork. I sit on a plastic milk crate and spread my stuff out on a cardboard box of bean sprouts. Last month I did forty-five minutes of calculus in there, derivatives. My fingers were stiff by the time I got back to the dining room. My manager is my mom. She doesn't always remember I have homework, or she remembers but there are tables to clear. I do homework in small pieces. Twenty minutes here, fifteen there. Sometimes in the cooler, sometimes at a corner table when it's slow. I've gotten good at stopping in the middle of a problem and picking it back up three hours later.

I don't know what I'm supposed to say about all this. I work weekends. I do my homework in a cooler. I teach people to fold spring rolls the way my grandma does. It's just what my life is.

b.text:
The register died on a Saturday at 6:40, right in the middle of the dinner rush. I was on the floor and my dad was in the kitchen. I knew because the screen went black and then came back with a blue error message. We had forty people in the dining room and a waitlist at the door.

I found a pen and a stack of the guest check pads we keep under the counter for when the printer jams. I started writing tickets by hand. Two bowls of pho, no onion. One vermicelli, extra fish sauce on the side. A large order of spring rolls to go. My handwriting is bad, so I wrote slowly and checked the math twice. My dad called out order numbers and I called them back. For two hours nobody used the computer. When the repair guy came Monday he asked why we didn't just close. My dad said, "We had food."

On Sundays a new hire, Danny, was on the schedule. He's a sophomore and he'd never cooked before. I taught him my grandma's spring roll fold because she was home with her knee and couldn't come in. She taught me when I was nine. You lay the rice paper flat, fold the sides in like an envelope, then roll tight so the shrimp shows through the wrapper. Danny's first four were loose and fell apart in the fryer. I showed him again. By the sixth he had it. He said it was like folding a burrito, and I said no, it's not, and we laughed because he was sort of right.

On my breaks I do calc homework in the walk-in cooler. It's the only place with no noise and no phone. It's cold enough that I wear my hoodie and sit on an upside-down bucket. The light is bad. I do derivatives and integrals and think about limits. Sometimes my mom comes in to grab bean sprouts and asks if I'm okay. I say yes. She brings me a jacket sometimes even though I already have one on.

I'm not sure what I want to say about any of this except that it's what I do. I'm not the kind of person who's one thing at school and another person at home. I'm the person who writes tickets by hand when the computer fails and teaches a kid to fold spring rolls and does homework in the cold. That's not a lesson I learned. It's just true. I'll keep doing it until I leave for school, and then I'll come back on weekends and do it again.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
Every morning, I watch my two middle-schoolers drag themselves out of bed in the dark, bleary-eyed and fumbling for cereal, and I think: *this can’t be right*. Their alarm clocks scream at 6:15, and we’re out the door before the sun has even thought about warming the pavement. I’m not a sleep scientist or a logistics expert—just a parent who’s read the school board’s proposal for an 8:45 start time and knows, deep in my bones, that it’s the right move for our kids.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has been clear for years: adolescents need 8 to 10 hours of sleep, and their natural sleep cycles shift later. Waking a teenager at 6 a.m. is like waking an adult at 4 a.m.—it works against biology, not with it. An 8:45 start isn’t an indulgence; it’s simply aligning school with what we know about growing brains.

But I don’t need a national study when we have proof here at home. Lincoln Middle’s pilot program shifted its first bell to 8:45, and the results were remarkable. Attendance rose, and first-period grades climbed. When I spoke with a teacher friend at Lincoln, she described a roomful of students who were actually *present*—not just physically, but mentally, ready to learn. That’s what every parent wants: kids who can focus on algebra, not on staying upright.

The main objection I hear is about bus schedules. I get it—changing start times feels like untangling Christmas lights. But the proposal on the table already re-tiers the routes. The transportation department has mapped it out, and it works without adding cost or leaving younger students waiting in the dark. We’re not being asked to choose between our middle-schoolers and the rest of the district; the plan is balanced and ready to go.

Next month, the school board will vote. I’m asking my neighbors to see this for what it is: a rare, evidence-backed chance to give our kids something as basic as enough sleep. Let’s stop fighting their biology and start giving them mornings that make sense. I’ll set a later alarm for that—happily.

b.text:
# Why I'm Supporting the 8:45 Start Time

Like most parents of middle-schoolers, I've watched my kids drag themselves out of bed at 6:15 a.m. for the past two years. They're not lazy. They're not staying up too late scrolling on their phones (though yes, that happens sometimes). They're adolescents, and their bodies are doing exactly what adolescent bodies do.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. They didn't pick that number out of thin air. Research shows that puberty shifts kids' internal clocks, making it nearly impossible for them to fall asleep before 11 p.m. — and meaning that a 7:30 first bell has them waking up at the lowest point of their sleep cycle.

I've read the school board's proposal closely, and I know some people are concerned about the bus schedule. That was my first question too. But the proposal already addresses this directly: it re-tiers the bus routes so that elementary runs shift earlier and middle school routes move later. No new buses. No new drivers. No new cost. Just a reordering of who gets picked up when.

If you want proof this works, look at what happened at Lincoln Middle School. After their pilot program pushed start times later, attendance went up. First-period grades went up. Not test scores three years down the road — immediate, measurable improvements in the class that currently suffers most from sleepy teenagers.

I understand change is inconvenient. Families have built their lives around the current schedule. But the current schedule was built around adult work hours and bus logistics, not around what we know about how kids actually learn. We now have that information. We have a pediatricians' organization telling us our adolescents need more sleep. We have a local pilot showing real results. We have a proposal that solves the transportation problem without spending a dime.

My kids will be in high school before long, and this change may not fully benefit them. But the kids coming up behind them — the fifth graders who will be middle-schoolers next fall — deserve a schedule that gives them a fighting chance.

The school board votes next month. I hope they'll look at the evidence, look at the proposal, and do right by our kids.

*Millbrook parent of two*

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
# How to Keep Your Dog’s Coat From Matting Between Grooming Visits

The biggest mistake I see owners make is bathing a matted dog because they think the water will loosen everything up. Unfortunately, it does the opposite. Once matted fur gets wet, it tightens as it dries and can turn into a felt-like pad against the skin.

Always brush your dog thoroughly **before** a bath at home, not after the mats have been soaked and set tighter. This is especially important for curly-coated dogs and double-coated breeds, whose loose undercoat can quickly become packed.

Use a slicker brush and work in small sections so you reach all the way through the coat instead of just smoothing the top. I recommend short, gentle “line brushing” strokes rather than brushing in circles. Circular brushing can twist the hair and contribute to tangles.

Start behind the ears and under the front legs. Those are two of the first places mats tend to form because of friction, movement, collars, and harnesses. Then work through the rest of the coat section by section, including the chest, belly, legs, tail, and areas where equipment rubs.

If you notice a mat beginning to form, don’t immediately pull at it with a brush or comb. First, work a little dog-safe conditioner or detangling product into the mat with your fingers. Gently separate the outer edges before using your slicker brush in short strokes. Hold the hair close to the skin while you work so you aren’t tugging on your dog.

If the mat is tight against the skin, covers a large area, or your dog seems uncomfortable, stop and call your groomer. Don’t try to cut it out with scissors—dog skin is thin and can easily be pulled up into the mat.

A few minutes of section-by-section brushing several times a week can make a huge difference. It keeps your dog more comfortable and makes the next grooming visit easier for everyone.

b.text:
If you run your hands through your dog’s coat, feel a tangle, and immediately think, “I’ll just throw them in the tub and wash it out,” I need you to step away from the faucet. 

I see this happen in the salon every single week, especially with our curly doodles and thick double-coated breeds. People think warm water and a good lather will soften up tangles, but water actually does the exact opposite. Think about what happens when you wash a wool sweater: the fibers shrink, knit together, and turn into a solid, impenetrable felt pad. That is exactly what happens to your dog's hair. Bathing a matted dog locks those knots in tighter, and once that happens, my clippers are usually the only safe option left. 

The golden rule at home is to always brush *before* the bath, never after. If water hits a knot, you’ve lost the battle. 

When you sit down to brush, throw out the idea of just casually sweeping over their back while you watch TV. That just fluffs the top layer while mats quietly build up right against the skin. Grab a slicker brush, and instead of moving in circles or long, sweeping arcs, use short, gentle line strokes. You want to part the hair with your free hand so you can see the pink of their skin, then brush down through that section, working your way up layer by layer. 

Don't just start randomly in the middle of their back, either. Work in small sections and go straight to the friction zones first, because that’s where mats always start. Check right behind the ears where their collar rubs, deep in the armpits under their front legs, and back around the groin and tail base. If you can keep those hidden friction areas clear, the rest of the body is easy.

Now, if you’re doing your routine check and you feel a mat that’s already formed, put the brush down. Raking through a tight knot with metal pins hurts, and it only takes one painful session for your dog to decide they hate being groomed. Instead, take a little bit of dog conditioner (or a dog-safe detangling spray) and work it directly into the knot with your bare fingers. Massage it in, gently teasing the hairs apart with your fingertips to break up the core of the mat. Only after you’ve worked it loose with your hands and given the hair some slickness should you take a metal comb or slicker brush to gently finish working it out, starting from the tips and moving toward the skin.

A few minutes of line brushing in the right spots a couple of times a week will save your dog from discomfort, save their coat length, and save you from the dreaded "we had to shave them" phone call at their next appointment. As always, if you run into a knot you can’t safely separate with your fingers, leave it alone and bring them in—we're always here to help tackle it before it gets out of hand.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
Members of the City Council:

I own a small, independent coffee shop on Main Street, and I oppose the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour. That is not a modest adjustment. It triples the hourly rate—a 200% increase—and adds a cost to the short, everyday visits that downtown businesses depend on.

My concern is grounded in numbers. In 2019, after a similar parking rate increase in the next town over, I tracked register activity for six weeks and observed an 18% decline in foot traffic there. That observation alone cannot establish that parking rates caused the entire decline. But an 18% drop is a serious warning, and it deserves consideration before we adopt a similar increase here.

My customers’ average visit lasts 22 minutes. The current one-hour minimum already more than covers that visit. If the minimum remains in place under this proposal, someone stopping for coffee will pay $1.50 instead of 50 cents, even though they typically use barely more than a third of the hour they purchase. That is an additional dollar for the same short stop, not for additional time or a better parking experience.

For a small shop, those brief visits are not incidental. They are the business. We rely on people deciding that stopping downtown is convenient and worthwhile. Council should not dismiss the cumulative effect of making that decision more expensive.

The city’s own report says meter revenue covers only 4% of the downtown budget. That does not mean parking revenue is irrelevant, but it does mean this increase should not be presented as a solution to the broader budget problem. Tripling the price also does not guarantee tripling revenue: that depends on whether people continue parking downtown at the same rate.

Before approving this proposal, I ask the council to explain the expected net revenue, account for possible changes in parking demand, and consider shorter paid increments that reflect actual visits.

Please reject the increase as proposed. A policy that triples the cost of parking deserves a stronger justification than we have been given—especially when the businesses bearing the risk are the same businesses that keep Main Street active.

b.text:
To the Members of the City Council:

My name is [Name], and I am the owner of [Coffee Shop Name], a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am submitting this testimony in opposition to the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from fifty cents to one dollar and fifty cents per hour.

The evidence that this increase will hurt small businesses is not theoretical. In 2019, when the neighboring town enacted a similar parking rate hike, I tracked my own register sales for six weeks to see how foot traffic would respond. The result was an eighteen percent drop in customer visits. That figure comes from six weeks of actual transaction data, not from speculation. Nearly one in five customers simply stopped coming through my door after parking became significantly more expensive.

This proposal is particularly misaligned with businesses like mine because of how our customers actually use downtown parking. The average visit to my shop lasts twenty-two minutes. Under the current rate, a customer pays fifty cents for a one-hour minimum, which already covers their stay with nearly forty minutes to spare. If this increase passes, that same twenty-two-minute visit will cost one dollar and fifty cents. We are asking our customers to triple their parking cost for time they do not use.

Furthermore, the city’s own report states that parking meter revenue covers only four percent of the downtown budget. This increase will not meaningfully address our fiscal needs. It will simply triple the burden on short-term parkers for a revenue stream that, by the city’s own accounting, contributes just four cents of every dollar in the downtown budget.

An eighteen percent decline in foot traffic is a proven consequence, not a possibility. A twenty-two-minute visit should not carry a one-dollar-and-fifty-cent parking fee. And a policy that impacts only four percent of the budget is not a financial solution. I respectfully urge the council to reject this proposed rate increase.

Respectfully submitted,  
[Name]  
Owner, [Coffee Shop Name]  
Main Street

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
Open campus lunch for juniors and seniors should be allowed at our school because it would reduce overcrowding, respect older students’ responsibility, and match what nearby districts are already doing successfully. Juniors and seniors are close to adulthood, and many of them are ready for the independence that comes with more freedom during the school day. A policy like this would not be reckless; it would be a practical change that benefits students and improves the lunch period for everyone.

The biggest reason to allow open campus lunch is that our cafeteria is already too crowded. The cafeteria seats only 220 students, but 340 students are in the lunch wave. That means more than 100 students do not have a real seat available at lunch. Instead of giving students enough space to eat comfortably, the school forces a large group to stand, squeeze together, or find awkward places to sit. Lunch is supposed to be a break in the day, but overcrowding turns it into a stressful and uncomfortable experience. If juniors and seniors were allowed off campus, the cafeteria would not have to serve as the only option for every student in that lunch period.

Another reason is that many students would use the privilege responsibly. I surveyed 80 students at our school, and 71 said they were in favor of open campus lunch. That is a strong majority. Students are not asking for something unreasonable; they are asking for a limited privilege for upperclassmen, who are generally older and more capable of managing their time. Juniors and seniors already handle harder classes, jobs, sports, and other responsibilities. If they can manage those commitments, they can manage a lunch break without being treated like younger students who need as much supervision. Open campus lunch would recognize that maturity.

Nearby districts have already shown that this policy can work. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow open campus lunch for upperclassmen, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness. That matters because one of the main concerns about open campus lunch is that students will come back late and disrupt the school day. However, those districts provide real evidence that this does not have to happen. If schools similar to ours can allow juniors and seniors to leave campus without increasing tardiness, then our school can do the same. We do not need to guess whether the policy works when other districts have already demonstrated it.

Some people may argue that open campus lunch could create safety problems or encourage students to leave and not come back on time. Those concerns are understandable, but they are also manageable. Juniors and seniors already earn more privileges than underclassmen in other parts of school life, and a lunch pass would simply be another privilege tied to age and responsibility. The school could require students to return on time and lose the privilege if they abuse it. That is a fair consequence and a better solution than keeping every student locked into an overcrowded cafeteria because of what a few might do.

Open campus lunch for juniors and seniors would improve lunch at our school in a realistic and responsible way. It would reduce overcrowding in a cafeteria that cannot fit the students assigned to it, give mature students a privilege they are ready for, and follow the example of nearby districts that have already made this work without increasing tardiness. This policy would not weaken the school; it would show trust in students who have earned it. For those reasons, our school should allow open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

b.text:
Our school should trust its upperclassmen with the privilege of leaving campus during lunch. Currently, juniors and seniors are required to stay on school grounds for the entire lunch period, a policy that ignores both practical problems and the maturity of older students. Implementing an open campus lunch for these students would relieve dangerous overcrowding in the cafeteria, align our school with nearby districts that have already adopted this policy successfully, and honor the clear preference of the student body.

The most immediate reason to allow juniors and seniors off campus is the severe overcrowding in our cafeteria. Our lunch wave includes 340 students, but the cafeteria only seats 220 people. That leaves 120 students without a designated place to sit and eat. Every day, students end up on the floor, in hallways, or packed shoulder to shoulder at tables, creating a chaotic and uncomfortable environment. This overcrowding is not just an inconvenience; it’s a safety hazard. In the event of an emergency, a packed room makes it harder to evacuate quickly. Simply allowing older students to leave campus would immediately reduce the number of bodies in the cafeteria during that wave, giving everyone more space and a better lunch experience.

Critics might worry that an open campus would lead to worse attendance after lunch, but evidence from other districts tells a different story. Three nearby districts—Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade—already permit open campus lunch for their upperclassmen. All three have publicly reported data on tardiness, and none have seen an increase since the policy began. Their administrators note that students return on time because they don’t want to lose the privilege. If these communities, with similar student populations and traffic patterns, can manage an open campus without attendance problems, there is no reason to assume our students would behave any differently. The fear of post-lunch tardiness is contradicted by real-world results just a few miles away.

Beyond logistics and outside evidence, the students themselves overwhelmingly support the change. I conducted a survey of 80 randomly selected juniors and seniors at our school, and 71 said they would prefer an open campus option. That’s nearly 89 percent in favor. This isn’t just a casual wish; it reflects a desire for more independence and a recognition that sitting in a cramped cafeteria is not the best use of a 45-minute break. Many students said they would use the time to grab food quickly, run a short errand, or simply eat in a quieter environment—all activities that require the trust and responsibility we’re supposed to be developing in high school. When a policy is this out of step with what the people it affects actually want, it deserves a hard look.

One possible objection is that off-campus lunch invites reckless driving or procrastination, but those concerns are manageable. Students who leave could be required to carry a school-issued pass, and the privilege could be revoked if they abuse it—just as Fairmont and West Linn handle it. Moreover, our school already trusts seniors with early release and dual-enrollment programs where they travel independently; adding a lunch break does not ask for a new kind of maturity, only extends an existing one. The benefits of a less crowded cafeteria and a more motivated student body outweigh hypothetical worst-case scenarios that have not materialized elsewhere.

Our school has a clear opportunity to solve a real problem with a simple, tested solution. The cafeteria cannot comfortably hold everyone, nearby districts prove open campus works without harming attendance, and the students making this request are nearly unanimous. It is time to give juniors and seniors the freedom they have earned and the practical relief our lunch period desperately needs.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
Every time it rains, we lose the girls’ soccer field.

Not because the girls don’t show up. Not because the team doesn’t have enough players. Not because the season is short. We lose it because the grass field floods, turns to mud, and becomes unplayable. Over the last two seasons, nine games have been rained out or moved because of it.

That is not a rare inconvenience. That is a pattern. And it is costing our girls real opportunities to play, compete, and finish their season on a field that is safe and usable.

Last October, one of my players tore her ACL stepping into a rut on that field. Anyone who coaches knows injuries happen in sports. But when a field is uneven, soft in some places and hard in others, and full of holes after rain, we are no longer talking about normal risk. We are talking about preventable danger.

That should matter to the school board. It should matter to parents. It should matter to anyone who believes our athletes deserve the same basic conditions we already gave the boys.

The boys football field got turf in 2019.

That is the plainest reason this should move forward: fairness. If the boys’ program deserves a safe, reliable playing surface, then the girls’ program does too. Our girls are not asking for something extra. They are asking for the same standard.

Turf would not solve every problem in girls’ athletics, but it would solve this one. It would keep more games on the schedule. It would reduce cancellations, make practice and competition more dependable, and give our athletes a field that can handle the weather we actually get here. It would also mean fewer dangerous holes, fewer muddy patches, and fewer excuses for why a team has to keep starting over.

And yes, it matters that this is girls’ soccer. When the boys’ field gets the investment and the girls’ field is left to flood, people notice. Our student-athletes notice. They know when they are being treated as an afterthought.

This is a facilities budget decision, but it is also a values decision. We can spend money on the field that serves half our athletes and say that is good enough, or we can do the right thing and make sure the girls have a field that is safe, usable, and equal.

I coach because I care about these kids, not because I enjoy writing letters and making budget arguments. I would much rather spend my time on the field than talking about turf. But after nine rainouts or moved games in two seasons, after an ACL injury tied to a rut in the grass, and after watching the boys already get the upgrade years ago, this should not be a hard call.

Give the girls turf.

b.text:
Nine games in the last two seasons. That's how many times my girls' soccer team has had a game rained out or moved because our field flooded. Not postponed because of lightning or a downpour during play — moved because two days after it rains, our grass field is still a swamp. The boys' football team hasn't lost a single home date in that time. Their field is turf. Ours isn't.

Last October, one of my players tore her ACL when her foot caught a rut on our field. She's a junior. She spent her recruiting season on crutches instead of in front of college coaches. I'm not going to pretend one injury proves anything by itself, but I will tell you what I see every practice: divots, standing water, bare patches, and a surface that changes depending on which week it is. We spend the first ten minutes of practice walking the field looking for holes. That's not conditioning. That's damage control.

The school board votes on next year's facilities budget soon, and turf for the girls' soccer field needs to be in it. Here's why.

First, safety. Turf isn't perfect — no surface is — but a consistent, level, well-drained field beats a rutted grass field that never fully recovers between rainstorms. When I can't tell my players the ground under them is predictable, I can't tell their parents it's safe.

Second, use. When a game gets moved, it doesn't just inconvenience my roster. Parents rearrange work schedules, opposing teams eat bus costs, our JV loses its game entirely because there's no field time left, and the athletic department scrambles to find officials for a new date. Nine times. A turf field drains, and you play. That's the whole pitch.

Third — and I'll be direct about this — fairness. The football field got turf in 2019. Nobody asked whether grass was good enough for the boys, because everyone understood it wasn't. Five years later, the girls are still playing on a field that floods. Title IX isn't just about roster spots. It's about facilities, and right now, ours don't match. I don't think anyone on the board intends that gap. But intent doesn't drain a field.

I've heard the objections. Turf is expensive up front — yes, and so is resodding, reseeding, and repainting a grass field every year, plus rescheduling costs and the field time we lose. Some people prefer grass — so do I, in theory. In practice, our grass field is unplayable for chunks of the season, and preference doesn't matter when the field is underwater.

I coach for the stipend, not the glory, and I'm not writing this because I enjoy writing letters. I'm writing it because I've stood on that field for years watching my players deal with conditions the boys stopped dealing with in 2019, and the fix is sitting right there in a budget line.

Board members: put it in the budget. Parents and neighbors: show up to the meeting or send an email and say you want it there. My girls have earned a field that lets them play. Nine canceled games and one torn ACL is enough.
