setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
Relieving the Pressure: Why Juniors and Seniors Deserve Open Campus Lunch

When the midday bell rings, high school upperclassmen are expected to demonstrate maturity, time management, and preparation for the adult world. Yet, for forty-five minutes every day, those same students are funnelled into a cafeteria that simply cannot handle them. Granting juniors and seniors open campus privileges for lunch is not merely a request for extra freedom; it is a practical solution to a severe logistical problem, backed by local data and overwhelming student support. 

The most immediate argument for open campus lunch is simple spatial reality: our cafeteria is currently failing to accommodate its population. The room has a legal seating capacity of 220 people. However, our current lunch wave forces 340 students into that exact same space. Every single day, 120 students are left to wander around looking for space, standing against the walls, or squeezing into overcrowded tables. This physical bottleneck leads to agonizingly slow lunch lines, leaving many students with barely ten minutes to eat before their next class. Allowing upperclassmen to step off campus during lunch would instantly eliminate this daily bottleneck, creating a manageable, safer environment for lowerclassmen who remain on school grounds.

Critics of open campus policies often raise concerns about safety, tardiness, and accountability, worrying that off-campus privileges will lead to chaotic afternoons and empty desks. However, regional evidence proves these fears are unfounded. Three neighboring districts—Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade—already allow open campus lunch for their upperclassmen. The published attendance and discipline statistics from all three districts reveal no measurable rise in tardiness or unexcused absences following the implementation of the policy. When high school students are treated like adults, they generally rise to the expectation. The real-world track record of our surrounding schools demonstrates that open campus lunch can be implemented smoothly without sacrificing academic discipline.

Furthermore, this policy reflects the clear consensus of the student body. In a recent survey conducted among 80 juniors and seniors at our school, 71 expressed strong support for an open campus policy. This overwhelming majority highlights a genuine readiness among students to take ownership of their day. High school is supposed to act as a bridge to college and the workforce, places where individuals are trusted to manage their own schedules, meal choices, and punctuality. Refusing to offer upperclassmen basic trust during a lunch break directly contradicts the school's stated goal of fostering independence.

Implementing open campus lunch for juniors and seniors is a logical win for everyone involved. It solves a real structural problem in our overcrowded cafeteria, relies on proven models from nearby districts, and honors the maturity of the upperclassmen. By trusting students with the responsibility of an open campus, our administration can turn a daily logistical headache into a step forward for school climate and student responsibility.

b.text:
Stepping Outside the Gates: Why Open Campus Lunch Works for Upperclassmen

Every day at fourth period, the bell triggers an uncoordinated sprint toward the cafeteria. The rush is not just about getting food; it is about securing a place to sit. For juniors and seniors who are months or a year away from living independently in college or entering the workforce, this daily routine feels less like preparation for adulthood and more like an overcrowded holding pattern. While our closed-campus policy was designed with safety and discipline in mind, it fails to meet the practical realities of our school today. Granting off-campus lunch privileges to juniors and seniors would resolve severe logistical strain on our facilities, encourage personal responsibility, and align our policy with proven regional standards.

The most immediate argument for an open campus is not philosophical; it is physical. Our cafeteria was built to seat 220 students, yet our current lunch wave serves roughly 340. The result is a daily bottleneck where over a third of the student body is displaced. Students are forced to eat sitting on the floor against locker banks, crowd onto stairwells, or spend twenty minutes in a line only to rush through their meal before the bell rings. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave during lunch would immediately draw down those numbers, freeing up seats and table space for freshmen and sophomores. It solves a physical capacity problem without requiring school renovation or additional staff supervision in the hallways.

The standard objection to off-campus privileges is almost always attendance: administrators worry that freedom will translate to empty desks during fifth period. However, this assumption is contradicted by real data from schools just outside our district line. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade high schools all operate with an open campus for upperclassmen. According to their published attendance records, none of these three districts experienced an increase in tardiness or unexcused absences after implementing the policy. Students quickly learn to manage their time because they recognize that tardiness puts their privileges at risk. If three neighboring communities with similar demographics and driving conditions can manage open lunch without academic disruption, there is no reason to assume our student body is incapable of doing the same.

Furthermore, this change carries overwhelming student support and offers a structured way to practice independence. In an informal survey conducted across our school last month, 71 out of 80 students surveyed favored implementing open campus lunch for upperclassmen. Most students do not view this policy as an excuse to wander, but as an earned milestone. High school is intended to prepare students for the demands of adulthood, where time management is an essential skill rather than a luxury. An open campus offers a low-stakes environment to practice that balance: students must plan a meal, coordinate transportation, watch the clock, and return ready to learn. For administrators who still harbor reservations, the policy could easily be tied to academic and behavioral standing, turning off-campus lunch into an incentive for maintaining passing grades and regular attendance.

A closed campus may feel like the safest default, but it ignores the strain on our cafeteria and underestimates the maturity of upperclassmen. With our facilities over capacity and clear evidence from Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade that attendance remains steady, the case for change is practical and timely. It is time to treat juniors and seniors with the trust they have earned, solve our overcrowding problem, and open the campus gates.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
**How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots to Prevent Burst Pipes in Minneapolis**

Every January, my crew and I run all over Minneapolis fixing burst pipes that could have been prevented with a five-minute chore. Let's get straight to it: here is exactly how to winterize your outdoor spigots so you don't end up paying for a major plumbing emergency when the temperature drops.

**Step 1: Disconnect your garden hoses**
I’m putting this first because leaving the hose attached is the absolute biggest mistake homeowners make. It is the number one cause of the burst-pipe calls we get mid-winter. If the hose is connected, water can't drain out of the spigot. It freezes, expands, and splits the pipe right inside your wall. Unscrew the hose, drain it, and put it in the garage.

**Step 2: Shut off the interior valve**
Head down to your basement or utility room and find the shutoff valve for your outdoor water supply. It’s usually located just a few feet inside from where the spigot sits on the exterior wall. Turn it completely off. 

*Note: If you’re looking around down there and realize you don’t actually have an interior shutoff valve—which is pretty common in some of these older Twin Cities homes—give us a call. We can come out and install an interior shutoff for you so you aren't at the mercy of the weather.*

**Step 3: Drain the outside spigot**
Go back outside and turn the spigot on. Let whatever water is trapped in that short section of pipe trickle out. Leave the handle in the "open" position for the rest of the winter. If a few drops of leftover water freeze, leaving the valve open gives the ice room to expand without snapping the metal.

**Step 4: Install a $3 foam cover**
Stop by the hardware store and spend three bucks on one of those hard foam insulated spigot covers. Hook it over the faucet and pull it tight against your siding or brick. It’s the cheapest insurance you can buy against sub-zero windchills.

That's it. It takes less time than drinking a cup of coffee. Take ten minutes this weekend to knock this out, and if you run into any plumbing issues you can't handle yourself, you know where to find us.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots (Minneapolis Homeowners)

Here's the whole job, start to finish. It takes about ten minutes per spigot.

**1. Find the interior shutoff valve and close it.**

Go inside to where that spigot's pipe enters the house — usually the basement, sometimes a crawlspace or a utility room. You're looking for a valve on that pipe, often a gate valve with a round handle or a stop-and-waste valve with a small bleeder cap on the side. Turn it clockwise until it stops.

If it's a stop-and-waste, open the little bleeder cap after you close the valve. That lets the water in the pipe drain out instead of sitting there.

**2. Open the outside spigot and let it drain.**

Go back outside, open the spigot all the way, and leave it open for the winter. Any water in that stretch of pipe runs out. On a stop-and-waste setup you'll hear it gurgle and stop. If nothing comes out and the pipe feels empty, you're done.

Leave it open. This isn't a mistake. If a little water is still trapped in there, an open spigot gives it somewhere to expand instead of splitting the pipe.

**3. Disconnect your hoses. This is the one that matters.**

If you only do one thing on this list, do this one.

A hose left connected to the spigot is the single biggest cause of our January burst-pipe calls. Here's why: most Minneapolis homes have a frost-free sillcock, which is designed to drain itself back into the house every time you shut it off. It can only do that if the hose is off. Leave the hose on and the spigot holds water right at the wall, where it freezes and splits the pipe.

Then it sits there frozen and harmless until we get a warm day in January or February, the ice thaws, and you've got water running down inside your basement wall. That's the call. Water in the basement, wet insulation, sometimes a finished ceiling coming down.

So: disconnect every hose, drain them, coil them up, and store them inside or in the garage. If you have a splitter, a quick-connect fitting, or a timer on that spigot, take all of it off too. Anything threaded onto the spigot counts.

**4. Cap it with a foam cover.**

These are about three dollars at any hardware store. They're a foam cup that fits over the spigot and hooks onto the siding. They are not what keeps your pipe from freezing — the interior shutoff and the drain are. But they keep cold air off the spigot, keep ice from forming in the body of the fixture, and they're cheap insurance. Slap one on each spigot.

## If you don't have an interior shutoff, call us

Plenty of older Minneapolis and St. Paul homes don't have one. Sometimes it's buried behind a finished basement wall, sometimes it was never installed, and sometimes there's one valve feeding the whole run and nobody labeled it.

Don't guess at it. If you can't find the shutoff, or you find one and aren't sure it's actually cutting off that spigot, call us at [phone number] and we'll come find it, tag it, and shut it down for you. We do this all fall. It's a quick visit, and it's a lot cheaper than a burst pipe in January.

## The short version

- Close the valve inside
- Open the spigot outside and leave it open
- Take the hoses and all fittings off
- Add a $3 foam cover
- No shutoff valve? Call us

Do the first three and you've handled 95% of it. The hoses are the part people skip, and they're the part that costs you a ceiling.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The couples who hand me a five-page shot list from Pinterest rarely end up with the photos they actually wanted. 

The ones who throw the list away? They get magic.

After eight years and nearly 300 weddings in the Texas Hill Country, I’ve seen this play out over and over: you can either perform for your wedding gallery, or you can live your wedding day. You can’t do both.

Take the Barrera wedding, for example. 

Thirty minutes before their outdoor ceremony, the sky opened up. Total downpour. The manicured lawn, the timeline, the planned backdrop—all gone. 

Instead of stressing over a checklist of missed photo ops, they looked at each other, laughed, and pivoted. We moved the entire setup under a massive, dripping pecan tree. 

Because they weren’t mentally tracking whether we got "Pose #14 by the arbor," they were completely dialed into the moment. When the hem of her dress soaked through with mud, she didn't care. When the wind blew the rain sideways during their vows, he just pulled her closer. 

The gallery from that afternoon remains one of my absolute favorites. Not because it was technically perfect—none of the original lighting setups worked—but because every single frame captured genuine, unfiltered emotion. 

To the couples currently planning: by all means, list out your family formal groupings so we don’t miss Grandma. 

Beyond that? Trust the vendor team you hired. 

When you free your photographer to watch for moments instead of hunting down clipboard items, and when you give yourself permission to just live the day as it unfolds, that’s when the real art happens. 

Ditch the list. Live the day. The photos will take care of themselves.

b.text:
The best wedding photos often happen when the shot list goes out the window.

In my 8 years shooting full-time in the Texas Hill Country, I’ve noticed a pattern. The couples who try to document every single pose sometimes miss the magic in between. The ones who trust the process? They end up with the most genuine images.

Take the Barrera wedding. We had a solid plan, then the rain rolled in. Instead of panicking, we moved everything under the old pecan tree. That forced change shifted the energy. Instead of stiff portraits, we got laughter, intimacy, and light filtering through the leaves. Those ended up being their favorite shots.

If you’re planning your day, make a list for sure. But also leave room for the unexpected. Trust your vendor, embrace the weather, and let the moments happen naturally.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
Council Members,

I own a small independent coffee shop on Main Street, and I am asking you to reject the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour. Tripling the rate would impose a noticeable new cost on short visits while doing little to address the city’s broader downtown budget.

My customers stay an average of 22 minutes. The current one-hour minimum already more than covers the typical visit to my shop. Raising the hourly charge to $1.50 would not create more turnover for these customers; it would simply make a brief stop for coffee three times as expensive to park.

I have also seen evidence that higher parking prices can reduce downtown activity. In 2019, after a similar meter-rate increase in the next town over, I tracked my own register data for six weeks and observed an 18% drop in foot traffic. That is not a vague concern about what might happen. It is a measurable decline that I documented following a comparable change. For a small independent business, losing nearly one in five customer visits can affect staffing, inventory, operating hours, and the ability to remain open.

The city’s own report further indicates that meter revenue covers only 4% of the downtown budget. Increasing the rate from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour therefore does not appear to solve the underlying budget problem. Instead, it risks discouraging the customers whose spending supports downtown shops, restaurants, employees, and tax revenue.

Downtown businesses depend on convenience and repeat visits. A customer deciding whether to stop for a 22-minute coffee, pick up an order, or visit another Main Street business may choose a location with free or less expensive parking. Each decision may seem small, but together they can produce the kind of 18% decline I have already observed.

I respectfully urge the council not to triple the downtown parking rate. Please consider alternatives that address the budget without placing a disproportionate burden on short-term visitors and small businesses. At minimum, the city should conduct a clear economic-impact analysis and consider short-term parking options before approving an increase.

Thank you for considering this testimony and for entering it into the public record.

b.text:
Honorable Members of the City Council,

My name is the owner of a small independent coffee shop on Main Street, and I appear before you today to submit this written testimony for the public record opposing the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from fifty cents to one dollar fifty per hour. As a business owner who relies every day on the steady flow of customers who stop in for coffee, conversation, and a brief respite, I have watched carefully how parking costs shape the habits of the people who keep our downtown alive. The numbers I bring you are not abstractions or vague warnings; they are concrete measurements drawn from my own experience and from the city’s own documents, and they show that this rate hike would inflict real and measurable harm without meaningfully advancing the city’s fiscal goals.

In 2019 the neighboring town implemented a nearly identical parking-meter increase. I immediately began tracking my own register and customer counts for a full six weeks afterward, isolating the effect as cleanly as a single shop owner can. Foot traffic through my door dropped eighteen percent. That is not a theoretical projection; it is what actually happened on the ground when people who once parked for a quick coffee decided the new cost was no longer worth the stop. Eighteen percent fewer customers means fewer cups sold, fewer tips for my baristas, and a thinner margin for an independent business that already operates on the edge. If the same pattern repeats here, my shop—and every other small retailer who depends on short, spontaneous visits—will absorb a direct and lasting loss.

Our customers already fit comfortably within the existing rate structure. I have timed hundreds of visits: the average customer stays twenty-two minutes. Under the current fifty-cent-per-hour rate with its one-hour minimum, they pay only for the time they actually need. Raising the rate to one dollar fifty an hour triples the cost of that same short stop without adding any extra service or convenience. For a person who wants only a latte and a few minutes of quiet, the new price becomes a deterrent rather than a fair user fee. The result is not that people will park longer; it is that many will simply choose not to come at all.

Finally, the city’s own recent report on downtown finances makes plain that meter revenue covers just four percent of the downtown budget. Even if every meter were occupied every hour at the higher rate, the additional dollars would still amount to a trivial fraction of overall needs. This proposal therefore cannot be justified as a serious solution to any fiscal shortfall. It is a disproportionate burden placed on the very people and businesses that generate sales-tax revenue, employment, and the lively street life that make downtown worth visiting in the first place.

I urge the Council to reject the proposed increase from fifty cents to one dollar fifty an hour. The evidence—an eighteen-percent drop in foot traffic after a comparable 2019 hike, an average customer visit of only twenty-two minutes already covered by the present rate, and the city’s own finding that meters supply merely four percent of the downtown budget—demonstrates that the change would damage local commerce without delivering meaningful public benefit. Please keep downtown accessible to the short-term visitors who sustain our independent shops. Thank you for considering this testimony as part of the public record.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
Hi everyone,

It’s that time of year when wedding season starts to heat up, and I’ve been getting quite a few calls about custom wedding cakes. So, I wanted to sit down over a cup of coffee and talk to you about a decision we’ve made here at the bakery.

We’ve decided to stop taking on custom wedding cake orders.

This wasn’t a light or easy decision, but it’s the right one for our little shop and, ultimately, for all of you who rely on us. Our workdays start around 4 AM, and while we love baking for celebrations of all kinds, we’ve realized that the wedding cakes, as much as we’ve adored them, were quietly pulling our focus away from the very heart of our bakery—the everyday case full of the pies, breads, pastries, and cookies that you all come in for. That case is what keeps the lights on and the ovens warm. It’s what allows us to show up for you every single day.

Beyond that, a custom wedding cake is a deeply personal and time-intensive project for a team of just the three of us. A single order can easily pull us away for about 14 hours each, not including the baking, of dedicated consultation and tasting time. And this year, we had three beautiful cakes, which we poured our hearts into, get canceled at the last minute. For a small bakery that costs us the ingredients, the labor, and the opportunity cost of what we could have been baking for you all in that time. It’s a risk that, frankly, we can’t sustain anymore if we want to keep our doors open and our daily cases full.

So, by stepping away from wedding cakes, we’re making a promise to you: to be even more present, more creative, and more available for the daily treats that bring you in week after week. We want our energy going into that chocolate sourdough you love, the apple hand-pies, the morning buns—that’s our true specialty, and we want to keep getting better at it for you.

We know some of you might be a little bit sad to hear this, and we are too, in a way! But we hope you understand. Your support, for our scones and our loaves and our cinnamon rolls, is what allows us to make choices like this—to choose quality over quantity, and to keep our little shop a happy, sustainable place for us and for you.

Thank you for being the reason we get up so early. For trusting us with your daily bread (and dessert). We’re excited to pour all that extra energy back into the bakery case and see what we can create next.

With so much gratitude,

[Your Name/The Baker]

b.text:
I should probably start this by saying that if you emailed me about a wedding cake in the last few months and I got back to you with a kind but vague “let me check our calendar,” I’m sorry for the slow dance. I knew the answer was probably no, but saying it out loud—or, well, typing it—took me longer than I expected.

We’re not taking custom wedding cake orders anymore. I want to tell you why, and I don’t want it to sound like one of those corporate policy memos, so bear with me while I just talk it through.

It’s four in the morning when I get here most days. The dark still feels different at four—thicker, quieter. I turn on the ovens, start the coffee, and by six we’re pulling the first scones and the regulars start filtering in. That’s the part I love. The rhythm of it. The woman who gets the same sourdough roll every Tuesday, the kid who presses his nose to the pastry case waiting for the chocolate croissants. That everyday case—the muffins, the loaves, the little birthday cakes you grab on the way home from work—is what keeps our lights on. It’s what pays the rent on this little shop.

Somewhere along the way, we started saying yes to wedding cakes. And don’t get me wrong, they were beautiful. There’s something about a three-tier cake that makes you feel like a real artist. But here’s the thing nobody tells you when you’re dreaming of buttercream flowers: before you even turn on the mixer, you’ve already given away about fourteen hours. Tastings, consultations, emails at midnight about whether the shade of blush is too peach, sketching, resketching, driving to venues, driving back. All of it unpaid. And for a shop our size—there’s three of us, and two of those hands are mine by four a.m.—that time has to come from somewhere. It was coming from the case. It was coming from sleep. It was coming from the bread that actually pays the bills.

Then this year, three couples cancelled last minute. Full stop, no deposit, no nothing. I’d already bought the specialty chocolate, the vanilla beans, the fondant, rented the stands. When you’re small, you can’t just absorb that. You also can’t get back the weeks of planning and the early mornings that went into a cake that never got made. I stood in the walk-in looking at ingredients for a wedding that wasn’t happening and I just... I couldn’t do it anymore. Not without letting down the part of this business that keeps us here.

I know some of you will be disappointed. Maybe you were saving up to ask us. I hate that. But I also know you come in because you trust that the sourdough will be ready at seven and the cinnamon rolls won’t sell out before eight. To keep that promise, I have to be here, fully, for the daily stuff. The stuff that smells like home when you walk through the door.

We’re still making cakes, of course. If you need something for a Saturday dinner or a small party, we’ll do our best. But the big, elaborate, months-in-the-making wedding cakes? That’s a chapter we’re closing. Not because we don’t love love—we do. But because we love this shop, and our regulars, and the quiet magic of an ordinary Tuesday morning too.

Thank you for understanding. See you tomorrow—I’ll have the coffee on.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
# A Later Start Is the Right Call for Millbrook's Kids

I have two kids at Millbrook Middle, and like a lot of parents in this town, I've spent more mornings than I can count trying to pry a groggy 12-year-old out of bed before sunrise. So when the school board proposed moving our middle school start time to 8:45, my first reaction wasn't about policy. It was relief.

Here's the thing I didn't fully understand until I read the proposal closely: this isn't about kids being lazy. The American Academy of Pediatrics has been clear for years that adolescents are biologically wired to fall asleep later and wake later than the rest of us. Their bodies literally don't produce the sleep hormones on the same schedule ours do. Asking a middle-schooler to be alert at 7:30 a.m. is like asking me to be sharp at 4:00 in the morning. It's not attitude. It's chemistry.

We don't have to guess whether a later start helps, either. Lincoln Middle, one county over, ran a pilot with a later bell. Their attendance went up. Their first-period grades went up. These are the exact numbers our board is looking at, and they point in one direction. Kids who sleep more show up more, and they learn more once they're there. As a parent, that's the whole ballgame.

I know the objection I'll hear at the coffee shop, because I had it myself: what about the buses? You can't just move one school's clock without the whole system going sideways. But if you actually read the proposal, the board already thought this through. The plan re-tiers the bus routes so the elementary and middle schedules swap slots. The younger kids, who are up at dawn anyway, catch the earlier runs. The buses don't need to multiply. They just need to run in a different order. It's a logistics fix, not a dealbreaker, and pretending otherwise is an excuse to do nothing.

I'm not a writer or an expert. I'm a parent who's tired of watching my kids drag through the school day running on too little sleep, when there's real evidence we could do better.

The board votes next month. If you've got kids in this district, or grandkids, or you just care about how our schools do, tell them you support the 8:45 start. Our kids have earned the chance to show up rested.

b.text:
I have a 12-year-old who cannot find his backpack at 7 a.m. I have a 13-year-old who fell asleep in first period last Tuesday. I love them both, and I am asking the school board to vote yes on the 8:45 start time.

If you've parented a middle-schooler, you know the mornings. The alarm goes off and you're watching a teenager try to fold a shirt and remember their name at the same time. It isn't laziness. Their bodies are genuinely fighting them. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m., because adolescent sleep cycles shift — teenagers physically cannot fall asleep early enough to get the rest they need before an 8 a.m. bell. The AAP puts the recommended nightly sleep at 8.5 to 9.5 hours. Do the math from a 7 a.m. wake-up and you get the picture most of us are already living at our kitchen tables.

We don't have to guess whether later starts help. Lincoln Middle ran a pilot last year, and two numbers stand out: attendance went up, and first-period grades went up. That isn't a theory. That's our neighbors' kids, in a school like ours, showing up more and learning more in the very class that used to feel like a sleep study.

I know the bus question is on a lot of minds. The proposal already accounts for it. The transportation team re-tiered the routes, which means a staggered pickup schedule replaces the old one-size-fits-all grid. It's not a hidden cost or an afterthought — it's built into the plan. Parents who want the details can see the new tier map at the district office. Reasonable people can disagree about specific tweaks, but "the buses won't work" is not a reason to deny a generation of kids the sleep their doctors say they need.

I am not a sleep researcher. I am a parent who has watched two children drag themselves through early-morning classes and come home too wiped out to do anything but stare at a screen. The board has a chance next month to fix that. Vote yes on 8:45.

a.text:
**The Case for Open Campus Lunch**

Lunch period is often the most anticipated part of the school day, yet for many juniors and seniors at [School Name], it has become a source of stress rather than relief. Overcrowding in the cafeteria, limited seating, and a growing desire for student autonomy have sparked discussion about whether open campus lunch should be implemented. While concerns about supervision and safety are frequently raised, the evidence from neighboring districts, combined with student sentiment and logistical necessity, strongly supports allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch. Open campus lunch should be adopted because a overwhelming majority of students favor it, nearby schools have implemented it without negative consequences, and the current cafeteria capacity is fundamentally insufficient for the student population.

A survey of 80 upperclassmen at [School Name] revealed that 71 respondents—approximately 87.5 percent—are in favor of open campus lunch. This data is not merely a majority opinion; it reflects a clear student desire for greater independence and a break from the confined school environment. When such a large portion of the affected student body voices support, it indicates that the policy aligns with student needs and morale. Disregarding this level of favoritism would ignore the very population the school serves, particularly in a curriculum that emphasizes student voice and democratic participation.

Beyond student preference, the practical reality of cafeteria overcrowding makes open campus a logistical imperative. The school’s cafeteria seats only 220 people, yet 340 students are assigned to the lunch wave that occurs during this period. This 120-student gap means that nearly half of the lunch cohort must eat in hallways, gymnasiums, or other makeshift spaces, creating an environment that is noisy, overstimulating, and sometimes unsafe. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus would naturally reduce the number of students in the building during lunch, easing congestion and improving the experience for those who remain. The physical space simply cannot accommodate the current student volume, and open campus offers a realistic solution to that mismatch.

Critics of open campus lunch often point to potential issues such as increased tardiness or students failing to return to class. However, three nearby districts—Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade—have already permitted open campus lunch for upperclassmen, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness rates following implementation. These real-world examples demonstrate that the feared drawbacks do not necessarily materialize when the policy is properly structured. The success of these districts provides a proven model that [School Name] could adapt, rather than starting from scratch with untested assumptions.

Implementing open campus lunch for juniors and seniors is not an administrative gesture; it is a data-supported, student-centered adjustment. With 71 of 80 surveyed students in favor, current cafeteria capacity grossly insufficient for the population, and neighboring districts demonstrating that the transition causes no increase in tardiness, the case is strong. Open campus lunch addresses genuine logistical strain, honors student preference, and aligns with the demonstrated practices of comparable schools. It is a practical change that improves the daily school experience for the majority of upperclassmen.

b.text:
When I grabbed a slice of pizza at lunch last Tuesday, I had to eat it standing in the hallway because every seat in the cafeteria was taken. I am not making this up, and I am not the only one. Across our school, 340 students are packed into a cafeteria built for 220 during the same lunch wave, and the overflow has become a daily fact of life. Our school should allow juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch, and the reasons are simpler than the policy currently suggests: we do not have the space to hold everyone, three nearby districts already do this without problems, and our own classmates overwhelmingly want the chance.

The overcrowding is not an exaggeration. With 120 more students than seats, lunch has become something to survive rather than enjoy. The lines for food stretch out the door, and once you finally get your tray, your options are eating on the floor, leaning against a locker, or hunting for a quiet corner of the building that is not technically a learning space. Teachers lose their rooms during lunch as students claim them as overflow seating, and staff spend part of their break redirecting students out of hallways. Open campus would not solve every problem with our lunch period, but it would solve this one immediately. Letting even a portion of the upperclassmen leave would shrink the crowd to a number the cafeteria can actually handle.

If the worry is that students will skip class or flood back late, three of our neighboring districts have already answered that question. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all permit open campus lunch for upperclassmen, and none of them have reported an uptick in tardiness or a drop in afternoon attendance in the data they publish. These are not experimental programs; they are established policies in schools similar to ours in size and demographics. If the policy caused real problems, we would expect to see them reflected in those numbers, and we do not. We would be copying a working model, not running an experiment.

It is also worth noting that this is what students actually want. In a survey of 80 students at our school, 71 said they would support an open campus policy for juniors and seniors. That is almost nine out of ten, and it crosses the usual social circles — it is not just the athletes, not just the honors kids, not just one friend group. When nearly everyone surveyed agrees on something, the administration should at least take that as a signal that the current system is not working for the people living inside it.

The counterargument worth taking seriously is the safety and accountability concern. If a student leaves campus and does not come back, who is responsible, and what happens to the rest of the school day? This is a fair question, and it is the one that keeps most closed-campus policies in place. The answer is that schools like Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade have worked it out through standard expectations: students sign out, parents are notified, and tardiness consequences still apply. A junior or senior is old enough to handle the responsibility, and the small number of students who might abuse the privilege already have ways to skip class without leaving the building. Holding the many responsible for the few is the reason we still have a cafeteria problem in the first place.

Open campus lunch is not a revolutionary idea. It is a practical response to a problem we already have, a policy that nearby schools have proven works, and a change that almost every student I surveyed supports. The hardest part of this argument is not finding reasons. It is explaining why a school that is already bursting at the seams during lunch would choose to keep everyone locked inside.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
When the Better Team Loses

Let's get this out of the way first: this was a good season. Eight wins. A school record for Dez Kowalski, who threw for 2,340 yards this year and made Friday nights a lot more fun to watch. That's real, and it shouldn't get buried under how the year ended.

But I'm not going to sit here and write a nice, tidy season wrap-up like the scoreboard in the second round didn't happen, because it did, and it's still bugging me a week later.

Here's the thing that gets me: this team lost to an opponent they beat by 20 points back in Week 3. Same team. Same coaching staff. And down by three in the second half — three points, in a game they were controlling on the ground — the offense stopped running the ball.

Not because it wasn't working. It was working. That's what makes it maddening instead of just disappointing. When the run game is moving the chains and you're down a single score, you don't need to get cute. You don't need to prove anything. You need to keep doing the thing that's working until they stop it. Instead, the offense drifted away from it, started leaning on the pass in obvious passing situations, and let a defense that had spent a whole half chasing tailbacks suddenly pin its ears back and tee off on Kowalski.

I get the instinct. When you fall behind, the coach's brain screams "we need points fast," and the pass looks like the quicker route there. But three points isn't a two-score deficit. Three points is one good drive. One good, patient, run-it-until-they-stop-it drive. This team had exactly that drive in its bag all night and put it away in favor of hope.

That's not a talent problem. It's not a Kowalski problem — the kid deserved better play-calling support in that stretch, not less of it. It's a discipline problem, and discipline problems are the kind you can actually fix.

So no, I'm not writing the "great year, on to next season" column, at least not only that one. This team was good enough to still be playing right now. They didn't lose to a better team. They lost to a version of a team they'd already beaten, and they helped them do it by walking away from what was working.

Next year's team will have the tools to be even better. Here's hoping somebody in that coaches' booth remembers this game the next time it's a one-score contest and the run is humming. Trust it. Ride it. Make the other team prove they can stop it before you decide to stop doing it yourself.

b.text:
**A Great Season, A Coaching Mistake, and an Early Winter**

An 8-2 record looks great framed on the wall at the diner. It’ll read nicely in the spring sports banquet program, too. But let’s not sugarcoat Friday night: the boys should still be playing football this week. 

Losing in the second round of the state playoffs is tough enough. Losing to a team you ran off their own field by 20 points back in September makes it a bitter pill that's going to stick in this town's throat all winter. 

Before we get to the autopsy, credit where it’s due: Dez Kowalski put together the finest season under center this town has ever seen. Setting the school single-season record with 2,340 passing yards is a massive achievement, and Kowalski played with heart and grit from August two-a-days all the way through Friday night. He earned every bit of that record. 

But relying exclusively on Dez’s right arm in the second half is precisely why the season is over.

Coming out of the locker room down just three points, the game plan inexplicably went into panic mode. The ground game was chewing up five yards a pop in the first half and keeping the defense honest, yet the coaching staff put it in mothballs the minute the third quarter kicked off. You don't abandon the run when you're within one field goal. When you become one-dimensional against a playoff defense out for revenge, you’re playing right into their hands. They pinned their ears back, brought pressure, and dared us to beat them with an empty backfield. We couldn't.

It’s easy to look at an 8-2 finish and call it a total success, and these kids have plenty to be proud of. But championships aren't won by getting cute with the playbook when a fistfight is required. Friday night was a winnable game that got away because we stopped doing what got us there.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
The state should not cut apprenticeship funding by 15%.

I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with the local IBEW, and I see what this funding does every day. It gives people a real path into a good job without crushing them with student debt. It also helps local contractors and the whole economy by creating skilled workers who are ready to work.

My own cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one finished and are now working journeyman jobs. That is a strong return on the state’s investment. These are not people who got trained and then sat on the sidelines. They are working, paying taxes, and building things this state needs.

The numbers speak for themselves. Apprentices start around $19 an hour. By the time they finish, they can top out around $46 an hour as journeymen. That means they move off assistance programs fast and become taxpaying workers instead of staying dependent on public aid.

The cost is also much lower than people might think. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to something like $48,000 in average public subsidy per four-year college graduate who finishes. If the state wants to spend money wisely, apprenticeship is one of the best deals out there.

A cut to apprenticeship funding would hurt working people, hurt contractors, and hurt the state’s future workforce. It would also make it harder for young people and adults trying to build a better life with their hands and their heads.

We should be growing apprenticeship programs, not cutting them. Keep the funding in place and keep investing in a system that works.

b.text:
## Don’t Cut Apprenticeship Funding—Invest in What Works

The state’s proposed 15% cut to apprenticeship funding is a bad decision for working people, contractors, unions, and the state economy.

I am a third-year electrical apprentice with the IBEW. I see every day what apprenticeship does for people who are willing to work and learn a skilled trade. It gives people a real path to a career without taking on years of debt. It also gives the state trained workers who build, repair, and maintain the electrical systems everyone depends on.

My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one finished and are now working as journeymen. That is not just a completion number on a report. That is 21 people who moved into solid careers, are paying taxes, supporting families, buying homes, and working on projects in their communities.

In our trade, apprentices start at around $19 an hour and work their way up as they gain skills and experience. A journeyman electrician can make around $46 an hour. That kind of wage growth changes a person’s life. It means people can get off assistance programs quickly, pay their bills, and build some stability. It means they are not stuck in low-wage jobs with no clear way forward.

Apprenticeship is also a smart use of public money. The total public cost for an apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to roughly $48,000 in average public subsidy for a student who completes a four-year degree. Both college and the trades have value, but the state should look honestly at the results it gets for its investment.

For about $14,000, the state helps train a worker who enters a high-demand field, earns a good wage, and helps meet the need for skilled labor. Electricians are needed everywhere: homes, schools, hospitals, factories, data centers, renewable energy projects, public transportation, and new infrastructure. Cutting apprenticeship funding when the state needs more skilled workers makes no sense.

A 15% cut may look like a number on a budget sheet, but it has real effects. It can mean fewer training opportunities, fewer instructors, less equipment, and fewer people able to enter the trades. It can make it harder for apprentices to complete their programs. It can also make the worker shortage worse at a time when contractors are already looking for qualified people.

Apprenticeship is not a handout. Apprentices work. We show up early, learn safety, study code, and train on the job while earning a paycheck. We are building our skills while helping build the state. The public support that goes into apprenticeship is an investment that comes back through taxes, wages, and completed projects.

Legislators should not treat apprenticeship funding as an easy place to cut. If the state wants more people in good jobs, more skilled workers, and less dependence on public assistance, it should protect apprenticeship programs and expand them.

My class is proof that the model works. Twenty-one out of 24 people finished and moved into journeyman jobs. That is a strong return for workers, employers, taxpayers, and the state.

Instead of cutting apprenticeship funding by 15%, lawmakers should invest in the programs that are already producing results.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/ I made a pricing mistake at Tallyup.

I raised prices 40% for everyone overnight.

Within a week, we lost 30 of 140 customers.

2/ The mistake wasn’t raising prices.

We needed to charge more to keep building a sustainable product.

The mistake was treating existing customers the same as new customers — with no warning, no context, and no choice.

3/ For a gym owner, Tallyup is another operating expense.

A sudden increase doesn’t feel like “we’re improving the product.”

It feels like: “this tool I rely on just got more expensive without asking.”

That’s on me.

4/ What I changed:

- Existing customers are grandfathered or moved gradually
- Price changes get communicated before they happen
- New pricing applies to new customers first
- I explain what’s changing and why

5/ The lesson:

Pricing is not just a number on a checkout page.

It’s a trust decision.

Especially when you’re a small SaaS asking customers to bet on you long-term.

6/ I still believe Tallyup should be priced sustainably.

But I won’t make another “overnight” decision that asks customers to absorb the cost of my learning curve.

b.text:
I raised Tallyup’s prices 40% on everyone overnight.

Within a week, 30 of our 140 customers had left.

Here’s the pricing mistake—and what I changed afterward 🧵

1/ I treated pricing like a spreadsheet problem.

The product had improved. The old price felt too low. A 40% increase seemed reasonable to me.

But customers didn’t experience it as a spreadsheet update.

They experienced it as a surprise bill.

2/ The biggest mistake wasn’t raising prices.

It was changing the deal without giving customers:

• Advance notice  
• Time to evaluate  
• A clear explanation  
• Any recognition for supporting Tallyup early

I optimized for simplicity on my side and created uncertainty on theirs.

3/ I also assumed existing customers saw the product the way I did.

I saw everything we’d built.

They saw the specific job they hired Tallyup to do: help track member retention.

More features don’t automatically make a sudden price increase feel fair.

4/ Losing 30 customers in a week made the lesson impossible to ignore:

Pricing isn’t just about what the product is worth.

It’s also about trust, timing, and how you communicate change.

5/ What I changed:

• No more overnight increases  
• Existing customers get advance notice  
• Pricing changes come with a clear reason  
• Early customers are treated differently from new signups  
• Customers have time to decide, ask questions, or adjust

6/ I’m not saying never raise prices.

Small SaaS companies need sustainable pricing.

But “we need to charge more” doesn’t mean “everyone pays 40% more starting now.”

The rollout is part of the pricing decision.

7/ My takeaway:

Raise prices when the business needs it.

Just don’t confuse having the right destination with taking the right route.

I learned that one by losing 30 of 140 customers in a week.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
On Saturdays the restaurant opens at eleven, but we get there at nine. My dad unlocks the back door and the first thing you smell is the fish sauce from the night before, and then the rice cooker starts and it smells like our house.

The register died on a Saturday in October. Not a slow reboot, not a frozen screen—dead, the little lights gone. My mom kept pressing the power button like it was a person she could wake up. So I got a pad of paper and started writing tickets by hand. Table four, two vermicelli bowls, one with extra pork, no peanuts. Table six wanted the pho with tendon, and I had to remember it wasn't on the paper receipt because there was no receipt, just my handwriting getting worse as it got busier. I did the math for everyone's change in my head. I got one order wrong all day, a spring roll count, and my dad only found out because I told him. The system came back around three. By then I didn't need it.

We hire people sometimes and they don't last. There's a lot to remember and the kitchen gets hot. In the spring we hired a guy named Danh who was maybe nineteen and he could cook but he couldn't fold a spring roll right. My grandma folds them a specific way, tight, so they don't come apart in the oil. She showed me when I was little and now I showed him. You lay the wrapper like a diamond, filling near the bottom, fold up once, fold the sides in, then roll and seal the edge with water. Danh's first ten fell apart. His eleventh held. I didn't tell my grandma I taught him because she likes to think only she can do it, and honestly she does it better, but his are fine now.

I do my homework in the walk-in cooler. This sounds worse than it is. The dining room is loud and there's nowhere to sit, but the cooler has a shelf at the right height and it's quiet in there with the boxes of vegetables and the sound of the fan. I did most of my calculus in the cooler this year. Related rates, integrals, all of it, sitting on a milk crate with my jacket on. My mom would open the door to grab lemongrass and see me and say don't stay too long, you'll get sick. I never got sick. I got a lot of problem sets done.

That's most of my Saturdays. I'll probably work them until I leave for school, and then my parents will figure something out, or they won't and it'll be harder for them, which I think about. I'm not going to pretend the restaurant taught me some big thing. It's just where I've been every weekend since tenth grade. I know how to run a register with no register. I know how my grandma folds a spring roll. I can do calculus at forty degrees. These are the things I know.

b.text:
I started working weekends at my parents’ restaurant when I was a sophomore. At first it was only when someone called out sick, but by junior year it was every Saturday and Sunday: open at ten, close at midnight, the same three rooms, the same smell of fish sauce and fried garlic.

The register system died on a Saturday in November. I had been there twenty minutes when the screen froze, flickered, and went black. My dad shrugged and said, “Paper.” So I pulled out the old receipt pad and started writing tickets by hand. I wrote “pho tai, extra herbs” and “bánh mì, pickled” over and over until my handwriting started to blur. The line backed up. A regular asked if the computer was broken. I said yes. He said it was always broken on Saturdays. I told him it was worse.

That same month I taught a new hire how to fold my grandma’s spring rolls. He was sixteen, maybe, and he was tearing the rice paper because he rolled too tight and too fast. My grandma had shown him once, but he was still doing it wrong—filling leaking out the ends. I stood next to him and showed him how she does it: one corner down, roll once, tuck both sides in, then roll slow so the paper doesn’t burst but the filling stays inside. After three tries he got it. I didn’t tell him I’d watched her do it for years, or that I still do it wrong sometimes when I’m rushing.

On breaks I sit in the walk-in cooler to do calc homework. It’s the only quiet place in the restaurant. The light flickers, it’s forty degrees, and I have my notebook open on top of the milk crates. I don’t finish everything. Sometimes I get through three problems before someone opens the door and I put the notebook away.

I work because my parents need the help and because I need the money for books and gas. The restaurant is loud and hot, and when I go home I smell like fryer oil and lime. I don’t think that makes me special. I just know how to write a ticket when the computer breaks, how to fold a roll so it doesn’t tear, and how to solve a derivative in forty degrees. That’s just what I do.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
If you have a Doodle, a Poodle, a Golden, or any dog with a thick, double or curly coat, you’ve probably felt that dreaded sinking feeling when your fingers hit a solid lump of tangled hair. Coat maintenance at home can feel like an uphill battle, especially in the weeks between your appointments with us, but a few small technique tweaks will completely change your routine.

First, let’s talk about the single biggest mistake I see pet parents make. A lot of folks notice their dog looking a little scruffy or tangled, so they pop them right into the bathtub thinking the warm water and shampoo will loosen everything up. Please, do not do this. Water does not untangle hair—it acts like a shrink-wrap machine on loose knots, binding them together into a dense, solid felt pad that even professional equipment can't gently save. You must *always* thoroughly brush and comb your dog out before the bath, never after. 

When you sit down to brush, throw out the idea of just running the brush over the top of their coat in big, circular sweeps. Surface brushing makes the outside look fluffy while the hair right against the skin is turning into dreadlocks. Grab a slicker brush and use short, straight "line" strokes. Part the hair with one hand so you can see the skin, and use gentle, short downward strokes with the other, working your way through the coat in small sections from the skin outward. 

I always recommend starting with the trouble zones where friction is highest. Mats almost always start behind the ears (from scratching and petting) and under the front legs in the armpit area (from walking and harnesses). Tackle those spots first while your dog is still patient, parting the fur and working through layer by layer. 

If you do find a knot that's already starting to clump together, step away from the brush for a second. Raking a brush directly over a tight mat just pulls the skin and hurts the dog, which makes them hate grooming time. Instead, take a small dab of dog-safe leave-in conditioner or detangler and work it deep into the knot using only your fingers. Gently wiggle and massage the hair apart with your fingertips to break up the core of the tangle. Once it’s softened and loosened with your hands, *then* you can gently tease it out with the edge of a slicker brush or the wide teeth of a metal comb.

Spending five to ten minutes doing this a couple of times a week will keep your pup comfortable, happy, and tangle-free until I see them next on the grooming table. And as always, if you're struggling with a specific spot, leave it alone so you don't hurt the skin, and let me know at drop-off—I'm always happy to show you the line-brushing motion in person!

b.text:
How to Keep Your Dog's Coat From Matting Between Grooming Visits

If your dog has a double coat or one of those wonderful curly coats, you already know they need a little more attention at home than a short-haired breed does. And the number one thing I want you to take away from this post is: brush before the bath, never after. I cannot stress this enough. So many owners come in and tell me they bathed their dog first because they figured the water and shampoo would help loosen up any tangles. It does the exact opposite. Wet fur, especially wet matted fur, basically felts itself together, like actual felting, the kind you'd do on purpose with wool and a needle. Once that happens, you're not dealing with a tangle anymore, you're dealing with a mat that's bonded to the skin, and that's a much bigger problem.

So brush first, every time, before any water touches the coat.

When you're brushing, grab a slicker brush and use short strokes, almost like little flicking motions in a line, not circles. Circular brushing just pushes the loose undercoat around and tangles it into itself instead of pulling it out. Short line strokes actually lift the loose hair out and away from the coat.

Work in sections rather than just running the brush over the whole dog in one go. I always tell people to pay special attention behind the ears and under the front legs, because that's where mats show up first, almost every single time. There's friction there, less airflow, and the fur is often finer in those spots, so it tangles faster than anywhere else on the body. If you're only going to spot check two areas between full brush-outs, make it those two.

And if you do find a mat that's already started, please don't just grab a comb or brush and start yanking at it. Work some conditioner into it with your fingers first, gently, until it softens up a bit. Let the product do some of the work before any tool touches it. Pulling a dry or half-formed mat with a brush usually just tightens it and makes it more painful for your dog, and honestly more frustrating for you too.

Keep up with this in between visits and you'll notice a real difference, less time on the table for your dog, less stress for both of you, and a coat that stays in much better shape overall.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Outdoor Spigots in Minneapolis

Disconnect every garden hose, shut off the indoor water supply to each outdoor faucet, and drain the water out. Then add a foam faucet cover. For most Minneapolis homes, that’s a quick job—and much cheaper than repairing a frozen pipe.

## 1. Disconnect the hoses first

**Leaving a hose connected is the biggest mistake we see. It’s behind most of our January burst-pipe calls.**

Remove hoses, splitters, timers, and spray attachments from every outdoor spigot. Drain your hoses and put them away for the season.

Even a “frost-free” faucet can freeze and split if a connected hose traps water inside it. The damage may stay hidden until you turn the faucet on again and water starts leaking inside the wall.

## 2. Close the interior shutoff valve

Look inside your basement or crawl space, near where the pipe runs through the wall to the outdoor faucet. There’s often a dedicated shutoff valve on that line.

Turn a round handle clockwise until it’s closed, or turn a lever handle a quarter-turn so it sits perpendicular to the pipe. Don’t force a stuck or badly corroded valve.

**Can’t find an interior shutoff? Call us.** Some frost-free faucets are designed to drain without one, but they need to be installed correctly and have nothing attached outside. We can check your setup and tell you whether you need a shutoff added.

## 3. Open the outdoor spigot and let it drain

With the interior valve closed, open the outdoor faucet. Let the water run out, then leave the faucet open for the winter.

If water keeps flowing instead of stopping, the interior valve may not be closing properly—or you may have shut off the wrong line. Don’t assume the faucet is winterized.

Some interior shutoffs also have a small drain or bleeder cap. If yours does, follow its draining instructions and use a bucket to catch the water. If you’re unsure, give us a call.

## 4. Add a foam faucet cover

A basic foam cover costs about $3 at many hardware stores. Fit it snugly against the house to help keep cold air away from the faucet.

**A cover is extra protection, not a substitute for disconnecting the hose and draining the line.** It won’t reliably protect a water-filled pipe through a Minneapolis cold snap.

Do this before the first hard freeze, and check every outdoor faucet—including the one behind the garage you rarely use.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots (Advice from a Minneapolis Plumber)

Every January, a big share of our burst-pipe calls trace back to the same thing: an outdoor spigot that didn't get winterized. The whole job takes about ten minutes and costs three bucks. Here's exactly how to do it.

Do this by mid-October. Around here the first hard freeze can hit early, and it only takes one cold night to split a pipe.

## 1. Disconnect your hoses

Start here, because everything else depends on it. Unscrew every hose, splitter, and timer from every outdoor faucet. Drain the hoses, coil them, and put them in the garage or shed — they'll last longer anyway.

This matters even if you have a frost-free spigot. A frost-free only works if water can drain out of it. A connected hose traps water inside, and then it's no better than the old-style faucet.

## 2. Shut the interior valve

Go down to the basement and find where the pipe runs from the spigot through the wall. There should be a shutoff valve on that line, usually within a few feet of where it exits the house. Turn it clockwise until it stops.

One valve per spigot — if you have faucets on multiple sides of the house, each one has its own shutoff.

## 3. Drain the spigot

Go back outside and open the spigot. Let it run until the water stops — that's the water trapped between the shutoff and the faucet, and it's the water that would otherwise freeze.

If your interior valve has a little bleeder cap on the side, open that too (hold a cup under it). It lets air into the line so it drains completely.

Leave the outdoor spigot in the open position all winter. If any water is left in there, it has somewhere to go when it expands.

## 4. Put on a foam cover

The hard foam faucet covers are about $3 at any hardware store. It slips over the spigot and cinches tight against the siding. It's cheap insurance against wind chill hitting the pipe where it comes through the wall.

## The mistake that causes most of our January burst-pipe calls

Leaving the hose connected. That's it — that's the big one.

Here's what happens. The hose traps water in the spigot, and because the hose is still on, most people never shut the interior valve either. So you've got a pressurized line, full of water, sitting against an exterior wall. January rolls around, we get a real cold snap — the minus-twenty kind Minneapolis does every year — and that water freezes, expands, and splits the pipe. Often it splits *inside* the wall, where you can't see it.

Then you've got water pouring into your wall cavity or basement, and a ten-minute job just became an emergency call, a plumbing repair, and drywall work.

Take the hoses off. It's the single most important step on this list.

## Don't have an interior shutoff?

A lot of older Minneapolis homes don't — the spigot line runs straight out through the wall with no way to isolate it. If that's your setup, don't try to get through winter with just a foam cover and good intentions.

Give us a call at [phone number]. We can install an interior shutoff valve, or swap the spigot for a frost-free sillcock that drains itself every time you turn it off. Either one is a quick, inexpensive job — and it's a whole lot cheaper than the burst-pipe version of the same visit.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots (And Avoid a January Burst Pipe)

Freezing temps in Minneapolis don't give you much room for error when it comes to outdoor plumbing. If water sits inside your outdoor faucet or the supply line behind it, it will freeze, expand, and split the pipe inside your wall. You won’t even know it happened until you turn the water back on in the spring—or worse, during a mid-winter thaw when it floods your basement.

Here is the exact four-step process to winterize your outdoor spigots before the hard freeze hits.

---

### Step 1: Disconnect All Garden Hoses Immediately
Do this today. If you take only one thing away from this post, make it this: **never leave a hose connected to an outdoor spigot over the winter.** 

Even if you have a modern "frost-free" sillcock, leaving a hose attached prevents the water inside the faucet body from draining out. The trapped water freezes right at the exterior wall, splits the brass tube, and causes a massive leak inside your home. Easily 80% of the burst-pipe calls our family takes in January and February happen because someone forgot to disconnect a hose.

Disconnect the hose, drain it, roll it up, and store it away. Remove any splitters, timers, or quick-connect adapters, too.

---

### Step 2: Locate and Shut Off the Indoor Valve
Head down to your basement, utility room, or crawlspace. Look for the water line heading directly toward the outside wall where your outdoor spigot is located. 

On that line, you should find a shutoff valve (either a round wheel-handle gate valve or a straight lever-handle ball valve). 

* Turn a **round wheel-handle** clockwise until it stops completely.
* Turn a **lever-handle** a quarter-turn until it is perpendicular (across) the pipe.

---

### Step 3: Drain the Residual Water Out of the Line
Shutting the indoor valve stops new water from entering, but there is still water trapped between the valve and the outside wall. You need to drain it.

1. Go outside and open the outdoor spigot all the way. Let whatever water is inside drain out. Leave the spigot in the **open** position all winter.
2. Go back inside to your shutoff valve with a small bucket or towel. Most indoor shutoff valves have a tiny brass "bleeder cap" on the side of the valve body. Unscrew that cap slowly. 
3. Let the trapped water drain into your bucket. 
4. Once the water stops dripping, screw the bleeder cap back on tightly.

---

### Step 4: Add a $3 Foam Faucet Cover
Go to your local hardware store and grab an insulated styrofoam faucet cover. They cost about $3 to $5 and hook right onto the spigot handle, pulling tight against your siding with a rubber gasket. 

While draining the line is the main defense, these covers add an extra barrier against biting Minneapolis wind chills, protecting the fixture itself from extreme cold drafts.

---

### Can’t Find an Indoor Shutoff Valve?
A lot of older homes in Minneapolis—especially in neighborhoods like South Minneapolis, Northeast, or Saint Paul—either don't have indoor shutoffs for the outside lines, or the old gate valves are seized shut and won't turn.

If you don't have a dedicated indoor shutoff, or if your valve is leaking when you try to turn it, don't force it. Give our team a call. We can install a reliable, modern ball valve and a proper frost-free sillcock so you never have to worry about a frozen pipe wrecking your basement.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
**Roadstar DC4 — 14 months, ~140k miles**

Bought this thing figuring it'd die by month six. It didn't, so here's the honest rundown.

**What earned it a permanent spot on my windshield:**

Guy changed lanes into me outside Amarillo. Front cam got the whole thing clean — his mirror, his signal that never came on, all of it. Sent the clip to my insurance and had the claim approved in 9 days. Nine. Last time I went through a claim without footage it took six weeks of phone calls and them squinting at my word against his. That alone paid for the camera about forty times over.

**Where it falls short:**

Rear cam night footage goes to mush past about 30 feet. Close-in stuff at the dock or somebody riding my bumper, fine. But if you're hoping to read a plate on a car that clipped you and kept going in the dark, you'll be disappointed. Daytime it's sharp enough.

The suction mount is garbage in summer. Fell off twice — once in Phoenix in July, once in Vegas. Both times it landed on the dash still recording, so no damage, but I'm not gambling on it. Switched to the adhesive mount and it hasn't budged since. If you buy this, just start with the adhesive mount and skip the aggravation.

The app is the other gripe. It needs WiFi to pull footage off the camera, and truck stop WiFi is a joke on a good day. I quit fighting it. Now I just pop the SD card and read it on my laptop, which is faster anyway. If the app being useless is a deal-breaker for you, look elsewhere — but I don't know many guys who are pulling clips off their dash cam in the sleeper for fun.

**Bottom line:** Front cam is solid and that's the one that matters for claims. Rear cam is a nighttime weak spot. Buy the adhesive mount, ignore the app, keep a spare SD card in the console. Held up through 140k miles of heat, cold, and washboard road without a hiccup, and it got me paid. Good enough.

b.text:
**Quick Review: Roadstar DC4 (140k Miles / 14 Months)**

Figured I’d drop a quick, no-BS review on the Roadstar DC4 after running it for 14 months and about 140,000 miles across the lower 48. 

**The Good:**
This thing has already paid for itself ten times over. Had a four-wheeler try to merge into my steer tire on I-80. The front camera caught the entire lane change clear as day. Handed the video to the adjuster, and the claim was approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6-week finger-pointing match. Front video quality in daylight and standard night driving is crisp.

**The Annoying:**
* **The Mount:** Toss the suction cup in the trash right out of the box. It melted off my windshield twice during summer runs through the southwest. Swapped over to the semi-permanent adhesive mount and it hasn't budged an inch since.
* **The App:** Total waste of time on the road. It forces you onto a Wi-Fi connection to download clips, which is completely useless sitting in a truck stop parking lot. Don't bother fighting it—just keep a $10 USB card reader in your glove box and pull the micro SD card directly.

**The Rear Cam:**
It’s decent for backing and close-quarters daytime, but night footage gets real grainy past 30 feet. It’ll prove whether someone rear-ended you, but don't expect to read a license plate at a distance in the pitch black.

**Bottom Line:**
It’s got a few quirks, but it works when it counts. If you buy one, stick it on with the adhesive pad, manage your footage via the SD card, and let it do its job. Worth the money just for the insurance protection.

a.text:
**Corlane SM6 After 8 Months: Beaten Up Daily By a Market Baker**

I've had the Corlane SM6 on my counter for 8 months now, and it's not had an easy life. I bake sourdough to sell at the farmers market on weekends, so this thing runs almost daily — levains, test loaves, and on Fridays, back-to-back sandwich loaves for market day.

Let's get to what you actually want to know.

The motor is a beast. I do a double batch of stiff, low-hydration bagel dough in it — the kind that used to make my old mixer walk across the counter and smell hot — and the SM6 doesn't stall, doesn't strain, doesn't even get warm. Just plows through 10 minutes of kneading. For heavy, weekly bread dough, this is why you buy it.

It's not perfect. Two real annoyances:

1. The bowl-lift lever squeaks like crazy. After about three weeks it starts up again, so I'm on a schedule of hitting it with WD-40 once a month. Takes 10 seconds, but on a $429 machine you shouldn't have to.

2. The stock dough hook is too short for the deep bowl. On a single loaf of sourdough it just spins above the dough and barely catches it. I gave up and bought a third-party extended hook for $28, and now it kneads perfectly. Factor that into the cost.

Speaking of cost: I paid $429. The equivalent KitchenAid bowl-lift is $80 less right now at $349. You're paying a premium for the Corlane, no question.

Verdict: Buy it if you knead heavy dough every week. For bagels, sourdough, stiff enriched doughs, it's worth the extra $80 over the KitchenAid and the annoying hook situation. It's paid for itself at market for me.

Skip it if you're mostly doing cookies and cake batter. You're overpaying for motor you'll never use, and you'll just be annoyed by the squeaky lever.

b.text:
# 8 Months with the Corlane SM6: An Honest Look from a Farmers Market Baker

I’ve had the Corlane SM6 on my counter for eight months now, and it hasn’t had an easy life. Prepping for my weekend sourdough drops means this machine gets put to work nearly every single day, often running back-to-back batches of high-hydration loaves and enriched doughs. 

If you’ve been eyeing this mixer and wondering if it justifies the price tag over the standard alternatives, here is the unvarnished reality.

---

### The Powerhouse: Motor Performance
The standout feature of the SM6 is, without question, the motor. 

Most consumer-grade mixers start groaning the second you load them with anything under 60% hydration. To test its limits, I threw a double batch of stiff, 54%-hydration bagel dough at it—a volume that would cause most tilt-head mixers to dance across the counter and overheat. The SM6 didn't stall, shudder, or click. The torque is consistent, the planetary action stays true under resistance, and the machine stays firmly planted on the counter. For raw kneading capability, it completely outclasses the competition in this size category.

---

### The Flaws: Cheap Trim and an Annoying Hook
That raw power comes with two frustrating oversights you need to know before buying:

1. **The Squeaky Lift Lever:** The bowl-lift mechanism has solid lockup, but the internal hinge started shrieking within three weeks. It requires a quick shot of WD-40 roughly once a month to keep it operating smoothly. It’s purely cosmetic/mechanical friction, but on a mixer at this price point, you shouldn't need a lubrication maintenance schedule just to raise the bowl.
2. **The Stock Dough Hook is Too Short:** The bowl is deep, but the factory spiral hook leaves too much clearance at the bottom. With smaller batches (under 800g of flour), the hook simply slaps the top of the dough instead of turning and kneading it against the base. I ended up spending an extra $28 on a third-party, extended spiral hook to make the machine fully functional for single-loaf bakes. 

---

### The Price Tag
The Corlane SM6 retails for **$429**. 

That puts it roughly **$80 higher** than the equivalent bowl-lift KitchenAid model. You are paying a premium almost entirely for the internal drivetrain and motor longevity, because the included attachments and lever finish certainly don't reflect that extra cash.

---

### The Verdict

**Buy it if:** You knead heavy, low-to-medium hydration doughs (sourdough, bagels, sandwich loaves, brioche) on a weekly basis. The motor reliability and torque under load are worth the extra $80 and the aftermarket hook purchase. It is a workhorse built for serious dough.

**Skip it if:** Your baking focuses primarily on cookies, layer cakes, meringues, and the occasional soft no-knead bread. You do not need the excess torque, and you will just be overpaying for a machine with an annoying lift lever and attachments poorly configured for smaller, lighter batters. Stick with a standard mixer instead.

a.text:
1/ On the Maple Ave kitchen job, we found [joist issue] when we opened up [area]. The problem wasn’t just how it looked: [what it meant for the floor and the remodel].

2/ The fix: [repair scope]. Added cost: $[amount], including [what that covered]. Schedule impact: [time added]. Not the part of a kitchen remodel anybody gets excited to spend money on, but it needed to be addressed.
