b.text:
Pulled up the kitchen subfloor on the Maple Ave job yesterday and found two joists notched almost halfway through their depth. Someone ran a drain line through them 20+ years ago and just hogged out whatever they needed. Floor had a noticeable bounce right over it.

Notch that deep in the middle third of a joist is basically cutting its strength in half. You're allowed a notch, but there are rules about depth and location for a reason. Whoever did this either didn't know or didn't care.

Fix was sistering both joists full length and rerouting the drain properly. Added about $1,400 and a day and a half to the schedule the client wasn't planning on.

The lesson: that bounce in your floor is rarely "just how old houses feel." It's usually something structural someone hid behind finishes. Open it up before you tile over it, not after.

setup: A retired rural mail carrier is writing a letter to the Kettle Falls Courier urging residents to oppose the post office counter closure at the July 28 forum.

a.text:
To the editor:

I drove Route 4 here in Kettle Falls for 22 years before retiring last year. Same 38 miles, day after day. I’m not much of a writer, but I know this town, and closing our post office counter is a bad idea.

USPS says the branch loses $40,000 a year. But they already cut the counter hours to 8 a.m. to noon. Of course traffic dropped. People who work mornings can’t get there. Now USPS is pointing to that drop as a reason to close the counter altogether. They ought to account for what their own cuts did before telling us the town doesn’t use its post office.

I think of Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She’s in her 80s and gets her heart medicine by mail. Closing the counter isn’t the same as stopping delivery, but that counter is still a service she needs. She can’t just drive twenty minutes to Fairview when she needs a money order. Neither can plenty of other folks around here.

A post office serves people, not just a balance sheet. Before the district manager takes our counter away, I’d like to hear what restoring useful hours would do for that $40,000 figure.

Please come to the public forum July 28 at the Grange Hall. Tell the district manager what you use the counter for and what losing it would mean. We need the people making this decision to hear from the people who have to live with it.

b.text:
To the Editor,

I’m writing as a retired rural mail carrier who drove Route 4 right here in and around Kettle Falls for 22 years before handing in my keys last year. I know every turn, driveway, and family in this valley because I’ve seen them all over the years. That’s why I’m speaking up about the talk of closing counter service at our post office.

USPS officials say the branch loses forty thousand dollars a year, which is their reason for taking away walk-in service. But anybody who’s actually dealt with these offices knows what really happened: they already cut our hours down to eight o’clock until noon. Of course the traffic dropped after that. You set the hours, watched the numbers fall, and then blamed those same numbers for shutting us down. That’s putting the cart before the horse.

This isn’t just accounting. It’s real people. Take Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She’s in her eighties, receives her heart medication by mail, and can’t safely drive twenty minutes into Fairview just to get a money order or handle a simple transaction once the counter closes. When you remove walk-in service, you don’t save money—you create a burden for seniors and folks without reliable transportation. They end up relying on neighbors or driving anyway, which defeats the whole point.

If you want to protect everyday services in this town, mark your calendar for July 28 at the Grange Hall. The USPS district manager will be attending that public forum, and he needs to look you in the eye and hear what’s happening on the ground. Don’t let them write off this county based on figures they helped create. Show up, speak plainly, and tell them to keep the counter open.

Sincerely,

A former Route 4 carrier

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots Before the Minneapolis Freeze

If you leave water sitting in your exterior sillcocks when the ground freezes solid in Hennepin County, that copper pipe will split open. You won’t notice it when it happens—you’ll notice it during the first spring thaw when water starts pouring into your finished basement or crawl space.

Here is the exact step-by-step process we tell our customers to follow every October. It takes ten minutes.

---

### Step 1: Disconnect all hoses, splitters, and timers immediately

If you only do one thing on this list, do this. 

Leaving a garden hose connected to an outside spigot is responsible for roughly 80% of the burst-pipe calls we run in January and February. Even if you have a modern "frost-free" spigot, leaving a hose attached traps water inside the barrel of the valve. The water cannot drain out. It freezes, expands, and splits the brass tube wide open inside your wall. 

Unscrew the hose, drain it, roll it up, and put it in the garage. Take off brass splitters and plastic timers, too.

### Step 2: Locate and close the interior shutoff valve

Head into your basement, utility room, or crawl space. Look at the wall roughly where the outdoor faucet sits outside, and follow that copper line inward. 

You’re looking for a shutoff valve. It will usually be either:
* **A round wheel handle (gate valve):** Turn it clockwise until it stops tight.
* **A lever handle (ball valve):** Turn it a quarter-turn so the handle sits perpendicular across the pipe.

### Step 3: Drain the trapped water (Don't skip the bleeder cap)

Turning off the interior valve only stops incoming water; you still have water sitting between the shutoff and the outside spigot. You need to get that water out.

1. **Go outside:** Turn the spigot handle all the way open. Let whatever water is inside run out. Leave this tap open all winter.
2. **Go back inside:** Grab a small bucket or a rag. On the side of your interior shutoff valve, you’ll usually see a tiny brass cap—that’s the bleeder port. Unscrew that cap with a pair of pliers. A cup or two of water will drain out into your bucket. 
3. Once it stops dripping, screw the tiny bleeder cap back on hand-tight.

If you don't open that bleeder cap, an airlock keeps the water trapped in the line, defeating the whole purpose of shutting off the valve.

### Step 4: Install a $3 foam faucet cover

Run down to your local hardware store and buy an insulated foam faucet cover—they usually cost less than five bucks. Hook the rubber loop over the spigot handle and slide the foam dome tight against the exterior siding. 

While this won't save an undrained pipe from twenty below zero, it blocks cold Minneapolis drafts from creeping directly through your foundation rim joist.

---

### What if you don't have an interior shutoff valve?

A lot of older homes in Minneapolis—especially in South Minneapolis, Northeast, and older parts of St. Paul—never had dedicated interior shutoff valves installed for the hose bibbs. Or, the old gate valve is corroded and won't turn without snapping.

If you can't find an interior shutoff, **give us a call.** We can get out to your house quickly, sweat in a reliable quarter-turn ball valve with a bleeder, or upgrade you to a true commercial frost-free hydrant before the hard freeze sets in. It costs far less to install a shutoff today than it does to remediate water damage in mid-winter.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

Winterizing your outside spigots—hose bibs, outdoor faucets, whatever you call them—is the most important step in protecting your home’s outdoor pipes before a Minneapolis freeze. Most of our January burst-pipe calls start the same way: a hose left hooked up to a spigot.

When water inside the hose and spigot freezes, it expands and pushes back into the pipe inside your wall. By the time you notice, you’re not dealing with a frozen faucet. You’re dealing with a burst pipe, water damage, and an emergency plumbing bill.

Here’s how to winterize your outside spigots the right way.

## The big mistake: leaving hoses connected

If you only do one thing, disconnect your hoses.

This is the mistake we see most. Homeowners shut off the spigot, wrap it, or throw a cover on it—but leave the hose attached. A connected hose traps water in the spigot and the hose itself. Even “frost-free” spigots aren’t magic; if a hose is attached, they can’t drain, and they will freeze.

That trapped water freezes, expands, and looks for somewhere to go. Too often, it goes into the pipe inside your home. This is the number one cause of the burst outdoor pipes we repair every January.

Disconnect hoses, drain them completely, coil them up, and store them indoors. Do it before the first hard freeze, not after.

## How to winterize outside spigots: 4 steps

### 1. Disconnect and drain hoses

Remove every hose from every outdoor spigot. Hold them up or lay them out so the water drains out, then store them in a garage, basement, or shed.

Do not leave a hose attached “just in case.” A hose left outside all winter will crack and split. A hose left attached can freeze your spigot and burst the line behind it.

### 2. Shut off the interior valve

Go inside and find the shutoff valve that feeds the outdoor spigot. In many Minneapolis homes, it’s in the basement, crawlspace, or utility room, often near the ceiling where the pipe heads outside.

Turn the valve clockwise until it stops. This cuts water to the outdoor line so there’s nothing left to freeze and expand.

**If you can’t find a shutoff—or your home doesn’t have one—call us.** Plenty of older Minneapolis homes don’t have a dedicated interior shutoff for exterior faucets, and no cover on earth will protect a line that still has water in it. We can install a shutoff or shut the line down the right way before the first deep freeze.

### 3. Drain the spigot

With the interior valve closed, go back outside and open the spigot. Let any remaining water drain out completely.

Once the water stops, close the spigot. If you skip this step, leftover water in the spigot body can still freeze and crack it.

### 4. Add a $3 foam cover

Finish with an inexpensive foam faucet cover from any hardware store. You can grab one for about $3. Slip it over the spigot and tighten it snug against the house.

It blocks wind and adds a layer of insulation. It’s cheap, it takes ten seconds, and it’s a lot better than paying for emergency pipe repair.

## Don’t have an interior shutoff? Call us.

If you can’t find a shutoff valve inside—or you know your outdoor spigots don’t have one—don’t just cover the faucet and hope for the best. That’s how small problems turn into January emergencies.

Call us before the first hard freeze. We’ll track down the line, install a shutoff if you need one, or winterize your exterior plumbing properly. It’s a quick, affordable fix compared to a burst pipe and water in your walls.

Keep those hoses off, shut the line down, and your outdoor pipes should make it through the winter just fine.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
**Turf the Girls Soccer Field. Now.**

*By a girls' soccer and track coach*

Nine games. That’s how many games my girls soccer team has had rained out or moved in the last two seasons because our grass field floods. Not because the other team was better. Not because we didn’t practice. Because the field can’t handle rain.

Last October, one of my players tore her ACL stepping in a rut on that same field. A rut. Not a collision, not a bad slide tackle. A hole in the grass. She’s still not back. That’s not bad luck. That’s a facility problem.

The boys football field got turf in 2019. They play on a surface that drains, that doesn’t rut, that doesn’t turn into mud. My girls are still playing on a field that floods every time it rains hard. That’s not a coaching issue. That’s not a talent issue. That’s a fairness issue.

I’m not asking for a new stadium. I’m asking for the same basic thing the boys already have: a field that’s playable when it rains and safe when it’s dry. The school board votes on next year’s facilities budget soon. Put turf on the girls soccer field in that budget.

Some people will say turf is expensive. You know what’s more expensive? Losing nine games a season. Losing a player to an ACL tear that didn’t have to happen. Losing the message that girls’ sports matter as much as boys’ sports.

I coach for a stipend. I’m not here to write pretty sentences. I’m here because I’ve watched my players warm up on a field with standing water and then get told their game is moved—again. I’ve watched a girl’s season end because of a rut. I’ve watched the football team practice on turf while we drag mud off our cleats.

The board has a choice. They can keep telling half the school’s athletes to wait their turn, or they can fix the field. My players have waited long enough.

Vote yes on turf for the girls soccer field.

b.text:
Nine games in two years. That’s how many times my girls’ soccer team has had a game rained out, postponed, or moved to an away field because ours turned into a swamp. This isn’t a minor inconvenience—it’s a pattern. And last October, it cost us more than a schedule shuffle. One of my starting defenders planted her foot in a deep rut that had been hidden by standing water the day before, heard a pop, and tore her ACL. That surgery, that recovery, that lost season—it all traces back to a grass field that can’t handle a hard rain.

I’m not a writer. I’m a coach. I do this for a small stipend because I care about the kids. So I’ll say it plainly: Our girls’ soccer field is dangerous and unfair. The boys’ football field got turf back in 2019. It drains perfectly, plays fast, and doesn’t chew up ankles when the weather turns. Meanwhile, my team dodges puddles and ankle-breakers every spring. We’ve had girls slide into a tackle and come up with mud in their mouths because the ground can’t take another step. We’ve had goal kicks that stop dead in a pool. The conditions are messing with our development—and our safety.

The numbers don’t lie. Over the past two seasons, nine games lost or relocated because of flooding. That’s nine fewer chances for these athletes to compete, to be scouted, to learn how to win and lose on their home soil. The football team hasn’t missed a single home game due to field conditions since their turf went in. They get a reliable, consistent surface. We get a lottery.

I’ve heard the argument: Grass is softer, cheaper to maintain. But our grass isn’t soft in October—it’s sodden and rutted. And the “cheaper” math ignores the cost of rescheduling buses, officials, and staff when we lose a home game. It ignores the cost of a knee surgery and months of PT. It ignores the simple message we send when we pour money into the boys’ Friday night lights while the girls’ soccer team is an afterthought.

The school board votes next month on the facilities budget. I’m asking them—and this community—to look at the facts, not the gender of the athletes who use the field. Turf for the girls’ soccer field isn’t a luxury. It’s a safety fix, an equity fix, and a long-overdue investment. We don’t need a new grandstand or a fancy press box. We need a surface that doesn’t flood, doesn’t rut, and doesn’t send my players to the emergency room.

One field. Two years. Nine lost games and one torn ACL. That should be enough. Fix the field. Fund the turf. It’s that simple.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/ I raised Tallyup's prices 40% on every customer overnight. A week later, 30 of 140 had cancelled. Here's what I got wrong and what I'm doing differently now.

2/ The reasoning felt solid. The product had gotten meaningfully better since launch. New customers were already paying more without blinking. Existing customers were on the old price and I figured the value was obvious.

3/ So I changed the Stripe plans, sent one email saying "prices are going up starting next billing cycle," and went to bed.

4/ The cancellations started before I woke up.

5/ What the replies taught me: it wasn't really the number. Gym owners run on thin margins and budget month to month. A 40% jump with no warning read as "this guy doesn't understand my business." Which, for a retention tool, is a bad look.

6/ A few said they'd have stayed at the new price if I'd just given them time. A few said they'd have stayed if I'd asked what they thought first. Most just left quietly.

7/ What I changed:

Existing customers are grandfathered at their old price for the rest of the year. If you signed up trusting a number, that number should mean something.

8/ New pricing only applies to new signups. Anyone who cancelled over this got an email offering their old rate back, no strings. Some came back. Not all.

9/ Going forward, any price change gets a real heads up. Months, not one billing cycle. And I'll talk to customers before I decide, not after.

10/ The lesson isn't "never raise prices." It's that the way you raise them tells customers what you think of them. I told 140 people I thought of them as line items. 30 of them believed me.

11/ Still here, still building. Back to the work.

b.text:
Here's a thread on the pricing mistake and what I changed 🧵

1/ Six months ago I raised Tallyup's prices 40% overnight. On everyone. No grandfathering, no warning emails, just flipped the switch on a Tuesday morning. Here's what happened: we lost 30 of our 140 customers in a week. ~21% churn, out of nowhere.

2/ The reasoning at the time felt solid. MRR was flat, I figured the product was underpriced, and I'd read enough "raise your prices" posts to think I was leaving money on the table. I was solving my boredom, not a real customer problem.

3/ What I missed: my customers are gym owners running small facilities. They don't have procurement budgets. A 40% jump in a line item they'd been paying for a year feels like a billing error before it feels like a value conversation. Most of the 30 who left didn't even email. Just canceled.

4/ First thing I changed: rolled back pricing for anyone who stayed. Sent a personal email, no template, explaining the jump was a mistake and their old price was locked in for 12 months. Kept 22 of the remaining 110 that way. The other 8 churned within the month anyway.

5/ Second change: any future price increase is on new customers only, for at least 6 months before existing customers see it. And existing customers get 30 days notice with a real explanation, not a Stripe receipt. Announcements > assumptions.

6/ Third change: I started charging new signups the new price and tracking conversion rate weekly instead of just MRR. Conversion dropped ~15% the first month, which told me the new price was probably 10-15% too high, not 40%. I'd been anchoring to the wrong number.

7/ What I'd tell other solo founders: your existing customers are your cheapest source of validated pricing. If you raise on them and a chunk leave instantly, the market just told you something your spreadsheet didn't. Listen to it before you keep raising.

8/ Tallyup today: ~115 customers, MRR is higher than it was at 140 because new signups come in at the new price, but the lesson wasn't "raise prices." It was "raise prices the way your customers can actually absorb them." Wild concept, I know.

(end 🧵)

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
Six months ago, I replaced my makeshift setup with the Jarvik L2 standing desk. As a remote software engineer spending 8 to 10 hours a day at my terminal, my desk is my primary tool. 

    As always: no affiliate links here, no gifted products. I bought this with my own money. Here is the unfiltered breakdown after half a year of daily use.

    ### The Good: The Motor
    The dual-motor system is easily the best part of the L2. It is fast, extraordinarily smooth, and genuinely quiet. I frequently transition from sitting to standing in the middle of Zoom calls without needing to mute my mic. The pitch is a low, discreet hum rather than a high-pitched whine, and it moves from my sitting height (28 inches) to standing height (44 inches) in about four seconds flat. 

    ### The Bad: Stability and Memory Drift
    If you type aggressively—which I do when I'm deep in a debugging session—you will run into stability issues. At sitting height, the frame is rock solid. But at full standing height, there is a clear, persistent wobble. It isn't going to collapse, but my dual 27-inch monitors shake noticeably while I'm typing hard. If your desk sits on carpet, expect it to be worse.

    Then there’s the controller firmware. The memory presets suffer from drift. Over a few weeks of daily toggling, my standing preset gradually creeps downward by about a centimeter. Every month or so, I have to clear the memory and re-program my heights because 44 inches slowly degrades to ~43.6 inches. It’s a minor annoyance, but sloppy engineering nonetheless.

    ### The Ugly: The Cable Management Tray
    The included cable tray is absolute garbage. It’s made of flimsy, stamped sheet metal that sags under the weight of a standard multi-outlet power strip and two chunky power bricks. The mounting brackets are awkward, and the cutouts have surprisingly sharp edges that will scrape your cables if you pull them through roughly. Toss it in the recycling bin immediately and buy a $15 wire mesh basket off Amazon instead.

    ### The Verdict
    Whether the Jarvik L2 is worth buying comes down entirely to price:

    *   **At $749 (Full Retail):** Pass. At this price point, you are too close to Uplift V2 territory, which offers far better crossbar stability, superior accessories, and controllers that don't drift.
    *   **At $549 (Sale Price):** Buy it. Jarvik runs $200-off sales constantly. For $549, a super-quiet, fast dual-motor frame is worth trading off a weak cable tray and minor top-end wobble.

b.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: The Six-Month Review

Six months ago I bought a Jarvik L2 with my own money, and I've been sitting and standing at it for roughly 50 hours a week ever since. Nobody sent me this desk, there are no affiliate links in this post, and Jarvik has no idea I exist. Here's what actually held up and what didn't.

## The motor is genuinely excellent

Let's start with the thing Jarvik got right, because they really did. The dual-motor system is fast — about 12 seconds from my sitting height (28.5") to my standing height (44") — and quiet enough that I've raised the desk mid-meeting with my mic hot and nobody noticed. I measured it at my desk with a phone app: roughly 42 dB during travel, which is quieter than my fridge. My previous desk (a Flexispot EC1) sounded like a garbage disposal by comparison and took nearly twice as long.

Six months in, zero motor issues. No grinding, no stalling, no weird hesitation under load, and I have about 60 pounds on this thing between two monitors, a monitor arm, and a small rack of audio gear. If the motor is your main concern, buy with confidence.

## The wobble is real, and it's height-dependent

Here's my biggest complaint. At sitting height and even at moderate standing heights (up to ~40"), the L2 is rock solid. But at my full standing height of 44", there's noticeable front-to-back wobble when I type hard — and I type hard. My monitors visibly shimmy during fast typing sessions. It's not enough to make anything fall over, and it settles the instant I stop, but if you're tall (I'm 5'10" and this is my ergonomically correct height, so taller folks will have it worse) and you're a heavy typist, you will notice it every single day.

I tried the usual fixes: releveled the feet, retorqued every bolt at the three-month mark, moved the heavy stuff toward the center of the desktop. Marginal improvement at best. This is a frame stiffness issue, not an assembly issue. The columns just don't have enough overlap at full extension.

If your standing height is under 40", ignore this entire section. Above 42", take it seriously.

## The memory presets drift, which defeats the purpose

The L2 has four memory presets, and they drift by about a centimeter over a few weeks of use. My sitting preset was 28.5" in January; by March it was landing at 28.9". A centimeter doesn't sound like much until you realize the entire point of an ergonomic setup is consistency — my keyboard tray clearance is tight, and that drift is the difference between my wrists being neutral and being cocked upward.

The fix is re-running the calibration routine (lower to minimum, hold down for 5 seconds until it beeps), which takes 30 seconds. I now do it monthly, like some kind of desk chore. It works, but I shouldn't have to do it. My guess is the controller loses track of position slightly with each cycle and the error accumulates. Firmware-fixable? Probably. Fixed? No.

## The cable tray is an insult

The included cable management tray is a flimsy plastic trough that clips to the underside of the desktop with two of the least confidence-inspiring clips I've ever handled. One clip snapped during installation — not from force, from *existing*. The tray is also too shallow to hold a standard power strip plus a laptop brick, so cables spill over the edge anyway.

I gave up after a month, unscrewed it, and bought a $20 steel under-desk raceway from Amazon that mounts with actual screws. Problem permanently solved. Budget for this. Do not attempt to live with the stock tray.

## Small stuff, quickly

- **Assembly:** 90 minutes solo, decent instructions, all holes lined up. Fine.
- **Desktop:** I got the 60" laminate. No warping, no peeling, edges have survived multiple chair collisions. Fine.
- **Controller:** The touch-style buttons are slightly laggy but the display is readable. Fine.
- **Anti-collision:** Triggered correctly the one time my chair arm got in the way. Fine.
- **Warranty:** Untested, thankfully. It's 5 years on the frame, 2 on electronics, which is middle-of-the-pack.

## The verdict: it's a $549 desk

I paid $549 on sale. At that price, this is an easy recommendation for most people: the motor is best-in-class for the money, the build is solid at normal heights, and the flaws are either fixable ($20 cable raceway) or manageable (monthly recalibration).

At the $749 list price, no. At $749 you're in range of frames with better column overlap that don't wobble at full extension, and you shouldn't be doing calibration chores or replacing included accessories on a desk that costs that much.

**Buy it if:** it's on sale, your standing height is under ~42", and you can live with a monthly 30-second recalibration ritual.

**Skip it if:** you're paying full price, you're over 6 feet tall, or preset precision matters to you and you refuse to babysit it.

Six months in, I'm keeping mine. But I'm keeping it as a $549 desk — because that's what it is.

a.text:
To the Editor:

I’m writing about the plan to close counter service at our post office. I drove Route 4 for this town for 22 years before I retired last year. I know these roads and the people on them. The USPS says the Kettle Falls branch loses forty thousand dollars a year, but that only started after they already cut our window hours from 8 a.m. to noon. Of course foot traffic dropped then. You can’t point to a problem you made yourself and call it a reason to make it worse.

Think about folks like Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She’s in her eighties, depends on the mail for her heart medication. If the counter closes, how is she supposed to get a money order? She can’t drive twenty minutes over to Fairview every time she needs one. She’s not the only one.

There’s a public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall. The USPS district manager will be there. If you want a post office that still serves this town, you need to show up and speak out. I’ll be there. I’m not a writer, but I know when our town is getting a raw deal. See you July 28.

— A Retired Route 4 Carrier, Kettle Falls

b.text:
To the Editor:

I carried mail on Route 4 for 22 years. Thirty-eight miles a day, six days a week, until I retired last year. I am not a writer, but I know this town about as well as anybody, so I want to say something about the Postal Service closing our counter.

The district office says the Kettle Falls branch loses $40,000 a year. What they leave out is why. Two years ago they cut the counter hours from a full day down to 8 to noon. Anybody who works a job could not get there anymore. Of course the traffic dropped. Now they are pointing at the drop in traffic as the reason to shut the window for good. They made the problem and now they are using it as the excuse.

Here is what that means for real people. Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill is in her eighties. She gets her heart medication through the mail and pays for it with money orders she buys at that counter. When it closes, the nearest window is Fairview, twenty minutes each way on the highway. She does not drive that road. I do not know what she is supposed to do, and I do not think the people making this decision have thought about her at all. There are more like her on every route out of this office. I delivered to them.

A post office counter is not a luxury in a town like ours. It is how people who do not have a computer or a car or a bank account do their business.

The Postal Service is holding a public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall. The district manager will be there. If you care about this, show up. Bring your neighbors. Bring your parents. Fill the chairs. If the hall is empty, they will take that as permission. If it is full, they will have to explain themselves to our faces.

I will be there. I hope to see you.

[Name]
Retired carrier, Route 4
Kettle Falls

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
My first clinical rotation was in the emergency room. I spent the week before it telling everybody I was ready. I wasn't. I don't think anybody is. But I learned more in that first week than in a whole semester of lectures, and most of it nobody could have taught me ahead of time.

The first thing that stuck with me was a man who needed a wound cleaned. It took a while, and it hurt the whole time. His wife was on her way but stuck in traffic, and every time the door opened, he looked at it. My preceptor had her hands full, so she looked at me, and I took his hand and told him I'd stay right there until his wife made it. I didn't say anything smart. I just held on while he squeezed and worked on his breathing. When his wife finally walked in, she took over and I stepped back. That's how it should work. Sometimes the whole job is being the person in the room until the right person gets there.

Later that shift a code got called. I followed my preceptor down the hall and she stopped me and pointed at the supply closet. Restock the gauze, she said. So I stood in that closet counting packets while behind the curtain somebody counted compressions out loud. I could hear everything through that curtain. I won't pretend I wasn't disappointed. I wanted to be in there. But somebody has to make sure there's gauze when the next person comes through the door bleeding, and that week that somebody was me. I restocked every shelf in that closet. I did it slow and I did it right.

The hardest one was a blood draw. A diabetic man, stuck a thousand times in his life, veins like thread. I missed. Then I missed again. Then a third time. Each one made me want to quit worse than the last. He never told me to stop. He just said I'd get it. On the fourth stick I got a good flash of blood, and I had to act like I wasn't about to cry from relief. What I keep coming back to is that he trusted me to keep going. Patients let students practice on them. That's a gift, and I don't want to waste it. That night I went home and watched videos on finding veins in hard cases. The next day I asked my preceptor what she looks for. I'll miss again someday. I just want to miss less.

Here's what I took from that week. Nursing isn't one skill. It's holding a stranger's hand because the person who should be holding it is stuck on the highway. It's counting gauze while other people count compressions, and knowing both counts matter. It's missing three times and going a fourth because the patient said you'd get it.

I'm a first-year student. I have a long way to go and a lot of shelves left to restock. This scholarship would mean less time figuring out how to pay for the next semester and more time learning the job. That's it, honestly. I want to keep showing up to that closet, that bed, that chair. I want to be worth the trust that man had in me on the fourth try.

b.text:
During my first week in the ER, I held a stranger’s hand while his wound was cleaned. His wife was stuck in traffic. I could not make the cleaning hurt less or get her there any faster, but I could stay beside him. So I did.

Before that week, I thought mostly about the skills I needed to learn. I wanted to take blood pressure correctly, remember what I had studied, and not freeze when someone needed me. I knew being kind mattered, but I had not understood how much it could matter in one small moment. Holding his hand did not require a test or a checkoff. It required me to notice that he was alone.

Other moments made me feel much less useful.

During a code, I was sent to restock gauze. Behind the curtain, I could hear the team counting. I wanted to be able to help, but I was a first-year student with more to learn than I knew how to do. At that moment, helping meant getting supplies where they belonged and staying out of the team’s way.

It felt strange to do such an ordinary task while something so serious was happening a few feet away. But the supplies still needed to be there. That experience taught me that I cannot judge the value of a task by how important I feel while doing it. Sometimes my job will be small. It will still be my responsibility to do it well.

Then there was the patient with diabetes whose veins were difficult to access. I missed his blood draw three times before getting it on the fourth try. I was relieved when I finally got it, but I was also aware that every missed attempt had happened to him, not just to my confidence.

I have thought about that blood draw since. I want to become skilled, but I do not want to get so focused on completing a task that I lose sight of the person going through it. I need to learn when to keep trying, when to pause, and when to ask for help. Getting something done matters. So does how the patient is treated along the way.

I left my first week in the ER knowing more, but also knowing how much I still had to learn. I had seen how quickly a room could change and how much trust patients place in people they have just met.

This scholarship would help me continue my nursing education and build the skills to meet that trust. I want to become a nurse who can act when things are urgent, admit when I need help, and notice when someone needs a hand to hold. My first week did not make me that nurse yet. It gave me a clearer idea of who I am working to become.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The Barrera wedding got rained out in October.

The ceremony site we'd scouted twice? Underwater. The golden hour portrait spot? A mud pit. And the shot list we'd carefully built over three planning calls? Useless by 2pm.

So we moved everything under the big pecan tree on the property. No plan. No list. Just a couple who trusted me and a tree that had clearly seen a hundred years of Hill Country storms.

Those are some of the best photos I've delivered in 8 years of shooting weddings.

Here's what I've noticed after 250+ weddings: the couples who hand me a rigid shot list get exactly what's on the list. The couples who tell me "capture how it feels" get the images they end up framing.

Shot lists have their place — family groupings, the heirloom details, the moments you'd genuinely regret missing. I always ask for those.

But when a couple gives me room to react to what's actually happening — the rain, the laughter during a botched toast, grandpa sneaking a dance with the flower girl — that's when the magic shows up.

The Barreras didn't get the wedding they planned. They got something better, and the photos prove it.

If you're planning your wedding: hire a photographer whose work you trust, give them your true non-negotiables, and then let them do their job. The best moments of your day haven't been invented yet.

📍 Texas Hill Country
#WeddingPhotography #HillCountryWeddings #TexasWeddings

b.text:
The Barrera wedding almost fell apart.

Rain came out of nowhere about an hour before the ceremony. The outdoor venue they'd planned around for months was suddenly off the table.

We moved everything under this massive old pecan tree near the property line. Not the plan. Not what anyone picked out during the planning meetings.

And here's the thing — they didn't panic. They didn't start trying to reshoot the timeline or hand me a list of "must-have" poses to make up for what they were losing. They just let it unfold.

The first look happened under wet branches, light filtering through in a way no venue would have given us. The dancing started early because why wait. The toasts happened in a circle of lawn chairs on wet grass.

Those photos are some of my favorites from 8 years of full-time shooting.

Here's what I've seen over and over: the couples who show up with a rigid shot list tend to get photos that look exactly like their shot list. Fine. Safe. Done.

The couples who trust the day — who let their photographer respond to what's actually happening in front of them — those are the ones who end up with images nobody else has.

The Barreras didn't get the wedding they planned. They got the one that happened. And it was better.

If you're planning your wedding right now, my advice is simple: pick a photographer whose work you trust, then let them work. Bring a short list of non-negotiables if you need to. But leave room for the pecan tree.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
# The Cereal Aisle

I flew home from my second deployment in October. My wife met me at the airport with our daughter, who was six.

I had a picture of that girl taped inside my locker for a year. In the picture she was five and missing a front tooth. The one at the airport had both her teeth back and was taller than I remembered, and when I came walking up she got behind her mother's leg and held on to it and looked at me like she was trying to place me. My wife put her hand on the back of our daughter's head and said, "That's Daddy." She didn't come out from behind the leg right away. I knelt down and waited. It took her a minute. I don't blame her. A year is a long time when you're six. A year is most of what you can remember.

She came around eventually. But I think about that minute a lot.

A few days later my wife sent me to the store for milk and a couple other things. I got the milk fine. Then she'd written cereal on the list, and I went to the cereal aisle, and I stood there.

I want to explain this right. There were maybe forty kinds of cereal. Probably more. I stood in front of them and I could not pick one. It wasn't that I couldn't decide which one tasted best. It was that I couldn't make the machinery in my head do the thing it was supposed to do. Over there you eat what they give you and you're grateful and you don't think about it. You don't stand in front of forty choices with nobody shooting at you and nothing to do but pick. I stood there long enough that a stocker asked me if I needed help finding something. I said no. I stood there some more. I want to say it was twenty minutes. It was a while.

I finally grabbed the one with the toucan on it because my daughter had that when she was little, and I left.

At home the hardest part came at night. For a year I'd slept facing the door. You do that so you can see it. You do it without thinking after a while, your body just turns you that way. And we kept our bedroom door shut at home, always had, and I couldn't do it. I'd lie there with the door shut and it felt wrong, like something was going to come through it and I wouldn't know. So I started leaving it open. My wife asked why. I said I liked the air. That wasn't it. I turned so I could see the open door and the hallway, and that was the only way I could get to sleep for a long time.

It got a little better. The door thing took months. My daughter warmed up faster than I did, honestly. By Christmas she was climbing on me like I'd never left.

I still don't love the cereal aisle.

b.text:
The automatic doors at the airport slid open and the noise of the terminal hit me. I dropped my duffel bag by the baggage claim. My wife was already there. She walked up and hugged me, but my daughter didn't. She was six years old, and she just stood there, holding onto the back of my wife’s leg. She peeked around her mother's hip, looking at me like I was somebody who had knocked on the wrong door. I had been gone for twelve months. I didn't push it. I just knelt down on the linoleum and talked to her quietly until she finally stepped out and let me put my arms around her.

A few days later, my wife told me we were out of milk and asked me to go to the store. I walked in, grabbed a basket, and turned down the cereal aisle. I stopped dead. There were forty different kinds of cereal on the shelves. Frosted, honey-glazed, chocolate, bran, shredded wheat, stuff with marshmallows. I stood there looking at the boxes for twenty minutes. An employee restocking the bread walked past me, gave me a weird look, and kept going. I couldn't pick one. Over there, you ate what the DFAC put on the tray or what was in the MRE. You didn't have to choose. I eventually put the empty basket on top of a display of oatmeal and walked out to my truck.

The nights took the longest to figure out. On my second deployment, I slept in a room where my cot faced the door. You always face the door. You sleep light, and if that handle turns, you're up. When I got back to our house, my wife liked to leave our bedroom door open a few inches to let the hallway air in. The first couple of weeks, I’d wake up at three in the morning, staring at that dark gap, waiting for someone to come through it. I asked her to shut it all the way. We kept it shut and locked for a while. After a month, I started leaving it open a crack. Then a few inches. It took me half a year to relearn how to sleep with the door wide open and my back turned to it.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
I am a third-year electrical apprentice with the local IBEW. I work with my hands, pull wire, and do the physical labor that keeps the lights on in our state. Right now, state lawmakers are proposing a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding. I am not an English professor or a politician, but I know how to look at numbers and see if something makes sense. Cutting this funding makes zero sense for working families or taxpayers.

Look at how this program actually works in the real world. My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished the training, and all 21 of those graduates are out in the field right now working full-time journeyman jobs. That is not a bloated government program sitting around doing nothing; that is 21 people trained, employed, and contributing directly to our local economy.

The financial path is straightforward. An apprentice starts out making around $19 an hour while learning the trade on the job. By the time you top out as a journeyman, you are making around $46 an hour. That kind of wage changes lives. It takes people off state assistance programs almost immediately. Instead of needing public support, trade workers are buying homes, raising families, and paying heavy tax dollars back into the system that helped train them.

Then look at what it costs the state. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes our program is about $14,000. Compare that to a traditional four-year public college degree, where the average public subsidy per graduating student is roughly $48,000. We turn out fully skilled, high-earning tradespeople at less than a third of the public cost of a four-year degree, and our graduates don't carry mountain loads of student debt.

A 15% cut to apprenticeship funding hurts a system that is already giving the state its best return on investment. It cuts off a proven pathway to the middle class for people willing to work hard. 

To our union brothers and sisters: contact your state representatives and tell them what this training did for you. And to the state legislators reading this: look at the math. Don't cut a program that works. Vote no on the 15% cut and keep investing in the trades that build this state.

b.text:
Don't Cut Apprenticeship Funding

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with the IBEW. I'm writing this because the state wants to cut apprenticeship funding by 15%. That is a bad idea and it will hurt working people.

Look at my own cohort. We started with 24 apprentices. 21 of us finished. All 21 are working journeyman jobs right now. That's 21 good paychecks, 21 taxpayers, 21 people not sitting on the sidelines.

Here's why this program works. You start earning right away. Apprentices start around $19 an hour. When you top out as a journeyman you're around $46 an hour. That means people get off assistance programs fast. You're working, you're paying taxes, you're supporting a family. You're not stuck with debt.

And it's cheap for what you get back. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to a four-year college grad. The average public subsidy per four-year grad who finishes is something like $48,000. So we cost less than a third and we all have jobs waiting.

If the state cuts 15%, what happens? Fewer spots. Bigger classes. Less hands-on training. Older equipment. More guys dropping out because they don't get the help they need. We already have a waitlist of people who want in. This cut will shut the door on them.

Legislators say they want to save money and create jobs. Cutting this program does the opposite. You save a little now and you lose a lot later. You lose electricians, you lose taxpayers, and contractors have to turn down work because they can't find hands.

I'm asking my union brothers and sisters to speak up. And I'm asking any legislator reading this to come out to the training center and see where your money goes. It works.

Don't cut what works.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
## How to Bleed Air Out of Baseboard Heating Before Winter

1. **Shut off the boiler and circulator.**  
   Turn the heating system off before bleeding the baseboards. Let the system cool down so you don’t get burned by hot water or steam.

2. **Start with the baseboard closest to the boiler.**  
   Find the first baseboard unit on the heating loop. The bleeder valve is usually located at one end of the baseboard cover or near the piping connection. It may have a small square head for a radiator key or a slot for a flathead screwdriver.

3. **Place a cup or small container underneath the valve.**  
   Have a towel ready, too. A little water will usually come out once the air is released.

4. **Open the bleeder valve slowly.**  
   Use a radiator key or flathead screwdriver and turn the valve slowly. You should hear air hissing out. Keep the cup underneath the valve while it vents.

5. **Close the valve when the water runs steadily.**  
   Once the hissing stops and water comes out in a steady stream with no air bubbles, close the valve. Tighten it snugly, but don’t overtighten it. Excessive force can damage or crack the valve seat.

6. **Move to the next baseboard unit.**  
   Continue bleeding each unit in order, working from the baseboard closest to the boiler outward through the rest of the loop.

7. **Do not skip the basement loop.**  
   The mistake behind many of our cold-radiator calls is bleeding only the upstairs baseboards. Air often collects in the basement loop, so make sure those units are included before moving on. If the basement loop is full of air, the upstairs baseboards may still stay cold even after you bleed them.

8. **Turn the system back on and check the heat.**  
   After all the valves are closed, restore power to the boiler and circulator. Give the system time to heat up, then check that the baseboards warm evenly.

If a bleeder valve leaks after you close it, won’t open, or releases water without stopping, shut the system down and have it checked. Repeated air in the system, cold baseboards after bleeding, or a boiler pressure problem can point to an issue that bleeding alone won’t fix.

b.text:
Shut off the circulator pump or boiler before you open any valves. If the system is running when you crack a bleeder, you’ll force air down the line instead of out of it, and you’ll probably get sprayed. Give the boiler ten minutes to settle and the pressure to flatten out.

Start with the baseboard unit closest to the boiler and work your way outward, one by one. Each unit has a bleeder valve on one end—usually a small brass fitting with a square nut or a slotted stem. Slide a cup, small bowl, or heavy rag underneath before you touch it.

Open the valve slowly with a bleeder key or a flathead screwdriver. You’ll hear hissing first. That’s the air leaving. Keep it cracked until the stream of water runs steady and quiet, with no sputtering or bubbles. Depending on how much air is trapped, this can take thirty seconds or several minutes.

Once the flow is solid, close the valve snug, but do not reef on it. These brass seats crack easily, and an overtightened bleeder will drip or weep all winter. Finger-tight plus a quarter turn is usually enough.

Repeat this at every unit in the house. The mistake that generates most of our cold-radiator calls is homeowners bleeding only the upstairs baseboards and skipping the basement loop. The air that collects at the top of the system usually got pushed there from below. If you skip the basement, you’ll be bleeding the upstairs again in a week.

When you finish the last unit, check the boiler pressure gauge. Bleeding drops the system pressure, so you may need to add water through the fill valve to get back to the manufacturer’s recommended range—usually 12 to 15 psi for a one- or two-story home. If you’re unsure how to add water or the pressure won’t hold, shut the boiler down and give us a call.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
# The 7am Walk

Last month I had first-time buyers, the Pruitts, scheduled to tour a house on Sycamore Street. The night before, they couldn't sleep—nerves, excitement, all of it. So at 7am they drove over and just... walked the neighborhood.

When we did the official tour later, they already knew the street. They'd seen the retired couple watering their garden. They'd noticed the coffee shop two blocks down. They'd watched the school buses load up. They'd felt what it was actually like to live there, not just visit.

They made an offer that day. Closed three months later. Last week I got photos of them on the porch.

In 12 years, I've noticed the buyers who are happiest long-term are almost always the ones who've done this. They walk at different times. They sit in the driveway. They check out the commute during rush hour. They talk to neighbors. By the time they buy, the house isn't a transaction anymore—it's a place they already know.

If you're looking at houses: go back at 7am. Go back at 6pm. Go back on a Saturday. You'll know if it's right. You really will.

b.text:
After 12 years of helping buyers in Asheville, I’ve noticed a pattern I can’t fully explain, but I trust it: the buyers who show up early and walk the neighborhood before we tour the house tend to be the calmest, happiest people at closing.

I thought about this again with the Pruitts, who were looking at a house on Sycamore Street. They got there around 7:00 that morning, before our showing, just to walk the block while it was still quiet. They noticed neighbors out with dogs and coffee, the way the light came through the trees, and how the street felt once the morning started picking up. By the time I got there, they weren’t just thinking about buying a house anymore. They were already testing whether their lives would fit on that street.

We still went through the house carefully, asked questions, and talked through the usual concerns. But the Pruitts had already done something important. They had given themselves a chance to feel the neighborhood before falling in love with the kitchen.

A lot of first-time buyers want to get straight to the tour, and I understand that. Inventory is tight, emotions run high, and there is a lot of pressure to move quickly. But sometimes the smartest move happens before the front door opens. Drive the street at a different hour. Walk it when it’s quiet. Notice what you hear, who’s outside, where the sunlight lands, and whether it feels like a place you would actually live.

The house matters. But the street you wake up on can be the difference between a good purchase and a happy one.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
# Don't Cut the Ladder Out From Under Us

I'm a third-year apprentice with our local. I want to tell you why the state's proposed 15% cut to apprenticeship funding is a bad idea, using real numbers from my own cohort.

We started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one finished. That's an 87% completion rate. Those 21 people are now working journeyman electricians, earning around $46 an hour. We started at about $19 an hour as first-years — enough to get by, not enough to get comfortable. But that number climbs fast, year over year, as we learn the trade and take on more responsibility. By the time you're a journeyman, you're not just off government assistance, you're paying good money back into the system through taxes.

Here's the number that should matter most to legislators looking to save money: the total public cost per apprentice who finishes our program runs about $14,000. Compare that to a four-year college degree, where the average public subsidy per graduate who finishes is around $48,000. That's not a small gap. That's more than three times the cost, for a program where a good chunk of students don't even finish and end up with debt and no degree to show for it.

Our program doesn't work that way. If you finish, you have a skill. You have a job waiting. You're not sending out a hundred resumes hoping someone calls back. The work is here, the pay is real, and the path is clear from day one.

Cutting apprenticeship funding by 15% doesn't save the state money in any real sense — it just shifts costs somewhere else. Fewer apprentices trained means fewer skilled electricians in five years, which means higher costs for every construction project, every repair, every new build that needs qualified people to do the work safely and correctly. It also means fewer working-class kids get a shot at a stable, well-paying career without taking on a mountain of student debt.

We're not asking for a handout. We're asking the state to keep funding something that already works, that already proves itself in the numbers. Twenty-one out of 24. $14,000 versus $48,000. Off assistance and into the middle class in four years. That's not a program that needs cutting. That's a program that needs protecting.

If you're reading this and you're one of our state legislators, I'd invite you to come see an apprenticeship class in session. Come see what your investment actually looks like on the ground. It looks like people learning a trade, showing up on time, and building a future for themselves and their families — at a fraction of the cost of a lot of other programs the state funds without blinking.

Don't cut the ladder out from under the next generation of tradespeople. We're proof it works.

b.text:
# Keep the Funding, Keep the Pipeline

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with the local IBEW, and I'm writing this because the state is talking about cutting apprenticeship funding by 15%. That's a bad idea, and I want to explain why using numbers that actually mean something.

My cohort started with 24 apprentices. 21 of us finished, and every one of us is working journeyman jobs right now. That's not a feel-good story. That's a success rate, and it's real. We didn't drop out because we got bored or because the program wasn't worth our time. We stuck with it because the path was clear: put in the work, learn the trade, come out making a living wage.

Apprentices in our program start around $19 an hour. By the time you top out as a journeyman, you're making around $46 an hour. That means within a few years, people who might have been on food stamps or other assistance are off it. Not because someone gave them a pep talk, but because they learned a skill that pays. I've watched guys in my cohort go from barely getting by to buying homes and supporting families. That happens because the training is funded and the jobs are there.

Now look at the cost side. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes our program is about $14,000. Compare that to roughly $48,000 in average public subsidy per four-year college graduate who finishes. I'm not knocking college. Some jobs need a degree, and that's fine. But if the state is looking at where it gets return on its money, apprenticeship programs are a better deal by a long shot. We produce working tradespeople at less than a third of the public cost, and those tradespeople start paying taxes and spending in their communities right away.

A 15% cut doesn't sound huge until you think about what it actually does. It means fewer apprentices accepted. It means less classroom instruction time. It means tools and materials that are already stretched thin get stretched thinner. When my cohort went through, we had what we needed. If you cut 15% off the budget, the next cohort won't. You can't train electricians on hopes and good intentions. You need funded seats, funded instructors, and funded materials.

Here's what I want the legislators reading this to understand: apprenticeship funding isn't a handout. It's an investment that pays back fast. Every apprentice who finishes becomes a taxpayer, a consumer, and a skilled worker the state needs. Every apprentice who doesn't get a seat because of budget cuts is someone who stays underemployed or on assistance longer. The math on that is simple, and it doesn't require a fancy economic study to figure out.

My cohort is proof this works. 21 out of 24 finished. We're working. We're paying taxes. We're not drawing on public assistance. And the state got all of us trained for $14,000 each. Find me a better deal than that anywhere in the budget.

Keep the funding where it is. Better yet, increase it. The trades are short on people, and the people are ready to do the work. All we need is the state to not pull the rug out from under the programs that get us there.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
If your baseboard heat is gurgling, uneven, or one room stays cold while the rest of the house heats fine, there’s a good chance air is trapped in the system. Bleeding the air out before winter can help restore proper flow and get the heat moving again.

### Before you start
Turn off the circulator or boiler first and let the system cool down enough to work on safely. You’ll also want a small cup or container, a flathead screwdriver or radiator key, and a rag or paper towel.

### 1. Find the bleeder valve
Look at the end of each baseboard heating unit for the bleeder valve. It’s usually a small valve on the end cap that lets trapped air escape.

### 2. Place a cup underneath
Set a cup or container directly under the valve before opening it. A little water will come out once the air is gone, and this helps keep the area clean.

### 3. Open the valve slowly
Use a radiator key or flathead screwdriver to open the valve slowly. Don’t crank it open all the way. At first, you may hear a hissing sound as air escapes.

### 4. Watch for steady water flow
Keep the valve open until the hissing stops and water comes out in a steady stream. That usually means the air is out of that section.

### 5. Close it snugly
Close the valve once the water runs steadily. Make it snug, but don’t overtighten it. Overtightening can crack the valve seat and cause a leak later.

### 6. Work one unit at a time
Bleed the system unit by unit, starting with the baseboard closest to the boiler and moving outward. That helps you clear the air in the right order and keeps you from missing a trapped pocket.

### Don’t skip the basement loop
One mistake that causes a lot of cold radiator calls is bleeding only the upstairs units and skipping the basement loop. In many homes, that’s actually where the air is sitting. If the basement loop has air in it, the rest of the system can still struggle to heat properly.

### When to call for help
If you bleed the baseboards and still have cold spots, repeated hissing, low pressure, or no heat at all in part of the house, there may be a bigger issue in the system. That can include a pressure problem, a bad circulator, a stuck zone valve, or a blockage that needs service.

If you want, I can also help with baseboard maintenance tips, signs of air in the system, or a short homeowner-friendly FAQ to add to this post.

b.text:
You'll need a bleeder key or small flathead screwdriver, a cup, and an old towel.

1. Shut the boiler and circulator off first. You don't want hot water moving while you're opening the valves. Let it cool for 20-30 minutes if it's been running.

2. Start with the baseboard unit closest to the boiler and work your way out. That's usually in the basement.

3. On the end of each baseboard unit, you'll find a small bleeder valve. Hold your cup right underneath it and have the towel handy — water will spit once the air clears.

4. Open it slow, just a quarter turn. You'll hear hissing as the air comes out. Leave it alone until that stops and you get a steady little stream of water with no sputter.

5. Close it snug. Don't crank on it. Overtighten it and you'll crack the valve seat and it'll drip all winter.

6. Go unit by unit through the house in order.

The thing I see on most of our cold radiator calls: folks only bleed the upstairs units because that's where they feel the cold. Don't skip the basement loop. That's usually where the air is actually trapped, and if you leave it there it'll just work its way back upstairs.

If you bleed everything and a unit is still cold top to bottom, or you're not getting any water out at all, shut it back down and call us out — that's usually pressure or a stuck zone valve, not just air.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam – 14-Month / 140k-Mile Review**

Put about 140,000 miles on the Roadstar DC4 over the last 14 months running cross-country. Figured I’d drop a quick write-up for anyone looking to upgrade their cab setup.

**The Good:**
It already paid for itself. Had a four-wheeler try to slide into my lane and clip my steer tire, then tried telling the trooper I ran him off the road. Handed the footage over, and my insurance claim was fully approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6-week headache. Front video quality is sharp day and night, license plates show up clear, and the unit hasn't frozen up once despite constant cab vibration.

**The Bad:**
* **The Mount:** Toss the suction cup straight into the trash. It dropped off my windshield twice during the heat of July. Swapped to the included 3M adhesive mount and haven't had an issue since.
* **Rear Cam:** Fine during the day, but night footage gets real grainy past about 30 feet. It’ll prove positioning if somebody rear-ends you, but don't expect to read a plate number at distance in the dark.
* **The App:** Total waste of time. It requires a solid Wi-Fi connection to pull footage to your phone, which is useless when you’re parked in the back row of a packed truck stop with zero signal. Save yourself the blood pressure spike and just keep a cheap USB-C/Lightning SD card reader in your glovebox. Pull the card, plug it into your phone or tablet, done.

**Bottom Line:**
It’s got quirks, but it turns on every time I key the ignition, survives rough roads, and kept an at-fault accident off my record. Good enough for me. Worth a look if you need reliable coverage without spending four figures.

b.text:
Roadstar DC4 dash cam — 14 months and about 140k miles on my rig. Posting for the other owner-operators.

Rear cam night footage gets grainy past 30 feet. It’s not a dealbreaker but know the limit.

The win: caught a lane-change accident that got my insurance claim approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6 weeks. That alone paid for the unit.

Suction mount fell off twice in summer heat. Switched to the adhesive mount and it’s been rock solid since.

App needs WiFi to pull footage. Most truck stops have garbage WiFi or none at all, so downloading through the app is useless out here. I just pull the SD card.

Bottom line: camera is good, app is annoying, suction mount is trash in heat. Go adhesive from day one. Rear night vision has limits but front is sharp. Would run it again.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/4 Opened up the ceiling on our Maple Ave kitchen remodel and found a classic shortcut. Someone sistered a 2x4 to a sagging 2x8 floor joist... but only for 4 feet in the middle of a 14-foot span. And they used drywall screws.

2/4 To fix it right, we had to temporarily jack the floor, pull the bad sister, and run a full-length LVL sister with through-bolts and structural adhesive. It added a full day of framing and about $1,800 to the budget. 

3/4 The actual lesson for my fellow builders and architects: a half-sister doesn't just fail to fix the sag. It creates a hard hinge point where the new lumber ends, concentrating stress and cracking the finishes above. Always span full length to the bearing walls.

4/4 And for homeowners: if your remodel involves opening up old ceilings or floors, keep a 10-15% contingency specifically for structural surprises. 100-year-old Pittsburgh houses always have at least one skeleton hiding in the framing.

b.text:
1/ On the Maple Ave kitchen, demo turned up a 2x8 floor joist under the sink run with a notch cut into the bottom edge for an old cast-iron drain. The notch took out roughly half the joist depth. Next bay over, someone had bored a 3" hole within an inch of the bottom edge. That floor had been carrying cabinets, tile, and a fridge.

2/ Fix: engineer detail, two sistered joists, new blocking, and re-supported the drain run. Cost about $1,850 and two extra days. Cabinet install got pushed. Not catastrophic, but none of it was in the original budget because none of it was visible until the ceiling came down.

3/ Lesson for contractors: on older kitchens, assume there are old plumbing notches/holes until you open a bay. Put exploratory demo and a framing repair allowance in the bid. For homeowners: ask what's under the floor before cabinets are ordered. For architects: keep a framing inspection in the schedule before millwork.

4/ The real lesson isn't "old houses are wild." It's that a kitchen remodel is a structural project with cabinets on top. The joists don't care about the finish schedule. Find the bad framing while it's cheap to fix, not after the counters are templated.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
**The Market Isn’t Crashing. Sellers Are Just In Denial.**

After ten years selling real estate in this town, I’ve learned to spot the difference between a market crash and a reality check. Right now, what we’re watching in our neighborhoods isn't a crash. It’s a standoff.

Look at the numbers for our zip code. Last spring, the median home was on the market for eight days. This spring, that number jumped to 34 days. Showings per listing have dropped by half. By those metrics alone, you might think the sky is falling. 

Except it isn't. List prices in our area are actually up 6% year-over-year. 

How do you cut foot traffic in half, quadruple the time a house sits on the market, and still see higher asking prices? It’s simple: buyers have reached their financial limit, but sellers are still living in 2022.

Right now, I personally have three sellers with homes sitting past the 60-day mark. All three are stubbornly refusing to drop their price. They see that 6% appreciation stat and assume it applies automatically to their house, regardless of condition, interest rates, or what buyers are actually willing to pay per month. They remember when putting a "For Sale" sign in the yard meant five over-ask offers by Sunday evening. 

That market is gone. But the narrative that the market is "dead" is equally false.

Let’s be completely direct about what is happening: the market hasn't broken; it has simply stopped subsidizing bad pricing strategies. 

Buyers haven't vanished. They are still out there, mortgage pre-approvals in hand, but high interest rates have made them selective and cautious. They aren’t going to stretch their budgets for a home that is priced like it’s peak-frenzy season. 

The proof is in the closing data. When a home is priced correctly for today’s reality—not last year’s memories—it doesn't sit. Homes that are launched at an accurate, compelling price point are still going under contract in under two weeks. 

If a house in our suburb is sitting at 45, 60, or 90 days right now, it isn’t because the local economy collapsed or because buyers disappeared into thin air. It’s sitting because the seller is overcharging for the current climate. 

The market hasn't crashed. It just shifted gears, and it's time for sellers to catch up.

b.text:
# The Market Isn't Crashing. Your Expectations Are.

I've been selling homes in this area for a decade, and I've never seen a sharper disconnect between what sellers believe and what buyers are actually doing.

Last spring, the median home in my zip code went under contract in 8 days. Eight. This spring it's 34. Showings per listing have dropped by half. And yet list prices are still up 6% year over year.

Read that again. Prices are up. Showings are down. Days on market have quadrupled.

That's not a contradiction. That's a market working through a transition, and a lot of sellers haven't gotten the memo.

I have three listings right now where the sellers have refused every price adjustment for over 60 days. I've shown them the data. I've shown them the showings they're not getting. I've shown them the comparable sales. They're holding firm because their neighbor sold in a week last March and they believe their house is better anyway.

Meanwhile, the homes priced correctly from day one are still moving in under two weeks. I sold one in 11 days last month. Another agent in my office had one go in 9. The buyers are here. They're just not desperate anymore, and they're not going to overpay for something that sits while they watch from the sidelines.

Here's what happened. During 2021 and 2022, buyers had no leverage and sellers had all of it. Prices climbed, terms got aggressive, and 8 days on market felt normal. That wasn't normal. That was a once-in-a-generation sellers' market, and we all knew it even while we were enjoying it.

What we have now is a market that's still good for sellers but requires them to be realistic. A 6% year-over-year price increase with mortgage rates where they are is a strong market. It's just not a market where you can throw a number at the wall and wait for someone to match it.

The homes that are sitting aren't sitting because something is wrong with them. They're sitting because the price was set for a world that no longer exists. The homes that are selling are selling because someone looked at the current data, not last year's, and priced accordingly.

If you're thinking about selling this summer, here's my honest advice. Don't ask me what your home would have sold for last year. Ask me what it will sell for this year. Those are two different numbers, and only one of them actually matters.

The market hasn't crashed. It's just grown up.

a.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam - 14 Months / 140k Mile Review**

Been running the Roadstar DC4 in my current rig for 14 months and about 140,000 miles. Here’s the straight dope for anyone looking at picking one up.

The biggest plus: It pays for itself. It caught a four-wheeler making a blind lane change right in front of me. Sent the clip to my insurance, and my claim was approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6-week BS. 

The drawbacks:
- Rear night vision: Gets pretty grainy past 30 feet. It's fine for seeing if someone is riding your bumper, but don't expect to read plates in the dark.
- The mount: The suction cup fell off the glass twice in the dead of summer. Switched to the adhesive mount and it's been rock solid. Do yourself a favor and just use the adhesive right out of the box.
- The app: It needs Wi-Fi to pull footage to your phone, which is completely useless at most truck stops. I just pull the SD card and use a reader on my laptop.

Bottom line: It’s a solid, no-frills workhorse that did exactly what it needed to do when it counted. Just ditch the suction cup and ignore the app.
