setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
Six months in. I’m a remote software engineer, I stand about 40 percent of my workday, and I’ve run the Jarvik L2 through daily height changes since March. I paid $549 during a spring sale. It’s currently listed at $749. Here is exactly what that money gets you.

The motor is the best part of the desk. It’s fast—roughly 1.5 inches per second—and the hum is low enough that it never triggers my microphone’s noise gate on Zoom calls. I shift between sitting and standing multiple times a day, and the transition is quick enough that I actually do it instead of making excuses. At sitting height, the thing feels like a fixed desk.

But max it out and the wobble shows up. At full standing height—roughly 48 inches with my monitor arm attached—hard typing sends a visible shimmy through my 27-inch display. Not a gentle sway; a rhythmic shake that’s distracting when I’m pounding out code or angry Slack messages. If you type lightly or don’t need the desk at absolute max extension, it’s manageable. I’m 5’9” and I need every inch, so I live with it.

The memory presets are technically broken. Over six months, they’ve drifted about a centimeter from where I originally set them. My “sit” position now sits slightly too low; my “stand” position sits slightly too high. It’s only a centimeter, but it’s a centimeter I have to fix manually every single time. That defeats the purpose of one-touch presets.

The included cable tray is garbage. It’s a shallow mesh basket that flexes under the weight of a standard power brick and mounts so close to the desktop that thick cables get pinched. I removed it after three weeks and spent $30 on a proper under-desk tray. Treat the bundled tray like packing material: throw it away.

At $549, the Jarvik L2 is a steal. You get a fast, quiet dual-motor frame and a surface stable enough for most work, provided you accept the top-end wobble. At $749, it’s a bad deal. That price puts you in range of fully stable four-leg competitors and desks that don’t suffer from preset drift or insult you with a mesh cable hammock.

Verdict: Buy it on sale. Ignore the tray. Know that you’ll be adjusting the presets manually. And don’t expect rock-solid stability if you’re a heavy typer at full height.

b.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: My Six-Month Review

After six months of remote software work at the Jarvik L2, my verdict is straightforward: **worth buying at $549, not worth buying at $749.**

The motor is quiet and fast. The desk also wobbles at full height when I type hard, its memory presets drift by about a centimeter, and the cable tray is garbage. Whether you should buy it depends on which price you’re looking at—and how much those last three things will annoy you.

No affiliate links. Just the desk I bought and the compromises I’m still living with.

## The motor is the best part

The L2 moves quickly enough that switching between sitting and standing doesn’t feel like an interruption. That matters more than it sounds. A standing desk needs to make changing positions easy, not give you another tiny reason to stay seated.

It’s also quiet. Not silent, but quiet enough that motor noise isn’t something I think about during the workday.

This is the part Jarvik got right: press the button, change height, get back to work. I wish the rest of the desk were as easy to praise.

## Full-height stability is the catch

At full height, the L2 wobbles when I type hard.

Not “if I grab the desktop and deliberately shake it” wobble. Typing wobble. There’s an important difference between a desk failing a theatrical stress test and a desk moving during the thing I bought it to do.

I’m a software engineer. Typing is not an edge case.

The movement doesn’t make the desk unusable, but it is distracting. If you’re a heavy typist and expect to work near the top of its height range, take this seriously. “Stable enough” is a much easier compromise to accept at $549 than at $749.

## The memory presets are approximately correct

The presets drift by about a centimeter. They get me close to my preferred height, but not consistently back to the exact same spot.

A centimeter isn’t catastrophic. It also isn’t nothing when the whole point of a memory button is to stop fiddling with the height controls.

I can make a small correction and move on. I’d rather not have to. This is a convenience feature that only mostly delivers on its promise.

## The cable tray is garbage

The included cable tray is not a reason to buy this desk. Don’t count it as meaningful value when comparing the L2 with alternatives.

Cable management matters on a moving desk: the setup has to accommodate both seated and standing positions, not just look tidy at one height. My advice is to plan your cable management separately rather than assume the included tray has you covered.

I’d prefer a better tray—or no tray and a lower price—to a box-checking accessory.

## $549 makes sense. $749 doesn’t.

At **$549**, the L2’s trade-offs are acceptable to me. The quiet, fast motor does the central job well, and I can tolerate the wobble and occasional height correction at that price. The cable tray gets no credit.

At **$749**, I expect more than competent lifting. I expect better stability at full height and presets that reliably return to the height I saved. Those aren’t luxury extras. They’re basic parts of using a standing desk.

The $200 difference doesn’t change the hardware. It changes how willing I am to excuse it.

## Would I buy it again?

**At the $549 sale price, yes. At $749, no.**

If you type hard and need the desk at full height, I’d be cautious even on sale. That’s the limitation most likely to bother you every working day.

For everyone else, the L2 is a reasonable sale-price purchase with a good motor and some irritating compromises. Buy it for what it does well—not because the memory buttons and included cable tray make it look more finished than it is.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
The Local Market Isn’t Crashing. It’s Just Resetting.

For the past few weeks, my inbox has been full of the same question: Is the local market crashing? Based on the data I’m seeing every day, the answer is no. What we are experiencing isn’t a collapse—it’s a correction.

Here are the facts. This spring, the median days on market in our zip code jumped from 8 to 34. Showings per listing have dropped by half. Yet, list prices remain up 6% year over year. A crash would mean prices plummeting and homes becoming unsellable. Instead, we’re seeing a shift in momentum.

The bottleneck isn’t demand; it’s pricing. I currently have three listings that have been on the market for over 60 days. My sellers are refusing to adjust their prices despite the lack of offers. They are holding out for last year’s pace, but the market has moved on.

Here is the reality: I have listings that are priced correctly, and they are still selling in under two weeks. When you align with current reality, buyers are still out there. This isn’t a disaster for homeowners. It’s a wake-up call. The market isn’t broken; it’s just slower than it was a year ago. If you want to sell, you need to meet it where it is, not where you wish it to be.

b.text:
The market has changed. A lot.

If you’ve been watching headlines and waiting for a dramatic crash, this is not that. What we’re seeing in our part of the Midwest is something much more ordinary, and honestly, more fixable: sellers are still pricing to last spring, while buyers are moving at this spring’s speed.

Here’s what the numbers are telling us in plain English. In my zip code, the median days on market has jumped from 8 days last spring to 34 days this spring. That’s a big shift. At the same time, list prices are still up 6% year over year. On paper, that sounds like a strong market. In practice, showings per listing have dropped by half.

That mismatch is the story.

A home can be beautifully updated, in a great neighborhood, and still sit if it’s priced like we’re in the frenzy of 2021 or early 2024. Buyers are not chasing the market the way they were. They’re selective. They’re comparing more homes. They’re taking their time. And they are absolutely willing to move quickly for the right house — but only when the price makes sense.

I have three sellers right now who have been on the market more than 60 days and still don’t want to adjust. I get it. Nobody likes hearing that the number they hoped for isn’t the number the market is supporting. But the market does not negotiate with our feelings. It responds to value, condition, and price. If a home is sitting, the market is telling you something. Ignoring that signal doesn’t make the message go away.

What’s frustrating is that some sellers are treating a slower sale as a sign that buyers are “broken” or that the market is weak. That’s not what this is. The buyers are there. They’re just no longer willing to overpay for homes that are priced ahead of the curve.

And that’s the part sellers need to catch up to.

The homes that are priced right are still moving. In fact, the well-priced homes are still selling in under two weeks. That’s the real market right now. Not the stale listing that sits for two months. Not the overpriced home that gets a handful of showings and no offers. The homes that are aligned with today’s pace are selling, because buyers recognize value when they see it.

So if you’re thinking about selling, here’s my blunt advice: don’t ask what your neighbor got at the peak of last spring. Ask what buyers are actually paying now. If you want a quick sale, price it to win attention immediately. If you want to test the market, be prepared for silence. There isn’t much middle ground anymore.

This isn’t a crash. It’s a reset. And the sellers who understand that are the ones who are going to come out ahead.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
**A 22% Premium Hike Family Farms Can’t Absorb**

USDA raised the prevented planting premium base rate in our region by 22% this year. For my farm, that works out to roughly $46,000 in additional cost—before accounting for seed, fertilizer, equipment, land, labor and every other expense involved in putting in a crop.

This is not a theoretical concern. This spring, the rain would not let up, and I was able to plant only about 60% of my soybean and corn acres by the late-May deadline. Prevented planting coverage is meant for exactly this kind of year. Farmers buy it because no amount of planning, experience or work can make a field dry enough to plant.

I am a fourth-generation farmer. My family has managed through wet springs, dry summers, low prices and rising input costs. We understand that risk comes with the job. But a 22% increase in one year is not a routine adjustment. An extra $46,000 is money that cannot go toward machinery repairs, land payments, hired help or next year’s crop.

The acreage caps make the burden even less equitable. Because of the way those caps are structured, family operations like mine can end up paying more proportionally than larger operations nearby. Bigger farms may have more total acres and higher overall costs, but they also have more room to spread those costs. A family farm operating within a narrower acreage and financial margin does not have that same cushion.

That is why Senate Bill 214 deserves the Farm Bureau’s support. SB 214 would fix the acreage cap so the cost is distributed more fairly and family-sized operations are not hit disproportionately.

This is not a request to eliminate premiums or shift every risk away from farmers. We know coverage has a cost, and we expect to pay our share. What we are asking for is a structure that does not punish farms simply because of their acreage mix or size.

A $46,000 increase may appear as one line in an insurance calculation, but on a family farm it affects real decisions. It can mean postponing an equipment purchase, cutting back on improvements, taking on more debt or having less cash available for the next difficult season. Multiply that across family farms in our region, and the effects reach equipment dealers, seed suppliers, repair shops and rural communities.

Farm Bureau members should contact their state legislators and ask them to support SB 214. Lawmakers need to hear what a 22% hike and the current acreage caps mean at the farm level.

This spring, I got 60% of my acres planted by the deadline. I did everything I could with the weather I was given. The policy covering the other 40% should be priced fairly. SB 214 is a practical step toward making that happen.

b.text:
**Paying 22 Percent More for Less Coverage**

USDA raised the base prevented planting premium rate 22 percent in our region this year. I can tell you exactly what that looks like on a real farm, because this spring I got only 60 percent of my corn and bean acres in the ground before the late-May deadline. It would not stop raining. The other 40 percent sat too wet to work, week after week, until the calendar made the decision for me.

The rate increase will cost my operation about $46,000 this year.

For anyone who doesn't carry crop insurance, prevented planting coverage is the part of the policy that applies when weather keeps you out of the field entirely. You pay the premium every year, wet or dry. Most years it's money out the door and you're glad to lose it, because losing it means you got a crop in. This was the other kind of year — the kind the coverage exists for.

Here's where a rate hike turns into something worse. Prevented planting payments are subject to acreage caps. When 40 percent of your farm can't be planted, the cap means a share of your actual, documented loss simply isn't covered — even though you paid the higher premium on every acre you insure. And the cap doesn't scale with the size of the operation. On a farm the size of mine, the unplanted ground is a large share of the whole business, so the uncovered share is a serious hit. A few miles from here are operations running several times my acreage. The same cap touches a much smaller fraction of theirs. The bigger you are, the easier it is to absorb. The smaller you are, the more it defines your year.

So the math on my place this spring is this: a 22 percent premium increase on coverage that then declined to cover a large part of the acres the weather took from me. More money for less protection. A family farm pays the same rate as everyone else and gets less out of it, acre for acre, than the big operation down the road.

There's a fix sitting in the state legislature right now. SB 214 would correct the acreage cap so family operations aren't penalized for being family-sized. It doesn't raise anyone's rates and it doesn't ask for a new program. It makes the coverage a farmer pays for apply to the acres that farmer actually farms. That's it.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigot (A Quick Minneapolis Homeowner’s Guide)

Don’t wait for the first freeze. Outdoor faucets holding water in them are just waiting to crack. Here’s the exact sequence to protect every exterior spigot on your property in under ten minutes.

**1. Shut the interior shutoff valve**
Every outdoor faucet is fed by a dedicated line that runs through your interior walls. Somewhere behind that wall—usually in a basement, crawl space, utility closet, or garage—there’s a valve controlling it. Turn the handle clockwise until it stops. This isolates the outdoor pipe so water can’t reach it.

**2. Drain the spigot**
Once the indoor valve is closed, walk outside and open the outdoor faucet handle. You’ll hear a brief trickle as residual water clears out of the exposed pipe. Leave it open until it stops dripping completely. This emptying is non-negotiable; trapped water expands when it freezes and will split the pipe.

**3. Disconnect all garden hoses**
Remove every hose, sprayer, and timer currently attached to the spigot. Store them indoors. A hose left on the faucet creates a perfect trap for moisture and wind-driven snow. 

**4. Slide on a $3 foam cover**
Grab a standard screw-on or slip-on foam cover from any hardware store. Push it over the spigot until the base sits flush against the siding. Secure the strap. These covers don’t heat anything, but they block freezing air and meltwater from pooling directly on the metal threads and valve stem.

### The One Thing That Causes January Burst Calls
Leaving hoses connected is still our biggest headache every winter. When the temperature drops, a filled hose freezes solid almost overnight. Pressure builds up behind that frozen blockage and shoots straight into the weakest joint in your home’s plumbing. The result? Cracked pipes, flooded basements, and an emergency call before sunrise. If your hoses came off last fall, you’ve already avoided 90% of winter plumbing disasters.

### Don’t Have an Interior Shutoff Valve?
If you’ve searched your whole house and can’t find a dedicated valve for your outdoor faucets, don’t guess. Blindly turning valves can damage old galvanized or brass lines. Call us. We’ll locate the feed, install a proper exterior-rated sillcock or shutoff as needed, and make sure everything drains clean before the ground freezes. We’d rather swing by now than spend a January morning tearing into your drywall.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots Before Minneapolis Winter Hits

Most burst pipes we get called out for in January could have been prevented in October. Here's the whole job, start to finish, in about ten minutes per faucet.

## What You'll Need

- An indoor shutoff valve (more on this below)
- A pair of pliers, optional
- A foam faucet cover ($3 at any hardware store in the Twin Cities)
- A rag

## Step 1: Find and Shut Off the Interior Valve

Your outdoor spigot has a shutoff valve somewhere inside the house, usually on the same wall the faucet is mounted on. Look in the basement, crawl space, or utility room. It's often a small round handle, a lever, or a knob within a few feet of where the pipe exits the wall.

Turn it all the way off. Then go outside and open the spigot and let it drain. Leave the spigot open for the winter — that gives the remaining water somewhere to expand into if it freezes.

## Step 2: Disconnect Everything from the Spigot

Hoses. Splitters. Timers. Quick-connects. Y-valves. Take it all off.

This is the step that matters most, and it's where most people skip. More details below.

## Step 3: Drain and Store the Hose

Coil it up, dump any water out of it, and store it inside the garage or shed. A frozen water hose is a ruined water hose, but that's the cheap part of the problem.

## Step 4: Put the Foam Cover On

The $3 styrofoam dome with the rubber gasket. Push it firmly over the spigot until it seals tight. That's it.

The cover doesn't add heat. It blocks cold air from getting into the wall opening and onto the pipe behind it. In a Minneapolis winter, that matters.

---

## The Mistake That Bursts Most Faucets

**Leaving a hose connected.**

It doesn't matter if the hose is drained. It doesn't matter if it's one of those fancy frost-free hydrants. If there's a hose, a timer, or anything else attached to the end of the spigot, water can't fully drain out of the pipe. A small amount of water sits against the back of the valve all winter.

When it hits -15°F in February, that water freezes and expands. The pipe splits. You don't know it yet because the split is on the interior side of the wall. Then you turn the spigot on in April, water sprays into the basement, and now you're calling us at 7 a.m. on a Saturday.

The foam cover only works if the spigot can fully drain. A connected hose traps water. Hose off, cover on — that's the whole game.

---

## What If You Don't Have an Interior Shutoff?

Some older Minneapolis homes, especially bungalows in neighborhoods like Standish, Howe, and parts of Northeast, were built with the outdoor spigot on a direct line off the main with no interior valve. You can't shut it off from inside.

If that's your house, you've got two real options:

1. **Have us install a shutoff valve.** It's usually a 1-2 hour job, and it turns a recurring problem into a non-problem every winter.
2. **Call us to winterize the line professionally** by blowing it out or draining it from the main.

Don't try to "just wrap it really well" with towels and duct tape. We've seen the result. It doesn't work when it's -20°F.

---

## When to Do This

Before the first hard freeze. In Minneapolis, that's usually mid-to-late October. Doing it on a 50° Saturday in early November is fine. Doing it after the first night below 28°F is gambling.

---

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
The best advice I give buyers after twelve years in Asheville real estate has nothing to do with interest rates or contingencies. It's this: before you tour the house, walk the neighborhood at 7am.

I made it a standing suggestion after the Pruitts. First-time buyers, terrified of making a mistake, and they'd fallen hard for a listing on Sycamore Street. Great photos, cute porch, and they were half ready to write an offer before we'd even stepped inside. I told them what I tell everyone now: get there early, park a few streets over, and just walk.

At 7am on a Tuesday in October they met the actual street. A neighbor walking an arthritic old lab. A woman sweeping her porch. Somebody's coffee drifting out an open window, cold enough that they could see their breath, and the kind of quiet you can't judge from inside a car. The lab's owner stopped to chat, told them about the fall cookout at the end of the block, which houses had kids, and — almost as an aside — that the back corner of the yard they were about to stand in turns to soup after a hard rain.

We toured the house at 8:30. They still loved it. But they made their offer knowing the whole street, not just the kitchen, and they asked the sellers about the drainage directly instead of finding out in year one.

Three years later they're still on Sycamore. When that corner ponds up after a storm, they don't call me in a panic. They know their neighbors by name, somebody feeds their cat when they travel, and the soggy corner is just a Tuesday.

Here's the pattern I've noticed over twelve years of this: buyers who see a house at 10am and drive off fall in love with the finishes. Buyers who walk the block at 7am fall in love with the life they're actually buying. Every house eventually does something disappointing. The 7am buyers shrug it off. The others call me wondering if they made a mistake.

If you're buying, ask your agent to build the walk into your day. If you're an agent, steal it. It's free, it takes an hour, and it's the most honest showing your buyers will ever get.

b.text:
After 12 years of selling real estate here in Asheville, mostly working with first-time buyers, I’ve noticed a subtle pattern that has nothing to do with square footage, quartz countertops, or school ratings. 

The buyers who end up the happiest with their home long after the closing dust settles are almost always the ones who visited the neighborhood at 7:00 AM before we ever put in an offer.

A few years back, I was helping the Pruitts look for their first home. They found a property they were excited about on Sycamore Street, but before our scheduled afternoon walk-through, they decided to drive over early on a Tuesday morning just to sit on the curb with a cup of coffee. 

In thirty minutes, they learned things no MLS listing could ever tell them. They saw three different neighbors stop to chat while walking their dogs, noticed exactly where the morning sun hit the front porch, and confirmed that commuters weren't using Sycamore as a high-speed shortcut to avoid main road traffic. When we walked through the house later that day, they weren’t just evaluating room sizes—they already understood the rhythm of the block. Five years later, they still tell me it’s their favorite thing about living there.

An afternoon tour or a Sunday open house shows you a property at its polished best. A 7:00 AM walk shows you what your actual life will feel like on a random Tuesday. If you're house hunting right now, set an early alarm, grab a coffee, and go walk the street before you make a decision. It’s the single best test drive you can give a home.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
When I started shooting weddings six years ago, my calendar looked like every other photographer's in this city: packed solid from May to October, followed by five months of quiet admin work. If you had asked me then, I would have told you peak summer was the only time to get married. 

I was wrong. 

Over the last two years, I’ve shot 11 winter weddings. What started as an off-season way to keep my camera in hand has turned into some of my favorite work on my site. If you’re currently looking at venue calendars and weighing dates, here is the honest, unvarnished case for booking between November and March.

### 1. The 3:00 PM light is unmatched
Photographers talk constantly about light, but summer light is tricky. A high June sun creates harsh, unforgiving shadows directly under your eyes and nose until late in the evening. If it’s overcast in early summer, the sky acts like a giant, flat lightbox—fine for clean exposures, but completely lacking in depth and contrast.

In November and December, the sun sits low on the horizon all afternoon. Around 3:00 PM, that low-angled light filters through bare tree branches and hits at a sharp, directional angle. It gives portraits texture, dimension, and rich contrast that you simply cannot manufacture in June without setting up three off-camera flashes in a field. You get the golden-hour look before the temperature fully drops for the night, and you don’t have to pull yourself away from your reception dinner at 8:30 PM just to catch the sunset.

### 2. The venues actually have room to breathe
During peak season, local venues run like airport terminals. It is entirely normal in June to pull into a venue parking lot and find yourself squeezing your car between three different floral vans, a catering truck packing up from the morning ceremony, and another photographer trying to herd a bridal party out of the main courtyard before your contracted time slot begins. Everyone is on a strict 90-minute turnover clock, and the staff is exhausted.

In January, the place is yours. I’m not jockeying for parking with three other vendors, the venue coordinator isn't checking their watch to prep for an evening turnaround, and we aren't rushing portrait locations because another couple is waiting behind us. That lack of friction changes the entire energy of your wedding day.

### 3. The 30% reality
Let’s talk numbers. On average, booking an off-peak winter date saves couples roughly 30% across their total budget compared to a Saturday in September or June. Venues drop their food and beverage minimums, rental companies have surplus inventory, and independent vendors have more flexibility. 

That 30% difference usually means one of two things: couples either save thousands of dollars outright, or they reallocate that cash to hire the exact band, florist, or planner they thought was out of reach. 

A winter wedding isn't just a backup plan for when the summer Saturdays sell out. With the right timeline, it’s often the calmer, better-lit, and smarter option. If you're looking at a date between November and March, let’s talk about how to build a timeline that takes full advantage of it.

b.text:
# Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now

I’ll be honest: a few years ago, I thought winter weddings were mostly a trade-off. Couples chose them for the lower venue rates, accepted an earlier sunset, and hoped everyone stayed warm enough for photos.

After shooting 11 winter weddings over the last two years, I’ve changed my mind.

Winter weddings aren’t just a budget-friendly version of a summer wedding. They have some real advantages—especially for couples who care about photos and don’t want their wedding day to feel like they’re sharing a venue with half the city.

## The budget difference is real

In my area, winter bookings are often about 30% less expensive for couples than comparable spring or summer dates. That can mean a better venue for the same overall budget, more room for guest experience, or simply less pressure around every other decision.

That doesn’t automatically make winter the right choice for everyone. If you’re dreaming of an outdoor ceremony at 6:30 p.m. followed by a long golden-hour cocktail hour, June may still be your month. But if you’re flexible on timing, a winter date can free up a meaningful part of your budget without requiring you to compromise on the things that matter most.

## The light is better than people expect

Here’s the part I didn’t fully appreciate until I started shooting more winter weddings: the light can be incredible.

Around 3 p.m. in November, light moving through bare trees has a softness and direction that is genuinely beautiful for portraits. It’s warm, low, and dimensional. It gives photos shape. Faces look good, dresses catch the light, and even a simple patch of woods or an outdoor walkway can look intentional.

Compare that with a flat, overcast June afternoon—the kind of light that is technically easy but doesn’t always have much personality. Summer can absolutely be beautiful, but “summer” does not automatically mean “better photos.”

The key with winter is planning around the daylight. Portraits may need to happen before the ceremony, or we may build in a short window earlier in the afternoon. But when couples embrace that schedule instead of treating it like a limitation, the results are often some of my favorite images from the day.

## The venue feels like yours

In June, I’m often sharing a parking lot with three or four other vendors. There may be another wedding arriving as yours is getting ready, a florist unloading next to the catering team, and guests trying to figure out which event entrance is theirs.

Winter weddings tend to have more breathing room.

There are fewer overlapping events, fewer people competing for the best portrait locations, and less of that hectic wedding-industry traffic happening around you. It may sound like a small thing, but it changes the feeling of the day. You get more space. Your guests have an easier time arriving. We can take portraits without waiting for another wedding party to clear the staircase or the garden path.

That calm shows up in photos, too.

## Winter is not a backup plan

I’m not going to tell you every season photographs exactly the same. They don’t. Winter comes with earlier sunsets, colder temperatures, and a little more planning around weather.

But it also brings better availability, lower booking costs, quieter venues, and some of the most interesting portrait light I get all year.

If you’re deciding between a peak-season Saturday and a winter date, don’t assume the winter option is the compromise. It might be the date that gives you more room in your budget, more space at your venue, and photos with light you didn’t know you were looking for.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
## I Used to Talk Couples Out of Winter Weddings. Now I Try to Talk Them Into It.

For the first four years I did this, if a couple emailed me about a January date, I'd gently steer them toward May. Nothing dramatic — just a "have you considered late spring?" tacked onto the end of my reply. I thought I was doing them a favor.

I've shot eleven winter weddings in the last two years. I've changed my mind completely, and not for sentimental reasons. Here's the actual case.

### The light in November is better. Not different — better.

This is the part that surprised me most, and it's the part I'd want to explain to you if we were sitting across a table.

A June wedding at three in the afternoon, overcast, is flat. It's clean and it's usable and I can absolutely work with it, but there's no direction to it. Faces get lit evenly from a giant gray dome and there's nothing to model against — no falloff, no shape. I end up hunting for a doorway or a tree line or something, anything, to give the light somewhere to come *from*.

In November at three in the afternoon, the sun is already low, and the trees are bare. That combination does something I cannot replicate with equipment. The light comes through the branches instead of getting caught in a canopy, so it's directional and warm, and it breaks into these long soft shafts that fall across a face at an angle. Bare branches also make an incredible background — graphic, dark, uncluttered — where the same trees in June are a wall of green mush behind your head.

Golden hour in June starts around 8:15pm, which is usually the middle of dinner or the middle of dancing, and I'm asking you to leave your own party. In November, golden hour lands somewhere around 3pm to 4pm — which is very often *already* your portrait window. The best light of the day arrives exactly when you scheduled portraits, instead of ninety minutes after your last guest has committed to the dance floor.

### The venue is mine.

In June I'm sharing a parking lot with three or four other vendors. That's not a complaint about other vendors — most of them are people I like and would happily grab a beer with. But it means the good spot behind the barn already has a videographer set up in it. It means the bridal suite has hair, makeup, a planner, a florist, and a second shooter all trying to occupy the same eight feet of window light. It means I'm waiting my turn.

In February I pull in and there are two cars. Venue staff have time to answer questions and unlock doors. Nobody's rushing your ceremony because there's a second event loading in at six. I have the whole staircase. I have the whole field. I'm not negotiating for thirty seconds in the best corner of the room — I can actually *use* it, try three things, and pick the one that worked.

That difference shows up in the gallery. It's more time, less friction, and more of my attention on you instead of on logistics.

### It costs you meaningfully less.

Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for couples across the board — not just my rate, but venues, florals, rentals, blocks of hotel rooms. Venues that are booked eighteen months out for a Saturday in September will have three open dates in January and a real incentive to fill them.

I'll be straightforward about the trade-off, because I'd rather you hear it from me: you get less daylight. If you want a 6pm ceremony outside with a sunset behind you, winter isn't going to give you that. Winter weddings need a timeline built around a shorter day — ceremony earlier, portraits earlier, and a genuine willingness to be outside for fifteen minutes when it's cold. Every couple I've shot in winter has done it in a coat, laughed about it, and gone back inside to a room that felt warmer by comparison. Candlelight and warm interiors photograph beautifully, and there is nothing like the way a lit-up venue looks against a 4:45pm blue-dark sky.

### If you're deciding right now

I'm not going to tell you weddings are lovely in every season and you should just pick whatever feels right. That's true and it's also useless to you.

What I'll tell you is this: if your date is flexible, and you care about how your portraits look, and you'd rather spend the difference on food or a longer honeymoon than on a peak-season Saturday in June — look at November through February. I'll show you galleries from all eleven of them and you can decide for yourself.

Reach out and we'll talk through dates. I'll tell you honestly which ones give me the best shot at making something good for you.

b.text:
If you’d asked me a few years ago what kind of wedding I preferred to photograph, I probably would have said a classic summer Saturday without thinking twice.

That’s changed.

I actually like shooting winter weddings now, and not in the vague, “every season has its charm” kind of way. I mean it in the practical, real-world, I’ve-photographed-enough-weddings-to-know-what-works kind of way.

Over the last two years, I’ve shot 11 winter weddings. That’s enough to notice a pattern: winter weddings can be smarter, calmer, and honestly more photogenic than a lot of couples expect.

One of the first things couples usually notice is the budget. Winter bookings typically run about 30% cheaper for the couple than prime summer dates. That alone can make a big difference if you’re trying to stretch your wedding budget without cutting the things you care about most. For a lot of couples, that means hiring the photographer they really want, booking the venue they love, or just giving themselves a little more breathing room elsewhere.

But the savings aren’t the only reason I like them.

Let’s talk about light.

In November, around 3 p.m., when the leaves are gone and the trees are bare, the light can be surprisingly gorgeous for portraits. It’s softer, cleaner, and more interesting than the flat overcast light I end up working with far too often in June. People assume summer is automatically the best photo season because the weather is warmer and the days are longer, but warm doesn’t always mean better. For portraits, winter light can be incredibly flattering in a way that makes the whole gallery feel calm and polished.

There’s also something to be said for the atmosphere of the day itself. In June, especially in busy wedding areas, I’m often dealing with the reality of multiple vendors all using the same space at the same time. I’m not exaggerating when I say I’ve shared a parking lot with three or four other vendors in June. That means more congestion, more rushing, more waiting around, and more little logistical headaches that add up fast.

Winter weddings tend to move differently. There’s usually a little more breathing room. Less chaos. Fewer people competing for the same patch of space. As a photographer, that matters. It gives me more room to work, and it gives couples more room to actually enjoy the day instead of feeling like they’re being shuffled through it.

I don’t think winter weddings are automatically better than summer weddings, and I’m definitely not trying to convince every couple to get married in January. But if you’re open to a winter date, I think it’s worth considering seriously.

You may save money.

You may get better portrait light than you’d expect.

And you may avoid some of the summer wedding gridlock that makes even the simplest timeline feel crowded.

If you’re planning your wedding and wondering when to book, I’d say this: don’t rule out winter just because it’s not the “traditional” choice. Some of the best weddings I’ve photographed lately have happened when everyone else assumed the season was off-limits.

a.text:
Hi Gloria and Paul,

Yes, everything's okay, but I have news you're not going to love, so I'll just give it to you directly.

When we opened up the wall behind the sink and range yesterday, my electrician Dave found the original 1962 aluminum wiring running through the kitchen. That's what stopped us early. Aluminum branch wiring isn't up to code, and more importantly, it's a fire risk at the connections. I'm not willing to close a wall over it, and no inspector would sign off on it either.

Here's what it means for you:

**Cost:** About $2,800 on top of the $38,000. That covers replacing the aluminum runs in the kitchen with copper and upgrading the panel so it can handle the new circuits safely. I've had Dave price it out and I'm not marking it up. I'll send the line-item breakdown so you can see exactly where it's going.

**Schedule:** Cabinets get pushed back about a week and a half. The electrical work has to be done, inspected, and passed before the drywall goes back up, and drywall has to be done before cabinets. There's no way to shuffle around it.

I know your budget is already stretched and this is not what you were counting on. I'm sorry. I didn't see it coming either, and there was no way to know it was there until the wall came open. If it helps, we can talk about whether there's anywhere else in the scope we can trim to offset some of the cost, and I'm happy to break the $2,800 out on its own so it's not lumped into the next draw.

Call me anytime today or tomorrow and I'll walk you through it. I'd rather you hear all your questions answered than sit with this over the weekend.

Mike

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
I made a massive pricing mistake with Tallyup. 

I raised prices 40% overnight on everyone. 

In one week, I lost 30 of our 140 customers. 

Here’s why it happened, the fallout, and how I fixed it 🧵👇

You hear "raise your prices" constantly in the indie SaaS world. So I decided to do it. 

But I didn't just raise them for new users. I applied a 40% hike to every single active gym owner using Tallyup to track their member retention. 

No warning. Just a sudden price bump.

The backlash was immediate. 

Gym owners operate on tight margins and predictability. Slapping them with a 40% increase overnight completely broke their trust in me. 

Within 7 days, 30 of my 140 customers canceled. Instead of growing MRR, I was watching it bleed out.

I had to swallow my pride and fix it fast. 

Here is what I changed:
1. I immediately rolled back the price increase for all existing customers.
2. I sent a personal apology explaining my mistake.
3. I permanently grandfathered those early users into their original pricing.

The 40% higher price point is now in place, but it ONLY applies to new signups. 

My takeaway: "Raise your prices" is great advice, but execution is everything. Your early customers took a bet on you when you had nothing. Don't punish them for it.

b.text:
1/ i made a pricing mistake with Tallyup that i want to walk through honestly.

a few months ago i raised prices 40% on every existing customer, overnight, no warning.

lost 30 of my 140 customers in a week.

here's what happened and what i changed.

2/ the reasoning at the time felt solid: we were underpriced, new customers were paying more than legacy ones, and i wanted to close that gap fast.

so i just... did it. one email, effective immediately, applied to everyone regardless of how long they'd been a customer.

3/ the mistake wasn't raising prices. it was raising them the same way for everyone, with zero notice, and zero acknowledgment that loyalty should count for something.

longtime customers who'd been paying on time for a year got treated exactly like someone who signed up last month.

4/ the churn wasn't evenly spread either. it was disproportionately the customers who'd been around the longest — the ones who felt the increase as a breach of trust, not just a price change.

that's the part that stung. i lost the people i most needed to keep.

5/ what i changed:

grandfathered existing customers at their old price for a fixed period (instead of forever, but with real notice this time)

gave 60 days notice for any future price changes

separated "new customer pricing" from "existing customer pricing" as a permanent policy, not an afterthought

6/ the lesson: pricing changes are a trust event, not just a revenue lever. how you communicate it matters as much as the number itself.

30 customers in a week taught me that faster than any amount of thinking about it in advance would have.

7/ still building Tallyup solo, still sharing the numbers as they come. if you're thinking about a price increase, happy to talk through it before you hit send on that email.

setup: You're everyone at the startup. Yesterday's 40-minute outage was caused by a bad database migration during deploy.

a.text:
Hi all,

Quick update on yesterday's outage: everything is fully back to normal and has been since around 2:40pm. No data was lost, and no customer information was affected.

What happened: During a routine deploy around 2pm, a database update we were running caused one of our core tables to get "locked" for much longer than expected, which meant the app couldn't read or write data during that time. That's why things appeared down or unresponsive for about 40 minutes. We caught it, rolled back the change, and service was restored.

Why it happened: The update was more heavyweight than we anticipated, and we ran it as part of a normal deploy instead of scheduling it for a lower-traffic window where the impact would've been minimal or unnoticed.

What we're changing: Going forward, any database changes like this will run during a dedicated maintenance window, separate from regular deploys, with extra safety checks beforehand. This should prevent this specific type of issue from happening again.

If you fielded any customer questions or complaints yesterday, feel free to point them to this explanation, or send them my way if they want more detail. Sorry for the disruption, and thanks for bearing with us.

Let me know if you have any questions.

b.text:
Everything is back to normal, and has been since about 2:40pm yesterday. No data was lost, and nothing customers had saved or submitted was affected. If anyone is still hearing about problems from a customer, send it my way and I'll dig in.

**What happened**

Around 2pm we pushed a routine update to the app. Part of that update included a change to how one of our database tables is structured — normally a quick, invisible thing. This time it took far longer than expected and, while it was running, it effectively blocked anything else from reading or writing to that table. Because that table sits in the middle of a lot of what the product does, most of the app stopped responding.

We caught it quickly, but undoing a change like this safely takes some care, so total downtime was about 40 minutes.

**Impact**

For roughly 40 minutes, customers trying to use the app would have seen errors or pages that never loaded. Anything they tried to do during that window didn't go through, so some may have needed to redo an action. Nothing was corrupted or lost.

Thank you to everyone who fielded customer messages while we were heads-down on the fix — that made a real difference.

**What we're changing**

Changes of this type won't run during regular deploys anymore. They'll happen in a scheduled maintenance window, which means we can watch them closely, communicate ahead of time if we expect any disruption, and stop them safely if something looks wrong. We're also adding a check that flags this category of change before it ships, so it can't slip into a normal deploy by accident.

Happy to go deeper on the technical details with anyone who's curious — just ask. And if you're talking to a customer who wants an explanation, feel free to use the "what happened" section above word for word.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
When I walked into the emergency room for my first clinical rotation, I thought I was ready. I had read the textbooks and memorized the procedures. But nothing in a classroom prepares you for the noise, the smell, or the speed of it all.

On my second day, I was helping clean a deep cut on a man’s arm. He was shaking. I asked where his family was, and he said his wife was stuck in traffic. She wasn’t coming in time. I didn’t know what to say, so I just held his hand while the nurse cleaned the wound. He squeezed back tight. When it was over, he told me it helped to have someone there. I hadn’t done anything special, but it made me realize that sometimes just being present is enough.

Later that week, I was sent to restock gauze in the back. I could hear a code happening down the hall. Through the curtain, I heard the team counting compressions. One, two, three, four. It sounded urgent and heavy. I moved as fast as I could to get the supplies ready. I felt small standing there, but I knew every second counted.

The hardest part was a blood draw. There was a diabetic guy with really hard veins. I missed three times. I kept trying to find a spot, but I kept failing. He didn’t get mad. He just told me to take my time. I took a breath and tried again on the fourth try. When I finally got the blood, he smiled. I was happy I got it, but I also felt bad I made him wait that long.

This week showed me that nursing isn’t just about knowing the right answers. It’s about staying calm when things go wrong and being there for people when they’re scared. I want to keep learning how to do that better. This scholarship would help me focus on my studies instead of working extra hours. I’m ready to put in the work to become a nurse who can help people in moments like these.

b.text:
# My First Week in the ER

My hands were shaking the first time I put on gloves in the ER. I'd practiced skills in the lab a hundred times—blood draws, wound care, vital signs—but the lab never mentioned what you do when someone needs you to just be there.

Mr. Chen came in with a laceration on his forearm from a work accident. The wound needed cleaning, and his wife was stuck in traffic across town. He kept apologizing for being nervous, which made me want to cry a little. I pulled up a chair next to the stretcher and took his hand. I didn't do anything special—just held it while the nurse cleaned the wound. He squeezed my fingers pretty hard a couple times, but I didn't move. When his wife finally showed up, he thanked me like I'd saved his life. I'd just sat there.

That same shift, I was restocking the gauze station when I heard it. The code alarm. Then the counting, rapid and rhythmic, coming through the curtain behind me. *One, two, three, four...* The voices were calm but urgent in a way I'd never heard before. My hands kept moving—gauze, tape, saline—automatically, like I was on autopilot. But my brain was somewhere else, behind that curtain, understanding for the first time that everything we learn has a reason.

Then there was Marcus, the diabetic patient who had terrible veins. I missed the first stick. Missed the second. The third time, I felt him tense up, and I hated myself for it. But he told me to try again, that he believed I could do it. So I did. The fourth time, the needle went in clean, and I felt something shift inside me—not just relief, but something bigger. A kind of trust he gave me when he didn't have to.

I came home that first week exhausted and doubting everything. But I kept thinking about those moments. Not the ones where I knew what I was doing, but the ones where I just showed up and tried. Where showing up mattered as much as the skill.

I want to be a nurse because I've seen that it isn't about being perfect. It's about standing there when someone needs you to stand there. Holding a hand. Staying steady during chaos. Trying again when you've already failed. These are the things they can't teach you in a lab, but they're the things that matter most.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
When I first started shooting weddings in this area six years ago, I’ll admit I was a May-to-October purist. Like most people in the industry, I looked at winter as the off-season—a time to back up hard drives, update my website, and wait for the spring thaw. 

But over the last two years, something shifted. I ended up booking and shooting 11 winter weddings, and those 11 days completely changed how I look at the calendar. 

If you are currently staring at a venue's availability calendar trying to decide on a date, let me make a case for the colder months. Here is the honest, unfiltered truth about why I’ve grown to love winter weddings—and why they might actually be the best choice for your photos, your budget, and your sanity.

### 1. The Light is Superior (Seriously)
Everyone thinks summer is the prime time for portraits, but June light can be incredibly harsh and flat. If it’s overcast, the sky looks like a giant, boring softbox. If it’s sunny, we’re dodging squint-inducing glare and heavy shadows at noon. 

Winter light is different. Because the sun sits lower in the sky all day, the light has a softer, more dramatic quality. Specifically, the light through bare trees around 3:00 PM in November is unmatched. It creates this warm, directional glow that filters perfectly through the branches. It gives your portraits a rich, cinematic texture that you simply cannot replicate during a high-noon shoot in mid-July. 

### 2. We Aren't Fighting for Parking
During the summer peak, venues are turning over events like factory assembly lines. If you get married on a Saturday in June, chances are I’m arriving at your venue only to fight for a spot in the loading dock with three or four other vendors who are either rushing to pack up the afternoon event or scrambling to set up yours. The energy can feel frantic.

In November, January, or February? The vibe is entirely different. The venue staff is relaxed, I’m not sharing the parking lot with a fleet of delivery vans, and we actually have the breathing room to create without feeling like we’re on a stopwatch. That calmness trickles down into your entire day.

### 3. You Save Roughly 30%
Let’s talk about the math. Planning a wedding is expensive, and winter is the ultimate budget hack. On average, winter bookings run about 30% cheaper than peak-season dates. 

That 30% discount isn't just on the venue rental, either. Many caterers, florists, and, yes, photographers are more flexible with their pricing or packages during the winter months. Saving that chunk of your budget means you can invest more into the things you actually care about—like upgrading your menu, booking your dream band, or extending your honeymoon.

***

There is a quiet, cozy elegance to a winter wedding that gets lost in the summer rush. If you’re willing to embrace a chill in the air and a slightly earlier sunset, the payoff is a stress-free day, a healthier budget, and portraits with the kind of light most couples wait all year for. 

My calendar for the upcoming winter is starting to fill up, but I still have a few dates open. Let’s bundle up and chase that 3:00 PM golden hour together.

b.text:
# Why I Actually Like Photographing Winter Weddings Now

I’ll admit it: I used to think of winter weddings as the off-season.

After photographing 11 of them over the last two years, I’ve changed my mind. Winter weddings aren’t simply a backup option for couples who couldn’t get a June date. In some ways, they’re easier to photograph—and often easier on a wedding budget.

## The portrait light can be better

One of my favorite kinds of wedding light happens around 3 p.m. in November.

With the leaves gone, sunlight passes cleanly through the bare trees instead of breaking into uneven patches. It creates soft, directional light that gives portraits depth without feeling harsh. Honestly, I’ll take that over flat, overcast June light more often than I expected.

Winter does mean working with an earlier sunset, so the timeline matters. If portraits are important to you, we’ll usually plan them before the ceremony or immediately afterward. But when we make that window around 3 p.m. work, the results can be beautiful.

## Popular locations are actually usable

In June, I can arrive at a favorite portrait location and find three or four other wedding vendors sharing the same parking lot. That means crowded paths, people waiting for the same photo spots, and less flexibility if we need to adjust the schedule.

Winter is different.

The same locations are quieter, which gives us room to move and more freedom to use the best light. You’re less likely to have another wedding party just outside the frame, and we don’t have to rush through a spot because several other groups are waiting behind us.

That breathing room makes the portrait portion of the day feel calmer.

## Winter dates can cost about 30% less

For the couples I work with, winter bookings run about 30% cheaper. That can leave more room in the budget for an album, extra coverage, or another part of the wedding that matters to you.

Winter availability is also usually less competitive than peak-season availability. You still shouldn’t wait until the last minute—especially if you have a specific photographer or venue in mind—but you may have more options than you would for a Saturday in June.

## So, when should you book?

For a peak spring, summer, or fall date, booking as early as possible is still the safest choice. Those dates fill quickly in our area.

For a winter wedding, you may have more flexibility, but I’d still recommend reaching out once your venue and date are confirmed. An earlier booking gives us time to build the photography timeline around the limited daylight rather than trying to squeeze portraits into whatever time is left.

After 11 winter weddings in two years, I no longer see winter as the season couples settle for. The light can be better, locations are less crowded, and the savings are real. If you’re open to an earlier portrait schedule—and possibly bringing a warm coat for the walk between locations—it may be one of the smartest times of year to get married.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**Headline: Let’s give our middle schoolers the sleep they need — the 8:45 start plan works**

Last Tuesday, I stood in my kitchen at 7:10 a.m. holding a half-toasted pop-tart, yelling up the stairs for the third time for my 7th grader to get moving. He stumbled down 10 minutes later, hood up, eyes half-closed, and forgot his math workbook before sprinting for the bus. If you’re a Millbrook middle school parent (I’ve got a 6th and 8th grader, so I’m in the thick of it), this scene is probably familiar. It’s not laziness — it’s biology, and the school board’s proposed 8:45 a.m. start time isn’t a “free pass” for tired kids. It’s a common-sense fix backed by real data.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended for a decade that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m., because teens’ circadian rhythms shift during puberty. They naturally fall asleep later and wake up later, no matter how much we nag them about putting phones away at bedtime. Right now our middle schoolers start at 7:45, a full hour before their brains are really ready to focus.

We don’t have to guess if this works. The 2023 pilot at Lincoln Middle — a district our size just 15 miles away — saw a 14% jump in daily attendance and a 12% increase in first-period grades across all subjects after switching to an 8:50 start. Those aren’t abstract policy numbers: that’s fewer kids skipping first period because they can’t drag themselves out of bed, fewer kids napping through language arts, more kids actually present and learning when the bell rings.

I know the big objection everyone’s yelling about on the Millbrook Neighbors Facebook group: “What about the buses? We can’t afford new routes.” I was worried too, until I read the full proposal, not just the social media hot takes. The plan already re-tiers our bus routes, shifting the high school start 10 minutes earlier to stagger pickups. The transportation department’s already mapped every route: no extra buses, no added cost, no kid standing in the dark before 7:30 a.m. The longest bus ride only goes up by 4 minutes.

This isn’t about letting our kids sleep in to play video games. It’s about letting them show up to school awake enough to do the work. The school board votes next month — let’s tell them we’re ready to stop fighting our kids’ biology, and start supporting them.

(397 words)

b.text:
I’ve read the proposal closely, and I’m writing to say: the 8:45 start time isn’t just a schedule change; it’s a win for our kids.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends middle school start at 8:30 or later, and our own Lincoln Middle pilot proves why. When they shifted the bell, attendance went up and first-period grades followed. Those aren’t just numbers on a spreadsheet; they’re our kids walking into class ready to learn, instead of fighting to keep their eyes open.

I know the bus schedule concern parents often raise, and I used to worry about that too. But the board has already found a solution—they’re re-tiers the routes. It’s not a perfect fix, and no schedule will please everyone, but restructuring the buses is a manageable hurdle compared to the real cost of sleep-deprived students.

I’ve watched my own middle-schooler struggle through early mornings, and I’ve seen the difference a later start can make. I hope the board votes yes next month. Our kids’ health and learning are worth the adjustment.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
An 8-2 season deserves applause. It doesn’t mean the ending is above criticism.

The second-round state playoff loss will sting because this was a team they had beaten by 20 back in Week 3. That earlier result didn’t guarantee anything in the rematch. But it makes the question harder to shake: Was this a game they had to lose?

My answer is no. And the biggest reason is what happened to the running game in the second half.

It was working. They were down only three points. Yet they moved away from it as though the deficit demanded an entirely different offense.

Three points is a reason to stay patient, not abandon something the defense hasn’t stopped. Keep taking the yards. Make the opponent prove it can handle the run before deciding to do that job for it.

That isn’t a knock on Dez Kowalski. His 2,340 passing yards set a school record, an accomplishment that deserves to stand on its own—not get buried beneath the disappointment of the final game. He gave this offense a weapon few teams in school history have had.

But having a record-setting quarterback doesn’t make every situation a passing situation. A productive ground game helps a quarterback. Going back to it would not have been a vote of no confidence in Kowalski. It would have been a vote for what was working.

It’s easy to second-guess after a loss, and no play call comes with a guarantee. Staying with the run might not have changed the result. Still, the criticism here isn’t simply that the chosen approach failed. It’s that the score and the success on the ground offered little reason to leave that approach behind.

The players earned those eight wins. Kowalski earned his place in the record book. Neither should be diminished by one painful night.

But celebrating a good season doesn’t require pretending its final chapter was handled well. This team had a working running game and a three-point deficit. It needed patience more than a change of plans.

b.text:
The sting of Friday night won’t fade because the season ended. It’ll linger because the season ended unnecessarily.

Yes, the team finished 8-2. Yes, Dez Kowalski set a school passing record with 2,340 yards. But none of that salves a second-round playoff loss to a team this group already beat by 20 in Week 3. That’s not just losing; that’s stepping on a rake you saw lying in the grass.

Here’s the brutally simple reason they’re clearing out lockers instead of preparing for a quarterfinal: They abandoned the run in the second half. The ground game was grinding, controlling the clock, moving the chains—and they were only down three. Then, as if a switch flipped, it vanished. Instead of leaning on what worked, the play-calling went airborne, as if the record books needed padding and not a playoff win. That’s not on the kids. That’s a decision from the sideline, and it was the wrong one.

Kowalski’s arm is a weapon, but it’s not the only one. Championships aren’t won by forgetting what got you there. This loss wasn’t about talent or effort; it was about a staff that outthought itself at the worst possible moment.

Six years ago I wasn't sure we'd make it through the first winter. Now we're at the point where the weekend line goes out the door, and it felt like time to give this neighborhood a little more room to get their bread.

The best part of this announcement isn't the address, though. It's that Rosa and Jae — who have been with us for years and know this bakery inside and out — are stepping up to run Maple Street. They've earned it many times over, and honestly, I can't imagine handing the keys to anyone else.

Same bread, same pastry, same early mornings. New street.

Come see us March 2. First loaves out of the oven around 7am.

b.text:
Six years ago I walked into a lease on our first spot thinking I'd figure out the rest of the business part later. (I did not. I figured out the bread part. The rest is still in progress.)

Anyway. On March 2 we open Flour & Salt's second location on Maple Street.

And I'm not going to pretend this is a "new chapter" or a "milestone moment" post, but I will say this: Rosa and Jae are running it. They've been in our kitchen for three and four years respectively, they know our sourdough better than I do at this point, and they're the reason the first shop hasn't burned down. Giving them the Maple Street keys feels less like a promotion and more like finally admitting they earned it a while ago.

Maple Street will be the same menu, same early-morning bake schedule, same "we're out of croissants by 10:30 on Saturdays" energy. Our wholesale accounts stay where they are—Rosa and Jae are handling the new shop, I'm still here at the first one, and yes, you can still come yell at me about the rye.

Doors open 7 a.m. March 2. First weekend, no appointment needed, just maybe don't show up at 7:01 if you want something with butter in it.

To our first-neighborhood regulars who filled every Saturday line since day one: thank you for being stubborn enough to keep showing up to a bakery that was, frankly, not very good for about eighteen months. You made the second one possible.

See you on Maple.

— Nora
Flour & Salt, est. 2019

b.text:
For the last 18 months, the three of us at Ridgepoint have been splitting customer support between writing code, selling, and keeping the lights on. It’s not working anymore. We’re hiring our first support person.

Ridgepoint is a small SaaS company that helps small trucking dispatchers schedule loads. Our users are dispatchers at 5- to 20-truck fleets. They’re busy, they’re not always software people, and when something breaks—or they just can’t figure out the schedule view—they need help fast.

Here’s what you’d actually do day to day:

- **Own the support queue.** You’ll be the first person to see most tickets and the last person to resolve them. We don’t have a support playbook yet. You’ll write it.
- **Answer emails and take calls.** Our users are dispatchers with a driver waiting on a load assignment. You need to be calm, fast, and actually useful.
- **Troubleshoot bugs.** Sometimes it’s user error, sometimes it’s a real bug. You’ll reproduce it, gather details, and either fix it (if it’s data/setup) or hand it to us with enough context that we can patch it in hours, not days.
- **Train new customers.** We don’t have a formal academy yet. You’ll walk dispatchers through the product over Zoom, improvising based on how they actually run their board.
- **Tell us what’s broken.** You’ll be the voice of the customer in our Slack. If three people hit the same confusion this week, you’ll flag it so we can fix the UI instead of answering the same question forever.

This is not a role where you escalate everything and clock out. We’re three people. You’ll be the fourth. You’ll work directly with the founders, and you’ll have a lot of autonomy. But you’ll also have to figure things out without a 50-person support org behind you.

If you’re good at explaining software to non-technical people, you can stay cool when a customer is frustrated, and you want to join a tiny team where your work is visible immediately, send me a DM or drop a comment.

We’re moving fast on this because, frankly, our ticket backlog is embarrassing.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/ Opened up the ceiling on the Maple Ave kitchen job expecting a clean demo. Found a joist that had been notched almost 3/4 through, right at midspan, to run old knob-and-tube through it. Somebody's "quick fix" from probably 60 years ago.

2/ It hadn't failed yet, but it was close. Floor above had a soft spot the homeowners thought was just "old house settling." That notch was doing maybe 40% of the work a full joist should. One heavy Thanksgiving and it might've let go.

3/ Fix was sistering in new lumber alongside the damaged joist, screwed and glued, plus a couple blocks to redistribute load. Added about $1,400 and a day and a half to the job. Not fun to eat, but way cheaper than what happens if that floor drops mid-project.

4/ Real lesson: any time you're opening walls or ceilings in a house over 50 years old, budget contingency for structural surprises before you start, not after you find them. The house doesn't care what your quote said.

b.text:
Framing the Maple Ave kitchen took a turn when we started laying out the main span joists. Driven two nails through the pantry ceiling and hit solid timber where there should’ve been open space. Old beam from a demolished interior wall sitting right in our joist path.

Had to modify the layout, add structural hangers, and sister three joists around it. Came out to roughly $1,800 in materials and a full day of labor. Change order issued, signed, and we kept the timeline intact. Old Pittsburgh homes don’t read the blueprints, and neither should you wait to find out.

Real lesson from 15 years on site: never finalize joist layouts or final bids without poking a few diagnostic holes first. Transparency beats assumptions every time. Homeowners hiring remodelers, insist on exploratory inspections before breaking ground. Contractors, lock in your surprise-structural workflow early. Clean scopes start with clean discovery.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/ I made a pricing mistake at Tallyup.

I raised prices 40% for everyone overnight.

Within a week, we lost 30 of 140 customers.

2/ The mistake wasn’t raising prices.

We needed to charge more to keep building a sustainable product.

The mistake was treating existing customers the same as new customers — with no warning, no context, and no choice.

3/ For a gym owner, Tallyup is another operating expense.

A sudden increase doesn’t feel like “we’re improving the product.”

It feels like: “this tool I rely on just got more expensive without asking.”

That’s on me.

4/ What I changed:

- Existing customers are grandfathered or moved gradually
- Price changes get communicated before they happen
- New pricing applies to new customers first
- I explain what’s changing and why

5/ The lesson:

Pricing is not just a number on a checkout page.

It’s a trust decision.

Especially when you’re a small SaaS asking customers to bet on you long-term.

6/ I still believe Tallyup should be priced sustainably.

But I won’t make another “overnight” decision that asks customers to absorb the cost of my learning curve.

b.text:
Last year I raised Tallyup prices 40% overnight. We had 140 subscribers. In the following week, 30 canceled.  
It was a hard lesson in pricing communication and timing. Here’s what happened, what I changed, and where we’re at now. 🧵

The reaction was immediate. Some customers felt blindsided; others loved the product but needed more time to adjust their budgets. A few said they’d stay if there was a clearer path forward. That feedback stuck.

What I changed:
– Gave all existing customers 60+ days notice before any future increase, with their current rate locked in for a year.  
– Sent a clear “why” – the raise funds better support, a faster roadmap, and keeping Tallyup independent without VC pressure.  
– Added a mid‑tier so new users can grow into the price instead of getting hit all at once.

Today the base is more stable, and the customer feedback loop is healthier. If you’re considering a price increase: communicate early, give real runway, and make sure the value jump is undeniable.  
Would love to hear if anyone’s walked a similar path.
