setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
**Stop Mats Before They Start: Coat Care for Double-Coated and Curly Dogs Between Grooming Visits**

I can usually tell within a few minutes of meeting a dog whether the mats I’m finding started at home—and most of the time, they did. Not because owners don’t care, but because the usual instinct is backward. We want to get the dog clean first and deal with the coat later. With double-coated and curly breeds, that one decision can turn a small tangle into a felted pad that’s nearly impossible to brush out.

The mistake I see constantly is people bathing the dog first, thinking the water and shampoo will loosen the mats. It does the opposite. Wet matted fur just tightens up as it dries; it basically turns into a felt pad. Bathing first doesn’t loosen mats, it locks them in tighter. So if you’re doing a home bath, always brush before the bath, never after. Start with a completely dry coat and get the tangles out first. Then bath time is actually relaxing instead of a battle.

When you’re brushing, grab a slicker brush and use short line strokes, not circles. Little strokes in the direction the coat grows are much kinder and more effective than scrubbing away with your hand in circles. Circles tend to bunch the hair together and make the tangle worse. Work in small sections so you can see the skin, don’t just skim over the topcoat. And start in the spots where I find mats first: behind the ears and under the front legs. Those friction areas are where it always begins, especially on curly doodles, double-coated breeds, and any dog with a thick undercoat.

If you already see a mat forming, resist the urge to go at it with a brush or comb. Rub a little conditioner right into the mat with your fingers first. You can use a dog-safe detangler if that’s what you have on hand. Work it in gently and give it a minute to soften things up. Only after it feels like the hairs have some slip should you pick up the slicker or a wide-tooth comb and tease it apart a little at a time. If it’s tight to the skin, your dog flinches when you touch it, or it’s bigger than a pea, please stop and let me handle it. And please don’t go in with scissors—I’ve seen too many good dogs end up with a vet visit that way.

A few minutes a few times a week will always beat one long session right before your appointment. Pay extra attention behind the ears, under the front legs, around the collar, the tail, and the feathering on the backs of the legs. If your brush catches in the same spot every single time, that’s your early warning sign.

When in doubt, send me a photo or bring your pup by the salon. I’d much rather spend five minutes showing you how to work a spot out than have to shave a whole coat later.

b.text:
I've been doing this for years now, and I will say this one thing over and over again, so grab a coffee and just trust me on this: do not bathe your dog before you brush them. I know, I *know*. The logic seems to go, "Well, if I get the water in there it'll loosen up those tangles and they'll just slide right out." They will not slide right out. What actually happens is the water swells the fur, the mat gets damp, and it dries back down into a little felt pad that's tighter and tougher than the tangle that was there before. You just cemented the problem into the coat. I can fix a mat in the salon. I can't fix the one you just made worse on Saturday night and now can't get a comb through.

So here's the sequence, and I really wish someone had laid this out plain when I was still a rookie with a shih tzu at home: brush first, dry and dirty and all. Always first. Then you bathe. Then you blow it out or let it air dry and give it one more quick pass. For the double-coated folks out there with your aussies and collies and huskies, and my curly-coated regulars with the poodles and doodles and Portuguese water dogs, this matters even more because the undercoat is what traps moisture and what knots first.

When you're doing that pre-bath brush, grab a slicker brush, the one with the fine wire pins. And here's the thing people get wrong on technique: you're not doing big circular scrubbing motions. You're doing short little strokes, almost like you're making tiny checkmarks or lines through the coat. Big circles just drag the top layer over a tangle you're not reaching and make it look smooth while the mat underneath stays right where it is. Small strokes, a couple inches at a time, so you can actually feel what's going on at the skin.

Work in sections. Don't just start at the head and sweep the whole side of the body in one go. You're gonna miss things. And start where the mats actually *start*, which is behind the ears and under the front legs, the armpit area. Those two spots are where a dog moves the most, where friction is highest, where the coat gets crushed against a collar or the other shoulder when they walk. If you catch a tangle there on Tuesday, it's a loose little knot. By the next visit it's a disc you can barely slide a comb under, and then it's a shave-out, and then you're having one of those sad conversations with your dog in my grooming room about why their ear looks different.

And if you already feel that little disc forming, or you can see a knot getting snug, do not pick up the brush and just start hacking at it. Do not pick up a comb. Go get your leave-in conditioner, or even just a little detangling spray, and work it into that mat with your fingertips. Massage it in. Let it sit for a minute or two. You're trying to get slip down into the fibers so the knot has somewhere to go when you finally touch it with a tool. If you drag a slicker through a bone-dry mat, you're pulling on skin, and now your dog learns that brushing means pain and starts squirming and growling, and you both lose. Conditioner first, fingers, *then* the tool, and go slow.

This is not meant to replace what we do here, honestly. If your boy or girl is double-coated and brushing goes every other day at best, you're still gonna need that pro de-mat and coat health check every four to six weeks, maybe tighter in shedding season. What this is, is giving you the tools to keep a small tangle from becoming the mat I have to shave out on Friday. You save your dog the clipper, you save yourself the stress of a wrestling match in your kitchen, and I get to do the full breed trim I actually trained for instead of the emergency "I can't get a comb in anywhere" special.

If you're not sure whether what you're seeing is "fine, I'll deal with it next visit" or "oh no, this is getting tight and I need a hand," just text me a photo. Seriously. Take a pic, send it to the salon number, I'll tell you if you're in trouble or if a little conditioner and some patience will sort it out. No charge for that. I'd rather answer three texts than see your dog get a bald patch because you weren't sure how to start.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
After 8 years shooting around 35 weddings a year, I’ve seen it enough to say it: couples who ditch the shot list always end up with the best photos.

Take the Barrera wedding. It was supposed to be outdoors, and then the rain came in hard. We moved everything under the big pecan tree and just went with it. There was no shot list to cling to, so nobody was stressed about what we were missing. The photos from under that tree feel like the actual day—not a checklist.

If you’re planning a wedding, my advice is simple: give your photographer a few must-haves, then let the rest unfold. The best images come from what actually happens, not what you planned to happen.

b.text:
After 8 years and hundreds of weddings, I've noticed a pattern: the couples who hand me a shot list and then let go of it get better photos than the ones who stick to it minute by minute.

Case in point: the Barrera wedding.

Rain moved in about an hour before the ceremony. The outdoor setup they'd planned for months was suddenly underwater. We ended up moving everything under this massive old pecan tree on the property, no arch, no draping, no aisle runner in place, just the tree and everyone crowded in under it.

It wasn't the plan. It wasn't on any shot list. And it produced some of the best images I've shot all year.

Here's what I think is actually happening: a shot list is a security blanket. It's couples trying to control an outcome months in advance because the whole process feels overwhelming. Totally understandable. But weddings don't run on schedules, they run on weather, on emotions, on 80 people in one place at one time. The second something doesn't go as planned, a rigid list becomes a source of stress instead of a source of comfort.

The couples who do best are the ones who tell me what matters to them (grandma's ring, dad's reaction, the first look) and then let me handle the rest. That trust is what lets me actually see what's happening in front of me instead of checking boxes.

The Barrera's didn't get the wedding they planned. They got a better one. And they got photos they'll be looking at for the next 50 years.

If you're planning a wedding right now: bring me your must-haves, then let the day do what it's going to do. That's usually where the best photos are hiding.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
By the late May planting deadline this spring, I only had 60% of my corn and soybean acres in the ground. The rain simply wouldn’t quit, keeping the planters parked when we desperately needed them rolling. Now, the USDA has handed us the bill for that wet spring: a 22% hike in the prevented planting premium base rate for our region.

Let’s look at exactly what that means on paper. For my operation, that 22% increase translates to an extra $46,000 out of pocket this year. That is real money that should be going toward next year's inputs, machinery maintenance, or paying down the operating note. Instead, it’s vanishing into a premium hike we had zero control over. 

What makes this pill even harder to swallow is the math behind the current acreage caps. Because of how these caps are structured, this premium increase hits mid-sized, family-run operations disproportionately harder than the massive, consolidated outfits down the road. The largest operations have the scale to dilute the impact of the caps. Meanwhile, fourth-generation family farms like mine get caught directly in the crosshairs, bearing a heavier percentage of the financial burden just for trying to protect the acres we were physically unable to plant.

We need a structural fix to level the playing field, and we have a viable one on the table right now. Senate Bill 214 specifically addresses and adjusts these acreage caps so that family operations aren't unfairly penalized by a flawed system. 

If we want to keep family farming viable in this state, we need a safety net that actually fits the farms it is supposed to protect. Pick up the phone and call your state legislators. Tell them exactly what this 22% hike is costing your bottom line, and tell them we need them to pass SB 214.

b.text:
**Commentary: The 22% Prevented Planting Hike That’s Hitting Family Farms Hardest**  
By [Name], 4th generation corn & soybean farmer, [County] Farm Bureau Member

This year, the USDA raised prevented planting premium base rates 22% for our region. For my 1,200-acre corn and soybean operation, that’s $46,000 extra out of pocket before we even get a crop in the ground.

I only got 60% of my acres planted by the late May deadline. It rained 21 out of 30 days in April, then another 12 in the first half of May—saturated ground that turned to muck the second you drove a tractor over it, no three-day window of dry weather to get the planter through before the cutoff. That leaves 480 acres of my farm on prevented planting coverage this year.

Here’s the math that doesn’t add up, and it’s tied to the acreage cap built into current prevented planting rules. The cap sets a maximum number of acres you can carry prevented planting coverage for, and it hasn’t been adjusted upward since 2008. For the 5,200-acre operation three counties over, their total prevented planting eligible acres hit that cap years ago—so only a small slice of their operation is on the hook for the rate hike. For them, prevented planting coverage makes up less than 9% of their total crop insurance premium, so the 22% hike only hits that 9% slice.

For my family farm? Those 480 prevented planting acres are all under the cap, so the full 22% rate hike applies to every single one. That makes prevented planting coverage 40% of my total crop insurance bill this year. Proportionally, that’s more than four times the financial hit the big operation takes, just because my farm is smaller and the cap was set when corn was $4.20 a bushel and a new pickup cost $22,000.

This isn’t about begrudging anyone else’s coverage. It’s about fixing a rule that penalizes mid-sized family farms for not being big enough to outgrow the cap. That’s where SB 214 comes in. The bill, currently before the state Senate Agriculture Committee, would tie our state’s prevented planting acreage caps to each farm’s 10-year average planted acreage, instead of the stagnant one-size-fits-all threshold we’re stuck with now. It won’t roll back the USDA’s 22% rate hike—no state bill can do that—but it will make sure the cost of that hike is distributed fairly, instead of falling disproportionately on farms like mine.

I know most of us don’t have time to track every bill winding through the capital. I’m usually too busy fixing planters or checking soybean stands to sit through committee hearings. But this one matters, and the math is clear: right now, we’re paying more for the same coverage just because we’re family-sized.

If you’re as tired of that as I am, do two things this week. First, call your state senator and representative and tell them to support SB 214. Second, mark your calendar for the county farm bureau’s legislative town hall on June 18 at the fairgrounds. Both of our district’s legislators are coming, and they need to hear from the people writing the premium checks, not just the lobbyists who don’t have to plant in the rain.

I’ve heard a lot of talk over the years about “supporting family farms.” SB 214 isn’t talk. It’s a fix that would save my farm $46,000 this year, and save hundreds of other family operations across the state tens of thousands more down the line. That’s the kind of support we actually need.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
Hey everyone,

Last week, I finally launched the game after three years of nights and weekends. It’s out there now, and that’s still a little surreal.

First week sales: 412 copies. Not life-changing numbers, but enough to feel like this was worth doing. The game hit the front page of a small subreddit for about six hours, which was cool to see—thanks to whoever posted it.

I’ve been reading feedback, and one thing that keeps coming up is that the movement feels a little floaty. Honestly, they’re right. I’m already working on tweaks for that, and it’ll be in the 1.1 patch next month.

That’s about it for now. More updates as they come. Thanks for being here.

b.text:
It’s been a week since launch. Honestly still feels surreal typing that.

412 copies sold in the first seven days. I know that’s not earth-shattering by any stretch, but for a solo project I’ve been chipping away at on nights and weekends for three years, it’s way more than I let myself hope for. A bunch of you grabbed it day one, and seeing usernames I recognize from the devlog pop up in the purchases was genuinely the best feeling.

Mid-week the game hit the front page of a small subreddit for about six hours. Nothing huge, but enough to give the Steam page a noticeable spike and bring in some really thoughtful early feedback. One post in particular stuck with me: a player said the movement feels “floaty.” I went back and replayed a few levels trying to see it from their perspective, and… yeah, they’re right. The air control has a bit too much hang time, and the deceleration isn’t snappy enough. Can’t un-feel it now. So I’m addressing that directly in patch 1.1, which I’m targeting for next month. I’m tightening up the horizontal drag, reducing the midair turn radius, and adding a tiny bit of downward pull on the jump apex so the character feels more planted without losing the sense of weight I originally wanted. I’ll post detailed patch notes when it’s closer.

Other things on the 1.1 list: fixing a rare softlock in the third area, some menu navigation polish (controller support was a little janky on certain screens), and a few audio balance tweaks people pointed out. Nothing massive, just cleanup.

After that, I want to take a real breath and finally play some games I’ve been ignoring for years. Then I’ll figure out what’s next—whether that’s a content update, porting to another platform, or starting the next thing. For now, just patching and catching up on sleep.

Thanks to everyone who’s played so far and sent bug reports, reviews, or just a nice message. It means a lot.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
**Put Our Girls On Turf Too**

The last two seasons, my team has had nine games rained out or moved. Not delayed. Rained out or moved to another school's field because ours was underwater.

I coach girls soccer and track at the high school. I'm not a writer, I do it for the coaching stipend. But I'm tired of telling 16-year-olds we don't have a place to play because it rained yesterday.

Our field is the low grass field behind the school. It doesn't drain. After any real rain it's ankle-deep mud for three days. We practice in it, we slide all over it, and we try not to get hurt in it. We sprint around the swampy spots and we tell parents to bring boots to sit on the hill.

Last October one of my sophomores tore her ACL in a game. She wasn't hit. She was dribbling, stepped in a rut in our own field where the grass had washed out, and her knee went. She missed basketball season and she's missing this whole season. I coach track, too. I know what a bad surface looks like. That field is a bad surface.

This is a safety problem and it's a fairness problem.

The boys football field got turf in 2019. It's great. It drains, it's lined, they never lose a home game to weather. Our girls have been playing on a field that floods if you look at it wrong for six more years. If this were the football field, it would have been fixed a long time ago. Actually, it was.

I get it, turf isn't cheap. The board has a lot to pay for. But we are not asking for a stadium or lights or a press box. We are asking for a flat field that works when it rains. A field where we don't have to bus to the other team's school and call it a "home" game. A field where kids aren't worrying about what hole they're going to step in.

The school board votes on the facilities budget next week. Put turf for the girls soccer field in it.

Our girls deserve the same shot the boys have had since 2019 - to actually play their home games, on their home field, without getting hurt.

b.text:
Nine games. That's what we lost to water in the last two seasons. Nine games where I told my girls the field was unplayable, or worse—where we played on it anyway because there was nowhere else to go and they'd been training for it since August. I watched a midfielder try to cut left in a mud pit in November and just... keep sliding, losing three yards, getting up angry and soaking. I watched a sophomore tear her ACL in October stepping into a rut I'd flagged to the athletic department three times. She's got a surgery on her calendar and a semester off the pitch. Her senior season is over.

I'm not telling you this for sympathy. I'm telling you because next week the school board votes on the facilities budget, and I need you to look at what "facilities" means when half your athletes can't play on them for half the fall.

Let's be plain about the geography here. Our grass field—our *only* grass field for girls' soccer—floods because the drainage was never adequate and the grade is wrong and every November we play on what is functionally a creek bed with grass sticking out of it. You could argue we've made it work. I've made it work. My assistant and I have spent more November afternoons pushing water off the pitch with brooms than I care to admit. But "make do" has a body count, and right now it's one blown knee per season minimum, and nine cancelled games means nine fewer chances to be scouted, to compete, to not forfeit a match on a Tuesday because some other field opened up on short notice.

Now. Here's the thing I want the board to answer to their own faces: the boys' football field got turf in 2019. Same athletic budget. Same drainage problem. A decade of complaints about mud, about ruts, about kids blowing out a knee in November—and they fixed it. Six figures, done, problem solved. And I'm glad, genuinely, I'm glad for Coach Daniels and his players. But I have to ask: why does the fix require four years and three budget cycles when the players are girls in cleats instead of pads? Why does a girl's ACL cost less to prevent than a boy's?

I don't want to make this a fight. I don't want parents pitting one team against another at a board meeting in a fluorescent-lit room in March. But I will not pretend the timeline is an accident. The drainage report for the football field was the same report—*the same report*—that listed our field as the second priority. Second priority. We are still second priority six years later.

What I'm asking for is not a favor. Turf installation on the girls' field is roughly in line with what was spent on the football field in 2019. It is a line item. It is a one-time cost that stops me from spending October writing rain-out notices and stops a girl's parents from getting a phone call from me at 6 a.m. saying their daughter is going to the hospital. It means my track kids get a dry warm-up area in the spring. It means the JV game against Whitmore next November actually gets *played*.

The board gets to vote on the budget. The voters get to call them. I just want my girls to have a field that holds a game.

I'll be at the meeting in March. I'll be there with two of my assistants and at least three players' parents. You can talk to us after, if you want. We'll be the loud ones in the gymnasium with our cleats still muddy.

—Coach [Name], Head Coach, [High School] Girls Soccer & Track

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
Somewhere around interview 200 I started noticing a pattern I can't unsee now.

Almost every candidate asks some version of "what does success look like in this role?" Fine question. Safe question. I've heard it so many times I could answer it in my sleep, and honestly the answer is usually whatever the hiring manager wrote in the req.

The candidates I end up fighting for ask a different one: what's the last thing this team tried that didn't work?

Had it happen last month. Ops analyst role, second round with our director of transportation. Candidate asks him what the team's last real miss was. He tells her about a route optimization pilot we ran in the Southeast — good software, decent data, died about five months in because the dispatchers never trusted the output and kept overriding it by hand.

She didn't nod and move on. She asked whether the dispatchers were involved before the pilot or after it was chosen. (After.) She asked if anyone tracked which overrides actually saved money versus which were just habit. (No.) Then she said something like: so the tool wasn't really the problem, you had a trust problem and no way to prove either side was right.

My director sat back in his chair. That was the whole interview, right there. She'd figured out in four minutes what took us five months and a written-off license fee.

Here's why I think it works. Asking about a failure tells you what the team actually does when things go sideways — do they blame the vendor, blame the frontline, or look at their own process? You learn whether the org is honest. You learn what kind of resistance you'll be walking into. And you find out whether your future boss can talk about a loss without getting defensive, which is genuinely one of the most useful things you can know before you sign.

It's also the hardest question to fake your way through as an interviewer. "What's our culture like" gets you the poster on the wall. "What did we get wrong recently" gets you the truth.

Job seekers: ask it. Hiring managers: have a real answer ready. The vague ones are telling on themselves.

b.text:
After roughly 200 interviews, one question has become a signal I pay attention to:

“What was the last project your team worked on that didn’t go well?”

The strongest candidates don’t just ask what success looks like. They want to know what happens when the plan falls apart.

In logistics, that’s worth understanding before you accept an offer.

The conversation might go something like this:

“We rolled out a new scheduling process, but it created more work for the warehouse team. We eventually pulled it back.”

“Were the warehouse supervisors involved before the rollout?”

“Not early enough.”

“What changed about how you planned the next one?”

That last question is the interesting part. They’re not just looking for a company willing to admit a mistake. They’re checking whether admitting it led to anything different.

As a recruiter, I also think this is a question we need to make room for. If I don’t know the answer, I should connect the candidate with someone who does—not turn it into a story about how every setback makes us stronger.

We ask candidates to tell us about a time they failed and what they learned.

It’s reasonable for them to ask us the same thing.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The couples who ditch the shot list always end up with the best photos.

I don’t say that as a photographer who dislikes planning. I’ve been a full-time wedding photographer in the Texas Hill Country for eight years, and I shoot around 35 weddings a year. In that time, the pattern is consistent: a long shot list turns a wedding day into a checklist. Trust turns it into a story.

The Barrera wedding—the one that got rained out—is the example I keep coming back to.

The original setup wasn’t going to work, so we moved everything under the pecan tree. No one was thinking about a posed list at that point. We were responding to the weather, the light, and the people right in front of us. What could have been a ruined timeline became the most memorable part of the day—and the photographs from under that tree are the ones that tell the real story of the day.

If you’re a couple researching photographers: bring your priorities, your timeline, and your trust. Then let your photographer watch for the moments you didn’t plan.

If you’re a vendor: the most valuable thing we bring to a wedding day isn’t a rigid plan. It’s the ability to adapt and the willingness to be present for what’s actually happening.

The best photos are never the ones on the list.

#WeddingPhotography #TexasHillCountry #WeddingVendors

b.text:
Over eight years shooting roughly 35 weddings a year here in the Texas Hill Country, I’ve learned something consistent: the couples who willingly set aside their detailed shot lists usually end up with the most powerful photos.

Shot lists are fantastic for keeping the day on track and making sure you don’t miss the cake cutting or the grand exit. But they’re pretty bad at capturing what actually happens. They can’t predict spontaneous laughter, an unexpected guest hug, or how the weather completely changes the mood of a venue.

Last month, we saw this play out perfectly during the Barrera wedding. We had a solid, printed timeline. Then, right before the ceremony, a heavy Texas downpour rolled in. Instead of stressing over missing checklist items, we made a quick call and moved everything under a sprawling old pecan tree. 

What unfolded in those next few hours wasn’t scheduled. It was the quiet conversations while waiting for the rain to ease, the intimate way families grouped together under the branches, and the soft, diffused light filtering through wet leaves. That unscripted moment didn’t just save the day—it became the emotional centerpiece of their gallery.

To the couples still drafting their photography checklists: keep the true must-haves, but leave room for flexibility. Trust your photographer to capture the day as it unfolds. And to my fellow vendors: when you build partnerships based on adaptability rather than rigid expectations, operations run smoother and results speak for themselves. You’ll still get your essentials. But you’ll also get the images that actually feel like your story.

How do you balance planning with spontaneity on event days? I’d love to hear how you and your teams navigate the unexpected.

#WeddingPhotography #TexasHillCountry #WeddingVendors #EventPlanning

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
**Confessions of a Peak-Season Photographer: Why I Actually Want You to Book a Winter Wedding**

After six years of shooting weddings in this metro area, I know the drill. Everyone wants a Saturday in June or September. For a long time, I was right there with you, secretly dreading the dark, cold days of the off-season. But over the last two years, I’ve shot 11 winter weddings, and my perspective has completely shifted. 

If you’re currently staring at a calendar trying to decide when to book your date, here is the unfiltered, behind-the-lens truth about why I actually prefer winter weddings now—and why you should seriously consider one, too.

**Your budget goes a lot further.**
Let’s talk numbers first. Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for the couple across the board. Venues know it’s the off-season, and they price accordingly. That 30% drop isn’t just a minor discount; it’s the difference between stressing over your catering minimum and effortlessly upgrading to the premium bar package you actually wanted. 

**The 3 PM lighting is unbeatable.**
As a photographer, light is everything. People assume summer guarantees great photos, but a flat, overcast June afternoon gives me dull, shadowless light that I have to work hard to make interesting. Compare that to a crisp November day. Around 3 PM, the sun sits low in the sky. When that late-afternoon light filters through the branches of bare trees, it creates a moody, dimensional backdrop for portraits that you simply cannot get in the middle of summer. It’s dramatic, it’s striking, and it makes my job incredibly easy.

**You actually get the venue to yourselves.**
In peak season, popular venues are booking machines. In June, I am routinely sharing the loading dock and parking lot with three or four other vendors from different weddings. You’re rushing through your timeline because the next couple’s florist is waiting to unload their truck, and the venue staff is exhausted from flipping the dining room. In the winter? The venue is yours. We have the space and the time to breathe, which means your photos look relaxed, not rushed.

I’m not going to give you a cheesy spiel about how "love is beautiful in every season." I’m just telling you that from a logistical, financial, and photographic standpoint, a winter wedding is a massive cheat code. 

If you’re on the fence about a November, January, or February date, take the leap. Head over to my contact page, and let’s get your winter date locked in.

b.text:
**Why Winter Weddings Are My New Favorite Secret**

When I first started shooting weddings six years ago, my calendar looked exactly how you’d expect: packed back-to-back from May to October, and totally quiet by December. Summer was the undisputed king of the wedding season. But lately, things have shifted. Over the last two years, I’ve shot 11 winter weddings right here in our metro area, and to my own surprise, they have become some of my absolute favorite days to photograph. 

If you are currently staring at a calendar and trying to decide when to book your date, I want to give you a few very specific reasons why you shouldn't write off the off-season. 

First, let’s talk about the light. As a photographer, light is everything, and there is a massive misconception that summer automatically equals beautiful photos. Honestly? I will take 3:00 PM in November over a flat, overcast Saturday in June any day of the week. Because the sun sits lower in the sky during the colder months, the afternoon light filtering through the bare winter trees creates a crisp, directional, and undeniably romantic glow. It gives your portraits an incredible depth that you just can't get when the sun is blazing directly overhead in the middle of summer. 

Then there is the sanity factor of your actual wedding day. During peak season, popular venues are often absolute zoos. I can’t tell you how many times in June I’ve had to fight for space in a venue parking lot with three or four other vendors, dodging catering trucks and florists just to load in my gear, while the couple feels rushed through a chaotic timeline. In the winter, all of that frenzy disappears. We have space to breathe, the venue staff isn't burned out, and you get everyone's undivided attention. The entire vibe of the day is noticeably more relaxed.

Finally, we have to talk about the budget. On average, booking a winter wedding runs about 30% cheaper for the couple than fighting for a prime summer date. That is a massive chunk of your budget that you get back. It's money that can be redirected toward upgrading your open bar, booking that dream honeymoon, or—dare I say it—splurging on the photography package you really want without stretching your wallet. 

I’m certainly not here to knock summer weddings; I’ve spent six years capturing them and will always love them. But if you want incredible portrait light, a relaxed timeline without a crowded parking lot, and a lot more mileage out of your budget, a winter wedding might just be the best decision you make.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
**When the Cap Doesn’t Fit**

This spring, I planted 60% of my acres. The other 40% sat underwater. It wasn’t a management decision—it just kept raining, and the late May final planting date came and went. Like a lot of you, I turned to prevented planting coverage, the safety net we pay for precisely because years like this happen.

Then the premium bill arrived. USDA raised the base rate for prevented planting in our region by 22% this year. For my operation, a fourth-generation corn and soybean farm, that increase alone adds $46,000 to my insurance cost. Forty-six thousand dollars. That’s a hard number to swallow after losing nearly half my planting window.

But the premium hike isn’t the whole story. What makes it truly lopsided is the acreage cap baked into the prevented planting program. That cap doesn’t scale with the size of your operation—it’s a fixed number of eligible acres per crop. On my farm, the cap already covers a big slice of my total ground before a single seed goes in. So a 22% rate hike on those capped acres cuts deep, eating into a much larger share of my potential revenue than it does for the 5,000-acre operation down the road. They might hit the same cap, but for them it’s a fraction of their total acres; for family-scale farms like mine, it’s a direct hit to our ability to keep the doors open.

The math is simple: a one-size-fits-all cap punishes smaller farms disproportionately, year after year, and a premium spike like this rubs salt in the wound. We need an acreage cap that reflects the reality of family farm scale, not just the averages for giant operations.

There’s a fix on the table. Senate Bill 214 restructures the prevented planting acreage cap so it’s proportional to actual farm size. That means your premium costs would align with your real exposure, not an arbitrary cutoff that treats a half-section farm the same as a 10,000-acre conglomerate. SB 214 gives family operations a fair shake, and it’s the kind of common-sense adjustment our state legislators can get behind.

Please take five minutes to call or email your state senator and representative. Tell them you’re a farmer, that the 22% prevented planting hike just cost your neighbor $46,000 on a rain-wrecked spring, and that SB 214 is the right tool to stop the cap from capping us out of business. If enough of us speak up, we can make sure the safety net actually catches the farms that need it most—ours.

b.text:
**A 22% Hike, 60% of My Acres, and a Bill Worth Your Phone Call**

This year USDA raised the base rate on prevented planting coverage in our region by 22 percent. On my operation that works out to roughly $46,000 more than I paid last year for the same protection.

I'd have paid it grudgingly in a normal spring. This wasn't a normal spring. The rain started the second week of April and did not quit in any meaningful way until it was too late to matter. By the late May final planting date I had 60 percent of my acres in the ground. The other 40 percent sat there with standing water in the low spots and mud you couldn't drive a four-wheeler across, let alone a planter. Anybody farming west of the river knows exactly what I'm describing because you were looking at the same thing out your own kitchen window.

So the year I actually needed prevented planting coverage is the year the premium jumped by nearly a quarter. That's the first thing I want people to sit with.

Here's the second thing, and it's the reason I'm writing.

The rate hike doesn't land evenly. The way the acreage caps are structured, the full increase applies across every acre on an operation my size. Once an operation crosses the cap threshold, the effective cost per acre starts coming down. The result is that the two large operations that farm on either side of me, both good neighbors, both running several times my acreage, are seeing a smaller percentage increase in their total premium cost than I am. Same county. Same rain. Same deadline. Same 40 percent left unplanted. Different bill.

I ran the numbers with my crop insurance agent, who I trust and who didn't argue with me. On a per-acre basis I'm paying meaningfully more for the same coverage than the operations next door. Not because I'm a worse risk. Because I'm smaller.

I don't begrudge the bigger outfits. They didn't write the rules. But a program that's supposed to help farmers stay in business through a bad spring shouldn't be quietly structured so that the fourth-generation operation on 1,200 acres carries a heavier share than the one on 6,000. That's backward, and I don't think it's what anybody intended when the caps were drawn up.

SB 214 would fix the acreage cap. It adjusts how the threshold applies so the premium increase falls proportionally instead of piling onto the operations least able to absorb it. It doesn't take anything away from the larger farms. It doesn't touch the coverage itself. It just corrects the math so that a 22 percent hike is a 22 percent hike for everybody, not 22 for some and less for others.

The bill has been sitting in committee since February. I'm told it's stalled less from opposition than from nobody making much noise about it. That part we can do something about.

If you farm in this county and you had ground you couldn't plant this spring, you already know what I'm talking about. If you didn't have that problem this year, you will eventually, and the cap will be waiting for you when you do.

Call your state senator. Call your representative. Their numbers are on the back page of this newsletter. Tell them you farm here, tell them how many acres you got planted by the deadline, and tell them you want SB 214 out of committee and onto the floor. You don't need to be eloquent. You need to be one more voice they can't ignore.

I'll be at the county meeting on the 14th. If you want to compare premium statements, bring yours. I'll have mine.

a.text:
**Subject: Launch week is over — here’s what actually happened (no big takeaways, I swear)**

Hey everyone,

If you’re reading this, I’ve finally stopped refreshing the Steam sales dashboard every 45 seconds, which feels like a win in itself. It’s been seven days since my first commercial launch dropped — three years of nights, weekends, skipping friend’s birthdays, and debugging collision at 2am all boiling down to this very weird, very unglamorous week.

First off, the numbers: 412 copies sold in the first seven days. I set a totally arbitrary, low-stakes goal of 100 copies when I started this, so 412 feels kind of insane, honestly. I spent $0 on marketing — just posted the trailer here, tweeted at three indie curation accounts that never replied, and crossed my fingers that someone would care.

The big surprise was hitting the front page of that small indie game subreddit I’ve lurked on since I started this project — you know the one — for about 6 hours on Wednesday. I found out because my Discord (which had 12 people in it pre-launch, all my IRL friends who let me bug test on their laptops) blew up while I was at my day job. I spent my entire lunch break refreshing the thread, half-convinced someone was gonna call out that one cave level texture I forgot to upscale. Most of the week’s sales came from that, I’m pretty sure. Shoutout to whoever crossposted the trailer — I owe you a coffee, or a Steam key for whatever my next game is, whichever you prefer.

The best feedback, though, was a Steam review that dropped on day two that just said “movement feels floaty” and nothing else. You’re right! That is 100% a valid complaint. I tuned the movement on my old work monitor that has like 20ms of uncalibrated input lag, so after three years of playing it that way, I didn’t even notice. I’ve been messing with acceleration curves and coyote time all week, and it’s already feeling way tighter. That’s gonna be the big focus for 1.1, which I’m aiming to put out next month.

1.1’s also gonna have a few other small things people have been asking for: rebindable controller buttons (I know, I know — how did I forget that? Solo dev brain rot is real), a fix for the final boss music cutting out if you skip the pre-fight cutscene, and that weird bug where the main character’s hair clips through their hat if you sprint up stairs. Nothing game-changing, just stuff that makes the whole thing feel a little more polished.

I don’t have some big, profound “lesson learned” to wrap this up with, if I’m being honest. Launch week was messy. I stayed up till 3am Tuesday fixing a crash that only happened on Windows 10 21H2, I forgot to eat on Wednesday because I was replying to Reddit comments, I cried a little on Thursday when someone left a review saying they played it with their 8-year-old kid and beat the final level together. It was just… a week. A really cool, really stressful week.

Next week I’m taking one (1) full day off to do nothing game dev related — no stats, no bug reports, no tweaking jump height at 10pm. Then I’m diving straight into 1.1, and I’ll probably post a devlog next week about the movement tuning process if anyone’s curious about the nitty gritty of adjusting acceleration curves without making the controls feel slippery.

If you bought the game, thank you. Seriously. If you left a review, good or bad, thank you — even the one that called the pixel art “mid” (you’re not wrong, I’m still learning). If you’re a fellow indie dev waiting for your own launch, it’s okay if it’s not perfect. It’s just a launch.

Alright, I’m gonna go heat up a frozen pizza and not look at my code editor for at least 8 hours. Talk soon.
[Your Name]

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
A note about wedding cakes

I’ve been putting off writing this because I knew it would feel a little like saying goodbye to something sweet. For the last few years we’ve taken a handful of custom wedding cakes each year, and every single one was an honor. When someone trusts a tiny bakery with one of the biggest days of their life, it means something. I have loved the consultations, the tasting plates, the sketches, the moment a couple tries a bite and their whole face changes. That part never got old.

But here’s the honest, slightly tired truth: behind each of those cakes was about fourteen hours of free consult and tasting time before we ever turned on the mixer. Emails back and forth, a sit-down consult, a tasting, flavor tweaks, sourcing special ingredients, planning delivery. None of that was charged for, because we always wanted to be generous. We know how quickly wedding costs add up, and saying yes to those custom cakes felt like the right thing to do. The thing is, in a three-person shop, fourteen hours is not small. It’s most of a work week for one of us. It’s two or three days where my attention is split, and I’m already up at four most mornings trying to make sure the case is full by seven.

Then this year, three weddings canceled at the last minute. That isn’t a complaint, by the way—weddings change, life happens, and I genuinely hope each of those couples is doing okay. But by the time those cancellations came in, we had already bought the butter, the vanilla, the fruit, sometimes the sugar flowers. That money was already spent, straight out of our pocket, with no cake to sell and no invoice to send. Those three hurt in a way I wasn’t quite expecting.

More than the money, though, the wedding cakes were quietly pulling us away from the thing that actually keeps this little bakery alive: the everyday case. The sourdough, the croissants, the morning buns, the cookies, the galettes, the coffee cake. Those are what pay the rent, keep the lights on, and let us pay our small team. When our attention went to wedding cakes, the daily baking started to feel rushed. I could feel it, and I didn’t like it. We never want the thing you pick up on a random Tuesday to feel like an afterthought, because it isn’t. It’s the heart of this place.

So after a lot of conversations—some of them at four in the morning, standing in the back with flour on our aprons—the three of us have decided to stop taking custom wedding cake orders.

I want to be clear about what this doesn’t mean. We’re not going anywhere, and we still love a celebration. Our cake case is still full of the cakes we make every day, and we’re always happy to set aside a whole one for you, write a little message on top, or pack up a few boxes of pastries for a wedding morning or a rehearsal dinner. If you’re getting married and you want us to feed your people a stack of croissants or a pile of cookies, please come see us. We would be so happy to be part of that. It’s the fully custom wedding cakes—the long consults, the tasting appointments, the flavors we don’t normally make—that we’re stepping away from.

To the couples who trusted us with their wedding cakes: thank you. It was a privilege we don’t take lightly. We learned so much, and a few of those cakes are still some of my favorite things we’ve ever made. I’m going to miss that part more than I expected.

But I’m also really looking forward to putting that time back into the case, back into the bread, back into the pastries you grab on your way to work. Thank you for supporting a small bakery, for understanding when we have to make a hard call, and for keeping us busy enough that we have to protect the everyday magic. See you at the counter.

b.text:
# A Little Change Around Here

I've been putting off writing this one, which is usually a sign I should just sit down and do it. So here I am, coffee in hand, flour probably still on my sleeve.

We're not going to be taking custom wedding cake orders anymore.

I want to tell you why, because you've been good to us and you deserve more than a line on the order form. The truth is that wedding cakes, as much as I've loved making them, were quietly pulling the shop in a direction we couldn't keep up with. Every cake starts long before I ever turn on the oven — the consultations, the tastings, the back-and-forth about buttercream shades and how many tiers and whether the flowers should be real. By the time a single cake is done, we've usually put somewhere around fourteen hours into it that no one ever sees. And with three of us running this place, those are hours that have to come from somewhere.

Where they came from was the everyday. The morning loaves, the case full of scones and tarts, the thing you grab on your way to work. That's the part of the bakery that actually keeps our lights on, and it's the part I love most — the regulars, the small daily rhythm of it. When I was buried in wedding planning, that case suffered, and so did I.

I'll be honest about the other piece too. This year we had three weddings cancel at the last minute, and each time we'd already bought the ingredients and blocked the time. That kind of thing happens, I understand it, life is complicated and weddings especially so. But for a shop our size, absorbing that a few times over is a real hit, and it made me look hard at whether this was something we could keep doing well.

So we're stepping back from it, at least for now. If you've got a wedding coming up, I'm genuinely happy to point you toward a few people I trust who do beautiful work and have the setup for it. Just ask.

And please know — we're not going anywhere, and neither is the sweet stuff. We'll still do birthday cakes and the smaller celebration cakes you order ahead. We'll still have the case full every morning. If anything, pulling back on the big commitments means we get to do the everyday things better, which was always the whole point.

Thanks for reading this far, and for being the reason there's a shop to write about. See you at the counter.

— Maggie

*(and the whole crew)*

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/5
I raised Tallyup’s prices 40% on everyone overnight.

We lost 30 of our 140 customers in a week.

Tallyup helps gym owners track member retention. That irony isn’t lost on me.

Here’s the pricing mistake I made—and what I changed.

2/5
I treated two decisions as one:

• Should Tallyup cost more?
• Should every existing customer pay more immediately?

Even if the answer to the first was yes, that didn’t automatically justify the second.

3/5
I can’t neatly separate the impact of the higher price from the impact of changing it overnight.

That’s part of the mistake. I changed both at once.

“Customers won’t pay more” would be too convenient a lesson to take from this.

4/5
What I changed:

[Add the actual changes you made: the new pricing, who it applies to, how much notice customers get, or how you handled affected customers. Include only what happened.]

5/5
My takeaway isn’t “never raise prices.”

It’s that the rollout is part of the pricing decision—not an admin detail to figure out afterward.

Sharing the uncomfortable part of building in public, not just the launches.

b.text:
**1/** Two weeks ago I raised prices 40% on every Tallyup customer. Overnight. No warning.

I lost 30 of 140 customers in a week.

Here's what happened and what I'd do differently. 🧵

**2/** The logic felt airtight at the time.

I'd shipped a lot. Support was eating my week. I was underpriced compared to everyone I benchmarked against. Every pricing post I'd ever read said "just raise your prices."

So I did. Flipped the switch on a Tuesday night.

**3/** What I actually did wrong wasn't the 40%.

It was that I did it to existing customers, with no notice, with no explanation, and with nothing new in their hands that day.

I gave people a bill increase and called it a price change. Those are different things.

**4/** The cancellations weren't angry, which was worse.

Most were some version of "no hard feelings, this just isn't in the budget at that number." A few said they would have stayed if I'd asked first.

Gym owners run on thin margins. I knew that. I priced like I didn't.

**5/** The other thing I underestimated: existing customers didn't buy the current product.

They bought the thing I was selling when they signed up, at the price I promised. Changing both sides of that deal unilaterally broke something I couldn't fix with a discount code afterward.

**6/** What I changed:

New pricing applies to new signups only. Everyone who was here before the change is back on what they were paying, and I told them so directly.

**7/** For future increases:

— 60 days notice, sent by me, not a system email
— ships alongside something they asked for
— existing customers get a grandfathered tier, permanently
— I ask a handful of customers first instead of benchmarking against strangers

**8/** The part I'm still sitting with:

I wasn't underpriced for my market. I was underpriced for the market I wished I was in. Those are very different problems and raising prices only solves one of them.

**9/** Reaching out to the 30 this week. Some will come back, some won't, and that's fair.

Posting this because "raise your prices" is advice I took without the second half of the sentence. The second half is *how*.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
# A 15% Cut to Apprenticeship Funding Is a Bad Deal for Everyone

Let me lay this out plain. The state wants to cut apprenticeship funding by 15%. I'm a third-year electrical apprentice, and I'm here to tell you that's a mistake. Not because it hurts me personally, but because the numbers don't add up.

Here's what an apprenticeship actually does.

My cohort started with 24 people. Twenty-one of us made it through and are now working journeyman jobs or on our way there. That's not a fluke. That's what a real program with real funding looks like. Nobody handed us anything. We worked full days and went to class on top of it. But the structure was there, and the structure works.

Now let's talk money, because that's what this cut is really about.

An apprentice starts out around $19 an hour. By the time you top out as a journeyman, you're making around $46 an hour. That's not minimum wage. That's a wage you can raise a family on, buy a house on, pay taxes on. And here's the part the legislators should pay attention to: people get off state assistance programs fast when they're earning like that. We stop being a cost to the state and start being a source of revenue. We pay in instead of taking out.

Here's the number that matters most. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to the average public subsidy for a four-year college grad who finishes, which runs around $48,000. So for the price of one college grad, the state can put more than three journeymen to work.

Three skilled workers for the price of one. And these are workers the state actually needs. You can't outsource wiring a building. You can't ship a hospital's electrical system overseas. This work stays here.

So what does a 15% cut actually buy the state? A little bit of savings on paper. What does it cost? Fewer people in one of the cheapest, most effective job programs there is. More people stuck in low-wage work or on assistance. Fewer skilled tradespeople right when we're already short on them.

That's not saving money. That's stepping over dollars to pick up dimes.

I'm not an English professor. I'm an electrician. But I know a bad deal when I see one, and this is a bad deal. Apprenticeships take people with nothing but willingness to work and turn them into skilled, taxpaying professionals for about a third of what college costs the public. That's exactly the kind of thing the state should be putting more money into, not less.

To the legislators reading this: look at the numbers again before you vote. Twenty-one out of twenty-four. Fourteen thousand versus forty-eight. Nineteen dollars to forty-six an hour. Those numbers make the case better than I ever could.

Don't cut what's working.

*— A third-year IBEW electrical apprentice*

b.text:
Stop the 15% Cut to Apprenticeship Funding

I am a third-year electrical apprentice with the local IBEW union. I am writing to oppose the proposed 15% cut to state apprenticeship funding. This cut would hurt workers who are trying to build a career.

Look at my cohort. We started with 24 apprentices. 21 of us finished the program and are now working journeyman jobs. That is a success rate most programs can only dream of.

The pay is good too. Apprentices start around $19 an hour. Once we finish and become journeymen, we top out around $46 an hour. Because we earn good wages early, people get off state assistance programs fast. We become taxpayers instead of relying on help.

The costs show why this matters. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to the average public subsidy per four-year college grad who finishes, which is something like $48,000. We cost less to train and we get to work sooner.

Cutting this funding is a mistake. It blocks people from learning a trade and earning a living wage. The state saves more money by keeping us supported than by cutting us off. Please do not vote for this cut.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
# Prevented Planting Premium: A Reminder That Family Farms Need Fair Policy

This spring, my fields stayed underwater through late May. By the time the soil dried enough to plant, I'd crossed the prevented planting deadline. I ended up getting only 60% of my usual acreage in the ground.

That's the reality of farming in our region some years. What's less inevitable is the policy that followed.

The USDA raised prevented planting insurance premiums by 22% in our area this year. For my operation, that's roughly $46,000 in additional costs annually. I'm paying more to insure against the same weather risk I've always faced.

But here's what really stings: the way the acreage cap is structured, operations like mine—family farms running four, five, maybe six thousand acres—get hit proportionally harder than the larger operations nearby. A 22% increase on capped acreage means I eat a bigger percentage loss than neighbors farming 20,000 acres or more. We're all paying more, but the formula punishes scale differently depending on where you fall.

This isn't about complaining. It's about asking our state legislators to act. Senate Bill 214 addresses exactly this problem by fixing how the acreage cap works. It's straightforward policy that would level an uneven playing field.

Family farming operations deserve insurance structures that don't inadvertently force consolidation. I'd ask everyone reading this to contact your legislators about SB 214. Tell them family farms matter—not just as nostalgia, but as the businesses they still are.

b.text:
22%.

That's how much USDA raised the base rate for prevented planting coverage in our region this year.

This spring I got 60% of my corn and soybean acres planted by the late May deadline. Not for lack of trying. It just wouldn't quit raining. Field after field sat too wet to carry equipment, and the calendar ran out.

That 22% hike is costing me about $46,000 extra this year — for coverage on acres I couldn't even plant.

I'm a fourth-generation farmer. My operation isn't small, but it's a family operation. And because of how the acreage caps are written, that $46,000 hits me a lot harder proportionally than it hits the bigger operations around me. They can spread that increase across more capped acres and different units. I can't. I'm capped out faster, with fewer planted acres to balance it against. Same rain, same county, same 22% increase on paper — very different bill in real life.

That's not risk protection. That's a penalty for being rained out at the wrong scale.

SB 214 would fix the acreage cap formula so it doesn't punish mid-size family farms for a wet spring we didn't cause. It's a straightforward correction, and it's sitting waiting for support.

If you farm, you already know what this spring was like. If you don't, ask your neighbor what 40% unplanted looks like in June. Then call your state senator and representative and tell them to back SB 214.

We can't control the rain. We should at least be able to afford the insurance we're told to buy for it.

# Week One Launch Recap: 412 Copies and Floaty Movement

Well, it’s out. After three years of nights, weekends, and staring at code after my day job, my first game is officially live. 

I wanted to drop a quick update on how the first seven days went.

### The Numbers and the Reddit Spike
We sold 412 copies in week one. For a solo project with basically zero marketing budget outside of this devlog, I'm really happy with that. Seeing actual people buy and play something I built in my spare room is a weird feeling, but a good one.

The biggest traffic push happened on Thursday. A post I made hit the front page of a small niche subreddit and stayed there for about six hours. That single window accounted for a solid chunk of the week's sales and brought in a wave of fresh wishlists.

### The Feedback (And the Floaty Controls)
The reviews and community messages have been coming in, which has been great to read through. 

One review specifically called out the movement mechanics, saying the player character feels "a bit floaty." I booted up the build, played through a few levels with fresh eyes, and... yeah. Honestly, they’re completely right. When you’ve been testing your own jump physics for three years, you get used to the quirks, but stepping back, it definitely lacks weight.

### What’s Next
I'm not doing a post-mortem or pulling out some big philosophical lesson from launch week—I'm just getting back to work.

Right now, I’m working on Patch 1.1, which will drop next month. The main priority is tightening up the movement physics so it feels far more responsive, along with fixing a few ultra-wide display bugs that players reported over the weekend.

Thanks to everyone who bought a copy, left a review, or has been reading these posts over the last three years. 

More updates soon.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
Got the Roadstar DC4 about 14 months and 140k miles ago.

Night footage on the rear cam gets grainy past 30 feet, but that’s standard for this price point. The real win was catching a lane-change accident on camera; got my insurance claim approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6 weeks.

The suction mount fell off twice in summer heat until I swapped to the adhesive mount. App needs Wi-Fi to pull footage, which is useless at most truck stops, so I just pull the SD card instead. Solid dash cam for the money.

b.text:
Roadstar DC4 after 14 months / 140k miles

Ran this cam hard for 14 months and about 140k miles. Overall it’s held up, but there’s some stuff you should know before buying.

The rear cam is the weak link at night. Anything past 30 feet gets grainy enough that you’re not reading plates or fine details. Daytime rear footage is fine, front cam is solid day and night. If you’re mostly running daytime or just want basic coverage, it’s workable. If you need clean night rear footage, look elsewhere.

The one time it mattered, it paid for itself. Caught a lane change accident on camera where the other driver tried to say I drifted into him. Sent the clip to insurance and the claim got approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6 weeks. That alone makes me keep it in the truck.

Mounting: the suction mount fell off twice in summer heat, both times while parked. Switched to the adhesive mount and haven’t had an issue since. If you buy this, throw the suction mount in the glove box and go straight to adhesive.

The app is basically useless on the road. It needs wifi to pull footage, and most truck stops don’t have wifi worth using. I just pull the SD card and plug it into my laptop. Faster and no app headaches.

For the price, it’s decent. Not perfect, but the front footage is good and it saved me a long insurance fight. If you can live with the rear cam limits and don’t care about the app, it’s worth a look.

You truly carried the event—from recruiting and coordinating volunteers to hauling boxes before and after school every day. I know how much time, energy, and persistence that required, and I’m incredibly grateful.

Because of your efforts, the fair raised more than double last year’s total. Those funds will provide classroom books for our students throughout the year, so your work will have a lasting impact every time a student discovers a new story or finds the right book.

b.text:
Hi Renata,

I wanted to reach out personally now that the used book fair is all wrapped up to say thank you—truly, there aren’t enough words to capture how much your work this week meant to me, the other English teachers, and most of all, our students.

When the usual book fair coordinator had to step back three weeks ago, I was convinced we’d have to scale way back, or even cancel entirely. I had no idea how we’d pull off a full week of the fair on top of midterm grading, lesson planning, and all the chaos of the spring semester. Then you showed up to that last-minute planning meeting and said you’d take the lead—and I don’t think any of us realized just how fully you’d mean that.

I still can’t stop thinking about all the unglamorous, relentless work you put in that no one else would have noticed if they didn’t show up at 7 a.m. before the bell: hauling those heavy cardboard boxes of donated books from the basement storage closet (I still laugh about Tuesday, when you toted a box of mystery novels so big it blocked your view of the door, and joked you’d built up enough arm strength to skip your workout for the month). You stayed every single night after dismissal until 5 p.m. or later, folding tables, sorting leftover books to donate to the middle school, and restocking shelves for the next day—all while recruiting a team of parent volunteers and even a handful of my 11th grade AP Lang students, who kept stopping by my class this week to say how fun you made the whole thing feel, even when the hallways were packed and the cash register ran out of ones.

And the total? When we counted the proceeds last night, we all stood there stunned: you helped raise more than double what we brought in last year. Last year, the fair funds only covered half the new classroom library titles I had on my wishlist—this year, we can replace all the tattered, page-teared copies of *The House on Mango Street* and *To Kill a Mockingbird* for 9th grade, add all the verse novels and graphic novel classics kids have been begging me for (I already put in the order for *The Poet X* and the *Heartstopper* Book 1 set—don’t tell the kids yet, I want it to be a surprise), and even put some money toward the creative writing club’s annual literary magazine. That’s hundreds of students getting to hold books they’re actually excited to read, all because you showed up and cared enough to do the work no one else was willing to take on.

I know you don’t do this for recognition, but I wanted you to know exactly how far your effort goes. As a small token of my thanks, I set aside that used copy of Mary Oliver’s *Devotions* I saw you pick up and flip through three different times last week—it’s on the front desk in my classroom, and you can stop by anytime to grab it (or just say hi, if you want). I also told all my classes about everything you did to make the fair happen, and a bunch of the kids asked if they could write you thank you notes—if that’s something you’d be okay with, I’d love to pass them along in a few weeks.

Seriously, Renata—you turned a small, scrappy used book fair into something that will shape our students’ love of reading for the whole year. I can’t thank you enough.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/ Pulled up the subfloor on the Maple Ave kitchen job yesterday and found three joists that had been notched halfway through by whoever ran the original plumbing. Probably 40 years ago. Someone just kept going and nobody ever fixed it.

2/ Notched joists are a structural problem that gets worse over time. Floor gets bouncy, tile cracks, cabinets go out of level. The fix was sistering new 2x10s alongside each one, full length, glued and through-bolted. Took a day and a half with two guys.

3/ Cost the homeowners about $1,100 in labor and material they weren't expecting. Could've been a lot worse. If we'd tiled over that floor without looking, it would've failed within a year and the repair would've been triple once everything was finished.

4/ The lesson isn't "always expect the worst." It's pull the subfloor before you commit to a tile scope. Ten minutes with a pry bar tells you what you're actually working with. Every old kitchen has a story underneath it and you want to know before you're four weeks in.

b.text:
1/4
Maple Ave kitchen. Opened the subfloor after demo: three consecutive 2x10s cut clean through at midspan for an old 4" stack. Previous “repair” was 2x4s toenailled on the sides. 3/4" sag right where the island was going.

2/4
Sistered them full length with 2x10s, added blocking, hangers, and a short LVL. Three extra days for our crew. Extra cost to the owner: $2,850 in labor and material. Cabinets and stone were already in the warehouse.

3/4
Homeowners see the cabinets. We see whether the floor can actually hold them. That’s the gap.

4/4
Lesson: don’t lock the finish package until you’ve seen the structure. If you’re bidding a kitchen without looking at the joists, you’re not pricing a remodel. You’re guessing.

Hi Nadine,

Here is what happened: My substitute helper was at the door when someone arrived saying they were there to pick up Mia. The sub didn't recognize the person and checked Mia’s approved pickup list. Seeing that the person wasn't on it, she stopped the pickup and called you to verify before doing anything else. That being said, it never should have gotten to the point of you getting that call. If someone isn’t on your authorized list, the answer is an immediate no. My sub should have asked for photo ID the second that person stepped up, matched it against our list, and turned them away immediately instead of calling you and causing that kind of scare. 

I take this very seriously, and here is what is changing immediately:
1. We are instituting a mandatory photo ID check right at the door for anyone picking up who isn't recognized, no exceptions. 
2. The substitute will not work another shift here until she has been completely retrained on our security protocols so she understands that an unlisted person is an automatic refusal on the spot.

Your trust means everything to me, and keeping Mia safe is my entire job. Please call me today if you'd like to talk through this more over the phone—I'm here anytime.

b.text:
Hi Nadine,

In a home licensed for just eight kids, I know every family and every approved pickup person, and the safety of the children here is the whole reason I do this. The fact that you were put in that position makes me sick.

Here's exactly what happened. Yesterday I had a substitute helper working with the kids. An adult came to pick up Mia who was not on her approved pickup list. My substitute didn't recognize the person, so before she released Mia, she stopped and called you to confirm. You didn't authorize it, and Mia was not handed over. That call is the only reason it didn't go any further.

But you're right—it should never have gotten that far. The substitute should have checked Mia's approved pickup list and asked for photo ID at the door before Mia was ever brought to the front, and before any call to you was needed. Instead, she let an unauthorized adult get close enough that we were one bad decision away from your daughter leaving with someone who had no business picking her up. The safety net caught it at the last second, but the safety net should never have been tested. I take full responsibility for that gap.

Here's what I'm doing about it:

- Starting immediately, every single pickup begins with an ID check at the door. If the person isn't on the approved list and can't show matching ID, they don't get the child. No exceptions, and no parent should ever have to get a call like that.
- The substitute will be retrained on our pickup and release policy before she works another shift. If she can't follow it, she won't be back.
