setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
Shut off the circulator pump or boiler before you open any valves. If the system is running when you crack a bleeder, you’ll force air down the line instead of out of it, and you’ll probably get sprayed. Give the boiler ten minutes to settle and the pressure to flatten out.

Start with the baseboard unit closest to the boiler and work your way outward, one by one. Each unit has a bleeder valve on one end—usually a small brass fitting with a square nut or a slotted stem. Slide a cup, small bowl, or heavy rag underneath before you touch it.

Open the valve slowly with a bleeder key or a flathead screwdriver. You’ll hear hissing first. That’s the air leaving. Keep it cracked until the stream of water runs steady and quiet, with no sputtering or bubbles. Depending on how much air is trapped, this can take thirty seconds or several minutes.

Once the flow is solid, close the valve snug, but do not reef on it. These brass seats crack easily, and an overtightened bleeder will drip or weep all winter. Finger-tight plus a quarter turn is usually enough.

Repeat this at every unit in the house. The mistake that generates most of our cold-radiator calls is homeowners bleeding only the upstairs baseboards and skipping the basement loop. The air that collects at the top of the system usually got pushed there from below. If you skip the basement, you’ll be bleeding the upstairs again in a week.

When you finish the last unit, check the boiler pressure gauge. Bleeding drops the system pressure, so you may need to add water through the fill valve to get back to the manufacturer’s recommended range—usually 12 to 15 psi for a one- or two-story home. If you’re unsure how to add water or the pressure won’t hold, shut the boiler down and give us a call.

b.text:
**How to Bleed Air Out of Baseboard Heat Before Winter**

Half the "my radiators are cold" calls we run in October end up being trapped air, and it's a fifteen-minute job you can do yourself with a towel and a screwdriver. Here's how we do it.

**What you need**

- A radiator key or a flathead screwdriver (depends on your bleeder valve)
- A cup or small container
- A rag or towel for drips

**Step 1: Shut off the system**

Turn off the boiler and the circulator pump. Don't skip this. If the pump is running while you open a bleeder, it'll push air around the loop instead of letting it collect where you can get at it. Give the system a few minutes to settle before you start.

**Step 2: Find the bleeder valve**

Look at the ends of each baseboard unit, usually behind the end cap or just inside it. You're looking for a small brass fitting with either a square stem (needs the key) or a slotted screw (flathead works). Some units have them at one end only, some at both. Check both.

**Step 3: Start closest to the boiler**

Go to the unit nearest the boiler first and work outward along the loop. Air travels with the water, so you're clearing it in the direction it moves. Bleeding in random order means you'll be chasing the same pocket of air around the house.

**Step 4: Open it slow**

Hold your cup underneath and crack the valve open slowly. You'll hear hissing first. That's the air. Keep it open until the hissing stops and you get a steady stream of water with no sputtering. A trickle with bubbles means you're not done. Steady water, no noise, you're done.

**Step 5: Close it snug, not tight**

Turn the valve closed until it stops leaking. That's it. People crank these down like a lug nut and crack the valve seat, and now instead of a cold radiator you've got a drip and a service call. Snug is enough.

**Step 6: Repeat on every unit**

Every one. Which brings me to the part most people get wrong.

**The mistake that causes most of our cold radiator calls**

Homeowners bleed the upstairs units because that's where they notice the cold. Then they stop. But the air is almost never up there. It collects in the basement loop, the runs of baseboard or pipe down near the boiler that nobody looks at. You bleed the second floor, feel good about it, and the same air works its way back up in a week.

If you have baseboard in the basement, or a loop that runs through an unfinished area, bleed those too. In a lot of houses that's where the air actually lives, and it's the one spot people never think to check.

**After you're done**

Turn the boiler and circulator back on. Check the pressure gauge on the boiler. If it's low (most residential systems run around 12 to 15 psi cold), the fill valve should bring it back up, but if it doesn't, or if you keep getting air after bleeding a few times, that's a different problem. Could be the auto-fill, could be the expansion tank, could be a small leak somewhere pulling air in.

That's the point where it's worth having us take a look. But bleeding the system is the first thing we'd do anyway, so you might as well do it yourself and save the trip.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The Barreras had a shot list. Then it rained.

Not a light drizzle. The kind of Hill Country downpour that turns a ceremony lawn into a creek in twenty minutes. The list said first look by the arbor, family formals on the stone steps, portraits at golden hour in the field.

None of that happened.

What happened instead: we grabbed the whole party and moved everything under the big pecan tree on the property. Ceremony, family photos, the two of them, all of it. Wet grass, borrowed umbrellas, people packed in shoulder to shoulder because that was the only dry ground.

Those are some of the best photos I've made in eight years of doing this.

Here's the thing I've noticed over a lot of weddings. The couples who hand me a rigid list and want it checked off, line by line, end up with photos that look like everyone else's. Technically fine. Nice enough. Interchangeable.

The couples who tell me what matters to them and then let the day be the day? Those are the galleries people cry over.

It's not that planning is bad. I want to know your grandmother is flying in from Monterrey and it's a big deal she made it. I want to know the two of you met at a bar with a pecan tree out back, so the fact that we ended up under one wasn't lost on anybody.

But a shot list can't anticipate the moment your dad ducks under the umbrella with you and the two of you just stand there laughing at the rain. It can't schedule the way light looks coming through wet leaves. It can only tell you what you thought you'd want, months ago, on a sunny afternoon at your kitchen table.

So if you're interviewing photographers right now: ask them about the wedding that went sideways. Ask what they did. The list is the floor, not the ceiling.

And if it rains, find the biggest tree on the property.

b.text:
After eight years shooting roughly 35 weddings a year in the Texas Hill Country, I’ve seen the same pattern repeat: the couples who ditch the shot list always end up with the best photos.

The Barrera wedding is my favorite proof. We had a plan—locations, timelines, a detailed shot list. Then it rained. Hard. We moved everything under the pecan tree. No staged portraits in the field, no formal group shots in the barn. Just family huddled together laughing about the weather, the bride holding her bouquet under the branches, the groom shielding her with his jacket.

Those are the frames that tell the story. Not the checklist.

If you’re planning a wedding: build the timeline, but don’t treat the photo list like a contract. Leave space for the moment. The best images usually happen when the plan breaks.

To vendors: encourage your couples to let go a little. The magic isn’t in the checklist—it’s in the reaction.

Ready for a Hill Country photographer who actually plans for the rain? Let’s talk.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6-Month Review (No Affiliate Links, Just A Dev Who Uses It 40+ Hours A Week)
I bought this desk 6 months ago for $549 on Jarvik’s holiday sale, after my $150 Amazon special’s motor died mid-2AM production bug debug. I’m a remote software engineer, so I’m at this desk 40+ hours a week, switching between sitting for deep coding and standing for meetings/stack trace squinting. No fluff, no sponsored links, just the good, the bad, and the completely useless.

## The Good: The Motor Is Actually As Advertised
Let’s lead with the best part: the L2’s motor is fast, quiet, and reliable. I timed it from my sitting height (71cm) to my standing height (117cm) — 46cm of travel — in 7.1 seconds. My old desk took 14 seconds for the same distance and sounded like a lawnmower. The L2’s motor is so quiet I adjust it mid-Zoom calls all the time, and no one’s ever asked about background noise. I record coding tutorials with a Blue Yeti 60cm from the desk edge, and the motor doesn’t register on the audio track at all. It’s also smooth — no jerky starts or stops, so my full mug of black coffee on the front edge never sloshes, even when I move it all the way up or down. I adjust the height 5-6 times a day, and the motor hasn’t slowed or made weird noises in 6 months. Zero complaints here.

The 152x76cm bamboo top is also solid: no scratches, dents, or warping after 6 months of spilled coffee, dropped screwdrivers, and stacked algorithm textbooks.

## The Bad: Three Annoying Flaws That Add Up
### Wobble at full height when typing hard
The desk’s max height is 122cm; I use 117cm (I’m 5’10”, elbows at 90 degrees for typing). At that height, when I’m typing hard — think angry git commit messages, mashing my heavy Keychron Q5 mechanical keyboard while chasing a bug, 110 WPM — the desk sways side to side enough that my 27” 4K monitor (clamped to the back with a monitor arm) has visible wobble. It’s not bad enough to make text unreadable, but it’s distracting when I’m alternating between typing and staring at a stack trace. I tested it with a full glass of water 15cm from the front edge: 10 seconds of hard typing left a few drops sloshed over the rim.
The wobble kicks in around 107cm and gets worse the higher you go. At sitting height? Zero wobble, rock solid. I checked my floor with a 4-foot level and adjusted the feet until the desk was perfectly level at sitting height — this is a frame design flaw, not my floor.

### Memory presets drift about 1cm
I calibrated all 3 presets the day I set the desk up, using a tape measure for exact heights: 71cm (sitting coding), 117cm (standing debugging), 91cm (lunch/light work). After 2 months, my standing preset felt off — measured it, it was 116cm, a full cm lower than I’d set it. I recalibrated, and 2 months later, it was off again, same 1cm downward drift. The sitting preset hasn’t drifted at all, which makes me think it’s a motor calibration issue under higher height tension.
It’s not a dealbreaker — I just nudge it up with the button when I notice — but for a desk that advertises “precision memory presets,” it’s a letdown

b.text:
I’ve been using the Jarvik L2 as my primary remote workstation for six months. Here’s the breakdown.

The motor is excellent. It’s whisper-quiet and fast, making position changes effortless even during deep work.

However, stability at full height is a problem. The desk wobbles noticeably when I type with any force. If you’re a heavy-handed typist, your screen will shake.

The memory presets are unreliable. After half a year, my saved heights have drifted about a centimeter. You have to micro-adjust every time you use them.

The cable tray is garbage. It’s flimsy plastic that rattles during height changes. I had to replace it immediately.

Verdict: Worth it at the $549 sale price. Not worth it at $749. Do not pay full retail for this level of wobble and drift.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
This spring the rain wouldn't quit, and by the late May deadline I had only 60 percent of my soybean and corn acres in the ground. That alone is hard enough. Then came the USDA's 22 percent base-rate hike on prevented-planting coverage for our region. On my operation that single change is costing an extra $46,000 this year.

The acreage caps make it worse. Those caps hit a fourth-generation family farm like mine harder, proportionally, than the larger operations down the road that can absorb the same percentage hit across far more acres. The numbers don't lie: smaller family outfits are paying a steeper relative price for the same weather risk.

Senate Bill 214 would fix the acreage-cap problem. It deserves our full support. Call your legislators, show up at the next Farm Bureau meeting, and make sure they know the math that family farmers are living with right now.

b.text:
When the late May planting deadline arrived, 40% of my corn and soybean acres were still too wet to turn a tractor. Like many of you, the relentless spring rains left me with only 60% of my crops in the ground. But the real hit to our ledger came when the bill arrived for our prevented planting coverage. 

This year, the USDA raised the base premium rate in our region by 22%. For my family’s fourth-generation operation, that 22% hike translates directly to an extra $46,000 out of pocket. That is $46,000 spent just to cover the ground we were physically prevented from planting.

While a rate hike of this size hurts any year, the current structure of the program makes it highly inequitable. Because of how the crop insurance acreage caps are structured, this hike hits family-sized operations like ours much harder proportionally than the mega-farms down the road. Larger, corporate operations can spread their risk across multiple counties and structure their holdings to stay under the caps, or easily absorb the flat cost. Mid-sized family farms hit those caps quickly, leaving us to bear a disproportionate share of the premium burden per acre. It is a regressive system that punishes the independent family farms it was originally designed to protect.

We cannot control the weather, but we can influence the policy that dictates how we survive it. 

Right now, State Senate Bill 214 is moving through the legislature. SB 214 would directly address this acreage cap loophole, restructuring state-level agricultural safety nets to provide targeted relief and level the playing field for family-scale operations when disaster strikes. 

I urge every member of this Farm Bureau to contact our state legislators today and voice your support for SB 214. Our representatives need to understand the real-world math behind these policy decisions. An extra $46,000 bill for unplanted dirt is unsustainable. Passing SB 214 is a necessary step to ensure that family farms in our county can survive the spring to plant another year.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
**Subject: Launch week is over — here’s what actually happened (no big takeaways, I swear)**

Hey everyone,

If you’re reading this, I’ve finally stopped refreshing the Steam sales dashboard every 45 seconds, which feels like a win in itself. It’s been seven days since my first commercial launch dropped — three years of nights, weekends, skipping friend’s birthdays, and debugging collision at 2am all boiling down to this very weird, very unglamorous week.

First off, the numbers: 412 copies sold in the first seven days. I set a totally arbitrary, low-stakes goal of 100 copies when I started this, so 412 feels kind of insane, honestly. I spent $0 on marketing — just posted the trailer here, tweeted at three indie curation accounts that never replied, and crossed my fingers that someone would care.

The big surprise was hitting the front page of that small indie game subreddit I’ve lurked on since I started this project — you know the one — for about 6 hours on Wednesday. I found out because my Discord (which had 12 people in it pre-launch, all my IRL friends who let me bug test on their laptops) blew up while I was at my day job. I spent my entire lunch break refreshing the thread, half-convinced someone was gonna call out that one cave level texture I forgot to upscale. Most of the week’s sales came from that, I’m pretty sure. Shoutout to whoever crossposted the trailer — I owe you a coffee, or a Steam key for whatever my next game is, whichever you prefer.

The best feedback, though, was a Steam review that dropped on day two that just said “movement feels floaty” and nothing else. You’re right! That is 100% a valid complaint. I tuned the movement on my old work monitor that has like 20ms of uncalibrated input lag, so after three years of playing it that way, I didn’t even notice. I’ve been messing with acceleration curves and coyote time all week, and it’s already feeling way tighter. That’s gonna be the big focus for 1.1, which I’m aiming to put out next month.

1.1’s also gonna have a few other small things people have been asking for: rebindable controller buttons (I know, I know — how did I forget that? Solo dev brain rot is real), a fix for the final boss music cutting out if you skip the pre-fight cutscene, and that weird bug where the main character’s hair clips through their hat if you sprint up stairs. Nothing game-changing, just stuff that makes the whole thing feel a little more polished.

I don’t have some big, profound “lesson learned” to wrap this up with, if I’m being honest. Launch week was messy. I stayed up till 3am Tuesday fixing a crash that only happened on Windows 10 21H2, I forgot to eat on Wednesday because I was replying to Reddit comments, I cried a little on Thursday when someone left a review saying they played it with their 8-year-old kid and beat the final level together. It was just… a week. A really cool, really stressful week.

Next week I’m taking one (1) full day off to do nothing game dev related — no stats, no bug reports, no tweaking jump height at 10pm. Then I’m diving straight into 1.1, and I’ll probably post a devlog next week about the movement tuning process if anyone’s curious about the nitty gritty of adjusting acceleration curves without making the controls feel slippery.

If you bought the game, thank you. Seriously. If you left a review, good or bad, thank you — even the one that called the pixel art “mid” (you’re not wrong, I’m still learning). If you’re a fellow indie dev waiting for your own launch, it’s okay if it’s not perfect. It’s just a launch.

Alright, I’m gonna go heat up a frozen pizza and not look at my code editor for at least 8 hours. Talk soon.
[Your Name]

b.text:
Well, it’s finally out. After three years of nights and weekends, I launched my first commercial game last week. It feels incredibly weird to actually have it out in the wild.

For the numbers nerds out there, we sold 412 copies in the first seven days. I’m really happy with that for a debut. We also caught a nice little wave of traffic when the game hit the front page of a smaller subreddit, though the spike only lasted for about six hours before dropping off. Still, it definitely helped push the algorithm at the right time.

As for the feedback, I’ve been reading through all the reviews. Most of it has been great, but one reviewer pointed out that the movement feels "floaty." And honestly? They’re completely right. I spent so long staring at the same project that I just got used to it and lost my perspective. 

So, that’s the main focus for the 1.1 patch. I’m tightening up the controls, adjusting the acceleration curves, and making the character actually feel grounded. Expect that update to roll out sometime next month.

For now, I'm going to take a few days to just sleep and catch up on my backlog before diving back into the engine. Thanks to everyone who bought the game, played it, and left a review. I'll see you all when 1.1 is ready.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
At 5:17 on a Saturday night, our register system went black.

There were already people waiting by the door, and the printer in the kitchen had stopped spitting out orders. My dad pressed the power button three times, as if the third time would be different. My mom stood at the counter holding a bowl of pho she did not know where to take.

I pulled a stack of guest checks from under the register and started writing.

T12: two pho tai, one no onions.  
T7: bun bo hue, extra spicy.  
Pickup: four spring rolls, one grilled pork banh mi.

I made a copy of each ticket, handed one to the kitchen, and kept the other beside me. I wrote totals with a calculator and called out orders when they were ready. My handwriting got worse as the line grew. At one point, I charged a table for three iced coffees instead of two and had to run after them in the parking lot with five dollars.

The system came back almost two hours later. By then, the counter was covered in scraps of paper, and my left hand was stained blue from the pen. My dad wanted to enter every order into the register. My mom looked at the pile and said, “Tomorrow.”

Every weekend since sophomore year, I have worked at my family’s Vietnamese restaurant. I usually arrive before the lunch rush and leave after we stack the chairs. My jobs change depending on who is busy. I take orders, refill water, pack takeout containers, wipe tables, and translate when my parents need help with a customer or a delivery driver. I know which regular wants extra basil and which one will ask if the broth is really made that morning.

Some jobs take longer to learn. When we hired a new kitchen worker, I showed her how my grandma folds spring rolls. The wrapper has to be tight enough to keep the filling in but not so tight that it tears in the fryer. First fold the bottom over the filling. Then bring in both sides. Roll once, brush the edge with egg, and finish.

My first few rolls were crooked when my grandma taught me. She would unwrap them without saying anything and push the wrapper back toward me. Now I do the same thing, except I usually explain why.

“Not too much filling,” I told the new hire. “It looks small now, but it expands.”

She tried again. The next roll was still uneven, but it held. We lined it up on the tray with the others. By the end of the afternoon, hers looked almost like mine. None looked exactly like my grandma’s.

The restaurant is also where I do a lot of homework. During busy shifts, the dining room is too loud, and someone always needs the table I am using. The walk-in cooler is quieter. On breaks, I sometimes sit on an upside-down bucket between boxes of herbs and containers of broth, wearing my work apron over my school clothes.

That is where I finished a calculus problem set on derivatives. I balanced my notebook on my knees and set a ten-minute timer because staying longer would make my fingers stiff. Every few minutes, the compressor turned on and covered the sound of the kitchen. When the timer rang, I took a picture of the last problem, put my phone in my pocket, and went back out to refill sauces.

My weekends do not have much separation between school, work, and family. My mom might ask about an English assignment while sealing takeout bags. My dad might quiz me about college deadlines while chopping cilantro. Sometimes I am annoyed that I cannot spend Saturday the way my friends do. Sometimes I am relieved to have somewhere I already know what to do.

At closing, I sweep rice from under the tables and count the cash drawer. The kitchen smells like fried garlic, dish soap, and broth that has been simmering all day. Before we leave, I check the next morning’s reservations and make sure there are blank guest checks under the register.

We still use the computer. I just keep a pen beside it now.

b.text:
I haven’t had a Saturday off since October of my sophomore year. While my classmates are at football games or sleeping in, my weekends belong to my family’s Vietnamese restaurant. I start at 10:00 AM, just as the broth from the day before is reaching a rolling boil, and I don't leave until the chairs are stacked on the tables at ten at night.

My breaks are twenty minutes long, and I spend them in the walk-in cooler. It is the only place in the restaurant where nobody is shouting in Vietnamese or clattering stainless steel bowls. I sit on an overturned five-gallon bucket of pickled carrots, my winter coat zipped to my chin, and do my AP Calculus homework. The pages of my textbook always curl from the humidity, and after fifteen minutes, my fingers get too stiff to grip my mechanical pencil. But the quiet is absolute. I solve for limits while staring at crates of cilantro and boxes of beef bones, finding a weird kind of peace in the cold.

If the walk-in is where I find quiet, the front counter is where I learn how to handle chaos. Last November, during our prime Saturday dinner rush, our digital register system went completely black. Twenty active orders vanished from the kitchen screen, and a line of hungry customers began to stretch out the door. My dad was already sweating over four gas burners in the back, and my mom was frantically trying to reboot the router. 

I didn't have time to panic. I grabbed a stack of green guest checks and a black pen. I took orders by hand, writing down "P1" for beef pho and "E2" for spring rolls in my own shorthand. I ran the physical tickets to the kitchen, shouting modifications over the hiss of the exhaust fan, and did the math for the tax and change in my head. I kept a metal lockbox under the counter for cash. By the time the rush ended, my thumb was calloused from the cheap pen, but we hadn’t missed a single order, and the cash drawer balanced to the penny. 

When I am not running the register, I am training the new hires. Most of them are high school kids who have never had a job before. Last month, I taught a junior named Marcus how to roll spring rolls using my grandmother’s technique. The rice paper is temperamental—if you wet it too much, it turns to mush; if you don't wet it enough, it cracks. 

I showed him how to lay down the pork, the noodles, and the mint, and then how to tuck the sides in tight, like making a small sleeping bag. The trick is getting the shrimp to lay flat against the translucent wrapper so it looks good when served. 

"If you roll it too loose, it falls apart in the peanut sauce," I told him. "If you roll it too tight, the paper rips. You just have to feel the tension." I watched him tear six wrappers before he got one clean roll. I didn't get frustrated; I just cleared the sticky rice paper away and handed him another sheet. 

I am not going to say that working at the restaurant taught me the secret to life. The truth is, my feet hurt every Sunday, my clothes always smell like star anise, and I have missed a lot of high school events that I probably would have enjoyed. But this is my reality. I know how to work under pressure, I know how to teach people, and I know how to find quiet in a busy room. When I start college, I won't just be bringing my textbooks. I’ll be bringing the work ethic I built twelve hours at a time.

setup: You're Nadine Alvarado, emailing the daycare owner after a near-miss pickup mistake involving Mia and asking what happened and what changes are being made.

a.text:
Nadine,

I'm sorry. I know how that call must have landed, and you deserve a straight account of what happened.

Yesterday afternoon a man came to the door saying he was there to pick up Mia. I wasn't in the room at that moment. Lisa, the substitute who was covering for me, didn't recognize him, checked Mia's file, saw his name wasn't on your approved list, and called you before letting him anywhere near the door with her. Mia never left the room. Once you said no, he was turned away. That's the whole sequence.

Lisa did the right thing in the end, and I'm glad she trusted her gut. But I'm not going to pretend the process worked, because it didn't. She should have been checking the list against an ID the second he said Mia's name, not after he'd already stated he was there for her and she'd started to think about it. The fact that it got far enough for you to receive that call is on me. The pickup list and the "if in doubt, don't" rule are things I've drilled into my regular staff for years, and I didn't drill them hard enough into someone who was here for one day.

Here's what's changing:

Starting today, anyone picking up any child shows a photo ID at the door before they come inside, no exceptions, including me being told "oh, that's so-and-so's grandpa." I know the regular parents by face, and I'll still be asking. It takes ten seconds and it means nobody has to rely on recognizing someone.

Lisa won't be working here again until I've gone through the full pickup procedure with her in person and she's walked through it with me watching. If I'm not confident, she doesn't come back.

I'm also going back through every child's file this week to make sure the approved lists are current and easy to find, so nobody is flipping through papers while a stranger is standing at the door.

I don't have an answer yet for who this man was or why he had Mia's name. If you have any idea, I'd like to know, and if you don't, I'd like to know that too, because it changes how worried I am about it.

Please call me if you want to talk this through. I'd rather have the hard conversation than have you wondering.

Karen

b.text:
Hi Nadine,

I’m sorry I put you in that position yesterday. Getting a call about someone you’ve never heard of picking up Mia would be terrifying, and you’re right to want an explanation.

The substitute helper almost moved forward with releasing Mia to someone who wasn’t on her approved pickup list. She didn’t recognize the person and called you to check before releasing Mia, which is what stopped it from going further. Mia was not released to that person. But it should never have gotten as far as a possible handoff—the approved pickup list should have been checked first, not treated as something to sort out along the way.

I’m responsible for making sure everyone working here follows our pickup process. We’re adding an ID check at the door and matching it against each child’s approved pickup list before moving forward with any pickup. The substitute will also be retrained on the full process before she works here again, including what to do when someone who isn’t approved comes to the door.

I know these are basic safeguards you should be able to count on. I’m sorry we fell short yesterday, and I understand why this has shaken your trust. I’m available to talk through what happened and answer your questions directly.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6-Month Review

**TL;DR:** Good motor, mediocre stability at height, sloppy presets, embarrassing cable management. Worth $549. Not worth $749. Buy it on sale or buy something else.

I bought the L2 in [month], paid the $549 sale price with my own money, and have used it 8+ hours a day, five days a week, ever since. No affiliate links in this post — nobody makes money if you buy this thing, including me. My setup: two 27" monitors on a gas-spring arm, mechanical keyboard, and a standing height of about 42.5". I switch positions 4–6 times a day, so the motor and presets have had a real workout — somewhere north of 700 cycles at this point.

## The motor is the best part of this desk

Genuinely. Sit-to-stand takes about 17 seconds under full load, it's smooth, and it's quiet enough that I've adjusted it mid-meeting with my mic unmuted and nobody noticed. There's a low hum, not a whine, and no grinding or hesitation at the top of travel. After 700+ cycles it sounds identical to day one.

This is the thing cheap desks get wrong — my previous budget frame started stuttering under two monitors within a year. The L2's motor has given me zero problems and I expect that to continue.

## Stability: fine sitting, wobbly standing

At sitting height, it's a rock. No complaints.

At my standing height (42.5"), there's front-to-back wobble when I type hard — and I type hard, because mechanical keyboard, because programmer. The monitors on my desk-mounted arm visibly sway for a second or two after I really get going. It's not alarming, nothing's going to fall, but it's noticeable and it's the kind of thing that bugs you more in month six than month one.

Two things made it better: torquing every frame bolt again after the first month (they settle), and moving my monitor arm's clamp closer to a leg. If you type gently or use a laptop, you may never notice. If you hammer a keyboard like you're mad at it, you will.

## The memory presets drift

There are four presets. Great. Except they drift by about a centimeter. I'll hit preset 2, the display says 42.5", and I can feel it's wrong — measure it, and it's at 41.6" or 43.1". It's not consistent in which direction it misses, which honestly offends me more. A centimeter doesn't sound like much until your elbows are slightly wrong for three hours.

I've done the factory recalibration (hold the down button, let it bottom out) three times. It helps for a week or two, then the drift creeps back. My fix is dumb but effective: I use the presets to get close, then nudge with the manual buttons and watch the readout. It works, but "the memory buttons get you within a centimeter" is a sad sentence to write about a desk that costs this much.

## The cable tray is garbage

I don't use that word lightly. It's a shallow stamped-metal trough that attaches to the underside of the desktop with four short screws into particle board. Here's what happened, in order:

1. I loaded it with one surge protector and the usual cable bundle. It sagged in the middle within a week.
2. The rear two screws loosened themselves from the desk's vibration. I re-seated them. One stripped the hole.
3. It's too shallow to close over a standard surge protector anyway, so the lid has been off since month one.

I ripped it out in month three, mounted a $15 under-desk cable raceway from [generic], and my cable situation is now better than the desk deserves. Budget for that. Plan on throwing the included tray directly in the trash and saving yourself the intermediate steps.

## Smaller stuff

- **The desktop** is laminate over particle board and it's fine. Edges haven't chipped, it wipes clean, and my monitor arm clamp hasn't dented it. Not premium, not a problem.
- **The controller** display is bright enough to read in a dark room, which also means it's bright enough to annoy you in a dark room. No way to dim it. I put a strip of electrical tape over half of it.
- **Assembly** took me about 50 minutes alone. Instructions were clear, hardware was labeled, nothing was missing. Genuinely good experience.
- **Anti-collision** works. It stopped on my chair arm once and reversed. Tested it deliberately a second time because I didn't trust it. It passed.

## The verdict

At **$549**, this desk is a good deal. The motor alone justifies it — quiet, fast, and proven over six months of daily abuse — and the flaws are livable if you know about them going in. Recalibrate occasionally, re-torque your bolts, replace the cable tray immediately, and you've got a desk that does its job.

At **$749**, it's overpriced. At that number you're in range of frames with better lateral stability and controllers that remember where 42.5 inches actually is. The wobble and the preset drift are forgivable at $549. They are insults at $749.

Jarvik runs sales constantly — I've seen it at $549 three separate times since I bought mine. So the advice is simple: if you want this desk, set a price alert and wait. Do not pay full price. Full price is for people who don't read reviews, and you just read 800 words about a cable tray.

b.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6-Month Review

I bought this desk with my own money at the $549 sale price. No affiliate links, no sponsorship, just an opinionated write-up after using it every workday for half a year.

## The good: motor performance

This is genuinely the best part of the desk. The motor is quiet — quieter than the Fully Jarvis I used at my last job, quieter than I expected for the price. It goes from sitting to standing height in about 8 seconds and doesn't sound like a garbage disposal while doing it. If you're on video calls all day and need to adjust height without your coworkers hearing a jet engine spin up, this matters more than people think. Six months in, no degradation in speed or noise. Still smooth.

## The bad: stability at height

At full extension (I'm 5'9" and run it near max height), there's a noticeable wobble when I type with any real force. Not a catastrophic shake, but enough that my monitor arm visibly moves if I'm typing fast or hitting keys hard during, say, a rough debugging session. This is a legs-and-crossbar issue — the frame just isn't as rigid as competitors in this price range once you're near the top of its range. If you're tall or you like standing at max height, factor this in. If you're shorter and mostly using the mid-range, you probably won't notice it.

## The annoying: memory preset drift

The four programmable height presets drift over time. Not dramatically — about a centimeter off after a few weeks of use before you have to recalibrate. It's not a dealbreaker, but it's a paper cut. You set your sitting and standing heights once, expect the desk to remember them precisely, and instead you're eyeballing whether it's actually landed where you told it to. Recalibration is easy (hold the down button for a few seconds), but you shouldn't have to do it every month on a desk in this price bracket.

## The genuinely bad: cable tray

Skip it. Don't even bother installing the included cable tray — it's flimsy, it doesn't hold cables securely, and it rattles against the underside of the desk when you're adjusting height, which adds insult to the wobble injury. I removed mine after month two and switched to a basic under-desk tray from a third party. Whoever designed this component clearly wasn't asked to actually live with it.

## Verdict

**Worth it at $549. Not worth it at $749.**

At the sale price, you're getting a quiet, fast motor and a functional desk with a couple of real but manageable flaws. That's a fair trade. At full price, you're competing directly with desks that have stiffer frames and better presets for the same money — the Jarvik doesn't have enough going for it to justify $749 when the wobble and drift issues exist at all.

If you catch it on sale: buy it, skip the cable tray, and don't run it at max height if you're a hard typist. If it's full price when you're shopping: keep looking.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
# Launch week: 412 copies, six hours on a front page, and one very fair review

The game launched last week. After three years of nights and weekends, I don't have a clever way to describe that, so I'll just say it plainly: it's out, people can buy it, and I've been refreshing the sales dashboard more than I'd like to admit.

Numbers, since that's what most of you are here for: **412 copies in the first week.** Before launch I told myself that 100 would make it worth doing and 500 would be a miracle, so I'm landing somewhere in the middle, and I'll take it. It's not quit-the-day-job money. It's "the last three years weren't for nothing" money, which is what I was actually hoping for.

Mid-week, a post about the game hit the front page of a small subreddit and stayed there for about six hours. I watched it happen in real time. Traffic spiked, a good chunk of the week's sales came out of that one window, and then it slid off the page and everything went back to normal. Six hours of internet fame, gone by dinner. It was fun while it lasted.

Now the reviews. They've been mostly kind so far. One of them said the movement feels floaty, and I sat with that for about a minute before admitting they're right. I've played this game for three years and somewhere along the way I lost the ability to feel it — you tune something a hundred times and your hands just adapt. Fresh eyes caught in an afternoon what I couldn't catch in three years.

So: **patch 1.1 is coming next month**, and the headline item is movement tuning. Tighter acceleration, faster stops, less sliding around. If the floatiness bugged you, it's being fixed. There's also a short list of bugs people reported that I've been able to reproduce, and those are going in too.

After that, I'm going to keep supporting the game for a while and see how sales settle before deciding on anything bigger.

Thanks to everyone who bought it, everyone who wishlisted it forever ago and actually showed up, and everyone who's been following along with this devlog. 412 of you took a chance on it.

Back to work.

b.text:
**Week one**

It's out. It's been out for eight days now, which is long enough that I've stopped refreshing the sales page every twenty minutes and moved on to refreshing it every hour or so.

Here's where things stand.

412 copies sold in the first week. I don't have a great sense of whether that's good or bad relative to other first-time solo releases, and honestly I've stopped trying to figure it out. It's 412 people who paid money for something I made at my kitchen table over three years of evenings and Saturdays. That's the number. I keep looking at it.

On day two, someone posted it to a subreddit I'd never heard of — small, a few thousand people, very specific about the kind of games it likes. It sat on the front page there for about six hours. I watched the comment thread the whole time like it was a sporting event. Most of the sales spike came from that window, and then it tapered off the way everyone told me it would. I did not post it there myself. I don't know who did. If it was one of you, thanks.

Reviews are mostly positive so far, which I'm relieved about. A handful mention the writing, a couple mention the art, one person wrote three paragraphs about a puzzle in the second area and I've read it maybe a dozen times.

One review said the movement feels floaty. It's a mixed review, not a negative one, and the person was pretty fair about it. And they're right. I've known the movement was a little soft for a long time — I'd tuned it early on, got used to it, and after a certain point I just stopped noticing. Reading someone describe it fresh made me boot the game up and play the first area again, and yeah. It's floaty. Jump apex hangs too long, air control is too generous, landing doesn't have enough weight to it. I'd convinced myself it was a stylistic choice. It wasn't really. It was just the first thing that felt okay and then I built everything else on top of it.

So that's the main thing going into 1.1, which I'm aiming to have out next month:

- Retuning jump gravity and air control. Tighter fall, less drift. I'll probably keep a hair of the floatiness because the level geometry was built around it and I don't want to break every gap in the game, but it'll be noticeably firmer.
- Landing feedback — a small squash and a bit more sound on touchdown.
- Two crash bugs that got reported on launch day. Both are fixed on my end already; they'll ride along with the patch.
- The settings menu doesn't remember your resolution between sessions. It will.
- A few text fixes people caught.

I'll put a beta branch up in a couple of weeks for anyone who wants to try the new movement before it goes live, since I'd rather hear "this is worse now" from thirty people than from four hundred.

After 1.1 I genuinely don't know yet. There's a list of things I cut during development that I'd like to look at again, but I'm not going to promise any of it until I've had a few weeks to not be exhausted.

That's it. That's the week. Thanks to everyone who bought it, everyone who told a friend, and the person who wrote three paragraphs about the puzzle.

More when there's more.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
Nine girls’ soccer games have been rained out or moved in the last two seasons because our grass field floods. The boys’ football field got turf in 2019.

The school board is about to vote on next year’s facilities budget. It’s time to put turf on the girls’ soccer field—with the drainage and maintenance plan needed to make it work.

I coach girls’ soccer and track at our public high school. I’m not asking for a showpiece. I’m asking for a field we can count on using.

When a game gets moved, families have to rearrange rides and work schedules. When it gets canceled, players lose a chance to compete after putting in the work to prepare. Coaches can adjust. So can kids. But nine games in two seasons is not an occasional inconvenience. It is a facilities problem.

Last October, one of my players tore her ACL stepping in a rut on our field. I’m not going to claim that turf prevents ACL injuries. It doesn’t, and the board should look carefully at the safety, heat and maintenance requirements of any surface it considers. But we cannot talk about the drawbacks of replacing this field while ignoring the condition of the field our girls use now.

Keeping what we have is also a decision. Our players live with that decision every season.

Then there is the fairness question.

The district invested in turf for boys’ football in 2019. I’m glad those athletes have it. This is not an argument for taking anything away from them. It is an argument for giving girls’ soccer the same serious attention when its field repeatedly fails.

Our girls practice, compete and represent this school. They deserve more than being told to make do with a flooded field while another program has had turf for years.

I know facilities money is limited. Classrooms need repairs. Other teams have needs. A responsible board has to weigh all of that. It also has to account for the full cost of turf, including upkeep and eventual replacement—not just installation.

So get solid bids. Require proper drainage. Ask hard questions about player safety and long-term costs. Then fund the project instead of pushing it into another budget year.

I expect my players to show up prepared and take care of their responsibilities. They should be able to expect the district to take care of its responsibilities, too.

They have put in the work. Give them a field that does.

b.text:
**Turf the girls' soccer field. It's past time.**

Nine games. That's how many the girls' soccer team has had rained out or moved off our home field in the last two seasons. Not because of storms you'd remember. Because the field floods after an ordinary Tuesday rain and doesn't drain for days.

When a game gets moved, here's what that actually looks like. I'm on the phone at 6 a.m. with the other coach trying to find a field. Parents who took off work to come watch find out at lunch that we're now playing 40 minutes away, or on a Saturday, or not at all. Girls who've been looking forward to a home game all week get on a bus instead. Senior night got moved last year. We played it on the visitors' field.

That's the inconvenient part. Here's the dangerous part.

Last October one of my players tore her ACL. She wasn't tackled. Nobody touched her. She was running for a ball and her foot went into a rut where the field had flooded, dried out, and been chewed up by the previous week's practice. She's had surgery. She's looking at nine months to a year of rehab. She may or may not play in college like she'd planned.

I'm not going to pretend a turf field prevents every knee injury. It doesn't. But that injury was not bad luck. It was a hole in the ground that shouldn't have been there, on a field that can't hold up to the use it gets. Anyone who has walked our field in the spring knows exactly what I'm talking about. You can't get through a practice without somebody rolling an ankle in a soft spot.

The football field got turf in 2019. I was glad when it happened. Nobody argued that the boys should keep playing on mud. The reasoning was that it would cut down on cancellations, reduce injuries from bad footing, and hold up to heavy use. All of that turned out to be true. The football field hasn't lost a home game to weather since.

Every one of those reasons applies to the girls' soccer field. The difference is we've been waiting six years and it's still not in the budget.

I don't think anybody on the board sat down and decided the girls matter less. I think the football field got done because it had loud support and it was in front of people. The soccer field is out behind the bus lot and the girls have mostly just dealt with it. That's on me too. I should have been making noise about this a long time ago.

So I'm making noise now, before the facilities vote.

The cost is real. I'm not going to wave it away. But this district already knows what a turf field costs and what it saves, because we did it once. We know the maintenance numbers. We know how many hours the football field gets used now compared to when it was grass, including by other teams and community groups. Run the same numbers for the soccer field. Then add in what it costs to bus a team to a rented field nine times, and what it costs a family when their kid needs knee surgery.

And if the answer is that we can only afford one turf field in this district, then we should be asking why it's fine for the boys to have it and not the girls. I don't think anyone wants to make that argument out loud. So let's not put ourselves in the position of having to.

I coach because I like the kids and I like the sport. I don't do this to write letters to the newspaper. But I've got a player on crutches and a schedule I can't trust, and I've run out of ways to explain to fifteen-year-olds why their field is the one that never gets fixed.

Put the turf in the budget. Come out to a practice first if you want. Bring boots.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
1. **Turn off the boiler and circulator, and let the system cool.**  
   Turn the thermostats down, then shut off the heating system at its service switch. Don’t bleed baseboards while the boiler is hot or the circulator is running—hot water can cause serious burns.

2. **Find the bleeder valve on the first baseboard.**  
   Start with the unit closest to the boiler, then work outward through each heating loop. Look near the end of the baseboard for a small manual bleeder valve. You may need to remove an end cover to reach it.

   These steps are for **hot-water baseboards with individual bleeder valves**, not electric baseboard heaters. Some hot-water systems don’t have bleeders at each unit and must be purged at the boiler instead. If you can’t find a bleeder, don’t loosen a pipe fitting or open a drain or pressure-relief valve as a substitute.

3. **Put a cup under the valve.**  
   Keep a towel underneath, too. The first water out may be dirty, and it can still be warm. Keep your face and hands out of the discharge path.

4. **Open the bleeder slowly.**  
   Use a radiator key or a flathead screwdriver, depending on the valve. Turn it counterclockwise just enough to release air—usually only a small fraction of a turn. **Do not remove the screw.**

   You may hear hissing, followed by sputtering water. Leave the valve slightly open until water flows steadily with no hissing or air spurts. You don’t need to drain a cupful once the air is gone.

5. **Close it snugly, not forcefully.**  
   Turn the valve clockwise until the water stops. Overtightening can damage or crack the valve seat and leave you with a leak. Wipe the valve dry and check for drips.

6. **Repeat at every baseboard—including the basement loop.**  
   Work unit by unit, starting closest to the boiler and moving outward. Don’t bleed only the upstairs units and call it done. A basement loop can hold trapped air, too, and skipping it may leave part of the house cold. Check every loop rather than assuming the air is all upstairs—or all downstairs.

7. **Check system pressure, then test the heat.**  
   Bleeding releases some water and can lower system pressure. Before restarting, check the boiler gauge against the cold-fill pressure specified for your system. If pressure is low, no water comes out of a bleeder, or you’re unsure what the gauge should read, stop and call for service rather than adding water blindly.

   Restore power, turn up a thermostat, and let the system run. Check that each baseboard warms up and that the bleeders stay dry.

**Still have a cold baseboard?** A zone valve, circulator, low system pressure, or a loop that needs proper purging could be the problem. If air keeps returning or a valve won’t stop dripping, contact us to have the system checked.

b.text:
If your baseboards are gurgling or they're hot on one end and ice cold on the other, you've got air trapped in the loop. Here's how I bleed them in the field.

**What you need:** small cup or plastic container, an old towel, and a radiator key or flathead screwdriver.

**1. Shut the system down first.**
Hit the emergency switch for the boiler and turn off the circulator. You don't want the pump pushing more air around while you're bleeding, and you don't want to get hit with scalding water. Give it 10-15 minutes to cool down if it's been running.

**2. Find the bleeder valve.**
It's on the end of each baseboard unit, under the end cap. Little brass fitting with a flat or square head. That's it.

**3. Put your cup underneath it and have the towel ready.**
Even when you do it right, it'll spit a little.

**4. Open it slow.**
Quarter-turn with the key or flathead until you hear hissing. Don't crank it wide open. Let the air come out until the water runs in a steady stream with no sputtering or hissing.

**5. Close it snug.**
Snug, not Hercules tight. If you overtighten these you'll crack the valve seat and then you really have a leak. Just firm until the water stops.

**6. Go unit by unit, closest to the boiler and work out.**
Start with the baseboard closest to the boiler and work your way to the end of each loop. Do every unit, even if it feels hot.

The mistake I see that causes 90% of our "cold radiator" calls: people only bleed the upstairs units and skip the basement loop. The basement loop is usually where the air is actually sitting. If you skip it, you'll be right back where you started.

Once you're done, turn the boiler and circulator back on. Check the pressure gauge on the boiler - you should be around 12-15 psi cold. If a zone is still cold after you've bled everything, or you're not getting any water out of a bleeder, give us a call and we'll get you on the schedule.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
**Bleed Your Baseboard Heat Before Winter: Start at the Boiler, Not the Upstairs**

If your baseboards are cold at the bottom or dead along the whole length, air is trapped in the loop—not a major drain, just enough to stop flow. I write this between jobs because every fall the same call comes in: homeowner bleeds the upstairs, skips the basement, and wonders why the zone is still cold. Do it in this order and you’ll fix most of it yourself.

1. **Kill power to the circulator and boiler first.** You do not want the pump pushing water while a valve is open.
2. **Find the bleeder valve on the end of each baseboard unit**—small brass slotted screw or square-key fitting.
3. **Slide a cup or rag underneath.** It will drip.
4. **Insert a key or flathead screwdriver and turn slow counter-clockwise.** Don’t force it.
5. **Leave it open until the stream runs steady with zero hissing air.** Once it’s a smooth water flow with no bubbles, you’re clear.
6. **Close it snug.** Overtightening cracks the valve seat, and then you’re buying a replacement instead of just bleeding it.
7. **Go unit by unit, starting closest to the boiler and working outward** to the far end of the loop.

The mistake that causes most of our cold-radiator calls is bleeding only the upstairs units and skipping the basement loop. Air collects low in hydronic systems, not high. The basement baseboards—especially the ones at the end of the loop—are usually where the bubble is actually sitting. If you skip them, your upstairs units stay cold no matter how many times you open the upstairs bleeders.

If you run this sequence and still have cold spots, the air may be stuck in a different zone or the pump may need checking. Give us a call—we handle this exact call every fall, and now you know the order to do it right.

b.text:
Before you call for service, try this quick fix if your baseboards aren't warming up. Start by shutting off the circulator or boiler completely so the system isn't under pressure while you work. Locate the bleeder valve on the end of each baseboard unit; it usually looks like a small hex nut or slot. Place a cup or shallow bowl underneath it to catch any drips.

Turn the valve slowly with a bleeding key or flathead screwdriver. Keep turning until the hissing stops and water flows out steadily. Close the valve snugly, but avoid overtightening—you can crack the valve seat if you use too much force. Move through your home unit by unit, starting with the ones closest to the boiler and working outward.

The most common mistake we see is only bleeding the upstairs units while skipping the basement loop. Air naturally rises and collects in the lower loops, leaving upper radiators cold even after you think you've bled the system. Check the basement first, then move up. If the pipes stay cold after this, give us a ring and we'll check the pressure.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
A three-point deficit is not a reason to abandon a running game that’s working.

That’s the part of this second-round state playoff loss that will stick with me. Not simply that the season ended, or that it ended against a team our guys beat by 20 back in Week 3. It’s that, with the game still within reach, they moved away from something the opponent hadn’t given them a good reason to quit.

The second-half decision to abandon the run cost them this game. That’s my read, and an 8-2 season doesn’t make that decision immune from criticism.

Dez Kowalski threw for a school-record 2,340 yards this year. That deserves its own place in the school’s football history, without a playoff loss attached to every mention. He gave this offense a weapon few teams around here have ever had.

But having a record-setting quarterback doesn’t mean every close game needs to become his rescue mission. A productive running game helps him. It makes a defense account for more than his arm. Staying with it wouldn’t have been timid football. It would have been sensible football.

And no, winning the first meeting by 20 didn’t guarantee anything in the rematch. Opponents adjust. Playoff games are their own games. But that cuts both ways: coaches have to respond to what’s working that night, not just lean on the season’s biggest strength.

These players earned the town’s applause. Eight wins and a school passing record are accomplishments worth celebrating.

They also earned a chance to finish this playoff game with the full offense available to them. Down three, the run should still have been part of the answer.

b.text:

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
I made a massive pricing mistake with Tallyup.

I raised our prices by 40% on everyone overnight.

In just one week, I lost 30 of our 140 customers.

Here is what went wrong, why it blew up, and what I changed: 🧵

1/ The background:

Every advice thread for indie SaaS founders says the same thing: "Charge more."

As a solo founder building Tallyup (a retention tool for gym owners), I knew the value was there. So I decided it was time to adjust our pricing up by 40%.

2/ The mistake wasn't the price increase itself—it was how I rolled it out.

- I applied the 40% hike to existing users overnight.
- I gave zero advance notice.
- I didn't grandfather the early users who supported the product from day one.

3/ The fallout was fast.

In 7 days, 30 out of our 140 customers canceled. 

In a close-knit niche like gym owners, trust matters. Forcing a sudden 40% jump on existing users broke that trust, and the cancellations poured in.

4/ What I changed to fix it:

- Reverted the price hike for all impacted existing users and reached out directly to explain.
- Grandfathered existing accounts at their original rate.
- Applied the new 40% higher pricing ONLY to new sign-ups moving forward.

5/ Lessons learned the hard way:

- Protect your early supporters. Grandfather existing users when making big leaps.
- Test new pricing on new traffic, not your existing base.
- If you ever do change rates for current customers, give plenty of advance notice and clear reasoning.

Building in public means sharing the bad decisions alongside the wins. Hopefully, this saves another solo founder from making the same mistake.

b.text:
1/
Last week I made the worst pricing decision since starting Tallyup.

Tallyup is a small subscription tool that helps gym owners track member retention.

We had 140 customers.

I raised prices 40% on everyone overnight.

30 of them canceled in a week.

Here’s what happened and what I changed.

2/
The change was blunt:

I updated our pricing, and every active customer’s next charge was 40% higher.

No warning email.
No grandfathering.
No explanation.
Just a bigger charge.

3/
Then the cancellations hit.

30 of our 140 customers canceled in 7 days.

These were gym owners already using Tallyup to track retention. They weren’t asking for a price increase—I just handed them one.

4/
The mistake wasn’t raising prices.

The mistake was doing it:
• overnight
• on existing customers
• without notice
• without explaining the value

Price is a promise. I broke it.

5/
What I changed:

First, I rolled the increase back for every customer who was active before the change.

They’re back on the old price. No surprise 40% renewal.

6/
Second, the higher price now applies only to new customers.

If I ever change pricing for existing customers again, they’ll get advance notice and the option to keep their current rate.

7/
Third, I emailed the 30 customers who canceled.

I apologized, took responsibility, and offered their old price back.

I’m not going to guess how many will return. Some conversations are still open.

8/
Fourth, I now write the pricing-change email before I change pricing.

If I can’t explain the increase honestly in one short email, I’m not ready to ship it.

9/
After those cancellations, 110 of the original 140 remained.

I traded short-term revenue for trust, and that’s the right trade.

If you’re building indie SaaS: don’t surprise the people who already said yes.

10/
That’s the update.

Back to building Tallyup—this time without breaking trust.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
**60% Planted, 22% Higher, $46,000 More: Fix the Acreage Cap**

By the late-May deadline, I had planted 60% of my corn and soybean acres. The other 40% went prevented. Not because I didn’t want to plant it. Because it would not stop raining.

Then USDA’s Risk Management Agency raised the base rate for prevented planting coverage by 22% in our region. On my operation, that hike costs about $46,000 this year.

That is not a rounding error. That is a new tractor. That is a year of health insurance. That is the margin on several hundred acres of beans. I buy prevented planting coverage for the same reason I carry insurance on my combine: one bad spring can take the year. But this year, the safety net got more expensive at the exact moment we needed it most.

The part that makes no sense is how the acreage caps work. They do not hit every farm the same. A bigger operation with more spread-out acreage and more insured units can absorb the cap. My family operation cannot. Proportionally, the 22% increase and the acreage cap take a bigger bite out of my farm than they do the bigger operations nearby. That is not risk management. That is a penalty for being family-sized.

SB 214 would fix the acreage cap. It would update the formula so prevented planting coverage reflects the acres a family farm actually operates. It does not create a new entitlement or ask taxpayers to bail out bad management. It simply stops the current cap from punishing the operations that need the coverage most when weather takes the spring.

I am not asking for a guarantee. I am asking for a fair rule. If you planted 60% of your acres this spring, or if you watched your neighbor do it, you know what I mean. Call your state senator and state representative. Tell them to support SB 214. The next wet spring is not a question of if. It is a question of whether the cap has been fixed before it arrives.

— A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer

b.text:
**When the Rain Won't Stop, and the Bill Keeps Growing**

The USDA raised the prevented planting base rate 22% this year in our region. That's not a typo—twenty-two percent, in a single year. For me, that translated to roughly $46,000 in additional costs I didn't budget for and can't control.

This spring, it wouldn't stop raining. I'm not looking for sympathy—every farmer in this county knows what I'm talking about. But the facts are the facts: I could only get 60% of my acres planted before the late May deadline. That left 40% of my operation hitting the prevented planting program, and the premium hike hit right alongside it.

Here's what makes this worse for families like mine. The acreage caps don't scale with the size of your operation. On a 450-acre farm, losing a chunk of plantable acres pushes you up against that cap fast. When you're running 2,400 acres, you've got more room to absorb the hit proportionally. The way the system is structured, the smaller family farms carry a heavier burden percentage-wise. That's not a fair system. That's a system that's slowly squeezing us out.

There's a fix on the table: SB 214. It would revise the acreage cap so the program actually serves the family operations it's supposed to protect—not just the operations big enough to work around the rules.

I'm not asking for a handout. I'm asking for the rules to be fair. A 22% rate hike with no cap adjustment is a penalty on doing the right thing: trying to keep land in production, trying to keep this farm in the family, trying to be responsible stewards of the soil.

If you're reading this, whether you're a fellow farmer or someone in the statehouse who's never set foot in a field after rain, I'd ask you to look at the numbers. Forty-six thousand dollars is not a rounding error for an operation like mine. It's the difference between making ends meet and falling behind.

Support SB 214. The math doesn't lie, and neither does the mud.

a.text:
Dear Editor,

I drove Route 4 out of Kettle Falls for 22 years. I'm retired now, but I know this town and I know the people on these roads, and I've got something to say about the post office closing our counter service.

The USPS says our branch loses $40,000 a year. Well, no wonder. They already cut our window hours from 8 to noon. Once that counter closes, the nearest full-service window is twenty minutes to Fairview. She doesn't drive. Tell me how she's supposed to manage that.

This isn't just about numbers on a spreadsheet. It's about people who've been here their whole lives and who counted on the post office being there the way it always has been.

There's a public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall. I'd like to ask every person who reads this to show up. Bring your neighbor. Bring your stories. The district manager is supposed to be there, and he needs to look us in the eye and hear what this means to Kettle Falls.

Gerald Whitmore
Kettle Falls

b.text:
To the Editor,

Most folks around here know me from Route 4. I drove those 38 miles six days a week for 22 years before retiring last year, so I have a pretty fair idea of how this town works and what people need. 

The Postal Service says our counter service in Kettle Falls is losing $40,000 a year. What they leave out is that they cut our window hours down to four hours a morning—8 a.m. to noon—a few years back. When you cut the hours in half, cut the staff, and make it hard for working people to get in the door, of course customer traffic is going to drop off. It doesn't take an accountant to see they’re pointing at a problem they made themselves to justify shutting the counter for good.

This isn’t just numbers on a balance sheet. Think about folks like Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She’s in her eighties, lives alone, and gets her heart medication through the mail. She doesn't use the internet, and she doesn't drive anymore. If she needs to send a package, buy stamps, or get a money order to pay her electric bill, she can’t just hop in a car and make the twenty-minute drive over to Fairview. There are dozens of people on my old route in the exact same boat.

The USPS district manager is coming to town for a public forum on Tuesday, July 28, at the Grange Hall. If you care about keeping our town whole, you need to show up and fill those seats. They need to look us in the eye and hear why Kettle Falls still needs a real post office.

Don Mason
Kettle Falls

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
**Open Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors**

Lunch is supposed to give students a break in the middle of the school day, but right now it is also one of the most crowded and stressful parts of the schedule. Our school should allow juniors and seniors to have open campus lunch because it would reduce cafeteria overcrowding, reflect what students actually want, and follow the example of nearby districts where the policy has worked. Allowing older students to leave campus for lunch would be a reasonable change that benefits both students and the school.

The most immediate reason to consider open campus lunch is overcrowding. Our cafeteria only seats 220 people, but one lunch wave has 340 students. That means there are more students than seats before even considering how long lines move or how much space people need to actually eat comfortably. When the cafeteria is that full, students have trouble finding seats, the noise level increases, and lunch becomes rushed. If juniors and seniors were allowed to leave campus, fewer students would need to eat in the cafeteria at the same time. This would make lunch more manageable for the students who remain and for the staff supervising them.

Students also strongly support the idea. In a survey I conducted with 80 students at our school, 71 said they were in favor of open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. That is almost 89 percent, which shows that this is not just a small preference but a clear opinion among the student body. Students are the ones most affected by lunch policies, and their views should matter when the school is deciding how to improve the daily schedule. Juniors and seniors are also older and more experienced students, so they can be trusted with a limited privilege like leaving campus for lunch.

Another reason to support open campus lunch is that similar schools have already tried it successfully. Nearby districts such as Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade already allow open campus lunch, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness. This is important because one of the biggest concerns about open campus lunch is that students will not return to class on time. However, the evidence from other districts suggests that students are able to handle the responsibility. If those schools can make the policy work without creating a tardiness problem, our school can do the same with clear expectations and consequences.

Some people may argue that open campus lunch is a bad idea because students might leave the allowed area, return late, or make poor choices while off campus. Those concerns are understandable, but they do not mean the policy should be rejected. Instead, the school can create rules to prevent problems. For example, open campus lunch could be limited to juniors and seniors who have signed permission forms. Students could also lose the privilege if they are late or break the rules. Since nearby districts have not seen an increase in tardiness, it seems likely that these concerns can be managed.

Open campus lunch for juniors and seniors would be a practical solution to a real problem. It would reduce overcrowding in the cafeteria, give students more independence, and follow the successful example of nearby schools. The evidence shows that students support it and that it does not have to create the problems people fear. Our school should consider open campus lunch as a responsible and reasonable change.

b.text:
# Open Campus Lunch: A Reasonable Privilege for Upperclassmen

Every school day at noon, 340 students crowd into a cafeteria built to seat 220. The math does not work, and neither does the policy behind it. Our school should allow juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch. An open campus lunch would ease a real overcrowding problem, reflect what nearby districts have already proven safe, and give students the responsibility they are ready for.

The most immediate reason to adopt open campus lunch is that our current setup is physically overcrowded. Our cafeteria seats 220 people, but 340 students share the same lunch wave. That leaves more than a hundred students without a real place to sit, forcing them into hallways, stairwells, and the floor. Overcrowding like this is not just uncomfortable; it makes the space harder to supervise and harder to keep clean. Letting upperclassmen leave for lunch would relieve the pressure directly, freeing up seats for the students who stay.

Critics might argue that letting students leave campus would cause them to come back late, disrupting afternoon classes. This is a fair concern, but the evidence from nearby districts suggests it is unfounded. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow open campus lunch for juniors and seniors, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness after the policy took effect. These are not distant, unfamiliar schools; they are districts right next to ours, with similar students and similar schedules. If open campus lunch worked without increasing tardiness for them, there is little reason to believe our students would behave differently.

Beyond the practical benefits, open campus lunch is also something students want and are ready for. When I surveyed 80 students at our school, 71 said they were in favor of the policy. That is nearly nine out of ten. Juniors and seniors are sixteen and seventeen years old, many of them working jobs, driving cars, and preparing for college, where they will manage their own time entirely. A short window to leave for lunch is a modest, age-appropriate step toward that independence.

Some may still worry that open campus lunch treats a privilege as if it were a right, or that not every student will use the freedom responsibly. But the policy would apply only to upperclassmen, and it could be tied to conditions like good standing or timely returns, just as it is in neighboring districts. A privilege can be earned and, if abused, taken away.

The case for open campus lunch is straightforward. Our cafeteria cannot hold the students assigned to it, nearby districts have shown the policy causes no increase in tardiness, and the overwhelming majority of students support it. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus for lunch is not a risky experiment. It is a practical, proven solution that our school should adopt.
