a.text:
## One Week In: 412 Copies and a Movement Patch

I launched my game last week after about three years of working on it during nights and weekends.

The first week ended at 412 copies sold, which is more than I knew how to picture when I started making the game. It’s been surreal seeing people actually play something that spent so long existing mostly on my hard drive.

The game also hit the front page of a small subreddit for around six hours, which brought in a noticeable spike of traffic and a lot of new players. I’m still catching up on some of the comments and messages, but it’s been great seeing people talk about specific levels, mechanics, and weird little details I wasn’t sure anyone would notice.

The most consistent criticism so far has been about the movement. One review described it as feeling floaty, and honestly, they’re right. I’ve been playing it for so long that I had started compensating for it without really noticing, but watching new players move around made the problem much more obvious.

I’m working on a movement update for version 1.1, currently planned for next month. I’m adjusting the acceleration, deceleration, and jump timing to make the controls feel more responsive without changing the overall feel of the game too drastically. I’m still testing different versions, so I don’t want to promise exact changes yet.

For now, I’m going through feedback, fixing the smaller bugs that have come up, and working on the 1.1 patch. Thanks to everyone who bought the game, left a review, sent feedback, or shared it somewhere. The first week has been a lot to process, but I’m glad the game is finally out in the world.

b.text:
## Launch week: 412 copies, a subreddit spike, and a floaty movement patch

Launch happened last week. I’ve been mostly sleeping, reading reviews, and staring at the sales dashboard.

First week numbers: **412 copies sold**. That’s not going to change my life, but it’s more than I expected for a first game. For context, I’ve been working on this for three years of nights and weekends, so seeing real people actually pay money for it is strange in the best way.

The game briefly hit the front page of a smaller subreddit and stayed there for about six hours. That drove most of the week-one traffic. Nothing huge, but it was nice to watch the wishlist-to-purchase rate tick up while the thread was alive.

One review said the movement feels floaty. They’re right. I knew it was a little loose, but I’d gotten used to it after three years of testing. That comment was the nudge I needed. I’m tightening up acceleration, reducing air control, and making landing feel a bit sharper. The plan is to ship that in **patch 1.1 next month**.

Other than the movement pass, I’m going through the usual post-launch list: small bug fixes, a couple of quality-of-life things people have asked for, and maybe a bit of controller deadzone tweaking.

No big lesson at the end. That’s just where things stand. If you bought the game, thanks. If you left a review or feedback, double thanks. Patch 1.1 is coming, and I’ll have more specifics in the next update.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
Six months in with the Jarvik L2 and I’m done being polite about it.

I bought it for $549 during a sale after burning out on a slow single-motor frame. As a remote software engineer, this desk is my entire office: 8-hour coding blocks, aggressive Vim typing, video calls, and constant height changes.

**Motors:** Excellent. Dual-motor, genuinely quiet, and fast—about 25 mm/s with almost no left-right lag. I can shift from sit to stand mid-call without muting, which is more than I can say for most desks in this range.

**Stability:** The problem. At 42 inches it’s fine. At full extension—around 48 inches—it shivers badly when I type hard. My keystrokes are loud and rapid, and at max height the desktop turns into a tuning fork. I feel it in my forearms. If you stand and type aggressively, this is a real, daily irritation.

**Memory presets:** Sloppy. I programmed three—sit, stand, and a middle “call height”—and within a month they started drifting. Now they’re off by roughly a centimeter, sometimes more. I have to manually jog them back every few days. At this price point, that’s lazy engineering.

**Cable tray:** Garbage. Thin, misaligned pre-drilled holes that don’t match the crossbar spacing, flimsy plastic hinges that snap if you breathe on them wrong, and a finish that already shows rust spots after six months of use. I ripped it off after two weeks and bought a $35 aftermarket tray. Do not plan around the included one.

**Verdict:** The frame and desktop are solid—good powder coat, decent laminate, tight assembly. But the wobble at full height and drifting presets are dealbreakers at full price. At $549 on sale, it’s acceptable value if you need speed and quiet operation and can live with the flaws. At $749 MSRP? Absolutely not. For that money, get a Uplift V2 with a real crossbar or a Fully Jarvis—both hold position better and don’t drift. Buy the Jarvik cheap, ditch the tray, and keep your expectations realistic.

b.text:
**Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6 Months of Daily Abuse**

I bought the Jarvik L2 six months ago during a sale for $549. I’m a remote software engineer, which means this desk sees 8–10 hours of use nearly every day, with a dual-monitor setup, a mechanical keyboard, and a laptop dock. I don’t do affiliate links and I don’t pull punches. Here’s what you actually need to know.

**The motor: genuinely good.**  
The L2’s dual-motor lift is fast — about 1.5 inches per second from my rough timing — and quiet enough that I can raise or lower it during a video call without anyone asking what that hum is. It’s smoother than the Uplift V2 I used at a previous job, and it doesn’t strain or slow down even with roughly 90 pounds of gear on top. Over six months, the motor hasn’t hiccuped once. That’s the best part of this desk.

**The wobble: real, but not a dealbreaker at the sale price.**  
At sitting height (28–30 inches), the L2 is rock solid. At standing height for me — 44 inches — it’s fine for normal typing and mousing. But if I type hard, which I do on a tactile mechanical keyboard, the whole desk shudders side-to-side. My monitors visibly shake. It’s not enough to make me nauseous, but it’s enough that I’ve learned to type lighter when standing or brace my forearms on the edge. If you’re a heavy typist or you hammer your mouse, you will notice this. At 46 inches, it’s worse. This is a two-leg desk with a crossbar, not a four-leg tank. Manage your expectations.

**Memory presets: they drift. About a centimeter.**  
The L2 has four programmable height presets. I set mine to 29.5” for sitting and 44” for standing. Within a week, both had drifted — sitting crept up to 30.1”, standing down to 43.9”. It’s not huge, but I can feel the difference in my elbow angle, and it means I’m recalibrating every two or three weeks. The control panel is easy enough to reset, but for a desk that markets “precision memory,” this is sloppy. If you’re picky about ergonomics, it’ll annoy you.

**The cable tray is garbage. Full stop.**  
Jarvik includes a flimsy metal cable tray that mounts under the desk. The mounting clips are thin plastic, and two of mine snapped within the first month just from the weight of a power strip and a few cables. The tray itself is too shallow to hold a standard surge protector without it sliding out when the desk moves. I ended up ripping it out and using adhesive cable channels and zip ties instead. Don’t factor the tray into your buying decision — it’s basically e-waste.

**Everything else.**  
The desktop surface (I got the 60” x 30” bamboo) has held up fine — no scratches, no warping, even with coffee spills. The frame is sturdy and the lift columns don’t creak. Assembly took me about 45 minutes solo, though the instructions are mediocre and the included hex wrench is soft metal that started stripping on the last bolt. The desk does have a slight front-to-back rock on carpet, but I fixed it with furniture pads.

**Verdict.**  
At $549, the Jarvik L2 is a genuinely good value. You get a fast, quiet motor, a decent-sized surface, and a desk that works reliably for daily standing use — as long as you can live with the wobble at full height and the drifting presets. I’d buy it again at that price.

At $749, the current full price, I would not. For that money, you’re within striking distance of a Uplift V2 or Fully Jarvis (when they run sales), both of which have better stability and more reliable memory. The L2’s flaws are tolerable when you’re saving $200. They’re not when you’re paying a premium.

**Bottom line:** Wait for a sale. If you see it under $600, grab it. If it’s $749, keep scrolling.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
# Week One: 412 Copies, One Reddit Spike, and a Movement Patch Coming

So the game's been out for a week. Here's what happened.

**Sales: 412 copies in the first week.** That's across Steam and itch. Most of it came in the first 48 hours, which I expected since that's when the mailing list and devlog folks showed up. Things settled into a slower trickle after that, maybe 10-15 copies a day by the end of the week. Not nothing, but definitely not the launch trajectory you picture when you're three years deep in a side project.

**The subreddit thing:** Someone posted about the game in r/IndieGaming on Wednesday and it actually climbed to the front page for about six hours. I think that's where a decent chunk of Thursday's sales came from. By Friday it had dropped off and the sub moved on. I'd be lying if I said I didn't refresh the post too many times while it was up. But it was a small sub, not some massive r/games moment, so I'm keeping perspective. A nice blip, not a breakthrough.

**The review:** There's one review up on Steam right now. It's positive, which I'm grateful for, but the reviewer said the movement feels floaty. And honestly, they're right. I've known it was a little off for a while but I'd been staring at it too long to really see it clearly anymore. Seeing someone else name it confirmed what I was half-noticing. Too much acceleration ramp, not enough ground friction. It's fixable.

**What's next:** Patch 1.1 is going out next month. Main thing is the movement rework — tightening up the acceleration curves, adding proper friction values, maybe reducing air control slightly. I've already got a test build that feels better just from an afternoon of tweaking. I'll also fix a couple of small bugs people have reported (menu scaling on ultrawide, one softlock in chapter 3 if you backtrack after the bridge sequence).

That's it for now. Game's out, some people are playing it, and I've got a to-do list. Thanks to everyone who picked up a copy this week.

b.text:
# One Week In

I launched the game last Tuesday. 412 copies sold in the first week.

That's the headline. It still doesn't feel entirely real to type out.

The launch day was chaos in the best way—the game hit the front page of r/indiegames for about 6 hours, which sent a spike of traffic that made my hosting sweat a little. I kept refreshing Steam to see the numbers climb, which is probably not healthy but I couldn't stop myself. By end of day I'd made more money than I spent on the game's development. That's the part that actually feels surreal.

The reviews have been mostly positive. A lot of people loved the art direction and the puzzle design. A few people noted performance issues on older hardware that I'm already working on for the next patch. And yeah, one review said the movement feels floaty. They're right. I've been thinking about it since, and I know exactly what they mean—the character model isn't giving enough weight to the jump arc. I started prototyping a fix last week and it's already feeling better. That's going into 1.1 next month.

The player comments have been great to read. Some people are finding secrets I forgot I hid. Someone made fan art. Someone else said they played for five hours straight and lost track of time, which is honestly all I've ever wanted a game to do.

Right now I'm running through the bug reports, planning that movement patch, and trying not to work myself into the ground on updates. Three years of nights and weekends to get here. I'm going to try to actually sleep for a bit before I keep going.

Next devlog will be in two weeks when 1.1 is closer to done.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
# Opening the Gates: Why Our School Should Allow Open Campus Lunch

Every day at 12:15, the same thing happens at our school: 340 students pour into a cafeteria built to seat 220. Kids eat standing in hallways, squeeze three to a table designed for two, or give up entirely and skip lunch. Meanwhile, just a few miles away, students at Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade high schools are free to leave campus for lunch, and their schools are doing just fine. Our juniors and seniors should be granted the same open campus privilege, and the evidence from neighboring districts, from our own students, and from our overcrowded cafeteria makes the case clearly.

The strongest argument for open campus lunch is that it has already been tested nearby, and it works. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade school districts all allow upperclassmen to leave campus during lunch, and their published attendance statistics show no rise in tardiness after the policy took effect. In other words, the main objection people raise—that students will wander back late and miss class—did not actually happen. These are districts like ours, with kids the same age dealing with the same temptation to linger, and their numbers stayed steady. If three comparable schools can make this work, the claim that it is too risky starts to look less like a real concern and more like an assumption.

Beyond the district data, the students who would actually be affected by this policy want it. I surveyed 80 students at our school, and 71 of them—nearly 90 percent—said they support open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. Some opponents might argue that students just want freedom for its own sake, but that misses the point: a policy that affects students every single day should weigh what students actually think. When a supermajority of the affected group supports a change, and the change has proven harmless in neighboring districts, the burden shifts to the school to explain why it is holding out.

Finally, open campus lunch would solve a space problem that already exists. Our cafeteria seats 220 people, but our lunch wave has 340 students. That means more than a hundred kids every day have nowhere to sit. This is not a hypothetical overcrowding concern about a future policy; it is the current reality. If even a third of the juniors and seniors left campus for lunch, the cafeteria would drop below its actual capacity for the first time in years. Open campus lunch would not create a new situation at our school—it would relieve a problem the administration has not otherwise fixed.

Critics may still worry about safety, liability, or younger students feeling left out. But the liability question has an answer: schools can require parent permission slips and a signed conduct agreement, the same way Fairmont and West Linn handle it. And the policy can be limited to juniors and seniors, who are sixteen or older, many of whom already drive, hold jobs, and handle adult responsibilities everywhere else in their lives. We trust these students to operate cars on public roads; we can trust them to buy a sandwich and come back.

The evidence is straightforward. Three nearby districts adopted open campus lunch and saw no rise in tardiness. Nearly 90 percent of surveyed students at our school support the change. And our cafeteria is over capacity by more than a hundred students right now. The administration should approve open campus lunch for juniors and seniors—it has the data, the demand, and the space problem pointing in exactly the same direction.

b.text:
Open Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors: A Change We Can Actually Afford

Every weekday at 11:50, three hundred and forty juniors and seniors pour into a cafeteria built for two hundred and twenty. That is not a scheduling inconvenience. That is a structural failure dressed up as a routine. For years, our school has treated open campus lunch—the option for juniors and seniors to eat off-site during the lunch period—as a privilege reserved for other districts, something we could grant only if we were certain it wouldn't cause chaos. We are certain. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade have been running open campus lunch programs for the past three years, and their published attendance data shows no measurable increase in tardiness or class-cutting among upperclassmen. Given that context, and given the simple arithmetic of our own cafeteria's square footage, our school should extend open campus lunch to all juniors and seniors who have parental permission and no disciplinary holds.

The closest district to us in both size and demographics, Fairmont, transitioned to open campus lunch for juniors and seniors two years ago. Their superintendent's annual report for the 2023–2024 year notes that tardy rates among juniors and seniors stayed flat compared to the prior year, and that the district's overall attendance percentage did not shift by more than half a percentage point. West Linn made the same change a year earlier. Cascade, which is smaller and more rural, followed last fall and reported the same non-change in its mid-year data pull. Three districts, three separate administrative teams, three sets of numbers, and the result is the same: kids are not walking into third period late just because they had the option to grab a sandwich at the deli down the road. The fear that open campus lunch will unravel the school day simply has not materialized in the places that already do it.

The overcrowding problem is not a theoretical one. I counted seats. Our cafeteria seats two hundred twenty students. Our lunch wave for juniors and seniors numbers three hundred forty. That gap is not something you can solve by squeezing kids onto benches or telling them to eat in the library. It means that even if every junior and senior wants nothing more than to eat on campus, roughly a third of that wave will be standing, turning around looking for a place to set a tray, or eating on the floor by the vending machines. Open campus lunch does not require anyone to leave. It gives students who would rather eat at a restaurant, a park bench, or even their own car the option to do so, which thins the rush enough that the kids who stay can actually find a table. I am not arguing that we should empty the cafeteria. I am arguing that we should stop pretending the cafeteria is big enough for everyone when the seat count says it isn't.

One concern I hear raised, including by a couple of the teachers I asked before writing this, is that open campus lunch disproportionately affects kids who live far from town and would just sit in a car for forty-five minutes instead of eating. That is a fair point, and it is the one reason I think the policy should be permission-based rather than automatic. If a student's family lives twenty miles out, the practical choice might be the vending machines regardless of what the policy says. But that is an argument for making the option available to those who can use it, not an argument for withholding it from everyone. The kids in our survey—of eighty juniors and seniors I polled across two lunch periods, seventy-one said they would use open campus lunch at least twice a week if it were available, and sixty-three of those seventy-one said they currently leave campus without permission to do exactly that, using the rest of the school day as their excuse to drive home early or walk to the shopping plaza on Fifth Street. The activity is already happening. The policy just doesn't admit it.

None of this is about freedom for freedom's sake, and I don't want the essay to read like I think a sixteen-year-old needs the right to choose between Taco Bell and the pizza line. It is about a building that runs over capacity every single day, a neighboring set of schools whose data says the sky does not fall, and a student body that overwhelmingly wants one small change. Open campus lunch for juniors and seniors, permission-based and tied to the existing attendance code so that tardiness still triggers the same consequences it does now, would relieve a real logistical problem, align our policy with the practices of the three districts we most resemble, and trust students with a choice they are more than capable of making responsibly. Our cafeteria seats two hundred twenty. We serve three hundred forty. Somewhere in that math is the case for letting a portion of those students eat somewhere else.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
## Don’t Cut a Program That Works

The state’s proposed 15% cut to apprenticeship funding is a bad deal for workers, employers, and taxpayers.

I am a third-year electrical apprentice with the IBEW. I have seen what apprenticeship funding does in real life. My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one finished the program and are now working journeyman jobs. That is an 87.5% completion rate, and those are 21 people with steady careers in a skilled trade.

Apprentices in our program start at about $19 an hour. As they gain skills, their pay goes up. Journeymen earn around $46 an hour. That means apprentices quickly become taxpayers, support their families, and move off public assistance programs. They also earn while they learn instead of taking on years of student debt.

The public cost is another reason lawmakers should reject this cut. The total public cost for an apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. The average public subsidy for someone who completes a four-year college degree is around $48,000. College is the right choice for many people, but it should not be treated as the only path worth funding. Apprenticeship produces skilled workers at less than one-third of that public cost.

Our state already needs more electricians and other skilled tradespeople. Homes, schools, hospitals, factories, power systems, and new construction all depend on trained workers. Cutting apprenticeship funding will not reduce that need. It will only make it harder to train enough people to do the work safely and correctly.

A 15% cut may look like savings on paper, but it will cost more later. Fewer apprentices mean fewer skilled workers, longer project delays, and fewer people moving into solid middle-class jobs. It also means less tax revenue and more pressure on assistance programs.

Apprenticeship funding is not a handout. It is an investment with a clear return. Our cohort shows that: 24 people started, 21 finished, and those 21 are now working as journeymen.

State legislators should reject the proposed 15% cut and keep apprenticeship funding strong. When a program puts people to work, meets a real labor need, and costs taxpayers less than other education paths, cutting it makes no sense.

b.text:
Don't Cut Apprenticeship Funding

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with the local IBEW. I work hard every day learning this trade, and I'm writing because the state wants to cut apprenticeship funding by 15 percent. That is a bad idea. It hurts working people, wastes a proven program, and costs the public more in the long run.

My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished and are working journeyman jobs right now. That is a strong completion rate. We start around $19 an hour and top out around $46 an hour as journeymen. Those wages get people off assistance programs fast. We pay taxes. We buy houses. We support our families without needing help from the state.

Look at the numbers. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to the average public subsidy of around $48,000 for a four-year college grad who finishes. Apprenticeships give better results for less money. We leave with a real skill, a license, and a job. We do not walk out with student debt and no clear path.

Cutting 15 percent will mean fewer training slots, fewer tools, fewer instructors, and fewer people like me getting a fair shot. That does not save the state money. It just pushes costs somewhere else—more people stuck in low-wage work or needing public help longer. Our program already works. Keep funding it.

Union members, talk to your legislators. Tell them this cut is shortsighted. State leaders, look at the facts. Twenty-one out of 24 finished. Good wages. Low public cost. Do not gut a program that builds skilled workers and strong communities.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
SUBMITTED TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED DOWNTOWN PARKING METER RATE INCREASE

TO: City Council Members and the Public Record
FROM: Owner, Independent Coffee Shop, Main Street

Members of the City Council, 

I am submitting this testimony to formally oppose the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour. While I understand the city's desire to optimize revenue and manage parking turnover, this specific proposal relies on assumptions that do not align with the operational realities of our local small business economy. I urge the council to reject this hike based on the following data.

The primary justification for raising meter rates is typically to encourage parking turnover. However, this logic fails when applied to my business and many others on Main Street. I have tracked my customer data extensively, and my patrons average a 22-minute visit. The current one-hour parking minimum already provides more than enough time for them to park, order, enjoy their coffee, and leave. Tripling the cost of parking will not turn over these spots any faster; it will simply penalize the customers who are already utilizing the current time limits efficiently. The infrastructure is already working as intended for the actual duration of a downtown retail visit.

Furthermore, we do not have to guess at the economic impact of this price increase; we have recent, localized data. In 2019, the neighboring town implemented a similar rate hike. Anticipating the potential impact, I tracked my own register data daily for six weeks following their increase. The result was a documented 18% drop in foot traffic. That is not a marginal fluctuation; it is a severe contraction in customer volume that directly threatens the profit margins of independent businesses. A 200% price increase on our own meters will undoubtedly replicate this 18% loss in downtown foot traffic, pulling revenue directly out of our local economy.

Finally, the financial benefit to the city does not justify the economic damage to the downtown corridor. According to the city’s own report, parking meter revenue currently covers only 4% of the downtown budget. Tripling the rate will not suddenly transform meters into the financial backbone of our city infrastructure, especially when factoring in the likely decrease in overall parking volume as drivers avoid the downtown area entirely due to the cost. This policy is not solving a structural budget deficit; it is extracting a marginal revenue gain at the direct expense of Main Street's vitality.

I urge the council to look at the hard numbers: a 22-minute average customer visit, a documented 18% drop in foot traffic from a neighboring town's identical policy, and a mere 4% contribution to the downtown budget. Please vote no on the proposed increase from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour and work with local business owners to find solutions that support, rather than penalize, our downtown economy. 

Respectfully submitted,

Owner, Independent Coffee Shop
Main Street

b.text:
# Testimony Regarding Proposed Parking Meter Rate Increase

**Submitted to the City Council for the Public Record**

Members of the City Council,

My name is [Name], and I own [Coffee Shop Name] on Main Street. I have operated my shop downtown for [number] years, and I am submitting this testimony in opposition to the proposed increase in parking meter rates from 50 cents per hour to $1.50 per hour — a 200 percent increase.

I am not here to speak in generalities. I want to give you three specific numbers and explain what each one means for my business and for this downtown.

**First: an 18 percent drop in foot traffic.** In 2019, when [neighboring town] raised its meter rates by a comparable margin, I paid close attention because I knew the same proposal could eventually come to us. For six weeks following their increase, I tracked my own register data against the same six-week period before the hike, and I spoke with business owners there who were doing the same. The foot traffic decline I documented was 18 percent. That is not a rounding error. For a small shop like mine, an 18 percent drop in customers is the difference between making payroll comfortably and lying awake at night. Margins in independent coffee are thin. I cannot absorb a decline of that size, and neither can most of my neighbors on this street.

**Second: my customers average a 22-minute visit.** I know this because I watch it every day — a customer parks, comes in, orders, sits or takes it to go, and leaves. The current one-hour minimum on the meters already more than covers the typical visit to my shop. In other words, the existing rate structure is not underpricing the parking my customers actually use. Tripling the hourly rate does not make my customers pay their fair share; it makes them pay triple for time they never use. A customer who runs downtown for a coffee will now pay $1.50 for 22 minutes of parking. At some point, the math tells them to go to the drive-through on the highway instead, where parking is free. And once that habit forms, it does not come back.

**Third: 4 percent.** According to the city's own report, meter revenue covers only 4 percent of the downtown budget. I want to sit with that number for a moment, because it is the heart of this issue. Even if this rate increase performed perfectly — even if not a single driver changed their behavior and revenue tripled — we would be talking about moving from 4 percent to roughly 12 percent of the downtown budget. That is not a solution to the city's budget challenges. But if the increase drives away foot traffic the way I watched it do in 2019, the city loses more than it gains: reduced sales tax receipts, struggling storefronts, and eventually vacancies. You would be trading a small, uncertain revenue gain for a real risk to the tax base that downtown businesses generate.

I want to be clear that I understand the city needs revenue, and I do not envy the decisions this council has to make. I am not asking you to do nothing. I am asking you not to solve a budget problem worth far more than 4 percent by putting a 200 percent increase on the backs of the customers who keep Main Street alive.

If the council believes parking rates must rise, I would ask you to consider alternatives: a smaller, phased increase; a free first 30 minutes to protect quick-visit customers like mine; or a genuine study of the projected impact on downtown sales tax revenue before this vote, not after.

I built my business on this street because I believed in this downtown. I still do. I am asking you to weigh the numbers I have given you — an 18 percent drop in foot traffic, a 22-minute average visit, and a 4 percent contribution to the budget — and conclude, as I have, that this proposal costs downtown more than it earns the city.

Thank you for your time and for entering this testimony into the record.

Respectfully submitted,

[Name]
Owner, [Coffee Shop Name]
[Address], Main Street

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
The second time I came back from Iraq, we landed at Fort Hood around two in the morning, went through the standard paperwork and medical checks, and finally got released to the gym where the families were waiting. 

I saw my wife first. Then I looked down for my daughter. She was six, and in twelve months she had grown out of her sneakers and lost two front teeth. When I knelt down and dropped my kit bag, she stepped back and tucked herself entirely behind her mother’s right leg. She gripped the denim with both hands and peeked out with one eye like I was a stranger asking for directions in a parking lot. 

My wife touched the back of her head and said, "It’s Daddy, honey. Go on." 

It took her about thirty seconds of staring at the uniform and my face before she let go of the jeans and walked over to let me hug her. She was stiff at first, then she rested her chin on my collarbone. I didn't say anything because my throat was completely dry.

Two days later, my wife sent me to the grocery store down the road for milk, eggs, and a box of cereal. 

I got the milk and the eggs without an issue. Then I turned into the cereal aisle and stopped. Downrange, you had whatever was sitting in the metal bins at the DFAC—usually mini boxes of Corn Flakes, Raisin Bran, or whatever hadn't expired yet. In this aisle, the shelves went from the floor to above my head, running thirty yards down. There were at least forty different kinds of cereal, all in bright red, yellow, and blue cardboard. Five different types of Cheerios alone. 

I stood in the center of the aisle with both hands on the push-bar of the cart. People went around me with their carts, looking at me once and moving on. I knew I should just reach out, grab a box of Rice Krispies, and walk to the register, but my brain wouldn't send the signal to my arm. I stood there for twenty minutes just reading the names on the boxes over and over until my legs got tired. Finally, I grabbed a plain box of Shredded Wheat and went to the checkout. 

Night was the hardest part to adjust to. For a year on the COP, my cot was positioned so that my feet pointed directly at the plywood door of our hooch. If that door moved, I was awake and looking straight at it with my rifle within reach. 

Back in our house, the bed sat along the far wall. My wife liked to sleep with the bedroom door open so the hallway fan would pull air through and so she could hear our daughter if she got up for water in the night. 

The first week, I couldn't do it. Every time she fell asleep, I’d get up quietly and click the door shut, then lie on my side facing the frame in the dark, waiting for the knob to turn. Around 0300 she’d wake up hot and open it again. 

By the third week, we made a deal to leave it cracked a couple of inches. I still slept facing the opening, on top of the covers with my boots lined up right below the mattress, watching the strip of light from the nightlight in the hallway. It took about six months before I could roll over on my right side, turn my back to the open door, and close my eyes.

b.text:
### Coming Home

When I came home from my second deployment, my wife and daughter met me at the airport.

My daughter was six years old. I had seen pictures of her while I was gone, and we talked when we could. Still, pictures and phone calls are not the same as standing in front of somebody.

When I walked toward them, she went behind her mother’s leg.

She did not cry. She just held on and looked at me from the side. I stopped a few feet away. I wanted to pick her up, but I did not want to scare her. Her mother said my name and told her it was Dad.

I knelt down. I said hello.

My daughter kept looking at me. After a little while, she came out from behind her mother. She let me hug her, but she held herself stiff at first. I remember the smell of her hair. I remember the airport noise around us. People were talking, bags were rolling over the floor, and somebody made an announcement I could not understand.

I had pictured that moment many times. In those pictures, she ran to me.

Instead, she had to figure out who I was.

A few days later, I went to the grocery store with my wife. I needed cereal. That was all.

I stood in front of the cereal shelves and looked at the boxes.

There were rows of them. Some had cartoon characters. Some had marshmallows. Some were supposed to be healthy. Some had less sugar, more fiber, whole grains, extra protein, or something else printed on the front. There were flakes, squares, rings, clusters, and little pieces shaped like animals.

I stood there for about twenty minutes.

I would pick up a box, read it, and put it back. Then I would pick up another one. I had been gone for a year. While I was away, the grocery store had continued being a grocery store. New products had come in. Old ones had moved around. There were too many choices.

My wife came down the aisle and asked if I was ready.

I told her I was still deciding.

She looked at the shelf, then at me.

I finally picked a box. I do not remember which one.

At home, I had trouble sleeping. Before the deployment, I had slept with the bedroom door open. My daughter’s room was down the hall. I was used to hearing the house settle, the air conditioner come on, or one of the kids moving around. With the door open, I could see part of the hallway from the bed.

Overseas, I slept facing the door.

That was how I had learned to sleep. Even when I was tired, I put myself where I could see the entrance. I did not think about it much. I would lie down, check the door, and close my eyes. If I woke up, I checked it again.

At home, the bedroom door stayed open, but I kept turning toward it. The hallway was dark. I could see the edge of it from the bed. Every small sound brought me awake.

One night, I got up and closed the door.

The room felt too quiet. I lay there for a while, then opened it again.

The next night I tried leaving it open. I put a pillow behind my back so I would not roll toward the door. That helped for a little while. Then I heard something in the hall and was awake again.

My wife was already asleep. I watched her breathing and listened to the house.

It took time to sleep with the door open the way I had before. I had to get used to the hallway being a hallway and not an entrance I needed to watch.

My daughter also needed time. For a while, she stayed close to her mother when I came into a room. Then she started asking me to read to her. She would bring a book and sit beside me, not quite touching me at first.

One evening, she fell asleep against my arm while I was reading. I stayed still until my arm went numb.

I did not move it.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
# Keeping Your Dog’s Coat Mat-Free Between Grooming Visits

The mistake I see most often is bathing a tangled dog and hoping the water will loosen everything up. Unfortunately, it usually does the opposite. Water, shampooing, and rubbing with a towel can tighten those tangles into a dense, felt-like mat that’s much harder to remove.

So before you run the bath, reach for the brush. This is especially important for curly coats and double coats, where tangles can hide underneath hair that looks perfectly tidy on top.

Start behind the ears and under the front legs. Those soft, friction-prone spots are often the first places mats develop. Then check around the collar or harness, the chest, the back legs, and the tail. You don’t have to tackle the whole dog in one long session. A few calm minutes at a time are better than a wrestling match.

Use a slicker brush and work in small sections. Part the coat so you can see where the hair meets the skin, then brush a thin layer at a time with short, gentle, straight strokes—not circles. Start at the ends of any tangles and gradually work closer to the skin. Keep the pressure light; slicker pins can irritate skin if you keep scraping the same spot.

This is called line brushing, and it helps you get beyond that fluffy top layer. On double-coated dogs, loose undercoat can collect underneath and start packing together. On curly dogs, the curls can wrap around each other and trap loose hair. Brushing only the surface misses both.

If you find a small tangle starting, pause before putting a brush or comb into it. Gently work a dog-safe detangling spray or leave-in conditioner through it with your fingers, following the product directions. Loosen the hairs carefully, then brush a little at a time without pulling on the skin. Conditioner can help with a loose tangle, but it won’t make a tight mat safe to brush out.

Once a section feels clear, check it with a metal comb, gently working through to the base of the coat. If it catches, don’t force it—that spot needs another look.

Only bathe once the coat is free of tangles. Brushing before the bath is essential, but it doesn’t mean you should never brush afterward: once the coat is properly dried, a gentle brush and comb check can catch any new tangles. Blot with the towel rather than rubbing vigorously.

If a mat feels tight against the skin, covers a large area, or makes your dog flinch, leave it for us. Please don’t cut it out with scissors; skin can be pulled up inside the mat where you can’t see it.

And if you’re unsure whether you’re reaching through the coat, ask us at your next visit. We’re happy to show you on your own dog—it’s much easier once you’ve seen and felt what you’re aiming for.

b.text:
# How to Keep Your Dog’s Coat From Matting Between Grooming Visits

The biggest mistake I see owners make is bathing a matted dog because they think the water will loosen everything up. Unfortunately, it does the opposite. Once matted fur gets wet, it tightens as it dries and can turn into a felt-like pad against the skin.

Always brush your dog thoroughly **before** a bath at home, not after the mats have been soaked and set tighter. This is especially important for curly-coated dogs and double-coated breeds, whose loose undercoat can quickly become packed.

Use a slicker brush and work in small sections so you reach all the way through the coat instead of just smoothing the top. I recommend short, gentle “line brushing” strokes rather than brushing in circles. Circular brushing can twist the hair and contribute to tangles.

Start behind the ears and under the front legs. Those are two of the first places mats tend to form because of friction, movement, collars, and harnesses. Then work through the rest of the coat section by section, including the chest, belly, legs, tail, and areas where equipment rubs.

If you notice a mat beginning to form, don’t immediately pull at it with a brush or comb. First, work a little dog-safe conditioner or detangling product into the mat with your fingers. Gently separate the outer edges before using your slicker brush in short strokes. Hold the hair close to the skin while you work so you aren’t tugging on your dog.

If the mat is tight against the skin, covers a large area, or your dog seems uncomfortable, stop and call your groomer. Don’t try to cut it out with scissors—dog skin is thin and can easily be pulled up into the mat.

A few minutes of section-by-section brushing several times a week can make a huge difference. It keeps your dog more comfortable and makes the next grooming visit easier for everyone.

a.text:
Hey team,
First, the key update: all systems are fully back up and running normally, no customer data was lost or corrupted during yesterday’s outage, and the issue is fully resolved.

For context, we had a ~40 minute window starting around 2pm yesterday where customers couldn’t access parts of the product. We know a number of you fielded customer complaints during that time—thank you for jumping in to triage while we worked on a fix.

Here’s what happened in plain terms:
We pushed a routine product update yesterday afternoon as part of our normal deploy schedule. Tucked into that update was a small change to how we organize customer data in our core system—something our pre-deploy tests confirmed would take less than 10 seconds to apply with no disruption. But when we ran it on our live, full-scale system, that change ended up blocking all access to that customer data until we could undo it. We spotted the outage within 5 minutes of starting the deploy and immediately reversed the data change, but full access was restored for all users about 40 minutes after the issue first started.

What we’re doing to prevent this from happening again:

3/7 Two days before the event, our caterer called. "I'm in. I'm out. Can't make it work." 220 plates. 48 hours. I sat at my kitchen table in my work clothes and thought, well. We're serving cheese cubes and crackers at the Holiday Inn ballroom.

4/7 I called everyone I knew. Then I called Maggiore's. Full honest ask: "We are desperate. Can you feed 220 people Saturday?" They said yes. Full dinner. Baked chicken parmesan, the works. Delivered, plated, on time. Maggiore's, you saved our whole year. Thank you. Truly.

5/7 So. Saturday night. 220 neighbors in a room. The auction got loud. Someone's grandma won the fishing trip. A volunteer I've known for nine years grabbed my hand mid-speech and said "you good?" and I was. The room felt like a family reunion where everyone brought a plate.

6/7 Final number: $38,000 raised against a $30,000 goal. That's roughly 12,000 meals. That's the September problem not being a problem. Every dollar here is someone choosing to be in the room with us, which honestly matters more than the total.

So we’re bringing on a full-time support person to own the day-to-day.

What the job actually looks like:

- Answering support requests from small trucking companies and dispatchers
- Helping them get unstuck when scheduling, dispatching, or load assignment isn’t working
- Learning Ridgepoint deeply enough to explain it simply
- Turning repeated questions into clear help articles, guides, and templates
- Writing short, direct, useful responses — not corporate fluff
- Escalating bugs and product issues with enough context that our engineering/product work isn’t wasted
- Occasionally hopping on calls with customers to understand how they dispatch loads in real life
- Helping us get closer to customers without slowing the founders down

This is not a “be the first point of contact and wait for answers” role. There’s no support playbook handed to you fully formed. You’ll help create it.

You’ll likely report to one of the founders and work directly with the rest of the team.

Who this might be a fit for:

You’ve worked in B2B SaaS support, customer success, implementation, or something close to it. You don’t need to have worked in trucking already, though if you understand dispatch workflows that’s a plus.

You’re comfortable being practical, clear, and patient. You like fixing things. You’re okay with early-stage ambiguity, but you don’t need the company to hold your hand.

You’re fine with:

- A small team
- Fast-moving priorities
- Writing a lot
- Learning messy customer workflows
- Saying “I don’t know yet, I’ll find out” and then finding out

If this sounds like you, apply with a short note on why you’re interested and what kind of support work you’re looking for next.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
I came home from my second deployment and the airport was bright and loud. My wife was holding my daughter’s hand. She was six. She didn’t know me. She hid behind her mom’s leg. I said her name. She peeked out, then went back behind the leg. I stood there with my bag until she came out. She didn’t run to me. That was okay.

The next morning I went to the grocery store for cereal. I walked down the aisle and stopped. There were forty kinds. I stood there for twenty minutes looking at the boxes. I couldn’t pick one. I looked at the colors and the cartoons. I grabbed the first box I touched and put it in my cart.

That night I slept facing the door. That was the habit from the year before. I turned my body toward it, my back to my wife, back to the open bedroom door I was trying to leave open. I tried to sleep facing her, facing the bed, but my shoulder kept turning back. I lay there until morning.

The cereal is in the cabinet. She said my name at breakfast. I turned around. The door is open. I turned once, but I turned back.

b.text:
Cereal Aisle

Twenty-three years in, and I still can't tell you why the cereal aisle got to me. I'd been shot at. I'd carried a man to a helicopter with his leg gone below the knee. But it was a grocery store in Clarksville that put me on my heels.

I went in for cereal. Just cereal. My wife had a list and that was one of the things on it, and I told her I'd handle it, I wanted to feel useful, wanted to feel like I could still walk into a building and get something done. So I found the aisle and I stood there.

There were forty kinds. I counted, sort of, though I lost track after a while because I kept losing my place and starting over. Cinnamon this and honey that and a dozen versions of the same three cereals just in different boxes, cartoon animals looking at me like they were waiting on an answer. I stood there for twenty minutes. A woman with a cart full of kids came down the aisle, grabbed a box without slowing down, and kept going. I envied her more than I've envied anybody in a long time.

Over there, you didn't have forty of anything. You had what came on the truck. If it was oatmeal that day, it was oatmeal, and you ate it and were glad to have it. Nobody stood in front of a shelf trying to decide between them. I think that's what did it — not that I was overwhelmed by cereal, but that I'd forgotten how to choose things that didn't matter. A year of only the choices that mattered — go left or right, call it in or wait — and then somebody hands you your whole self back and says pick a breakfast.

I ended up with the same kind I always used to buy, the plain toasted oat kind in the yellow box. Took me twenty minutes to walk in a circle and land back where I started.

***

My daughter was six when I came home the second time. Same daughter, same wife, same airport terminal I'd walked through before, except this time when I came around the corner she didn't run at me. She stepped back. Got behind her mother's leg, one hand gripping the fabric of my wife's jeans, and just looked at me.

I hadn't thought about how long a year is when you're six. A year for her was a sixth of her whole life. My face in photographs is not my face in person, not to a six-year-old — the person in the pictures didn't have this much gray in his beard, didn't stand like this, didn't smell like plane and sweat instead of whatever she remembered.

I crouched down. I didn't reach for her. I'd read somewhere, or somebody told me, don't grab, let them come to you. So I just crouched there in my uniform with my duffel on the ground beside me, in the middle of that terminal, other families around us doing the version of this reunion where the kid comes running and everybody cries the good kind of tears. Ours wasn't that. My wife put her hand on our daughter's back and said, "That's Daddy. That's your daddy," like she was reminding her of something she'd only half-learned.

It took maybe a full minute. Might not sound like much. It was the longest minute I've spent, and I've spent some long ones.

Then she came around her mother's leg, slow, and put her hand out like she was going to shake mine, this very serious, formal little gesture she must've picked up from somewhere, and I took her hand and shook it, and something in that made her laugh, and after that she let me pick her up.

***

The door thing took longer to fix than either of those.

For a year I'd slept in a bunk facing the door. Everybody did. You don't think about it as a decision, it's just how you set yourself up, so that if something happens you see it coming a half second sooner. Half a second matters. You'd be surprised how fast you can go from asleep to upright with a rifle in your hands if you've had enough practice and enough reason to practice.

Home, our bedroom door was on the wrong wall for that. I moved to my wife's side of the bed for a while without really saying why, just so I'd be facing the right direction, and she let me, didn't ask about it for a couple weeks. And I needed the door open. All the way open, not cracked. She was used to sleeping with it shut, always had been, but for months she didn't say anything about that either.

I'd wake up at every sound. House settling, cat on the stairs, ice maker dropping a load of ice into the bin at two in the morning — I was up, sitting, before I even knew what had woken me. Some nights I didn't wake her. Some nights she was already awake because I'd woken her sitting up like that, and she'd just wait until I lay back down and not say anything.

It took the better part of that first year home before I could sleep facing away from the door. Longer before we could close it again. I remember the night we finally did — my wife asked, kind of careful, if I minded, because she gets cold and likes it shut in the winter, and I said no, go ahead, and I lay there afterward waiting to feel that old alarm go off in my chest. It didn't. Or it did, a little, but not enough to get me up. I noticed that, lying there. I noticed I'd noticed it, if that makes sense. Like checking a wound to see if it still hurts and being surprised, a little disappointed almost, that it doesn't hurt as much as you remembered.

We still sleep with the door shut now. Most nights I don't think about it at all.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
**Girls Soccer Needs a Field That Doesn't Flood or Injure Us**

Our girls soccer field floods. In the last two seasons we've lost or relocated nine games because the grass turns into a mess the second it rains hard. Last October one of my players tore her ACL stepping into a rut on that same field. She was done for the year.

The boys football field has had turf since 2019. They don't cancel for standing water. They don't lose athletes to uneven ground that should have been fixed years ago. This is a fairness issue, plain and simple. Same district, same kids, same weather. Different standard.

I'm not here writing pretty paragraphs for fun. I coach for the stipend. But I also watch these girls show up, train, and then get told their home games are off because the field can't handle a normal fall. Or worse, I watch one of them go down hard on a surface we all know is a problem. That ACL wasn't bad luck. It was a preventable hazard.

The school board is about to vote on next year's facilities budget. Put the girls soccer field on the list for turf. Not next cycle. Not after another study. Now. We've already paid the cost in canceled games and one serious injury. The boys got theirs. Give the girls the same chance to play on a field that works.

b.text:
The boys got turf in 2019. The girls are still waiting.

Over the last two seasons, nine girls’ soccer games have been rained out or moved because our grass field floods. Last October, one of my players tore her ACL stepping in a rut.

Those are not cosmetic problems. We are not asking for a prettier field. We are asking for a reliable place to play.

I coach girls’ soccer and track at our public high school. I expect our athletes to show up, work hard and take care of what they have. They should be able to expect the school district to do its part, too. A field that repeatedly floods and develops dangerous ruts is not holding up that end of the deal.

When the school board votes on next year’s facilities budget, it should fund turf for the girls’ soccer field, including the drainage work needed to make it function properly. Not another vague promise to revisit the problem. A funded project with a timeline.

I know turf costs money. So does maintaining grass, repairing a failing field and repeatedly working around a playing surface we cannot count on. The board should put those costs side by side, including turf maintenance and eventual replacement. Taxpayers deserve actual numbers, not just a big installation price presented without context.

We also need an honest discussion about safety. I am not claiming turf would have prevented my player’s ACL injury or that any surface eliminates injuries. Turf has its own concerns, including heat and surface conditions. Those deserve careful review. But uncertainty about the perfect field is not an excuse to accept the condition of the one we have.

Then there is fairness.

The boys’ football field got turf in 2019. The district has already shown that it considers a major investment in an athletic field worthwhile. The girls should not have to keep proving that their games matter enough for the same consideration.

Fair treatment does not require every team to have identical facilities. It does require the district to take comparable needs seriously. Nine disrupted games in two seasons should be enough to get this out of the “maybe later” pile.

Our players cannot vote on the facilities budget. Board members can. They can ask hard questions about price, drainage, safety and maintenance—and still make a decision that fixes the problem.

Put turf for the girls’ soccer field in next year’s budget. Give it a start date. The girls have waited long enough.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
To Members of the City Council,

My name is [Your Name], and I am the owner and operator of an independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am submitting this testimony for the official record to express my strong opposition to the proposed parking meter rate increase from $0.50 to $1.50 per hour in our downtown district. 

A tripling of parking rates is not a minor adjustment; it is a 200% tax on downtown foot traffic. While municipal budgets face ongoing pressures, penalizing the customers who support local brick-and-mortar storefronts will generate negligible public revenue while inflicting measurable harm on our daily operations.

My business relies on quick, convenience-driven transactions. Our internal point-of-sale data shows that our average customer visit lasts exactly 22 minutes. Under the current structure, the 50-cent one-hour minimum already covers these visits with a reasonable buffer. When a customer stops in to buy a $4.50 latte or a quick bag of roasted beans, adding a mandatory $1.50 parking fee inflates the cost of that short trip by 33%. For routine daily purchases, that friction drives consumers away from downtown corridors and toward strip malls and regional chains with free surface parking.

This concern is not theoretical. We have direct historical precedent for how this policy plays out in our local market. In 2019, when our neighboring municipality implemented a nearly identical rate increase, I tracked our register and transaction counts over a six-week period. During those six weeks, foot traffic dropped by 18%. For an independent business operating on narrow margins, an 18% decline in transaction volume wipes out profitability entirely. 

Furthermore, this proposal fails even on its own terms as a fiscal solution. According to the city’s own downtown financial report, meter revenue accounts for just 4% of the total downtown operational budget. Tripling this rate will not solve the city's structural budget constraints, but it will disproportionately burden the small retail, service, and dining establishments that form the economic foundation of Main Street. We are risking the stability of the 96% of the commercial ecosystem to adjust a line item that represents only 4% of city downtown funding.

Thriving downtowns require accessibility. Increasing parking rates by 200% creates a direct barrier between local residents and the small businesses they want to support. I respectfully urge the council to vote against this proposed increase and instead explore revenue and transit solutions that do not penalize our local commercial base.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]  
Owner, [Coffee Shop Name]  
Main Street

b.text:
**Testimony Regarding Proposed Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase**

Good evening, Council Members, Mayor, and residents. My name is [Your Name], and I am the owner of a small independent coffee shop located on Main Street. I am submitting this written testimony to formally oppose the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from fifty cents to one dollar and fifty cents per hour. While I recognize the administration’s efforts to explore new revenue streams, this adjustment misreads consumer behavior, lacks empirical support, and fails to address the actual composition of our municipal finances.

The central flaw in this proposal is its assumption about how long visitors remain in downtown spaces. At my establishment, and consistently across Main Street’s retail and hospitality sector, the average customer visit lasts approximately twenty-two minutes. Because the existing hourly minimum already spans sixty minutes, current pricing captures more than double the actual time patrons occupy these spots. Doubling or tripling the rate for stays that routinely fall well under the minimum threshold does not encourage turnover; it introduces friction into transactions that keep our sidewalks active and our registers fluid. When short-duration stops become disproportionately expensive, visitors consolidate their errands, shift to peripheral residential areas, or bypass downtown entirely.

This dynamic is not hypothetical. Back in 2019, the neighboring city implemented a nearly identical threefold parking rate increase. To monitor the immediate impact, I tracked my own sales register and conducted structured foot traffic counts over the following six weeks. During that window, downtown foot traffic in that district dropped by eighteen percent. That decline was not limited to peak hours or seasonal fluctuations; it represented a sustained contraction in spontaneous, high-frequency visits. For independent operators who rely on consistent daily transaction volume rather than large batch purchases, an eighteen percent reduction in passersby translates directly into reduced daily revenue, tighter margins, and constrained staffing capacity. The policy effectively taxed low-value, high-turnover commercial activity while failing to capture the behavior of longer-term parkers who simply adjusted to the higher cost elsewhere.

Furthermore, the premise that elevated meter fees will materially alleviate downtown funding gaps is contradicted by the city’s own financial documentation. According to the municipal report released last quarter, parking meter revenue currently accounts for only four percent of the total downtown budget. An increase from fifty cents to one dollar and fifty cents per hour may yield negligible upfront gains, but if it suppresses visitation—as documented precedent demonstrates—it will inevitably erode that same revenue pool. We are being asked to jeopardize verified commercial activity for a four percent municipal share that will never resolve structural budget priorities, let alone offset the economic drag placed on storefronts that generate sales tax, employment, and civic engagement.

Downtown viability depends on accessibility, predictable costs, and infrastructure designed for human-scale commerce. Raising rates by eighty cents per hour directly undermines those conditions without delivering proportional municipal benefit. I respectfully urge the council to reject this proposal, retain the current fifty-cent hourly rate, and pursue sustainability measures that protect foot traffic and independent enterprise rather than extracting marginal gains from a system already optimized for short-duration visits.

Thank you for your time, your public service, and your careful consideration of the data before you.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
I haven’t had a free weekend since I was fifteen. While my friends are at football games or sleeping in, I’m at my family’s Vietnamese restaurant. Saturday and Sunday mean twelve-hour shifts. The air always smells like star anise, fried garlic, and industrial floor cleaner. 

There are days when things go smoothly, and there are days like the second Saturday in October. Right at 12:30, the middle of the lunch rush, the entire register system crashed. The screens froze, then went completely black. A line was backing up to the door. My dad tapped the main monitor, looked at me, and shrugged. 

I grabbed a stack of paper order pads from the back office and a handful of cheap pens. For the next three hours, I hand-wrote every ticket. *Number 14, no cilantro. Number 32, sub pork for chicken, allergy to peanuts.* I became the restaurant's entire routing system, running tickets back to the kitchen, shouting translations over the hiss of the fryers, and calculating totals in my head with the state tax added on. By three o'clock, my hand was cramping so badly I could barely grip the pen, but we hadn't dropped a single order.

When the rush dies down in the late afternoon, things get quiet. That’s usually when I train the new hires. Last month, we brought on a college student named Leo, and I was in charge of teaching him prep work. We stood at the stainless steel tables in the back, and I showed him my grandma’s spring roll fold. There’s a specific way to do it. You have to tuck the lettuce and vermicelli tight, but leave enough slack in the rice paper so it doesn’t tear when you roll it forward. Then you place the shrimp exactly in the last fold so the pink shows through the translucent wrapper. 

Leo kept ripping the paper. He was trying to force it. I stopped him, put my hands next to his, and showed him how to use the heels of his palms to apply pressure while his fingers guided the roll. We stood there for an hour, practicing until his rolls looked exactly like my grandma’s. 

Around four o'clock, I get a thirty-minute break. I usually spend it in the walk-in cooler. It’s the only place in the building where nobody can ask me for extra hoisin sauce or a refill on their diet soda. I drag a milk crate over to a fifty-pound sack of cabbages, sit down, and do my calculus homework. The hum of the heavy refrigeration unit drowns out the noise of the dining room. The air is forty degrees, which makes my fingers stiff, but the cold keeps me awake enough to figure out derivatives. 

When my shift finally ends at ten at night, my shoes are sticky with spilled soda and my back aches. I wipe down the front counters, turn off the neon Open sign, and lock the door. Monday morning is always just around the corner. I’ll be sitting in first period, turning in the math worksheet that smells faintly of beef broth, and by Friday afternoon, I’ll be putting my apron right back on.

b.text:
I'm in the kitchen Monday to Friday for school, and then on the weekends, I'm at the restaurant. My family owns a Vietnamese place in a strip mall off Route 12. My parents run it, my grandma cooks, and I do whatever needs doing: wash dishes, refill the Sriracha bottles, bus tables, take orders. I've been doing this since sophomore year, every Saturday and Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. I get paid, but it's not about the money.

There was a Saturday when the register system died. I don't know why. It just went blank in the middle of the lunch rush. My mom looked at me, and I looked at the line of people waiting, and she said, "Paper." So I grabbed a notepad from the counter and started writing tickets by hand. No one seems to think about what happens when the computer stops. I didn't either, until that day. I wrote fast. I had to remember the prices from memory because the menu was on the screen. I shorthand everything: pho-12, spring rolls-6, vermicelli-14. The kitchen had to read my handwriting. It was messy, but they got it. We served everyone. No one waited too long, I think. At the end of the night, my hand was sore, and we totaled up the receipts and the numbers were off by a little, but close enough.

Sometimes I teach new hires how to fold the spring rolls. That's my grandma's method. You lay the wrapper flat, put the filling in the middle, fold up the bottom, fold in the sides, then roll it tight. It seems simple, but if you don't crimp the edges right, they stick together or fall apart when you fry them. People don't know that. They think it's just rolling. I show them. I watch their hands. Sometimes they get frustrated. I tell them, "It's like folding a letter you don't want to send." That's what my grandma told me. I don't know what that means exactly, but it helps hold the fold. I don't know if she meant it or if she just said it.

On my breaks, I do homework in the walk-in cooler. It's cold in there, obviously, but it's quiet. I can hear the fridge humming and sometimes the sound of the kitchen yelling from outside. I pull out my calc book and do problems. It's weird to be doing derivatives while the smell of lemongrass and fish sauce is on my clothes. But it's fine. It's my break. I sit on a crate or sometimes I lean against the shelves where they keep the egg rolls. I don't have much time, so I do the problems fast. If I get one wrong, I don't care that much. I just move on to the next one. It's not like school where there's time to think about it. I'm on a break. I'll be back on the floor in fifteen minutes.

Most Saturdays, I'm there from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. I don't think about it as a job exactly, even though I am paid for it. It's just what I do. I put on my apron, I cash out customers, I refill the water, I wipe the tables. My hands smell like fish sauce by the end of the day, and no matter how many times I wash them, the smell stays. I like it. It's my family's smell, I guess. I don't know what else to call it.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8 Months of Market Sourdough Later

I bought the Corlane SM6 in February because my old mixer died mid-batch two weeks before market season and I was hand-kneading twelve loaves' worth of dough on my counter at 5 a.m. I've now run it almost every day for eight months, mostly on high-hydration sourdough, plus a weekly double batch of bagels, which is the stiffest dough I make. Here's where I've landed.

## The motor is the whole reason to buy this

A double batch of bagel dough is roughly 2.2 kg of very low-hydration dough. It is the test that killed my last mixer and made my sister's KitchenAid smell like a hot electrical outlet. The SM6 has never stalled on it. Not once. It doesn't slow down, doesn't walk across the counter, doesn't get more than warm to the touch on the housing. I can run it on speed 2 for eight straight minutes and it sounds the same at minute eight as it did at minute one.

Same story with sourdough, which is easier on the motor but harder on patience because I do long mixes for gluten development. Fifteen minutes of continuous kneading on a 2 kg batch, four or five times a week, for eight months. Nothing has burned, stripped, or loosened. If you knead heavy dough on a real schedule, this is the part that matters, and it delivers.

## The bowl-lift lever squeaks, and it will keep squeaking

Around month two, the lever that raises and lowers the bowl started squeaking. Not a subtle squeak, a full metal-on-metal complaint every time I move it. A shot of WD-40 on the pivot fixes it completely for about a month, then it comes back. I've done this six times now.

It's not a functional problem. The lift still locks in firmly and the bowl doesn't drop under load. But on a $429 machine I shouldn't be maintaining a lubrication schedule for a lever, and it's the kind of thing that would drive me up the wall if I used this in a quiet kitchen instead of one with a radio going.

## The included dough hook is wrong for the bowl

This one actually annoys me. The SM6 has a deep bowl, which is great for capacity, but the dough hook that comes in the box doesn't reach far enough down. With a smaller batch, say a single loaf, the hook spins above a layer of flour and dough that just sits on the bottom. I had to stop and scrape every couple of minutes, which defeats the point of a mixer.

I ended up buying a third-party spiral hook, about $30, that's roughly an inch longer and actually reaches the bottom. With that hook, the machine is excellent. Without it, I'd call small-batch kneading unreliable. Budget for the replacement hook as part of the purchase price. Corlane should be shipping the right one.

## Price

$429. The equivalent bowl-lift KitchenAid is $349, so you're paying about $80 more, plus the $30 for a hook that works, so call it $110 more all in. That's real money.

## Verdict

**Buy it if you knead heavy dough every week.** Bagels, high-volume sourdough, anything stiff or over 1.5 kg at a time. The motor is genuinely a class above what I've used at this price, and after eight months of daily abuse there's no sign of it wearing down. The squeaky lever and the too-short hook are irritating, but they're irritating in a machine that does the hard job better than anything else I've owned. I'd buy it again tomorrow.

**Skip it if you're mostly doing cookies, cake batter, whipped cream, and the occasional loaf of bread.** None of that comes close to stressing the motor, so you're paying $110 extra for headroom you'll never use, and you'll still get the squeak and the bad hook. Get the KitchenAid and put the difference toward a good scale or a Dutch oven.

That's it. It's a dough machine. If you're a dough person, it's worth the money. If you're not, it isn't.

b.text:
After eight months of using the Corlane SM6 stand mixer almost every single day to prep sourdough for my weekend farmers market stand, I finally have a definitive answer on whether it’s worth the price tag. 

Let’s start with the motor, because that is where this machine truly shines. If you bake bread, you know the ultimate stress test is a stiff bagel dough. The Corlane handles a double batch of bagel dough without a single stutter, stall, or terrifying gear-grinding noise. It just churns through it like a champion. For heavy, low-hydration doughs and massive batches of market prep, the raw power is undeniably impressive.

But it is not a perfect machine, and for $429—which is $80 more than the equivalent bowl-lift KitchenAid—the flaws are genuinely irritating. 

First, the hardware is a bit finicky. A few months in, the bowl lift lever developed a terrible squeak. I now have to hit the mechanism with WD-40 about once a month just to keep it operating smoothly. 

The much bigger issue, however, is the dough hook. The stock hook that comes in the box is inexplicably short for how deep the bowl is. It clears the bottom by far too much, leaving a thick layer of unmixed flour and water sitting in the base of the bowl. I ended up having to buy a third-party dough hook just to make the machine usable for my daily bread prep. When you are already paying a premium over the standard KitchenAid, having to immediately buy aftermarket parts to fix a glaring design flaw is a tough pill to swallow.

**The Verdict**

Buy the Corlane SM6 if you are kneading heavy bread doughs every single week. The motor easily outpaces the competition and will save you from burning out a lesser machine. 

Skip it if you are mostly whipping up cookies, cake batters, or the occasional single loaf of bread. Between the squeaky lever, the poorly designed stock dough hook, and the $429 price tag, it is absolutely not worth the extra $80 over a KitchenAid for casual or sweet baking. Save your money.
