setup: A retired rural mail carrier is writing a letter to the Kettle Falls Courier urging residents to oppose the post office counter closure at the July 28 forum.

a.text:
To the Editor:

I drove Route 4 out of the Kettle Falls post office for 22 years. Thirty-eight miles, six days a week, in mud season and in January. I retired last year. I am not a writer, so I will say this plainly.

The Postal Service wants to close our counter service. The reason they give is that the branch loses about $40,000 a year. I would like people to think about where that number comes from.

A few years back they cut the window hours from a full day down to eight to noon. Anybody who has ever run a business could tell you what happens next. Folks who work days can't get in. Folks who used to mail a package on their lunch hour go to Fairview instead, or they order a label online, or they just quit bothering. Traffic dropped. Of course it dropped. Then the receipts dropped with it.

So now they hold up the low numbers as proof the counter isn't needed. That is pointing at a problem they made themselves. It is like cutting a man's hours to half time and then firing him for not getting enough done.

I want to say something about what the counter actually does, because a report in an office somewhere does not show it.

Mrs. Halloran lives up on Kettle Hill. She is in her eighties. Her heart medication comes by mail, and it has come by mail for years, and I carried it up that hill more times than I could count. She does not drive to Fairview. Twenty minutes each way on that road is not a small thing when you are her age and the weather turns. When she needs a money order — and she does, she pays some bills that way, the way a lot of older people around here still do — she walks into our post office and a person she knows helps her. There is no website that replaces that. There is no cluster box that replaces that.

She is not the only one. There are dozens of people on that route in the same position, and most of them will not write a letter to the paper about it.

The district manager is coming to the public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall. I am asking people to show up. Not to yell at anybody — the folks who work in our office are our neighbors and this is not their doing. Just show up, so the man from the district can see the room is full and can hear it from people who live here.

Numbers on a page are easy to close. A room full of your customers is harder.

Please come.

— [Name], Kettle Falls
Retired rural carrier, Route 4

b.text:
To the Editor,

I drove Route 4 for 22 years before I retired last year, so I think I know this town and the people in it pretty well. I’m writing because the post office is talking about closing our counter service, and I don’t think that’s right.

The USPS says the branch loses $40,000 a year. But they already cut the hours from 8 to noon. Of course fewer people could use it after that. A lot of folks work, or they can’t get there in the middle of the day. If you take away the service, then people stop coming, and then you say the service isn’t needed. That’s pointing at a problem they made themselves.

This isn’t just about numbers. Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill is in her 80s and gets her heart medicine by mail. If the counter closes, how is she supposed to get a money order? She can’t drive 20 minutes to Fairview. That’s not fair to her, and she’s not the only one.

A post office isn’t just a building. It’s part of how people take care of business, especially older folks and people out in the country.

I hope people will show up to the public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall. If you can come, come. Let the district manager know this town still needs its counter service.

Sincerely,  
A retired Route 4 carrier

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
USDA raised the prevented planting premium base rate 22% this year in our region. On my operation, that increase costs about $46,000 extra this spring. That number is not an abstract policy problem. It is cash that has to come from somewhere else: seed, fertilizer, equipment notes, rent, interest, reserves, or next year’s operating budget.

The reason is simple. This spring, it would not stop raining. By the late May planting deadline, I had only about 60% of my acres planted. The unplanted acres became prevented planting acres, and with the higher base rate, those acres now cost more to insure than they did last year. The rain did not change between planting seasons. The premium base rate did.

That raises a hard question: why should a family operation pay a larger proportional bite for a risk event it did not create and could not avoid?

This is where the acreage caps matter. Under the current structure, family operations like mine are hit harder proportionally than the bigger operations nearby. A large, diversified farm can absorb a 22% hike across a broader land base. A family farm cannot. We may have similar weather, similar planting dates, and similar prevented acres, but the premium hike lands harder because our margins are tighter and our land base is smaller. The acreage cap structure magnifies that difference.

That is why I am asking readers to support SB 214. SB 214 fixes the acreage cap problem so family farms are not penalized harder simply because they are family farms. It gives the prevented planting program the fairness and flexibility producers expected when we signed up to manage risk in the first place.

If you want to help, contact your state legislator and ask them to support SB 214. Tell them the facts: a 22% base rate hike in our region cost this operation about $46,000 this year. Tell them that only 60% of my acres were planted by the late May deadline because of weather beyond my control. Tell them that acreage caps are making the problem worse for family operations than for larger nearby farms.

Farmers do not need perfect seasons. We deal with weather every year. But we should not have to carry a larger share of an insurance premium increase because the current acreage cap structure works better for big operations than it does for family farms.

Tell legislators to support SB 214.

b.text:
**A 22% Premium Hike Is a Real Cost to Family Farms**

This spring, I was able to get only about 60 percent of my acres planted before the late-May deadline. It simply would not stop raining.

That left prevented planting coverage as the only practical option on a significant share of our ground. But this year, USDA raised the base prevented planting premium rate in our region by 22 percent. For my operation, that increase means roughly $46,000 in additional crop-insurance cost this year alone.

That is not a small adjustment. It is money that would otherwise go toward seed, fertilizer, machinery repairs, land payments, payroll, or keeping more working capital available for the next season.

The increase is especially hard on family operations because of the way the acreage caps are structured. Once those caps apply, farms like mine can end up paying a much higher share of the cost than larger operations with more acres spread across their business. The weather does not distinguish between a family farm and a larger operation, but the current premium structure can.

Prevented planting coverage is not a windfall. It is a risk-management tool for the years when conditions make planting impossible. This year, many of us faced exactly that situation: fields too wet to plant, deadlines approaching, and no realistic way to make up the lost time.

State legislators have an opportunity to address the inequity in this system through SB 214. The bill would fix the acreage-cap issue that disproportionately burdens family-sized farms when prevented planting coverage is needed most.

I encourage Farm Bureau members and rural residents to contact their state senator and representative and ask them to support SB 214. A fairer acreage-cap structure will not change the weather, but it can make sure family farms are not carrying an unfair share of the cost when the rain will not let up.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
I’ve sat through just north of 200 interviews for our operations and frontline logistics leadership roles so far this year, and for the longest time I thought the most thoughtful candidates were the ones who asked nuanced questions about team culture or upward mobility.
I was dead wrong.
The standout candidates? They all lead with the same first question when we get to Q&A: “What’s the last project your team tried that didn’t work, and what did you learn from it?”

Last week I interviewed a senior ops lead for our Northeast regional role, and he opened his Q&A with that exact line before he even asked what a typical day in the role looked like.
I didn’t sugarcoat it. I told him about the Brooklyn last-mile e-bike pilot we launched back in March: we’d crunched the spreadsheets and swore switching 2 dense urban routes from box trucks to cargo e-bikes would cut delivery times by 25% and slash fuel costs. We completely missed that our micro-fulfillment center in Bushwick had zero secure overnight bike parking, and we underestimated how many of our B2C deliveries for that route were large furniture items that didn’t fit in the bike cargo holds. We pulled the plug after 6 weeks, ate $12k in unused vendor contracts, and had to reset SLAs with 3 key retail clients we’d already promised faster delivery to.
Most candidates would nod politely, say “that makes sense,” and move on to the next prepped question.
This guy leaned in. First follow-up: “Did your team do an on-site audit of the fulfillment center footprint before you signed the bike vendor, or was that all planned from the corporate office?” Second: “Were those 3 retail clients looped into the pilot testing at all, or did you just announce the new SLA to them out of the blue?” Then he walked me through a nearly identical failed same-day delivery pilot he’d run at his last company, and laid out exactly what he’d do in his first 30 days if we wanted to revisit the e-bike idea—starting with a cross-functional kickoff with our facilities and client success teams before we spent a dime on new equipment.
He got the offer 2 days later.

Here’s the thing: no team is perfect, especially not in logistics where plans shift faster than a surprise port delay can derail your entire Q3 forecast.
For job folks reading this: This question isn’t a gotcha. It’s the fastest way to prove you’re not just interviewing for a paycheck—you’re interviewing to solve real problems for a team that’s still figuring it out. It also tells you way more about how a team operates than “what’s the culture like” ever will. Do they blame individual frontline team members for the failure? Do they brush it off like it was no big deal? Do they actually have takeaways they’ve implemented across the team? All the intel you need, in one question.
For my fellow recruiters and hiring managers: If a candidate asks you this, don’t default to the polished “we had a small misalignment” corporate answer. Be honest. The best candidates don’t want to join a “perfect” team—they want to join a team that’s self-aware enough to admit when they messed up, and hungry to fix it.

Curious to hear from both sides: Job seekers, do you ask about failed projects in your interviews? Hiring managers, what’s the most memorable question a candidate has asked that made you stop and take notice?

b.text:
I've done ~200 interviews for ops and dispatch roles in the last two years.

The candidates I still think about a week later almost always do the same thing at the end. They ask me about a project that failed here.

Not "what's the culture like." They want to know what happens here when things go sideways.

Had this happen last month. Final round for a Site Supervisor role in Louisville.

He goes: "Can you tell me about the last big thing that didn't work out at your site?"

I told him: "We tried to flip Louisville to 6-day receiving last Q3 to get ahead of peak. Looked great on a spreadsheet. We didn't staff for it right, burned out our two best leads, OT blew up, and service actually got worse. We killed it after four weeks and went back to five."

He didn't miss a beat. He said: "How did you guys talk about it with the floor team after you rolled it back?"

That follow-up is the whole ballgame.

He wasn't looking for gossip. He was trying to figure out if we blame people or fix the plan. If he'd get cover when he inevitably makes a bad call, too.

I was honest with him about it. He took the offer.

Curious for other hiring managers - is there a failure story you're actually willing to share in interviews?

b.text:
We're hiring our first support person.

Here's the honest version: the three of us have been answering every ticket ourselves since we started. It worked for a while. It doesn't anymore. We need someone to take that over so we can stop doing it badly at 11pm.

**What the job actually is day to day:**

- You're in our inbox and chat tool most of the day. Our customers are small trucking dispatchers—usually 1-5 person shops. Their questions are mostly about how to do something in the app, why a load didn't sync right, or why something looks weird on their schedule.
- You'll reproduce their issues, figure out if it's a bug or user error, file bugs when it's us, and explain things clearly when it's them.
- You'll write up common answers so we can stop typing the same reply forty times.
- You'll sit in on our weekly product call and tell us what customers are actually asking for, because right now that signal is buried in our inboxes.

- Not a managerial role. It's you, the tickets, and the three of us.
- Not a path to product or engineering in the next six months. We need someone who wants to do support well.

**What we care about:**

- You write clearly. Most of this job is explaining things in writing to people who are not technical and are often in a hurry.
- You're okay with ambiguity. We're a small team, processes are loose, and you'll have to figure things out on your own.
- Some familiarity with logistics or trucking helps but isn't required. Being patient and genuinely useful is required.

If this sounds like what you're looking for, DM me or email [address]. Please include a note on why this specific role appeals to you—generic applications will get generic responses.

setup: A chef and restaurant owner is replying to a viral post about tipping and service charges to disagree from her own experience.

a.text: Respectfully disagree. We actually trialed a flat 20% auto-charge instead of tipping for eight months. Had to roll it back. Turned out we just couldn’t compete for staff with nearby spots still offering tips. Great concept on paper, but until pay scales equalize, tipping’s still how we keep good people on the floor. Learned it firsthand running a small NOLA spot.

b.text: We actually tried the no-tip model with a flat 20% service charge for 8 months at my 40-seat spot. We had to roll it back because we couldn't compete in hiring—our front-of-house staff made significantly more down the street at traditional tipped restaurants. Sounds simple on paper, but the reality of the labor market makes it really tough to sustain.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
**Launch week: 412 copies, six hours on a subreddit, and yes — the movement is floaty**

The game is out. It's been out for a week. Here's where things landed.

It sold 412 copies in the first week. First commercial release, three years of nights and weekends, a few hundred people following the devlog. I don't have a frame of reference for whether that's good, so I'm just writing it down.

The other thing that happened: a post on a small subreddit hit their front page for about six hours. Six hours on a small subreddit isn't a milestone anyone puts on a store page. But it was the first time I watched the sales graph move on its own, without me posting anything, and I refreshed the backend page more times in those six hours than I'd like to admit.

Then there was the review. Someone said the movement feels floaty.

They're right.

I've been playing this build for three years. My hands know it. I stopped feeling it somewhere around month eight. Watching someone else actually move around in it — not just reading the note, watching — it's obvious. The character takes too long to reach top speed and keeps drifting after you let go, so every input has this little smear on the end of it. In a game that's mostly about moving around, that's not a nitpick. That's the thing.

I spent a day being annoyed about it and then started fixing it.

**1.1, next month**

The patch is mostly the movement. Tighter acceleration curve. Stops when you tell it to stop. More gravity on the descent so jumps don't hang in the air. And coyote time — I've watched enough people miss a jump by a frame or two to know that's on me and not on them.

There's also a list of smaller bug fixes from launch reports, plus a couple of settings people asked for. Nothing exciting. Just cleanup.

After that, back to building.

Thanks to everyone who bought it, played it, and especially the ones who wrote down what was wrong. I read all of it.

1.1 goes out next month. I'll post again when it's up.

b.text:
Launch Week

It's out. After three years of nights and weekends, v1.0 went live last week.

I don't really know how to start these things other than just saying the numbers, so: 412 copies sold in the first week.

That's not a lot by Steam standards, but it's about 400 more than I was honestly expecting. I kept refreshing the dashboard on day one like an idiot.

The weirdest part was Tuesday(?) when someone posted it to a small subreddit and it hit the front page of that sub for like 6 hours. Traffic just spiked out of nowhere. I sat there watching the wishlist graph go vertical and didn't know what to do with myself.

Got the first real negative-ish review too. Said the movement feels floaty. And... yeah, they're right. I tuned it on my machine for so long I just got used to it. I reread the review like five times and then opened the controller code.

So what's next:

I'm working on 1.1 now. Main thing is tightening up the movement — more gravity, less drift on the jump landing, better air control. Shooting to have that out next month.

Thanks for playing it / wishlisting it / reading these posts while I was still just posting broken screenshots. I'll put up the full 1.1 patch notes when it's closer.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
A little note about wedding cakes

I’ve been putting off writing this one, because I don’t want anyone to feel like we’re letting them down. But I also believe in being straight with you, so here it is: we’re not taking on custom wedding cake orders anymore.

It’s not because we stopped loving weddings. We haven’t. I still get a little teary when someone tells me they got engaged at our counter or when a regular brings in photos of a cake we made years ago. Wedding cakes were a joy in a lot of ways.

But the honest truth is, they don’t work for a bakery our size. There are only three of us. I’m up at 4am most days, and by the time a wedding cake is done—the emails back and forth, the tasting, the sketching, the scheduling, the hunting down exactly the right ribbon or flower—it’s usually about 14 hours before I even turn on the oven. That’s 14 hours I’m not spending on the things that keep our doors open: the morning buns, the bread, the cookies, the case full of everyday stuff you actually come in for.

This year we also had three wedding cakes cancel on us at the last minute. I don’t blame anyone—big life plans change, things fall apart, I get it. But by then the ingredients were ordered, some of the prep was already done, and for a business this small, those losses stung. It’s hard to bounce back from that when you’re also trying to make payroll and keep the lights on.

And honestly, the wedding cake work was pulling us away from the everyday case, which is what actually pays rent. That case is our heartbeat. It’s what you count on when you come in for a coffee and a croissant, or a last-minute birthday cake, or just something good after a long week. I don’t want to lose that. I don’t want to be too busy with a five-tier cake to make sure the sourdough is right.

So we’re making the call to focus on what we do best, and to do it really well. If you’re already on our calendar or mid-conversation with us about a wedding cake, we’ll honor that. We’ll still have cakes in the case, and if you need something for a smaller gathering, come talk to us—we’ll do what we can. If you’re looking for a wedding cake, I’m happy to point you toward some local bakers I truly trust.

Thank you for understanding. Thank you for being the reason we get to do this at all. And thank you for still coming in for the daily stuff—that’s the part I never want to lose.

See you at the counter.

b.text:
Hey friends,

I wanted to share something that’s been on my mind for a while, because you’re the ones who keep showing up for us every week and I figure you deserve to hear it straight from me.

We’re stepping away from custom wedding cakes.

I know that might land a little heavy for a few of you who’ve been dreaming about one of our cakes for your day, and I want you to know how much it means that you’d even think of us for something that important. Truly. We’ve loved every single wedding cake we’ve made—the late-night sketching, the tasting plates we put together after the morning bake, the pure joy of watching a couple’s face when they try the first bite. But after this year especially, it’s become clear that continuing isn’t fair to the bakery, to the three of us, or honestly to the everyday customers who keep the lights on.

Here’s the real talk: each custom wedding order ends up taking about fourteen hours of free time—consults, sketches, multiple tastings, endless back-and-forth emails—before we even start baking. That’s time when one of us isn’t at the bench or helping with the morning rush. On top of that, we had three last-minute cancellations this year alone. We’d already bought the ingredients, blocked the days, and then… nothing. That cost lands square on a tiny shop like ours. And the biggest piece is that every hour spent on a wedding cake is an hour pulled away from the case you all actually come in for—the croissants, the cookies, the bread that pays the rent and keeps us open for you at 7 a.m. when you need your coffee and something warm.

I bake starting at 4 most mornings, and the blog (and everything else) gets written in whatever scraps of time are left. We’re three people. We love this work with our whole hearts, but we also have to protect the part of it that sustains us so we can keep doing it for years. Focusing on the everyday case—the things you grab on your way to work or for Sunday breakfast—is what lets us stay independent and keep showing up for this neighborhood.

So for now, no more custom wedding cakes. We’ll still have beautiful cakes in the case every day, and if you’re looking for something special for a smaller celebration, come talk to us. We just can’t take on the full custom wedding route anymore.

Thank you for understanding, for supporting us through all the early mornings and flour-dusted days, and for being the reason we get to keep baking at all. See you soon for a croissant—or three.

With love and a little butter on my sleeves,
[Your Name]

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
It’s just past five in the morning as I write this, sitting at the little table by the window while the first batch of croissants of the day is baking. It’s my favorite hour in the bakery—quiet, warm, and smelling of caramelized butter. Usually, my mind is spinning with the day’s bake list, but today I wanted to sit down and share a big decision we’ve made about the shop. 

Starting next season, we’ve decided to step away from doing custom wedding cakes. 

This wasn’t an easy choice to make. Being a small part of someone's wedding day is an incredible honor, and we have loved bringing those sweet visions to life. But as a tiny three-person team, we’ve had to take a hard, honest look at where our time and energy go, and how we can best keep serving this community we love so much.

The truth is, custom wedding cakes are a massive undertaking behind the scenes. By the time we sit down for initial tastings, exchange dozens of emails, sketch out designs, and source specialized decorations, we’ve easily poured about fourteen hours of work into a single cake before we even crack the first egg. When there are only three of us running the entire show, those hours have to come from somewhere, and lately, it has felt like we’re constantly running on empty.

We also had a tough run of luck this year with three last-minute wedding cancellations. While we completely understand that life happens and plans change, for a business of our size, absorbing the cost of expensive, specialty ingredients that we’ve already purchased—and can't reuse—is a really heavy blow. 

Most importantly, we realized that pouring so much of our limited time into these massive, one-off custom projects was pulling us away from the heart of our bakery: our daily pastry case. It’s the morning buns, the sourdough loaves, the chocolate chip cookies, and the casual birthday cakes that actually pay our rent and keep our doors open. More than that, it’s the daily connection with you—our regulars who pop in on your way to work or bring your kids in for a weekend treat. You are the reason we get up at 4:00 AM, and we want to make sure our pastry case is always packed with the very best we have to offer.

We will absolutely still be baking our signature cakes, and we'd still love to be a part of your birthdays, anniversaries, and casual celebrations—we'll just be sticking to our set menu of favorite flavors and styles rather than doing fully custom, bespoke wedding commissions. 

Thank you all so much for your warmth, your understanding, and your incredible support as we navigate what it means to grow and stay sustainable as a neighborhood bakery. The timer on the oven is buzzing, so I have to run—but I hope to see you at the counter later this week.

b.text:
**On Wedding Cakes, and Why We're Saying Goodbye to Them**

I've been putting off writing this one for a few weeks, mostly because I kept thinking I'd find a way to say it that didn't feel like a letdown. I haven't found it yet, so I'm just going to say it: starting this fall, we're not taking custom wedding cake orders anymore. If you've already got a date on our books, nothing changes — we'll be there, and your cake will be exactly what we promised. But we're not booking anything new.

I want to tell you why, because you've been good to us and you deserve more than a line on the order page.

The short version is that wedding cakes were quietly eating the shop.

The longer version starts with the part nobody sees. A custom cake isn't really a baking job — it's a project. There's the first conversation, usually an hour, sometimes two, where we talk through what you're imagining. Then there's the tasting, which means baking four or five small cakes and three or four fillings on a day we're already baking everything else, and then sitting down for another ninety minutes to go through them. Then the follow-up emails about whether the buttercream can be a shade warmer. Then the second tasting, because your mother couldn't make the first one. Then the sketch, the revision to the sketch, the call about whether we can match the ribbon. Then the delivery logistics, which are their own small novel.

I finally sat down and added it up this spring, and it came to somewhere around fourteen hours per cake before I ever start the actual cake. Fourteen hours that aren't billed, because that's how the industry does it — the consult is free, the tasting is free, the eight rounds of emails are free. I don't blame anyone for that. It's just how it's always worked. But there are three of us here, and fourteen hours is most of a person's week.

Then there's the other thing, which is harder to talk about without sounding sour, so I'll just be plain about it. We had three cancellations this year inside of two weeks of the date. Weddings fall apart, and I genuinely mean it when I say I hope those folks are all right — I'm not telling you this to shame anybody. But by two weeks out, the flour and the butter and the good vanilla and the fruit are bought. The specialty order for the particular chocolate is in. The day is blocked off, which means we turned down other work to hold it. When it goes away, that all just sits there. Three times in one year is real money for a shop our size, and it's money that came out of a place where there isn't a lot of slack.

But honestly, if it were only those two things, we'd have figured out a way. Deposits, contracts, a consult fee, something. The real reason is the third one, and it's the one that took me longest to admit.

Every hour I spent on wedding cakes was an hour I wasn't spending on the case.

The case is what pays rent. It's the morning buns and the sourdough and the seeded rye and the cardamom knots that go by ten-thirty on a Saturday. It's the birthday sheet cakes and the pie orders in November. It's you, coming in on a Tuesday because you always come in on a Tuesday. That's the actual business. That's what's been here for six years. And I kept noticing that on the weeks with a wedding in them, the case got thinner, or the laminated stuff didn't get the attention it wanted, or I ran out of the rye and just didn't have it in me to fix it. I'd be in the back at 4am piping sugar flowers for eighty people I'd never met while the thing that actually feeds us got the leftovers of my attention.

That's backwards. It took me an embarrassingly long time to see that it was backwards.

So here's what we're doing instead. We're keeping celebration cakes — the eight and ten-inch rounds, the sheet cakes, the ones you order with a week's notice and pick up at the counter. We'll still write on them. We'll still do the flavors you like. We just won't be doing tiers, or sugar work, or delivery, or the whole long courtship that a wedding cake requires. And we're putting that reclaimed time straight back into the case, which is where I've wanted it for a while now.

If you're getting married and you were hoping we'd do it, I'm sorry, truly. Come talk to me anyway — I know most of the good people in town doing this work and I'll happily point you at whoever's right for what you want.

And thank you for reading a long one. See you Tuesday.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
When I came home from my second deployment, the first place I got stuck was the cereal aisle at the commissary.

I had gone in for a few things because the house was low on milk and bread. My wife had made a list, short and clear. I was glad for the list. I put the milk in the cart, then the bread, then laundry detergent. Cereal was on the list too.

I turned down the aisle and stopped.

There were shelves on both sides, bright boxes all the way down. Different kinds of Cheerios. Different kinds of Raisin Bran. Cereal with marshmallows, cereal with chocolate, cereal that claimed to be healthy, cereal aimed at kids with cartoon characters I did not recognize. There were family-size boxes, single-serving boxes, boxes with prizes inside.

I stood there trying to pick one.

Over there, I had eaten whatever came in the box or on the tray. You ate when you could. You did not spend time deciding if you wanted cinnamon or berries or extra protein. Food was food. You learned not to complain about it.

At the commissary, I kept thinking I needed to make a good choice. Not just any choice. The right one.

A woman pushed her cart past me and gave me a look. Not mean. Just wondering why a grown man in a ball cap was standing in the middle of the aisle staring at cereal.

I picked up one box and put it back. Then another. I checked the price tags, though I had no idea what I was comparing. At some point I realized I had been there a long time. Maybe twenty minutes. It could have been longer.

I finally grabbed a box of plain corn flakes because it looked like something that had been around before I left. I took it home.

My daughter was six when I got back.

At the airport, I came through the doors with my duffel bag over one shoulder. There were people waiting along the railings, holding signs and balloons. Kids were running around. Somebody was crying. Somebody else was laughing too loud.

I saw my wife first. She was holding our daughter’s hand.

My wife smiled, and I smiled back. Then I looked at my daughter.

She looked at me for a second. I had seen pictures of her while I was gone. My wife sent them whenever she could. School pictures. Birthday pictures. Pictures of her missing front tooth. I knew the shape of her face from those pictures. I knew the pink backpack she was wearing.

But she looked at me like I was a stranger.

Then she stepped behind her mother’s leg.

I remember setting down my duffel bag. I remember kneeling because that seemed like what I should do. I held my arms out, but not too far. I did not want to scare her.

“Hey, sweetheart,” I said.

She pressed her face against my wife’s leg.

My wife reached down and touched her hair. “That’s Daddy,” she said.

My daughter looked again. She was trying to figure it out. I could see that. She had heard my voice on the phone. She had seen me on a screen sometimes, when the connection worked. But I was taller than the screen. I had a beard I did not have before. I smelled like airports and travel and the inside of a duffel bag.

After a minute, she came out from behind my wife. She did not run to me. She walked slowly, holding one finger in her mouth.

I stayed where I was.

When she got close enough, I asked if I could have a hug.

She nodded.

It was a small hug at first. Her arms barely went around my neck. I held her carefully. Then she held on tighter.

At home, I had trouble sleeping.

The bedroom door had always been shut while I was gone. My wife liked it closed. The house was quiet that way. The hallway light did not come in. The air conditioning did not make the door move.

But I could not sleep with it shut.

For a year, I had slept where I could see the door. I had learned which doors opened inward and which opened outward. I had noticed hinges, locks, windows, corners. I did not think about doing it. I just did it.

The first night home, my wife shut the bedroom door before getting into bed.

I lay there in the dark for a while.

“You okay?” she asked.

“Yeah,” I said.

A few minutes passed.

Then I got up and opened the door.

The hallway was dark. My daughter’s room was down the hall, her night-light making a faint yellow line under her door. I stood there looking at it.

My wife did not say anything.

I got back into bed, leaving our door open.

For a while, every sound in the house woke me up. The refrigerator turning on. The ice maker dropping cubes. Pipes knocking when somebody used water. The dog moving around downstairs. I would wake up and look toward the open doorway before I knew I was awake.

After a few weeks, I started sleeping longer.

One night, my wife fell asleep before me. The door was open. The hallway was dark except for that line of light from my daughter’s room.

I got up and closed the door most of the way.

Not all the way. Just enough that it stayed open a few inches.

Then I went back to bed.

b.text:
The plane touched down at Fort Bragg, and just like that, I was home. Again. The first time, I’d come back from Iraq with a duffel bag full of dirty uniforms and a head full of things I didn’t want to talk about. This time, Afghanistan. Different sand, same weight.

I stood in the cereal aisle at the commissary, staring at the shelves like they were a puzzle I couldn’t solve. Forty kinds of cereal. Forty. Back in the FOB, we got whatever was in the MREs—peanut butter, crackers, maybe some Skittles if you were lucky. Here, there were boxes with cartoon characters, organic labels, granola that cost more than a six-pack. I picked up a box of Frosted Flakes, put it back. Grabbed the Raisin Bran, set it down. Twenty minutes later, I walked out with a loaf of bread and a jar of peanut butter. Old habits.

The airport was worse. My wife had texted me a picture of our daughter a few weeks before I left—missing her two front teeth, grinning like she’d just won a prize. I’d kept that picture in my pocket the whole deployment. Now, standing there in the terminal, I saw her peeking out from behind my wife’s leg, eyes wide like she wasn’t sure who I was. She was six. I’d been gone a year.

“Hey, kiddo,” I said, crouching down. She didn’t move. My wife gave me that look—the one that said *give her time*. So I did. I sat on the floor and pulled out the little wooden camel I’d carved for her in the downtime. She took it, turned it over in her hands, then finally stepped forward and hugged my neck. I held on tight.

Sleeping was the hardest part. For a year, I’d slept with one eye open, always facing the door, always ready. Now, back in our house, my wife left the bedroom door open like she always did. I lay there, staring at the ceiling, listening to the quiet hum of the fridge, the occasional car passing outside. No mortars, no generators, no guys talking in their sleep. Just silence. I got up and shut the door. The next night, I left it open for an hour before closing it. The night after that, two hours. Eventually, I stopped noticing.

Some mornings, I’d wake up and forget where I was. Then I’d see my wife’s hair spread out on the pillow next to me, hear my daughter laughing in the other room, and remember. Home. Again.

setup: You're everyone at the startup. Yesterday's 40-minute outage was caused by a bad database migration during deploy.

a.text:
Hi team,

**Current Status:** All systems are fully operational, healthy, and stable. 

I want to share a quick update on what happened during yesterday’s 40-minute outage around 2:00 PM, especially for those of you who were fielding customer questions and concerns.

**What Happened**
During a routine software deploy yesterday afternoon, we ran a database update (a "migration") that was meant to reorganize how some data is stored. Instead of applying instantly as expected, the update locked up a core database table, which prevented the app from reading or writing data and caused the platform to become unresponsive for roughly 40 minutes.

**How It Was Resolved**
Once we identified the lockup, the engineering team rolled back the deployment to the previous working version, which unlocked the database and restored full service to customers.

**What We’re Changing**
To make sure this doesn’t happen again:
* **Maintenance Windows:** Moving forward, any database updates that carry a risk of locking tables will only be run during scheduled, off-peak maintenance windows rather than during regular daytime deploys.
* **Testing:** We are adding additional staging tests to measure database lock times before changes go anywhere near production.

Thank you to everyone who stepped up to manage customer communication while we were working through the fix. If anyone needs specific context for follow-ups with customers, or if you have any questions, please feel free to reach out to me directly.

b.text:
Hi everyone,

We’re back up and stable. The outage yesterday lasted about 40 minutes around 2pm and is fully resolved.

What happened, in plain terms: we were doing a routine deploy that included a database migration—a change to how some data is stored. That change accidentally locked a key database table (temporarily blocked access to data the app depends on) for much longer than it should have, which made the app unavailable. We identified the issue, rolled back the change, and service was restored.

Some of you were hearing from customers during the outage—thank you for stepping in, and sorry for the disruption and extra stress.

Going forward, these migrations will run in a scheduled maintenance window rather than during regular deploys. That way, a routine release won’t be able to cause an outage like this again.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
The whistle blew for the third time this season. The game wasn’t over; the field was. Girls jogged off the pitch, mud-spattered and frustrated, while the varsity boys squad took the adjacent football field—pristine, dry, and ready for overtime.

We’ve lost nine games to rain in the last two seasons. The grass turns into a swamp, and the ball doesn’t bounce; it gets stuck. Last October, one of my sophomores planted her foot to change direction and went down. An ACL tear. Nine months of rehab. All because the ground gave way under her.

The football team got turf installed in 2019. They practice on a surface that doesn’t flood, doesn’t turn into holes, and doesn’t threaten their athletes’ careers. My girls are playing on a patch of dirt that the city treats like a decorative afterthought.

It’s not just about scheduling headaches. It’s about equity. It’s about keeping kids in the game instead of on the sidelines with a surgeon. The school board is voting on the budget next month. They know the football field is turf. They know ours floods. At this point, not upgrading is a choice.

b.text:
**The football field got turf in 2019. The girls' soccer field still floods.**

Nine. That's how many games our girls' soccer team has had rained out or moved in the past two seasons because our grass field floods. Not snowed out. Not forfeited. Flooded. My players stand at the fence in full uniform, watching standing water where the midfield should be, and then we call their parents to come pick them up.

"Moved" usually means handing our home game to the opponent because their field drains and ours doesn't. And rained-out games don't disappear. They get crammed into the back of the schedule — three games in five days on tired teenage legs, which is how knees get hurt even before you factor in the ruts.

About those ruts. When the field floods and then dries, it dries hard and uneven, with troughs where the puddles sat and footprints baked in like concrete. Last October, one of my players planted her foot in one of those ruts on a routine cut — the kind of cut she's made a thousand times in practice — and tore her ACL. Surgery. Nine months of rehab. She lost her junior season to a hole in the ground that never should have been there. I won't use her name here. She's a kid, not a talking point. But her injury is the reason I'm writing, and her parents know it.

Now let's talk about 2019.

That's the year the district put turf on the football field. I want to be clear: I'm glad they did. Those kids deserve a safe, playable surface. So do mine. The school board already decided that athletes in this town get to play on turf. They just decided it for some athletes.

Since then, the girls' soccer program has been told to wait. Wait for the next budget cycle. Wait for the five-year facilities plan. My freshmen who were promised "soon" are now juniors.

People ask why the girls don't just play on the football turf. Because it's spoken for — football practices, games, and everything else the district schedules there. And because "you can borrow the boys' field when they're not using it" is not the same as having your own. Ask the football team if they'd take that deal.

Title IX turned fifty a few years back. Equity was never just about counting roster spots. It's the ground under your feet. Right now, the ground under our girls' feet is a swamp after every hard rain and a washboard when it dries.

I can hear the objection already: turf costs money. It does. So does resodding and reseeding a field that drowns twice a season. So do the hours parents spend driving forty minutes to borrowed fields for games that were supposed to be at home. So does an ACL surgery and nine months of physical therapy. The district found the money in 2019. The field hasn't gotten cheaper since then. It's just gotten worse.

And this isn't a gift to one team. A turf field gets used — both soccer programs, PE classes, youth leagues on weekends, community events. Grass fields around here sit empty half the year because nobody can play on them. Turf works every day. The football field has proven that for five years.

The school board votes on next year's facilities budget in [month]. Turf for the girls' soccer field needs to be in it. Not in "phase two." Not in some long-range plan that kicks the can past my current freshmen's graduation. In this budget, this year.

If you're a parent, an alum, or a taxpayer who thinks girls should play on the same quality field as boys, come to that meeting and say so. I'll be easy to spot. I'll be the one in the school windbreaker, holding a list of nine rained-out games and one torn ACL.

*The writer is the head girls' soccer and track coach at [School] High School.*

b.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8 Months of Near-Daily Market Baking

I've had the Corlane SM6 on my counter for eight months now, and unlike most of the gear that passes through my kitchen for a review, this one has earned its spot by actually working for a living. I bake sourdough for the farmers market most weekends, which means this machine gets fired up almost every day. Here's what I've learned.

## The Motor Is the Real Deal

This is where the SM6 justifies itself. I regularly run a double batch of stiff bagel dough through it, which is the kind of dense, low-hydration dough that makes lesser mixers whine, walk across the counter, or shut off entirely to protect themselves. The Corlane doesn't flinch. No stalling, no burning smell, no motor overheating cutoff. If you knead heavy dough, this is the headline feature, and it delivers.

## The Annoyances

Two of them, and I want to be honest about both.

First, the bowl lift lever squeaks. It started a couple months in, and I now hit it with a shot of WD-40 about once a month to keep it quiet and smooth. It's not a dealbreaker, but at this price point I shouldn't have to babysit a moving part on a schedule.

Second, and more irritating: the included dough hook is too short for the depth of the bowl. It doesn't reach the bottom well, so flour and shaggy dough get left behind and you're scraping constantly. I bought a third-party hook that fits properly, and it fixed the problem entirely. Frustrating that I had to spend extra to make the machine do its main job, but the fix is cheap and easy.

## The Price

It's $429. That's $80 more than the comparable KitchenAid. There's no getting around the fact that you're paying a premium, and you should know that going in.

## The Verdict

**Buy it if you knead heavy dough every week.** If you're running stiff bagel, bagel-adjacent, or high-volume sourdough batches the way I do, the extra $80 buys you a motor that won't quit, and that's worth every penny over the life of the machine. Budget another twenty bucks for a proper dough hook and expect to keep a can of WD-40 in the drawer.

**Skip it if you're mostly baking cookies and cake batter.** The SM6's whole advantage is its muscle, and you'll never use it. For lighter work, the cheaper KitchenAid does the same job, comes with a hook that actually fits, and doesn't squeak. Save your $80.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
I shot 8 years in the Hill Country. I'll tell you the one thing that separates "nice" wedding photos from the ones a couple actually frames on their wall.

It's usually the couple who said "we'll trust you on the day" and tossed the 47-point shot list in a drawer.

Last spring. Barrera wedding. Two weeks out, they send me a shot list. Four pages. Specific angles, specific family groupings, "I want a photo in front of the big rock at 4:15." I respect it. I make a plan.

Then it rains.

Not drizzle. The kind of sideways Hill Country rain where your 200mm lens fills with water in about eleven seconds. Ceremony's in a field. Reception's in a tent that's now a swimming pool. The whole timeline is garbage.

I text them: "We can pivot. All of it. Or we can stand in the mud and make sure we check off your list."

Daniella writes back, three words: "Wherever's dry. Go."

We hauled everything—officiant, string quartet, chairs, the whole 70-person mess—under this massive old pecan tree behind the venue. The canopy broke the rain enough to keep people mostly dry. The light going through the leaves was, honestly, the best natural light I'd seen in two years. Nobody was checking a list. Nobody was watching the clock. They were just there, a little wet, laughing, holding hands under a tree that had been growing since before either of them was born.

I got forty frames from that afternoon that I still think about. And none of them were on page four.

Couples, here's what I'm actually asking for: give me your family formals. I need to know about Aunt Linda who'll cry if she's not in the photo. But the "creative" shots? The golden-hour portraits? Let me be a photographer instead of a checklist. The day will not go as written. It's not a failure. That's just the day being the day.

And if you're a vendor reading this—planner, DJ, venue owner—you know this instinct too. The moment you stop managing the script and start managing the energy, the room shifts. The best moments we build are the ones nobody wrote down.

The Barreras still text me when they get a good one off the tree. I keep every text.

That's the whole job right there.

b.text:
The couples who ditch the shot list always seem to end up with the best photos.

Not because planning doesn’t matter—it does. I still want the family groupings, meaningful details, and moments you don’t want missed.

But an exhaustive list of poses can pull everyone out of the day they’re actually living.

The Barrera wedding is a perfect example. Rain changed the plan, and we moved everything under the pecan tree. Instead of trying to force the original vision, they trusted the moment, embraced the weather, and stayed present.

That flexibility created photographs that felt like them—not a checklist.

Give your photographer the must-haves. Then leave room for the unexpected.

That’s often where the best images are hiding.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/ I raised Tallyup’s prices 40% on everyone overnight.

We lost 30 of our 140 customers in a week.

I build a tool that helps gym owners track member retention. This was a painful lesson in my own.

Here’s the mistake—and what I changed.

2/ The mistake wasn’t necessarily charging more.

It was treating a price increase like a switch I could flip, rather than a change customers needed time to consider.

Everyone. Overnight. No transition.

3/ I can’t tell you what would have happened with a slower rollout.

But losing 30 customers doesn’t prove the old price was right, either.

I changed the price and the rollout at the same time. Now I can’t cleanly separate the two.

4/ What I changed:

[Insert the actual changes you made: how you handled existing customers, whether you changed the price again, and what you changed about notice or rollout.]

5/ My takeaway: deciding what to charge and deciding how to introduce that price are two different jobs.

I treated them as one.

Sharing this because “charge more” is common indie SaaS advice. The rollout deserves just as much attention.

b.text:
Here's a thread on the pricing mistake and what I changed 🧵

1/ Six months ago I raised Tallyup's prices 40% overnight. On everyone. No grandfathering, no warning emails, just flipped the switch on a Tuesday morning. Here's what happened: we lost 30 of our 140 customers in a week. ~21% churn, out of nowhere.

2/ The reasoning at the time felt solid. MRR was flat, I figured the product was underpriced, and I'd read enough "raise your prices" posts to think I was leaving money on the table. I was solving my boredom, not a real customer problem.

3/ What I missed: my customers are gym owners running small facilities. They don't have procurement budgets. A 40% jump in a line item they'd been paying for a year feels like a billing error before it feels like a value conversation. Most of the 30 who left didn't even email. Just canceled.

4/ First thing I changed: rolled back pricing for anyone who stayed. Sent a personal email, no template, explaining the jump was a mistake and their old price was locked in for 12 months. Kept 22 of the remaining 110 that way. The other 8 churned within the month anyway.

5/ Second change: any future price increase is on new customers only, for at least 6 months before existing customers see it. And existing customers get 30 days notice with a real explanation, not a Stripe receipt. Announcements > assumptions.

6/ Third change: I started charging new signups the new price and tracking conversion rate weekly instead of just MRR. Conversion dropped ~15% the first month, which told me the new price was probably 10-15% too high, not 40%. I'd been anchoring to the wrong number.

7/ What I'd tell other solo founders: your existing customers are your cheapest source of validated pricing. If you raise on them and a chunk leave instantly, the market just told you something your spreadsheet didn't. Listen to it before you keep raising.

8/ Tallyup today: ~115 customers, MRR is higher than it was at 140 because new signups come in at the new price, but the lesson wasn't "raise prices." It was "raise prices the way your customers can actually absorb them." Wild concept, I know.

(end 🧵)

setup: An IT helpdesk technician is writing an essay to a hiring manager for a junior product and UX role.

a.text:
Dear Hiring Manager,

I spend 40 hours a week inside your product. I'm an IT helpdesk technician at a mid-size hospital system, and for the past five years, your ticketing tool has been the center of my workday. I field around 35 tickets a day through it, which means I know its workflows, its friction points, and its rough edges better than most users ever will.

That daily exposure turned me into an unofficial product consultant. Over the last three years, I've submitted 14 feature requests to your team—four of them shipped. I don't say that to boast; I say it because it shows I already think like someone who wants to improve the product, not just use it.

I've also channeled that instinct internally. I built a wiki of 60+ troubleshooting articles that reduced our repeat tickets by roughly a third. Translating messy institutional knowledge into clear, usable guidance is the part of my job I love most—and it's the bridge between helpdesk work and UX.

What I'm looking for now is the chance to do that work upstream, where the decisions get made. I've seen healthcare workers struggle with software at the point of care. I've also seen what happens when a product team listens and iterates. I want to be part of that loop.

I know I'm coming from the support side, not a traditional design background. But I'm applying for a junior role because I have the domain knowledge, the user empathy, and the track record of shipping feedback that actually helps people. I'd welcome the chance to talk about how that translates.

Thank you for your time.

Best,
[Name]

b.text:
Dear Hiring Manager,

I've spent the last five years living in your ticketing tool.

As an IT helpdesk technician for a mid-size hospital system, I field about 35 tickets a day through your platform — from password resets in the ER to clinical workflow breakdowns. I know where users rage-click, where they get confused, and where a small fix saves hours.

Because I see those patterns every day, I built an internal wiki with 60+ troubleshooting articles that cut our repeat tickets by about a third. And over the last three years, I've submitted 14 feature requests to your product team. Four of them shipped — which was the moment I realized I want to be on the side building it, not just requesting it.

I understand your users because I am one, and I support hundreds more just like me. I'd love to bring that front-line perspective to your Junior UX and Product Support role.

Thank you for your consideration,
[Your Name]

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
**COLUMN: Abandoning the ground game cost us a deeper playoff run**

It’s tough to swallow a season ending the way ours did on Friday night. Going 8-2 is a banner year for this program, and nobody is taking that away from these kids. But losing in the second round of the state playoffs to a team we beat by 20 points back in Week 3 leaves a bad taste in your mouth. 

We didn’t lose because we were out-athleted. We lost because of a baffling second-half game plan.

Let’s look at the facts. At halftime, we were down by just three points. More importantly, our run game was dictating the tempo. We were moving the chains, controlling the clock, and keeping their defense on their heels. Then the third quarter started, and for some reason, the coaching staff decided to put the ball entirely in Dez Kowalski’s hands.

Don't get me wrong, Dez is a phenomenal talent. He threw for 2,340 yards this season, shattering the school record, and he’s got the arm to make any throw on the field. But you don’t abandon a working ground game just to chase highlight-reel passes, especially when you’re only trailing by a single field goal. 

By going pass-heavy in the second half, we became one-dimensional. We let their defensive line pin their ears back and hunt our quarterback. We gave up the clock, we gave up the physical advantage we’d established in the first half, and ultimately, we gave up the game. 

You have to play to your strengths, and on Friday, our strength was right between the tackles. Next year’s squad will need to remember that when the lights are brightest, you don't get cute. You just line up and run it down their throats.

b.text:
**One Play Call Haunts the Season**

Eight wins, two losses, and a school-record 2,340 passing yards for Dez Kowalski—by the numbers, this was a season to celebrate. But numbers don’t tell the whole story, and neither does the final score of last Friday’s playoff loss. The truth stings because it’s avoidable: we lost because we stopped doing what was working.

Up 20 points on that same opponent back in Week 3, we ran the ball down their throats. Last Friday, down just three in the second half, we abandoned the run. Four straight pass plays, three incompletions, a sack, and suddenly the momentum was gone. The defense, gassed from long drives earlier in the game, couldn’t hold up when we needed them most.

Football is a game of adjustments, sure, but sometimes the best adjustment is sticking with what got you there. We had them on their heels. Instead of pounding the rock, we put it all on Dez’s arm—and for the first time all season, it wasn’t enough. That’s not on him. It’s on the play-calling.

This team had heart, talent, and a shot at something special. But in the end, we outsmarted ourselves. And that’s the hardest loss to swallow.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
**The Spring Market Reality Check: It’s Not a Crash, It’s a Price Tag Problem**

If you’ve driven around our neighborhoods lately, you’ve probably noticed something we haven't seen in a while: yard signs that are actually sticking around for more than a weekend. 

Last spring, selling a home in our ZIP code was a sprint. The median days on market was a breakneck 8 days. You put a sign in the yard on Thursday, went away for the weekend, and sorted through a dozen offers on Monday. 

This spring, the median days on market has climbed to 34 days. At the same time, the number of showings per listing has cut clean in half. 

Looking at those two stats, it’s easy to jump to the conclusion that the sky is falling. But here is the kicker: local list prices are still up 6% year-over-year. 

So, how do we reconcile fewer buyers through the door and longer wait times with prices that are still climbing? 

I’ll give you the honest answer, because I’m living it every day. Right now, I personally have three listings sitting at over 60 days on the market. The sellers are frustrated, and they are flatly refusing to drop their prices. They are holding out for the frenzy of 2021 and 2022, convinced that the perfect buyer is just around the corner.

But the reality is, that buyer isn't coming. Not at that price. 

There is a lot of talk in the national news about a housing crash, and plenty of pundits hedging their bets by saying "the market is complex and depends on many factors." 

I’ve been doing this in our community for ten years, and I’m here to tell you: it’s not that complex. We are not experiencing a crash. What we are experiencing is a massive disconnect between sellers who haven’t caught up to the new pace of the market, and buyers who are pushing back against high interest rates. 

The buyers are still out there. They are qualified, and they want to buy. But they are tired of being stretched to their absolute financial limits for homes that need work or are priced at the very top of the market. 

The proof is in the data. The homes in our neighborhoods that are priced correctly from day one—not priced where the seller *wishes* the market was, but where the market actually *is*—are still selling in under two weeks. 

If you are thinking of selling this spring, you don't need to panic, but you do need a reality check. The days of naming your price and waiting for a bidding war are over. If your home has been sitting for over a month, it’s not because the market is broken. It’s because your price is. 

Price it right, and it will sell. Price it for three years ago, and you'll be joining my sellers on day 61.

b.text:
**The Market Didn’t Crash—Sellers Just Haven’t Caught Up**

After 10 years selling in this suburb, I’ve learned that the most dangerous words in real estate are “let’s just see what happens.” Last spring, that phrase was harmless. Median days on market in our zip code was 8. Eight days. You could overprice a house by five or ten grand and still have multiple offers before the weekend was over. The market moved so fast that mistakes didn’t matter.

This spring is different. Median days on market has stretched to 34. Showings per listing have dropped by half. And yet list prices are still up 6 percent year over year. So sellers look at that number and think the old rules still apply. They don’t.

I currently have three sellers who have been on the market for over 60 days. All three have refused to lower their price. All three are getting a handful of showings, no offers, and the same feedback on repeat: “Nice house, but it’s priced too high.” These aren’t bad houses. They aren’t in bad locations. They are priced for a market that no longer exists.

This is not a crash. Let me say that clearly, because I know the headlines love that word. A crash is when prices fall hard and demand disappears. That is not what is happening here. Prices are still up year over year. Buyers are still out there. The problem is tempo. Last spring, the market was so fast that an overpriced listing could still get saved by a buyer who was tired of losing. This spring, buyers are slower. They are seeing more inventory. They compare. They negotiate. They don’t panic. An overpriced house now sits while the correctly priced one down the street goes under contract in under two weeks.

I’ve watched it happen all spring. The houses priced at or just below recent comparable sales are still moving in 10 to 14 days. The houses priced 5 to 10 percent above the comps are sitting, collecting days on market like a stain that gets harder to wash out.

Here is the hard truth for sellers: your list price is not a statement of what your house was worth last spring. It is a statement of what a buyer is willing to pay this week. The market does not owe you last year’s momentum. If you have been on the market for more than 30 days without an offer, the problem is not your photos, your staging, or your agent’s marketing. The problem is the price. Buyers are telling you with their silence.

I know price reductions feel like defeat. They aren’t. They are catching up to reality. A price cut after 45 days often costs you more than pricing honestly from day one, because buyers start to wonder what’s wrong with the house. The longer you sit, the more leverage you hand to the buyer who eventually does make an offer. The best time to reduce your price was two weeks ago. The second-best time is today.

For buyers, this is not a fire sale, but it is a moment of opportunity. The desperation is gone. You can read the inspection report without being told to waive it. You can negotiate on closing dates, repairs, and some contingencies. You have room to breathe. After three years of bidding wars, that is a real shift. But do not expect prices to fall off a cliff. The fundamentals here have not changed: good schools, steady jobs, limited new construction. What changed is the speed.

The agents telling their sellers to “wait for the right buyer” are doing them a disservice. The right buyer is not coming at the wrong price. This spring is separating the honest actors from the wishful thinkers. My advice to sellers is plain: if you want to sell in this market, price like you actually want to sell. If you want to list high and hope, don’t be surprised when you are still on the market in August.

This is not a crash. It is a correction in expectations. The sellers who understand that are still selling. The ones who don’t are still on the market.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
I've been doing this for years now, and I will say this one thing over and over again, so grab a coffee and just trust me on this: do not bathe your dog before you brush them. I know, I *know*. The logic seems to go, "Well, if I get the water in there it'll loosen up those tangles and they'll just slide right out." They will not slide right out. What actually happens is the water swells the fur, the mat gets damp, and it dries back down into a little felt pad that's tighter and tougher than the tangle that was there before. You just cemented the problem into the coat. I can fix a mat in the salon. I can't fix the one you just made worse on Saturday night and now can't get a comb through.

So here's the sequence, and I really wish someone had laid this out plain when I was still a rookie with a shih tzu at home: brush first, dry and dirty and all. Always first. Then you bathe. Then you blow it out or let it air dry and give it one more quick pass. For the double-coated folks out there with your aussies and collies and huskies, and my curly-coated regulars with the poodles and doodles and Portuguese water dogs, this matters even more because the undercoat is what traps moisture and what knots first.

When you're doing that pre-bath brush, grab a slicker brush, the one with the fine wire pins. And here's the thing people get wrong on technique: you're not doing big circular scrubbing motions. You're doing short little strokes, almost like you're making tiny checkmarks or lines through the coat. Big circles just drag the top layer over a tangle you're not reaching and make it look smooth while the mat underneath stays right where it is. Small strokes, a couple inches at a time, so you can actually feel what's going on at the skin.

Work in sections. Don't just start at the head and sweep the whole side of the body in one go. You're gonna miss things. And start where the mats actually *start*, which is behind the ears and under the front legs, the armpit area. Those two spots are where a dog moves the most, where friction is highest, where the coat gets crushed against a collar or the other shoulder when they walk. If you catch a tangle there on Tuesday, it's a loose little knot. By the next visit it's a disc you can barely slide a comb under, and then it's a shave-out, and then you're having one of those sad conversations with your dog in my grooming room about why their ear looks different.

And if you already feel that little disc forming, or you can see a knot getting snug, do not pick up the brush and just start hacking at it. Do not pick up a comb. Go get your leave-in conditioner, or even just a little detangling spray, and work it into that mat with your fingertips. Massage it in. Let it sit for a minute or two. You're trying to get slip down into the fibers so the knot has somewhere to go when you finally touch it with a tool. If you drag a slicker through a bone-dry mat, you're pulling on skin, and now your dog learns that brushing means pain and starts squirming and growling, and you both lose. Conditioner first, fingers, *then* the tool, and go slow.

This is not meant to replace what we do here, honestly. If your boy or girl is double-coated and brushing goes every other day at best, you're still gonna need that pro de-mat and coat health check every four to six weeks, maybe tighter in shedding season. What this is, is giving you the tools to keep a small tangle from becoming the mat I have to shave out on Friday. You save your dog the clipper, you save yourself the stress of a wrestling match in your kitchen, and I get to do the full breed trim I actually trained for instead of the emergency "I can't get a comb in anywhere" special.

If you're not sure whether what you're seeing is "fine, I'll deal with it next visit" or "oh no, this is getting tight and I need a hand," just text me a photo. Seriously. Take a pic, send it to the salon number, I'll tell you if you're in trouble or if a little conditioner and some patience will sort it out. No charge for that. I'd rather answer three texts than see your dog get a bald patch because you weren't sure how to start.

b.text:
The easiest way to prevent painful mats is to catch them before bath day. Once fur is wet, any small tangles can tighten into dense, felt-like pads that are much harder to remove.

This is especially important for double-coated and curly-coated dogs. Areas like behind the ears, under the front legs, around the collar, and along the belly tend to tangle first because they get a lot of rubbing and movement.

Before bathing your dog at home, make sure the coat is completely brushed out. Don’t rely on the bath to loosen knots. That’s a mistake I see constantly, and it usually has the opposite effect: water pulls the tangled hairs together and can lock the mats in even tighter.

Use a slicker brush and work with short, gentle line strokes. Think of brushing a small section at a time, moving the brush away from the skin and then checking your progress. Avoid scrubbing in circles, since circular brushing can twist the hair and create more tangles.

Start behind the ears and under the front legs, then work through the rest of the coat in sections. Part the hair with your fingers so you can see down toward the skin instead of only brushing over the surface. For a double-coated dog, you’ll need to work through the outer coat and the undercoat. For a curly-coated dog, take your time so the brush reaches all the way through each curl.

If you notice a mat beginning to form, don’t immediately attack it with a brush or comb. First, work a little dog-safe conditioner into the mat with your fingers. Gently loosen the outside edges before trying to separate the hairs. Never yank or force a brush through a tight mat, especially if your dog is uncomfortable.

A quick brush before the bath is much kinder and more effective than trying to deal with a tightened, wet coat afterward. If you find mats close to the skin, large areas of matting, or a dog who is painful or upset when you touch the coat, stop and contact your groomer. Some mats need to be safely clipped out rather than brushed out, and trying to remove them at home can injure your dog’s skin.
