setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
The single most common thing I see on my table is a dog who got a bath at home last weekend, and now has a coat that feels like a car mat. The owner did everything with good intentions. That's what makes it worth writing about.

Here's the thing nobody tells you: water is what turns a loose tangle into a mat. Wet fur swells, then it shrinks as it dries, and every one of those little knots cinches down on itself like a wet shoelace. Add shampoo, which strips the slip right out of the hair, and you've essentially wet-felted your dog. It's the same process people use on purpose to make wool hats. So when you bathe a matted dog hoping the suds will loosen things up, you get the exact opposite. That mat is now denser, tighter, and closer to the skin than it was an hour ago. On a really bad one, I can't get a comb under it at all, and my only honest option is to shave it out.

So: brush first. Always. Before the bath, on a dry coat, top to bottom. Then bathe. Never the other way around.

**Brushing a dry coat, the way it actually works**

Get yourself a decent slicker brush — the flat rectangular kind with the fine bent wire pins. If you have a doodle, a Poodle, a Bichon, a Cocker, anything curly, you'll want a metal greyhound comb too, because that's your only real way to know if you got all the way down. On a Husky, Pomeranian, Golden, Aussie, or any of the other double coats, the slicker plus an undercoat rake will do most of the heavy lifting.

Use short, straight strokes in a line, and lift the brush off the coat at the end of each one. Little flicking strokes, an inch or two long. What you don't want is that big sweeping circular motion people naturally fall into — circles push hair around and tangle it against itself, and they only skim the surface anyway. You end up with a coat that looks brushed on top and is packed solid underneath. Straight lines, off and back, off and back.

Work in sections instead of wandering all over the dog. I like to part the coat with my free hand, brush the hair right at the part line, then move my hand up a half inch and do it again. It's slow the first few times and then it becomes second nature.

Start behind the ears and under the front legs. That's where mats show up first on nearly every dog I touch, and it's where most people brush last, if at all. Behind the ears the hair is fine and it rubs against the ear leather all day. Under the front legs and in the armpit it's constant friction from walking, plus harness straps. Same story around the collar, the base of the tail, and the back of the hind legs where they brush together. If you only have five minutes, spend them in those spots and you'll prevent most of your problems.

**If you can already feel a mat**

Don't attack it with a brush. Dry mats are welded together and dragging a slicker through one hurts — that's the tug that teaches a dog to hate being brushed, and once they've learned that, everything gets harder for both of us.

Instead, put a little conditioner or a detangling spray right on it and work it in with your fingers. Squish it, roll it, pull it apart into smaller pieces, hair by hair if you have to. Give it a minute to actually soak in. Conditioner works by coating the strands so they slide past each other instead of gripping, and that's a chemical job, not a mechanical one. Only once it feels softer and you can see some separation should the comb or slicker come near it. Work from the outside edge of the mat inward, holding the base of the hair with your other hand so you're not pulling on skin.

And be honest with yourself about size. A mat bigger than a quarter, or one that's flat against the skin and won't lift, is a phone call, not a project. There can be moisture and irritation trapped under there, sometimes a hot spot, and forcing it out at home usually means a stressed dog and a nick in the skin. I'd much rather see you early with two or three tangles than three months later with a coat that has to come off.

Ten minutes, two or three times a week, in the spots I listed. Dry coat, straight strokes, sections. That's genuinely the whole thing — and it's the difference between your dog leaving here with the haircut you wanted and leaving with a summer shave.

b.text:
# Keeping Your Dog’s Coat Mat-Free Between Grooming Visits

The mistake I see most often is an owner bathing their dog because they think the water will loosen up a few tangles. I understand the thinking, but it usually makes the job harder. Water, rubbing, and drying can tighten those tangles until you’re dealing with a felt-like pad instead of a little knot.

The rule I tell my clients is simple: brush before the bath. Don’t leave the detangling until afterward.

This matters especially for double-coated dogs and curly-coated breeds. Loose undercoat can get trapped close to the skin, and curls can wind around each other as your dog moves. A coat can look lovely on top and still have tangles underneath.

Start behind the ears and under the front legs. Those soft, high-friction spots are often the first places mats develop. Then check around the collar or harness, the chest, the back legs, and the tail.

Work in small sections rather than sweeping your brush over the whole dog. Gently lift a little coat so you can see where you’re working, then use a slicker brush with short, straight strokes—not circles. This is called line brushing. You’re brushing one small line of hair at a time, then moving to the next, so you don’t just skim over the surface and miss everything underneath.

Keep your touch light. The pins should work through the hair, not scrape the skin. If you keep catching in the same place, stop rather than brushing harder.

If you spot a small tangle starting, work a little dog-safe detangling spray or leave-in conditioner into it with your fingers before reaching for a brush or comb. Follow the product directions, gently tease the hairs apart, and support the coat near the skin so you aren’t pulling on your dog. Conditioner can help with a loose tangle; it won’t make a tight mat safe to brush out.

After each section, check your work with a metal comb. It should pass gently through the coat, not just through the ends. If it catches, that spot needs another look—not a stronger tug.

Once the coat is tangle-free, you can bathe your dog. Dry thoroughly afterward, especially through a dense undercoat. A gentle brush-through once dry is fine; the important thing is not using the bath as your first attempt at detangling.

A few minutes of regular checking is much easier on your dog than one long session tackling a week’s worth of knots. How often you need to brush depends on the coat, so ask us what makes sense for yours.

And if a mat is tight, close to the skin, or uncomfortable to touch, leave it for us. Please don’t cut it out with scissors—skin can be pulled up inside the mat where you can’t see it. Give the salon a call, and we’ll help you work out the kindest next step.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
WHEN THE RUN GAME LEFT, SO DID THE SEASON

I said it on my radio show the morning after the loss, and I’ll say it again in print: this team didn’t lose because the other team suddenly got better. We lost because, in the second half, we stopped doing the one thing that was working.

Eight-and-two is a good season. Nobody around here is going to complain about eight wins and a trip to the second round of the state playoffs. But seasons are remembered by how they end, and this one ended against a team we beat by 20 back in Week 3.

Dez Kowalski threw for 2,340 yards this year, a school record. That’s a heck of an achievement, and it ought to be celebrated. But a passing record doesn’t win playoff games by itself. Against that team, chasing the big play might have been part of the problem.

Go back to Week 3. We didn’t win by 20 because we turned Dez loose on every snap. We won because we were more physical. The offensive line moved people, the backs ran hard, and Dez took what the defense gave him. The run set everything up. That’s how this team was built to play.

Then came the rematch.

Down only three in the second half, the game was right there for the taking. And the run was still working. You could see it on the few carries we did give our backs—positive yards, the line getting a push, the defense on its heels. That’s when good teams get stubborn. That’s when you keep handing it to the guy who’s moving the pile and dare the other team to stop it.

Instead, we got away from it.

That’s my take, plain and simple. Down three, with a running game that had been effective all night, we started dropping back to throw. Not because the run had stopped working—because it hadn’t. We just stopped calling it. And once you do that in the playoffs, you give the other team exactly what it wants. Three-and-outs. Your defense back on the field. A one-score game turning into a two-score game before you can settle down.

I’m not putting this on Dez. The kid set a school record, and he gave this program a season to remember. But no quarterback should be asked to win a playoff second half by himself when the running game is rolling. Playoff football is still played at the line of scrimmage. You run it to stay ahead of the chains, you run it to protect your defense, and you run it because in November, the team that flinches usually goes home.

There’s no disgrace in 8-2. This group gave the town a lot to be proud of, and Dez’s name will be in the record book for a long time. But if there’s one lesson to carry into the offseason, it’s this: don’t abandon what got you here. We already proved we could beat that team doing what we do best. In the biggest half of the year, we should have done it again.

That’s why the season ended. Not because we weren’t good enough. Because we stopped being us.

b.text:
**They Had It in Hand. Then They Let It Slip Away.**

Eight wins. A school-record quarterback. A playoff run that ended in Round 2.

And yet, if you watched the last few minutes of Saturday night, you probably didn’t leave with the feeling you watched a team that got beaten up. You probably left with the feeling you watched a team beat itself.

The loss stings for the obvious reason. This is the same opponent the team had already beaten by twenty yards, maybe more depending on which stat sheet you trust, in Week 3. In basketball, sometimes you say teams match up differently. In football, when you’ve already won a game like that, and then you’re down only three in the second half of the rematch, the answer usually isn’t to throw the playbook at the wall and start looking for heroics.

That’s where my head is at with this one.

This team didn’t lose because it wasn’t good enough. It lost because it stopped trusting what had been working. The run game was there. It was moving the ball, it was controlling the clock, and it was giving the defense a break. Then, with the game still on the line, that identity started to disappear. Suddenly it felt less like execution and more like hope. Hope is not a game plan in the second half of a one-score playoff game.

Now, none of that takes away from Dez Kowalski’s season. Two thousand, three hundred and forty yards is a school record, and it didn’t happen by accident. He carried the offense for stretches, made throws under pressure, and kept this thing alive more times than anyone in these parts should remember. But here’s the uncomfortable part: a school-record season from your quarterback doesn’t erase a lost playoff game if the rest of the team was taken out of it. Sometimes the best answer is the boring one. And the boring one Saturday night was the run game.

Eight and two is a good season. Nobody should act like it isn’t. You don’t get to pretend playoff losses are just another Tuesday in a small town like ours. People cared. That matters. But if we’re being honest—and this column should be honest—the disappointment isn’t that this team got exposed. It’s that it got close, had something solid in its hands, and then let the game drift away because it forgot what made it good in the first place.

That’s what makes this one ache.

Not that they lost.

That they only lost by three.

a.text:
Subject: A change we've been putting off telling you about

I've rewritten this post about six times now, always at some ridiculous hour after the ovens are already going, because I keep wanting to explain myself instead of just talking to you. So let me try again, plainly this time.

We're not taking custom wedding cake orders anymore.

If you've been in the shop, you probably know how much I've loved doing them. There's something about a couple sitting at that little table up front, nervous and giddy, trying five kinds of buttercream and pretending they're not going to just pick the one that reminds them of their grandmother's kitchen. I've gotten to be a small part of some really big days, and I don't say that lightly.

But here's the truth of it. Each of those orders took about fourteen hours of my time before a single cake was ever baked — consults, tastings, follow-up emails, redesigns after someone's aunt had opinions about fondant. Fourteen hours doesn't sound like much until you realize it's coming out of the same twenty-four hours that start at 4am with the sourdough and don't really end until the case is stocked and the last regular's coffee order is called out. It was time that used to go toward the everyday bread and pastries — the stuff that actually keeps the lights on and lets the three of us keep doing this at all.

And then this year we had three cancellations, all last minute, all after we'd already bought the ingredients and blocked out the days. I'm not telling you that to complain — weddings get cancelled, plans change, that's life — but three in one year, on top of everything else, made it clear something had to give.

So we sat with it for a while, the three of us, and decided the honest thing to do was step back from wedding cakes and put that time back into what's actually paying the rent and what most of you actually come in for every day. The morning pastries. The birthday cakes. The bread that sells out by ten. That's the bakery, really, at its core, and lately it's been getting the leftover hours instead of the good ones.

If you're planning a wedding and were hoping we'd be part of it, I'm genuinely sorry, and I mean that. We may still do smaller celebration cakes down the line, and if that changes I'll tell you here first, same as always. But for now, this is us choosing to take care of the everyday thing that got us all here in the first place.

Thank you for understanding, and for still showing up for the regular stuff. It matters more than you know.

— [Your name], still icing something at an hour I won't admit to

b.text:
I need to tell you all something, and I'd rather just say it straight than make some big announcement.

After a lot of thinking (and a few sleepless nights, if I'm being honest), we've decided to stop taking custom wedding cake orders.

This wasn't a snap decision. I love wedding cakes. I love sitting with couples and hearing how they met, I love sketching tiers on napkins, and there is nothing like seeing a cake set up in a venue with the light coming in and everyone milling around with champagne. Some of my favorite memories in this shop have come from wedding cakes.

But here's what I've had to be honest about. Each custom order eats up about fourteen hours of my time before I ever bake a single layer. Consultations, tastings, emails back and forth about flavors and design, sketches and revisions, logistics. Fourteen hours. And that's time I'm not spending on the case, on the sourdough, on the things that walk out the door every day and keep the lights on.

This year we had three last-minute cancellations. I don't say that to shame anyone, things happen, life falls apart sometimes. But the ingredients for a wedding cake are expensive, and when someone cancels two weeks out, that cost doesn't come back. Three times in one year was enough to make me sit down with the numbers and realize I was running part of this business at a loss while working harder than ever.

What it really came down to is this. I started this shop to bake for you all every day. The case, the breads, the cookies, the things you grab on your way to work or bring to a dinner party. That's the heartbeat of this place. And every time I disappeared into a wedding cake, the case got thinner and the everyday stuff suffered. I can't keep doing that to the people who come in every week.

So that's it. No more custom wedding cakes. We'll still have plenty of beautiful things in the case for showers and parties and just-because celebrations. If you need a cake for a big gathering, talk to me and we'll figure something out from what we already do well. But the big custom orders are done.

Thank you for understanding, and thank you for being the reason we're still here.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
First Week in the ER

My first week in the ER, I learned that nursing is not about knowing everything. It is about showing up.

On my second day, a man came in with a deep cut on his arm. His wife was stuck in traffic, so he was alone. The doctor had to clean the wound, and the man was in a lot of pain. He reached out and grabbed my hand. I did not know what to say, so I just stood there and let him hold on. When his wife finally walked in, he let go and thanked me. I had not given him medicine or done a procedure. But I had stayed. That mattered.

A few days later, a code was called. I was too new to help, so a nurse told me to restock gauze. I stood outside the curtain with the boxes and heard them counting compressions. One, two, three, four. I kept counting gauze packs. It felt strange to do something so small while they worked to save someone. But then I realized the room needed gauze too. Even the small jobs have a place in a big emergency.

The hardest moment came with a diabetic man who had bad veins. I was supposed to draw blood. I missed three times. My hands were shaking, and I wanted to go get someone else. But the man looked at me and said, "Take your time. I know you are learning." On the fourth try, I got it. I almost cried. He just nodded. He did not complain or ask for another nurse. He gave me a chance to learn.

Before that week, I thought nursing was about being fast and knowing everything. Now I think it is about staying calm when things are not calm. It is about holding a hand, counting gauze, and trying again.

I am applying for this scholarship because I want to keep learning. I work part-time, and school and clinicals take most of my time. I do not want to cut back on clinical hours because that is where I learn the most. Every shift teaches me something I cannot get from a lecture.

My first week in the ER was not dramatic. I did not save a life. But I saw what saving looks like up close. It looks like a hand held, a small task done, and a fourth try. I want to be part of that for a long time.

b.text:
I thought my first week in the ER would teach me how to do things. It mostly taught me how to stand there.

The first man whose hand I held was named Walter. He was seventy-one and he'd caught his forearm on a piece of sheet metal in his garage. The wound wasn't the worst thing I saw that week, but it was long, and it needed a lot of cleaning, and the nurse working on it was thorough in a way that took time. Walter kept looking toward the doorway. His wife was on the highway somewhere, stuck behind an accident, which he said out loud about four times like saying it would move traffic.

I wasn't doing anything. I was a first-year student with a name badge and no skills yet. So I asked if he wanted me to sit with him, and he said yes so fast it surprised me.

He took my hand. Not gently. He held it like a man holding a railing. His grip went tight when the saline hit the deep part and loosened when it didn't, and I just sat there and let him squeeze and told him his wife was probably three exits away. I made that up. I had no idea where she was. But it was the only useful thing I had, so I gave it to him.

She got there twenty minutes later. He let go of my hand and took hers and didn't say anything to me, and that was fine. That was the whole point.

Later that week, a code came in. I heard it before I saw anything — the overhead page, and then the sound of six people moving fast in a small space. A nurse turned to me and said, "Gauze. Supply room. Go."

I want to be honest about how that felt. I felt useless. I felt like I was being moved out of the way, which I was. I walked to the supply room and stood in front of the shelves and picked out four-by-fours, and on the way back I had to pass the curtain, and I could hear them counting compressions. One, two, three, four. Somebody's voice steady on top of it, calling out the rhythm.

I stopped walking. I don't know for how long. Probably four seconds. It felt like a lot longer.

Then I brought the gauze where it needed to go, and I restocked the rest of the shelf, because that was my job and somebody had to do it. Later I found out the patient didn't make it. I went home that night and sat in my car in the driveway for a while before I went inside.

Here's what I keep coming back to about that. Somebody had to restock the gauze. Not that day — the next day, the next patient. The shelf being full is why the nurse's hand finds it without looking. I didn't save anybody. But I understood for the first time that a hospital is a hundred small jobs stacked on top of each other, and the person doing the smallest one still has to do it right.

The blood draw was the hardest part of the week, and it wasn't even close.

The patient was a man in his fifties, diabetic, in for something unrelated. His veins were rough — scarred up from years of sticks, rolling, deep. My preceptor said I could try. She stood next to me the whole time.

I missed. I missed again. I missed a third time.

By the third one my hands were shaking and my face was hot and I was about two seconds from asking her to just take over. I apologized so many times he finally said, "You're gonna have to stop that, it's making me nervous." Which made us both laugh, a little, which helped more than anything anybody said to me that whole week.

My preceptor didn't take the needle. She said, "Feel again. Don't look for it, feel for it." So I put my fingers on his arm and closed my eyes for a second like an idiot, and I found something soft and springy near his wrist that I'd skipped over three times because it didn't look like anything.

Fourth stick. Flash of red in the hub. He said, "There you go," like he'd been rooting for me, and I think he actually had been.

I've thought about why that one stuck with me. It's not because I finally got it. It's because he let me try four times. He was tired, he'd been poked by better nurses than me his whole adult life, and he still put his arm out. People do that. They hand you their body and their bad day and they let you learn on them, and most of them never get thanked for it.

I don't have a big statement about what kind of nurse I'm going to be. I've had one week. But I know I want to be the person who sits down when there's nothing else to do, who keeps the shelf full for the next person, who feels for the vein instead of just looking at it.

This scholarship would help me keep going. I'm working part-time and the schedule is tight and the program is not going to get easier. But I'd like to be there for week two, and week fifty, and however many after that.

I'd like to get good at this. I think I could.

It is just past 4:30 in the morning right now. The deck oven is humming, the shop smells like yeast and cinnamon, and I’m sitting at the prep table with my first cup of coffee trying to get this typed out before the first timers go off. 

I wanted to share a decision our tiny three-person team made recently. Starting next season, we’re officially stepping back from taking on custom wedding cakes. 

It wasn't an easy call to make, because being a small part of so many love stories over the years has been truly special. But as a crew of three, we’ve had to take a hard look at where our time and energy go. Custom wedding cakes are a massive labor of love, but between the initial emails, the design sketches, the back-and-forth emails, and the tasting sessions, we realized each order eats up about fourteen hours of work before we even crack an egg for the actual cake. 

On top of that, running a small bakery comes with very thin margins. We had three last-minute wedding cancellations this year alone, and for a team our size, absorbing those wasted ingredient costs and holding open prime calendar slots really hurts. 

Most of all, we’ve realized that pouring so much of ourselves into one or two big weekend cakes was pulling us away from the heart of this shop: our everyday pastry case. The morning croissants, the fresh loaves of sourdough, the cookies you pick up on your way home—that everyday case is what keeps our lights on and our rent paid. It’s also what connects us to you, our regulars, every single day. 

We want to get back to doing what we do best without burning out. We want to have the time and creative energy to experiment with new seasonal pastries, keep your favorite loaves on the shelves, and greet you with fresh bakes every morning. 

If you’re planning a celebration, please know we aren't abandoning cake entirely! We’ll still be offering our standard signature layer cakes available to order straight from our everyday menu for birthdays, small gatherings, and yes, sweet and simple weddings too. When I adopted your platform in my AP Biology classroom two years ago, I didn't just gain a teaching tool—I gained insight into exactly what makes your product work. More importantly, I learned what breaks it, and how to fix it with frustrated users on the fly.

For eight years, I've done customer success work without the title. Every semester meant onboarding 30 new students who didn't want to be there, troubleshooting technical issues mid-lesson, and talking down parents who didn't understand what their kid was doing in the LMS. I became my school's de facto admin for your platform—managing permissions, running trainings, and fielding questions from teachers who'd never used anything like it before.

That experience taught me what your CS team needs to know: educators are pragmatic. They care less about features than about whether something saves them time or creates more work. They abandon tools that require explanation. They evangelize tools that just work.

I'm leaving the classroom because I want to scale that advocacy work. I want to help your customers succeed the way you helped me succeed—by understanding their world, anticipating their friction points, and making sure they get actual value from what they're paying for.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots (Before Minneapolis Cold Snaps Break Your Pipes)

Every January we get the same calls: a burst pipe behind the wall where an outdoor spigot connects. Almost every single time, it's because a hose was left hooked up over the winter. That one mistake causes more cold-weather plumbing damage in this city than anything else we see.

Here's how to actually protect your spigots, in the right order.

## 1. Disconnect every hose

Do this first. If a hose is attached, water can't drain out of the spigot, even if you turn everything off. That trapped water freezes, expands, and splits either the spigot or the pipe behind it. Coil up the hoses and store them somewhere warm.

## 2. Find your interior shutoff valve

Most Minneapolis homes built in the last 40 years have a dedicated shutoff valve for each outdoor spigot, usually in the basement, right where the pipe goes through the wall to the outside. It'll be a separate small valve, not your main water shutoff.

Turn that valve off. This stops water from feeding into the outdoor line all winter.

**If you can't find one, or your house doesn't have one:** stop here and give us a call. Older homes and some additions were never plumbed with an interior shutoff, and that changes what you need to do. Don't guess on this one.

## 3. Drain the spigot

Once the interior valve is off, go back outside and open the spigot. Let any remaining water drain out completely. Most outdoor faucets have a small cap or bleeder valve near the handle, open that too so water isn't sitting trapped in the pipe between the valve and the spigot. Leave the outdoor spigot open (in the "on" position) all winter. This gives any water that does get in somewhere to expand into, instead of building pressure inside the pipe.

## 4. Cover the spigot

Grab a foam spigot cover, the styrofoam dome kind, at any hardware store for about three dollars. Slide it over the spigot and secure it. This adds a layer of insulation against direct freezing air, especially important during Minneapolis's stretches of single-digit and below-zero days.

## The mistake to avoid

We can't say this enough: **disconnect your hoses.** We understand it's an easy thing to forget in October when you're just trying to get the yard put away for the season. But a forgotten hose is the single biggest reason homeowners end up calling us in the dead of winter with water coming through a wall or ceiling.

Takes two minutes. Saves you a very expensive January.

## No interior shutoff? Call us.

If you've checked your basement and can't find a valve for your outdoor spigot, don't wait until the pipes freeze to deal with it. We can install one, or walk you through what your specific setup needs. It's a straightforward job now, and a much bigger one after a freeze.

**[Phone number] — we're happy to help before it becomes an emergency.**

b.text:
## How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots (Minneapolis Homeowners, Do This Before Halloween)

Four steps. Twenty minutes. Do them both — front and back of the house, plus the garage if you've got a hose bib out there.

### 1. Shut off the interior valve

Every outdoor spigot should have a shutoff valve inside the house on the pipe that feeds it. In most Minneapolis homes that's in the basement, along the rim joist, near where the pipe runs out through the wall. Older houses in Nokomis, Longfellow, Northeast — it's usually a small gate valve or a ball valve within a few feet of the exterior wall.

Turn it off. Gate valve, that's clockwise until it stops. Ball valve, quarter turn so the handle sits crosswise to the pipe.

### 2. Drain the spigot

Go outside and open the spigot all the way. Let it run until it stops dripping. This is the step people skip, and it's the whole point of the exercise — the interior valve keeps new water out, but whatever's already sitting in that pipe is what freezes and splits it.

Leave the outdoor spigot open all winter. Nothing's feeding it, and an open valve gives any leftover moisture somewhere to expand.

If your interior shutoff has a small bleeder cap on the side, put a bucket under it, unscrew it a turn or two, and let the rest drain out. Snug it back down when it quits dripping.

### 3. Disconnect your hoses

Read that again, because this is the one that costs people money.

### 4. Put a $3 foam cover on it

Hardware store, insulation aisle, styrofoam dome with a rubber strap. Loop the strap over the spigot handle, tighten it, push the cover flat against the siding. It's not doing the heavy lifting — steps 1 and 2 did that — but it buys you a margin when we hit a stretch of below-zero nights and it cuts down on wind chill hitting that pipe where it passes through the wall.

## The mistake that keeps us busy every January

A garden hose left attached to the spigot holds water. That water freezes and backs pressure up into the spigot and the pipe behind it. Even a frost-free hose bib — the long ones designed to shut off inside the heated part of the wall — can't drain if there's a hose hanging on the end of it. That's the part homeowners don't know. People install a frost-free bib and figure they're covered, then leave the hose on and split the pipe anyway.

Here's how it plays out: the pipe cracks in December, but it's holding no water, so nothing happens. Nobody notices. Then in May somebody hooks up a hose to water the tomatoes, turns on the interior valve, and water comes pouring into the basement through the rim joist. Or worse — it cracked on the interior side of the wall and it's been running down inside the wall cavity since the first thaw.

Coil your hoses, drain them, hang them in the garage. Takes five minutes.

## What if you don't have an interior shutoff?

A lot of Minneapolis houses don't — especially anything pre-war where a spigot got added at some point without a dedicated valve, or where a previous owner's remodel buried the valve behind finished basement wall.

If you go down to the basement and can't find a shutoff for that line, don't guess and don't just cover the spigot and hope. **Give us a call.** Adding an interior shutoff valve is a small job — usually an hour or two — and it's a lot cheaper than the drywall, insulation, and framing repair after a burst line lets go behind a finished wall.

Same goes if the valve is there but seized, or if you shut it off and the spigot outside is still dripping steady after ten minutes. That means the valve isn't holding, and it needs to be replaced before it gets cold.

We're a family business and we've been pulling apart frozen hose bibs in this city for a long time. We'd rather set you up in October than cut open your ceiling in January.

**Call us or book online — we'll get someone out.**

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
**What I Learned in the ER**

Before my first clinical rotation, I thought I knew what nursing was. I had passed my classes. I could label a diagram of the heart. I knew what to do on a test. Then I spent a week in the emergency room, and I found out how much I didn't know.

On my second day, a man came in with a deep cut on his arm from a work accident. The nurse had to clean it out, and it was going to hurt. His wife was stuck in traffic and kept calling him, upset that she couldn't get there. He was trying to sound calm on the phone, but his free hand was shaking. When the cleaning started, I didn't have a real job to do. I was a student. So I held his hand. He squeezed hard enough that my fingers went white, and he apologized, and I told him not to. We didn't talk much. He just needed someone there until his wife could be. I always figured nursing was about the skills — the needles, the medications, the machines. That day the most useful thing I did was stand still and let a stranger hold on to me.

Later that week there was a code. A patient's heart stopped, and the room filled up fast with people who knew exactly what they were doing. I did not know what I was doing, and a nurse told me to go restock gauze in the supply room. At first I felt useless, like I was being sent out of the way. And I was — but restocking still needed to happen, and I was the person who could do it. Through the curtain I could hear them counting compressions out loud, steady and even, like a heartbeat the team was making with their own voices. I stacked gauze and listened and understood something: everyone in that department had a job, and every job mattered, even mine. Someday I'll be the one counting. Right now I'm the one making sure the shelf isn't empty when somebody reaches for it.

The hardest lesson came from a blood draw. The patient was a man with diabetes, and his veins were hard to find. I missed. He told me it was fine, try again. I missed a second time. Then a third. I wanted to hand the needle to someone else and disappear. My face was hot and my hands didn't feel like mine. He looked at me and said, "You'll get it. I've had worse." The nurse supervising me could have taken over, but she talked me through it instead. On the fourth try, I got it. The flash of blood in that tube was the best thing I saw all week. What stayed with me wasn't the success, though. It was that he trusted me after I had already failed him three times. Patients give students that kind of grace all the time, and I don't ever want to take it for granted.

I went into that week thinking the goal was to look competent. I came out understanding that the goal is to be useful, honest, and present, and that competence comes from staying in the room when it's uncomfortable — during the pain, the missed sticks, the moments when the most you can offer is your hand.

I'm a first-year student. I have a lot left to learn, and I know it. But that week in the ER showed me I'm in the right place, doing work I want to spend my life getting better at. This scholarship would help me keep showing up — to class, to clinicals, to the patients who are willing to let a student learn on them. I owe them my best effort. I intend to give it.

b.text:
My first week in the ER taught me more than any classroom could.

I came in nervous, trying to keep up and not get in the way. The ER moves fast. People are hurting, scared, tired, and sometimes all three at once. I knew that before I started, but it felt different once I was actually there. It is one thing to read about care. It is another to stand in a room and see what people need in real time.

One moment that stayed with me was when I helped with a wound cleaning for an older man. His wife was stuck in traffic and could not get there yet. He kept looking toward the door. He was trying to act calm, but I could tell he was worried. I stood beside him and held his hand while the nurse cleaned the wound. I did not do anything dramatic. I just stayed there. But I could see it helped. Sometimes people do not need a speech. Sometimes they just need someone to sit with them and not make them face it alone.

Another moment happened during a code. I was sent to restock gauze, and as I stood outside the room, I could hear the team counting through the curtain. It was organized, fast, and serious. Even though I was not in the room, I could feel how much everyone mattered in that moment. I learned that nursing is not just one person at the center. It is a team working together, each person doing their part. Even something as simple as bringing supplies back quickly can make a difference.

I also had a hard time with a blood draw on a diabetic patient who had very poor veins. I missed the first time. Then I missed again. And again. I felt awful. I did not want to give up, but I also did not want to keep poking him and making it worse. On the fourth try, I finally got it. I was relieved, but I also knew I had to be honest with myself. I was frustrated, and I was embarrassed, but I kept going. That patient was patient with me, and I will not forget that. It reminded me that learning takes time, and that skill comes with practice, patience, and respect for the person in front of you.

That first week showed me that nursing is not only about being right the first time. It is about staying calm, paying attention, and caring even when things are busy or hard. It is about being useful in the small moments and steady in the hard ones. I left that week more sure than ever that I want to do this work.

I am applying for this scholarship because I want to keep learning and keep growing into the kind of nurse my patients can count on. My first week in the ER did not just teach me skills. It showed me the kind of nurse I want to become: someone who shows up, stays steady, and treats every patient like they matter.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
The milk crates in our walk-in cooler are stacked three high next to the five-gallon buckets of fish sauce. That is where I sit on my fifteen-minute breaks on Saturdays. It stays thirty-eight degrees in there, which is cold enough to see my breath, but it is the only room in the building where nobody is yelling an order or dropping a wire basket into boiling oil. 

I wear my apron over my jacket and prop my calculus binder against a cardboard case of cabbage. Limits and derivatives make more sense when your teeth are slightly chattering; the cold keeps me from nodding off after four hours on my feet. If I stay in past minute twelve, my fingers get too stiff to hold the mechanical pencil, so I pack up, shove the binder back into my tote bag, and push open the heavy metal door.

I’ve worked weekends at my family’s restaurant since sophomore year. I take orders, bus tables, chop scallions, and run the floor depending on who called out sick. Last fall, my dad hired a high school junior named Tyler who had never touched rice paper before. The first few spring rolls he tried to make looked like wet paper towels stuffed with shredded pork. 

"Watch," I told him, wiping down a section of the stainless steel prep table. 

You dip the rice paper in warm water for two seconds, not three. If it feels soft when you pull it out of the bowl, it’s already ruined—it will tear the second the vermicelli hits it. You lay it flat, stack the lettuce, mint, and noodles across the bottom third, and lay three shrimp pink-side down near the top so they show through the translucent wrapper once it’s closed. Then the fold: pull the bottom edge up tight, tuck both sides in like an envelope, and roll forward with the flats of your palms, never your fingertips. 

My grandma showed me that fold when I was nine. She didn’t speak much English, and Tyler didn’t speak any Vietnamese, but the motion doesn't need translation. You don’t squeeze; you just guide it. By his third tray, Tyler was turning out rolls tight enough to be sliced on a bias without the filling spilling onto the cutting board.

That kind of routine keeps the restaurant moving, but things still fall apart. A few months ago, right at the peak of the 6:30 dinner rush on a rainy Saturday, the touchscreen POS terminal let out a long beep, flickered, and went entirely black. There were forty people seated in the dining room, three tables waiting at the door, and four delivery drivers pacing by the counter. 

My dad tapped the screen twice with his knuckle, looked over at me, and said, "Paper."

I grabbed a legal pad from under the counter, tore the sheets into quarters, and dug three pens out of my apron pocket. For the next two and a half hours, I did the math by hand. Table 4 wanted two bowls of phở tái, one extra broth, no cilantro. Table 8 wanted three broken rice plates with pork chops, well done. I had to keep the menu prices straight, calculate the 8.25% sales tax in the margins, and translate each ticket into the kitchen’s shorthand before sliding it onto the order wheel. "PT-X-NC" for Table 4. "Com Tam Suon" for Table 8. 

My handwriting started out neat and ended up looking like a seismograph readout, but the kitchen never stopped firing bowls, and the wrong food never went to the wrong table. When we finally flipped the door sign to "Closed" at nine, my thumb was dented from the ballpoint pen, and the back of my neck burned from looking down. 

My friends ask me why I don't quit and find an easier job where I don't go home smelling like star anise and dish soap. But on Sunday nights, after the dining room chairs are flipped onto the tables and my dad turns off the neon "Open" sign, there is a half-hour where the restaurant is completely silent. My mom counts down the cash drawer, my dad sweeps the entryway, and I run the wide mop across the red floor tiles, working my way toward the back exit. 

Tomorrow morning is AP Chemistry at 7:45. I lean the mop against the sink, pack my backpack, and sit down at the front booth to finish my lab report while the floor dries.

b.text:
The first sign was the receipt printer making a noise like it was chewing paper. Then the screen froze, blinked once, and went black.

It was 12:15 on a Saturday, and the restaurant was already full. Every table had at least one bowl of pho or plate of broken rice. The kitchen tickets were hanging on the rail, but the new ones stopped coming. My mom tapped the screen a few times, then looked at me.

I grabbed a stack of order pads and a handful of pens.

For the next three hours, I wrote every ticket by hand. Table number, dish, modifications, no onions, extra broth, one order rare, one order well done. I used different colors so the kitchen would not mix up appetizers and entrees. Red for drinks, blue for food. When I ran out of red, I used pencil and underlined twice.

The kitchen did not slow down. If anything, it got louder because nobody trusted the system anymore. My dad called out orders from the pass. My aunt asked if table six got their egg rolls. Someone said table twelve had been waiting twenty minutes, but table twelve had just ordered. I kept the pad in front of me and wrote everything down before I moved.

At one point, a server handed me a ticket with coffee stains all over it. I could still read the table number, but not the drinks. I went to the table and asked the customers to repeat the order. They were patient, which surprised me. Usually people get annoyed when something goes wrong in a restaurant. Maybe they could tell we were trying.

By the time the repair guy came, my hand hurt. I had filled six order pads. The register came back on, printed a long list of errors, and then started working like nothing had happened. I kept the last page of my order pad. It had a smear of fish sauce on the corner.

When things calm down, I usually help prep. My favorite job is spring rolls, but only if nobody rushes me. My grandma taught me the fold when I was little. She did not explain it much. She just put a rice paper wrapper on the damp towel, added shrimp, pork, herbs, and noodles, then folded the sides in tight and rolled it once. The trick was not to overfill it and not to tear it.

Last month we hired a new girl named Lan. She was fast, but her spring rolls kept splitting. She kept putting too much lettuce near the edge. I showed her how to leave room at the sides and tuck the filling down before rolling.

“Like this,” I said. “Don’t be nice to it.”

She laughed and tried again. The next one looked better. The one after that looked almost like my grandma’s.

My grandma does not work full shifts anymore, but she still comes in and checks everything. She picked up one of Lan’s rolls and turned it over in her hand. She did not say anything for a second. Then she said, “Okay.”

That was enough.

During slow stretches, I do homework. The best place is the walk-in cooler. It is quiet, and nobody asks me to refill sauces or wipe down tables. I sit on a milk crate with my backpack and my calculator. The fan blows cold air behind the shelves of basil, cilantro, and sliced onions. Sometimes my nose runs. Sometimes my fingers get stiff. But I can focus.

Calc is hardest in there. Not because of the cold, but because if I lose track of one step, I have to start over. I keep my notebook on my knees and write small so I can fit more work on one page. Last week I was doing derivatives while someone behind me stacked boxes of frozen shrimp. He asked if I was studying chemistry. I said no, but then I had to explain what a derivative sort of is, and by the time I finished, my problem was all wrong.

I do not always finish homework before my shift ends. Sometimes I have to take it home, and sometimes I fall asleep with the notebook open on my bed. But I like knowing where everything is: the order pads, the spring roll wrappers, the calculator, the stack of clean towels by the sink.

On weekends, the restaurant smells like garlic and star anise. My shoes get sticky. My shirt smells like broth even after I wash it. I know which table wobbles, which fan squeaks, which customer asks for extra limes without asking nicely.

When the last customers leave, I stack chairs, sweep under the tables, and count the register drawer. My dad turns off the hood fan, and the room gets suddenly quiet. I take the trash out back, lock the side door, and check it twice.

Then I get in the car and ride home.

setup: You're Priya and Sam. A freelance videographer is following up on an overdue $1,800 wedding video invoice with a soft Friday deadline.

a.text:
Hi Priya and Sam,

Hope you're both doing well and enjoying married life!

Since I haven't heard back from my last email, I wanted to follow up once more on invoice #47 for $1,800, which was due on the 14th and is now three weeks overdue. I know how chaotic inboxes and life can get, so I'm sure this just slipped through the cracks — no hard feelings at all.

That said, I do need to get this wrapped up, so could you please take care of it by end of day this Friday? If splitting the amount into two payments would make it easier, I'm happy to do that — just let me know and I'll set it up.

The payment link in my earlier email is still active, or I'm glad to resend it if that's easier.

Thanks so much, and congrats again!

b.text:
Hi Priya and Sam!

Hope you're settling into married life beautifully. I'm sorry to chase you again on invoice #47 ($1,800) — it's now three weeks past due, and I haven't heard back, so I wanted to make sure it didn't get lost in the shuffle.

Could you get this settled by this Friday, 5pm your time? That'll give me a clear answer and let me close out the books on my end.

If a single payment is tight right now, I'm absolutely happy to split it into two installments — just say the word and I'll resend a revised invoice. Totally understand that post-wedding finances can be a lot to juggle.

Thanks so much, both — really appreciate you, and I hope you loved the video! Let me know either way by Friday and we'll sort it out.

Warmly,
[Your name]

setup: A high school English teacher is replying to a viral post about AI ruining writing, sharing a counterpoint about better handwritten first drafts.

a.text: 16 years in. I moved every first draft to timed/unplugged this year because of AI, and my students’ handwritten essays got noticeably better. Turns out when you make them generate ideas first, they actually write—this isn’t illiteracy, it’s just fixing assignments that had gotten lazy.

b.text: "Funny enough, my students' handwritten essays actually improved this year—turns out making first drafts timed and unplugged forced me to rethink assignments in a good way. AI’s just another tool; the real work is adapting."
